Factoring is the physical act of arranging them into a perfect rectangle.} \\ \text{The dimensions of that rectangle are your factors.} Visual Learner: Visions of Zero \text{Look for the "Sign Crossings." Every factor } (x-c) \text{ is a visual instruction to cross the origin at point } c. \\ \text{Factoring is drawing the map of the crossing points.} Special factoring forms — both directions a^2 - b^2 = (a-b)(a+b) \qquad \text{(difference of squares)} \\ a^3 - b^3 = (a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2) \qquad \text{(difference of cubes)} \\ a^3 + b^3 = (a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2) \qquad \text{(sum of cubes)} The ac method — step by step \text{Factor } ax^2+bx+c: \\ 1.\; \text{compute } ac. \quad 2.\; \text{find } p,q \text{ with } pq=ac \text{ and } p+q=b. \\ 3.\; \text{rewrite: } ax^2+px+qx+c. \quad 4.\; \text{factor by grouping.} Sum/difference of cubes memory: SOAP (a \pm b)(a^2 \mp ab + b^2) \\ \text{S: Same sign as original. O: Opposite sign. A: Always positive.} \\ a^3 + b^3 = (a+b)(a^2 - ab + b^2) \quad \text{same, opposite, always}+ The Rational Roots Theorem \text{For a polynomial with integer coefficients: any rational zero must be } \frac{\text{factor of constant term } a_0}{\text{factor of leading coeff } a_n}. \\ \text{This provides the list of all possible "DNA candidates" for factoring.} Proof of the Zero Product Property \text{If } a \cdot b = 0 \text{ and } a \neq 0, \text{ then } \frac{1}{a}(a \cdot b) = \frac{1}{a}(0) \implies b = 0. \\ \text{This logic is why factoring is a mandatory tool for solving equations.} Factoring as Rectangle Area Each cell of the grid is one term from the multiplication. Factoring recovers the dimensions. GCF first, then trinomial \text{Factor completely: } 6x^3 - 24x^2 + 18x Never skip the GCF step. It reduces the degree of the remaining factor, making the next step easier. = 6x(x^2 - 4x + 3) GCF is $6x$. Always pull this out first — it simplifies everything inside. = 6x(x-1)(x-3) Factor the trinomial $x^2 - 4x + 3$. Need two numbers that multiply to $3$ and add to $-4$: those are $-1$ and $-3$. The ac method on a hard trinomial \text{Factor: } 6x^2 + 7x - 3 The ac method removes all guesswork. It turns a hard trinomial into a grouping problem. a=6,\; c=-3 \Rightarrow ac = -18. \text{ Need } p+q=7,\; pq=-18. Compute $ac$. Find two numbers with that product and sum equal to $b = 7$. p = 9,\; q = -2 \quad (9 \times -2 = -18,\; 9 + (-2) = 7) List factor pairs of $-18$: try $(9,-2)$. It works. 6x^2 + 9x - 2x - 3 Rewrite middle term using the two numbers found. = 3x(2x+3) - 1(2x+3) = (3x-1)(2x+3) Factor by grouping. The common factor $(2x+3)$ appears in both groups. Sum of cubes — recognising the pattern \text{Factor: } 8x^3 + 27 The quadratic factor from a sum/difference of cubes is usually irreducible over the reals. Always check by computing the discriminant. 8x^3 + 27 = (2x)^3 + 3^3 Recognise as sum of cubes with $a = 2x$ and $b = 3$. = (2x + 3)\bigl((2x)^2 - (2x)(3) + 3^2\bigr) Apply the sum of cubes formula: $(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2)$. = (2x+3)(4x^2 - 6x + 9) Simplify. Note: $4x^2 - 6x + 9$ has discriminant $36 - 144 < 0$ — it does not factor over the reals. Factoring by grouping — four terms \text{Factor: } x^3 + 2x^2 - 9x - 18 Grouping works when the four terms split into two pairs that share a common factor. If the first grouping does not work, try a different pairing. = x^2(x+2) - 9(x+2) Group first two and last two terms. Factor GCF from each pair: $x^2$ from the first, $-9$ from the second. = (x^2 - 9)(x + 2) The common factor $(x+2)$ appears — pull it out. = (x-3)(x+3)(x+2) $x^2 - 9$ is a difference of squares. Factor again. Completely factored. Advanced Structure: Rational Exponents \text{Factor completely: } x^{3/2} - x^{1/2} - 6x^{-1/2} Even with negative or fractional exponents, the "Lowest Power" is always your GCF. This unlocks the quadratic structure inside. = x^{-1/2}(x^2 - x - 6) Step 1: Always pull out the GCF. Here, the lowest power $x^{-1/2}$ is the factor common to all terms. = x^{-1/2}(x-3)(x+2) Step 2: Factor the remaining quadratic trinomial. Need product $-6$ and sum $-1$. Factoring in Quadratic Form \text{Factor completely: } x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 Many high-degree polynomials are just quadratics in disguise. Scaling the variable (substitution) reveals the path. (x^2)^2 - 5(x^2) + 4 Step 1: Recognise the structure as $u^2 - 5u + 4$ where $u = x^2$. (x^2 - 1)(x^2 - 4) Step 2: Factor the trinomial. Need product $4$ and sum $-5$. (x-1)(x+1)(x-2)(x+2) Step 3: Each factor is a Difference of Squares. Break them down completely. \text{Factor completely: } x^4 - 16 Treat $x^4$ as $(x^2)^2$ — this is a difference of squares. Then check if the factors continue to factor. (x-2)(x+2)(x^2+4) x^4 - 16 = (x^2)^2 - 4^2 = (x^2-4)(x^2+4) Difference of squares with $a = x^2$, $b = 4$. (x^2-4) = (x-2)(x+2) Difference of squares again. (x^2+4) \text{ is irreducible over } \mathbb{R} Sum of squares never factors over the reals. x^4 - 16 = (x-2)(x+2)(x^2+4) Fully factored over the reals. Over $\mathbb{C}$: $(x-2)(x+2)(x-2i)(x+2i)$. \text{Factor } x^6 - 1 \text{ completely over the reals.} First treat as difference of squares $(x^3)^2 - 1^2$, then as difference/sum of cubes. (x-1)(x+1)(x^2+x+1)(x^2-x+1) x^6-1 = (x^3-1)(x^3+1) Difference of squares with $a=x^3$, $b=1$. x^3-1 = (x-1)(x^2+x+1) Difference of cubes. x^3+1 = (x+1)(x^2-x+1) Sum of cubes. x^6-1 = (x-1)(x+1)(x^2+x+1)(x^2-x+1) Both quadratic factors have negative discriminants — irreducible over $\mathbb{R}$. This is the complete factorisation. \text{Factor completely using the "Sophie Germain" identity: } x^4 + 4. Add and subtract a term ($4x^2$) to complete a perfect square. The original is not a difference of squares... yet. (x^2+2x+2)(x^2-2x+2) x^4 + 4 = (x^4 + 4x^2 + 4) - 4x^2 Step 1: Complete the square $(x^2+2)^2$ by adding and subtracting $4x^2$. = (x^2+2)^2 - (2x)^2 Step 2: Recognize the difference of squares: $a = (x^2+2)$ and $b = (2x)$. = (x^2 + 2x + 2)(x^2 - 2x + 2) \qquad \blacksquare Step 3: Factors are the sum and difference. Both are irreducible over the reals. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step

documents.assignment: Converting to vertex form \text{Write } f(x) = 2x^2 - 12x + 7 \text{ in vertex form.}   The vertex $(h,k) = (3,-11)$ gives the minimum value, axis of symmetry $x = 3$, and tells you the parabola opens upward. All this information is invisible in standard form. = 2(x^2 - 6x) + 7 Factor the coefficient of $x^2$ out of the first two terms only. = 2(x^2 - 6x + 9) + 7 - 18 Add $(6/2)^2 = 9$ inside the bracket. Because of the factor of 2 outside, we added $2 \times 9 = 18$ to the expression — subtract 18 outside to compensate. = 2(x-3)^2 - 11 Vertex form. Vertex is at $(3, -11)$, which is the minimum (since $a = 2 > 0$). Using the discriminant before solving \text{Without solving, determine the nature of the roots of } 3x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0.   The discriminant is a preliminary test — compute it before solving. It tells you how many solutions to expect and whether complex numbers are needed. \Delta = b^2 - 4ac = 25 - 4(3)(4) = 25 - 48 = -23 Compute $\Delta$ directly. \Delta = -23 < 0 \Rightarrow \text{no real roots} Negative discriminant means the parabola does not intersect the $x$-axis. The roots exist but are complex conjugates. Constructing a quadratic from its roots — Vieta's formulas backwards \text{Find a monic quadratic with roots } r_1 = 3 + \sqrt{2} \text{ and } r_2 = 3 - \sqrt{2}.   Irrational roots always come in conjugate pairs $p \pm \sqrt{q}$ when the coefficients are rational. Vieta's formulas let you reconstruct the quadratic directly from the roots. r_1 + r_2 = 6 \qquad r_1 r_2 = (3+\sqrt{2})(3-\sqrt{2}) = 9 - 2 = 7 Compute sum and product of roots — no need to use the full values until the product step. x^2 - (r_1+r_2)x + r_1 r_2 = x^2 - 6x + 7 The monic quadratic with these roots is $x^2 - (\text{sum})x + (\text{product})$. Physics: Tracking a Projectile \text{A ball is thrown with height } h(t) = -5t^2 + 20t + 2. \text{ Find the maximum height and the time it hits the ground.}   The vertex is the peak of the journey, and the roots are the endpoints. Every projectile is a quadratic experiment. t_{\text{peak}} = -\frac{b}{2a} = -\frac{20}{2(-5)} = 2 \text{ seconds} Step 1: The maximum height occurs at the vertex. Use $t = -b/2a$. h(2) = -5(4) + 20(2) + 2 = -20 + 40 + 2 = 22 \text{ meters} Step 2: Substitute $t=2$ into the height function to find the peak. 0 = -5t^2 + 20t + 2 \implies t = \frac{-20 \pm \sqrt{400 - 4(-5)(2)}}{2(-5)} = \frac{-20 \pm \sqrt{440}}{-10} Step 3: Ground impact occurs when height $h(t) = 0$. Solve using the Quadratic Formula. t \approx \frac{-20 - 20.98}{-10} \approx 4.1 \text{ seconds} Step 4: Only the positive time root is physically meaningful. Economics: Profit Maximisation \text{A company's profit follows } P(x) = -x^2 + 100x - 1200, \text{ where } x \text{ is units sold. Find the "Break-Even" points and the optimal sales volume.}   The "sweet spot" of any quadratic system is its vertex. Symmetry ensures that the optimum is always perfectly balanced between the zero-points. 0 = -x^2 + 100x - 1200 \implies x^2 - 100x + 1200 = 0 Step 1: Break-even is where $P(x) = 0$. Solve by factoring: $(x-20)(x-80) = 0$. x_{\text{break-even}} = 20, 80 \text{ units} Step 2: These are the roots. Any sales between 20 and 80 result in profit. x_{\text{opt}} = -\frac{100}{2(-1)} = 50 \text{ units} Step 3: The vertex gives the maximum profit. $x=50$ is exactly half-way between 20 and 80.  \text{Find the value of } k \text{ so that } x^2 + kx + 25 = 0 \text{ has exactly one real solution.} Exactly one solution means the discriminant equals zero. k = \pm 10  \Delta = k^2 - 4(1)(25) = 0 Set $\Delta = 0$ for a repeated root. k^2 = 100 \Rightarrow k = \pm 10 Two values of $k$ work: the quadratic $x^2 + 10x + 25 = (x+5)^2$ and $x^2 - 10x + 25 = (x-5)^2$.  \text{A parabola has vertex } (2, -3) \text{ and passes through } (5, 6). \text{ Find its equation in standard form.} Start from vertex form $f(x) = a(x-2)^2 - 3$, then use the given point to find $a$. f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 1  f(x) = a(x-2)^2 - 3 Vertex form with vertex $(2, -3)$. 6 = a(5-2)^2 - 3 = 9a - 3 \Rightarrow a = 1 Substitute $(5, 6)$ and solve for $a$. f(x) = (x-2)^2 - 3 = x^2 - 4x + 1 Expand to standard form.  \text{A parabola has roots at } x = -1 \text{ and } x = 5. \text{ If the maximum value of the function is } 18, \text{ find its standard form equation.} The x-coordinate of the vertex must be the midpoint of the roots. Once you have the vertex, use $y = a(x-h)^2 + k$ to find $a$. f(x) = -2x^2 + 8x + 10  h = \frac{-1 + 5}{2} = 2 Step 1: The vertex $x$ is the average of the roots. \text{Vertex} = (2, 18) Step 2: The given "maximum value" is the $y$-coordinate of the vertex. 18 = a(5-2)^2 \text{ (Relative to roots, use intercept form)} \\ f(x) = a(x+1)(x-5) \implies 18 = a(2+1)(2-5) Step 3: Substitute $(2, 18)$ into the factored form to solve for $a$. 18 = a(3)(-3) \implies 18 = -9a \implies a = -2 Step 4: Solve for the scale factor. The negative $a$ confirms it was a maximum. f(x) = -2(x+1)(x-5) = -2(x^2 - 4x - 5) = -2x^2 + 8x + 10 Step 5: Expand to standard form.

documents.content: Where does the quadratic formula come from? Most students are handed it without explanation. It is actually a geometric argument — and seeing it makes the formula unforgettable. Quadratic equations model projectile motion, profit maximisation, lens optics, and electrical circuit resonance. The discriminant ($b^2 - 4ac$) tells engineers whether a system oscillates, is critically damped, or overdamped — before solving anything. In calculus, completing the square is the technique that makes certain integrals solvable by converting a quadratic into a perfect square form. **Where you are in the story:** Lesson 2 gave you the tools to factor polynomials. Now those tools are applied to the single most important polynomial class: the quadratic. If a trinomial factors nicely over the integers, you can solve it in seconds. But most quadratics in the real world do not have integer roots — and that is where completing the square and the quadratic formula come in. A quadratic $ax^2 + bx + c$ is a parabola. Its vertex — the minimum or maximum point — is the geometric heart of the function. Vertex form $a(x-h)^2 + k$ makes the vertex $(h, k)$ immediately readable. Completing the square is the algebraic procedure that converts standard form into vertex form. The geometric intuition: $x^2 + bx$ is a square of side $x$ plus a rectangle of width $b$ and height $x$. To complete it into a perfect square, split the rectangle in half and attach one piece to each side of the square. The missing corner is a square of side $b/2$, area $(b/2)^2$. Add it in — and subtract it to keep the value the same. Now you have $(x + b/2)^2 - (b/2)^2$. The discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$ is not just a formula component — it is the quantity under the square root, telling you how far the vertex is from the $x$-axis. Positive: two real roots (vertex and $x$-axis are on opposite sides). Zero: one repeated root (vertex touches $x$-axis). Negative: no real roots (vertex does not reach the $x$-axis). **The Symmetry of Change**: Every parabola is perfectly symmetrical. The **Axis of Symmetry** is the vertical line passing through the vertex, dividing the path into mirror images. In physics, this represents the moment an object stops rising and begins to fall—the perfect midpoint of a journey through time and space. **Turning Points**: Unlike linear relationships that go in one direction forever, quadratics have a **Turning Point**. This vertex represents the absolute limit of the system—the maximum profit, the minimum fuel consumption, or the peak of a projectile's flight. **Where this is heading:** The discriminant analysis introduced here appears again immediately in Lesson 6 (Complex Numbers), which explains what happens when $\Delta < 0$ and the "impossible" roots are computed. The vertex form and completing-the-square technique recur in Lesson 4 when simplifying certain rational expressions. The completing-the-square procedure for $ax^2 + bx + c$: first divide everything by $a$ to get a leading coefficient of 1. Then move $c/a$ to the other side. Add $(b/2a)^2$ to both sides. Factor the left side as a perfect square. Take the square root of both sides (both $\pm$). Solve for $x$. This procedure, done in full generality, produces the quadratic formula. The vertex formula $h = -b/(2a)$ comes directly from completing the square: the vertex is at the $x$-value that makes $(x - h) = 0$, which is $x = h = -b/(2a)$. You do not need to memorise it separately from the quadratic formula — it is just the middle term of the formula without the $\pm\sqrt{\Delta}$ part. Vieta's formulas connect the roots to the coefficients without solving: for $ax^2+bx+c = 0$ with roots $r_1, r_2$: $r_1 + r_2 = -b/a$ and $r_1 r_2 = c/a$. These are useful for checking solutions and for constructing quadratics with given roots. Logical Learner: The Midpoint Constraint \text{Because of symmetry, the x-coordinate of the vertex (h) is ALWAYS the exact average of the roots.} \\ h = \frac{r_1 + r_2}{2}. \text{ This connects Vieta's formulas directly to the geometry of the vertex.} Physical Learner: The Parabola of Gravity \text{A ball thrown in the air follows a quadratic path } y = at^2 + vt + s. \\ \text{The vertex is the maximum height, and the roots represent the time of launch and the time of impact.} Visual Learner: The Turning Point \text{The vertex is a snapshot of Momentum in Transition.} \\ \text{It is where the "speed" of the y-value hits zero before reversing direction. Look for where the slope mirrors itself.} The quadratic formula ax^2 + bx + c = 0 \implies x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} Vieta's formulas for quadratics r_1 + r_2 = -\frac{b}{a} \qquad r_1 r_2 = \frac{c}{a} \\ \text{Example: roots of } x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 \text{ sum to } 5 \text{ and multiply to } 6 \Rightarrow r_1=2, r_2=3. The leading coefficient matters when completing the square 2x^2 + 8x + 3: \text{ factor out 2 first.} \\ 2(x^2 + 4x) + 3 = 2(x^2 + 4x + 4) + 3 - 8 = 2(x+2)^2 - 5 \\ \text{Note: adding 4 inside the bracket adds } 2 \times 4 = 8 \text{ to the expression — subtract 8 outside.} The Average of Roots Proof ($h = -b/2a$) \text{By the Quadratic Formula, roots are } \frac{-b}{2a} \pm \frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}. \\ \text{The average is } h = \frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{-b}{2a} + \frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}\right) + \left(\frac{-b}{2a} - \frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}\right)\right] = -\frac{b}{2a}. \\ \text{The axis of symmetry is the center of the roots.} Vieta's Algebraic Symmetries ax^2+bx+c = a(x-r_1)(x-r_2) = a(x^2 - (r_1+r_2)x + r_1r_2). \\ \text{Matching coefficients gives } -a(r_1+r_2) = b \implies r_1+r_2 = -b/a \text{ and } ar_1r_2 = c \implies r_1r_2 = c/a. Completing the Square — Watch the Geometry Adding and subtracting $(b/2)^2$ is adding zero in disguise — it changes the form but not the value. Converting to vertex form \text{Write } f(x) = 2x^2 - 12x + 7 \text{ in vertex form.} The vertex $(h,k) = (3,-11)$ gives the minimum value, axis of symmetry $x = 3$, and tells you the parabola opens upward. All this information is invisible in standard form. = 2(x^2 - 6x) + 7 Factor the coefficient of $x^2$ out of the first two terms only. = 2(x^2 - 6x + 9) + 7 - 18 Add $(6/2)^2 = 9$ inside the bracket. Because of the factor of 2 outside, we added $2 \times 9 = 18$ to the expression — subtract 18 outside to compensate. = 2(x-3)^2 - 11 Vertex form. Vertex is at $(3, -11)$, which is the minimum (since $a = 2 > 0$). Using the discriminant before solving \text{Without solving, determine the nature of the roots of } 3x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0. The discriminant is a preliminary test — compute it before solving. It tells you how many solutions to expect and whether complex numbers are needed. \Delta = b^2 - 4ac = 25 - 4(3)(4) = 25 - 48 = -23 Compute $\Delta$ directly. \Delta = -23 < 0 \Rightarrow \text{no real roots} Negative discriminant means the parabola does not intersect the $x$-axis. The roots exist but are complex conjugates. Constructing a quadratic from its roots — Vieta's formulas backwards \text{Find a monic quadratic with roots } r_1 = 3 + \sqrt{2} \text{ and } r_2 = 3 - \sqrt{2}. Irrational roots always come in conjugate pairs $p \pm \sqrt{q}$ when the coefficients are rational. Vieta's formulas let you reconstruct the quadratic directly from the roots. r_1 + r_2 = 6 \qquad r_1 r_2 = (3+\sqrt{2})(3-\sqrt{2}) = 9 - 2 = 7 Compute sum and product of roots — no need to use the full values until the product step. x^2 - (r_1+r_2)x + r_1 r_2 = x^2 - 6x + 7 The monic quadratic with these roots is $x^2 - (\text{sum})x + (\text{product})$. Physics: Tracking a Projectile \text{A ball is thrown with height } h(t) = -5t^2 + 20t + 2. \text{ Find the maximum height and the time it hits the ground.} The vertex is the peak of the journey, and the roots are the endpoints. Every projectile is a quadratic experiment. t_{\text{peak}} = -\frac{b}{2a} = -\frac{20}{2(-5)} = 2 \text{ seconds} Step 1: The maximum height occurs at the vertex. Use $t = -b/2a$. h(2) = -5(4) + 20(2) + 2 = -20 + 40 + 2 = 22 \text{ meters} Step 2: Substitute $t=2$ into the height function to find the peak. 0 = -5t^2 + 20t + 2 \implies t = \frac{-20 \pm \sqrt{400 - 4(-5)(2)}}{2(-5)} = \frac{-20 \pm \sqrt{440}}{-10} Step 3: Ground impact occurs when height $h(t) = 0$. Solve using the Quadratic Formula. t \approx \frac{-20 - 20.98}{-10} \approx 4.1 \text{ seconds} Step 4: Only the positive time root is physically meaningful. Economics: Profit Maximisation \text{A company's profit follows } P(x) = -x^2 + 100x - 1200, \text{ where } x \text{ is units sold. Find the "Break-Even" points and the optimal sales volume.} The "sweet spot" of any quadratic system is its vertex. Symmetry ensures that the optimum is always perfectly balanced between the zero-points. 0 = -x^2 + 100x - 1200 \implies x^2 - 100x + 1200 = 0 Step 1: Break-even is where $P(x) = 0$. Solve by factoring: $(x-20)(x-80) = 0$. x_{\text{break-even}} = 20, 80 \text{ units} Step 2: These are the roots. Any sales between 20 and 80 result in profit. x_{\text{opt}} = -\frac{100}{2(-1)} = 50 \text{ units} Step 3: The vertex gives the maximum profit. $x=50$ is exactly half-way between 20 and 80. \text{Find the value of } k \text{ so that } x^2 + kx + 25 = 0 \text{ has exactly one real solution.} Exactly one solution means the discriminant equals zero. k = \pm 10 \Delta = k^2 - 4(1)(25) = 0 Set $\Delta = 0$ for a repeated root. k^2 = 100 \Rightarrow k = \pm 10 Two values of $k$ work: the quadratic $x^2 + 10x + 25 = (x+5)^2$ and $x^2 - 10x + 25 = (x-5)^2$. \text{A parabola has vertex } (2, -3) \text{ and passes through } (5, 6). \text{ Find its equation in standard form.} Start from vertex form $f(x) = a(x-2)^2 - 3$, then use the given point to find $a$. f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 1 f(x) = a(x-2)^2 - 3 Vertex form with vertex $(2, -3)$. 6 = a(5-2)^2 - 3 = 9a - 3 \Rightarrow a = 1 Substitute $(5, 6)$ and solve for $a$. f(x) = (x-2)^2 - 3 = x^2 - 4x + 1 Expand to standard form. \text{A parabola has roots at } x = -1 \text{ and } x = 5. \text{ If the maximum value of the function is } 18, \text{ find its standard form equation.} The x-coordinate of the vertex must be the midpoint of the roots. Once you have the vertex, use $y = a(x-h)^2 + k$ to find $a$. f(x) = -2x^2 + 8x + 10 h = \frac{-1 + 5}{2} = 2 Step 1: The vertex $x$ is the average of the roots. \text{Vertex} = (2, 18) Step 2: The given "maximum value" is the $y$-coordinate of the vertex. 18 = a(5-2)^2 \text{ (Relative to roots, use intercept form)} \\ f(x) = a(x+1)(x-5) \implies 18 = a(2+1)(2-5) Step 3: Substitute $(2, 18)$ into the factored form to solve for $a$. 18 = a(3)(-3) \implies 18 = -9a \implies a = -2 Step 4: Solve for the scale factor. The negative $a$ confirms it was a maximum. f(x) = -2(x+1)(x-5) = -2(x^2 - 4x - 5) = -2x^2 + 8x + 10 Step 5: Expand to standard form. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step

How do you integrate $\dfrac{1}{x^2 - 1}$? You cannot directly. But if you split it into $\dfrac{1/2}{x-1} - \dfrac{1/2}{x+1}$, each piece integrates to a $\ln$. That splitting is partial fractions — and it is pure algebra. Partial fractions are used in control systems engineering to analyse the step response of a transfer function — breaking a complex rational function into simple poles that each contribute a decaying exponential. In signals processing, every filter response is a rational function that gets decomposed this way. A rational expression is a fraction where numerator and denominator are polynomials. They behave exactly like numeric fractions — same rules for multiplying, dividing, adding, subtracting. The only new complication is that you must track which values make the denominator zero (the domain restrictions). Partial fraction decomposition is the reverse of adding fractions. When you add $ rac{A}{x-1} +  rac{B}{x+1}$, you get a single fraction over $(x-1)(x+1)$. Partial fractions asks: given that combined fraction, recover the $A$ and $B$. The technique: multiply both sides by the denominator, then solve for the coefficients. The key insight: a fraction with a linear factor in the denominator integrates to a logarithm. A fraction with a repeated or quadratic factor needs different forms. Decomposing into these simple pieces is exactly what makes integration possible. **The Ratio in Rational**: Just as a rational number is the ratio of two integers, a rational expression is the ratio of two functions. It describes how the "Growth Rate" of the numerator competes with the "Growth Rate" of the denominator. This tension is what creates the unique terrain of rational graphs. **Algebraic Decompression**: Think of a complex rational expression as a "Zipped File." Partial Fraction Decomposition is the tool that "Un-zips" it. It takes a dense, single formula and expands it into a series of atomic, simple elements that are much easier to process, model, and integrate. The procedure for partial fractions: (1) ensure the fraction is proper; (2) factor the denominator completely; (3) set up the partial fraction template matching each factor type; (4) multiply through by the denominator to clear all fractions; (5) solve the resulting system for the unknown coefficients. Operations on rational expressions follow the same rules as numeric fractions. For multiplication: multiply numerators and denominators, then cancel common factors. For division: multiply by the reciprocal. For addition: find a common denominator, convert, then add numerators. Always state domain restrictions. A rational expression is undefined wherever the denominator is zero. After simplification (cancellation), a hole appears where the cancelled factor was zero — the domain restriction remains even though the expression looks defined there. documents.assignment: Elimination on a 2×2 system \text{Solve: } 3x - 2y = 8, \quad 5x + y = 11   Solution: $(30/13, -7/13)$. This is the intersection point of the two lines. 3x - 2y = 8 \quad \text{and} \quad 10x + 2y = 22 Multiply the second equation by 2 to make $y$ coefficients opposites. 13x = 30 \Rightarrow x = \tfrac{30}{13} Add equations. $y$ eliminated. y = 11 - 5(\tfrac{30}{13}) = \tfrac{143-150}{13} = -\tfrac{7}{13} Back-substitute. Recognising a dependent system \text{Solve: } 2x - 4y = 6, \quad -x + 2y = -3   Infinitely many solutions: every point on the line $2x - 4y = 6$. Geometrically, the two equations represent the same line. \text{Multiply equation 2 by 2: } -2x + 4y = -6 Prepare for elimination. \text{Add: } 0 = 0 All variables cancel. The statement $0=0$ is always true — infinitely many solutions. y = \frac{2x-6}{4} = \frac{x-3}{2} \quad \text{(parameterise: let } x = t\text{)} The equations are multiples of each other. Express solutions in terms of a free parameter. Structural Intersection: Parabola meets Line \text{Solve for } (x,y): \; y = x^2, \quad y = x + 2   The system has two solutions: $(2,4)$ and $(-1,1)$. Non-linear systems can have more than one intersection point. x^2 = x + 2 \implies x^2 - x - 2 = 0 Step 1: Use direct substitution. Set the two expressions for $y$ equal to each other. (x-2)(x+1) = 0 \implies x = 2, -1 Step 2: Solve the resulting quadratic. This is the first link between Chapters 3 and 5. x=2 \Rightarrow y=4, \quad x=-1 \Rightarrow y=1 Step 3: Pair the $x$-values with their corresponding $y$-values. Two equations in two unknowns: geometrically, each is a line. The solution is where they cross. What if they are parallel? What if they are the same line? Systems of equations are everywhere in engineering: structural analysis (force balance at every joint), electrical networks (Kirchhoff's laws), economics (supply-demand equilibrium), and computer graphics (ray-surface intersection). Every finite element analysis solves a system of thousands of equations simultaneously using the matrix methods introduced here. A linear system is a set of constraints that must all be satisfied simultaneously. Each equation in two variables is a line — its solution set is a whole line of points. The system's solution is the set of points satisfying all equations at once. For two lines in a plane, there are exactly three cases: one intersection point (unique solution), parallel lines (no solution), or the same line (infinitely many solutions). Three methods — substitution, elimination, and matrix row reduction — all find this intersection. They differ in what they manipulate: substitution replaces one variable; elimination adds equations to cancel a variable; matrix methods automate elimination systematically. The Gaussian elimination algorithm is just elimination applied by an organised procedure. Matrices are a compact notation for systems. The augmented matrix $[A|\mathbf{b}]$ stores the coefficients and constants. A system is the point where the strands cross. It represents a "Structural Consensus"—the only place where every rule in the environment is obeyed simultaneously. **Equilibrium: The Tug of War**: In physics, an object stays still when the forces on it cancel out. A system of equations is a mathematical equilibrium. Each equation is a "Force" pulling the solution in a certain direction, and the intersection is the only place where the tension is perfectly balanced. Substitution: solve one equation for one variable, substitute into the other. Best when one equation is already solved or easily solved for a variable. Elimination: multiply equations by constants so that one variable has equal (or opposite) coefficients, then add/subtract to eliminate it. Best for balanced-looking systems. documents.assignment: Dividing complex numbers \text{Compute } \dfrac{3+4i}{1-2i}.   Always multiply by the conjugate to divide. The denominator becomes real (a sum of squares), and the result is in standard form. = \frac{(3+4i)(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)} Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. = \frac{3+6i+4i+8i^2}{1+4} = \frac{3+10i-8}{5} Expand. Use $i^2 = -1$. = \frac{-5+10i}{5} = -1+2i Simplify. The answer is a complex number in standard form. Finding all cube roots of 1 \text{Find all solutions to } z^3 = 1 \text{ in } \mathbb{C}.   The $n$ nth-roots of any complex number are equally spaced on a circle in the complex plane. This geometric regularity is only visible through the complex plane. 1 = e^{i \cdot 0} = e^{i \cdot 2\pi} = e^{i \cdot 4\pi} Write 1 in polar form with all equivalent angles. z = e^{i \cdot 2\pi k/3}, \quad k = 0, 1, 2 Apply De Moivre for cube roots: divide angles by 3. z_0=1, \quad z_1=e^{2\pi i/3}=-\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i, \quad z_2=e^{4\pi i/3}=-\tfrac{1}{2}-\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i Three roots equally spaced at 120° on the unit circle. The Orbit of i: Periodic Powers \text{Compute } i^{2026} \text{ and } i^{-1}.   Powers of $i$ are a 4-step cycle: $i, -1, -i, 1$. This is the simplest example of a cyclic group in algebra. 2026 = 4(506) + 2 Step 1: Divide the power by 4 to find the remainder. Every 4 rotations return to 1. i^{2026} = i^2 = -1 Step 2: $i^{2026}$ is at the same location as $i^2$. 180° rotation. i^{-1} = \frac{1}{i} = \frac{-i}{-i^2} = -i Step 3: A negative power is a "Backwards" rotation. 90° clockwise is $-i$. Resurrecting the Roots: Solving the Impossible \text{Solve } x^2 - 2x + 10 = 0.   No polynomial ever has "No Solution" again. Complex numbers make algebra complete by filling the geometric gaps in the real line. x = \frac{-(-2) \pm \sqrt{(-2)^2 - 4(1)(10)}}{2(1)} Step 1: Apply the Quadratic Formula. The discriminant is negative. x = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{-36}}{2} Step 2: The discriminant $-36$ was a dead-end before $i$. Now, $\sqrt{-36} = 6i$. x = 1 \pm 3i Step 3: Simplify. The roots form a conjugate pair $(1+3i, 1-3i)$.  \text{Use Euler's formula to prove: } \cos(2\theta) = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta. Expand $e^{i \cdot 2\theta} = (e^{i\theta})^2$ using Euler's formula on both sides. \cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta  e^{i \cdot 2\theta} = \cos 2\theta + i\sin 2\theta Euler on the left. (e^{i\theta})^2 = (\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^2 = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta + 2i\sin\theta\cos\theta Expand the square. \text{Equate real parts: } \cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta \qquad \blacksquare Imaginary parts give $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ as a bonus.  \text{Find all 4th roots of unity (solutions to } z^4=1 \text{) and prove their sum is zero.} The roots form a square in the complex plane. Use the symmetry of the square to explain the sum. 1, i, -1, -i \text{ and Sum } = 0  z = e^{2\pi i k/4} \implies z = 1, i, -1, -i Step 1: The roots are the four points 90° apart on the unit circle. \text{Sum} = 1 + i + (-1) + (-i) = 0 Step 2: Each root has an opposite that cancels it out perfectly. \text{Geometrically: The "Center of Mass" of a regular n-gon centered at the origin is } 0. Step 3: This symmetry holds for any $n$; the sum of the $n$ nth-roots of unity is always zero.

documents.content: What does it mean to rotate a number? Multiplying by $i$ does exactly that — rotates 90° in the complex plane. This is not a coincidence. It is the key to Euler's formula $e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$. Complex numbers are not a mathematical curiosity — they are the language of electrical engineering (impedance $Z = R + jX$), signal processing (Fourier transforms), and quantum mechanics (wavefunctions are complex-valued). Every AC circuit analysis uses complex exponentials. Every digital filter is designed in the complex plane. The real numbers have a gap: $x^2 = -1$ has no solution. Rather than accepting this as impossible, mathematicians defined $i$ as the number satisfying $i^2 = -1$. This is not magic — it is the same move made when extending naturals to integers (to solve $x + 5 = 3$) and integers to rationals (to solve $2x = 3$). Each extension filled a gap. A complex number $a + bi$ is a point $(a, b)$ in the complex plane. The real axis is the $x$-axis; the imaginary axis is the $y$-axis. Addition of complex numbers is vector addition — add the real parts, add the imaginary parts. Multiplication is more interesting: it rotates and scales simultaneously. Multiplying by $i$ rotates 90° counterclockwise: $1 \to i \to -1 \to -i \to 1$. Four multiplications by $i$ bring you full circle. This is where the mysterious pattern $i^1=i, i^2=-1, i^3=-i, i^4=1$ comes from — it is rotation, not arithmetic magic. **The Quest for Closure**: In algebra, "Closure" means that an operation on members of a set always produces a result that is also a member of that set. Real numbers are NOT closed under square roots. Complex numbers provide the "Algebraic Closure"—they are the universal set where every polynomial has a home and every root is reachable. **The Geometry of the Imaginary**: Calling these numbers "Imaginary" was a historical mistake by René Descartes. They are as "real" as any other number; they simply represent a second dimension of momentum. In the complex plane, every number is a Vector—a magnitude and a direction. The fundamental theorem of algebra — every polynomial of degree $n$ with complex coefficients has exactly $n$ roots in $\mathbb{C}$ (counted with multiplicity) — means the complex numbers are algebraically closed. This is WHY } i \cdot i = -1 \text{ geometrically.} Complex arithmetic (a+bi)+(c+di) = (a+c)+(b+d)i \\ (a+bi)(c+di) = (ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i \\ \overline{a+bi} = a-bi \quad (\text{conjugate}) \\ \frac{a+bi}{c+di} = \frac{(a+bi)\overline{(c+di)}}{|c+di|^2} \quad (\text{multiply by conjugate over conjugate}) De Moivre's theorem (r\,e^{i\theta})^n = r^n e^{in\theta} = r^n(\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta) \\ \text{Used to find }n\text{th roots: each root is } r^{1/n}e^{i(\theta+2\pi k)/n}, \; k=0,1,\ldots,n-1 The Conjugate Symmetry Theorem \text{For a polynomial with real coefficients: if } z \text{ is a root, then } \overline{z} \text{ is also a root.} \\ \text{Complex roots must always travel in "Conjugate Pairs."} Algebraic Completeness of C \text{The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra states that every polynomial of degree } n \text{ has exactly } n \text{ complex roots.} \\ \mathbb{C} \text{ is an "Algebraically Closed" field—no further definitions of numbers are required.} The Complex Plane — Multiplication as Rotation Multiplying by $e^{i\theta}$ is a pure rotation by $\theta$ — no scaling. Absolute value inequalities always split into two cases. $|f(x)| < k$ means $-k < f(x) < k$ — a compound inequality. $|f(x)| > k$ means $f(x) > k$ OR $f(x) < -k$ — a disjunction. documents.assignment: Maximizing profit with two variables \text{Maximize } P = 3x + 2y \text{ subject to: } \\ x + 2y \leq 4, \quad x - y \leq 1, \quad x \geq 0, \quad y \geq 0.   The maximum profit of 8 is achieved by producing 2 units of $x$ and 1 unit of $y$. \text{Vertices: } (0,0), (1,0), (2,1), (0,2) Graphing reveals the vertices. $(2,1)$ is the intersection of $x+2y=4$ and $x-y=1$. P(0,0)=0, \quad P(1,0)=3, \quad P(2,1)=3(2)+2(1)=8, \quad P(0,2)=4 Plug each vertex into $P = 3x + 2y$. P_{max} = 8 \text{ at } (2,1) Compare the values. Minimizing Cost: The Diet Problem \text{Minimize Cost } C = 2x + 5y \text{ subject to: } \\ x + y \geq 10, \quad x \geq 2, \quad y \geq 3.   Survival math: often we want to minimize distance or cost while staying above a threshold of necessity. \text{Vertices: } (7,3), (2,8) Step 1: Graph the constraints. This is a minimization problem on a "Bottom-Bounded" feasible region. C(7,3) = 2(7) + 5(3) = 14+15 = 29 \\ C(2,8) = 2(2) + 5(8) = 4+40 = 44 Step 2: Evaluate cost at the vertices. C_{min} = 29 \text{ at } (7,3) Step 3: The lowest cost is found at $(7,3)$—the point most "Opposite" to the direction of cost increase.  \text{Analyze the system subject to: } x - y \leq 1, \; x \geq 0, \; y \geq 0. \\ \text{Why does } P = x+y \text{ have NO maximum value here?} Graph the region. It is open at the top. Think about what happens as $x$ and $y$ both get larger and larger. The region is unbounded in the positive y-direction.  \text{Feasible Region: } y \geq x - 1 Step 1: The region is the entire area above the line $y=x-1$ in the first quadrant. P(x,y) \to \infty \text{ as } y \to \infty Step 2: Since $y$ has no upper bound, we can pick a larger $y$ forever, increasing $P$ without limit. \text{Conclusion: Unbounded region } \implies \text{ No Maximum} Step 3: Linear Programming requires a "Container" to find a peak. documents.content: A factory makes two products with different profit margins and different resource requirements. How many of each should they make to maximize profit without running out of materials? Linear programming is the backbone of logistics and supply chain management. From airline scheduling to hospital staffing and diet optimization, the goal is always to maximize a benefit (profit, throughput) or minimize a cost (waste, time) given limited resources (fuel, beds, budget). Problems involving thousands of variables are solved daily using the simplex algorithm, which builds on the graphical methods taught here. Linear programming is a technique for finding the maximum or minimum value of a **linear objective function** (like profit $P = 5x + 3y$) subject to a set of **linear constraints** (inequalities like $x + y leq 10$). The set of all points that satisfy all constraints simultaneously is called the **feasible region**. Because the constraints are linear, this region is always a polygon (in 2D). The **Vertex Theorem** (or Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming) states that the optimal value (max or min) always occurs at one of the vertices (corners) of the feasible region. This means instead of checking infinitely many points, you only need to check the corners. **The Grammar of Scheduling**: "Programming" in this context does not mean computer code; it comes from the older sense of "Creating a Schedule" or a "Plan of Action." It is the science of optimal coordination between competing rules. **Resource Scarcity**: In the real world, you never have "Infinite" anything. You have limited time, limited fuel, and limited space. Linear programming is the mathematical language of Scarcity—how to thrive within the boundaries of what is available. To solve a linear programming problem: (1) Graph each constraint inequality to find the feasible region. (2) Find the coordinates of every vertex (intersection of boundary lines). (3) Evaluate the objective function at each vertex. (4) The largest resulting value is the maximum; the smallest is the minimum. Finding vertices involves solving systems of two linear equations (the boundary lines) at each corner of the polygon. Every point in this region is a "possible" solution.} Sweeping with Iso-Profit Lines \text{Every point on } ax+by=k \text{ gives the same value } k. \\ \text{Solving is finding the largest } k \text{ such that the line } ax+by=k \text{ still touches the feasible region.} The Simplex Algorithm Path \text{In high dimensions (thousands of variables), we cannot graph.} \\ \text{The Simplex Algorithm starts at one vertex and "hops" to an adjacent vertex with a better value, step by step, until no better vertex exists.} Maximizing profit with two variables \text{Maximize } P = 3x + 2y \text{ subject to: } \\ x + 2y \leq 4, \quad x - y \leq 1, \quad x \geq 0, \quad y \geq 0. documents.assignment: Converting between degrees and radians \text{Convert: (a) } 135° \text{ to radians, (b) } \frac{7\pi}{4} \text{ to degrees.}   $\pi$ always cancels in radian-to-degree conversion. If it does not cancel cleanly, leave the answer in terms of $\pi$. 135° \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{135\pi}{180} = \frac{3\pi}{4} Multiply by $\pi/180$. Simplify the fraction: $\gcd(135,180)=45$, so $135/180 = 3/4$. \frac{7\pi}{4} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = \frac{7 \times 180}{4} = \frac{1260}{4} = 315° Multiply by $180/\pi$. The $\pi$ cancels. Arc length and sector area \text{A circle has radius 8 cm. Find (a) the arc length and (b) sector area for a central angle of } 150°.   Both formulas are clean in radians. In degrees they would each need a $\pi/180$ factor — one more reason radians are the natural choice. 150° = 150 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{5\pi}{6} \text{ rad} Convert to radians first — the formulas require it. s = r\theta = 8 \times \frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{40\pi}{6} = \frac{20\pi}{3} \approx 20.9 \text{ cm} Arc length formula. A = \tfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}(64)\cdot\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{320\pi}{12} = \frac{80\pi}{3} \approx 83.8 \text{ cm}^2 Sector area formula. Finding coterminal angles \text{Find a positive and a negative angle coterminal with } \frac{2\pi}{3}.   Infinitely many coterminal angles exist. The one in $[0, 2\pi)$ is the "principal" representative. To find it, add or subtract $2\pi$ repeatedly until the result lands in range. \frac{2\pi}{3} + 2\pi = \frac{2\pi}{3} + \frac{6\pi}{3} = \frac{8\pi}{3} Add one full rotation for a positive coterminal angle. \frac{2\pi}{3} - 2\pi = \frac{2\pi}{3} - \frac{6\pi}{3} = -\frac{4\pi}{3} Subtract one full rotation for a negative coterminal angle. Navigating the Globe: DMS to Decimal \text{Convert } 48^\circ 51^\prime 24^{\prime\prime} \text{ (the latitude of Paris) to decimal degrees.}   DMS is the historical legacy of Babylonian navigation. Digital systems (GPS) prefer decimal degrees for easier computation. 48 + \frac{51}{60} + \frac{24}{3600} Step 1: Convert minutes to 1/60th of a degree and seconds to 1/3600th. 48 + 0.85 + 0.00667 = 48.85667^\circ Step 2: Sum the parts to find the decimal equivalent. Angular Synchrony: Connected Gears \text{A small gear (r=2) is connected to a large gear (r=8). If the small gear turns } 120^\circ, \text{ how far does the large gear turn?}   Large gears turn less but with more torque. The ratio of angles is the inverse of the ratio of radii. 120^\circ = \frac{2\pi}{3} \text{ rad} Step 1: Convert to radians for rotation modeling. s = r_1 \theta_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{2\pi}{3} = \frac{4\pi}{3} Step 2: Calculate the arc length travel along the small gear. \frac{4\pi}{3} = 8 \cdot \theta_2 \implies \theta_2 = \frac{4\pi}{24} = \frac{\pi}{6} \text{ rad} Step 3: The arc length travel is identical for the large gear. Solve for the large angle. \theta_2 = 30^\circ Step 4: Convert back to degrees for the final answer.  \text{A wheel of radius 30 cm rotates at 120 rpm. Find the linear speed of a point on the rim in m/s.} Convert rpm to radians per second first: 1 revolution = $2\pi$ rad. v = 1.2\pi \approx 3.77 \text{ m/s}  \omega = 120 \times 2\pi = 240\pi \text{ rad/min} = \frac{240\pi}{60} = 4\pi \text{ rad/s} Angular velocity in rad/s. v = r\omega = 0.30 \times 4\pi = 1.2\pi \approx 3.77 \text{ m/s} Linear speed = radius × angular velocity. Convert radius to metres.  \text{Two supplementary angles are in the ratio } 2:7. \text{ Find each in degrees and radians.} If the angles are $2k$ and $7k$, they sum to $180°$. 40° \text{ and } 140°  2k + 7k = 180° \Rightarrow 9k = 180° \Rightarrow k = 20° Set up and solve. 2k = 40° = \frac{2\pi}{9} \text{ rad} \qquad 7k = 140° = \frac{7\pi}{9} \text{ rad} The two angles, in both units.  \text{The Earth has a radius of } 6400 \text{ km and rotates once every } 24 \text{ hours. Calculate the linear speed (km/h) of a person standing on the equator.} Find the angular velocity in radians per hour first. One rotation = $2\pi$ radians. \approx 1675 \text{ km/h}  \omega = \frac{2\pi \text{ rad}}{24 \text{ hours}} = \frac{\pi}{12} \text{ rad/h} Step 1: Calculate the angular speed of the planet. v = r\omega = 6400 \times \frac{\pi}{12} = \frac{1600\pi}{3} \approx 1675 \text{ km/h} Step 2: Linear speed = radius × angular velocity. Multiply and simplify.

documents.content: Degrees are completely arbitrary — someone decided a full turn is 360, and that number stuck for thousands of years. Radians are different. They are the only angle measure that makes calculus formulas simple. Why? The Babylonians chose 360 for a full circle around 2000 BCE, probably because 360 has many divisors and approximates the days in a year. Radians were not formalised until the 19th century — but they are the reason $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$ holds without any ugly constants. In engineering, rotational speed in radians per second connects directly to frequency in a way degrees cannot. **Where you are in the story:** You are stepping into Trigonometry fresh from Precalc-2 (Algebra), where you built fluency with functions, equations, and the coordinate plane. Algebra gave you the tools to manipulate symbols; now Trigonometry gives those symbols geometric meaning. Before you can work with sine and cosine, you need to understand what an angle actually is and why mathematicians chose a particular unit to measure it. That gap — between "angles as turns" and "angles as lengths" — is exactly what this lesson fills. An angle is formed by two rays sharing a common endpoint called the vertex. The angle measures the rotation from one ray (the initial side) to the other (the terminal side). Direction matters: counterclockwise is positive by convention, clockwise is negative. Degrees divide a full rotation into 360 equal parts. This is arbitrary but convenient — 360 is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24, 30, 36, 40, 45, 60, 72, 90, 120, 180. Almost any fraction of a circle comes out to a whole number of degrees. Radians measure angles by arc length. One radian is the angle subtended by an arc equal in length to the radius. Since the circumference is $2\pi r$, a full circle subtends $2\pi$ radians. This is not a convention — it follows directly from the definition of $\pi$. Radians are dimensionless: they are a ratio of lengths. The calculus reason radians win: $\lim_{\theta \to 0} \frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} = 1$ only when $\theta$ is in radians. This limit is the foundation of every trig derivative. In degrees, the limit gives $\pi/180$ instead — a constant that would infect every derivative formula forever. **The Cosmic Constant**: While 360 is a human choice (based on the Babylonian calendar), $2\pi$ is a property of the Universe itself. Radians represent the "True Language" of circles—where the distance traveled along the edge is directly linked to the angle turned at the center. **Circular Measure**: If you unrolled a circle onto a flat line, the distance you walked would be the "Arc Length." Trigonometry is the study of how that linear walk translates into rotational position. The radian is the only unit that keeps this relationship scale-free. **Where this is heading:** Now that you understand angle measurement and why radians exist, the next lesson (Triangle Geometry) builds the geometric scaffolding — similar triangles, the Pythagorean theorem, and Thales' theorem — that makes the trig ratios well-defined. Every trig ratio you will learn is secretly a similar-triangle relationship, and the radian definition you just mastered ensures arc length and sector area formulas work without conversion factors. Degrees-minutes-seconds (DMS) notation subdivides degrees the same way hours subdivide time: $1° = 60^\prime$ (arcminutes) and $1^\prime = 60^{\prime\prime}$ (arcseconds). GPS coordinates use decimal degrees; astronomical measurements often use DMS. Converting: $37°22^\prime 48^{\prime\prime} = 37 + 22/60 + 48/3600 = 37.38°$. An angle in standard position has its vertex at the origin and its initial side along the positive $x$-axis. The terminal side determines the angle. Coterminal angles have the same terminal side but differ by full rotations: $\theta$ and $\theta + 360°k$ (or $\theta + 2\pi k$) are coterminal for any integer $k$. The arc length formula $s = r\theta$ (radians) and area of a sector $A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ (radians) are direct consequences of the radian definition. These formulas are used constantly in physics and engineering — rotational kinetic energy, moment of inertia, angular velocity. documents.assignment: Using similar triangles to find an unknown side \triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF. \text{ If } AB=6, BC=9, AC=12, \text{ and } DE=4, \text{ find } EF \text{ and } DF.   Similar triangles: find the scale factor from any pair of corresponding sides, then multiply all others by it. \text{Scale factor: } k = \frac{DE}{AB} = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3} Find the ratio of corresponding sides. DE corresponds to AB. EF = k \cdot BC = \frac{2}{3} \times 9 = 6 \qquad DF = k \cdot AC = \frac{2}{3} \times 12 = 8 Multiply all sides of the original triangle by the scale factor. Verifying and generating Pythagorean triples \text{(a) Verify 8-15-17 is a Pythagorean triple. (b) Generate a triple using } m=3, n=1.   The generating formula produces all primitive triples when $\gcd(m,n)=1$ and $m-n$ is odd. Multiples of primitives also work. 8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289 = 17^2 \checkmark Check: does $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$? m=3, n=1: \quad a = m^2-n^2 = 8, \quad b = 2mn = 6, \quad c = m^2+n^2 = 10 Apply the generating formula. This gives the triple (6, 8, 10) — a multiple of (3, 4, 5). 3D distance between two points \text{Find the distance between } A(1, -2, 4) \text{ and } B(3, 1, -1).   The 3D distance formula is exactly the Pythagorean theorem applied in three dimensions. There is nothing new to memorise — just one more square under the root. d = \sqrt{(3-1)^2 + (1-(-2))^2 + (-1-4)^2} Apply the 3D distance formula. = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 25} = \sqrt{38} Two applications of the Pythagorean theorem: first in the $xy$-plane, then adding the $z$ component. The Room Diagonal: Distancing in Space \text{A box has dimensions 3m } \times \text{ 4m } \times \text{ 12m. What is the longest distance between two opposite corners?}   3D distance is just Pythagoras twice. The "Diagonal of the Box" is the ultimate test of spatial geometry. d_{floor} = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5 Step 1: Calculate the diagonal of the floor. This is a 3-4-5 triangle. d_{room} = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = 13 Step 2: Use the floor diagonal as one leg and the height (12) as the other. This is a 5-12-13 triangle. The Triple Factory: Generating Primitives \text{Use Euclid's formula with } m=5, n=2 \text{ to generate a primitive Pythagorean triple.}   Euclid's formula is a powerful engine for discovery. It proves that there are infinitely many integer solutions to the right-triangle problem. a = 5^2 - 2^2 = 25 - 4 = 21 Step 1: Calculate the first leg. b = 2(5)(2) = 20 Step 2: Calculate the second leg. c = 5^2 + 2^2 = 25 + 4 = 29 Step 3: Calculate the hypotenuse. 21^2 + 20^2 = 441 + 400 = 841 = 29^2 \checkmark Step 4: Verify the result. 21-20-29 is a primitive triple.  \text{A 10-foot ladder leans against a wall. Its base is 6 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach? Is the foot-to-top distance a Pythagorean triple?} This is a right triangle with hypotenuse 10 and one leg 6. h = 8 \text{ ft; yes, } (6,8,10) = 2\times(3,4,5)  h^2 + 6^2 = 10^2 \Rightarrow h^2 = 100-36 = 64 \Rightarrow h = 8 Pythagorean theorem. The height is 8 feet. (6, 8, 10) = 2 \times (3, 4, 5) \checkmark Yes — a multiple of the 3-4-5 triple. Recognising triples saves time on exams.  \text{Prove: the midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is equidistant from all three vertices.} Place the right angle at the origin. The midpoint of the hypotenuse is the average of the two other vertices. |OM| = |AM| = |BM| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} = \tfrac{1}{2}|AB|  \text{Let the right angle be at } O=(0,0), A=(2a,0), B=(0,2b). \text{ Midpoint } M = (a,b). Convenient coordinates. Using $2a$ and $2b$ makes the midpoint calculation clean. |OM| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} \quad |AM| = \sqrt{(2a-a)^2+b^2} = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} \quad |BM| = \sqrt{a^2+(2b-b)^2} = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} All three distances equal $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ — the midpoint is equidistant from all three vertices. \therefore M \text{ is the circumcentre of the right triangle, and the circumradius} = \tfrac{1}{2}|AB|. \qquad \blacksquare This is why Thales' theorem works: the circumcentre of a right triangle lies exactly at the midpoint of the hypotenuse.  \text{Verify Thales' Theorem for a triangle with vertices } (0,0), (6,0), \text{ and } (0,8). \text{ Find the midpoint of the hypotenuse and check its distance to all three corners.} The midpoint is the center of the circumscribed circle. It should be equidistant from the right angle and the two sharp corners. Distances to (0,0), (6,0), (0,8) are all 5.  M = (3,4) Step 1: Calculate the midpoint of the hypotenuse from (6,0) to (0,8). d_{origin} = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5 Step 2: Calculate the distance from (3,4) to the origin (0,0). d_{A} = \sqrt{(3-6)^2 + (4-0)^2} = 5 \\ d_{B} = \sqrt{(3-0)^2 + (4-8)^2} = 5 Step 3: Calculate the distance to the other two corners. All are equal.
documents.applications: Similar triangles are the engine behind trigonometry: the trig ratios are defined for a right triangle, but they work for any angle because all right triangles with the same angle are similar. Pythagorean triples appear in construction (the 3-4-5 rope trick to make a right angle), GPS signal processing, and error-correcting codes. The 3D distance formula underlies every computation in 3D graphics and physics. documents.content: Thales of Miletus, around 600 BCE, proved that any angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle. He reportedly discovered this while looking at reflections in water. How do you prove something that visually obvious — and why does it matter for trigonometry? Similar triangles are the engine behind trigonometry: the trig ratios are defined for a right triangle, but they work for any angle because all right triangles with the same angle are similar. Pythagorean triples appear in construction (the 3-4-5 rope trick to make a right angle), GPS signal processing, and error-correcting codes. The 3D distance formula underlies every computation in 3D graphics and physics. **Where you are in the story:** In the previous lesson (Angles & Radians) you established how to measure angles and why radians are the natural unit. Now you need the geometric scaffolding that makes trigonometry work: specifically, why the trig ratios are well-defined at all. The answer is similar triangles — and this lesson fills that gap by building up from the angle sum theorem through Thales' theorem to the Pythagorean theorem and its triples. The angles of any triangle always sum to 180°. This is not just a rule — it follows from the parallel line axiom of Euclidean geometry. Draw a line through the apex of any triangle parallel to the base. The three angles of the triangle line up along it, making a straight angle of 180°. This proof works for every triangle, every time. Two triangles are similar (∼) if their angles match — one is a scaled copy of the other. Similar triangles have equal ratios of corresponding sides. This is why the trigonometric ratios are well-defined: in any right triangle with a given acute angle, the ratio opposite/hypotenuse is always the same number, regardless of the triangle's size. That number is the sine of the angle. Two triangles are congruent (≅) if they have the same angles and the same side lengths — they are identical, not just scaled copies. The congruence conditions (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL for right triangles) tell you the minimum information needed to guarantee two triangles are identical. **The Language of Inclosure**: A triangle is the simplest possible enclosure in flat space. It is the only polygon that is 'Rigid'—meaning its shape is completely determined by its side lengths. This unique property makes it the universal building block of stable structures. **Structural Rigidity**: Unlike a square, which can 'shear' into a rhombus without changing its side lengths, a triangle cannot be deformed. To change an angle, you MUST change a side length. This is WHY bridges, cranes, and roof trusses are built from interconnected triangles. **Where this is heading:** With triangle geometry solid, the next lesson (Trig Ratios in Right Triangles) defines all six trig functions as ratios of the sides — and the similar-triangle argument you just saw is exactly why those ratios depend only on the angle, not on the triangle's size. Every SOH-CAH-TOA ratio is a similar-triangle relationship in disguise. The Pythagorean theorem $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ has over 370 known proofs. The most visual is the area rearrangement: start with a square of side $(a+b)$, place four copies of the right triangle inside it, and the remaining area is $c^2$. Rearrange the triangles differently and the remaining area shows $a^2 + b^2$. Same total area → same result. A Pythagorean triple is a set of three positive integers $(a, b, c)$ satisfying $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. All primitive triples (no common factor) are generated by $m^2-n^2$, $2mn$, $m^2+n^2$ for coprime integers $m > n > 0$ with $m-n$ odd. The 3-4-5 triple has been used in construction since ancient Egypt — stretch a 12-unit rope into a 3-4-5 triangle and you have a perfect right angle. The 3D distance formula extends the 2D version by one more Pythagorean step. Given points $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2,z_2)$: first find the horizontal distance $d_{xy} = \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}$, then the full 3D distance $d = \sqrt{d_{xy}^2 + (\Delta z)^2} = \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2+(\Delta z)^2}$. It is the Pythagorean theorem applied twice. Distance Between Points Using similar triangles to find an unknown side \triangle ABC \sim \triangle DEF. \text{ If } AB=6, BC=9, AC=12, \text{ and } DE=4, \text{ find } EF \text{ and } DF. Similar triangles: find the scale factor from any pair of corresponding sides, then multiply all others by it. \text{Scale factor: } k = \frac{DE}{AB} = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3} Find the ratio of corresponding sides. DE corresponds to AB. EF = k \cdot BC = \frac{2}{3} \times 9 = 6 \qquad DF = k \cdot AC = \frac{2}{3} \times 12 = 8 Multiply all sides of the original triangle by the scale factor. Verifying and generating Pythagorean triples \text{(a) Verify 8-15-17 is a Pythagorean triple. (b) Generate a triple using } m=3, n=1. The generating formula produces all primitive triples when $\gcd(m,n)=1$ and $m-n$ is odd. Multiples of primitives also work. 8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289 = 17^2 \checkmark Check: does $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$? m=3, n=1: \quad a = m^2-n^2 = 8, \quad b = 2mn = 6, \quad c = m^2+n^2 = 10 Apply the generating formula. This gives the triple (6, 8, 10) — a multiple of (3, 4, 5). 3D distance between two points \text{Find the distance between } A(1, -2, 4) \text{ and } B(3, 1, -1). The 3D distance formula is exactly the Pythagorean theorem applied in three dimensions. There is nothing new to memorise — just one more square under the root. d = \sqrt{(3-1)^2 + (1-(-2))^2 + (-1-4)^2} Apply the 3D distance formula. = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 25} = \sqrt{38} Two applications of the Pythagorean theorem: first in the $xy$-plane, then adding the $z$ component. The Room Diagonal: Distancing in Space \text{A box has dimensions 3m } \times \text{ 4m } \times \text{ 12m. What is the longest distance between two opposite corners?} 3D distance is just Pythagoras twice. The "Diagonal of the Box" is the ultimate test of spatial geometry. d_{floor} = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5 Step 1: Calculate the diagonal of the floor. This is a 3-4-5 triangle. d_{room} = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = 13 Step 2: Use the floor diagonal as one leg and the height (12) as the other. This is a 5-12-13 triangle. The Triple Factory: Generating Primitives \text{Use Euclid's formula with } m=5, n=2 \text{ to generate a primitive Pythagorean triple.} Euclid's formula is a powerful engine for discovery. It proves that there are infinitely many integer solutions to the right-triangle problem. a = 5^2 - 2^2 = 25 - 4 = 21 Step 1: Calculate the first leg. b = 2(5)(2) = 20 Step 2: Calculate the second leg. c = 5^2 + 2^2 = 25 + 4 = 29 Step 3: Calculate the hypotenuse. 21^2 + 20^2 = 441 + 400 = 841 = 29^2 \checkmark Step 4: Verify the result. 21-20-29 is a primitive triple. \text{A 10-foot ladder leans against a wall. Its base is 6 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach? Is the foot-to-top distance a Pythagorean triple?} This is a right triangle with hypotenuse 10 and one leg 6. h = 8 \text{ ft; yes, } (6,8,10) = 2\times(3,4,5) h^2 + 6^2 = 10^2 \Rightarrow h^2 = 100-36 = 64 \Rightarrow h = 8 Pythagorean theorem. The height is 8 feet. (6, 8, 10) = 2 \times (3, 4, 5) \checkmark Yes — a multiple of the 3-4-5 triple. Recognising triples saves time on exams. \text{Prove: the midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is equidistant from all three vertices.} Place the right angle at the origin. The midpoint of the hypotenuse is the average of the two other vertices. |OM| = |AM| = |BM| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} = \tfrac{1}{2}|AB| \text{Let the right angle be at } O=(0,0), A=(2a,0), B=(0,2b). \text{ Midpoint } M = (a,b). Convenient coordinates. Using $2a$ and $2b$ makes the midpoint calculation clean. |OM| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} \quad |AM| = \sqrt{(2a-a)^2+b^2} = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} \quad |BM| = \sqrt{a^2+(2b-b)^2} = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} All three distances equal $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ — the midpoint is equidistant from all three vertices. \therefore M \text{ is the circumcentre of the right triangle, and the circumradius} = \tfrac{1}{2}|AB|. \qquad \blacksquare This is why Thales' theorem works: the circumcentre of a right triangle lies exactly at the midpoint of the hypotenuse. \text{Verify Thales' Theorem for a triangle with vertices } (0,0), (6,0), \text{ and } (0,8). \text{ Find the midpoint of the hypotenuse and check its distance to all three corners.} The midpoint is the center of the circumscribed circle. It should be equidistant from the right angle and the two sharp corners. Distances to (0,0), (6,0), (0,8) are all 5. M = (3,4) Step 1: Calculate the midpoint of the hypotenuse from (6,0) to (0,8). d_{origin} = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5 Step 2: Calculate the distance from (3,4) to the origin (0,0). d_{A} = \sqrt{(3-6)^2 + (4-0)^2} = 5 \\ d_{B} = \sqrt{(3-0)^2 + (4-8)^2} = 5 Step 3: Calculate the distance to the other two corners. documents.assignment: Finding all six trig ratios from one side ratio \text{If } \sin\theta = \frac{3}{5} \text{ and } \theta \text{ is acute, find all six trig ratios.}   One trig ratio in a right triangle determines all six. Draw the triangle, find the missing side, read off the ratios. \text{opp} = 3, \text{ hyp} = 5 \Rightarrow \text{adj} = \sqrt{25-9} = 4 Draw the triangle: opposite = 3, hypotenuse = 5. Pythagorean theorem gives the adjacent side. (Recognise 3-4-5!) \sin = \frac{3}{5}, \; \cos = \frac{4}{5}, \; \tan = \frac{3}{4} The three primary ratios. \csc = \frac{5}{3}, \; \sec = \frac{5}{4}, \; \cot = \frac{4}{3} The three reciprocals — flip each primary ratio. Exact values from the unit circle for angles beyond 90° \text{Find the exact value of } \sin(150°), \cos(225°), \tan(300°).   Reference angle method: (1) find which quadrant, (2) find the reference angle (acute angle to the x-axis), (3) apply the ASTC sign rule. \sin(150°) = \sin(180°-30°) = \sin(30°) = \frac{1}{2} QII: sin is positive. Reference angle is $180°-150°=30°$. Use the known value. \cos(225°) = -\cos(45°) = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} QIII: cos is negative. Reference angle is $225°-180°=45°$. \tan(300°) = -\tan(60°) = -\sqrt{3} QIV: tan is negative. Reference angle is $360°-300°=60°$. Reciprocal Reconstruction: Working Backwards \text{If } \sec\theta = \sqrt{5} \text{ and } \sin\theta < 0, \text{ find all six trig ratios.}   A single reciprocal ratio locks in the entire unit circle possibility. Sign analysis is the final filter. \cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, \quad \theta \in QIV Step 1: Reciprocal of secant is cosine. Since sec is positive and sin is negative, we must be in Quadrant IV. \text{adj} = 1, \text{ hyp} = \sqrt{5} \implies \text{opp} = -\sqrt{(\sqrt{5})^2 - 1^2} = -2 Step 2: Use Pythagoras to find the opposite side. It MUST be negative because of QIV. \sin\theta = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}, \quad \tan\theta = -2, \quad \cot\theta = -\frac{1}{2}, \quad \csc\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2} Step 3: Read off all remaining ratios from the side lengths. The Complement Equation: Symmetry in Action \text{Solve for } x: \sin(20^\circ) = \cos(x).   Co-functions are identical once you cross the 45° boundary of the complement. \cos(x) = \sin(90^\circ - x) Step 1: Use the co-function identity. \sin(20^\circ) = \sin(90^\circ - x) \implies 20 = 90 - x Step 2: Equate the arguments. x = 70^\circ Step 3: Solve for x.  \text{If } \tan\theta = -\frac{5}{12} \text{ and } \theta \text{ is in QIV, find } \sin\theta \text{ and } \cos\theta. $\tan = $ opp/adj. In QIV, sin is negative and cos is positive. \sin\theta = -5/13, \; \cos\theta = 12/13  \text{opp} = 5, \text{ adj} = 12 \Rightarrow \text{hyp} = \sqrt{25+144} = 13 In QIV: opposite is $-5$ (below x-axis), adjacent is $+12$. Hypotenuse is always positive. \sin\theta = -\frac{5}{13}, \quad \cos\theta = \frac{12}{13} QIV: sin negative, cos positive. Verify: $(-5/13)/(12/13) = -5/12 = \tan\theta$ ✓  \text{Prove that } \tan\theta + \cot\theta = \sec\theta \csc\theta. Write everything in terms of sin and cos, then combine fractions. \tan\theta + \cot\theta = \sec\theta\csc\theta  \tan\theta + \cot\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} + \frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} Convert to sin and cos. = \frac{\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \frac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} Common denominator, then Pythagorean identity. = \frac{1}{\sin\theta} \cdot \frac{1}{\cos\theta} = \csc\theta \cdot \sec\theta \qquad \blacksquare Split and recognise the reciprocal definitions.  \text{Start with the fundamental identity } \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1. \text{ Derive the identity relating cotangent and cosecant.} Divide the entire identity by $\sin^2\theta$. 1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta  \frac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} + \frac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} = \frac{1}{\sin^2\theta} Step 1: Perform the same algebraic operation (division) on every term. 1 + \left(\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\right)^2 Step 2: Group the squared terms. 1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta \qquad \blacksquare Step 3: Recognition. The ratio of cos-to-sin is cotangent; the reciprocal of sin is cosecant.

documents.content: Why is it called the co-sine? And what does the "co" mean in co-secant and co-tangent? The naming hides a beautiful symmetry that makes half the unit circle values free once you know the other half. Every GPS location, every 3D rendering, every robot arm position uses trig ratios. In manufacturing, the angle of a machined surface is specified as a trig ratio — not as an angle — because ratios are dimensionless and therefore independent of units. Structural engineers compute forces along and perpendicular to members using sine and cosine decomposition. **Where you are in the story:** The previous lesson (Triangle Geometry) established that similar triangles have equal side ratios — and that any two right triangles with the same acute angle are similar. That similarity is the entire reason trig ratios exist: they are the names we give to those locked-in ratios. This lesson fills the gap between "ratios exist" and "here are all six, where they come from, and how they connect." In a right triangle, the six trig ratios are just the six ways to form a fraction from the three side lengths. With sides labelled relative to an acute angle $\theta$: opposite (opp), adjacent (adj), hypotenuse (hyp), the six ratios are $\sin = \text{opp/hyp}$, $\cos = \text{adj/hyp}$, $\tan = \text{opp/adj}$, and their reciprocals $\csc = \text{hyp/opp}$, $\sec = \text{hyp/adj}$, $\cot = \text{adj/opp}$. The "co" prefix means complementary. The co-sine of an angle is the sine of its complement: $\cos\theta = \sin(90°-\theta)$. Similarly $\cot\theta = \tan(90°-\theta)$ and $\csc\theta = \sec(90°-\theta)$. This is why co-functions appear in pairs — they share the same values, just on opposite angles of the same right triangle. These ratios are well-defined because of similar triangles. Every right triangle with a given acute angle $\theta$ is similar to every other — same angles, just different scale. The ratio opposite/hypotenuse is the same for all of them. That common ratio is exactly what we call $\sin\theta$. The ratio does not depend on the size of the triangle. **The Grammar of Proportion**: The word "Sine" has a messy history—starting as "Jiva" (bowstring) in Sanskrit, becoming "Jaib" (fold) in Arabic, and being mistranslated into "Sinus" (bay/pocket) in Latin. Regardless of the name, it represents the "Vertical Chord"—the height of a point on the circle. **The Scale-Free Universe**: Trigonometry is the math of Ratios, and ratios are the only true units in physics. Whether you are measuring the angle of an atom or the angle of a distant galaxy, the Sine of 30° is ALWAYS 0.5. It is a universal constant of shape, independent of size. **Where this is heading:** Once you have the six trig ratios defined in a right triangle, the next lesson (Graphing Trig Functions) takes those ratio values and plots them as functions of the angle — turning the static triangle picture into dynamic waves. The periodicity, asymptotes, and range of every trig graph follow directly from the definitions and the unit circle you see here. The exact values for 30°, 45°, and 60° come from two special triangles. The 45-45-90 triangle has legs equal; if each leg is 1, the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$. The 30-60-90 triangle comes from cutting an equilateral triangle in half; if the hypotenuse is 2, the short leg is 1 and the long leg is $\sqrt{3}$. The unit circle ($r=1$) unifies all of this. At angle $\theta$ measured from the positive $x$-axis, the terminal point is $P = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. This is because in a unit-radius right triangle, the adjacent side has length $\cos\theta$ (by definition of cosine) and the opposite side has length $\sin\theta$. The unit circle extends trig to all angles — not just acute ones. For angles beyond 90°, the right-triangle definition breaks down (you cannot have an obtuse angle in a right triangle). The unit circle definition takes over: $\sin\theta$ is always the $y$-coordinate of the terminal point, $\cos\theta$ is always the $x$-coordinate, for any angle. The Cosine is just the Sine seen from the other corner's perspective.} Logical Learner: The Scale-Free Universe \text{Geometry is scale-invariant.} \\ \text{Because a triangle is "Rigid," every angle is locked to a specific ratio of sides. Trigonometry is the catalog of these universal proportions.} Physical Learner: The Clinometer and Shadow \text{Ancient Egyptians found the height of pyramids by measuring shadows.} \\ \text{The Tangent ratio is the "Shadow Factor"—tell me the angle of the sun, and I will tell you exactly how many times longer your shadow is than your height.} Visual Learner: The Tangent as Slope \text{Visualize a mountain climb.} \\ \text{The Sine is your vertical gain; the Cosine is your horizontal travel; the Tangent is the "Steepness" of the path.} \\ \tan\theta \text{ is the literal slope (rise/run) of the terminal side.} Exact values — the two special triangles \begin{array}{c|ccc} \theta & 30° & 45° & 60° \\ \hline \sin & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \cos & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \frac{1}{2} \\ \tan & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 1 & \sqrt{3} \end{array} Memory pattern for sin/cos exact values \sin 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° = \frac{\sqrt{0}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{1}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{4}}{2} \\ = 0, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, 1 \\ \text{Cosine is the same sequence reversed.} Unit circle definition — extends trig to all angles \text{Terminal point of angle } \theta: P = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta) \\ \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \quad (x \neq 0) \\ \text{Signs by quadrant: ASTC — All, Sin, Tan, Cos (positive)} ASTC — which functions are positive in each quadrant \text{"All Students Take Calculus"} \quad \text{QI: All | QII: Sin | QIII: Tan | QIV: Cos} \\ \text{This follows from the }(x,y) \text{ signs of the unit circle point } (\cos, \sin). The Unit Circle Projection (Pythagorean Identity) \text{For any point } (x,y) \text{ on the unit circle: } x^2 + y^2 = 1^2. \\ \text{Substituting the trig coordinates: } \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1. \\ \text{This is the fundamental constraint of the trigonometric world.} The Similarity Necessity \text{If triangles } T_1, T_2 \text{ share angle } \theta, \text{ they share ALL angles (A-A similarity).} \\ \text{Side ratios are fixed by similarity scale factors. Therefore, any two students solving the same trig problem will find the SAME numerical ratio.} All Six Ratios — One Draggable Triangle The ratio is the number. The triangle size is irrelevant. Trigonometric Ratios Sine & Cosine of Common Angles All Six Trig Functions on the Unit Circle Sin and cos are coordinates. Tan is a segment on the tangent line. Sec is the distance to the tangent point. Finding all six trig ratios from one side ratio \text{If } \sin\theta = \frac{3}{5} \text{ and } \theta \text{ is acute, find all six trig ratios.} One trig ratio in a right triangle determines all six. Draw the triangle, find the missing side, read off the ratios. \text{opp} = 3, \text{ hyp} = 5 \Rightarrow \text{adj} = \sqrt{25-9} = 4 Draw the triangle: opposite = 3, hypotenuse = 5. Pythagorean theorem gives the adjacent side. (Recognise 3-4-5!) \sin = \frac{3}{5}, \; \cos = \frac{4}{5}, \; \tan = \frac{3}{4} The three primary ratios. \csc = \frac{5}{3}, \; \sec = \frac{5}{4}, \; \cot = \frac{4}{3} The three reciprocals — flip each primary ratio. Exact values from the unit circle for angles beyond 90° \text{Find the exact value of } \sin(150°), \cos(225°), \tan(300°). Reference angle method: (1) find which quadrant, (2) find the reference angle (acute angle to the x-axis), (3) apply the ASTC sign rule. \sin(150°) = \sin(180°-30°) = \sin(30°) = \frac{1}{2} QII: sin is positive. Reference angle is $180°-150°=30°$. Use the known value. \cos(225°) = -\cos(45°) = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} QIII: cos is negative. Reference angle is $225°-180°=45°$. \tan(300°) = -\tan(60°) = -\sqrt{3} QIV: tan is negative. Reference angle is $360°-300°=60°$. Reciprocal Reconstruction: Working Backwards \text{If } \sec\theta = \sqrt{5} \text{ and } \sin\theta < 0, \text{ find all six trig ratios.} A single reciprocal ratio locks in the entire unit circle possibility. Sign analysis is the final filter. \cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, \quad \theta \in QIV Step 1: Reciprocal of secant is cosine. Since sec is positive and sin is negative, we must be in Quadrant IV. \text{adj} = 1, \text{ hyp} = \sqrt{5} \implies \text{opp} = -\sqrt{(\sqrt{5})^2 - 1^2} = -2 Step 2: Use Pythagoras to find the opposite side. It MUST be negative because of QIV. \sin\theta = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}, \quad \tan\theta = -2, \quad \cot\theta = -\frac{1}{2}, \quad \csc\theta = -\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2} Step 3: Read off all remaining ratios from the side lengths. The Complement Equation: Symmetry in Action \text{Solve for } x: \sin(20^\circ) = \cos(x). Co-functions are identical once you cross the 45° boundary of the complement. \cos(x) = \sin(90^\circ - x) Step 1: Use the co-function identity. \sin(20^\circ) = \sin(90^\circ - x) \implies 20 = 90 - x Step 2: Equate the arguments. x = 70^\circ Step 3: Solve for x. \text{If } \tan\theta = -\frac{5}{12} \text{ and } \theta \text{ is in QIV, find } \sin\theta \text{ and } \cos\theta. $\tan = $ opp/adj. In QIV, sin is negative and cos is positive. \sin\theta = -5/13, \; \cos\theta = 12/13 \text{opp} = 5, \text{ adj} = 12 \Rightarrow \text{hyp} = \sqrt{25+144} = 13 In QIV: opposite is $-5$ (below x-axis), adjacent is $+12$. Hypotenuse is always positive. \sin\theta = -\frac{5}{13}, \quad \cos\theta = \frac{12}{13} QIV: sin negative, cos positive. Verify: $(-5/13)/(12/13) = -5/12 = \tan\theta$ ✓ \text{Prove that } \tan\theta + \cot\theta = \sec\theta \csc\theta. Write everything in terms of sin and cos, then combine fractions. \tan\theta + \cot\theta = \sec\theta\csc\theta \tan\theta + \cot\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} + \frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} Convert to sin and cos. = \frac{\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \frac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} Common denominator, then Pythagorean identity. = \frac{1}{\sin\theta} \cdot \frac{1}{\cos\theta} = \csc\theta \cdot \sec\theta \qquad \blacksquare Split and recognise the reciprocal definitions. \text{Start with the fundamental identity } \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1. \text{ Derive the identity relating cotangent and cosecant.} Divide the entire identity by $\sin^2\theta$. 1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta \frac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} + \frac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} = \frac{1}{\sin^2\theta} Step 1: Perform the same algebraic operation (division) on every term. 1 + \left(\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\right)^2 Step 2: Group the squared terms. 1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta \qquad \blacksquare Step 3: Recognition. The ratio of cos-to-sin is cotangent; the reciprocal of sin is cosecant. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step
