documents.assignment: Identifying features of a trig graph from its equation \text{For } y = 3\sec(2x): \text{ find the period, amplitude (if any), asymptotes, and range.}   For reciprocal trig functions: period from the inner function, asymptotes from denominator zeros, range stretched by the amplitude factor. \sec(2x) = 1/\cos(2x) \Rightarrow \text{period of } \cos(2x) = \frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi \Rightarrow \text{period of } \sec(2x) = \pi Secant inherits the period of cosine. The coefficient 2 halves the period. \text{Amplitude: undefined (sec is unbounded). Vertical stretch: 3.} Amplitude is only defined for bounded functions like sin and cos. For sec, the 3 is a vertical stretch factor. \text{VAs: } \cos(2x) = 0 \Rightarrow 2x = \frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi \Rightarrow x = \frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{k\pi}{2} Find where the denominator is zero. \text{Range: } (-\infty, -3] \cup [3, \infty) The stretch factor 3 scales the range: $|\sec| \geq 1$ becomes $|3\sec| \geq 3$. Matching equations to graphs \text{A trig graph has: period } \pi/2, \text{ asymptotes at } x = \pi/4 + k\pi/2, \text{ passes through origin. Which function?}   Work backwards from features: period determines $B$, asymptote positions identify the function family, key points distinguish between candidates. \text{Asymptotes at } x = \pi/4 + k\pi/2 \Rightarrow \cos(Bx) = 0 \Rightarrow \text{tangent or secant} Asymptotes with this structure come from where cosine is zero. \text{Passes through origin} \Rightarrow \text{tangent (not secant, which never passes through origin)} Secant has range $\leq -1$ or $\geq 1$, so it cannot pass through $(0,0)$. \text{Period } \pi/2 = \pi/B \Rightarrow B = 2 \Rightarrow y = \tan(2x) The period of tangent is $\pi/B$. Solve for $B$. The Multi-Stage Wave: Total Transformation \text{Sketch one period of } y = -2\sin(2x - \pi/2) + 1.   Combine the "Four Pillars": Amplitude, Period, Phase, and Vertical Shift. Map the five key points starting from the shifted origin. A = |-2| = 2, \quad \text{Reflected over x-axis} Step 1: Amplitude is 2. The negative sign means it starts by going DOWN. T = \frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi Step 2: Period is pi. 2x - \pi/2 = 0 \implies x = \pi/4 Step 3: Phase shift is pi/4 to the right. D = 1 Step 4: Vertical shift is up 1. The midline is y=1. Signal Reconnaissance: Equation from Two Peaks \text{Find the cosine equation for a wave with a peak at } (1, 10) \text{ and the next peak at } (5, 10), \text{ with a minimum valley at } y = 2.   Every physical signal can be reconstructed by identifying its boundary box (max/min) and its temporal cycle (period). v = \frac{10+2}{2} = 6, \quad A = 10-6 = 4 Step 1: Find the midline and amplitude. Midline is the average of max/min; amplitude is the distance from max to midline. T = 5 - 1 = 4 \implies \frac{2\pi}{B} = 4 \implies B = \frac{\pi}{2} Step 2: Period is the horizontal peak-to-peak distance. x = 1 \implies y = A\cos(B(x-C)) + D Step 3: Since the maximum is at x=1, the phase shift is 1 to the right. y = 4\cos(\frac{\pi}{2}(x-1)) + 6 Step 4: Assemble the pieces.  \text{Sketch one full period of } y = -2\csc(x/2) \text{ and state its domain, range, and period.} Find where $\sin(x/2) = 0$ for the asymptotes, then sketch $y = -2\sin(x/2)$ as a guide curve. \text{Period } 4\pi. \text{ Domain: } x \neq 2k\pi. \text{ Range: } (-\infty,-2]\cup[2,\infty).  \text{Period of } \sin(x/2) = \frac{2\pi}{1/2} = 4\pi \Rightarrow \text{period of csc} = 4\pi The $1/2$ stretches the period to $4\pi$. \text{Asymptotes: } \sin(x/2) = 0 \Rightarrow x/2 = k\pi \Rightarrow x = 2k\pi At $x = 0, \pm 2\pi, \pm 4\pi, \ldots$ \text{Range: } (-\infty,-2]\cup[2,\infty) $-2\csc$ means we multiply by $-2$: the graph flips AND stretches. Arcs that normally go up now go down and vice versa.  \text{Find the horizontal shift } C \text{ such that } \sin(x + C) = \cos(x) \text{ for all } x. \text{ Verify your result by sketching the relation.} The cosine wave is just the sine wave shifted so its peak appears where the sine wave is at zero. C = \pi/2  \sin(x + \pi/2) = \sin(x) \cos(\pi/2) + \cos(x) \sin(\pi/2) Step 1: Use the sum identity. $\cos(90^\circ)=0$ and $\sin(90^\circ)=1$. 0 + \cos(x) \cdot 1 = \cos(x) Step 2: Simplify. This reveals the identity. C = \pi/2 \qquad \blacksquare Step 3: The cosine function is simply a sine function that has been "phase-advanced" by 90 degrees.

Tangent appears in slope calculations and optics (angle of refraction). Secant appears in navigation and in calculus integrals. Knowing these graphs deeply — not just their shapes but exactly why each feature is where it is — makes reading physical phenomena from equations automatic. Linguistic Learner: The Language of Oscillation \text{The word "Sinusoidal" comes from "Sinus" (fold/pocket), but in physics, we call it a "Wave."} \\ \text{The "Period" is the time it takes to complete one full "Trip" around the circle. It is the heartbeat of the function.} Logical Learner: The Periodic Signature \text{Rotation is the only motion that is infinite yet bounded.} \\ \text{Because you cannot go farther "Up" than one radius, the graph MUST turn back. This creates the local maxima and minima that define the wave's intensity.} Physical Learner: The Harmonic Pendulum \text{Every vibrating thing—a bridge in the wind, a guitar string, a light wave—follows a sine graph.} \\ \text{Even your own heart rate is a sequence of non-sinusoidal periodic waves. Why does the tangent graph have vertical asymptotes at $\pi/2$, $3\pi/2$, $5\pi/2$... but the sine graph never has any? The answer is in the definition: $	an x = \sin x / \cos x$, and the denominator hits zero exactly at those points. Sine and cosine graphs model every oscillation in physics: sound waves, light waves, AC current, spring motion. Tangent appears in slope calculations and optics (angle of refraction). Secant appears in navigation and in calculus integrals. Knowing these graphs deeply — not just their shapes but exactly why each feature is where it is — makes reading physical phenomena from equations automatic. Sine and cosine are the foundation. Their graphs are identical in shape — cosine is just sine shifted left by $\pi/2$. Both oscillate between $-1$ and $+1$, completing one full cycle every $2\pi$. The sine graph starts at $(0,0)$; the cosine graph starts at $(0,1)$. Everything else about them follows directly from the unit circle. Tangent and cotangent have a completely different character. They are not bounded — they shoot to $\pm\infty$ at their asymptotes. Tangent has period $\pi$ (not $2\pi$), because $	an(x+\pi) = 	an x$ — the sine and cosine both flip sign, and the negatives cancel. Tangent is zero where sine is zero and undefined where cosine is zero. Secant and cosecant are the reciprocals of cosine and sine. Wherever cosine is 1, secant is 1; wherever cosine approaches 0, secant shoots to infinity. The secant graph looks like a series of upward and downward parabola-like arcs, never crossing the band $(-1, 1)$ — because $|\sec x| = 1/|\cos x| \geq 1$ always. **The Circle Unrolled**: Visualize a point spinning around the unit circle at a constant speed. If you track its vertical height over "time" (the angle), you trace out the sine curve. If you track its horizontal position, you trace out the cosine curve. A "wave" is just a circular rotation laid out flat. **The Periodic Signature**: Nature repeats. Because a circle returns to its starting point every $2\pi$, every trigonometric relationship MUST restart its story at that same interval. This is the "Periodic Signature"—the mathematical fingerprint of everything that oscillates. The domain of each trig function excludes the points where it is undefined. $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are defined everywhere. $	an x$ and $\sec x$ are undefined where $\cos x = 0$: $x 
eq \pi/2 + k\pi$. $\cot x$ and $\csc x$ are undefined where $\sin x = 0$: $x 
eq k\pi$. The five key points of one cycle of $y = \sin x$ on $[0, 2\pi]$ are: $(0,0)$, $(\pi/2, 1)$, $(\pi, 0)$, $(3\pi/2, -1)$, $(2\pi, 0)$. For $y = \cos x$: $(0,1)$, $(\pi/2, 0)$, $(\pi, -1)$, $(3\pi/2, 0)$, $(2\pi, 1)$. Memorise these — they anchor every graph. The tangent graph on $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$ passes through $(-\pi/4, -1)$, $(0, 0)$, $(\pi/4, 1)$ and increases without bound at both ends. Cotangent is the reflection: it passes through $(\pi/4, 1)$, $(\pi/2, 0)$, $(3\pi/4, -1)$ and has asymptotes at $x = 0$ and $x = \pi$. documents.assignment: Evaluating inverse trig exactly \text{Find: } (a)\; \arcsin\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \quad (b)\; \arctan(-1), \quad (c)\; \arccos 0.   Always check the principal range. The answer must lie in the correct interval for each inverse function. \arcsin\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \tfrac{\pi}{3} $\sin(\pi/3) = \sqrt{3}/2$ and $\pi/3 \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ — it is in the principal range. \arctan(-1) = -\tfrac{\pi}{4} $\tan(-\pi/4) = -1$ and $-\pi/4 \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)$. The negative angle is correct — arctan output is negative for negative inputs. \arccos 0 = \tfrac{\pi}{2} $\cos(\pi/2) = 0$ and $\pi/2 \in [0, \pi]$. Note: $\arcsin 0 = 0$ but $\arccos 0 = \pi/2$ — different principal ranges give different answers. Chain rule with inverse trig \text{Differentiate } f(x) = \arctan(x^2).   Chain rule with inverse trig: apply $1/(1+u^2)$ or $1/\sqrt{1-u^2}$ at the inner function, then multiply by the inner derivative. f'(x) = \frac{1}{1+(x^2)^2} \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(x^2) Chain rule: derivative of arctan is $1/(1+u^2)$ evaluated at the inner function, times the inner derivative. = \frac{1}{1+x^4} \cdot 2x = \frac{2x}{1+x^4} Simplify. Note the denominator is $1+x^4$ not $1+x^2$ — the inner function was $x^2$, so it gets squared again. Inverse trig antiderivative — completing the square first \text{Evaluate } \displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{x^2 - 4x + 8}.   Completing the square converts a general quadratic denominator into the arctan standard form. This is the reverse path from the calculus bridge in the quadratics lesson. x^2 - 4x + 8 = (x-2)^2 + 4 Complete the square on the denominator. This converts it to the arctan standard form $u^2 + a^2$. \int \frac{dx}{(x-2)^2 + 4} Let $u = x-2$, $du = dx$. Then $a^2 = 4$, $a = 2$. = \frac{1}{2}\arctan\frac{x-2}{2} + C Apply $\int \frac{du}{u^2+a^2} = \frac{1}{a}\arctan\frac{u}{a} + C$ with $a=2$. The Nested Triangle: Composition without Angles \text{Evaluate } \cos(\arcsin(4/5)) \text{ without finding the angle.}   Nested trig functions are solved by drawing the representative triangle. You do not need to know the angle to know its other ratios. \theta = \arcsin(4/5) \implies \sin(\theta) = 4/5 Step 1: Let the inner expression represent an angle theta. \text{opp} = 4, \text{ hyp} = 5 \implies \text{adj} = \sqrt{25-16} = 3 Step 2: Draw the triangle. Opposite is 4, Hypotenuse is 5 (a standard 3-4-5 triangle). \cos(\theta) = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}} = 3/5 Step 3: Read the required ratio directly from the geometry. The Arctan Shift: Solving for x \text{Solve for } x: \arctan(5x - 2) = \frac{\pi}{3}.   Equations are "unwrapped" layer-by-layer. To remove an inverse trig function, apply its standard trig counterpart. 5x - 2 = \tan(\frac{\pi}{3}) Step 1: Apply tangent to both sides to "undo" the arctan. 5x - 2 = \sqrt{3} Step 2: Substitute the exact value for tan(60°). x = \frac{2 + \sqrt{3}}{5} Step 3: Solve for x algebraically.  \text{Differentiate } g(x) = x\arcsin x + \sqrt{1-x^2}. documents.content: If $\sin(\pi/6) = 1/2$, then $\sin^{-1}(1/2)$ should be $\pi/6$. But $\sin(5\pi/6) = 1/2$ too — and infinitely many other angles. How does $\sin^{-1}$ give a single answer? Inverse trig functions appear any time you need an angle from a ratio: surveying (finding an angle from measured distances), robotics (computing joint angles from end-effector position), physics (finding launch angles for projectile motion). In calculus, $\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x = \frac{1}{1+x^2}$ is one of the most important antiderivative formulas — it is how integrals like $\int \frac{1}{1+x^2}\,dx$ are solved. The sine function is not one-to-one — it takes the same value at infinitely many angles. $\sin(\pi/6) = \sin(5\pi/6) = \sin(13\pi/6) = \cdots = 1/2$. A function that is not one-to-one has no inverse — there is no way to say "the angle whose sine is $1/2$" because there are infinitely many. The solution is domain restriction: we agree to only use a specific portion of the sine curve — the piece from $-\pi/2$ to $\pi/2$. On that interval, sine is strictly increasing and therefore one-to-one. The inverse of this restricted function is $\arcsin$. The output is always in $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ — the "principal value." No ambiguity. Each inverse trig function has a different restriction, chosen to cover the full output range while keeping the function one-to-one: $\arcsin$ uses $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$, $\arccos$ uses $[0, \pi]$, $\arctan$ uses $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$. These choices are conventions — but they are universal conventions, and every calculator uses them. **The Language of the Arc**: The prefix "Arc-" refers to the arc length on the unit circle. While "Sine" asks for the ratio of a given angle, "Arc-sine" asks for the length of the arc that produces that ratio. It is the language of reverse-engineering rotation. **The Domain Trade**: To gain an inverse function, we must sacrifice the periodic nature of the original. We "Trade" the entire sine wave for a single strictly increasing piece that passes the horizontal line test. This segment becomes the "Reference Standard" for all reverse calculations. The derivatives of the inverse trig functions are algebraic — no trig appears in them. This is surprising until you see how they are derived: using implicit differentiation on $y = \arcsin x$ means differentiating $\sin y = x$, giving $\cos y \cdot y' = 1$, so $y' = 1/\cos y$. Then using the Pythagorean identity $\cos y = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 y} = \sqrt{1 - x^2}$, the final result is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ — no trig at all. The key derivatives to know: $\frac{d}{dx}\arcsin x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$, $\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x = \frac{1}{1+x^2}$. These also give the two most important inverse trig antiderivatives, which appear constantly in calculus. The identity $\arcsin x + \arccos x = \pi/2$ holds for all $x \in [-1,1]$. Geometrically: in a right triangle, the two acute angles sum to $\pi/2$, and if one is $\arcsin x$, the other is $\arccos x$. This means you only really need to remember $\arcsin$ and $\arctan$ — the others follow from complementary angle relationships. This spans } [-1, 1] \text{ continuously.} \\ \text{Cosine outputs are positive in Q1 and negative in Q2. This also spans } [-1, 1] \text{ continuously.} \\ \text{These choices minimize the "distance" from the standard 0-threshold.} Restricting the Domain to Create an Inverse The inverse function is the reflection of the restricted portion — not the whole periodic curve. documents.title: Solving Triangles: Law of Sines, Law of Cosines, and the Ambiguous Case
documents.subtitle: Every triangle can be solved — if you know which law to use and when

documents.assignment: AAS triangle — Law of Sines \text{In } \triangle ABC: A=35°, B=82°, a=9. \text{ Find } b \text{ and } c.   AAS: find the third angle first, then use Law of Sines twice. Always use the most accurate known pair $(a, A)$ as your reference ratio. C = 180° - 35° - 82° = 63° Find the third angle using the triangle angle sum. \frac{b}{\sin 82°} = \frac{9}{\sin 35°} \Rightarrow b = \frac{9\sin 82°}{\sin 35°} \approx \frac{9(0.9903)}{0.5736} \approx 15.53 Law of Sines: set up the ratio using the known side-angle pair $(a, A)$. c = \frac{9\sin 63°}{\sin 35°} \approx \frac{9(0.8910)}{0.5736} \approx 13.98 Same ratio, solve for $c$. SAS triangle — Law of Cosines \text{In } \triangle ABC: a=7, b=10, C=52°. \text{ Find } c, \text{ then complete the triangle.}   SAS: Law of Cosines gives the unknown side, then switch to Law of Sines for angles. Find the smaller angle first to avoid the ambiguous case. c^2 = 7^2 + 10^2 - 2(7)(10)\cos 52° = 49 + 100 - 140(0.6157) \approx 149 - 86.2 = 62.8 Law of Cosines: the included angle C is opposite the unknown side c. c \approx \sqrt{62.8} \approx 7.92 Take the square root. \sin A = \frac{a\sin C}{c} = \frac{7\sin 52°}{7.92} \approx \frac{7(0.7880)}{7.92} \approx 0.696 \Rightarrow A \approx 44.0° Now use Law of Sines for angle A. Since $a < c$, angle $A < C$ — no ambiguous case here. B = 180° - 52° - 44° = 84° Third angle by subtraction. SSA — the ambiguous case \text{In } \triangle ABC: a=8, b=11, A=35°. \text{ How many triangles exist? Solve all cases.}   SSA with two triangles: solve for both possible angles B, check that each gives a positive C, then complete each triangle separately. documents.content: Given two sides of a triangle and an angle not between them (SSA), you might expect one answer. But you can get zero, one, or two valid triangles from the same information. Why — and how do you tell which case you're in? Surveyors use the Law of Sines to compute distances they cannot measure directly. GPS systems use the Law of Cosines to compute positions from three known signal distances (trilateration). Ship navigation uses triangle solving to determine position from bearings. The ambiguous SSA case is not a mathematical curiosity — it appears whenever you're given a bearing and two distances but don't know which side the target is on. Right triangle trig (SOH-CAH-TOA) only works when there is a right angle. For oblique triangles (no right angle), two laws extend the power of trig: the Law of Sines and the Law of Cosines. The Law of Sines says: in any triangle, the ratio of a side to the sine of its opposite angle is constant. $a/\sin A = b/\sin B = c/\sin C$. This ratio is actually the diameter of the circumscribed circle. Use it when you know two angles and one side (AAS or ASA), or two sides and a non-included angle (SSA — but beware the ambiguous case). The Law of Cosines generalises the Pythagorean theorem to non-right triangles. $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$. When $C = 90°$, $\cos C = 0$ and it reduces to $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ exactly. Use it when you know two sides and the included angle (SAS), or all three sides (SSS). **The Language of the Oblique**: "Oblique" means slant. While right triangles are the "Special Forces" of geometry, oblique triangles are the everyday reality. Solving them is the process of forced symmetry—breaking a slanted world into right-angled components to find the hidden truths of length and angle. **Degrees of Freedom**: A triangle is "Locked" when its shape cannot change without breaking a side. In geometry, this requires 3 pieces of independent information. Two angles and a side lock the scale; three sides lock the rigidity. Without these, the triangle has a "Degree of Freedom" to wobble or collapse. The ambiguous case (SSA) arises because the sine function is not one-to-one: $\sin\theta = \sin(180°-\theta)$. If you compute $\sin B$ from the Law of Sines and get a value in $(0,1)$, there are two angles in $[0°, 180°]$ with that sine value — $B$ and $180°-B$. Both might produce a valid triangle, only one might, or neither might (if the computed sine exceeds 1). The ambiguous case conditions: given sides $a$, $b$ and angle $A$ (opposite to $a$): if $A$ is obtuse, there is either 0 or 1 triangle. If $A$ is acute, compare $a$ to the height $h = b\sin A$: if $a < h$ there are 0 triangles, if $a = h$ there is exactly 1 (right triangle), if $h < a < b$ there are 2 triangles, if $a \geq b$ there is 1 triangle. The area of any triangle can be computed from two sides and the included angle: $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$. This is because the height of the triangle with base $a$ is $b\sin C$. Combined with Heron's formula for SSS triangles, you can always find the area once the triangle is solved. documents.title: Trig Identities: Where They Come From
documents.subtitle: From the unit circle to the identities you actually use in calculus
documents.tags: trigonometry identities unit circle pythagorean identity angle addition
documents.assignment: Evaluating $\sin(75°)$ exactly using angle addition \text{Find the exact value of } \sin(75°).   Angle addition lets you find exact trig values for any angle that splits into 30°, 45°, or 60° pieces. \sin(75°) = \sin(45° + 30°) Split into angles whose exact values we know. = \sin 45°\cos 30° + \cos 45°\sin 30° Apply the angle addition formula for sin. = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} Substitute exact values from the unit circle. = \frac{\sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2}}{4} Combine fractions. This is the exact answer — no calculator needed. Power Reduction — the setup for $\int \sin^2 x\, dx$ \text{Rewrite } \sin^2 x \text{ so it can be integrated.}   Power reduction is the only way to integrate even powers of sin and cos. It converts $\sin^2$ into a $\cos 2x$ term, which integrates cleanly. \cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x Start from the double angle formula. Choose the form that has $\sin^2 x$ in it. 2\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos 2x Rearrange to isolate $\sin^2 x$. \sin^2 x = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2} Now the right side has no powers — it integrates directly term by term. \int \sin^2 x\, dx = \int \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}\, dx = \frac{x}{2} - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + C Integrate. Without power reduction this integral has no direct antiderivative. Why $\sin^2 x$ averages to $\frac{1}{2}$ The power reduction rewrite shows that $\sin^2 x$ oscillates symmetrically around $\frac{1}{2}$ — its area over a full period is exactly $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Choosing the right Pythagorean form under pressure \text{Simplify } \frac{\sin^2 x}{1 - \cos x}.   When you see $1 \pm \cos x$ or $1 \pm \sin x$ in a denominator, your first instinct should be the Pythagorean identity — it almost always creates a factorable numerator. \sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x Rewrite numerator using the Pythagorean identity. Key move: recognize $1 - \cos^2 x$ factors. = \frac{(1 - \cos x)(1 + \cos x)}{1 - \cos x} Factor as difference of squares: $a^2 - b^2 = (a-b)(a+b)$. = 1 + \cos x \qquad (x \neq 0, 2\pi, \ldots) Cancel the $(1 - \cos x)$ factor. Valid wherever the denominator is nonzero. The Rational Strategy: Complex Verification \text{Verify: } \frac{\sin \theta}{1+\cos \theta} + \frac{1+\cos \theta}{\sin \theta} = 2\csc \theta.   Common denominators and Pythagorean recognition are the "Master Keys" for complex rational identities. \frac{\sin^2 \theta + (1+\cos \theta)^2}{\sin \theta(1+\cos \theta)} Step 1: Find a common denominator. \frac{\sin^2 \theta + 1 + 2\cos \theta + \cos^2 \theta}{\dots} Step 2: Expand the squared binomial. \frac{2 + 2\cos \theta}{\sin \theta(1+\cos \theta)} Step 3: Recognize the Pythagorean identity $\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta = 1$. \frac{2(1+\cos \theta)}{\sin \theta(1+\cos \theta)} = \frac{2}{\sin \theta} = 2\csc \theta \qquad \blacksquare Step 4: Factor out 2 and cancel the common term. Triple Angle Expansion: Predicting the Future \text{Derive an expression for } \sin 3x \text{ in terms of } \sin x.   Higher harmonics can be systematically decomposed by nesting addition formulas. \sin(2x + x) = \sin 2x\cos x + \cos 2x\sin x Step 1: Treat 3x as 2x + x. (2\sin x\cos x)\cos x + (1 - 2\sin^2 x)\sin x Step 2: Use double angle identities for sin and cos. 2\sin x(1 - \sin^2 x) + \sin x - 2\sin^3 x Step 3: Convert all terms to sine using the Pythagorean identity. 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x \qquad \blacksquare Step 4: Distribute and combine like terms.  \text{Prove: } \tan^2 x + 1 = \sec^2 x Start from $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$ and divide every term by $\cos^2 x$. \tan^2 x + 1 = \sec^2 x  \frac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x} + \frac{\cos^2 x}{\cos^2 x} = \frac{1}{\cos^2 x} Divide the Pythagorean identity through by $\cos^2 x$. \tan^2 x + 1 = \sec^2 x \qquad \blacksquare By definition $\sin/\cos = \tan$ and $1/\cos = \sec$. This identity is crucial for integrals involving $\sqrt{1 + x^2}$.  \text{Derive } \sin^2\frac{x}{2} = \frac{1 - \cos x}{2} \text{ from the double angle formula.} Use $\cos 2A = 1 - 2\sin^2 A$ and substitute $A = x/2$. \sin^2\tfrac{x}{2} = \tfrac{1 - \cos x}{2}  \cos 2A = 1 - 2\sin^2 A Start from the double angle formula (the $\sin^2$ form). \text{Let } A = \frac{x}{2}: \quad \cos x = 1 - 2\sin^2\frac{x}{2} Substitute $A = x/2$ so $2A = x$. \sin^2\frac{x}{2} = \frac{1 - \cos x}{2} \qquad \blacksquare Rearrange. This is the half-angle identity — useful for integrating $\sin^2(x/2)$ and appears in Fourier series.  \text{Combine the addition and subtraction formulas to prove: } \sin A\cos B = \frac{1}{2}\left[\sin(A+B) + \sin(A-B)\right]. Write out the full expansion for both sine formulas and add them together. \sin A\cos B = \frac{1}{2}[\sin(A+B) + \sin(A-B)]  \sin(A+B) = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B Step 1: Write the addition formula. \sin(A-B) = \sin A\cos B - \cos A\sin B Step 2: Write the subtraction formula. \sin(A+B) + \sin(A-B) = 2\sin A\cos B Step 3: Combine. Notice the matched terms add up, while the opposite terms cancel out exactly. \sin A\cos B = \frac{1}{2}\left[\sin(A+B) + \sin(A-B)\right] \qquad \blacksquare Step 4: Algebraic isolation for the product.
documents.proofs: We can prove $\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta$ using only the distance formula and the unit circle definition. All other angle addition formulas follow from this one.

Signal processing, AC circuit analysis, and wave mechanics all reduce to identity manipulation. documents.content: Why does $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$ always? And how does knowing that save you in a calculus problem? Trig identities are not facts to memorize — they are tools. In calculus, the choice of which identity to apply transforms an impossible integral into a trivial one. Signal processing, AC circuit analysis, and wave mechanics all reduce to identity manipulation. Every trig identity is a geometric fact in disguise. The unit circle — radius 1, centered at the origin — is the source of all of them. A point on the unit circle at angle $\theta$ has coordinates $(\cos\theta,\, \sin\theta)$ by definition. Because the circle has radius 1, the Pythagorean theorem applied to that point gives $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$ immediately. This is not a coincidence — it IS the Pythagorean theorem, just stated for a circle. The other identities flow from the same picture. The angle addition formulas come from rotating a point and reading off its new coordinates. The double angle formulas are just the angle addition formulas applied to $\theta + \theta$. Nothing is arbitrary. **The Language of Sameness**: An identity is a "Mathematical Synonym." Unlike an equation (which you solve for x), an identity is a statement that two expressions are identical for ALL x. It is the art of re-reading the same geometric reality in a different algebraic dialect. **The Area Puzzle**: Imagine a large rectangle with a diagonal. If you tilt the rectangle by an angle, its vertical height changes. The Sine Addition formula is the geometric account of how the "Components" of that tilt add up to the final height. It is a puzzle of rotational assembly. The Pythagorean identity $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ has two children you derive by dividing both sides. These are the identities that appear in calculus integrals involving $\tan$ and $\sec$. The angle addition formulas are the workhorses. Every other compound identity derives from them. You should be able to re-derive the double angle formula in seconds by setting $\beta = \alpha$. Power reduction identities — expressing $\sin^2 x$ and $\cos^2 x$ as single-angle terms — are the key to integrating even powers of trig functions. If you see $\int \sin^2 x\, dx$ in calculus, power reduction is the move. We can prove $\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta$ using only the distance formula and the unit circle definition. All other angle addition formulas follow from this one. The single identity that generates all others \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1 Two more Pythagorean identities — divide, don't memorize \text{Divide by } \cos^2\theta: \tan^2\theta + 1 = \sec^2\theta \qquad \text{Divide by } \sin^2\theta: 1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta How to see the angle addition formula geometrically \sin(\alpha+\beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta The identity family tree \text{Pythagorean} \xrightarrow{\theta+\theta} \text{Double Angle} \xrightarrow{\div 2} \text{Half Angle} \xrightarrow{\text{rearrange}} \text{Power Reduction} Linguistic Learner: The Language of Sameness \text{"Identity" comes from the Latin "Idem" (The Same).} \\ \text{Think of identities as "Aliases." In identity proofs, the goal is to reveal that the masked stranger on the left is actually the familiar friend on the right.} Logical Learner: Algebraic Morphing \text{Identity proofs are "Non-Destructive."} \\ \text{You are not "Solving"—you are "Simplifying" and "Mapping." Every step is a logical equivalence. If } A = B \text{ and } B = C \text{, then } A = C \text{ is the engine of the entire deep dive.} Physical Learner: Rotational Synchrony \text{Double and Triple angle formulas describe "Harmonics."} \\ \text{In acoustics or power electronics, } \sin 2\theta \text{ is the first harmonic—a wave that spins twice as fast. Identities allow us to mix and separate these signals in the physical world.} Visual Learner: The Area Puzzle \text{Visualize tiling a rectangle with smaller blocks.} \\ \text{The Sine Addition formula } \sin(A+B) \text{ is the area-equivalent of placing two rotations together in space. The resulting total height is the sum of the rotated components.} Angle Addition Formulas \sin(A \pm B) = \sin A\cos B \pm \cos A\sin B \qquad \cos(A \pm B) = \cos A\cos B \mp \sin A\sin B Double Angle Formulas (set $B = A$ above) \sin 2A = 2\sin A\cos A \qquad \cos 2A = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A = 1 - 2\sin^2 A = 2\cos^2 A - 1 Power Reduction (solve double angle for $\sin^2$ and $\cos^2$) \sin^2 A = \frac{1 - \cos 2A}{2} \qquad \cos^2 A = \frac{1 + \cos 2A}{2} The most common calculus mistake with $\cos 2A$ \cos 2A \text{ has THREE equivalent forms. Pick the one that eliminates the variable you want.} \\ \text{Seeing } \sin^2? \text{ Use } 1 - 2\sin^2 A. \quad \text{Seeing } \cos^2? \text{ Use } 2\cos^2 A - 1. The Tangent Construction \tan(A+B) = \frac{\tan A + \tan B}{1 - \tan A\tan B}. \\ \text{This is derived by dividing } \frac{\sin(A+B)}{\cos(A+B)} \text{ and then dividing all terms by } \cos A\cos B. The Energy of the Wave \text{In physics, Intensity (Power) is proportional to } \sin^2(t). \\ \text{Power reduction reveals } (1 - \cos 2t)/2 \text{, which proves that the power of an oscillating wave is itself a wave of double the frequency, centered around an average value of 1/2.} Unit Circle — Identities as Geometry Every trig value is a length on or inside the unit circle. Intro to Trig Identities & Proofs Pythagorean Trig Identities Symmetry, Conjugates & Reflections Sum & Difference Identities Double & Half Angle Identities Double Angle — Geometric Derivation The double angle formula is the angle addition formula applied to itself. Proof: x² + y² = r²  →  dy/dx = −x/y See what happens when calculus meets the Pythagorean identity: implicit differentiation of x² + y² = r². Evaluating $\sin(75°)$ exactly using angle addition \text{Find the exact value of } \sin(75°). Angle addition lets you find exact trig values for any angle that splits into 30°, 45°, or 60° pieces. \sin(75°) = \sin(45° + 30°) Split into angles whose exact values we know. = \sin 45°\cos 30° + \cos 45°\sin 30° Apply the angle addition formula for sin. = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} Substitute exact values from the unit circle. = \frac{\sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2}}{4} Combine fractions. This is the exact answer — no calculator needed. Power Reduction — the setup for $\int \sin^2 x\, dx$ \text{Rewrite } \sin^2 x \text{ so it can be integrated.} Power reduction is the only way to integrate even powers of sin and cos. It converts $\sin^2$ into a $\cos 2x$ term, which integrates cleanly. \cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x Start from the double angle formula. Choose the form that has $\sin^2 x$ in it. 2\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos 2x Rearrange to isolate $\sin^2 x$. \sin^2 x = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2} Now the right side has no powers — it integrates directly term by term. \int \sin^2 x\, dx = \int \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}\, dx = \frac{x}{2} - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + C Integrate. Without power reduction this integral has no direct antiderivative. Why $\sin^2 x$ averages to $\frac{1}{2}$ The power reduction rewrite shows that $\sin^2 x$ oscillates symmetrically around $\frac{1}{2}$ — its area over a full period is exactly $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Choosing the right Pythagorean form under pressure \text{Simplify } \frac{\sin^2 x}{1 - \cos x}. When you see $1 \pm \cos x$ or $1 \pm \sin x$ in a denominator, your first instinct should be the Pythagorean identity — it almost always creates a factorable numerator. \sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x Rewrite numerator using the Pythagorean identity. Key move: recognize $1 - \cos^2 x$ factors. = \frac{(1 - \cos x)(1 + \cos x)}{1 - \cos x} Factor as difference of squares: $a^2 - b^2 = (a-b)(a+b)$. = 1 + \cos x \qquad (x \neq 0, 2\pi, \ldots) Cancel the $(1 - \cos x)$ factor. Valid wherever the denominator is nonzero. The Rational Strategy: Complex Verification \text{Verify: } \frac{\sin \theta}{1+\cos \theta} + \frac{1+\cos \theta}{\sin \theta} = 2\csc \theta. Common denominators and Pythagorean recognition are the "Master Keys" for complex rational identities. \frac{\sin^2 \theta + (1+\cos \theta)^2}{\sin \theta(1+\cos \theta)} Step 1: Find a common denominator. \frac{\sin^2 \theta + 1 + 2\cos \theta + \cos^2 \theta}{\dots} Step 2: Expand the squared binomial. \frac{2 + 2\cos \theta}{\sin \theta(1+\cos \theta)} Step 3: Recognize the Pythagorean identity $\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta = 1$. \frac{2(1+\cos \theta)}{\sin \theta(1+\cos \theta)} = \frac{2}{\sin \theta} = 2\csc \theta \qquad \blacksquare Step 4: Factor out 2 and cancel the common term. Triple Angle Expansion: Predicting the Future \text{Derive an expression for } \sin 3x \text{ in terms of } \sin x. Higher harmonics can be systematically decomposed by nesting addition formulas. \sin(2x + x) = \sin 2x\cos x + \cos 2x\sin x Step 1: Treat 3x as 2x + x. (2\sin x\cos x)\cos x + (1 - 2\sin^2 x)\sin x Step 2: Use double angle identities for sin and cos. 2\sin x(1 - \sin^2 x) + \sin x - 2\sin^3 x Step 3: Convert all terms to sine using the Pythagorean identity. 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x \qquad \blacksquare Step 4: Distribute and combine like terms. \text{Prove: } \tan^2 x + 1 = \sec^2 x Start from $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$ and divide every term by $\cos^2 x$. \tan^2 x + 1 = \sec^2 x \frac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x} + \frac{\cos^2 x}{\cos^2 x} = \frac{1}{\cos^2 x} Divide the Pythagorean identity through by $\cos^2 x$. \tan^2 x + 1 = \sec^2 x \qquad \blacksquare By definition $\sin/\cos = \tan$ and $1/\cos = \sec$. This identity is crucial for integrals involving $\sqrt{1 + x^2}$. \text{Derive } \sin^2\frac{x}{2} = \frac{1 - \cos x}{2} \text{ from the double angle formula.} Use $\cos 2A = 1 - 2\sin^2 A$ and substitute $A = x/2$. \sin^2\tfrac{x}{2} = \tfrac{1 - \cos x}{2} \cos 2A = 1 - 2\sin^2 A Start from the double angle formula (the $\sin^2$ form). \text{Let } A = \frac{x}{2}: \quad \cos x = 1 - 2\sin^2\frac{x}{2} Substitute $A = x/2$ so $2A = x$. \sin^2\frac{x}{2} = \frac{1 - \cos x}{2} \qquad \blacksquare Rearrange. This is the half-angle identity — useful for integrating $\sin^2(x/2)$ and appears in Fourier series. \text{Combine the addition and subtraction formulas to prove: } \sin A\cos B = \frac{1}{2}\left[\sin(A+B) + \sin(A-B)\right]. Write out the full expansion for both sine formulas and add them together. \sin A\cos B = \frac{1}{2}[\sin(A+B) + \sin(A-B)] \sin(A+B) = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B Step 1: Write the addition formula. \sin(A-B) = \sin A\cos B - \cos A\sin B Step 2: Write the subtraction formula. \sin(A+B) + \sin(A-B) = 2\sin A\cos B Step 3: Combine. Notice the matched terms add up, while the opposite terms cancel out exactly. \sin A\cos B = \frac{1}{2}\left[\sin(A+B) + \sin(A-B)\right] \qquad \blacksquare Step 4: Algebraic isolation for the product. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step

documents.assignment: Encrypting the Spot: Infinite Names \text{Give four unique names for the polar point } (2, 30^\circ).   A single coordinate in polar is an "Iterative State"—it can be described by infinitely many angle-radius combinations. (2, 30^\circ + 360^\circ) = (2, 390^\circ) Name 1: Add a full rotation. (-2, 30^\circ + 180^\circ) = (-2, 210^\circ) Name 2: Negative radius—look at 210 degrees but step backward 2 units. (2, 30^\circ - 360^\circ) = (2, -330^\circ) Name 3: Standard radius with a negative angle. (-2, 30^\circ - 180^\circ) = (-2, -150^\circ) Name 4: Negative radius with a negative angle. Identifying the Curve: The Displaced Circle \text{Convert } r = 6\cos\theta \text{ to rectangular form and identify the curve.}   This is a circle centered at (3, 0) with radius 3. Simple polar forms often describe shifted circles. r^2 = 6r\cos\theta Step 1: Multiply both sides by r. This creates the r² and r cos coefficients we need. x^2 + y^2 = 6x Step 2: Substitute r² = x² + y² and x = r cos. (x-3)^2 + y^2 = 9 Step 3: Complete the square on the x terms.  \text{The area of a polar sector is } A = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta. \text{ Use this to prove } A = \pi r^2 \text{ for a full circle.} Substitute the total angle of a full circle into the sector formula. \text{Area} = \pi r^2  \theta = 2\pi \text{ radians} Step 1: A full circle is a rotation of 2 pi. A = \frac{1}{2}r^2(2\pi) Step 2: Plug the total rotation into the area ratio. A = \pi r^2 \qquad \blacksquare Step 3: Simplify. The fundamental area of a circle is simply a full-rotation polar sector.

documents.content: If you're at the center of a lake, does it make more sense to say 'Go 3 miles North and 4 miles East' (Rectangular) or 'Look 53 degrees and travel 5 miles' (Polar)? Radar, Sonar, and planetary orbits all use Polar coordinates. Submarines and Air Traffic Controllers track objects by distance and bearing, not by X-Y grids. Master this, and you master the geometry of the sweep. **The Radial Map**: Every point on the plane can be identified by its "Distance from the Center" ($r$) and its "Rotation" ($\theta$). This is the Polar Coordinate system—a method that mirrors natural scanning motion like the turning of a neck or the sweep of a radar beam. **The Infinite Address**: Unlike the unique X-Y grid, every polar point has "Infinite Names." Because you can spin around a circle and land back in the same spot, $(r, \theta)$ is the same as $(r, \theta + 2k\pi)$. You can even have negative radii—which mean "Look this way, but step backwards." Conversion between Polar and Rectangular forms relies on the standard definition of sine and cosine in a right triangle. The distance to the origin is the hypotenuse, and the x and y coordinates are the horizontal and vertical projections. To convert from $(r, \theta)$ to $(x, y)$, used the formulas $x = r\cos\theta$ and $y = r\sin\theta$. To go backwards from $(x, y)$ to $(r, \theta)$, use $r^2 = x^2 + y^2$ and $\tan\theta = y/x$. documents.assignment: Chain Rule with Trig: $\frac{d}{dx}\sin(x^3)$ \text{Differentiate } f(x) = \sin(x^3).   Chain rule with trig: differentiate the trig function (sin→cos, cos→−sin etc.), keep the inner function as the argument, then multiply by the inner derivative. f'(x) = \cos(\underbrace{x^3}_{\text{inner}}) \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(x^3) Chain rule: derivative of outer (sin → cos) evaluated at inner, times derivative of inner. = 3x^2\cos(x^3) Power rule on the inner. Notice the argument of cos stays $x^3$ — never simplify it away. Odd Power Strategy: $\int \sin^3 x\, dx$ \text{Evaluate } \int \sin^3 x\, dx.   Odd power → peel one off, convert the rest with Pythagorean identity, $u$-substitute. Works every time. \int \sin^3 x\,dx = \int \sin^2 x \cdot \sin x\,dx Odd power of sin: factor off one $\sin x$ to pair with $dx$ for the substitution. = \int (1 - \cos^2 x)\sin x\,dx Convert $\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x$. Now let $u = \cos x$, $du = -\sin x\,dx$. = -\int (1 - u^2)\,du = -u + \frac{u^3}{3} + C Substitute. Clean polynomial integral. = -\cos x + \frac{\cos^3 x}{3} + C Back-substitute $u = \cos x$. Trig Sub with $\sqrt{x^2 + 4}$ \text{Evaluate } \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 + 4}}.   Pattern recognition is everything: see which radical form you have, choose the substitution, and the Pythagorean identity does the rest. \sqrt{x^2 + 4} = \sqrt{4 + x^2} \Rightarrow \text{form } \sqrt{a^2 + x^2},\ a=2 \Rightarrow x = 2\tan\theta Pattern: $\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}$ → use $x = a\tan\theta$. The identity $1 + \tan^2 = \sec^2$ will eliminate the radical. dx = 2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta \qquad \sqrt{x^2+4} = \sqrt{4\tan^2\theta + 4} = 2\sec\theta Compute $dx$ and simplify the radical using $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$. \int \frac{2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta}{2\sec\theta} = \int \sec\theta\,d\theta = \ln|\sec\theta + \tan\theta| + C Simplify and integrate. $\int \sec\theta\,d\theta$ is a standard result. = \ln\left|\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{2} + \frac{x}{2}\right| + C = \ln\bigl|\sqrt{x^2+4} + x\bigr| + C Back-substitute: $\tan\theta = x/2$ so $\sec\theta = \sqrt{x^2+4}/2$. Absorb the constant $\ln(1/2)$ into $C$. Implicit Oscillation: Hidden Derivatives \text{Find } dy/dx \text{ for the curve } x^2 + \sin y = xy.   Trig functions in implicit equations behave like any other function, but the chain rule for the dependent variable ($y$) is the engine. 2x + \cos y \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = y + x\frac{dy}{dx} Step 1: Differentiate implicitly. Remember the chain rule for the sin(y) term and product rule for the xy term. \frac{dy}{dx}(\cos y - x) = y - 2x Step 2: Collect all dy/dx terms on one side. \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y-2x}{\cos y - x} \qquad \blacksquare Step 3: Solve for the derivative. The Tracking Problem: Related Rates of Sweep \text{A lighthouse is 2km from a shore. The light rotates at 3 rad/min. Find the beam speed on the shore when it is 1km from the point nearest the lighthouse.}   Polar sweeps translate into linear speeds through the derivative of the tangent function. x = 2\tan\theta \implies \frac{dx}{dt} = 2\sec^2\theta \cdot \frac{d\theta}{dt} Step 1: Set up the geometric relationship. $x$ is the distance on shore, $2$ is the lighthouse distance. x=1 \implies \tan\theta = 1/2 \implies \sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta = 5/4 Step 2: Find the trigonometric state at the moment of interest. \frac{dx}{dt} = 2(5/4) \cdot 3 = 7.5 \text{ km/min} \qquad \blacksquare Step 3: Plug in the rotation rate (3 rad/min) and solve for the beam velocity.  \text{Differentiate } g(x) = \tan^2(3x). This is a chain rule twice — power rule on the outer square, then chain through tan, then chain through 3x. g'(x) = 6\tan(3x)\sec^2(3x)  g(x) = [\tan(3x)]^2 \Rightarrow g'(x) = 2\tan(3x) \cdot \frac{d}{dx}[\tan(3x)] Power rule on the outer square: bring down the 2, reduce the exponent. \frac{d}{dx}[\tan(3x)] = \sec^2(3x) \cdot 3 Chain rule again: derivative of tan is $\sec^2$, times derivative of inner $3x$. g'(x) = 6\tan(3x)\sec^2(3x) Combine. This pattern — trig squared composed with a linear function — appears constantly.  \text{Evaluate } \int \sin^2 x \cos^3 x\, dx. cos has an odd power. Factor one cos off, convert the remaining $\cos^2$ using Pythagorean identity, let $u = \sin x$. \dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3} - \dfrac{\sin^5 x}{5} + C  \int \sin^2 x \cdot \cos^2 x \cdot \cos x\, dx Factor off one $\cos x$ to sit with $dx$. = \int \sin^2 x (1 - \sin^2 x) \cos x\, dx Replace $\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x$. u = \sin x,\quad du = \cos x\,dx \Rightarrow \int u^2(1 - u^2)\,du Let $u = \sin x$. The $\cos x\, dx$ is absorbed as $du$. = \int (u^2 - u^4)\,du = \frac{u^3}{3} - \frac{u^5}{5} + C = \frac{\sin^3 x}{3} - \frac{\sin^5 x}{5} + C Integrate and back-substitute.  \text{Find the second derivative of } f(x) = \sin^2 x. Either use the power chain rule on two layers, or use the power reduction identity FIRST to make the calculation trivial. f''(x) = 2\cos 2x  f(x) = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2} Step 1: Apply the identity. This is the "Master Move" before doing any calculus. f'(x) = \frac{1}{2}(2\sin 2x) = \sin 2x Step 2: Differentiate the linear terms. Derivative of -cos(2x) is +sin(2x)*2. f''(x) = 2\cos 2x \qquad \blacksquare Step 3: Differentiate again. The acceleration of the energy wave is a cosine wave with double frequency.

documents.applications: In signal processing, Fourier transforms decompose any signal into trig components. The integrals that arise are exactly the type covered here. In mechanics, the period of a pendulum involves an elliptic integral that requires trig substitution to approximate. Knowing the pattern lets you see the structure before you compute. documents.content: You see $\int \sqrt{1 - x^2}\, dx$. What do you do first — and why does $x = \sin\theta$ magically work? In signal processing, Fourier transforms decompose any signal into trig components. The integrals that arise are exactly the type covered here. In mechanics, the period of a pendulum involves an elliptic integral that requires trig substitution to approximate. Knowing the pattern lets you see the structure before you compute. Trig shows up in calculus in three distinct situations, each with its own strategy. Recognizing which situation you're in is more than half the work. Situation 1: you're differentiating a trig function (possibly composed with something else). This is chain rule territory. The inner function tells you what to multiply by. Situation 2: you're integrating a power of $\sin$ or $\cos$. The exponent tells you the strategy: odd power → factor one out and use $u$-sub. Even power → power reduction identity first. Situation 3: you see $\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$, $\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}$, or $\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}$ under a radical. This screams trig substitution — the substitution is chosen so the Pythagorean identity eliminates the radical entirely. **The Sine Approximation**: For very small angles, $\sin x$ is indistinguishable from $x$. This logical bridge—the "Linearization" of circular motion—is why physics formulas for pendulums and waves can be simplified into linear equations at the limit. **The Harmonic Slope**: Differentiating a wave reveals its velocity. The slope of a Sine wave is exactly the value of a Cosine wave. When the shadow of a rotating wheel moves fastest (at the origin), the cosine is at its peak. This physical synchrony is the heart of oscillatory calculus. The derivatives of all six trig functions follow from $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$ and the quotient rule. You should be able to derive $\frac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^2 x$ on demand — it takes three lines. For integration strategy with $\sin^m x\cos^n x$: if either exponent is odd, save one copy of that function and convert the rest using $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$, then $u$-substitute. If both are even, power reduce first. The trig substitution table is derived from three Pythagorean identities. You are not memorizing three arbitrary substitutions — you are choosing which Pythagorean identity will eliminate the square root. This is the area under a semicircle — it should equal $\frac{\pi}{4}$ over $[0,1]$. We'll verify that too. Three trig situations — three different moves \text{Differentiating trig} \to \text{chain rule} \qquad \text{Integrating } \sin^n/\cos^n \to \text{parity strategy} \qquad \sqrt{a^2 \pm x^2} \to \text{trig substitution} Why trig substitution works geometrically \sqrt{1 - x^2} \text{ is the height of a point on a unit circle at horizontal position } x. \text{ Setting } x = \sin\theta \text{ makes } \sqrt{1-x^2} = \cos\theta \text{ — a leg of the same right triangle.} Linguistic Learner: The Instantaneous Limit \text{"Limit" comes from the Latin "Limes" (a boundary or threshold).} \\ \text{Trig in calculus is the art of pushing the boundary. "Instantaneous" change is simply the average change over a distance that becomes infinitely small.} Logical Learner: The Sine Approximation \text{Why is } \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1 \text{?} \\ \text{Logic: As the arc shrinks, the vertical height and the arc length become identical.} \\ \text{In the limit, the curve and the straight line are one.} Physical Learner: The Harmonic Slope \text{Visualize a mass on a spring.} \\ \text{The position is a sine wave. The velocity (the derivative) is a cosine wave. The velocity is highest when the position is zero (passing the center), and zero when the position is maxed. Calculus is the language of this trade-off.} Visual Learner: The Squeeze Theorem \text{Imagine a thin slice of pizza (a sector) squashed between two triangles.} \\ \text{One triangle is smaller (height } \sin x\text{), one is larger (height } \tan x\text{). As the slice gets thinner, the area of the three shapes must converge to the same point.} Trig Derivatives (the six you must know cold) \frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x \quad \frac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x \quad \frac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^2 x \\ \frac{d}{dx}\csc x = -\csc x\cot x \quad \frac{d}{dx}\sec x = \sec x\tan x \quad \frac{d}{dx}\cot x = -\csc^2 x Trig Substitution Table — read from the radical \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} \to x = a\sin\theta \quad (\text{uses } 1 - \sin^2 = \cos^2) \\ \sqrt{a^2 + x^2} \to x = a\tan\theta \quad (\text{uses } 1 + \tan^2 = \sec^2) \\ \sqrt{x^2 - a^2} \to x = a\sec\theta \quad (\text{uses } \sec^2 - 1 = \tan^2) Odd-power integration strategy \int \sin^5 x\cos^2 x\,dx: \quad \text{odd power of sin} \Rightarrow \text{factor out } \sin x, \text{ convert } \sin^4 = (1-\cos^2)^2, \text{ let } u = \cos x Don't forget $dx$ when substituting x = a\sin\theta \Rightarrow dx = a\cos\theta\,d\theta. \text{ The } dx \text{ replacement is essential and easy to drop under pressure.} The Unit Threshold \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1. \\ \text{This is the single most important identity in trig calculus. It states that the arc and its sine merge at the limit.} The Domain of Substitution \text{For } x = a\sin\theta \text{, we restrict } \theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]. \\ \text{This restriction ensures the substitution is "One-to-One," allowing us to invert back to arcsin at the end.} Why $x = \sin\theta$ Kills the Radical Drag $x$ along the circle to see how $\sqrt{1 - x^2}$ corresponds to $\cos\theta$. Two Function Machines — Inner and Outer Shrinking Δx — Why Derivatives Multiply Rates Multiplying — Leibniz Notation Integration Strategy Decision Tree The strategy is determined by the structure of the integrand, not the specific numbers. The sin(x³) Proof — Step by Step Practice — 10 Forms of the Chain Rule Chain Rule with Trig: $\frac{d}{dx}\sin(x^3)$ \text{Differentiate } f(x) = \sin(x^3). Chain rule with trig: differentiate the trig function (sin→cos, cos→−sin etc.), keep the inner function as the argument, then multiply by the inner derivative. f'(x) = \cos(\underbrace{x^3}_{\text{inner}}) \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(x^3) Chain rule: derivative of outer (sin → cos) evaluated at inner, times derivative of inner. = 3x^2\cos(x^3) Power rule on the inner. Notice the argument of cos stays $x^3$ — never simplify it away. Odd Power Strategy: $\int \sin^3 x\, dx$ \text{Evaluate } \int \sin^3 x\, dx. Odd power → peel one off, convert the rest with Pythagorean identity, $u$-substitute. Works every time. \int \sin^3 x\,dx = \int \sin^2 x \cdot \sin x\,dx Odd power of sin: factor off one $\sin x$ to pair with $dx$ for the substitution. = \int (1 - \cos^2 x)\sin x\,dx Convert $\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x$. Now let $u = \cos x$, $du = -\sin x\,dx$. = -\int (1 - u^2)\,du = -u + \frac{u^3}{3} + C Substitute. Clean polynomial integral. = -\cos x + \frac{\cos^3 x}{3} + C Back-substitute $u = \cos x$. Trig Sub with $\sqrt{x^2 + 4}$ \text{Evaluate } \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 + 4}}. Pattern recognition is everything: see which radical form you have, choose the substitution, and the Pythagorean identity does the rest. \sqrt{x^2 + 4} = \sqrt{4 + x^2} \Rightarrow \text{form } \sqrt{a^2 + x^2},\ a=2 \Rightarrow x = 2\tan\theta Pattern: $\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}$ → use $x = a\tan\theta$. The identity $1 + \tan^2 = \sec^2$ will eliminate the radical. dx = 2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta \qquad \sqrt{x^2+4} = \sqrt{4\tan^2\theta + 4} = 2\sec\theta Compute $dx$ and simplify the radical using $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$. \int \frac{2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta}{2\sec\theta} = \int \sec\theta\,d\theta = \ln|\sec\theta + \tan\theta| + C Simplify and integrate. $\int \sec\theta\,d\theta$ is a standard result. = \ln\left|\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{2} + \frac{x}{2}\right| + C = \ln\bigl|\sqrt{x^2+4} + x\bigr| + C Back-substitute: $\tan\theta = x/2$ so $\sec\theta = \sqrt{x^2+4}/2$. Absorb the constant $\ln(1/2)$ into $C$. Implicit Oscillation: Hidden Derivatives \text{Find } dy/dx \text{ for the curve } x^2 + \sin y = xy. Trig functions in implicit equations behave like any other function, but the chain rule for the dependent variable ($y$) is the engine. 2x + \cos y \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = y + x\frac{dy}{dx} Step 1: Differentiate implicitly. Remember the chain rule for the sin(y) term and product rule for the xy term. \frac{dy}{dx}(\cos y - x) = y - 2x Step 2: Collect all dy/dx terms on one side. \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y-2x}{\cos y - x} \qquad \blacksquare Step 3: Solve for the derivative. The Tracking Problem: Related Rates of Sweep \text{A lighthouse is 2km from a shore. The light rotates at 3 rad/min. Find the beam speed on the shore when it is 1km from the point nearest the lighthouse.} Polar sweeps translate into linear speeds through the derivative of the tangent function. x = 2\tan\theta \implies \frac{dx}{dt} = 2\sec^2\theta \cdot \frac{d\theta}{dt} Step 1: Set up the geometric relationship. $x$ is the distance on shore, $2$ is the lighthouse distance. x=1 \implies \tan\theta = 1/2 \implies \sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta = 5/4 Step 2: Find the trigonometric state at the moment of interest. \frac{dx}{dt} = 2(5/4) \cdot 3 = 7.5 \text{ km/min} \qquad \blacksquare Step 3: Plug in the rotation rate (3 rad/min) and solve for the beam velocity. \text{Differentiate } g(x) = \tan^2(3x). This is a chain rule twice — power rule on the outer square, then chain through tan, then chain through 3x. g'(x) = 6\tan(3x)\sec^2(3x) g(x) = [\tan(3x)]^2 \Rightarrow g'(x) = 2\tan(3x) \cdot \frac{d}{dx}[\tan(3x)] Power rule on the outer square: bring down the 2, reduce the exponent. \frac{d}{dx}[\tan(3x)] = \sec^2(3x) \cdot 3 Chain rule again: derivative of tan is $\sec^2$, times derivative of inner $3x$. g'(x) = 6\tan(3x)\sec^2(3x) Combine. This pattern — trig squared composed with a linear function — appears constantly. \text{Evaluate } \int \sin^2 x \cos^3 x\, dx. cos has an odd power. Factor one cos off, convert the remaining $\cos^2$ using Pythagorean identity, let $u = \sin x$. \dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3} - \dfrac{\sin^5 x}{5} + C \int \sin^2 x \cdot \cos^2 x \cdot \cos x\, dx Factor off one $\cos x$ to sit with $dx$. = \int \sin^2 x (1 - \sin^2 x) \cos x\, dx Replace $\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x$. u = \sin x,\quad du = \cos x\,dx \Rightarrow \int u^2(1 - u^2)\,du Let $u = \sin x$. The $\cos x\, dx$ is absorbed as $du$. = \int (u^2 - u^4)\,du = \frac{u^3}{3} - \frac{u^5}{5} + C = \frac{\sin^3 x}{3} - \frac{\sin^5 x}{5} + C Integrate and back-substitute. \text{Find the second derivative of } f(x) = \sin^2 x. Either use the power chain rule on two layers, or use the power reduction identity FIRST to make the calculation trivial. f''(x) = 2\cos 2x f(x) = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2} Step 1: Apply the identity. This is the "Master Move" before doing any calculus. f'(x) = \frac{1}{2}(2\sin 2x) = \sin 2x Step 2: Differentiate the linear terms. Derivative of -cos(2x) is +sin(2x)*2. f''(x) = 2\cos 2x \qquad \blacksquare Step 3: Differentiate again. The acceleration of the energy wave is a cosine wave with double frequency. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step instantaneous rate of change slope dy/dx velocity marginal change

documents.title: Logarithms: Why $\ln$ Is Everywhere in Calculus
documents.subtitle: Log laws from geometry, the natural log as an area, and why $e$ is the right base
documents.tags: logarithms natural log ln exponentials log laws integration

documents.assignment: Logarithmic Differentiation — when the exponent has a variable \text{Differentiate } f(x) = x^x.   When the exponent contains the variable, take $\ln$ of both sides first. This converts the exponential into a product and makes differentiation possible. \ln(f(x)) = \ln(x^x) = x\ln x Take $\ln$ of both sides. Use $\ln(a^r) = r\ln a$ to bring the exponent down. Now it's a product, not an exponential — much easier to differentiate. \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} = \ln x + x \cdot \frac{1}{x} = \ln x + 1 Differentiate both sides. Left side uses $\frac{d}{dx}\ln(f) = f'/f$. Right side uses product rule. f'(x) = f(x)(\ln x + 1) = x^x(\ln x + 1) Multiply both sides by $f(x) = x^x$. This technique works for any function where the variable appears in the exponent. Integrating $\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ — recognizing the log form \text{Evaluate } \int \frac{2x}{x^2 + 1}\,dx.   Any time the numerator is (close to) the derivative of the denominator, $\ln$ is the antiderivative. Check for this pattern before trying anything else in rational integrals. \text{Numerator is } 2x = \frac{d}{dx}(x^2 + 1) Check: is the numerator the derivative of the denominator? Yes. This is the $\frac{f'}{f}$ pattern. u = x^2 + 1,\quad du = 2x\,dx Let $u$ equal the denominator. The numerator $2x\,dx$ becomes $du$ exactly. \int \frac{du}{u} = \ln|u| + C = \ln|x^2 + 1| + C = \ln(x^2+1) + C Standard $\int 1/u\,du = \ln|u|$. Since $x^2+1 > 0$ always, we drop the absolute value. Expanding with log laws before differentiating \text{Differentiate } y = \ln\!\left(\frac{x^3\sqrt{x+1}}{(2x-1)^4}\right).   Always expand $\ln$ using log laws before differentiating a product/quotient/power inside a log. It converts one hard problem into several easy ones. y = 3\ln x + \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(x+1) - 4\ln(2x-1) Apply log laws to break apart the single log: product → sum, quotient → difference, power → coefficient. Always do this before differentiating a complex log. y' = \frac{3}{x} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{x+1} - 4 \cdot \frac{2}{2x-1} Differentiate term by term. Each term is a simple $\frac{d}{dx}\ln(u) = u'/u$. y' = \frac{3}{x} + \frac{1}{2(x+1)} - \frac{8}{2x-1} Simplify. Without log expansion, this would have required the quotient rule and product rule on a complex expression. The Natural Descent: Nested Logarithms \text{Differentiate } f(x) = \ln(\ln(\ln x)).   Nested logarithms create a product of inverse terms. This demonstrates the slow growth of logs—their derivatives diminish exponentially. f'(x) = \frac{1}{\ln(\ln x)} \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(\ln(\ln x)) Step 1: Apply the outermost chain rule. Derivative of ln(u) is 1/u. \frac{d}{dx}(\ln(\ln x)) = \frac{1}{\ln x} \cdot \frac{1}{x} Step 2: Chain again through the middle log. f'(x) = \frac{1}{x \ln x \ln(\ln x)} \qquad \blacksquare Step 3: Combine. The derivative cascades down the tower of logs. The Bridge of Base e: Solving Different Bases \text{Solve for x: } 2^x = 3^{x+1}.   Base e acts as the 'Universal Language' for all exponential equations. It allows us to compare different growth rates on a single scale. x \ln 2 = (x+1) \ln 3 Step 1: Take the natural log of both sides. x \ln 2 = x \ln 3 + \ln 3 Step 2: Distribute. x(\ln 2 - \ln 3) = \ln 3 Step 3: Collect x terms. x = \frac{\ln 3}{\ln 2 - \ln 3} \approx -2.71 \qquad \blacksquare Step 4: Isolate x.  \text{Differentiate } f(x) = \ln(\sin x). Chain rule: $\frac{d}{dx}\ln(u) = \frac{u'}{u}$. What is $u$ here? f'(x) = \cot x  f'(x) = \frac{1}{\sin x} \cdot \cos x Chain rule: outer is $\ln$ (derivative $1/u$), inner is $\sin x$ (derivative $\cos x$). = \frac{\cos x}{\sin x} = \cot x Simplify. This result is the antiderivative of $\cot x$: $\int \cot x\,dx = \ln|\sin x| + C$.  \text{Evaluate } \int_1^e \frac{(\ln x)^2}{x}\, dx. Spot the $f'/f$ or let $u = \ln x$. What is $du$? \dfrac{1}{3}  u = \ln x,\quad du = \frac{1}{x}\,dx Let $u = \ln x$. Then $du = (1/x)\,dx$ — which is exactly what appears in the integrand. x=1 \Rightarrow u=0;\quad x=e \Rightarrow u=1 \qquad \int_0^1 u^2\,du Change limits using $u = \ln x$. Clean power integral. \bigl[\tfrac{u^3}{3}\bigr]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3} Evaluate. The original definite integral equals $\frac{1}{3}$.  \text{Solve for x: } \log_x(100) = 2. Apply the Change of Base formula to rewrite the log in terms of natural logs. 10  \frac{\ln 100}{\ln x} = 2 Step 1: Universal Change of Base. \ln 100 = 2 \ln x \implies \ln 10^2 = 2 \ln x Step 2: Recognize 100 as 10 squared. 2 \ln 10 = 2 \ln x \implies \ln 10 = \ln x Step 3: Use the log power rule. x = 10 \qquad \blacksquare Step 4: Solve for x. The base of the logarithm is 10.

documents.applications: The natural log is not just a base-$e$ curiosity. It appears in entropy, information theory, population growth models, RC circuit discharge, radioactive decay, and every integral involving $1/x$ or rational functions. Understanding why $\ln$ is natural — not just that it is — changes how you recognize when to use it.

documents.assignment: Building a sinusoidal model from a description \text{A tide oscillates between 0.5 m and 3.5 m with a period of 12.4 hours. High tide occurs at } t=2 \text{ h. Write a model.}   Systematic model building: amplitude, midline, period, phase shift — in that order. Cosine is natural when you know where the maximum occurs. A = \frac{3.5 - 0.5}{2} = 1.5 \qquad D = \frac{3.5 + 0.5}{2} = 2 Amplitude = half the range. Midline = average of max and min. B = \frac{2\pi}{12.4} \approx 0.507 $B = 2\pi/\text{period}$. h(t) = 1.5\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi}{12.4}(t - 2)\right) + 2 Use cosine — peaks at the phase shift. High tide at $t=2$ means shift right by 2. Check: $h(2) = 1.5 + 2 = 3.5$ ✓ Solving a trig equation using a double angle identity \text{Solve: } \sin 2x = \sin x \text{ on } [0, 2\pi).   When you see a double angle in an equation, apply the identity immediately to get everything in terms of the same angle. Then factor algebraically. 2\sin x\cos x - \sin x = 0 Replace $\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$, move everything to one side. \sin x(2\cos x - 1) = 0 Factor out $\sin x$. \sin x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0, \pi \qquad \cos x = \tfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow x = \tfrac{\pi}{3}, \tfrac{5\pi}{3} Set each factor to zero. Four solutions total in $[0, 2\pi)$. Calculus connection — rate of change of a sinusoidal model \text{For the tide model } h(t) = 1.5\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi}{12.4}(t-2)\right) + 2, \text{ how fast is the tide rising at } t=5 \text{ h?}   The derivative of a sinusoidal model is another sinusoidal model — same period, amplitude scaled by the frequency, phase shifted by $\pi/2$. h'(t) = -1.5 \cdot \frac{2\pi}{12.4}\sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi}{12.4}(t-2)\right) Differentiate: amplitude $\times$ frequency becomes the new amplitude. Cosine → negative sine. h'(5) = -1.5 \cdot \frac{2\pi}{12.4} \cdot \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi}{12.4}(3)\right) \approx -0.507\sin(1.532) \approx -0.507 \times 0.9996 \approx -0.507 Substitute $t=5$. The negative value means the tide is falling at about 0.507 m/h at $t=5$.  \text{Solve } 2\sin^2 x + 3\cos x = 3 \text{ on } [0, 2\pi). Replace $\sin^2 x$ using the Pythagorean identity to get a quadratic in $\cos x$. x = 0,\; \pi/3,\; 5\pi/3  2(1-\cos^2 x) + 3\cos x = 3 Substitute $\sin^2 x = 1-\cos^2 x$. 2\cos^2 x - 3\cos x + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow (2\cos x - 1)(\cos x - 1) = 0 Rearrange and factor the quadratic. \cos x = \tfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow x = \tfrac{\pi}{3}, \tfrac{5\pi}{3} \qquad \cos x = 1 \Rightarrow x = 0 Three solutions: $x = 0, \pi/3, 5\pi/3$.  \text{A particle oscillates with position } s(t) = 3\sin(2t) + 4\cos(2t). \text{ Write this as } A\sin(2t + \phi) \text{ and find the amplitude and phase shift.} Use the identity $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\sin(\theta + \phi)$ where $\tan\phi = b/a$. A = 5, \; \phi = \arctan(4/3) \approx 0.927 \text{ rad}  A = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5 Amplitude from the combining formula. \tan\phi = \frac{4}{3} \Rightarrow \phi = \arctan\frac{4}{3} \approx 0.927 \text{ rad} Phase shift from $\tan\phi = b/a$ where $b=4$, $a=3$. s(t) = 5\sin(2t + 0.927) Combined form. Amplitude 5, phase shift $\approx 53.1°$. The maximum of 5 is larger than either original amplitude (3 or 4) — the two oscillations partially reinforce each other.

documents.assignment: Reading a graph and identifying transformations f(x) = -2 \cdot 3^{x+1} + 4. \text{ Identify all transformations, domain, range, and asymptote.}   The key point $(0,1)$ of $3^x$ maps to: shift $x$ by $-1$ gives $(-1,1)$; stretch/reflect gives $(-1,-2)$; shift up 4 gives $(-1, 2)$. \text{Base function: } g(x) = 3^x \text{ (growth, base 3)} Always start by identifying the parent function. h = -1: \text{ shift left 1} \quad k = 4: \text{ shift up 4} \quad a = -2: \text{ reflect over x-axis, stretch by 2} Read off each parameter from $f(x) = a \cdot b^{x-h} + k$. Note: $x+1 = x-(-1)$ so $h = -1$. \text{Asymptote: } y = k = 4 \qquad \text{Domain: } (-\infty, \infty) The vertical shift moves the asymptote. \text{Range: } (-\infty, 4) \quad \text{because } a = -2 < 0 \text{ (reflected, so approaches 4 from below)} Negative $a$ flips the range. Without the reflection, range would be $(4, \infty)$. Compound interest — finding the amount \$5000 \text{ is invested at 4.5\% annual interest. Find the amount after 10 years (a) compounded monthly, (b) compounded continuously.}   Continuous compounding always gives the maximum possible amount for a given rate. The gap shrinks as rates decrease. (a)\; A = 5000\left(1+\frac{0.045}{12}\right)^{12 \times 10} = 5000(1.00375)^{120} \approx \$7841.10 $n=12$ (monthly), $r=0.045$, $t=10$. (b)\; A = 5000e^{0.045 \times 10} = 5000e^{0.45} \approx 5000(1.5683) \approx \$7841.56 Continuous compounding. Notice: only $\$0.46$ more than monthly — the difference is tiny at moderate rates. Doubling time \text{An investment grows continuously at 6\%. How long to double?}   Doubling time for continuous growth at rate $r$ is always $t = \ln 2 / r$. The Rule of 72 ($\approx 72/r\%$) is a quick mental estimate. 2P = Pe^{0.06t} \Rightarrow 2 = e^{0.06t} Set $A = 2P$ (doubled). Divide both sides by $P$. \ln 2 = 0.06t \Rightarrow t = \frac{\ln 2}{0.06} \approx \frac{0.6931}{0.06} \approx 11.55 \text{ years} Take the natural log of both sides. Rule of 72 approximation: $72/6 = 12$ years — close!  \text{An account compounds quarterly at 5\%. How long until \$3000 grows to \$5000?} Set up the compound interest formula, divide both sides by $P$, then take the logarithm of both sides. t \approx 10.28 \text{ years}  5000 = 3000\left(1 + \frac{0.05}{4}\right)^{4t} \Rightarrow \frac{5}{3} = (1.0125)^{4t} Set up and simplify. \ln\frac{5}{3} = 4t \ln(1.0125) \Rightarrow t = \frac{\ln(5/3)}{4\ln(1.0125)} \approx \frac{0.5108}{4(0.01242)} \approx 10.28 \text{ years} Take ln of both sides, use log power rule, solve for $t$.  \text{Show that if a quantity grows continuously at rate } r\text{, it increases by } (e^r - 1) \times 100\% \text{ per year. What is the effective annual rate for 5\% continuous compounding?} Compare $A = Pe^{r \cdot 1}$ to $A = P(1 + r_{\text{eff}})$ for $t = 1$ year. r_{\text{eff}} = e^r - 1 \approx 5.127\% \text{ for } r=5\%  Pe^r = P(1 + r_{\text{eff}}) \Rightarrow r_{\text{eff}} = e^r - 1 Equate one year of continuous and annual growth. Solve for the effective rate. r = 0.05: \; r_{\text{eff}} = e^{0.05} - 1 \approx 1.05127 - 1 = 0.05127 = 5.127\% The effective annual rate is 5.127% — slightly higher than the stated 5% continuous rate.

A population of bacteria doubles every hour. After 24 hours starting from 1 bacterium, how many are there? The answer — 16,777,216 — is why exponential growth is called explosive. But what makes the function $f(t) = 2^t$ so fundamentally different from $f(t) = t^2$? Exponential functions model anything that grows or decays at a rate proportional to its current size: compound interest, radioactive decay, viral spread, cooling of a hot object, charging of a capacitor. In manufacturing, the learning curve — the observation that production cost drops by a fixed percentage each time cumulative output doubles — is an exponential relationship. Every one of these models uses the same family of functions. **Where you are in the story:** You are coming from Precalc-3 (Trigonometry), where functions were defined by ratios of sides in triangles and wrapped around the unit circle. Now the story shifts to a completely different kind of function — one where the variable lives in the exponent, not the base. That single change transforms the entire shape of the curve and its behavior. In $f(x) = b^x$, the variable $x$ is in the exponent and $b$ is a constant called the base. This is the opposite of power functions like $x^b$ where the variable is the base. The distinction matters enormously: $x^2$ grows like a parabola, but $2^x$ eventually overtakes any polynomial, no matter how high the degree. The base $b$ determines everything about the shape. When $b > 1$, the function grows — each unit increase in $x$ multiplies the output by $b$. This is multiplicative growth, which is why it accelerates so dramatically. When $0 < b < 1$, the function decays — each unit increase in $x$ multiplies the output by a fraction less than 1. Every exponential function $f(x) = b^x$ passes through $(0, 1)$ because $b^0 = 1$ for any valid base. The $x$-axis is a horizontal asymptote: the function approaches but never touches it. For growth functions, as $x 	o -\infty$; for decay functions, as $x 	o +\infty$. **Where this is heading:** Next you will meet $e$ and $\ln$ — where the choice of base $e \approx 2.71828$ turns out to be the one that makes all calculus simplest. You will also meet logarithms: the operation that "undoes" exponentiation, and the key to solving any equation where the unknown is trapped in an exponent. Transformations of exponential functions follow the same master formula as all functions: $f(x) = a \cdot b^{x-h} + k$. Here $a$ is a vertical stretch/reflection, $h$ is a horizontal shift, and $k$ is a vertical shift that also moves the horizontal asymptote from $y=0$ to $y=k$. When $a < 0$, the function reflects over the $x$-axis and the range becomes $(-\infty, k)$. The natural base $e \approx 2.71828$ is the most important base in calculus. It is defined as $e = \lim_{n 	o \infty}\left(1 +  rac{1}{n}ight)^n$, which emerges naturally from compound interest. The function $f(x) = e^x$ is its own derivative — the only function with this property — which is why it dominates in calculus, differential equations, and physics. Compound interest is the direct application of exponential functions to finance. If principal $P$ grows at annual rate $r$, compounded $n$ times per year for $t$ years: $A = P\left(1 +  rac{r}{n}ight)^{nt}$. As $n 	o \infty$ (continuous compounding), this becomes $A = Pe^{rt}$. The difference between monthly and continuous compounding is small but real. documents.assignment: Evaluating $\ln$ Expressions Without a Calculator Evaluate exactly: (a) $\ln(e^5)$, (b) $\ln(1)$, (c) $e^{\ln 7}$, (d) $\ln(e^{-3})$, (e) $\ln\!\left(\dfrac{1}{e^2}\right)$.   Pattern: whenever you see $\ln(e^{\text{something}})$ or $e^{\ln(\text{something})}$, they immediately simplify to "something." Memorize the cancel identities — they are used in virtually every calculus problem involving $e$ or $\ln$. (a)\; \ln(e^5) = 5 Direct: $\ln(e^x) = x$. The logarithm and exponential are inverses — they cancel. (b)\; \ln(1) = \ln(e^0) = 0 $1 = e^0$. Rewrite 1 as $e^0$, then apply $\ln(e^x) = x$. (c)\; e^{\ln 7} = 7 Direct: $e^{\ln x} = x$. The exponential undoes the logarithm. (d)\; \ln(e^{-3}) = -3 $\ln(e^x) = x$ works for negative exponents too. (e)\; \ln\!\left(\tfrac{1}{e^2}\right) = \ln(e^{-2}) = -2 Rewrite $1/e^2 = e^{-2}$ using the negative exponent rule, then cancel. Cancel Identity Visualizer The cancel identities make these evaluations immediate once you see the pattern. Expanding and Condensing $\ln$ Expressions Using Properties (a) Expand $\ln\!\left(\dfrac{x^3 \sqrt{y}}{z^2}\right)$ fully. (b) Condense $3\ln(x) - \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(y) + \ln(5)$ into a single logarithm.   Expansion: work outward from the structure (quotient → product → powers). Condensation: reverse the steps (powers → product/quotient → single log). The order of rules must be reversed. (a)\; \ln\!\left(\frac{x^3 \sqrt{y}}{z^2}\right) = \ln(x^3 \sqrt{y}) - \ln(z^2) Apply the quotient rule first: $\ln(A/B) = \ln(A) - \ln(B)$. = \ln(x^3) + \ln(\sqrt{y}) - \ln(z^2) Apply the product rule: $\ln(AB) = \ln(A) + \ln(B)$. = 3\ln(x) + \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(y) - 2\ln(z) Apply the power rule: $\ln(a^n) = n\ln(a)$. Note $\sqrt{y} = y^{1/2}$ and $\ln(z^2) = 2\ln(z)$. (b)\; 3\ln(x) - \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(y) + \ln(5) Start condensing. Power rule reverses the coefficients into exponents. = \ln(x^3) - \ln(y^{1/2}) + \ln(5) Power rule: $n\ln(a) = \ln(a^n)$. = \ln\!\left(\frac{5x^3}{\sqrt{y}}\right) Product rule adds logs: $\ln(x^3) + \ln(5) = \ln(5x^3)$. Quotient rule subtracts: $- \ln(\sqrt{y}) = \ln(1/\sqrt{y})$. Combined: single logarithm. Solving Exponential Equations with $\ln$ Solve exactly: (a) $e^{2x} = 7$, (b) $3e^{x-1} + 5 = 20$, (c) $e^{2x} - 5e^x + 6 = 0$.   Strategy: (1) Isolate the exponential. (2) Take $\ln$ of both sides. (3) Use $\ln(e^x) = x$ to cancel. (4) Solve the resulting linear/algebraic equation. When you see $e^{2x}$ and $e^x$ together — substitute $u = e^x$ to get a quadratic. (a)\; e^{2x} = 7 \implies \ln(e^{2x}) = \ln(7) Take $\ln$ of both sides. This is always the first move when the exponential is isolated. 2x = \ln(7) \implies x = \frac{\ln 7}{2} Cancel: $\ln(e^{2x}) = 2x$. Divide by 2. Exact answer — do not try to compute $\ln(7)$ by hand. (b)\; 3e^{x-1} = 15 \implies e^{x-1} = 5 Isolate the exponential first: subtract 5, divide by 3. x - 1 = \ln 5 \implies x = 1 + \ln 5 Take $\ln$ of both sides: $\ln(e^{x-1}) = x - 1 = \ln 5$. Solve for $x$. (c)\; e^{2x} - 5e^x + 6 = 0 \implies u = e^x: \quad u^2 - 5u + 6 = 0 Substitution! This is disguised as a quadratic in $u = e^x$. Notice $e^{2x} = (e^x)^2$. (u-2)(u-3) = 0 \implies u = 2 \text{ or } u = 3 Factor the quadratic. e^x = 2 \implies x = \ln 2 \qquad e^x = 3 \implies x = \ln 3 Both solutions valid since $e^x > 0$ always. Two exact answers. To solve $\ln + \ln = \ln$: use log laws to combine, then set arguments equal. Always check that all arguments of $\ln$ are positive in the final answer — extraneous solutions are common. (a)\; \ln(x) = 4 \implies e^{\ln x} = e^4 \implies x = e^4 Exponentiate both sides (raise $e$ to the power of each side). The left side simplifies immediately via $e^{\ln x} = x$. (b)\; \ln(2x-1) = 3 \implies 2x-1 = e^3 Exponentiate: $e^{\ln(2x-1)} = e^3$ gives $2x - 1 = e^3$. 2x = 1 + e^3 \implies x = \frac{1 + e^3}{2} \approx 10.54 Solve for $x$. Always check: the argument $2x - 1 = e^3 > 0$ ✓. (c)\; \ln(x) + \ln(x-2) = \ln(8) \implies \ln(x(x-2)) = \ln(8) Apply product rule: $\ln(A) + \ln(B) = \ln(AB)$. Both sides are now $\ln$ of something. x(x-2) = 8 \implies x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0 \implies (x-4)(x+2) = 0 Since $\ln$ is one-to-one, $\ln(A) = \ln(B) \implies A = B$. Factor the quadratic. x = 4 \text{ or } x = -2. \quad \text{Check: } x = -2 \text{ makes } \ln(-2) \text{ undefined — reject.} Always check domain! $x = -2$ gives $\ln(-2)$, which does not exist for real numbers. The only solution is $x = 4$. The Continuous Growth Model — Radioactive Decay Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. An artifact contains 35% of its original carbon-14. How old is it? (Use the continuous decay model $A = A_0 e^{kt}$.)   The pattern for all exponential problems with unknown $k$: (1) Use a known condition (half-life, doubling time) to find $k$ exactly. (2) Use that $k$ to solve the target question. Both steps use "take $\ln$, bring the exponent down." \text{Step 1: Find } k \text{ using the half-life.} \quad \frac{A_0}{2} = A_0 e^{k \cdot 5730} At $t = 5730$, exactly half the original amount remains. $A_0$ cancels. \frac{1}{2} = e^{5730k} \implies \ln\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = 5730k Take $\ln$ of both sides. k = \frac{\ln(0.5)}{5730} = \frac{-\ln 2}{5730} \approx -0.0001209\ \text{yr}^{-1} Exact value: $k = -\ln(2)/5730$. Negative confirms decay. \text{Step 2: Solve } 0.35 A_0 = A_0 e^{kt} Now use $k$ to find $t$ when 35% remains. 0.35 = e^{kt} \implies \ln(0.35) = kt Cancel $A_0$, take $\ln$ of both sides. t = \frac{\ln(0.35)}{k} = \frac{\ln(0.35)}{-\ln 2 / 5730} = \frac{5730 \ln(0.35)}{-\ln 2} \approx \frac{5730(-1.0498)}{-0.6931} \approx 8684\ \text{years} Divide both sides by $k$. Compute numerically. The artifact is approximately 8684 years old. Radioactive Decay — Exponential Model Drag the slider to the half-life (5730 yr). Notice exactly half the original remains. Then find the time for 35% remaining.  Without a calculator, determine which is larger: $e^\pi$ or $\pi^e$. (Hint: take $\ln$ of both and compare.) You need to compare $\pi$ and $e \ln \pi$. Is $\pi/e > \ln \pi$? Consider the function $f(x) = x/e - \ln(x)$. e^\pi > \pi^e \approx 23.14 > 22.46  \text{Compare } e^\pi \text{ vs } \pi^e. \text{ Take } \ln \text{ of both: compare } \pi \text{ vs } e\ln\pi. Since $\ln$ is increasing, $e^\pi > \pi^e \iff \ln(e^\pi) > \ln(\pi^e) \iff \pi > e\ln\pi$. \text{Equiv: is } \pi/e > \ln \pi? Divide both sides by $e$. f(x) = x/e - \ln(x). \quad f'(x) = 1/e - 1/x = 0 \implies x = e $f$ has a minimum at $x = e$. f(e) = e/e - \ln e = 1 - 1 = 0. The minimum value of $f$ is exactly 0, achieved only at $x = e$. \text{For } x \neq e: f(x) > 0 \implies x/e > \ln x. At $x = \pi \neq e$: $\pi/e > \ln\pi$. Therefore $\pi > e\ln\pi$, so $e^\pi > \pi^e$. ∎  Show that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt} = e^{rt}$ for any rate $r$ and time $t$. This is the derivation of the continuous compounding formula. Let $m = n/r$ (so $n = mr$). Rewrite the expression in terms of $m$ and use the definition of $e$. e^{rt} — the general continuous compounding formula. ∎  \left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt} = \left[\left(1+\frac{1}{n/r}\right)^{n/r}\right]^{rt} Rewrite: factor the exponent as $rt$ and combine the base to create the pattern $(1 + 1/m)^m$. Let\ m = n/r. \text{ As } n\to\infty,\ m\to\infty. \text{ The expression becomes } \left[(1+1/m)^m\right]^{rt} Substitution maps the $r$-dependent expression to the standard form. \lim_{m\to\infty}\left[(1+1/m)^m\right]^{rt} = e^{rt} \quad \blacksquare The inner limit $\lim_{m\to\infty}(1+1/m)^m = e$ by definition. The outer exponent $rt$ passes through the limit. So the continuous compounding formula is proved.
documents.proofs: We define $e$ as the limit $e = \lim_{n \to \infty}\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n$. But how do we actually know this limit exists? And how does this connect to the derivative of $b^x$? The argument runs through the derivative of $b^x$ from first principles. The difference quotient is $\frac{b^{x+h} - b^x}{h} = b^x \cdot \frac{b^h - 1}{h}$. The factor $b^x$ just comes out, so the derivative of $b^x$ always equals $b^x$ times the constant $\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{b^h - 1}{h}$. This constant depends only on $b$ — call it $L(b)$. We want the base where $L(b) = 1$: that is the base where its derivative equals itself exactly. One can show (using the substitution $h = 1/n$ and the squeeze theorem) that $L(b) = \ln(b)$ — the natural log. So $L(b) = 1$ when $\ln(b) = 1$, i.e., when $b = e$. This completes the circle: $e$ is both the compound-interest limit AND the unique base whose exponential is its own derivative.
