This is not a trick question — it is the paradox that Newton and Leibniz independently solved in the 1670s, and their solution is called the derivative. Every speedometer, every radar gun, every physics simulation, every machine-learning gradient computation, every economic "marginal" analysis uses the derivative. It is the mathematical language of instantaneous change, and it is the central idea of this entire chapter. Chapter 2 Road Map — The Full Journey **Act 1 — The Question (Lessons 1–2)**
• Lesson 1 (you are here): Four perspectives, the paradox, and what a derivative IS
• Lesson 2: The rigorous limit definition — difference quotient → derivative

**Act 2 — The Toolkit (Lessons 3–5)**
• Lesson 3: Power, product, quotient rules — shortcuts proven from limits
• Lesson 4: The chain rule — most important rule in all of calculus
• Lesson 5: Product + chain trap drill — the #1 mistake, fixed immediately

**Act 3 — Special Functions (Lessons 6–8)**
• Lesson 6: Trig derivatives — why the slope of sin is cos
• Lesson 7: Exponential and log derivatives — e^x equals its own derivative
• Lesson 8: Inverse function derivatives — arcsin, arctan formulas

**Act 4 — Synthesis (Lessons 9–10)**
• Lesson 9: Implicit differentiation — when y can't be solved for
• Lesson 10: Reading f, f', f'' from graphs — the visual language You Already Have Both Ingredients The derivative = limit of a slope formula. You know slope from Chapter 0: Δy/Δx. You know limits from Chapter 1: what expressions approach as variables get close to a value. This lesson snaps those two together. Nothing new is required — just synthesis. The Same Math in Four Domains **Physics**: s(t) = position → s'(t) = velocity → s''(t) = acceleration. **Economics**: C(x) = cost → C'(x) = marginal cost (cost of one more unit). **Biology**: P(t) = population → P'(t) = growth rate. **Machine Learning**: L(w) = loss → ∂L/∂w = gradient (used in every neural network update). Same limit, four completely different worlds. The Three Most Common Beginner Mistakes 1. **Confusing the derivative with the difference quotient**: The difference quotient [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h is the slope of the SECANT line. The derivative is the LIMIT of that, and is the slope of the TANGENT line.
2. **Thinking dy/dx is a fraction**: It looks like one and behaves like one in many situations, but it is defined as a limit. Treating it as a literal fraction leads to errors.
3. **Forgetting the derivative is a function**: f'(x) is not just a number — it is a new function that gives you the slope at EVERY point x.
documents.content:
Your car's speedometer reads 62 mph. But speed = distance ÷ time — and at a single instant you travel zero distance in zero time. That's 0/0, which is undefined. So how can your speed be 62 mph at a single moment? This is not a trick question — it is the paradox that Newton and Leibniz independently solved in the 1670s, and their solution is called the derivative. Every speedometer, every radar gun, every physics simulation, every machine-learning gradient computation, every economic "marginal" analysis uses the derivative. It is the mathematical language of instantaneous change, and it is the central idea of this entire chapter. **The Problem: Speed at a Single Instant** Imagine a car trip. You drive 120 miles in 2 hours — your average speed is 60 mph. That calculation is easy: distance divided by time, a single fraction. But now think about your speedometer at exactly 2:17:43 PM. It says 72 mph. How? At a single instant, you travel no distance in no time. The formula gives 0/0 — an undefined quantity. Yet 72 mph is a completely meaningful, measurable, physical number. How can that be? The same paradox appears everywhere: the instantaneous growth rate of a population, the exact slope of a curve at a point, the rate at which a drug concentration is dropping at a specific moment. We want to talk about rates "right now," but every formula for rate requires an interval of time or distance. Calculus — specifically, the derivative — resolves this paradox with mathematical precision. **Step 1: Start with Average Rate of Change** Before solving the paradox, let's be precise about the simpler quantity: average rate of change. If f(t) gives your position at time t, the average velocity from t = a to t = b is: [f(b) - f(a)] / (b - a). This is Δy/Δx — the slope of the straight line connecting the two points (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)) on the graph. That straight line is called a **secant line** (from the Latin "secare" — to cut; it cuts across the curve at two points). Everything starts here. The secant line slope is measurable, concrete, and computable. The question is: what happens to that slope as b gets closer and closer to a? **Step 2: Shrink the Interval Toward Zero** Watch what happens as we take smaller and smaller time intervals. Suppose f(t) = t² (think of a freely falling object where t is time and t² is proportional to distance fallen). At t = 2, let's compute the average velocity from t = 2 to t = 2 + h for shrinking values of h: h = 1 gives [f(3) - f(2)]/1 = [9 - 4]/1 = 5. h = 0.1 gives [f(2.1) - f(2)]/0.1 = [4.41 - 4]/0.1 = 4.1. h = 0.01 gives [f(2.01) - f(2)]/0.01 = [4.0401 - 4]/0.01 = 4.01. h = 0.001 gives 4.001. The numbers are converging — they approach 4 as h approaches 0. This is the derivative! The derivative of f(t) = t² at t = 2 is 4. We never divided by zero — we watched the ratio approach a limit as h approached zero. The limit resolved the paradox: we don't evaluate at h = 0 (that would be 0/0). We ask what the ratio *approaches* as h gets arbitrarily small. Those are completely different questions. **The Geometry: Secant Lines Rotating into the Tangent Line** Geometrically, here is what is happening. Each secant line through (2, f(2)) and (2+h, f(2+h)) has slope [f(2+h) - f(2)]/h. As h shrinks, the second point slides along the curve toward (2, 4). The secant line rotates. In the limit, it becomes a line that touches the curve at exactly one point — it just brushes the curve — and has the same slope as the curve at that point. This is the **tangent line**. The derivative at a point is the slope of the tangent line at that point. **This is not abstract.** Zoom in on any smooth curve near a point with a microscope. Zoom in far enough and the curve stops looking curved — it looks like a straight line. That straight line is the tangent line. Its slope is the derivative. Mathematicians call this property **local linearity**: every differentiable function looks linear when you zoom in close enough. **Four Ways to See the Same Thing** The derivative has four equivalent interpretations. Master all four, because different problems call for different lenses: (1) **Geometric**: the slope of the tangent line to the graph of f at the point (x, f(x)). (2) **Physical**: the instantaneous velocity — if f(t) is position, f'(t) is how fast position is changing at time t. (3) **Algebraic**: the limit of the difference quotient [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h as h → 0. (4) **Computational**: the best linear approximation to f near x — meaning f(x+h) ≈ f(x) + f'(x)·h for small h. All four describe the same object. The visualization below the Perspective Synchronization Block lets you switch between them. **The Sensitivity Interpretation — the Most Useful One** The most powerful practical interpretation of the derivative is as a **sensitivity**: f'(x) tells you how much f(x) responds to a tiny change in x. If f'(2) = 5, it means that near x = 2, a change of +0.01 in x produces a change of approximately +0.05 in f(x) — it amplifies the change by a factor of 5. If f'(2) = -3, a change of +0.01 in x produces a change of approximately -0.03 in f(x) — it reverses and amplifies. This sensitivity interpretation is the key to understanding the chain rule (sensitivities multiply), the product rule, and every application in optimization, physics, and economics. The formal statement of this sensitivity is the **local linearity formula**: f(x + h) ≈ f(x) + f'(x) · h for small h. This says: the function near x looks like the line f(x) + (slope) · h. The derivative is the slope of that local line. The error in this approximation shrinks faster than h does — it is "better than linear" as a model of f near x. **The Derivative Appears Everywhere** The same mathematical object — the limit of a ratio — describes completely different physical phenomena: In **kinematics**: if s(t) is position at time t, then v(t) = s'(t) is instantaneous velocity, and a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t) is acceleration. In **economics**: if C(x) is the cost to produce x units, then C'(x) is the marginal cost — the additional cost of producing one more unit. Economists design entire pricing strategies around marginal cost. In **biology/medicine**: if P(t) is a population (or drug concentration) at time t, then P'(t) is the growth rate (or absorption rate) — negative when the population shrinks. In each case, the derivative answers: "How fast is this quantity changing right now?" **Connecting to What You Already Know** You have both ingredients. From Chapter 0: you know slope = Δy/Δx = rise/run, and you can compute it for any two points. From Chapter 1: you know how to take limits — what a function approaches as its input gets close to a value. The derivative is *exactly* the limit of the slope formula: lim[h→0] [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h. You already know both halves. This lesson puts them together. **Notation — Multiple Names for the Same Thing** Mathematicians write the derivative in several equivalent ways. If y = f(x), all of the following mean the same thing: f'(x) (Lagrange notation — compact, good for algebra), dy/dx (Leibniz notation — looks like a fraction, excellent for chain rule and related rates), d/dx[f(x)] (operator notation — emphasizes that d/dx is an operation applied to f), and ẏ (Newton's dot notation — used in physics for time derivatives). Leibniz notation dy/dx is particularly powerful because it behaves algebraically like a fraction in many situations (it is not literally a fraction — it is a limit — but the chain rule makes it look like one). You will use all four notations in this course; learn to recognize each. **Not Every Function Has a Derivative Everywhere** The derivative requires the limit [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h to exist as h→0. Three things can make that limit fail: (1) A **corner** or **cusp** — like |x| at x=0 — where the slope from the left and from the right are different numbers, so the limit doesn't exist. (2) A **vertical tangent** — like x^(1/3) at x=0 — where the slope grows without bound (slope → ∞). (3) A **discontinuity** — at a jump or break in the graph, there is no well-defined tangent line. The failure modes table at the bottom of this section lists these cases explicitly. **How to Use the Visualizations Below** Work through the four interactive visualizations in order. First, LineFoundationsLab refreshes slope — run your mouse along the line and watch Δy/Δx stay constant. Second, CalculusFoundationsLab decodes the notation — every symbol in the derivative formula is mapped to a concrete meaning before you see the formula. Third, TangentLineViz shows the geometric derivative — drag the point along the curve and watch the tangent slope change. Fourth, DerivativeFromFirstPrinciplesViz is the key animation — drag h toward zero and watch the secant line rotate into the tangent line. That rotation IS the limit definition. Finally, PositionVelocityAcceleration shows the derivative chain in physics — three graphs live, connected by differentiation. We are now ready to state the formal definition. There are two closely related versions: the derivative at a specific point a (a number), and the derivative function f'(x) (a new function of x). **Definition at a point**: The derivative of f at x = a is the number f'(a) = lim[h→0] [f(a+h) - f(a)] / h, provided this limit exists and is finite. If the limit exists, we say f is **differentiable** at a. **Derivative function**: By letting a vary, we get the derivative function f'(x) = lim[h→0] [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h. For each x where f is differentiable, f'(x) gives the slope of f at that x. The derivative function encodes the slope of f at every point simultaneously. **All common notations mean the same thing**: If y = f(x), then f'(x) = y' = dy/dx = d/dx[f(x)] = Df(x) = ẏ (in physics). Leibniz notation dy/dx is powerful in chain rule and integration. Lagrange notation f'(x) is compact for algebra. Newton's ẏ appears in physics textbooks. **Higher derivatives**: Differentiating once gives f'(x). Differentiating f'(x) gives f''(x) — the second derivative. Then f'''(x), and so on. In Leibniz notation: d²y/dx², d³y/dx³. Second derivative measures the rate of change of the rate of change — geometrically, it measures concavity (whether the curve bends up or down). We use nothing except the limit definition. The key step is expanding (x+h)² algebraically, then canceling the h in numerator and denominator. We are allowed to cancel h because in the limit process, h approaches zero but is never equal to zero — canceling is legal for h ≠ 0. After canceling, we get a polynomial in h that is defined at h = 0. Taking the limit is then just substituting h = 0. This is the prototype for computing all power rule derivatives from first principles. Why This Generalizes to xⁿ For f(x) = xⁿ, expanding (x+h)ⁿ by the binomial theorem gives xⁿ + nxⁿ⁻¹h + (terms with h²). After subtracting xⁿ, dividing by h, and taking h→0, only the nxⁿ⁻¹ term survives. This proves the power rule: d/dx[xⁿ] = nxⁿ⁻¹ for any integer n. (The extension to all real n uses logarithmic differentiation, proved in Lesson 7.) Chapter 2 Road Map — The Full Journey **Act 1 — The Question (Lessons 1–2)**
• Lesson 1 (you are here): Four perspectives, the paradox, and what a derivative IS
• Lesson 2: The rigorous limit definition — difference quotient → derivative

**Act 2 — The Toolkit (Lessons 3–5)**
• Lesson 3: Power, product, quotient rules — shortcuts proven from limits
• Lesson 4: The chain rule — most important rule in all of calculus
• Lesson 5: Product + chain trap drill — the #1 mistake, fixed immediately

**Act 3 — Special Functions (Lessons 6–8)**
• Lesson 6: Trig derivatives — why the slope of sin is cos
• Lesson 7: Exponential and log derivatives — e^x equals its own derivative
• Lesson 8: Inverse function derivatives — arcsin, arctan formulas

**Act 4 — Synthesis (Lessons 9–10)**
• Lesson 9: Implicit differentiation — when y can't be solved for
• Lesson 10: Reading f, f', f'' from graphs — the visual language You Already Have Both Ingredients The derivative = limit of a slope formula. You know slope from Chapter 0: Δy/Δx. You know limits from Chapter 1: what expressions approach as variables get close to a value. This lesson snaps those two together. Nothing new is required — just synthesis. The Same Math in Four Domains **Physics**: s(t) = position → s'(t) = velocity → s''(t) = acceleration. **Economics**: C(x) = cost → C'(x) = marginal cost (cost of one more unit). **Biology**: P(t) = population → P'(t) = growth rate. **Machine Learning**: L(w) = loss → ∂L/∂w = gradient (used in every neural network update). Same limit, four completely different worlds. The Three Most Common Beginner Mistakes 1. **Confusing the derivative with the difference quotient**: The difference quotient [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h is the slope of the SECANT line. The derivative is the LIMIT of that, and is the slope of the TANGENT line.
2. **Thinking dy/dx is a fraction**: It looks like one and behaves like one in many situations, but it is defined as a limit. Treating it as a literal fraction leads to errors.
3. **Forgetting the derivative is a function**: f'(x) is not just a number — it is a new function that gives you the slope at EVERY point x. The Formal Limit Definition f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} \qquad \text{(provided the limit exists)} Five Equivalent Notations f'(x) = y' = \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx}[f(x)] = Df(x) \qquad \text{(all mean the same thing)} Differentiability Implies Continuity If f is differentiable at x = a, then f is continuous at x = a. The converse is FALSE — continuous does not imply differentiable (corners are continuous but not differentiable). Preview: The Rules You Will Prove in Lessons 3–4 After the limit definition is established, the following shortcuts are proved from it:
- **Power Rule**: $\frac{d}{dx}[x^n] = nx^{n-1}$ (for any real $n$)
- **Sum Rule**: $\frac{d}{dx}[f+g] = f' + g'$
- **Product Rule**: $\frac{d}{dx}[fg] = f'g + fg'$
- **Chain Rule**: $\frac{d}{dx}[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)$

These are theorems — proved once from the limit definition, used forever. dy/dx is NOT Literally a Fraction dy/dx looks like a fraction and behaves like one in the chain rule and separable differential equations, but it is defined as a limit. You cannot 'cancel' the dx in general. The notation is brilliantly suggestive — Leibniz designed it that way — but it is notation, not arithmetic. Step 1 — Foundations: What is Slope? Prerequisite check: drag the two points and confirm that slope = rise/run = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁) no matter where you place them. A constant slope is the defining property of a line. Step 2 — Decoding the Symbols Before They Appear Pick a function and a point x. Set h to a value like 0.5. The lab shows you f(x), f(x+h), and the difference — these are the rise and run of the secant line. Step 3 — The Geometric Derivative: Tangent Lines Drag the point. At a local maximum the tangent is horizontal (slope = 0). At a steep rise it is steep (slope > 0). At a steep fall it is steep the other way (slope < 0). Read the slope value displayed. Step 4 — The Limit in Action: Secant Becoming Tangent Drag h from large to small. The secant slope stabilizes to a definite number — that is f'(a). The paradox is resolved: we never divide by zero; we take the limit as we approach zero. Step 5 — The Derivative Chain: Position → Velocity → Acceleration Watch all three graphs update simultaneously. Click and drag the position curve to reshape it. This physical picture — not just algebra — is what differentiation means. Chapter 2 Review Board A complete map of Chapter 2 Derivatives, highlighting the core concepts and common traps before entering Chapter 3. Chapter 2 Applied Problems Real-world applications of derivatives: related rates, marginal analysis, and kinematics. Computing a Derivative from the Definition Use the limit definition to find f'(x) for f(x) = 3x + 5. The derivative of a linear function is its slope constant. This confirms the rule: d/dx[mx + b] = m. f'(x) = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{[3(x+h)+5]-[3x+5]}{h} Write out the definition with f(x) = 3x + 5 substituted = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{3x+3h+5-3x-5}{h} Expand the numerator = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{3h}{h} The 3x and 5 terms cancel = \lim_{h\to 0} 3 = 3 Cancel h, then substitute h=0. Result: the derivative of a line is its slope — no surprise. Velocity from a Position Function A ball is thrown upward with position s(t) = -4.9t² + 20t meters. Find its instantaneous velocity at t = 1 second. Is it still rising or already falling? At t = 1 s, the ball is moving upward at 10.2 m/s (positive means upward). The ball reaches its peak when v = 0: −9.8t + 20 = 0 → t ≈ 2.04 s. After that, v < 0 and the ball falls. v(t) = s'(t) = \frac{d}{dt}[-4.9t^2 + 20t] Velocity is the derivative of position = -4.9 \cdot 2t + 20 \cdot 1 = -9.8t + 20 Power rule on each term: d/dt[t²] = 2t, d/dt[t] = 1 v(1) = -9.8(1) + 20 = 10.2 \text{ m/s} Evaluate at t = 1 Marginal Cost in Economics A factory's cost to produce x items is C(x) = 0.01x² + 5x + 200 dollars. What is the marginal cost at x = 100 items? What does it mean? At 100 items, producing one more item costs approximately $7. Notice the actual cost of going from 100 to 101 items is C(101) - C(100) = (0.01·10201 + 505 + 200) - (0.01·10000 + 500 + 200) = $7.01 — the derivative predicted $7, which is accurate to within 1 cent. This is local linearity in action. C'(x) = \frac{d}{dx}[0.01x^2 + 5x + 200] Marginal cost = derivative of total cost = 0.01(2x) + 5 + 0 = 0.02x + 5 Power rule on each term C'(100) = 0.02(100) + 5 = 2 + 5 = 7 \text{ dollars/item} Evaluate at x = 100 Using the limit definition, prove that the derivative of f(x) = x³ is f'(x) = 3x². (Hint: expand (x+h)³ and cancel h.) (x+h)³ = x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³. After subtracting x³ and dividing by h, you get 3x² + 3xh + h². Take the limit. f'(x) = 3x² \frac{(x+h)^3 - x^3}{h} = \frac{x^3 + 3x^2h + 3xh^2 + h^3 - x^3}{h} Expand (x+h)³ using the cube expansion = \frac{3x^2h + 3xh^2 + h^3}{h} Cancel x³ terms = 3x^2 + 3xh + h^2 Cancel h from every term (valid since h ≠ 0) \lim_{h\to 0}(3x^2 + 3xh + h^2) = 3x^2 Substitute h = 0. The 3xh and h² terms vanish. The tangent line to f(x) = x² at the point (3, 9) passes through what y-intercept? Write the equation of the tangent line. Find the slope using f'(3), then use point-slope form with the point (3, 9). y = 6x − 9 (y-intercept is −9) f'(x) = 2x \implies f'(3) = 6 Derivative gives slope at x=3 y - 9 = 6(x - 3) Point-slope form: slope 6, point (3,9) y = 6x - 18 + 9 = 6x - 9 Simplify to slope-intercept form assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step instantaneous rate of change slope dy/dx velocity marginal change

documents.assignment: Derivative of x² from the Definition \text{Let } f(x) = x^2. \text{ Use the limit definition to find } f'(x). \text{ Then find the slope at } x=3 \text{ and write the equation of the tangent line at } (3, 9).   f'(x) = 2x. At x = 3, slope = 6, tangent line y = 6x - 9. Algebra keys: (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 (NOT a^2 + b^2); factor h by the distributive law in reverse; cancel h/h because h is nonzero during the limit process. f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} Always start by writing the limit definition. This is the algorithm — do not skip it. Every derivative we compute follows these exact steps. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(x+h)^2 - x^2}{h} Substitute f(x) = x^2. To find f(x+h): wherever x appears in the formula x^2, replace it with the quantity (x+h). So f(x+h) = (x+h)^2. Gotcha: this is NOT x^2 + h^2. You cannot distribute a square across a sum — that is one of the most common algebra mistakes in calculus. (x+h)^2 = (x+h)(x+h) Prerequisite algebra — what squaring means: raising a quantity to the power 2 means multiplying it by itself. We must expand this product before we can simplify anything. = x \cdot x + x \cdot h + h \cdot x + h \cdot h Prerequisite algebra — FOIL method for multiplying two binomials: multiply EVERY term in the first factor by EVERY term in the second. Four products total. First: x times x. Outer: x times h. Inner: h times x. Last: h times h. Write all four products before combining anything. Do not skip steps here. = x^2 + xh + xh + h^2 = x^2 + 2xh + h^2 Combine like terms: the outer and inner products are both xh, so xh + xh = 2xh. Final rule to know: (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2. The 2ab middle term is what everyone drops. It is not optional — if you omit it, your derivative will be wrong. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - x^2}{h} Substitute the full expansion back into the difference quotient numerator. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{2xh + h^2}{h} Cancel x^2 and -x^2 in the numerator: x^2 - x^2 = 0. This cancellation always happens in a derivative — the original function terms subtract away, leaving only terms that contain h. If any term without h survives after this step, you made an expansion error. Go back and check. 2xh + h^2 = h \cdot 2x + h \cdot h = h(2x + h) Prerequisite algebra — factoring using the distributive property in reverse: the rule ab + ac = a(b + c) says that if EVERY term in an expression shares a common factor, you can pull that factor out front. Check: does 2xh contain h? Yes — it equals h times 2x. Does h^2 contain h? Yes — it equals h times h. Since both terms share h as a factor, we factor h out. Verify by expanding back: h(2x + h) = h times 2x plus h times h = 2xh + h^2. Correct. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{h(2x + h)}{h} Substitute the factored numerator. Now h appears explicitly in both numerator and denominator. = \lim_{h \to 0} (2x + h) Prerequisite algebra — why canceling h/h is legal here: for any nonzero number k, k divided by k = 1. In the limit process, h is approaching zero but is NEVER actually zero. So at every stage, h is a nonzero quantity, and h/h = 1 is a perfectly valid cancellation. We are not dividing by zero. We are dividing by a nonzero number that happens to be getting very small. This distinction — approaching zero versus equaling zero — is the conceptual core of the entire limit idea. = 2x + 0 = 2x Now, and only now, substitute h = 0. The denominator is completely gone, so there is no risk of division by zero. Replace every h with 0: 2x + h becomes 2x + 0 = 2x. f'(x) = 2x The derivative of x^2 is 2x. This is a function, not a single number. At any x it gives the slope of the parabola at that point. At x = 0 the slope is 0 (the vertex is flat). At x = 1 the slope is 2. At x = -3 the slope is -6. f'(3) = 2(3) = 6 Evaluate the derivative function at x = 3. Plugging x = 3 into f'(x) = 2x gives 6. That is the slope of the tangent line at the point (3, 9). \text{Point-slope form: } y - y_1 = m(x - x_1) Prerequisite algebra — point-slope form: the equation of any line through a known point (x_1, y_1) with known slope m. We know slope m = f'(3) = 6. We need the point. The point lies on the ORIGINAL curve, so the y-coordinate is f(3) = 3^2 = 9. Point: (3, 9). Do not use f'(3) = 6 as the y-coordinate — that is the slope, not the height. y - 9 = 6(x - 3) Substitute point (3, 9) and slope 6 into point-slope form. y - 9 = 6x - 18 Distribute 6 across (x - 3): 6 times x = 6x, 6 times -3 = -18. y = 6x - 18 + 9 = 6x - 9 Add 9 to both sides to isolate y. Verification: plug x = 3 back in: y = 6(3) - 9 = 18 - 9 = 9. The line passes through (3, 9) as required. Derivative of x³ from the Definition \text{Let } f(x) = x^3. \text{ Use the limit definition to find } f'(x).   f'(x^3) = 3x^2. Critical step: expand (x+h)^3 into all four terms. Dropping the middle terms 3x^2 h and 3xh^2 is the most common error. f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(x+h)^3 - x^3}{h} Write the definition and substitute f(x) = x^3. This example forces you to expand a cube — a step that causes more errors than almost anything else in early calculus. (x+h)^3 = (x+h)^2 \cdot (x+h) Prerequisite algebra — strategy for a cube: x^3 means x times x times x, so (x+h)^3 = (x+h)(x+h)(x+h). A practical two-step approach: use the result we proved in ex1 — (x+h)^2 = x^2 + 2xh + h^2 — and then multiply that result by (x+h) once more. Splitting into two steps makes the expansion manageable and checkable. = (x^2 + 2xh + h^2)(x+h) Substitute the known expansion of (x+h)^2. We now need to multiply a trinomial (three terms) by a binomial (two terms). = x^2(x+h) + 2xh(x+h) + h^2(x+h) Prerequisite algebra — distributing a trinomial: multiply EACH of the three terms in the first factor by the COMPLETE second factor (x+h). The distributive law is the same rule used for binomials; it just has to be applied three times instead of twice. = (x^3 + x^2 h) + (2x^2 h + 2xh^2) + (xh^2 + h^3) Expand each pair. x^2 times x = x^3, x^2 times h = x^2 h. Then 2xh times x = 2x^2 h, 2xh times h = 2xh^2. Then h^2 times x = xh^2, h^2 times h = h^3. Six terms total. = x^3 + 3x^2 h + 3xh^2 + h^3 Collect like terms: x^2 h + 2x^2 h = 3x^2 h. And 2xh^2 + xh^2 = 3xh^2. Final expansion: (x+h)^3 = x^3 + 3x^2 h + 3xh^2 + h^3. Gotcha: the most common mistake here is writing only x^3 + h^3 and omitting both middle terms. Both 3x^2 h and 3xh^2 are real — confirm by multiplying back. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{x^3 + 3x^2 h + 3xh^2 + h^3 - x^3}{h} Substitute the full expansion into the difference quotient numerator. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{3x^2 h + 3xh^2 + h^3}{h} Cancel x^3 - x^3 = 0. Three terms remain; every one of them contains h. 3x^2 h + 3xh^2 + h^3 = h \cdot 3x^2 + h \cdot 3xh + h \cdot h^2 = h(3x^2 + 3xh + h^2) Prerequisite algebra — factoring h from three terms: check that each term contains h as a factor. 3x^2 h = h times 3x^2. 3xh^2 = h times 3xh. h^3 = h times h^2. All three have h, so apply the distributive law in reverse: ab + ac + ad = a(b + c + d). Factor h out of all three at once. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{h(3x^2 + 3xh + h^2)}{h} Rewrite the numerator with h factored out. = \lim_{h \to 0} (3x^2 + 3xh + h^2) Cancel h/h = 1. Legal because h is nonzero in the limit process. Denominator is gone. = 3x^2 + 3x(0) + (0)^2 = 3x^2 Substitute h = 0 safely. Both 3xh and h^2 contain h and become zero. Only 3x^2 — the constant-in-h term — survives. f'(x) = 3x^2 Pattern check: for x^2 the derivative was 2x. For x^3 it is 3x^2. In each case the exponent dropped down as the coefficient and the power decreased by one. You are watching the power rule emerge from first principles. Derivative of \sqrt{x} from the Definition f(x) = \sqrt{x}. \text{ Use the limit definition to find } f'(x) \text{ for } x > 0.   f'(sqrt(x)) = 1/(2 sqrt(x)) for x > 0. Technique: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate to eliminate the radical difference. The difference of squares identity produces a plain h in the numerator that cancels the denominator h. f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x+h} - \sqrt{x}}{h} Write the definition. Substituting h = 0 immediately gives 0/0. But unlike polynomials, there is no h to factor out of a square root. A completely different algebraic technique is needed: the conjugate method. \text{Prerequisite: difference of squares — } (a-b)(a+b) = a^2 - b^2 This identity is the key. Reading it left-to-right: multiplying a difference by its conjugate gives a difference of squares. Reading it right-to-left: a difference of squares factors into a product of a sum and difference. We want to use it right-to-left on the numerator: we will force the numerator into the form a^2 - b^2 to eliminate the square roots. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x+h} - \sqrt{x}}{h} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x+h} + \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x+h} + \sqrt{x}} Multiply the entire expression by the conjugate fraction. The conjugate of (a - b) is (a + b) — same two terms, but with the sign between them flipped. Multiplying by (conjugate)/(conjugate) equals 1, so the value is unchanged. This is called rationalizing the numerator. \text{Numerator: }(\sqrt{x+h} - \sqrt{x})(\sqrt{x+h} + \sqrt{x}) = (\sqrt{x+h})^2 - (\sqrt{x})^2 Apply the difference of squares identity directly: (a - b)(a + b) = a^2 - b^2, where a = sqrt(x+h) and b = sqrt(x). = (x+h) - x = h Prerequisite algebra — square root and squaring are inverse operations: by the definition of square root, (sqrt(A))^2 = A. So (sqrt(x+h))^2 = x+h and (sqrt(x))^2 = x. After subtracting: (x+h) - x = h. The radical signs are completely eliminated from the numerator. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{h}{h(\sqrt{x+h} + \sqrt{x})} The numerator is now simply h. The denominator is the original h multiplied by the conjugate factor. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{1}{\sqrt{x+h} + \sqrt{x}} Cancel h/h = 1 (h nonzero in the limit). After canceling, h appears only inside the square root in the denominator — it is safe to take the limit now. = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x+0} + \sqrt{x}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{x}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} Substitute h = 0. sqrt(x+0) = sqrt(x). The denominator becomes sqrt(x) + sqrt(x) = 2 sqrt(x). Domain requirement: x > 0 is needed to ensure sqrt(x) is a real number and the denominator is nonzero. f'(x) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} Equivalently written as (1/2) x^{-1/2}. Power rule verification: x^{1/2} should give (1/2) x^{1/2 - 1} = (1/2) x^{-1/2} = 1/(2 sqrt(x)). Confirmed — the power rule works for fractional exponents too. Derivative of 1/x from the Definition f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}. \text{ Use the limit definition to find } f'(x) \text{ for } x \neq 0.   f'(1/x) = -1/x^2. Key algebra: convert the fraction subtraction to a common denominator x(x+h), distribute the minus sign carefully, then cancel -h/h. The sign on h is the most frequent error. f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\dfrac{1}{x+h} - \dfrac{1}{x}}{h} Write the definition and substitute. The numerator is now a difference of two fractions — a compound fraction. Strategy: simplify the top fraction first, before dividing by h. \text{Focus on the numerator: } \frac{1}{x+h} - \frac{1}{x} Prerequisite algebra — subtracting fractions with unlike denominators: you cannot subtract fractions unless they share a common denominator. The denominators are (x+h) and x. These are different expressions (h makes them different), so we must convert both to a common denominator first. \text{Least common denominator (LCD)} = x(x+h) Prerequisite algebra — finding the LCD: when two denominators share no common factor, their LCD is simply their product. x and (x+h) share no common factor (h is nonzero), so LCD = x times (x+h) = x(x+h). \frac{1}{x+h} = \frac{1 \cdot x}{(x+h) \cdot x} = \frac{x}{x(x+h)} Convert the first fraction: multiply top and bottom by x. Multiplying by x/x = 1 does not change the value, only the form. \frac{1}{x} = \frac{1 \cdot (x+h)}{x \cdot (x+h)} = \frac{x+h}{x(x+h)} Convert the second fraction: multiply top and bottom by (x+h). \frac{1}{x+h} - \frac{1}{x} = \frac{x}{x(x+h)} - \frac{x+h}{x(x+h)} = \frac{x - (x+h)}{x(x+h)} Prerequisite algebra — subtracting fractions with the same denominator: a/c - b/c = (a - b)/c. Combine into one fraction. CRITICAL: keep the parentheses around (x+h) in the numerator. If you write x - x + h instead of x - (x+h), you get the wrong sign on h and your answer will have the wrong sign. = \frac{x - x - h}{x(x+h)} Prerequisite algebra — distributing a negative sign: -(x+h) = -x - h. The minus sign distributes to every term inside the parentheses. x becomes -x and h becomes -h. = \frac{-h}{x(x+h)} Simplify the numerator: x - x = 0, leaving -h. This negative sign is important — it is why the derivative of 1/x is negative. f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{1}{h} \cdot \frac{-h}{x(x+h)} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{-h}{h \cdot x(x+h)} The full difference quotient: the fraction difference is divided by h, meaning multiply by 1/h. Combine h terms together. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{-1}{x(x+h)} Cancel -h/h = -1 (h is nonzero in the limit). The negative sign carries through. = \frac{-1}{x(x+0)} = \frac{-1}{x \cdot x} = -\frac{1}{x^2} Substitute h = 0. Denominator becomes x times x = x^2. f'(x) = -\dfrac{1}{x^2} Power rule verification: 1/x = x^{-1}. Power rule gives (-1) x^{-1 - 1} = -x^{-2} = -1/x^2. Confirmed. Derivative of a Linear Function f(x) = 3x + 5. \text{ Find } f'(x) \text{ from the limit definition. Explain why the constant term disappears.}   f'(3x+5) = 3. The constant 5 cancels because it appears identically in both f(x) and f(x+h). Only the slope coefficient 3 survives the subtraction. f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} Start from the definition. Even for a simple function, writing this out explicitly keeps you from making sign errors. f(x+h) = 3(x+h) + 5 Substitute (x+h) wherever x appears in 3x + 5. Replace the x in '3x' with (x+h). The constant 5 does not change because it does not depend on x at all. = 3x + 3h + 5 Prerequisite algebra — distribute 3 over (x+h): 3 times x = 3x, 3 times h = 3h. The constant 5 is unchanged. f(x+h) - f(x) = (3x + 3h + 5) - (3x + 5) Write the subtraction with brackets around both expressions. This protects you from forgetting to distribute the minus sign. = 3x + 3h + 5 - 3x - 5 Prerequisite algebra — distributing a minus sign: -(3x + 5) = -3x - 5. Every term inside the parentheses gets its sign flipped. This is the step where sign errors most often happen. = 3h Collect like terms: 3x and -3x cancel. 5 and -5 cancel. Only 3h survives. Why does 5 disappear? Because 5 is a constant — it appears identically in both f(x) and f(x+h). When you subtract them, the 5s cancel. The intercept tells you WHERE the line is vertically, but it does not affect the steepness. Steepness — slope — depends only on the coefficient of x. \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} = \frac{3h}{h} = 3 Prerequisite algebra — cancel h/h = 1 (h nonzero). The entire difference quotient equals the constant 3 for every nonzero value of h. There is nothing left to take a limit of. f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} 3 = 3 Prerequisite: the limit of a constant is that constant. No matter how h changes, the value 3 never moves. So the limit is 3. f'(x) = 3 Geometric meaning: y = 3x + 5 is a straight line with constant slope 3 everywhere. The tangent line at any point IS the line itself. The derivative is the same at every x because a line has the same steepness everywhere. \text{General rule: if } f(x) = mx + b \text{ then } f'(x) = m Proof of the general rule: f(x+h) - f(x) = [m(x+h) + b] - [mx + b] = mx + mh + b - mx - b = mh. Dividing by h and taking the limit gives m. The intercept b always cancels. Is |x| Differentiable at x = 0? \text{Determine whether } f(x) = |x| \text{ is differentiable at } x = 0 \text{ by computing left and right-hand derivatives.}   |x| is continuous everywhere but not differentiable at x = 0. One-sided derivatives exist but disagree: +1 from the right, -1 from the left. The corner kills the derivative. f'(0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{|0 + h| - |0|}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{|h|}{h} Write the limit definition at x = 0. Since |0| = 0, the numerator simplifies to |h|. The problem: |h| behaves differently depending on whether h is positive or negative. We cannot evaluate this limit without splitting into cases. |h| = \begin{cases} h & \text{if } h > 0 \\ -h & \text{if } h < 0 \end{cases} Prerequisite algebra — definition of absolute value: absolute value returns the non-negative version of a number. For a positive input, return it unchanged. For a negative input, negate it to make it positive. Example: |-5| = -(-5) = 5. This piecewise definition forces us to analyze from the left and from the right separately. f'_+(0) = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{|h|}{h} Right-hand derivative: h approaches 0 from the positive side, so h > 0 the whole time. Apply the h > 0 branch of the absolute value: |h| = h. = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{h}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^+} 1 = 1 For h > 0: |h| = h, so the ratio is h/h = 1. Limit of the constant 1 is 1. Right-hand derivative = +1. f'_-(0) = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{|h|}{h} Left-hand derivative: h approaches 0 from the negative side, so h < 0 the whole time. Apply the h < 0 branch: |h| = -h. = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{-h}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-} (-1) = -1 For h < 0: |h| = -h. So the ratio is (-h)/h = -1. Gotcha: h itself is negative here, which means -h is a positive number. But the RATIO (-h)/h simplifies to -1 for all h, positive or negative. The left-hand derivative = -1. f'_+(0) = 1 \neq -1 = f'_-(0) The two one-sided derivatives are not equal. \text{Prerequisite: two-sided limit exists} \iff \lim_{h \to 0^-} = \lim_{h \to 0^+} Rule from Chapter 1: a two-sided limit exists if and only if both one-sided limits exist AND have the same value. Here the left limit is -1 and the right limit is +1. They disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist. \therefore f'(0) \text{ does not exist} The derivative at x = 0 does not exist. Geometrically: the graph of |x| has a corner at the origin. The left branch has slope -1; the right branch has slope +1. There is no single tangent line at a corner — two different lines are competing for the same point. \lim_{x \to 0} |x| = 0 = f(0), \text{ so } f \text{ is continuous at } 0 By contrast: is |x| at least continuous at 0? Yes — the limit equals the function value (both are 0). This confirms the one-way relationship: differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does NOT imply differentiability. |x| is the standard counterexample. See the Calculation on the Graph The two secants never converge — they are locked at +1 and -1 forever. That is why the limit does not exist and f is not differentiable at 0. Instantaneous Velocity from First Principles \text{A particle's position is } s(t) = 4t^2 + 3t \text{ meters, } t \text{ in seconds. Find its instantaneous velocity at } t = 2 \text{ s.}   Instantaneous velocity at t = 2 s is 19 m/s. The algebra is identical to ex1 — expand (t+h)^2, cancel terms, factor h, cancel h/h, substitute h = 0. Only the interpretation changes. v(t) = s'(t) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{s(t+h) - s(t)}{h} Physical setup: instantaneous velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time. The same limit-of-difference-quotient formula applies — we just interpret the result as meters per second. s(t+h) = 4(t+h)^2 + 3(t+h) Substitute (t+h) everywhere t appears in s(t) = 4t^2 + 3t. Two substitution sites: in the squared term and in the linear term. 4(t+h)^2 = 4(t^2 + 2th + h^2) Expand (t+h)^2 using (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2, with a = t and b = h. = 4t^2 + 8th + 4h^2 Distribute 4 to each term: 4 times t^2 = 4t^2, 4 times 2th = 8th, 4 times h^2 = 4h^2. 3(t+h) = 3t + 3h Distribute 3: 3 times t = 3t, 3 times h = 3h. s(t+h) = 4t^2 + 8th + 4h^2 + 3t + 3h Combine the two expanded pieces into the full expression for s(t+h). s(t+h) - s(t) = (4t^2 + 8th + 4h^2 + 3t + 3h) - (4t^2 + 3t) Subtract s(t) = 4t^2 + 3t. Use parentheses around s(t) to protect every sign inside. = 4t^2 + 8th + 4h^2 + 3t + 3h - 4t^2 - 3t Distribute the minus sign: -(4t^2 + 3t) = -4t^2 - 3t. = 8th + 4h^2 + 3h Collect like terms: 4t^2 - 4t^2 = 0, 3t - 3t = 0. Three h-terms remain. Every surviving term contains h, as expected. 8th + 4h^2 + 3h = h(8t + 4h + 3) Prerequisite: factor h from all three terms. 8th = h times 8t. 4h^2 = h times 4h. 3h = h times 3. All three terms have h as a factor. Apply distributive law in reverse: h(8t + 4h + 3). \frac{s(t+h)-s(t)}{h} = \frac{h(8t + 4h + 3)}{h} = 8t + 4h + 3 Cancel h/h (legal: h is nonzero in the limit process). The simplified difference quotient is 8t + 4h + 3. v(t) = \lim_{h \to 0}(8t + 4h + 3) = 8t + 3 \text{ m/s} Take h to 0. The 4h term vanishes. Velocity function: v(t) = 8t + 3 m/s. v(2) = 8(2) + 3 = 16 + 3 = 19 \text{ m/s} Evaluate at t = 2 s. Instantaneous velocity at exactly 2 seconds is 19 m/s. \text{Units check: } \frac{d}{dt}[\text{meters}] = \frac{\text{meters}}{\text{seconds}} = \text{m/s} Units: the derivative of position (meters) with respect to time (seconds) always has units m/s. If you get different units, recheck your setup. Galileo's Falling Ball: Velocity and Acceleration from First Principles Galileo showed that objects fall with position $y(t) = \frac{1}{2}g t^2$ (measured downward from rest), where $g \approx 9.8$ m/s\textsuperscript{2}. Use the limit definition to find velocity $v(t) = y'(t)$, then find acceleration $a(t) = v'(t)$. Evaluate velocity at $t = 3$ s.   From y(t) = (1/2)gt^2: v(t) = gt, v(3) = 29.4 m/s, a(t) = g (constant). Galileo proved that all objects fall with the same constant acceleration regardless of mass — and here you derived it algebraically. v(t) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{y(t+h) - y(t)}{h} Write the definition. Treat g as a constant (about 9.8) throughout — it is a fixed number, not a variable. y(t+h) = \frac{1}{2}g(t+h)^2 Substitute (t+h) for t. The factor (1/2)g is a constant multiplier that passes through the expansion unchanged. (t+h)^2 = t^2 + 2th + h^2 Expand using (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 with a = t, b = h. Same rule as ex1. y(t+h) = \frac{g}{2}(t^2 + 2th + h^2) = \frac{g}{2}t^2 + \frac{g}{2} \cdot 2th + \frac{g}{2}h^2 Distribute g/2 to each of the three terms. = \frac{g}{2}t^2 + gth + \frac{g}{2}h^2 Simplify the middle term: (g/2) times 2th = gth (the 2s cancel). y(t+h) - y(t) = \frac{g}{2}t^2 + gth + \frac{g}{2}h^2 - \frac{g}{2}t^2 Subtract y(t) = (g/2)t^2. The (g/2)t^2 terms cancel. = gth + \frac{g}{2}h^2 Two h-terms remain: gth and (g/2)h^2. Check: both contain h. gth + \frac{g}{2}h^2 = h \cdot gt + h \cdot \frac{g}{2}h = h\left(gt + \frac{g}{2}h\right) Factor h: gth = h times gt, and (g/2)h^2 = h times (g/2)h. Both terms contain h, apply the distributive law in reverse. \frac{y(t+h)-y(t)}{h} = \frac{h(gt + \frac{g}{2}h)}{h} = gt + \frac{g}{2}h Cancel h/h (h is nonzero). Difference quotient equals gt + (g/2)h. v(t) = \lim_{h \to 0}\left(gt + \frac{g}{2}h\right) = gt Take h to 0. The (g/2)h term vanishes. Velocity function: v(t) = gt. v(3) = 9.8 \times 3 = 29.4 \text{ m/s} At t = 3 s, the object is falling at 29.4 m/s. Plug in g = 9.8 and t = 3. a(t) = v'(t) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{v(t+h) - v(t)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{g(t+h) - gt}{h} Find acceleration by differentiating velocity. v(t) = gt is a linear function — use the same definition. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{gt + gh - gt}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{gh}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} g = g The gt terms cancel. gh/h = g (cancel h/h). Limit of constant g is g. a(t) = g \approx 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2 Acceleration is constant — the same 9.8 m/s^2 regardless of how long the object has been falling. Gotcha: constant acceleration does NOT mean constant velocity. Velocity v(t) = gt increases linearly with time. Constant acceleration means velocity increases by g every second — the change in velocity is steady, not the velocity itself. Full Quadratic — Profit Function A company's weekly profit from selling $x$ units is $P(x) = -2x^2 + 120x - 500$ dollars. Find $P'(x)$ from first principles. Evaluate at $x = 20$ units and find the unit count that maximizes profit.   P'(x) = -4x + 120. Marginal profit at x = 20 is $40/unit. Maximum profit ($1300) occurs at x = 30 units where P'(30) = 0. P'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{P(x+h) - P(x)}{h} Write the definition. In economics, P'(x) is called marginal profit — the rate at which profit changes per additional unit sold. P(x+h) = -2(x+h)^2 + 120(x+h) - 500 Substitute (x+h) wherever x appears. Three terms: quadratic, linear, and constant. -2(x+h)^2 = -2(x^2 + 2xh + h^2) Expand (x+h)^2 first using (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2. = -2x^2 - 4xh - 2h^2 Distribute -2 to every term: -2 times x^2 = -2x^2, -2 times 2xh = -4xh, -2 times h^2 = -2h^2. The negative coefficient distributes to all three. 120(x+h) = 120x + 120h Distribute 120. P(x+h) = -2x^2 - 4xh - 2h^2 + 120x + 120h - 500 Combine all expanded pieces. P(x+h) - P(x) = (-2x^2 - 4xh - 2h^2 + 120x + 120h - 500) - (-2x^2 + 120x - 500) Subtract P(x) with parentheses. The entire expression (-2x^2 + 120x - 500) gets negated. = -2x^2 - 4xh - 2h^2 + 120x + 120h - 500 + 2x^2 - 120x + 500 Prerequisite: distribute the minus sign. -(-2x^2 + 120x - 500) = +2x^2 - 120x + 500. Every sign inside the parentheses flips. = -4xh - 2h^2 + 120h Collect like terms: -2x^2 + 2x^2 = 0, 120x - 120x = 0, -500 + 500 = 0. Three h-terms survive. Good — every remaining term has h. -4xh - 2h^2 + 120h = h(-4x - 2h + 120) Factor h: -4xh = h times (-4x), -2h^2 = h times (-2h), 120h = h times 120. All three terms share h as a factor. Apply distributive law in reverse. \frac{P(x+h)-P(x)}{h} = -4x - 2h + 120 Cancel h/h (h nonzero in the limit). P'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}(-4x - 2h + 120) = -4x + 120 Take h to 0. The -2h term vanishes. P'(20) = -4(20) + 120 = -80 + 120 = \$40 \text{ per unit} Marginal profit at x = 20 is $40 per unit. If you sell the 21st unit, profit increases by approximately $40. P'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow -4x + 120 = 0 Prerequisite algebra — finding a zero of a linear expression: set P'(x) = 0 and solve. 4x = 120 \Rightarrow x = 30 Add 4x to both sides: 4x = 120. Divide both sides by 4: x = 30. At x = 30, slope of the profit curve is zero — the profit is at its peak. Below 30 units, P'(x) > 0 (profit growing). Above 30, P'(x) < 0 (profit shrinking). This is a preview of optimization — finding maximum/minimum values using derivatives. P(30) = -2(30)^2 + 120(30) - 500 = -1800 + 3600 - 500 = \$1300 Maximum weekly profit is $1,300, achieved at exactly 30 units. Rational Function — Dose-Response Model The fraction of drug receptors activated at dose $x$ follows $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x+1}$. Find $f'(x)$ from the limit definition. This tells a pharmacologist how sensitive receptor activation is to a small change in dose.   f'(x/(x+1)) = 1/(x+1)^2. Key algebra: combine the fraction difference using LCD, let the numerator simplify to h, then cancel h with the division by h. f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\dfrac{x+h}{x+h+1} - \dfrac{x}{x+1}}{h} Write the definition and substitute. f(x+h) means replace x with (x+h) in x/(x+1): get (x+h)/((x+h)+1) = (x+h)/(x+h+1). The result is a compound fraction whose numerator is a difference of two rational expressions. \text{LCD of } (x+h+1) \text{ and } (x+1) \text{ is } (x+h+1)(x+1) Prerequisite: to subtract rational expressions, convert both to a common denominator. These two denominators share no common factor (h makes them different), so the LCD is their product. \frac{x+h}{x+h+1} - \frac{x}{x+1} = \frac{(x+h)(x+1) - x(x+h+1)}{(x+h+1)(x+1)} Convert both fractions to the LCD and combine into one fraction by subtracting the numerators. (x+h)(x+1) = x^2 + x + xh + h Expand using FOIL: x times x = x^2, x times 1 = x, h times x = xh, h times 1 = h. x(x+h+1) = x^2 + xh + x Distribute x: x times x = x^2, x times h = xh, x times 1 = x. (x+h)(x+1) - x(x+h+1) = (x^2 + x + xh + h) - (x^2 + xh + x) Write the subtraction of both expanded numerators. = x^2 + x + xh + h - x^2 - xh - x = h Distribute the minus sign and collect like terms: x^2 - x^2 = 0, x - x = 0, xh - xh = 0. Only h remains. The numerator collapses to a single h. \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} = \frac{1}{h} \cdot \frac{h}{(x+h+1)(x+1)} = \frac{1}{(x+h+1)(x+1)} The full difference quotient: divide the fraction difference by h. The h from the numerator cancels the h we are dividing by. f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{1}{(x+h+1)(x+1)} = \frac{1}{(x+1)^2} Substitute h = 0: (x+h+1) becomes (x+1). Denominator becomes (x+1)^2. f'(x) = \frac{1}{(x+1)^2} The derivative is always positive — receptor activation always increases with dose. But f'(x) shrinks as x grows. At dose 0: f'(0) = 1 (steep response, each extra unit of drug has big effect). At dose 9: f'(9) = 1/100 (nearly saturated, extra drug has tiny effect). This is diminishing returns — a universal biological pattern. Marginal Cost and the Approximation Error A factory's total daily cost is $C(x) = 0.02x^2 + 40x + 300$ dollars to produce $x$ units. Find marginal cost $C'(x)$ from first principles. Evaluate at $x = 100$ and compute the actual cost of the 101st unit to see how close the derivative approximation is.   C'(x) = 0.04x + 40. At x = 100, C'(100) = $44/unit. Actual cost of 101st unit = $44.02. The derivative gives a linear approximation; the error of $0.02 comes from the quadratic term. C'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{C(x+h) - C(x)}{h} Marginal cost is the derivative of total cost. Economic interpretation: C'(x) is the approximate cost of producing one more unit when already producing x. C(x+h) = 0.02(x+h)^2 + 40(x+h) + 300 Substitute (x+h) wherever x appears. 0.02(x+h)^2 = 0.02(x^2 + 2xh + h^2) = 0.02x^2 + 0.04xh + 0.02h^2 Expand (x+h)^2, then distribute 0.02: 0.02 times x^2 = 0.02x^2, 0.02 times 2xh = 0.04xh, 0.02 times h^2 = 0.02h^2. 40(x+h) = 40x + 40h Distribute 40. C(x+h) - C(x) = 0.04xh + 0.02h^2 + 40h Subtract C(x) = 0.02x^2 + 40x + 300. All non-h terms cancel: 0.02x^2 - 0.02x^2 = 0, 40x - 40x = 0, 300 - 300 = 0. Three h-terms remain. = h(0.04x + 0.02h + 40) Factor h: 0.04xh = h times 0.04x, 0.02h^2 = h times 0.02h, 40h = h times 40. Apply distributive law in reverse. C'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}(0.04x + 0.02h + 40) = 0.04x + 40 Cancel h/h, take h to 0. Marginal cost function: C'(x) = 0.04x + 40. C'(100) = 0.04(100) + 40 = 4 + 40 = \$44 \text{ per unit} Derivative says the 101st unit costs approximately $44. C(101) = 0.02(101)^2 + 40(101) + 300 Now compute the exact cost at 101 units to verify the approximation. 101^2 = (100+1)^2 = 10000 + 200 + 1 = 10201 Prerequisite: expand 101^2 using (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 with a = 100, b = 1. C(101) = 0.02(10201) + 40(101) + 300 = 204.02 + 4040 + 300 = 4544.02 Arithmetic: 0.02 times 10201 = 204.02, 40 times 101 = 4040. C(100) = 0.02(10000) + 4000 + 300 = 200 + 4000 + 300 = 4500.00 Cost at exactly 100 units. C(101) - C(100) = 4544.02 - 4500.00 = \$44.02 Exact cost of producing the 101st unit: $44.02. C'(100) = \$44 \approx \$44.02 = C(101) - C(100) The derivative approximation ($44) is very close to the exact discrete cost ($44.02). The $0.02 error exists because the derivative measures the instantaneous rate at x = 100, but the actual question asks about a finite step from 100 to 101. As the step size shrinks (say, a half unit instead of a full unit), the approximation error also shrinks. This is the fundamental link between derivatives and differences. Rate of Cooling — Newton's Law Word Problem A casserole at 400\textdegree{}F cools after removal from the oven. Its temperature model is $T(t) = 400 - 150t + 20t^2$ (degrees F, $t$ in hours, $0 \leq t \leq 4$). Find $T'(t)$ from first principles. Evaluate at $t = 1$ hr and find when cooling is fastest.   T'(t) = -150 + 40t deg-F/hr. At t = 1 hr, T'(1) = -110 deg-F/hr. Fastest cooling is at t = 0: T'(0) = -150 deg-F/hr. T'(t) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{T(t+h) - T(t)}{h} T'(t) gives instantaneous rate of temperature change in degrees F per hour. A negative value means the temperature is dropping. T(t+h) = 400 - 150(t+h) + 20(t+h)^2 Substitute (t+h) for t. Three terms need expansion. -150(t+h) = -150t - 150h Distribute -150. Note: -150 times h = -150h (negative coefficient, so h-term is negative). 20(t+h)^2 = 20(t^2 + 2th + h^2) = 20t^2 + 40th + 20h^2 Expand (t+h)^2 then distribute 20. T(t+h) = 400 - 150t - 150h + 20t^2 + 40th + 20h^2 Assemble the full expansion. T(t+h) - T(t) = (400 - 150t - 150h + 20t^2 + 40th + 20h^2) - (400 - 150t + 20t^2) Subtract T(t) = 400 - 150t + 20t^2 with parentheses. = -150h + 40th + 20h^2 Collect like terms: 400 - 400 = 0, -150t + 150t = 0, 20t^2 - 20t^2 = 0. Three h-terms remain. -150h + 40th + 20h^2 = h(-150 + 40t + 20h) Factor h: -150h = h times (-150), 40th = h times 40t, 20h^2 = h times 20h. All three share h. T'(t) = \lim_{h \to 0}(-150 + 40t + 20h) = -150 + 40t Cancel h/h, take h to 0. T'(1) = -150 + 40(1) = -110 \;{^\circ}\text{F/hr} At t = 1 hour, temperature is dropping at 110 degrees F per hour. Negative sign confirms cooling. \text{Units: } T \text{ in }^\circ\text{F},\; t \text{ in hours} \Rightarrow T'(t) \text{ in }^\circ\text{F/hr} Units check: derivative of temperature (degrees F) with respect to time (hours) must be degrees-F per hour. T'(t) = -150 + 40t \text{ is an increasing function of } t The cooling rate T'(t) has slope +40 with respect to t. As t increases, T'(t) becomes less negative — the food cools more slowly over time. This matches Newton's law of cooling: cooling rate is proportional to the temperature difference from the surroundings. T'(0) = -150 \;{^\circ}\text{F/hr} \text{ (fastest cooling)} Cooling is fastest at t = 0, the moment the casserole is removed. The temperature difference from room temperature is greatest then. As it cools, the difference shrinks and the rate of cooling slows. Building the Power Rule: f(x) = x\u2074 f(x) = x^4. \text{ Find } f'(x) \text{ from the limit definition. Then compare your results from ex1, ex2, and this example to state the general power rule pattern.}   f'(x^4) = 4x^3. Confirmed: the power rule pattern d/dx[x^n] = nx^{n-1} holds for n = 2, 3, 4. The next lesson proves it for all n. f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(x+h)^4 - x^4}{h} Set up the definition. The challenge: expand (x+h)^4 completely. (x+h)^4 = [(x+h)^2]^2 Prerequisite strategy: do not expand (x+h)^4 all at once. Instead, rewrite it as [(x+h)^2]^2, use the result (x+h)^2 = x^2 + 2xh + h^2 from ex1, then square that result. Breaking into two steps makes the algebra manageable. = (x^2 + 2xh + h^2)^2 Substitute (x+h)^2 = x^2 + 2xh + h^2. Now we need to square this trinomial. = (x^2 + 2xh + h^2)(x^2 + 2xh + h^2) Write it as the trinomial times itself. = x^2(x^2 + 2xh + h^2) + 2xh(x^2 + 2xh + h^2) + h^2(x^2 + 2xh + h^2) Prerequisite: distribute each of the three terms in the first factor across the entire second factor. Three groups — one per term. = (x^4 + 2x^3 h + x^2 h^2) + (2x^3 h + 4x^2 h^2 + 2xh^3) + (x^2 h^2 + 2xh^3 + h^4) Expand each group. x^2 times x^2 = x^4, x^2 times 2xh = 2x^3 h, x^2 times h^2 = x^2 h^2. Then 2xh times each term. Then h^2 times each term. = x^4 + 4x^3 h + 6x^2 h^2 + 4xh^3 + h^4 Collect like terms: 2x^3 h + 2x^3 h = 4x^3 h. x^2 h^2 + 4x^2 h^2 + x^2 h^2 = 6x^2 h^2. 2xh^3 + 2xh^3 = 4xh^3. The coefficients 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 match row 4 of Pascal's triangle — this is the binomial theorem. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{4x^3 h + 6x^2 h^2 + 4xh^3 + h^4}{h} Substitute into the difference quotient. Cancel x^4 - x^4 = 0. Four h-terms remain. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{h(4x^3 + 6x^2 h + 4xh^2 + h^3)}{h} Factor h from all four terms: 4x^3 h = h(4x^3), 6x^2 h^2 = h(6x^2 h), 4xh^3 = h(4xh^2), h^4 = h(h^3). = \lim_{h \to 0}(4x^3 + 6x^2 h + 4xh^2 + h^3) = 4x^3 Cancel h/h, take h to 0. The three h-containing terms vanish. Only 4x^3 survives. f(x) = x^2 \Rightarrow f'(x) = 2x^1 Pattern review — n = 2: exponent 2 became coefficient 2, new power is 1. f(x) = x^3 \Rightarrow f'(x) = 3x^2 n = 3: exponent 3 became coefficient 3, new power is 2. f(x) = x^4 \Rightarrow f'(x) = 4x^3 n = 4: exponent 4 became coefficient 4, new power is 3. \frac{d}{dx}[x^n] = nx^{n-1} Power rule — observed pattern: the exponent drops down as the leading coefficient, and the new exponent is n - 1. You have now confirmed this for n = 2, 3, and 4 by grinding through the limit definition. The next lesson proves this for all n using the binomial theorem. Once proved, you will never have to repeat this process — you will just use the rule instantly. But you needed to see where it comes from. Derivative of a Quadratic with Linear Term: x² + 3x \text{Let } f(x) = x^2 + 3x. \text{ Use the limit definition to find } f'(x). \text{ Then evaluate } f'(2) \text{ and interpret the result as slope and marginal change.}   f'(x) = 2x + 3. At x = 2 the slope is 7. This example shows how the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives — a preview of the linearity of differentiation that we will prove formally later. Algebra keys: always expand fully before subtracting, factor h completely, and remember why h/h cancellation is legal in the limit. f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} Always begin with the exact limit definition. This is the fundamental algorithm for every derivative we compute from first principles. Never skip it — it keeps sign errors and algebra mistakes visible. f(x+h) = (x+h)^2 + 3(x+h) Substitute (x+h) for every occurrence of x in the original function. There are two places: inside the square and in the linear term. (x+h)^2 = x^2 + 2xh + h^2 Prerequisite algebra from ex1: expand the square using (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2. Do not write (x+h)^2 as x^2 + h^2 — the middle term 2xh is essential and is the most common early mistake. 3(x+h) = 3x + 3h Distribute the 3. The coefficient 3 multiplies both x and h. f(x+h) = x^2 + 2xh + h^2 + 3x + 3h Combine both expanded pieces. f(x+h) - f(x) = (x^2 + 2xh + h^2 + 3x + 3h) - (x^2 + 3x) Write the subtraction with full parentheses around f(x) to protect every sign when distributing the negative. = x^2 + 2xh + h^2 + 3x + 3h - x^2 - 3x Distribute the minus: every term in f(x) flips sign. This is another high-error step — forgetting to change the sign of 3x is common. = 2xh + h^2 + 3h Cancel like terms: x^2 - x^2 = 0 and 3x - 3x = 0. Only terms containing h survive — this is the expected pattern in any derivative calculation. 2xh + h^2 + 3h = h(2x + h + 3) Factor h out of every term using the distributive property in reverse: each piece contains h (2xh = h·2x, h^2 = h·h, 3h = h·3). Verify by distributing back if needed. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{h(2x + h + 3)}{h} Substitute the factored form back into the difference quotient. = \lim_{h \to 0} (2x + h + 3) Cancel h/h = 1. This cancellation is valid because h approaches 0 but is never actually zero during the process — we are not dividing by zero. = 2x + 0 + 3 = 2x + 3 Now safely substitute h = 0. The h term disappears, leaving the derivative function. f'(x) = 2x + 3 The derivative is 2x + 3. Pattern check: the derivative of x^2 is 2x (from ex1), the derivative of 3x is 3 (from the linear case in ex5), and constants would give 0. The operations are linear — derivatives respect addition. f'(2) = 2(2) + 3 = 7 Evaluate at x = 2. This is the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where x = 2 (the point itself is (2, f(2)) = (2, 4 + 6) = (2, 10)).  Use the limit definition of the derivative to find the equation of the tangent line to f(x) = 2x^2 - 3x at x = 1. First find f'(x) using the definition, then evaluate at x = 1 to get the slope. Use f(1) for the y-coordinate of the point. y = x - 2  f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{[2(x+h)^2 - 3(x+h)] - [2x^2 - 3x]}{h} Set up the difference quotient for f(x) = 2x² - 3x. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{2(x^2+2xh+h^2) - 3x - 3h - 2x^2 + 3x}{h} Expand (x+h)² = x²+2xh+h² and distribute the 2 and -3. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{2x^2 + 4xh + 2h^2 - 3x - 3h - 2x^2 + 3x}{h} Distribute fully. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{4xh + 2h^2 - 3h}{h} Cancel: 2x² - 2x² = 0 and -3x + 3x = 0. = \lim_{h \to 0} (4x + 2h - 3) = 4x - 3 Factor h and cancel, then let h → 0. f'(1) = 4(1) - 3 = 1, \quad f(1) = 2(1)^2 - 3(1) = -1 Evaluate slope f'(1) = 1 and y-coordinate f(1) = -1. y - (-1) = 1 \cdot (x - 1) \implies y = x - 2 Use point-slope form with point (1, -1) and slope 1.  Prove from the limit definition that \dfrac{d}{dx}[x^4] = 4x^3. You will need the expansion (x+h)^4 = x^4 + 4x^3h + 6x^2h^2 + 4xh^3 + h^4. Expand (x+h)^4 using the given binomial expansion, subtract x^4, divide by h, then let h→0. Identify which terms survive after h→0. \dfrac{d}{dx}[x^4] = 4x^3  \frac{d}{dx}[x^4] = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(x+h)^4 - x^4}{h} Apply the limit definition. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(x^4 + 4x^3 h + 6x^2 h^2 + 4xh^3 + h^4) - x^4}{h} Substitute the binomial expansion of (x+h)^4. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{4x^3 h + 6x^2 h^2 + 4xh^3 + h^4}{h} Cancel x^4 - x^4 = 0. = \lim_{h \to 0} (4x^3 + 6x^2 h + 4xh^2 + h^3) Divide every term in the numerator by h. Every term had at least one factor of h. = 4x^3 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 4x^3 Let h → 0. Every term containing h vanishes. Only 4x³ survives.  Let f(x) = x\sin(1/x) for x \neq 0 and f(0) = 0. Prove that f is differentiable at x = 0 by evaluating the limit definition directly. Use the Squeeze Theorem. Set up the difference quotient at a = 0. You will have [f(h) - f(0)] / h = h·sin(1/h) / h = sin(1/h). But sin(1/h) oscillates wildly — think about what bounds sin always satisfies, then squeeze. f(x) = x\sin(1/x) \text{ is NOT differentiable at } 0. \text{ The correct differentiable version is } g(x) = x^2\sin(1/x),\text{ for which } g'(0) = 0 \text{ by the Squeeze Theorem.}  f'(0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(0+h) - f(0)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(h) - 0}{h} Write the derivative at x = 0 using f(0) = 0. = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{h \sin(1/h)}{h} Substitute f(h) = h·sin(1/h) (valid for h ≠ 0, which is exactly what the limit requires). = \lim_{h \to 0} \sin\left(\frac{1}{h}\right) Cancel h/h. Now we have the limit of sin(1/h) as h → 0. This limit does NOT exist in the ordinary sense — sin(1/h) oscillates infinitely often near h = 0. -1 \leq \sin\left(\frac{1}{h}\right) \leq 1 \quad \text{for all } h \neq 0 Wait — we made an error above. We should NOT have canceled so quickly. Let us restart from the difference quotient before canceling. \frac{f(h) - f(0)}{h} = \frac{h \sin(1/h)}{h} = \sin(1/h)? \quad \text{Hmm — but this limit does not exist!} This seems to show f is NOT differentiable at 0. But wait — go back to the un-canceled form: f(h)/h = sin(1/h). Indeed this has no limit. So... is f differentiable? \text{Reconsider: } \frac{f(h)}{h} = \frac{h\sin(1/h)}{h} = \sin(1/h) The cancellation is correct. The issue is that sin(1/h) does NOT have a limit as h→0. Therefore f'(0) does not exist for f(x) = x·sin(1/x). This function is actually NOT differentiable at 0. \text{Compare with } g(x) = x^2 \sin(1/x),\; g(0)=0 The function x·sin(1/x) is NOT differentiable at 0. The differentiable version requires the extra factor of x. With g(x) = x²·sin(1/x), the difference quotient becomes h·sin(1/h), which DOES go to 0 by the Squeeze Theorem. g'(0) = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{h^2 \sin(1/h)}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0} h\sin(1/h) For g(x) = x² sin(1/x), the difference quotient reduces to h·sin(1/h). -|h| \leq h\sin(1/h) \leq |h| Since |sin(1/h)| ≤ 1 for all h ≠ 0, we have |h·sin(1/h)| ≤ |h|, giving the squeeze inequality. \lim_{h\to 0}(-|h|) = 0 \leq \lim_{h\to 0} h\sin(1/h) \leq \lim_{h\to 0}|h| = 0 Both bounding functions approach 0 as h → 0. By the Squeeze Theorem, the middle term also approaches 0. \therefore g'(0) = 0 The Squeeze Theorem gives g'(0) = 0. So g(x) = x²·sin(1/x) IS differentiable at 0, with derivative 0.  Let $f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & x \leq 1 \\ 2x - 1 & x > 1 \end{cases}$. Is $f$ differentiable at $x = 1$? Compute both one-sided difference quotients. Compute the left-hand and right-hand limits of [f(1+h)−f(1)]/h separately. For h<0, use the x² branch; for h>0, use the 2x−1 branch. Check if they agree. f is differentiable at x=1 with f'(1)=2. Both pieces meet smoothly: the parabola's slope at x=1 is 2x|_{x=1}=2, which matches the linear piece's slope of 2.  f(1) = 1^2 = 1 At x=1 we use the left branch: f(1)=1. f'_-(1) = \lim_{h \to 0^-}\frac{(1+h)^2 - 1}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-}\frac{1+2h+h^2-1}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-}(2+h) = 2 For h<0, 1+h<1 so use the x² branch. Factor and cancel h. f'_+(1) = \lim_{h \to 0^+}\frac{[2(1+h)-1] - 1}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^+}\frac{2h}{h} = 2 For h>0, 1+h>1 so use the 2x−1 branch. f(1+h)=2(1+h)−1=1+2h. f'_-(1) = 2 = f'_+(1) Both one-sided derivatives agree. f'(1) = 2 Since the one-sided limits match, f is differentiable at x=1 with derivative 2.
documents.proofs: There is a profound relationship between differentiability and continuity. Intuitively, if a function has a well-defined tangent slope at a point, it cannot have a jump or hole there — a broken function cannot have a smooth tangent. This is made precise by an important theorem. THEOREM (Differentiability Implies Continuity): If f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a. PROOF: We want to show that the limit of f(x) as x approaches a equals f(a), or equivalently that the limit of [f(x) - f(a)] as x approaches a is 0. We write f(x) - f(a) = [f(x) - f(a)] / (x - a) times (x - a). The first factor, [f(x)-f(a)]/(x-a), approaches f'(a) as x → a (by the alternative definition of the derivative). The second factor, (x - a), approaches 0. By the product law for limits, the product approaches f'(a) · 0 = 0. Therefore f(x) - f(a) → 0, which means f(x) → f(a). This proves continuity. The converse of this theorem is FALSE. A function can be continuous at a point without being differentiable there. The classic example is f(x) = |x| at x = 0. This function is continuous everywhere — there are no jumps or holes. But it has a "corner" at x = 0 where the graph changes direction sharply, and at that corner the derivative does not exist. PROOF that |x| is not differentiable at 0: We compute the left and right derivatives. From the right (h → 0⁺): [|0+h| - |0|] / h = |h|/h = h/h = 1, so the right-hand derivative is 1. From the left (h → 0⁻): [|0+h| - |0|] / h = |h|/h = (-h)/h = -1, so the left-hand derivative is -1. Since 1 ≠ -1, the two-sided limit does not exist, and f is not differentiable at 0. There are exactly three geometric ways a function can fail to be differentiable at a point, even while remaining continuous there. First: a corner, where the left and right derivatives both exist but are unequal (example: |x| at 0). Second: a cusp, where one or both one-sided derivatives are infinite but with opposite signs, causing the curve to come to a sharp pointed tip (example: x^(2/3) at 0 — the tangent line becomes vertical). Third: a vertical tangent, where the difference quotient grows without bound as h → 0, meaning the tangent line would be vertical (example: x^(1/3) at 0). In all three cases, the function is continuous but the limit of the difference quotient fails to be a finite real number. A function can also fail to be differentiable at a point of discontinuity, of course — but that failure is less subtle, since differentiability requires continuity. Differentiability Implies Continuity \text{If } f \text{ is differentiable at } a, \text{ then } f \text{ is continuous at } a. The Converse is False f(x) = |x| \text{ is continuous at } 0 \text{ but } f'(0) \text{ does not exist.} Three Ways to Fail Differentiability \text{(1) Corner: } f'_-(a) \neq f'_+(a) \\ \text{(2) Cusp: one-sided derivatives are } \pm\infty \\ \text{(3) Vertical tangent: } \left|\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}\right| \to \infty
