Dependency Hierarchy Solver: H(x) = sin(x³) Visualize the full dependency graph of a composition and read off the chain rule product from the graph edges. Recursive Proof Stepper: d/dx[sin(x³)] Step through the chain rule proof one sub-problem at a time, deepening the recursive structure of the argument. Why Chain Rule Works (Check by Expansion) Differentiate f(x) = (x^2+1)^3 two ways: (1) expand first, (2) use chain rule. Verify both match. Both methods agree exactly. Chain rule is the compact form of algebra you would otherwise repeatedly expand. (x^2+1)^3 = x^6 + 3x^4 + 3x^2 + 1 Method 1: expand using the binomial identity. f'(x)=6x^5+12x^3+6x Differentiate the expanded polynomial term by term. \text{Method 2: let } u=x^2+1,\;f=u^3 Set up outer and inner layers for chain rule. f'(x)=3u^2\cdot u'=3(x^2+1)^2\cdot2x=6x(x^2+1)^2 Apply outer derivative times inner derivative. 6x(x^2+1)^2=6x(x^4+2x^2+1)=6x^5+12x^3+6x Expand to confirm exact agreement with Method 1. Chain Rule with Power Function f(x) = (3x^2 - 1)^5. \text{ Find } f'(x). f'(x) = 30x(3x²-1)⁴. The chain rule contributed the factor of 6x (the derivative of the inner function), which is what distinguishes this from just differentiating u⁵. \text{Outer function: } F(u) = u^5 \quad \text{Inner function: } u = g(x) = 3x^2 - 1 Identify the outer and inner functions. The outer function is "raise to the fifth power" and the inner is 3x²-1. F'(u) = 5u^4, \quad g'(x) = 6x Differentiate the outer function (power rule: bring down 5, reduce exponent to 4) and differentiate the inner function separately. f'(x) = F'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x) = 5(3x^2-1)^4 \cdot 6x Apply the chain rule: differentiate the outer function (giving 5u⁴) evaluated at the inner function (replacing u with 3x²-1), then multiply by the derivative of the inner function. = 30x(3x^2-1)^4 Multiply the constants 5 and 6 together: 5·6 = 30. The (3x²-1)⁴ factor remains as is. Chain Rule with Square Root f(x) = \sqrt{x^2+1}. \text{ Find } f'(x). f'(x) = x/√(x²+1). Note that the derivative is 0 at x = 0 (horizontal tangent at the bottom of the U-shaped curve) and grows toward ±1 as x → ±∞. f(x) = (x^2+1)^{1/2} Rewrite the square root as a power of 1/2 to clearly see the power function structure. \text{Outer: } F(u) = u^{1/2}, \quad \text{Inner: } u = x^2 + 1 Identify the outer function as the square root (or equivalently the 1/2 power) and the inner function as x²+1. F'(u) = \frac{1}{2}u^{-1/2} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}, \quad g'(x) = 2x Differentiate outer (power rule with n=1/2) and inner separately. f'(x) = \frac{1}{2}(x^2+1)^{-1/2} \cdot 2x Chain rule: F'(g(x)) · g'(x). Replace u with x²+1 in the outer derivative, then multiply by 2x. = \frac{2x}{2(x^2+1)^{1/2}} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} Simplify: the factor of 2 in the numerator cancels with the 2 from the power rule denominator. Rewrite the negative power as a square root. Chain Rule with Sine f(x) = \sin(5x^3). \text{ Find } f'(x). f'(x) = 15x² cos(5x³). This illustrates the general pattern: d/dx[sin(g(x))] = cos(g(x))·g'(x). The argument of cosine is the same as the argument of sine was. \text{Outer: } F(u) = \sin(u), \quad \text{Inner: } u = 5x^3 The outer function is the sine function and the inner function is 5x³. F'(u) = \cos(u), \quad g'(x) = 15x^2 The derivative of sine is cosine (covered in the trig derivatives lesson). The derivative of the inner function 5x³ is 15x² by the power and constant multiple rules. f'(x) = \cos(5x^3) \cdot 15x^2 Apply the chain rule: differentiate the outer function (giving cos(u)), evaluated at the inner (replacing u with 5x³), then multiply by the inner derivative 15x². = 15x^2 \cos(5x^3) Rewrite with the constant factor first for standard form. Chain Rule with Exponential (Preview) f(x) = e^{x^2}. \text{ Find } f'(x). \text{ (Use the fact that } \frac{d}{du}[e^u] = e^u.) f'(x) = 2xe^(x²). The function e^(x²) grows enormously fast but its derivative is not just itself — the chain rule contributes the factor of 2x from the exponent. \text{Outer: } F(u) = e^u, \quad \text{Inner: } u = x^2 The outer function is e to the power u, and the inner function is x². F'(u) = e^u, \quad g'(x) = 2x The key property of e^u is that it equals its own derivative (proved in the exponential derivatives lesson). The inner derivative is 2x. f'(x) = e^{x^2} \cdot 2x Apply the chain rule: the outer derivative e^u evaluated at u = x² gives e^(x²), times the inner derivative 2x. = 2x\,e^{x^2} Rewrite with the constant factor first. Chain Rule: Do Not Confuse (sin x)⁴ with sin(x⁴) f(x) = (\sin x)^4. \text{ Find } f'(x). \text{ Also note why this is different from } \sin(x^4). f'(x) = 4(sin x)³ cos x = 4 sin³(x) cos(x). The position of the exponent completely changes the meaning: (sin x)⁴ means sin^4(x) [sine, then power], while sin(x⁴) means the sine of x⁴ [power, then sine]. \text{Outer: } F(u) = u^4, \quad \text{Inner: } u = \sin x In (sin x)⁴, the outer function is "raise to the fourth power" and the inner function is sin x. The entire sine is being raised to a power. F'(u) = 4u^3, \quad g'(x) = \cos x Differentiate outer: 4u³. Differentiate inner: d/dx[sin x] = cos x. f'(x) = 4(\sin x)^3 \cdot \cos x Chain rule result. This is often written as 4 sin³(x) cos(x). \text{Compare: } \frac{d}{dx}[\sin(x^4)] = \cos(x^4) \cdot 4x^3 For sin(x⁴), the outer function is sine and the inner is x⁴. The derivative of sine is cosine evaluated at x⁴, times the inner derivative 4x³. These are completely different functions. Triple Composition f(x) = \sin^4(x^2). \text{ Find } f'(x). \text{ (This is } (\sin(x^2))^4.) f'(x) = 8x sin³(x²) cos(x²). Triple compositions peel away one layer at a time, each contributing its own derivative as a multiplicative factor. f(x) = [\sin(x^2)]^4 Rewrite explicitly to show the structure: we are raising sin(x²) to the fourth power. This is a triple composition: the outermost is u⁴, the middle is sin, the innermost is x². \text{Layer 1 (outermost): } F(u) = u^4 Peel layer 1: apply the power rule outside and keep sin(x²) completely untouched inside the brackets. \text{Layer 2 (middle): } G(v) = \sin(v) Peel layer 2: now derive sine, again keeping its inner argument x² exactly as-is. \text{Layer 3 (innermost): } H(x) = x^2 The innermost function is x². F'(u) = 4u^3, \quad G'(v) = \cos(v), \quad H'(x) = 2x Core layer: derive x² last to get 2x, then multiply by everything collected from outer and middle layers. f'(x) = F'(G(H(x))) \cdot G'(H(x)) \cdot H'(x) Apply the extended chain rule: outer derivative (evaluated all the way at the inside) times middle derivative (evaluated at innermost) times innermost derivative. = 4[\sin(x^2)]^3 \cdot \cos(x^2) \cdot 2x Substitute: F'(G(H(x))) = 4[sin(x²)]³, G'(H(x)) = cos(x²), H'(x) = 2x. = 8x\sin^3(x^2)\cos(x^2) Collect constants: 4·2x = 8x. Write in standard form. Leibniz Form of Chain Rule If y = u^5 \text{ and } u = 3x^2 - 1, \text{ find } dy/dx \text{ using Leibniz form.} This gives the same answer as the composition form: dy/dx = 30x(3x²-1)⁴. The Leibniz form is particularly clear for related rates problems where the intermediate variable u has physical meaning. \frac{dy}{du} = 5u^4 Differentiate y = u⁵ with respect to u, treating u as the independent variable. \frac{du}{dx} = 6x Differentiate u = 3x² - 1 with respect to x. \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx} = 5u^4 \cdot 6x Multiply the two rates together per the chain rule in Leibniz form. The du "terms" appear to cancel like fractions, though this is a notational convenience, not literal cancellation. = 30x \cdot u^4 = 30x(3x^2-1)^4 Substitute back u = 3x²-1 to express everything in terms of x. The final answer must be in terms of the original variable x. Chain Rule Combined with Quotient Rule f(x) = \dfrac{(x^2+1)^{3/2}}{x+1}. \text{ Find } f'(x). f'(x) = √(x²+1) · (2x²+3x-1) / (x+1)². Factoring out the common (x²+1)^(1/2) factor from the quotient rule numerator is a key simplification technique. f(x) = \frac{N(x)}{D(x)} \text{ where } N(x) = (x^2+1)^{3/2}, \; D(x) = x+1 Identify the numerator and denominator. The numerator requires the chain rule; the denominator is simple. N'(x) = \frac{3}{2}(x^2+1)^{1/2} \cdot 2x = 3x(x^2+1)^{1/2} = \frac{3x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} \cdot (x^2+1) Differentiate the numerator using the chain rule: outer is u^(3/2) giving (3/2)u^(1/2), inner is x²+1 giving 2x. Simplify: (3/2)·2x = 3x. N'(x) = 3x(x^2+1)^{1/2} The derivative of the numerator is 3x√(x²+1). D'(x) = 1 The derivative of the denominator x+1 is simply 1. f'(x) = \frac{N'(x)D(x) - N(x)D'(x)}{[D(x)]^2} Apply the quotient rule formula. = \frac{3x(x^2+1)^{1/2}(x+1) - (x^2+1)^{3/2}(1)}{(x+1)^2} Substitute N, N', D, D' into the quotient rule. = \frac{(x^2+1)^{1/2}\left[3x(x+1) - (x^2+1)\right]}{(x+1)^2} {{algebra:factoring-fractional-powers|Factor out the lowest exponent (1/2)}} from both terms in the numerator. = \frac{(x^2+1)^{1/2}(3x^2 + 3x - x^2 - 1)}{(x+1)^2} Expand inside the brackets: 3x(x+1) = 3x²+3x, then subtract x²+1. = \frac{\sqrt{x^2+1}\,(2x^2 + 3x - 1)}{(x+1)^2} Combine like terms in the numerator: 3x²-x²=2x². Rewrite (x²+1)^(1/2) as √(x²+1). Mini Backprop Chain (Single Neuron) Let y = \sigma(z), z = wx+b, L = \tfrac12(y-t)^2. Find dL/dw. This local product is exactly the pattern repeated layer-by-layer in deep learning backpropagation. \frac{dL}{dy} = y-t Differentiate the squared loss with respect to output y. \frac{dy}{dz} = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z)) = y(1-y) Derivative of sigmoid activation. \frac{dz}{dw} = x For z = wx+b, derivative with respect to w is x. \frac{dL}{dw} = \frac{dL}{dy}\cdot\frac{dy}{dz}\cdot\frac{dz}{dw} = (y-t)\,y(1-y)\,x Multiply local derivatives along the computation graph. Hook Problem: Balloon Volume Rate A sphere has radius r(t)=2t. With V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3, find dV/dt at t=3. At t=3, volume is increasing at 288\pi cubic units per time unit. V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3,\quad r=2t Volume depends on radius, and radius depends on time. \frac{dV}{dr}=4\pi r^2,\quad \frac{dr}{dt}=2 Differentiate each stage with respect to its own variable. \frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{dV}{dr}\cdot\frac{dr}{dt}=4\pi r^2\cdot 2=8\pi r^2 Apply Leibniz chain form for related rates. Unit tracker: (cm^3/cm)*(cm/s)=cm^3/s, so multiplication is physically required. t=3 \Rightarrow r=2(3)=6 Evaluate the intermediate quantity first. \left.\frac{dV}{dt}\right|_{t=3}=8\pi(6)^2=288\pi Substitute r=6 into the rate formula. Abstract Function Trap — Reading a Table \begin{array}{l} \text{Let } h(x) = f(g(x)). \text{ The table gives values at selected points:} \\[6pt] \begin{array}{c|cccc} x & f(x) & g(x) & f'(x) & g'(x) \\\hline 1 & 4 & 3 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 7 & 2 & -2 & 4 \end{array} \\[6pt] \text{Find } h'(2) \text{ and } h'(3). \end{array} h'(2)=6 and h'(3)=20. The two-step rule: evaluate the inner function first, then look up the outer derivative at that value. On exams, reading f'(a) instead of f'(g(a)) is by far the most common Chain Rule error with tables. h'(x) = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x) Write the Chain Rule formula. This holds for any differentiable f and g — no explicit formula needed. h'(2) = f'\!\left(\underbrace{g(2)}_{?}\right) \cdot g'(2) To compute h'(2): we need f' evaluated at g(2), not at 2. Look up g(2) from the table first. g(2) = 1, \quad g'(2) = 3 \quad \text{(row } x=2\text{)} From the x=2 row: g(2)=1 and g'(2)=3. h'(2) = f'(\underbrace{1}_{g(2)}) \cdot 3 Substitute g(2)=1. We now need f'(1) — read from the x=1 row, not the x=2 row. f'(1) = 2 \implies h'(2) = 2 \cdot 3 = 6 From the x=1 row: f'(1)=2. Final answer: 2·3=6. h'(3) = f'(g(3)) \cdot g'(3) = f'(2) \cdot 4 = 5 \cdot 4 = 20 For h'(3): g(3)=2 (row x=3), g'(3)=4 (row x=3). Then f'(g(3))=f'(2)=5 (row x=2). Result: 5·4=20. Combo Rule Boss Fight — Product Rule + Chain Rule f(x) = x^3\sqrt{4x-1}. \text{ Find } f'(x). f'(x) = x²(14x-3)/√(4x-1). The outer rule was Product Rule; Chain Rule fired inside √(4x-1). The #1 mistake is reaching for Chain Rule first on a product — always identify the outermost operation before picking a rule. f(x) = \underbrace{x^3}_{A(x)} \cdot \underbrace{\sqrt{4x-1}}_{B(x)} The outermost operation is multiplication of x³ and √(4x-1). Product Rule is the outer rule. Chain Rule will appear only when differentiating B(x). A(x) = x^3 \implies A'(x) = 3x^2 Differentiate A = x³ by the power rule. B(x) = (4x-1)^{1/2} \implies B'(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}(4x-1)^{-1/2}\cdot 4 = \frac{2}{\sqrt{4x-1}} Differentiate B = (4x-1)^(1/2) by Chain Rule: outer gives (1/2)u^(-1/2), inner gives 4. Simplify: (1/2)·4 = 2. f'(x) = A'B + AB' = 3x^2\sqrt{4x-1} + x^3 \cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{4x-1}} Apply Product Rule: d/dx[AB] = A'B + AB'. = \frac{3x^2(4x-1) + 2x^3}{\sqrt{4x-1}} Write over common denominator √(4x-1). Multiply the first term top and bottom by √(4x-1). = \frac{x^2(12x - 3 + 2x)}{\sqrt{4x-1}} = \frac{x^2(14x-3)}{\sqrt{4x-1}} Factor out x² from the numerator: 3x²(4x-1)+2x³ = 12x³-3x²+2x³ = 14x³-3x² = x²(14x-3). The Ultimate Chain Rule Boss Fight h(x) = (2x + 1)^5 (3x - 2)^7. \; \text{Find } h'(x). h'(x) = (2x + 1)⁴(3x - 2)⁶(72x + 1). This is the 'Ultimate Boss' check: Product Rule on the outside, two Chain Rules on the inside, and a sophisticated factoring finale. h(x) = f(x)g(x) \implies h'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x) This is first and foremost a Product Rule problem because two distinct blocks are being multiplied. f(x) = (2x+1)^5 \implies f'(x) = 10(2x+1)^4 Differentiate the first factor using the Chain Rule (outer power 5, inner deriv 2). g(x) = (3x-2)^7 \implies g'(x) = 21(3x-2)^6 Differentiate the second factor using the Chain Rule (outer power 7, inner deriv 3). h'(x) = 10(2x+1)^4(3x-2)^7 + 21(2x+1)^5(3x-2)^6 Substitute derivatives into the Product Rule formula. h'(x) = (2x+1)^4(3x-2)^6 \left[ 10(3x-2) + 21(2x+1) \right] Factor out the common terms: the lowest powers (4 and 6) of each block. = (2x+1)^4(3x-2)^6 (72x + 1) Expand and simplify inside the square brackets: 30x - 20 + 42x + 21 = 72x + 1. \text{Differentiate } f(x) = (2x+1)^{10}. Treat (2x+1)^10 as a composition: outer function u^10, inner function 2x+1, and inner derivative 2. f'(x) = 20(2x+1)^9 \text{Outer: } F(u) = u^{10},\quad \text{Inner: } u = 2x+1 Identify the composition structure. F'(u) = 10u^9, \quad u' = 2 Differentiate each piece. f'(x) = 10(2x+1)^9 \cdot 2 = 20(2x+1)^9 Apply the chain rule and simplify. \text{Differentiate } f(x) = \sqrt{\dfrac{x^2+1}{x-1}}. Write as ((x²+1)/(x-1))^(1/2). The outer function is u^(1/2) and the inner function is the quotient (x²+1)/(x-1), which requires the quotient rule to differentiate. f'(x) = \dfrac{x^2-2x-1}{2(x-1)^{3/2}\sqrt{x^2+1}} f(x) = \left(\frac{x^2+1}{x-1}\right)^{1/2} Rewrite the square root as a power. \text{Let } u = \frac{x^2+1}{x-1}, \text{ so } f = u^{1/2} Define the inner function as the quotient. \frac{df}{du} = \frac{1}{2}u^{-1/2} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} Differentiate the outer square root. \frac{du}{dx} = \frac{2x(x-1) - (x^2+1)(1)}{(x-1)^2} = \frac{2x^2-2x-x^2-1}{(x-1)^2} = \frac{x^2-2x-1}{(x-1)^2} Apply the quotient rule to u = (x²+1)/(x-1). f'(x) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(\frac{x^2+1}{x-1}\right)^{-1/2} \cdot \frac{x^2-2x-1}{(x-1)^2} Combine via chain rule. = \frac{x^2-2x-1}{2(x-1)^2} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{x-1}{x^2+1}} = \frac{x^2-2x-1}{2(x-1)^{3/2}\sqrt{x^2+1}} Simplify u^(-1/2) = √((x-1)/(x²+1)) and combine with the denominator. \text{If } f \text{ is differentiable and } g(x) = [f(x^2+1)]^2, \text{ find } g'(x) \text{ in terms of } f \text{ and } f'. This is a triple composition: the outermost is squaring, the middle is f, the innermost is x²+1. Apply the extended chain rule. g'(x) = 4x\,f(x^2+1)\,f'(x^2+1) g(x) = [f(x^2+1)]^2 Recognize this as a composition of three layers: outermost is u², middle is f, innermost is x²+1. \text{Outer: } H(u) = u^2, \quad \text{Middle: } f(v) \text{ (given)}, \quad \text{Inner: } v = x^2+1 Name each layer. H'(u) = 2u, \quad f'(v) \text{ (given)}, \quad v' = 2x Differentiate each layer. g'(x) = H'(f(x^2+1)) \cdot f'(x^2+1) \cdot (x^2+1)' Apply the extended chain rule: outer derivative evaluated at middle-of-inner, times middle derivative evaluated at inner, times inner derivative. = 2[f(x^2+1)] \cdot f'(x^2+1) \cdot 2x Substitute: H'(f(x²+1)) = 2f(x²+1), the middle derivative at x²+1 is f'(x²+1), inner derivative is 2x. = 4x\,f(x^2+1)\,f'(x^2+1) Collect constants: 2·2x = 4x. \text{Given: } g(4)=2,\; g'(4)=-3,\; f(2)=7,\; f'(2)=5. \text{ Let } h(x)=f(g(x)). \text{ Find } h'(4). Apply h'(a) = f'(g(a))·g'(a). Read g(4) first, then look up f' at that value — not at 4. h'(4) = -15 h'(4) = f'(g(4)) \cdot g'(4) Write the Chain Rule formula for h = f∘g. g(4) = 2, \quad g'(4) = -3 Read the given values: the inner function value is 2 and its rate of change is −3. f'(g(4)) = f'(2) = 5 Evaluate f' at g(4)=2, not at 4. The given data says f'(2)=5. h'(4) = 5 \cdot (-3) = -15 Multiply the two factors: f'(g(4))·g'(4) = 5·(−3) = −15. \text{Differentiate } f(x) = \sin^2(x) \cdot e^{3x}. Outermost operation is multiplication (two factors) — Product Rule is outer. Each factor requires its own Chain Rule: d/dx[sin²x] and d/dx[e^(3x)]. f'(x) = e^{3x}\sin(x)\bigl[2\cos(x) + 3\sin(x)\bigr] f(x) = \underbrace{\sin^2(x)}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{e^{3x}}_{B} Outermost operation is multiplication — Product Rule governs the structure. A'(x) = 2\sin(x)\cos(x) Differentiate A = (sin x)² by Chain Rule: outer is u², inner is sin x. Result: 2sin(x)·cos(x). B'(x) = 3e^{3x} Differentiate B = e^(3x) by Chain Rule: outer is e^u, inner is 3x. Result: e^(3x)·3. f'(x) = 2\sin(x)\cos(x)\cdot e^{3x} + \sin^2(x)\cdot 3e^{3x} Apply Product Rule: A'B + AB'. = e^{3x}\sin(x)\bigl[2\cos(x) + 3\sin(x)\bigr] Factor out e^(3x) and sin(x) from both terms to reach the fully simplified form. Power, Product, Quotient Rules The chain rule is combined with these rules constantly. The generalized power rule is chain rule plus power rule. The Combo Rule Boss Fight (Example 12) shows how to identify which outer rule applies. Trig Derivatives — sin(x²) vs sin²(x) The most common Chain Rule mistake in trig: sin²(x) has outer u² and inner sin x, while sin(x²) has outer sin and inner x². The NestedTrigMachine visualization on the Trig Derivatives page shows this side-by-side. Implicit Differentiation Implicit differentiation is the chain rule applied to expressions in y where y = y(x). assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step instantaneous rate of change slope dy/dx velocity marginal change

documents.assignment: Classic trap expression h(x)=x(6x+6)^{-3}.   The missing inner factor 6 is the trap. Inline chain completion prevents it. u=x,\;v=(6x+6)^{-3},\;u'=1 Choose factors for product rule. v'=-3(6x+6)^{-4}\cdot 6=-18(6x+6)^{-4} Chain rule completes v': outer power gives -3(·)^{-4}, inner derivative of (6x+6) is 6. h'=(1)\cdot(6x+6)^{-3}+x\cdot\bigl(-18(6x+6)^{-4}\bigr) Assemble only after full v'. The canonical sin(3x) trap h(x)=x^2\sin(3x). Find h'(x).   The factor of 3 in v'=3cos(3x) is what the trap omits. Without it the answer is off by that factor everywhere. u=x^2,\quad v=\sin(3x) Step 1: label u and v. u'=2x Step 2: differentiate u. Plain power rule suffices — no composition. v=\sin(\underbrace{3x}_{\text{inner}}),\quad v'=\cos(3x)\cdot 3=3\cos(3x) Step 3: differentiate v FULLY. Outer is sin (derivative cos), inner is 3x (derivative 3). Both factors required. h'(x)=u'v+uv'=2x\cdot\sin(3x)+x^2\cdot 3\cos(3x) Step 4: assemble. Both ingredients are complete. h'(x)=2x\sin(3x)+3x^2\cos(3x) Simplified final answer. At x=1: 2\sin 3+3\cos 3\approx 0.282-2.970\approx -2.688, matching the numerical estimate. Both factors composite h(x)=e^{2x}\cdot(x^3-1)^2. Find h'(x).   When both factors are composite, both require chain rule before assembly. The 4-step checklist handles this without extra thought. u=e^{2x},\quad v=(x^3-1)^2 Step 1: label. Both u and v are composites. u'=e^{2x}\cdot 2=2e^{2x} Step 2: u' by chain rule. Outer is e^{(\cdot)}, inner is 2x with derivative 2. v'=2(x^3-1)^1\cdot 3x^2=6x^2(x^3-1) Step 3: v' by chain rule. Outer is (\cdot)^2, inner is (x^3-1) with derivative 3x^2. h'=2e^{2x}(x^3-1)^2+e^{2x}\cdot 6x^2(x^3-1) Step 4: assemble. Factor out e^{2x}(x^3-1). h'(x)=e^{2x}(x^3-1)\bigl[2(x^3-1)+6x^2\bigr]=e^{2x}(x^3-1)(2x^3+6x^2-2) Fully simplified. Both chain rules were required before assembly. Find and fix the error A student differentiates h(x) = x^3 \cdot \cos(x^2) and writes h'(x) = 3x^2\cos(x^2) + x^3(-\sin(x^2)). Is this correct? If not, find the error and give the correct derivative. Check whether v'=−sin(x²) is the complete derivative of cos(x²).   Numerical verification challenge Differentiate h(x) = \sqrt{x} \cdot e^{x^2}. Then verify numerically at x = 1: compute (h(1.001)-h(1))/0.001 to 3 decimal places and confirm it matches your formula. u=\sqrt{x}=x^{1/2}, u'=\tfrac{1}{2}x^{-1/2}. v=e^{x^2} requires chain rule for v'.
documents.content:
Why does this very common workflow fail: write u'v + uv', then partially differentiate v' and move on? In every applied derivative model with layered dependencies, one incomplete inner derivative quietly corrupts the entire final result. This lesson isolates that exact failure mode and gives a repeatable anti-trap workflow. **Where you are in the story:** You just learned both the product rule and the chain rule. They are separate tools, each correct on its own. This lesson exists for one reason only: to show you what happens when you combine them carelessly — and to give you a workflow that prevents the mistake permanently. The trap is not about forgetting a formula; it is about the order in which you complete steps. **The trap, stated precisely:** When you apply the product rule h'(x) = u'v + uv' to a function h(x) = u(x)·v(x), every term is a multiplication of already-completed derivatives. If v(x) is itself a composite function — meaning v(x) = f(g(x)) for some inner function g — then v'(x) REQUIRES the chain rule: v'(x) = f'(g(x))·g'(x). Stopping at just the outer derivative f'(g(x)) and skipping the multiplication by g'(x) is the trap. The algebra looks plausible, the answer has the right shape, but it is numerically wrong at every single point. **Worked wrong example — so you can recognize it:** Let h(x) = x² · sin(3x). Choose u = x² and v = sin(3x). The product rule gives h'(x) = u'v + uv'. Now: u' = 2x (correct). For v = sin(3x), the outer function is sin and the inner function is 3x. The WRONG move is to write v' = cos(3x), keeping only the outer derivative of the sine. This gives the wrong answer: h'(x) = 2x·sin(3x) + x²·cos(3x). This expression looks clean and reasonable. It is completely wrong. **Worked correct example — the same function done right:** h(x) = x² · sin(3x), u = x², v = sin(3x). Correctly: u' = 2x. For v' we must apply the chain rule to sin(3x): the outer derivative is cos(3x), and the inner derivative of 3x is 3. So v' = cos(3x)·3 = 3cos(3x). Now assemble: h'(x) = 2x·sin(3x) + x²·3cos(3x) = 2x·sin(3x) + 3x²cos(3x). The only difference is that factor of 3 in the second term — but it changes the numerical value at every point. **Numerical verification that the wrong answer is wrong:** Plug in x = 1. First evaluate the original function: h(1) = 1²·sin(3) ≈ 1·(0.1411) ≈ 0.1411. Now estimate h'(1) numerically using a small step: compute (h(1.001) − h(1))/0.001. We have h(1.001) = (1.001)²·sin(3.003) ≈ (1.002001)·(0.1382) ≈ 0.1385. So (0.1385 − 0.1411)/0.001 ≈ −2.6. Now compare: the WRONG formula gives h'(1) = 2(1)·sin(3) + (1)²·cos(3) ≈ 2(0.1411) + (−0.9900) ≈ 0.282 − 0.990 ≈ −0.708. The CORRECT formula gives h'(1) = 2sin(3) + 3cos(3) ≈ 0.282 + 3(−0.990) ≈ 0.282 − 2.970 ≈ −2.688. The numerical estimate is approximately −2.6, which matches the correct answer (≈−2.69), not the wrong one (≈−0.71). The discrepancy is a factor of roughly 3.8 — not a rounding issue, a structural error. **The fix — the Assembly Rule:** Treat product-rule assembly as a shopping list with exactly four ingredients: u, v, u', and full-v'. You are not allowed to proceed to step 3 (assembly) until all four ingredients are completely finished. Step 1: identify u and v. Step 2: compute u' fully — if u is a composition, use chain rule. Step 3: compute v' fully — if v is a composition, use chain rule all the way through. Step 4: ONLY NOW, assemble h' = u'v + uv'. This sequencing removes the trap structurally: there is no moment when partial v' is in your hand and you are tempted to assemble. **Second worked example — h(x) = e^(2x) · (x³ − 1)²:** Step 1 — choose u = e^(2x) and v = (x³ − 1)². Step 2 — compute u' fully: u = e^(2x) is a composition with outer e^(·) and inner 2x, so u' = e^(2x)·2 = 2e^(2x). Step 3 — compute v' fully: v = (x³ − 1)² is a composition with outer (·)² and inner (x³ − 1), so v' = 2(x³ − 1)·3x² = 6x²(x³ − 1). Step 4 — assemble: h'(x) = [2e^(2x)]·(x³ − 1)² + e^(2x)·[6x²(x³ − 1)]. Factor out the common e^(2x)(x³ − 1) to simplify: h'(x) = e^(2x)(x³ − 1)[2(x³ − 1) + 6x²] = e^(2x)(x³ − 1)(2x³ + 6x² − 2). Both u' and v' required chain rule, and both were completed before assembly. **Pattern recognition — how to know when v' needs chain rule:** Ask one question about v before you differentiate it: "Is the thing I am differentiating a simple power xⁿ, or does it contain a sub-expression inside?" If v is simply xⁿ, power rule alone suffices. If v is ANYTHING composed with something other than x — like sin(3x), e^(2x), (x³−1)², ln(x²+1), arctan(5x) — then the chain rule is mandatory. The tell-tale sign is: do I see a function applied to something that is not just plain x? If yes, chain rule is required for v'. For h(x)=u(x)v(x), the product rule is h'=u'v+uv'. This formula is a final assembly template, not a substitute for computing derivatives inside u' and v'. If v is composite, v' must be computed by chain rule inline: v' = f'(g(x))g'(x). Missing g'(x) is the exact mechanism behind the trap. A fast quality check is numeric verification at one or two points. Wrong and correct derivatives often diverge sharply away from special cancellation points. Lesson 5 of 10 — Act 2: Trap Drill **Previous:** The chain rule — differentiating composed functions by multiplying outer and inner derivatives.
**This lesson:** The #1 mistake when combining product and chain rules — recognize it, confirm it's wrong numerically, replace it with the correct workflow.
**Next:** Trig derivatives — applying your full toolkit to sin, cos, tan and friends. Wrong vs Correct: side by side \textbf{Example: } h(x) = x^2 \sin(3x), \quad u=x^2,\; v=\sin(3x)\\ \textbf{Wrong:}\quad v'=\cos(3x) \;\Rightarrow\; h'=2x\sin(3x)+x^2\cos(3x) \\ \textbf{Correct:}\quad v'=\cos(3x)\cdot 3=3\cos(3x) \;\Rightarrow\; h'=2x\sin(3x)+3x^2\cos(3x) 4-Step Assembly Checklist \text{1) Label } u \text{ and } v.\\ \text{2) Compute } u' \text{ fully (apply chain rule if } u \text{ is composite).}\\ \text{3) Compute } v' \text{ fully (apply chain rule if } v \text{ is composite).}\\ \text{4) Only now assemble: } h'=u'v+uv'. Quick Drill: Does This v' Need Chain Rule? \text{1) } v=x^5 \;\to\; \textbf{No} \text{ (plain power)}\\ \text{2) } v=\sin(3x) \;\to\; \textbf{Yes} \text{ (trig of } 3x \text{)}\\ \text{3) } v=(x^2+1)^4 \;\to\; \textbf{Yes} \text{ (power of expression)}\\ \text{4) } v=e^{x^2} \;\to\; \textbf{Yes} \text{ (exponential of } x^2 \text{)}\\ \text{5) } v=\ln(5x) \;\to\; \textbf{Yes} \text{ (log of } 5x \text{)} Assembly rule h'(x)=u'v+uv' \text{ is valid only after } u' \text{ and } v' \text{ are fully complete.} Combined-rule workflow \text{1) Choose }u,v.\; \text{2) Compute complete }u',v'.\; \text{3) Assemble }u'v+uv'.\; \text{4) Simplify and check numerically.} Product Rule Chain Trap Lab Dedicated anti-pattern lesson: identify the trap, apply the shopping-list workflow, and verify correctness numerically. Classic trap expression h(x)=x(6x+6)^{-3}. The missing inner factor 6 is the trap. Inline chain completion prevents it. u=x,\;v=(6x+6)^{-3},\;u'=1 Choose factors for product rule. v'=-3(6x+6)^{-4}\cdot 6=-18(6x+6)^{-4} Chain rule completes v': outer power gives -3(·)^{-4}, inner derivative of (6x+6) is 6. h'=(1)\cdot(6x+6)^{-3}+x\cdot\bigl(-18(6x+6)^{-4}\bigr) Assemble only after full v'. The canonical sin(3x) trap h(x)=x^2\sin(3x). Find h'(x). The factor of 3 in v'=3cos(3x) is what the trap omits. Without it the answer is off by that factor everywhere. u=x^2,\quad v=\sin(3x) Step 1: label u and v. u'=2x Step 2: differentiate u. Plain power rule suffices — no composition. v=\sin(\underbrace{3x}_{\text{inner}}),\quad v'=\cos(3x)\cdot 3=3\cos(3x) Step 3: differentiate v FULLY. Outer is sin (derivative cos), inner is 3x (derivative 3). Both factors required. h'(x)=u'v+uv'=2x\cdot\sin(3x)+x^2\cdot 3\cos(3x) Step 4: assemble. Both ingredients are complete. h'(x)=2x\sin(3x)+3x^2\cos(3x) Simplified final answer. At x=1: 2\sin 3+3\cos 3\approx 0.282-2.970\approx -2.688, matching the numerical estimate. Both factors composite h(x)=e^{2x}\cdot(x^3-1)^2. Find h'(x). When both factors are composite, both require chain rule before assembly. The 4-step checklist handles this without extra thought. u=e^{2x},\quad v=(x^3-1)^2 Step 1: label. Both u and v are composites. u'=e^{2x}\cdot 2=2e^{2x} Step 2: u' by chain rule. Outer is e^{(\cdot)}, inner is 2x with derivative 2. v'=2(x^3-1)^1\cdot 3x^2=6x^2(x^3-1) Step 3: v' by chain rule. Outer is (\cdot)^2, inner is (x^3-1) with derivative 3x^2. h'=2e^{2x}(x^3-1)^2+e^{2x}\cdot 6x^2(x^3-1) Step 4: assemble. Factor out e^{2x}(x^3-1). h'(x)=e^{2x}(x^3-1)\bigl[2(x^3-1)+6x^2\bigr]=e^{2x}(x^3-1)(2x^3+6x^2-2) Fully simplified. Both chain rules were required before assembly. Find and fix the error A student differentiates h(x) = x^3 \cdot \cos(x^2) and writes h'(x) = 3x^2\cos(x^2) + x^3(-\sin(x^2)). Is this correct? If not, find the error and give the correct derivative. Check whether v'=−sin(x²) is the complete derivative of cos(x²). Numerical verification challenge Differentiate h(x) = \sqrt{x} \cdot e^{x^2}. Then verify numerically at x = 1: compute (h(1.001)-h(1))/0.001 to 3 decimal places and confirm it matches your formula. u=\sqrt{x}=x^{1/2}, u'=\tfrac{1}{2}x^{-1/2}. v=e^{x^2} requires chain rule for v'. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step instantaneous rate of change slope dy/dx velocity marginal change

documents.assignment: Sine with Chain Rule f(x) = \sin(3x). \text{ Find } f'(x).   f'(x) = 3cos(3x). The chain rule "multiplies in" the factor of 3 from the inner function. Without the chain rule, the answer would be cos(3x) — missing the crucial factor of 3. \text{Outer: } F(u) = \sin(u), \quad \text{Inner: } u = 3x Identify the composition. The outer function is sine; the inner is 3x. F'(u) = \cos(u), \quad u' = 3 Derivative of sine is cosine; derivative of the inner function 3x is 3. f'(x) = \cos(3x) \cdot 3 = 3\cos(3x) Apply chain rule: outer derivative (cosine, evaluated at inner) times inner derivative (3). The argument of cosine is the same as the original argument of sine. Product Rule with Cosine f(x) = x^2 \cos(x). \text{ Find } f'(x).   f'(x) = 2x cos(x) - x² sin(x). The product rule gives two terms: the first represents the rate of change from the x² factor, and the second from the cos(x) factor. \text{Identify: } u(x) = x^2, \quad v(x) = \cos x This is a product of two functions. Assign the first factor and second factor for the product rule. u'(x) = 2x, \quad v'(x) = -\sin x Differentiate each factor separately. d/dx[x²] = 2x by the power rule; d/dx[cos x] = -sin x. f'(x) = u'v + uv' = (2x)(\cos x) + (x^2)(-\sin x) Apply the product rule: (first)(second)' + (first)'(second). = 2x\cos x - x^2 \sin x Simplify by writing the two terms separately. This is the fully simplified form. = x(2\cos x - x\sin x) Optionally factor out x from both terms. This factored form can be useful for finding zeros. Tangent with Chain Rule f(x) = \tan(x^2+1). \text{ Find } f'(x).   f'(x) = 2x sec²(x²+1). The derivative of tangent is always sec², and when the argument is a function of x, the chain rule contributes the derivative of that argument. \text{Outer: } F(u) = \tan u, \quad \text{Inner: } u = x^2 + 1 Identify the composition. The outer function is tangent; the inner is x²+1. F'(u) = \sec^2 u, \quad u' = 2x The derivative of tan(u) is sec²(u). The inner derivative is 2x. f'(x) = \sec^2(x^2+1) \cdot 2x = 2x\sec^2(x^2+1) Apply chain rule: outer derivative (sec², evaluated at x²+1) times inner derivative (2x). Power of Sine — Chain Rule f(x) = \sin^2(x). \text{ Find } f'(x).   f'(x) = 2 sin(x) cos(x) = sin(2x). The double angle identity provides a beautiful simplification here. f(x) = (\sin x)^2 Logic narrator: this is a power-rule shell first, not a trig-first move. See a square around something, peel the square before touching the sine. \text{Outer: } F(u) = u^2, \quad \text{Inner: } u = \sin x Identify the layers. F'(u) = 2u, \quad u' = \cos x Differentiate each layer. f'(x) = 2\sin x \cdot \cos x Chain rule: 2u evaluated at u = sin x gives 2 sin x, times the inner derivative cos x. = \sin(2x) Apply the double angle identity: 2 sin(x) cos(x) = sin(2x). This is a nice simplification, though both forms are correct. Composition of Two Trig Functions f(x) = \cos(\sin x). \text{ Find } f'(x).   f'(x) = -cos(x) sin(sin x). Note that the argument of the outermost sine is sin(x), not x — we evaluate the outer derivative at the inner function, preserving the inner function completely. \text{Outer: } F(u) = \cos u, \quad \text{Inner: } u = \sin x Both outer and inner functions are trigonometric. The outer is cosine (acting on the result of sine) and the inner is sine. F'(u) = -\sin u, \quad u' = \cos x Differentiate each layer: derivative of cosine is negative sine; derivative of sin x is cos x. f'(x) = -\sin(\sin x) \cdot \cos x Apply chain rule: outer derivative -sin(u) evaluated at u = sin x gives -sin(sin x), times the inner derivative cos x. Product Rule with Chain Rule: Secant Times Tangent f(x) = \sec(5x)\cdot\tan(5x). \text{ Find } f'(x).   f'(x) = 5 sec(5x)[tan²(5x) + sec²(5x)]. This can be further simplified using the identity tan²(x) + 1 = sec²(x), giving tan²+sec² = sec²-1+sec² = 2sec²-1. \text{Let } u(x) = \sec(5x), \quad v(x) = \tan(5x) This is a product of two functions, each requiring the chain rule. u'(x) = \sec(5x)\tan(5x) \cdot 5 = 5\sec(5x)\tan(5x) Differentiate sec(5x) using the chain rule: d/dx[sec u] = sec u tan u times u'. Here u = 5x and u' = 5. v'(x) = \sec^2(5x) \cdot 5 = 5\sec^2(5x) Differentiate tan(5x) using the chain rule: d/dx[tan u] = sec² u times u'. Here u = 5x and u' = 5. f'(x) = u'v + uv' = [5\sec(5x)\tan(5x)]\cdot\tan(5x) + \sec(5x)\cdot[5\sec^2(5x)] Apply the product rule. = 5\sec(5x)\tan^2(5x) + 5\sec^3(5x) Expand: tan(5x) · tan(5x) = tan²(5x) and sec(5x) · sec²(5x) = sec³(5x). = 5\sec(5x)[\tan^2(5x) + \sec^2(5x)] Factor out 5 sec(5x) from both terms. Quotient Rule with Sine f(x) = \frac{1+\sin x}{1-\sin x}. \text{ Find } f'(x) \text{ and simplify.}   f'(x) = 2cos(x) / (1-sin x)². The simplification of the numerator was made possible by factoring out cos x. \text{Numerator: } N = 1+\sin x, \quad \text{Denominator: } D = 1-\sin x Identify numerator and denominator for the quotient rule. N' = \cos x, \quad D' = -\cos x Differentiate numerator: d/dx[1+sin x] = cos x. Differentiate denominator: d/dx[1-sin x] = -cos x. f'(x) = \frac{N'D - ND'}{D^2} = \frac{\cos x(1-\sin x) - (1+\sin x)(-\cos x)}{(1-\sin x)^2} Logic narrator: run quotient rule cleanly, then hunt for identity-style collapse opportunities in the numerator to escape complexity. = \frac{\cos x(1-\sin x) + \cos x(1+\sin x)}{(1-\sin x)^2} Distribute the negative sign on the second term: -(1+sin x)(-cos x) = +cos x(1+sin x). = \frac{\cos x[(1-\sin x) + (1+\sin x)]}{(1-\sin x)^2} Factor cos x from both terms in the numerator. = \frac{\cos x \cdot 2}{(1-\sin x)^2} = \frac{2\cos x}{(1-\sin x)^2} Simplify inside the brackets: (1-sin x)+(1+sin x) = 2. The sin x terms cancel. Tangent Line to Sine Curve \text{Find the equation of the tangent line to } f(x) = \sin x \text{ at } x = \pi/3.   The tangent line is y = (1/2)x + (√3/2 - π/6). At x = π/3 ≈ 1.047, the sine curve has slope exactly 1/2 — the curve is rising gently as it approaches its peak at x = π/2. f'(x) = \cos x The derivative of sin x is cos x — no chain rule needed since the argument is just x. f'(\pi/3) = \cos(\pi/3) = \frac{1}{2} Logic narrator: this derivative value is the steerable slope. Plugging x = pi/3 locks the steering wheel to one tangent line. f(\pi/3) = \sin(\pi/3) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} Find the y-coordinate of the tangent point. From the unit circle, sin(π/3) = √3/2. y - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\left(x - \frac{\pi}{3}\right) Write in point-slope form with point (π/3, √3/2) and slope 1/2. y = \frac{1}{2}x - \frac{\pi}{6} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} Distribute 1/2 across (x − π/3) = x − π/3, giving (1/2)x − π/6, then add √3/2.  \text{Differentiate } f(x) = 3\cos x - 4\sin x. Differentiate each trig term separately: d/dx[cos x] = -sin x and d/dx[sin x] = cos x, then keep the constants 3 and -4 attached. f'(x) = -3\sin x - 4\cos x  f'(x) = 3 \cdot \frac{d}{dx}[\cos x] - 4 \cdot \frac{d}{dx}[\sin x] Apply the sum rule and constant multiple rule. = 3(-\sin x) - 4(\cos x) Use d/dx[cos x] = -sin x and d/dx[sin x] = cos x. = -3\sin x - 4\cos x Final simplified form.  Prove from the quotient rule that \dfrac{d}{dx}[\sec x] = \sec x \tan x. Write sec x = 1/cos x and apply the quotient rule with numerator 1 and denominator cos x. \dfrac{d}{dx}[\sec x] = \sec x \tan x  \sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x} Write secant in terms of cosine. \frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{1}{\cos x}\right] = \frac{0 \cdot \cos x - 1 \cdot (-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} Apply the quotient rule: numerator is (N'D - ND'). N = 1, N' = 0, D = cos x, D' = -sin x. = \frac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x} Simplify numerator: 0·cos x = 0 and -1·(-sin x) = sin x. = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} \cdot \frac{1}{\cos x} = \tan x \cdot \sec x Split the fraction: sin x / cos x = tan x and 1/cos x = sec x. = \sec x \tan x \quad \blacksquare Rewrite in standard order.  \text{Find all } x \in [0, 2\pi] \text{ where } f(x) = 2\sin x - \sin(2x) \text{ has a horizontal tangent line.} Set f'(x) = 0. You will need the chain rule for sin(2x). Then use the identity sin(2x) = 2sin(x)cos(x) or factor the resulting equation. There are 4 solutions in [0, 2π]. x = 0,\; \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\; \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \; (\text{and } 2\pi \text{ if counted})  f'(x) = 2\cos x - \frac{d}{dx}[\sin(2x)] Differentiate term by term. \frac{d}{dx}[\sin(2x)] = \cos(2x) \cdot 2 = 2\cos(2x) Apply the chain rule to sin(2x): outer derivative is cosine, inner is 2x with derivative 2. f'(x) = 2\cos x - 2\cos(2x) Combine the derivatives. f'(x) = 0 \implies 2\cos x - 2\cos(2x) = 0 \implies \cos x = \cos(2x) Set equal to zero and divide by 2. \cos(2x) = 2\cos^2 x - 1 Use the double angle identity to express cos(2x) in terms of cos(x). \cos x = 2\cos^2 x - 1 \implies 2\cos^2 x - \cos x - 1 = 0 Substitute and rearrange into a quadratic in cos x. (2\cos x + 1)(\cos x - 1) = 0 Factor the quadratic: check that (2u+1)(u-1) = 2u²-u-1. — \cos x = -\frac{1}{2} \quad \text{or} \quad \cos x = 1 Set each factor equal to zero. \cos x = 1 \implies x = 0 \text{ (and } 2\pi \text{, but that's the endpoint)} In [0, 2π], cos x = 1 at x = 0 (and at 2π = 0 again at the boundary). \cos x = -\tfrac{1}{2} \implies x = \frac{2\pi}{3} \text{ or } x = \frac{4\pi}{3} In [0, 2π], cos x = -1/2 at x = 2π/3 (second quadrant, reference angle π/3) and x = 4π/3 (third quadrant). x \in \left\{0,\; \frac{2\pi}{3},\; \frac{4\pi}{3}\right\} \text{ on } [0,2\pi] Collect all solutions. (x = 2π is the same point as x = 0 on the circle, included if the interval is closed.)
documents.proofs: We now prove d/dx[sin x] = cos x rigorously from the limit definition. This proof depends on two fundamental trigonometric limits, which we state but do not re-derive here (they were established in the limits chapter): lim(h→0) sin(h)/h = 1 and lim(h→0) (1 - cos h)/h = 0. PROOF that d/dx[sin x] = cos x: Using the limit definition, d/dx[sin x] = lim(h→0) [sin(x+h) - sin(x)] / h. Apply the sine addition formula: sin(x+h) = sin(x)cos(h) + cos(x)sin(h). So the numerator becomes: sin(x)cos(h) + cos(x)sin(h) - sin(x) = sin(x)[cos(h) - 1] + cos(x)sin(h). Dividing by h: sin(x) · [cos(h)-1]/h + cos(x) · sin(h)/h. Use the live-link panel below while reading this line: hover cos(x)·sin(h)/h to glow the vertical velocity arrow, and hover sin(x)·(cos(h)-1)/h to blink the horizontal correction that vanishes as h approaches 0. As h → 0: the first term has sin(x) (a constant with respect to h) times [cos(h)-1]/h. Rearranging, [cos(h)-1]/h = -(1-cos h)/h → -0 = 0. The second term has cos(x) (constant) times sin(h)/h → 1. Therefore the entire expression approaches sin(x)·0 + cos(x)·1 = cos(x). This completes the proof. PROOF that d/dx[cos x] = -sin x: Using the limit definition with the cosine addition formula cos(x+h) = cos(x)cos(h) - sin(x)sin(h): [cos(x+h)-cos(x)]/h = cos(x)·[cos(h)-1]/h - sin(x)·sin(h)/h. As h→0, the first term approaches cos(x)·0 = 0 and the second approaches sin(x)·1 = sin(x). So d/dx[cos x] = -sin(x). The minus sign comes from the minus sign in the cosine addition formula. The two key limits sin(h)/h → 1 and (1-cos h)/h → 0 as h → 0 are the real engine of these proofs. The first was established geometrically by the squeeze theorem (the arc length h is squeezed between sin h and tan h for small h > 0). The second follows from the first via the identity (1-cos h)/h = sin²(h) / [h(1+cos h)] = [sin(h)/h] · [sin(h)/(1+cos h)] → 1·0/2 = 0. Fundamental Trig Limits \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\sin h}{h} = 1 \qquad \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{1-\cos h}{h} = 0 Proof Strategy Tags \text{Isolation: expand }\sin(x+h).\;\text{Hunting: group }\frac{\sin h}{h}\text{ and }\frac{\cos h-1}{h}.\;\text{Survival: cosine term times 1 remains.} Proof: d/dx[sin x] = cos x \frac{d}{dx}[\sin x] = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\sin(x+h)-\sin x}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0}\left[\sin x\cdot\frac{\cos h - 1}{h} + \cos x \cdot\frac{\sin h}{h}\right] = \sin x\cdot 0 + \cos x\cdot 1 = \cos x
documents.applications:
Periodic phenomena dominate science and engineering: alternating current in electrical circuits, vibrations in mechanical systems, sound waves, ocean tides, the positions of planets. All of these are modeled using sine and cosine. To analyze how these quantities change — how quickly a current switches direction, how rapidly a spring approaches equilibrium, how fast a tide is rising — we need derivatives of trigonometric functions. The fact that d/dx[sin x] = cos x is not just elegant mathematics; it is the foundation of all oscillation and wave analysis. Lesson 6 of 10 — Act 3: Special Functions Begin **Previous:** Product + chain trap drill — the correct workflow for combining rules.
**This lesson:** Trig derivatives — why the slope of sin(x) is cos(x), and all six trig derivative formulas.
**Next:** Exponential and logarithmic derivatives — the self-referential property of e^x and the derivative of ln(x). Geometric Intuition: Unit Circle \text{At } \theta: \text{slope of } \sin\theta = \cos\theta Velocity-Vector Proof in One Line \vec r(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta),\;\vec r'(\theta)=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)\Rightarrow\frac{d}{d\theta}[\sin\theta]=\cos\theta The "co-" Functions All Have Minus Signs \frac{d}{dx}[\cos x] = -\sin x, \quad \frac{d}{dx}[\csc x] = -\csc x\cot x, \quad \frac{d}{dx}[\cot x] = -\csc^2 x Chain Rule Trap: sin(x^2) vs sin^2(x) \sin(x^2) \neq (\sin x)^2.\; \frac{d}{dx}[\sin(x^2)] = 2x\cos(x^2),\; \frac{d}{dx}[(\sin x)^2] = 2\sin x\cos x

A point moves around the unit circle at constant angular speed. Its y-coordinate is y = sin(theta). When theta = 0, the point is at (1, 0) and is moving straight upward, so height increases as fast as possible. When theta = pi/2, the point is at (0, 1) moving sideways, so height is not changing at all. When theta = pi, the point is at (-1, 0) moving downward, so height decreases at maximum rate. These rates, 1, 0, and -1, are exactly cos(0), cos(pi/2), and cos(pi). Why does this happen for every angle? Periodic phenomena dominate science and engineering: alternating current in electrical circuits, vibrations in mechanical systems, sound waves, ocean tides, the positions of planets. All of these are modeled using sine and cosine. To analyze how these quantities change — how quickly a current switches direction, how rapidly a spring approaches equilibrium, how fast a tide is rising — we need derivatives of trigonometric functions. The fact that d/dx[sin x] = cos x is not just elegant mathematics; it is the foundation of all oscillation and wave analysis. **Where you are in the story:** You now have a complete differentiation toolkit: power, product, quotient, and chain rules. That toolkit applies to any function — but we have only tested it on polynomials. This lesson and the next two apply the same toolkit to the three fundamental families of functions that appear throughout science and engineering: trigonometric functions (this lesson), exponential and logarithmic functions (next lesson), and inverse functions (the lesson after). **The central question of this lesson:** The sine function oscillates smoothly. At some angles it is rising fast, at others it is flat, and at others it is falling. Can we find a formula for that rate of change at every angle? The answer turns out to be startlingly clean: the rate of change of sin(θ) is cos(θ). The cosine curve IS the derivative of the sine curve. This lesson shows why — geometrically, analytically, and through the unit circle. Imagine tracing around the unit circle as the angle theta increases from 0. The y-coordinate follows the sine function. Let's watch what happens to the slope of the sine curve as theta varies. At theta = 0: the point (1, 0) is moving straight upward. The y-coordinate is increasing at maximum rate. The slope of sin(theta) is 1, and cos(0) = 1. At theta = pi/2: the point (0, 1) is moving horizontally. The y-coordinate is at a local maximum, so its instantaneous rate is 0. The slope is 0, and cos(pi/2) = 0. At theta = pi: the point (-1, 0) is moving straight downward. The y-coordinate decreases at maximum rate. The slope is -1, and cos(pi) = -1. This pattern is a theorem, not a coincidence: d/dtheta[sin(theta)] = cos(theta). Geometric proof bridge: position is (cos(theta), sin(theta)) and velocity is perpendicular to radius, so velocity has direction (-sin(theta), cos(theta)). The y-component of velocity is cos(theta), and that y-component is exactly d/dtheta[sin(theta)]. Why the minus sign for cosine? As theta increases through the first quadrant, cosine tracks horizontal position moving left, so its rate of change is negative. That directional fact is d/dx[cos x] = -sin x. Expert intuition: each derivative is a 90-degree phase rotation of the trig wave. sin -> cos -> -sin -> -cos -> sin. **Where this is heading:** You now have derivatives for all six trig functions. The next lesson introduces the other great family: exponential and logarithmic functions. The highlight is e — the one base for which the exponential function literally equals its own derivative. That self-referential property is one of the most surprising facts in mathematics. **The 90-degree phase shift pattern — a cycle of four:** Each derivative of a trig function is a quarter-period (90-degree) shift of the wave. Starting from sin(x): its derivative is cos(x), which is sin(x) shifted left by π/2. The derivative of cos(x) is −sin(x), another 90-degree shift. The derivative of −sin(x) is −cos(x), and the derivative of −cos(x) returns to sin(x). So the cycle is sin → cos → −sin → −cos → sin, repeating every four derivatives. This means: to find the 47th derivative of sin(x), compute 47 mod 4 = 3, so the 47th derivative is −cos(x). This four-step cycle is unique to trigonometric functions and reflects the geometric fact that rotating the unit-circle velocity vector by 90 degrees four times returns to the original direction. **Chain rule with trig — the most important application:** Once you have d/dx[sin(x)] = cos(x) and d/dx[cos(x)] = −sin(x), the chain rule extends these to any composite argument. The pattern is: d/dx[sin(g(x))] = cos(g(x))·g'(x) and d/dx[cos(g(x))] = −sin(g(x))·g'(x). The outer derivative uses the trig formula as usual, but the result must be multiplied by the derivative of the inner function g'(x). Example 1: d/dx[sin(3x)] = cos(3x)·3 = 3cos(3x). Example 2: d/dx[cos(x²)] = −sin(x²)·2x = −2x·sin(x²). Forgetting the inner derivative is the chain-trap in trig form — the same mistake isolated in the previous lesson now appears in trig context. We state all six trigonometric derivative formulas. The first two (sine and cosine) are proved from the limit definition. The other four are derived using the quotient rule, since tan, csc, sec, and cot are all rational combinations of sine and cosine. Once we have d/dx[sin x] and d/dx[cos x], the quotient rule handles everything else. Recall that tan x = sin x / cos x, csc x = 1/sin x, sec x = 1/cos x, and cot x = cos x / sin x. The memory device for the four derived formulas: all three "co-" functions (cosine, cosecant, cotangent) have negative derivatives. The remaining three (sine, tangent, secant) have positive derivatives. Within each pair: sine and cosine swap (but cosine gets a minus sign), tangent becomes sec², cotangent becomes -csc², and secant and cosecant follow their own symmetric patterns. Every one of these formulas extends to compositions via the chain rule. For any differentiable function u = g(x): d/dx[sin(u)] = cos(u)·u', d/dx[cos(u)] = -sin(u)·u', d/dx[tan(u)] = sec²(u)·u', and so on. These extended forms are the versions used in 90% of calculations. We now prove d/dx[sin x] = cos x rigorously from the limit definition. This proof depends on two fundamental trigonometric limits, which we state but do not re-derive here (they were established in the limits chapter): lim(h→0) sin(h)/h = 1 and lim(h→0) (1 - cos h)/h = 0. PROOF that d/dx[sin x] = cos x: Using the limit definition, d/dx[sin x] = lim(h→0) [sin(x+h) - sin(x)] / h. Apply the sine addition formula: sin(x+h) = sin(x)cos(h) + cos(x)sin(h). So the numerator becomes: sin(x)cos(h) + cos(x)sin(h) - sin(x) = sin(x)[cos(h) - 1] + cos(x)sin(h). Dividing by h: sin(x) · [cos(h)-1]/h + cos(x) · sin(h)/h. Use the live-link panel below while reading this line: hover cos(x)·sin(h)/h to glow the vertical velocity arrow, and hover sin(x)·(cos(h)-1)/h to blink the horizontal correction that vanishes as h approaches 0. As h → 0: the first term has sin(x) (a constant with respect to h) times [cos(h)-1]/h. Rearranging, [cos(h)-1]/h = -(1-cos h)/h → -0 = 0. The second term has cos(x) (constant) times sin(h)/h → 1. Therefore the entire expression approaches sin(x)·0 + cos(x)·1 = cos(x). This completes the proof. PROOF that d/dx[cos x] = -sin x: Using the limit definition with the cosine addition formula cos(x+h) = cos(x)cos(h) - sin(x)sin(h): [cos(x+h)-cos(x)]/h = cos(x)·[cos(h)-1]/h - sin(x)·sin(h)/h. As h→0, the first term approaches cos(x)·0 = 0 and the second approaches sin(x)·1 = sin(x). So d/dx[cos x] = -sin(x). The minus sign comes from the minus sign in the cosine addition formula. The two key limits sin(h)/h → 1 and (1-cos h)/h → 0 as h → 0 are the real engine of these proofs. The first was established geometrically by the squeeze theorem (the arc length h is squeezed between sin h and tan h for small h > 0). The second follows from the first via the identity (1-cos h)/h = sin²(h) / [h(1+cos h)] = [sin(h)/h] · [sin(h)/(1+cos h)] → 1·0/2 = 0. Fundamental Trig Limits \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\sin h}{h} = 1 \qquad \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{1-\cos h}{h} = 0 Proof Strategy Tags \text{Isolation: expand }\sin(x+h).\;\text{Hunting: group }\frac{\sin h}{h}\text{ and }\frac{\cos h-1}{h}.\;\text{Survival: cosine term times 1 remains.} Proof: d/dx[sin x] = cos x \frac{d}{dx}[\sin x] = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\sin(x+h)-\sin x}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0}\left[\sin x\cdot\frac{\cos h - 1}{h} + \cos x \cdot\frac{\sin h}{h}\right] = \sin x\cdot 0 + \cos x\cdot 1 = \cos x Lesson 6 of 10 — Act 3: Special Functions Begin **Previous:** Product + chain trap drill — the correct workflow for combining rules.
**This lesson:** Trig derivatives — why the slope of sin(x) is cos(x), and all six trig derivative formulas.
**Next:** Exponential and logarithmic derivatives — the self-referential property of e^x and the derivative of ln(x). Geometric Intuition: Unit Circle \text{At } \theta: \text{slope of } \sin\theta = \cos\theta Velocity-Vector Proof in One Line \vec r(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta),\;\vec r'(\theta)=(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)\Rightarrow\frac{d}{d\theta}[\sin\theta]=\cos\theta The "co-" Functions All Have Minus Signs \frac{d}{dx}[\cos x] = -\sin x, \quad \frac{d}{dx}[\csc x] = -\csc x\cot x, \quad \frac{d}{dx}[\cot x] = -\csc^2 x Chain Rule Trap: sin(x^2) vs sin^2(x) \sin(x^2) \neq (\sin x)^2.\; \frac{d}{dx}[\sin(x^2)] = 2x\cos(x^2),\; \frac{d}{dx}[(\sin x)^2] = 2\sin x\cos x Six Trig Derivatives \begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dx}[\sin x] &= \cos x \\ \frac{d}{dx}[\cos x] &= -\sin x \\ \frac{d}{dx}[\tan x] &= \sec^2 x \\ \frac{d}{dx}[\csc x] &= -\csc x\cot x \\ \frac{d}{dx}[\sec x] &= \sec x\tan x \\ \frac{d}{dx}[\cot x] &= -\csc^2 x \end{aligned} Six Trig Derivatives with Chain Rule \begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dx}[\sin u] &= \cos u \cdot u' \\ \frac{d}{dx}[\cos u] &= -\sin u \cdot u' \\ \frac{d}{dx}[\tan u] &= \sec^2 u \cdot u' \end{aligned} Deriving d/dx[tan x] via Quotient Rule \frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right] = \frac{\cos x \cdot \cos x - \sin x \cdot (-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} = \frac{\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x} = \frac{1}{\cos^2 x} = \sec^2 x Derivative as 90-Degree Phase Shift \frac{d}{dx}[\sin x]=\cos x=\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right),\quad \frac{d}{dx}[\cos x]=-\sin x=\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right) Deriving d/dx[csc x] via Quotient Rule \frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{1}{\sin x}\right] = \frac{0 \cdot \sin x - 1 \cdot \cos x}{\sin^2 x} = \frac{-\cos x}{\sin^2 x} = -\frac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\frac{\cos x}{\sin x} = -\csc x\cot x Deriving d/dx[cot x] via Quotient Rule \frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\right] = \frac{-\sin x \cdot \sin x - \cos x \cdot \cos x}{\sin^2 x} = \frac{-(\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x)}{\sin^2 x} = \frac{-1}{\sin^2 x} = -\csc^2 x Deriving cos(arcsin x) \theta = \arcsin x \Rightarrow \sin\theta = x = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}} = \frac{x}{1}.\\ \text{Then } \text{adj} = \sqrt{1 - x^2}.\\ \cos(\arcsin x) = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}} = \sqrt{1 - x^2}. Deriving sin(arccos x) \theta = \arccos x \Rightarrow \cos\theta = x = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}} = \frac{x}{1}.\\ \text{Then } \text{opp} = \sqrt{1 - x^2}.\\ \sin(\arccos x) = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}} = \sqrt{1 - x^2}. Deriving tan(arcsin x) \theta = \arcsin x \Rightarrow \sin\theta = x = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}} = \frac{x}{1}.\\ \text{Then } \text{adj} = \sqrt{1 - x^2}.\\ \tan(\arcsin x) = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}. Deriving tan(arccos x) \theta = \arccos x \Rightarrow \cos\theta = x = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}} = \frac{x}{1}.\\ \text{Then } \text{opp} = \sqrt{1 - x^2}.\\ \tan(\arccos x) = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}} = \frac{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}{x}. Deriving sec(arctan x) \theta = \arctan x \Rightarrow \tan\theta = x = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}} = \frac{x}{1}.\\ \text{Then } \text{hyp} = \sqrt{1 + x^2}.\\ \sec(\arctan x) = \frac{\text{hyp}}{\text{adj}} = \sqrt{1 + x^2}. The "Moving Point" Deep Sync Watch one angle drive three views at once: motion on the circle, slope of sine, and value of cosine. They stay synchronized because the sine slope is exactly cosine. Velocity Vector Lab (Zero Algebra Proof) Drag theta and verify: radius is (cos(theta), sin(theta)) while velocity is (-sin(theta), cos(theta)). The y-component of velocity is cos(theta), so d/dtheta[sin(theta)] = cos(theta). Trig Motion Bridge Lab Predict derivative signs from unit-circle motion and verify them instantly with the cosine readout. Why the Minus Sign? Co-Direction Compass Track vertical and horizontal motion signs as theta increases. This turns d/dx[cos x] = -sin x into directional geometry. The Higher-Order Derivative Clock Click d/dx to take successive derivatives. Every 4 steps returns to sin(x). Think of each derivative as a 90-degree phase rotation. Simple Harmonic Motion — Derivatives in Action Position x(t)=A cos(t), velocity v(t)=-A sin(t), acceleration a(t)=-A cos(t). Each graph is the derivative of the one above. Why tan(x) Explodes — Quotient Rule Intuition Drag toward x = pi/2. cos(x) shrinks toward 0 while sin(x) stays near 1, so tan(x)=sin(x)/cos(x) explodes. Interactive Quotient Rule Builder for tan(x) Step through "low d high minus high d low" and watch cos²(x)+sin²(x) collapse to 1. Nested Machine: sin(x²) vs sin²(x) Swap machine order to fix the most common chain-rule mistake. Square-then-sine and sine-then-square produce different derivatives. Peel-the-Onion Chain Rule Lab Practice peeling compositions in order. The outside changes first, the inside stays intact, then multiply by the core derivative. Sine-of-a-Sum Proof Builder Follow the formal proof with strategy tags. The colored limit blobs show exactly where the final cosine comes from. Inverse Bridge: From sin to arcsin Use a right triangle plus implicit differentiation to derive d/dx[arcsin x] = 1/√(1−x²). arcsin Derivative: Triangle + Meaning of Every Symbol Every symbol is mapped: x is a ratio, arcsin returns an angle, the triangle converts angle back into algebra. The square root appears from geometry, not memorization. Domain restriction ensures the square root stays positive. Inverse Reflection + Reciprocal Slopes (Calc Bridge) Try multiple invertible families and verify slope reciprocity at reflected points. Live-Link: Proof Terms ↔ Circle Geometry Hover the proof terms to light up the matching geometry. Use the theta and h sliders to verify at any angle. Sine with Chain Rule f(x) = \sin(3x). \text{ Find } f'(x). f'(x) = 3cos(3x). The chain rule "multiplies in" the factor of 3 from the inner function. Without the chain rule, the answer would be cos(3x) — missing the crucial factor of 3. \text{Outer: } F(u) = \sin(u), \quad \text{Inner: } u = 3x Identify the composition. The outer function is sine; the inner is 3x. F'(u) = \cos(u), \quad u' = 3 Derivative of sine is cosine; derivative of the inner function 3x is 3. f'(x) = \cos(3x) \cdot 3 = 3\cos(3x) Apply chain rule: outer derivative (cosine, evaluated at inner) times inner derivative (3). The argument of cosine is the same as the original argument of sine. Product Rule with Cosine f(x) = x^2 \cos(x). \text{ Find } f'(x). f'(x) = 2x cos(x) - x² sin(x). The product rule gives two terms: the first represents the rate of change from the x² factor, and the second from the cos(x) factor. \text{Identify: } u(x) = x^2, \quad v(x) = \cos x This is a product of two functions. Assign the first factor and second factor for the product rule. u'(x) = 2x, \quad v'(x) = -\sin x Differentiate each factor separately. d/dx[x²] = 2x by the power rule; d/dx[cos x] = -sin x. f'(x) = u'v + uv' = (2x)(\cos x) + (x^2)(-\sin x) Apply the product rule: (first)(second)' + (first)'(second). = 2x\cos x - x^2 \sin x Simplify by writing the two terms separately. This is the fully simplified form. = x(2\cos x - x\sin x) Optionally factor out x from both terms. This factored form can be useful for finding zeros. Tangent with Chain Rule f(x) = \tan(x^2+1). \text{ Find } f'(x). f'(x) = 2x sec²(x²+1). The derivative of tangent is always sec², and when the argument is a function of x, the chain rule contributes the derivative of that argument. \text{Outer: } F(u) = \tan u, \quad \text{Inner: } u = x^2 + 1 Identify the composition. The outer function is tangent; the inner is x²+1. F'(u) = \sec^2 u, \quad u' = 2x The derivative of tan(u) is sec²(u). The inner derivative is 2x. f'(x) = \sec^2(x^2+1) \cdot 2x = 2x\sec^2(x^2+1) Apply chain rule: outer derivative (sec², evaluated at x²+1) times inner derivative (2x). Power of Sine — Chain Rule f(x) = \sin^2(x). \text{ Find } f'(x). f'(x) = 2 sin(x) cos(x) = sin(2x). The double angle identity provides a beautiful simplification here. f(x) = (\sin x)^2 Logic narrator: this is a power-rule shell first, not a trig-first move. See a square around something, peel the square before touching the sine. \text{Outer: } F(u) = u^2, \quad \text{Inner: } u = \sin x Identify the layers. F'(u) = 2u, \quad u' = \cos x Differentiate each layer. f'(x) = 2\sin x \cdot \cos x Chain rule: 2u evaluated at u = sin x gives 2 sin x, times the inner derivative cos x. = \sin(2x) Apply the double angle identity: 2 sin(x) cos(x) = sin(2x). This is a nice simplification, though both forms are correct. Composition of Two Trig Functions f(x) = \cos(\sin x). \text{ Find } f'(x). f'(x) = -cos(x) sin(sin x). Note that the argument of the outermost sine is sin(x), not x — we evaluate the outer derivative at the inner function, preserving the inner function completely. \text{Outer: } F(u) = \cos u, \quad \text{Inner: } u = \sin x Both outer and inner functions are trigonometric. The outer is cosine (acting on the result of sine) and the inner is sine. F'(u) = -\sin u, \quad u' = \cos x Differentiate each layer: derivative of cosine is negative sine; derivative of sin x is cos x. f'(x) = -\sin(\sin x) \cdot \cos x Apply chain rule: outer derivative -sin(u) evaluated at u = sin x gives -sin(sin x), times the inner derivative cos x. Product Rule with Chain Rule: Secant Times Tangent f(x) = \sec(5x)\cdot\tan(5x). \text{ Find } f'(x). f'(x) = 5 sec(5x)[tan²(5x) + sec²(5x)]. This can be further simplified using the identity tan²(x) + 1 = sec²(x), giving tan²+sec² = sec²-1+sec² = 2sec²-1. \text{Let } u(x) = \sec(5x), \quad v(x) = \tan(5x) This is a product of two functions, each requiring the chain rule. u'(x) = \sec(5x)\tan(5x) \cdot 5 = 5\sec(5x)\tan(5x) Differentiate sec(5x) using the chain rule: d/dx[sec u] = sec u tan u times u'. Here u = 5x and u' = 5. v'(x) = \sec^2(5x) \cdot 5 = 5\sec^2(5x) Differentiate tan(5x) using the chain rule: d/dx[tan u] = sec² u times u'. Here u = 5x and u' = 5. f'(x) = u'v + uv' = [5\sec(5x)\tan(5x)]\cdot\tan(5x) + \sec(5x)\cdot[5\sec^2(5x)] Apply the product rule. = 5\sec(5x)\tan^2(5x) + 5\sec^3(5x) Expand: tan(5x) · tan(5x) = tan²(5x) and sec(5x) · sec²(5x) = sec³(5x). = 5\sec(5x)[\tan^2(5x) + \sec^2(5x)] Factor out 5 sec(5x) from both terms. Quotient Rule with Sine f(x) = \frac{1+\sin x}{1-\sin x}. \text{ Find } f'(x) \text{ and simplify.} f'(x) = 2cos(x) / (1-sin x)². The simplification of the numerator was made possible by factoring out cos x. \text{Numerator: } N = 1+\sin x, \quad \text{Denominator: } D = 1-\sin x Identify numerator and denominator for the quotient rule. N' = \cos x, \quad D' = -\cos x Differentiate numerator: d/dx[1+sin x] = cos x. Differentiate denominator: d/dx[1-sin x] = -cos x. f'(x) = \frac{N'D - ND'}{D^2} = \frac{\cos x(1-\sin x) - (1+\sin x)(-\cos x)}{(1-\sin x)^2} Logic narrator: run quotient rule cleanly, then hunt for identity-style collapse opportunities in the numerator to escape complexity. = \frac{\cos x(1-\sin x) + \cos x(1+\sin x)}{(1-\sin x)^2} Distribute the negative sign on the second term: -(1+sin x)(-cos x) = +cos x(1+sin x). = \frac{\cos x[(1-\sin x) + (1+\sin x)]}{(1-\sin x)^2} Factor cos x from both terms in the numerator. = \frac{\cos x \cdot 2}{(1-\sin x)^2} = \frac{2\cos x}{(1-\sin x)^2} Simplify inside the brackets: (1-sin x)+(1+sin x) = 2. The sin x terms cancel. Tangent Line to Sine Curve \text{Find the equation of the tangent line to } f(x) = \sin x \text{ at } x = \pi/3. The tangent line is y = (1/2)x + (√3/2 - π/6). At x = π/3 ≈ 1.047, the sine curve has slope exactly 1/2 — the curve is rising gently as it approaches its peak at x = π/2. f'(x) = \cos x The derivative of sin x is cos x — no chain rule needed since the argument is just x. f'(\pi/3) = \cos(\pi/3) = \frac{1}{2} Logic narrator: this derivative value is the steerable slope. Plugging x = pi/3 locks the steering wheel to one tangent line. f(\pi/3) = \sin(\pi/3) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} Find the y-coordinate of the tangent point. From the unit circle, sin(π/3) = √3/2. y - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\left(x - \frac{\pi}{3}\right) Write in point-slope form with point (π/3, √3/2) and slope 1/2. y = \frac{1}{2}x - \frac{\pi}{6} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} Distribute 1/2 across (x − π/3) = x − π/3, giving (1/2)x − π/6, then add √3/2. \text{Differentiate } f(x) = 3\cos x - 4\sin x. Differentiate each trig term separately: d/dx[cos x] = -sin x and d/dx[sin x] = cos x, then keep the constants 3 and -4 attached. f'(x) = -3\sin x - 4\cos x f'(x) = 3 \cdot \frac{d}{dx}[\cos x] - 4 \cdot \frac{d}{dx}[\sin x] Apply the sum rule and constant multiple rule. = 3(-\sin x) - 4(\cos x) Use d/dx[cos x] = -sin x and d/dx[sin x] = cos x. = -3\sin x - 4\cos x Final simplified form. Prove from the quotient rule that \dfrac{d}{dx}[\sec x] = \sec x \tan x. Write sec x = 1/cos x and apply the quotient rule with numerator 1 and denominator cos x. \dfrac{d}{dx}[\sec x] = \sec x \tan x \sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x} Write secant in terms of cosine. \frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{1}{\cos x}\right] = \frac{0 \cdot \cos x - 1 \cdot (-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} Apply the quotient rule: numerator is (N'D - ND'). N = 1, N' = 0, D = cos x, D' = -sin x. = \frac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x} Simplify numerator: 0·cos x = 0 and -1·(-sin x) = sin x. = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} \cdot \frac{1}{\cos x} = \tan x \cdot \sec x Split the fraction: sin x / cos x = tan x and 1/cos x = sec x. = \sec x \tan x \quad \blacksquare Rewrite in standard order. \text{Find all } x \in [0, 2\pi] \text{ where } f(x) = 2\sin x - \sin(2x) \text{ has a horizontal tangent line.} Set f'(x) = 0. You will need the chain rule for sin(2x). Then use the identity sin(2x) = 2sin(x)cos(x) or factor the resulting equation. There are 4 solutions in [0, 2π]. x = 0,\; \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\; \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \; (\text{and } 2\pi \text{ if counted}) f'(x) = 2\cos x - \frac{d}{dx}[\sin(2x)] Differentiate term by term. \frac{d}{dx}[\sin(2x)] = \cos(2x) \cdot 2 = 2\cos(2x) Apply the chain rule to sin(2x): outer derivative is cosine, inner is 2x with derivative 2. f'(x) = 2\cos x - 2\cos(2x) Combine the derivatives. f'(x) = 0 \implies 2\cos x - 2\cos(2x) = 0 \implies \cos x = \cos(2x) Set equal to zero and divide by 2. \cos(2x) = 2\cos^2 x - 1 Use the double angle identity to express cos(2x) in terms of cos(x). \cos x = 2\cos^2 x - 1 \implies 2\cos^2 x - \cos x - 1 = 0 Substitute and rearrange into a quadratic in cos x. (2\cos x + 1)(\cos x - 1) = 0 Factor the quadratic: check that (2u+1)(u-1) = 2u²-u-1. — \cos x = -\frac{1}{2} \quad \text{or} \quad \cos x = 1 Set each factor equal to zero. \cos x = 1 \implies x = 0 \text{ (and } 2\pi \text{, but that's the endpoint)} In [0, 2π], cos x = 1 at x = 0 (and at 2π = 0 again at the boundary). \cos x = -\tfrac{1}{2} \implies x = \frac{2\pi}{3} \text{ or } x = \frac{4\pi}{3} In [0, 2π], cos x = -1/2 at x = 2π/3 (second quadrant, reference angle π/3) and x = 4π/3 (third quadrant). x \in \left\{0,\; \frac{2\pi}{3},\; \frac{4\pi}{3}\right\} \text{ on } [0,2\pi] Collect all solutions. (x = 2π is the same point as x = 0 on the circle, included if the interval is closed.) The Chain Rule Every trig derivative formula extends to compositions via the chain rule. Most applied trig differentiation involves the chain rule. Limit Definition The proof of d/dx[sin x] = cos x uses the limit definition and the fundamental trig limits. Implicit Differentiation Trig functions appear frequently in implicit equations; their derivatives are used in implicit differentiation. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step approach approaching value as x approaches end behavior instantaneous rate of change slope dy/dx velocity marginal change trig sine cosine tangent unit circle

documents.title: Derivatives of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
documents.subtitle: The function that equals its own derivative — and the logarithm that unlocks it
