documents.assignment: Absolute Extrema on a Closed Interval Find the absolute maximum and minimum of $f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 4$ on $[-2, 3]$.   Absolute maximum of 11 at x = −1; absolute minimum of −16 at x = 2. Note that x = −2 and x = 3 (endpoints) are candidates but did not give the extrema here. f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6x - 12 = 6(x^2 - x - 2) = 6(x-2)(x+1) Find and factor the derivative. f'(x) = 0 \implies x = 2 \text{ or } x = -1 Both critical points are in (−2, 3). ✓ f'(x) \text{ exists everywhere (polynomial). No additional critical points.}  \textbf{Evaluate at candidates: } x = -2, -1, 2, 3  f(-2) = 2(-8) - 3(4) - 12(-2) + 4 = -16 - 12 + 24 + 4 = 0  f(-1) = 2(-1) - 3(1) - 12(-1) + 4 = -2 - 3 + 12 + 4 = 11  f(2) = 2(8) - 3(4) - 12(2) + 4 = 16 - 12 - 24 + 4 = -16  f(3) = 2(27) - 3(9) - 12(3) + 4 = 54 - 27 - 36 + 4 = -5  \text{Absolute max: } f(-1) = 11 \qquad \text{Absolute min: } f(2) = -16 Compare all four values: {0, 11, −16, −5}. Largest = 11, smallest = −16. Absolute Extrema of a Trig Function Find the absolute max and min of $f(x) = \sin x + \cos x$ on $[0, 2\pi]$.   Absolute max = √2 ≈ 1.414 at x = π/4; absolute min = −√2 at x = 5π/4. Note: f(0) = f(2π) = 1, illustrating that endpoints don't always give extrema. f'(x) = \cos x - \sin x = 0 \implies \cos x = \sin x \implies \tan x = 1  x = \frac{\pi}{4}, \;\frac{5\pi}{4} \quad \text{(in } [0, 2\pi]\text{)} tan x = 1 in Q1 at π/4 and in Q3 at 5π/4. f(0) = 0 + 1 = 1 \qquad f(\pi/4) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \sqrt{2}  f(5\pi/4) = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = -\sqrt{2} \qquad f(2\pi) = 0 + 1 = 1  \text{Absolute max: } \sqrt{2} \text{ at } x = \pi/4 \qquad \text{Absolute min: } -\sqrt{2} \text{ at } x = 5\pi/4 Values: {1, √2, −√2, 1}. Largest = √2, smallest = −√2.  Find the absolute max of $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3$ on $[0, 5]$. f'(x) = 2x − 4. Set equal to zero, then evaluate f at all candidates. Absolute max = 8 at x = 5; absolute min = −1 at x = 2 (the vertex).  f'(x) = 2x - 4 = 0 \implies x = 2  f(0) = 3, \quad f(2) = 4 - 8 + 3 = -1, \quad f(5) = 25 - 20 + 3 = 8  \text{Absolute max: } f(5) = 8 \qquad \text{Absolute min: } f(2) = -1   Give an example of: (a) a function with no absolute maximum on (0, 1), and (b) a function defined on [0, 1] with no absolute maximum. What EVT conditions fail in each case? For (a): try f(x) = x. For (b): introduce a discontinuity. (a) open interval; (b) discontinuity at x = 1 — both violate EVT conditions.  (a)\;f(x) = x \text{ on } (0,1): \text{ approaches 1 but never reaches it.} Interval is NOT closed — EVT does not apply. No absolute maximum. (b)\;g(x) = \begin{cases}x & 0 \leq x < 1 \\ 0 & x=1\end{cases}: \text{ approaches 1 but jumps to 0.} f is NOT continuous on [0,1] — EVT does not apply. No absolute maximum.
documents.proofs: **Proof sketch of EVT** (Bolzano-Weierstrass approach): Let f : [a, b] → ℝ be continuous. We claim f is bounded above. Suppose not. Then for each n ∈ ℕ, there exists xₙ ∈ [a, b] with f(xₙ) > n. The sequence (xₙ) is bounded (since a ≤ xₙ ≤ b), so by Bolzano-Weierstrass it has a convergent subsequence (xₙₖ) → c ∈ [a, b]. By continuity: f(c) = lim f(xₙₖ) = ∞, contradiction. So f is bounded above. Similarly f is bounded below. The supremum M = sup{f(x) : x ∈ [a, b]} exists. Again by Bolzano-Weierstrass and continuity, M is attained by some point in [a, b]. ■ The EVT fails without the closed interval condition (the sup may not be attained) or without continuity (the function may jump over its supremum). Fermat's Theorem — Precise Statement If $f$ has a local maximum or minimum at an interior point $c \in (a,b)$, and $f'(c)$ exists, then $f'(c) = 0$. \\ \text{Contrapositive: if } f'(c) \neq 0, \text{ then } c \text{ is not a local extremum (f is increasing or decreasing at } c\text{).}
documents.applications: Not always — but the Extreme Value Theorem tells you exactly WHEN you can. An airline must find the flight paths that minimize fuel cost (absolute minimum). A structural engineer must ensure a bridge's deflection never exceeds a maximum — the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees this maximum exists if the function is continuous on a closed interval. Without this guarantee, optimization is impossible: you can't minimize what might not have a minimum. EVT is the mathematical license that makes all of Chapter 3's optimization problems solvable.

documents.assignment: Verifying Rolle's Theorem for a Quadratic \text{Verify Rolle's Theorem for } f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 \text{ on } [1, 3] \text{ and find the value of } c.   Rolle's Theorem is verified: $c = 2$ is the point where $f'(c) = 0$. Geometrically, $f(x) = (x-1)(x-3)$ is a parabola opening upward with roots at 1 and 3, and its vertex (minimum) is at $x = 2$ — the horizontal tangent. f(1) = 1 - 4 + 3 = 0, \quad f(3) = 9 - 12 + 3 = 0 Check that $f(a) = f(b)$. Both endpoints give 0, so condition (iii) is satisfied. f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 \text{ is a polynomial} Polynomials are continuous everywhere and differentiable everywhere. Conditions (i) and (ii) hold on any interval. f'(x) = 2x - 4 Differentiate $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3$. 2x - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2 Solve $f'(c) = 0$. The only solution is $c = 2$. c = 2 \in (1, 3) \; \checkmark Confirm that $c = 2$ lies in the open interval $(1, 3)$. Canonical Example: Rolle's on the Parabola \text{Verify Rolle's Theorem for the canonical case } f(x) = x^2 \text{ on } [-1, 1] \text{ and find } c.   The canonical Rolle's example. $c = 0$ is the vertex where the tangent is horizontal. Graphically: a symmetric bowl shape with equal endpoint heights, one flat point at the bottom. f(-1) = (-1)^2 = 1, \quad f(1) = 1^2 = 1 Check condition (iii): $f(-1) = f(1) = 1$. Equal. f(x) = x^2 \text{ is a polynomial} \Rightarrow \text{continuous on } [-1,1], \text{ differentiable on } (-1,1) Conditions (i) and (ii) hold automatically. f'(x) = 2x Power rule. 2c = 0 \Rightarrow c = 0 Set $f'(c) = 0$. The only solution is $c = 0$. c = 0 \in (-1, 1) \; \checkmark Check: $0$ is strictly inside $(-1, 1)$. This is the vertex of the parabola — the horizontal tangent at the bottom. Rolle's Theorem with a Trigonometric Function \text{Show that } f(x) = \sin(x) \text{ on } [0, \pi] \text{ satisfies Rolle's Theorem and find all values of } c.   The unique value is $c = \pi/2$. This is the peak of the sine arch — exactly where the sine function changes from increasing to decreasing, with a horizontal tangent at its crest. f(0) = \sin(0) = 0, \quad f(\pi) = \sin(\pi) = 0 Condition (iii): $f(0) = f(\pi) = 0$. \sin(x) \text{ is continuous on } [0, \pi] \text{ and differentiable on } (0, \pi) Sine is infinitely differentiable everywhere. Conditions (i) and (ii) hold. f'(x) = \cos(x) Differentiate. \cos(c) = 0 \Rightarrow c = \frac{\pi}{2} Solve $f'(c) = 0$ on $(0, \pi)$. The only solution is $c = \pi/2$. f(\pi/2) = \sin(\pi/2) = 1 \text{ (the maximum)} At $c = \pi/2$, the function attains its maximum on $[0, \pi]$. The horizontal tangent occurs at the peak of the sine wave. Why Rolle Fails Without Differentiability \text{Show that } f(x) = |x| \text{ on } [-1, 1] \text{ does NOT satisfy the conclusion of Rolle's Theorem, and identify which hypothesis fails.}   The absolute value function satisfies conditions (i) and (iii) but not (ii) — it is not differentiable at $x = 0$. This single point of non-differentiability is enough to break Rolle's Theorem. f(-1) = |-1| = 1, \quad f(1) = |1| = 1 Condition (iii): $f(-1) = f(1) = 1$. This condition holds. f(x) = |x| \text{ is continuous on } [-1, 1] \; \checkmark Condition (i): The absolute value function is continuous everywhere. This holds. f'(0) \text{ does not exist: } \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{|h|}{h} = 1, \quad \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{|h|}{h} = -1 At $x = 0$, the left and right derivatives differ. The function has a corner at the origin. f'(x) = \begin{cases} -1 & x < 0 \\ +1 & x > 0 \end{cases} For $x \neq 0$, $f'(x)$ is either $-1$ or $+1$. Neither value is zero. \text{No } c \in (-1, 1) \text{ with } f'(c) = 0 There is no point in $(-1, 1)$ where the derivative is zero. Rolle's conclusion fails because hypothesis (ii) fails at $x = 0$. Using Rolle to Prove a Polynomial Has Exactly One Real Root \text{Prove that } p(x) = x^3 + 3x + 1 \text{ has exactly one real root.}   The polynomial $p(x) = x^3 + 3x + 1$ has exactly one real root (in $(-1, 0)$). The IVT gives existence, and Rolle's Theorem (via the contrapositive) gives uniqueness. p(0) = 1 > 0, \quad p(-1) = -1 - 3 + 1 = -3 < 0 By the Intermediate Value Theorem, since $p$ is continuous and changes sign on $[-1, 0]$, there is at least one root in $(-1, 0)$. p'(x) = 3x^2 + 3 = 3(x^2 + 1) Differentiate $p(x)$. 3(x^2 + 1) > 0 \text{ for all real } x Since $x^2 \geq 0$, we have $x^2 + 1 \geq 1 > 0$. So $p'(x) > 0$ everywhere — $p$ is strictly increasing. \text{Suppose } p \text{ had two roots } r_1 < r_2 Assume for contradiction that $p$ has two distinct roots. \text{Rolle's Theorem} \Rightarrow \exists\, c \in (r_1, r_2) \text{ with } p'(c) = 0 Rolle's Theorem would guarantee a point $c$ between the roots where $p'(c) = 0$. \text{But } p'(x) > 0 \text{ for all } x. \text{ Contradiction.} We showed $p'(x) = 3(x^2 + 1) > 0$ everywhere, so no such $c$ can exist. The assumption of two roots is false. Rolle's Theorem with Multiple Interior Zeros \text{Find all values of } c \text{ satisfying Rolle's Theorem for } f(x) = \sin(2\pi x) \text{ on } [0, 1].   There are two values: $c = 1/4$ and $c = 3/4$. Rolle's Theorem guarantees at least one, but this function — a complete period of a sine wave — has two horizontal tangents: a maximum at $x = 1/4$ and a minimum at $x = 3/4$. f(0) = \sin(0) = 0, \quad f(1) = \sin(2\pi) = 0 Condition (iii): $f(0) = f(1) = 0$. f'(x) = 2\pi\cos(2\pi x) Differentiate using the chain rule. 2\pi\cos(2\pi c) = 0 \Rightarrow \cos(2\pi c) = 0 Set $f'(c) = 0$. Since $2\pi \neq 0$, we need $\cos(2\pi c) = 0$. 2\pi c = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \Rightarrow c = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{n}{2} Solve for $c$. c \in (0, 1): \quad c = \frac{1}{4} \;(n=0), \quad c = \frac{3}{4} \;(n=1) Keep only values in the open interval $(0, 1)$. Canonical MVT Example \text{Apply the Mean Value Theorem to } f(x) = x^2 \text{ on } [0, 2] \text{ and find the guaranteed } c.   The MVT guarantees $c = 1$. At this point the tangent line to $f(x) = x^2$ is parallel to the secant from $(0,0)$ to $(2,4)$. Both have slope 2. f(0) = 0, \quad f(2) = 4 Compute endpoint values. \text{Average slope} = \frac{f(2) - f(0)}{2 - 0} = \frac{4 - 0}{2} = 2 Compute the secant slope. f'(x) = 2x Differentiate. 2c = 2 \Rightarrow c = 1 Set $f'(c) = $ average slope. Solve for $c$. c = 1 \in (0, 2) \; \checkmark Check that $c$ is inside the interval. At $x=1$, the tangent slope equals 2 = the secant slope. MVT with a Rational Function \text{Apply the MVT to } f(x) = \frac{1}{x} \text{ on } [1, 2].   The MVT guarantees $c = \sqrt{2}$. At this point the tangent to $y = 1/x$ is parallel to the secant from $(1,1)$ to $(2,1/2)$. Both have slope $-1/2$. f(1) = 1, \quad f(2) = \tfrac{1}{2} Evaluate endpoints. \text{Average slope} = \frac{1/2 - 1}{2 - 1} = -\frac{1}{2} The secant slope is negative — $f$ is decreasing on $[1,2]$. f'(x) = -\frac{1}{x^2} Differentiate using the power rule ($f(x) = x^{-1}$). -\frac{1}{c^2} = -\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow c^2 = 2 \Rightarrow c = \sqrt{2} Set $f'(c) = $ secant slope. Take positive root since $c \in (1,2) > 0$. c = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414 \in (1, 2) \; \checkmark $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$ lies strictly between 1 and 2. MVT verified.  Use Rolle's Theorem to prove that the equation $x^5 + 10x + 3 = 0$ has at most one real root. Compute $f'(x)$ and show it is always positive. Then use Rolle's Theorem by contradiction. \text{Since } f'(x) = 5x^4 + 10 > 0 \text{ for all } x, \text{ Rolle's Theorem precludes two or more roots.}  f(x) = x^5 + 10x + 3 \Rightarrow f'(x) = 5x^4 + 10 Differentiate the polynomial. 5x^4 + 10 \geq 10 > 0 \text{ for all } x Since $x^4 \geq 0$, we have $f'(x) \geq 10 > 0$ everywhere. \text{If } f \text{ had two roots } r_1 < r_2, \text{ Rolle's gives } c \in (r_1, r_2) \text{ with } f'(c) = 0 Apply Rolle's Theorem to the interval $[r_1, r_2]$. f'(c) \geq 10 > 0 — contradiction No such $c$ exists since $f'$ is always positive.  Verify Rolle's Theorem for $f(x) = x(x-2)e^x$ on $[0, 2]$ and find the value(s) of $c$. Check $f(0) = f(2) = 0$. Use the product rule to find $f'(x)$ and solve $f'(c) = 0$. c = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414  f(0) = 0 \cdot (-2) \cdot 1 = 0, \quad f(2) = 2 \cdot 0 \cdot e^2 = 0 Verify $f(0) = f(2) = 0$. f(x) = (x^2 - 2x)e^x \Rightarrow f'(x) = (2x - 2)e^x + (x^2 - 2x)e^x = (x^2 - 2)e^x Product rule: combine $(2x-2) + (x^2 - 2x) = x^2 - 2$. (c^2 - 2)e^c = 0 \Rightarrow c^2 = 2 \Rightarrow c = \pm\sqrt{2} Since $e^c > 0$ always, we need $c^2 - 2 = 0$. c = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414 \in (0, 2) \; \checkmark Only $c = \sqrt{2}$ lies in $(0, 2)$.  If $f$ is a polynomial of degree 4 with 4 distinct real roots, how many real roots does $f'$ have at minimum? What about $f''$? Apply Rolle's Theorem between each consecutive pair of roots, then repeat for $f'$. f' \text{ has at least 3 real roots (exactly 3). } f'' \text{ has at least 2 real roots (exactly 2).}  \text{Let } f \text{ have roots } r_1 < r_2 < r_3 < r_4 Label the four distinct real roots in order. \text{Rolle's: } f' \text{ has roots } c_1 \in (r_1,r_2),\; c_2 \in (r_2,r_3),\; c_3 \in (r_3,r_4) Between each consecutive pair of roots, Rolle gives at least one root of $f'$. At least 3 roots. f' \text{ has degree 3, so exactly 3 real roots} A cubic has at most 3 roots. Combined with at least 3, $f'$ has exactly 3 real roots. \text{Apply Rolle's again: } f'' \text{ has at least 2 real roots} Between consecutive roots of $f'$, Rolle gives roots of $f''$. Since $f''$ has degree 2, it has exactly 2 real roots.
documents.proofs:
**Proof of Rolle's Theorem (complete).** Assume $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and $f(a) = f(b)$. By the Extreme Value Theorem (which requires only continuity on a closed bounded interval), $f$ attains its absolute maximum $M$ at some $x_M \in [a, b]$ and its absolute minimum $m$ at some $x_m \in [a, b]$. If $M = m$, then $f$ is constant on $[a, b]$. Every point $c \in (a, b)$ satisfies $f'(c) = 0$, and the theorem holds trivially. If $M 
eq m$, then at least one of $M, m$ differs from $f(a) = f(b)$. Without loss of generality, suppose $M 
eq f(a)$. Then the maximum is not attained at $a$, and since $f(a) = f(b)$, it is not attained at $b$ either. So $x_M \in (a, b)$. Since $f$ is differentiable at $x_M$ and $x_M$ is an interior maximum, Fermat's Theorem gives $f'(x_M) = 0$. Set $c = x_M$. $\square$ **Fermat's Theorem (used above).** If $f$ has a local extremum at an interior point $c$ and $f'(c)$ exists, then $f'(c) = 0$. Proof: Suppose $c$ is a local maximum. For small $h > 0$, $f(c + h) \leq f(c)$, so $ rac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \leq 0$. Taking $h 	o 0^+$: $f'(c) \leq 0$. For small $h < 0$, $f(c + h) \leq f(c)$, but now the denominator $h$ is negative, so $ rac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \geq 0$. Taking $h 	o 0^-$: $f'(c) \geq 0$. Together: $f'(c) = 0$. (Symmetric argument for local minimum.) $\square$ **Why the hypotheses cannot be weakened.** (1) Continuity failure: define $f(x) = x$ for $x \in [0, 1)$ and $f(1) = 0$. Then $f(0) = f(1) = 0$ but $f'(x) = 1 
eq 0$ for all $x \in (0, 1)$. The jump at $x = 1$ breaks the Extreme Value Theorem. (2) Differentiability failure: $f(x) = 1 - |x|$ on $[-1, 1]$ has $f(-1) = f(1) = 0$, is continuous, but has a corner at $x = 0$ (the maximum) where $f'$ does not exist. The derivative is $-1$ for $x > 0$ and $+1$ for $x < 0$ — never zero. **Generalized Rolle's Theorem.** If $f$ vanishes at $n + 1$ distinct points, then $f'$ vanishes at $n$ distinct points (between consecutive roots of $f$), $f''$ vanishes at $n - 1$ points, and by induction $f^{(n)}$ vanishes at least once. This is used to prove error bounds in polynomial interpolation and Taylor's Theorem with remainder — topics we reach shortly. Fermat's Theorem (Interior Extrema) If $f$ has a local extremum at $c$ and $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then $f'(c) = 0$. WARNING: the converse is false. $f'(c) = 0$ does NOT imply $c$ is a local extremum — consider $f(x) = x^3$ at $c = 0$. Counterexamples When Hypotheses Fail Continuity dropped: $f(x) = x$ for $x \in [0,1)$ and $f(1) = 0$. Then $f(0) = f(1) = 0$ but $f'(x) = 1 
eq 0$. Differentiability dropped: $f(x) = 1 - |x|$ on $[-1,1]$ has $f(-1) = f(1) = 0$ but the maximum at $x = 0$ is a corner — no derivative exists there.
documents.applications: Imagine tossing a ball straight up. It leaves your hand going upward and returns to your hand going downward. At some instant in between, the ball's velocity must have been exactly zero — the peak of the trajectory. This is Rolle's Theorem in action: whenever a continuous quantity starts and ends at the same value, its rate of change must hit zero at some intermediate point. This principle underlies root-counting arguments in algebra, stability analysis in engineering, and error bounds in numerical analysis. Rolle's Theorem is also the stepping stone to the Mean Value Theorem — one of the most powerful results in all of calculus — which we prove directly from it in the Math section below. Extreme Value Theorem + Fermat — The Proof Engine The proof of Rolle's Theorem relies on two earlier results working together. The EVT (continuity on a closed interval → max and min exist) hands you a candidate interior point. Fermat's Interior Extremum Theorem (differentiability at that interior extremum → derivative = 0) hands you the conclusion. Neither result alone is sufficient. All Three Hypotheses Are Necessary Rolle's Theorem requires: (1) $f$ continuous on $[a, b]$, (2) $f$ differentiable on $(a, b)$, (3) $f(a) = f(b)$. Drop any one and the conclusion can fail. A jump discontinuity, a corner, or unequal endpoint values can each prevent the existence of a horizontal tangent. The Mountain Pass Analogy Imagine hiking from a trailhead at elevation $h$ to another trailhead at the same elevation $h$, following a continuous smooth path. If you go uphill at any point, you must come back down — and at the highest point your trail is momentarily flat (horizontal tangent). If you go downhill first, the lowest point is flat. Either way, a flat point exists. Multiple Horizontal Tangents Are Fine Rolle's Theorem guarantees at least one $c$ with $f'(c) = 0$, but there may be many. $f(x) = \sin(x)$ on $[0, 2\pi]$ has $f(0) = f(2\pi) = 0$ and two such points: $c = \pi/2$ and $c = 3\pi/2$. The theorem guarantees a minimum of one — finding all of them requires solving $f'(x) = 0$. Michel Rolle (1652–1719) Ironically, Michel Rolle was a vocal critic of calculus who considered infinitesimals to be logically unsound. His theorem, published in 1691, was originally stated only for polynomials. The modern version for differentiable functions came later, after the foundations of calculus were made rigorous by Cauchy and Weierstrass.

If you drive from your house to a friend's house and back home again, must there be a moment during the trip when your velocity is exactly zero? Why? Imagine tossing a ball straight up. It leaves your hand going upward and returns to your hand going downward. At some instant in between, the ball's velocity must have been exactly zero — the peak of the trajectory. This is Rolle's Theorem in action: whenever a continuous quantity starts and ends at the same value, its rate of change must hit zero at some intermediate point. This principle underlies root-counting arguments in algebra, stability analysis in engineering, and error bounds in numerical analysis. Rolle's Theorem is also the stepping stone to the Mean Value Theorem — one of the most powerful results in all of calculus — which we prove directly from it in the Math section below. You have spent all of Chapter 2 building the derivative — limit definitions, power rule, chain rule, implicit differentiation. But so far, derivatives have been about computing. Chapter 3 is about what derivatives TELL you. We start with the simplest possible question: if a function starts and ends at the same height, what must be true between those endpoints? The answer — Rolle's Theorem — looks almost obvious when you draw a picture, but its proof requires everything you learned about continuity and differentiability in Chapters 1 and 2. **Prerequisites you need (review them now if shaky).** (1) *Continuity on a closed interval*: $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ if it has no breaks, jumps, or holes. (2) *Differentiability on an open interval*: the derivative $f'(x) = \lim_{h 	o 0}  rac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ exists at every interior point — no corners, cusps, or vertical tangents. (3) *Extreme Value Theorem (EVT)*: if $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, it attains both a global maximum $M$ and global minimum $m$ on $[a,b]$. This is the key engine inside the proof. (4) *Fermat's Interior Extremum Theorem*: if $f$ has a local max or min at an interior point $c$ and $f'(c)$ exists, then $f'(c) = 0$. Quick sketch of why: at a local max, the difference quotient is $\leq 0$ from the right and $\geq 0$ from the left, so the limit (the derivative) must be exactly 0. (5) *Secant slope* (the average rate of change): $ rac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$. **The core idea, in plain language.** Rolle's Theorem makes a beautifully simple claim: if a function starts and ends at the same height on some interval, and if the function is smooth enough (continuous on the closed interval, differentiable on the open interval), then somewhere in between there must be a point where the tangent line is perfectly horizontal — the derivative is zero at that point. Think about it graphically. You are drawing a curve that starts at $(a, f(a))$ and must end at $(b, f(b))$ where $f(a) = f(b)$. The curve must be unbroken and smooth. If the curve goes up at any point, it must eventually come back down to the same height at $b$ — meaning there is a peak somewhere with a horizontal tangent. If it goes down first, there must be a valley. If it stays perfectly flat, then $f'(c) = 0$ everywhere. No matter what, a horizontal tangent is unavoidable. **The ball-tossing example.** Let $f(t)$ be the height of a ball at time $t$. You throw it at time $a$ and catch it at time $b$ at the same height: $f(a) = f(b)$. The height function is continuous and differentiable. Therefore, there exists some time $c$ between $a$ and $b$ where $f'(c) = 0$ — the ball is momentarily stationary at its peak. You do not need to solve any equation to know this; Rolle's Theorem guarantees it purely from the boundary conditions. **Why every hypothesis is needed.** Continuity: if the function can jump, it could leap from $f(a)$ up to some value and then jump back down to $f(b)$ without ever having a horizontal tangent. Differentiability: the function $f(x) = |x|$ on $[-1, 1]$ has $f(-1) = f(1) = 1$ and is continuous, but its only candidate for a horizontal tangent is $x = 0$, where the function has a corner and is not differentiable — so Rolle's Theorem does not apply and indeed no $c$ with $f'(c) = 0$ exists. Equal endpoints: without $f(a) = f(b)$ the curve can slope straight through from one height to another, never flattening. **Rolle's Theorem is an existence theorem.** It tells you that a point $c$ with $f'(c) = 0$ exists, but it does not tell you what $c$ is or how to find it. This is a common pattern in analysis — many of the deepest results guarantee existence without providing a formula. To actually locate $c$, you must solve $f'(x) = 0$ by other means (algebra, Newton's method, etc.). **Connection to the Mean Value Theorem.** Rolle's Theorem is actually a special case of the MVT. The MVT says: for any continuous, differentiable function on $[a, b]$, there exists $c$ with $f'(c) =  rac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$. When $f(a) = f(b)$, the right-hand side is zero, and the MVT reduces exactly to Rolle's Theorem. Historically, however, Rolle's Theorem came first, and the MVT is proved using Rolle's Theorem — the logical order is the reverse of the historical order. **Root-counting application.** One of the most elegant uses of Rolle's Theorem is proving bounds on the number of roots a function can have. If a polynomial $p(x)$ of degree $n$ had $n + 1$ roots, then between each consecutive pair Rolle's would give a root of $p'(x)$, producing $n$ roots of $p'$. But $p'$ has degree $n-1$ and can have at most $n-1$ roots — contradiction. Therefore $p(x)$ has at most $n$ roots. **Rolle's Theorem (Formal Statement).** Let $f$ be a function satisfying: (i) $f$ is continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$, (ii) $f$ is differentiable on the open interval $(a, b)$, and (iii) $f(a) = f(b)$. Then there exists at least one point $c \in (a, b)$ such that $f'(c) = 0$. **Proof (every step).** By the Extreme Value Theorem — which requires continuity on a closed bounded interval — $f$ attains its absolute maximum $M$ at some point $x_M \in [a, b]$ and its absolute minimum $m$ at some point $x_m \in [a, b]$. Case 1: $M = m$. Then $f$ is constant on $[a, b]$, so $f'(c) = 0$ for every $c \in (a, b)$. Done. Case 2: $M > m$. Since $f(a) = f(b)$, the two endpoints give the same function value. If $M = f(a) = f(b)$ then $m < M = f(a)$, so the minimum is attained at some interior $c \in (a, b)$. If $m = f(a) = f(b)$ then $M > m = f(a)$, so the maximum is attained at some interior $c \in (a, b)$. In either sub-case, $c$ is an interior local extremum. Since $f$ is differentiable at $c$, Fermat's Theorem gives $f'(c) = 0$. $\square$ **Canonical example: $f(x) = x^2$ on $[-1, 1]$.** $f$ is a polynomial — continuous and differentiable everywhere. $f(-1) = (-1)^2 = 1$ and $f(1) = 1^2 = 1$, so $f(-1) = f(1)$. By Rolle's, there exists $c \in (-1, 1)$ with $f'(c) = 0$. Compute: $f'(x) = 2x$. Set $2c = 0 \Rightarrow c = 0$. Check: $0 \in (-1, 1)$. The horizontal tangent is at the vertex of the parabola. **Working example 1: $f(x) = x^3 - 4x$ on $[-2, 2]$.** Continuous and differentiable everywhere. $f(-2) = -8 + 8 = 0$ and $f(2) = 8 - 8 = 0$. Equal. $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 4$. Set $3x^2 - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow x^2 =  rac{4}{3} \Rightarrow x = \pm  rac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \approx \pm 1.155$. Both values lie in $(-2, 2)$. Rolle's guarantees at least one; we found two. (Multiple roots are allowed.) **Working example 2: $f(x) = \sin x$ on $[0, 2\pi]$.** $f(0) = 0$, $f(2\pi) = 0$. $f'(x) = \cos x = 0 \Rightarrow x =  rac{\pi}{2},  rac{3\pi}{2}$ (both in $(0, 2\pi)$). Shows Rolle's works for trig functions. **Proof of the Mean Value Theorem from Rolle's.** The MVT states: if $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, then there exists $c \in (a, b)$ with $f'(c) =  rac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$. We reduce this to Rolle's with a clever auxiliary function. Define $g(x) = f(x) - f(a) -  rac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}(x - a)$. This subtracts the secant line (the straight line through $(a, f(a))$ and $(b, f(b))$) from $f(x)$. Step 1: Check $g$ satisfies Rolle's hypotheses. $g$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$ (same as $f$). $g(a) = f(a) - f(a) - 0 = 0$ and $g(b) = f(b) - f(a) - (f(b)-f(a)) = 0$. So $g(a) = g(b)$. Step 2: Apply Rolle's to $g$: there exists $c \in (a,b)$ with $g'(c) = 0$. Step 3: Compute $g'(x) = f'(x) -  rac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$. Step 4: $g'(c) = 0$ gives $f'(c) =  rac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$. $\square$ The auxiliary $g(x)$ is designed so the secant term cancels exactly at both endpoints — no extra terms survive. **Canonical MVT example: $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 2]$.** Average slope: $ rac{f(2)-f(0)}{2-0} =  rac{4}{2} = 2$. By MVT, exists $c \in (0,2)$ with $f'(c) = 2$. $f'(x) = 2x = 2 \Rightarrow c = 1 \in (0,2)$. The tangent at $x = 1$ is parallel to the secant from $(0,0)$ to $(2,4)$. **MVT working example 1: $f(x) =  rac{1}{x}$ on $[1, 2]$.** Average slope: $ rac{1/2 - 1}{1} = - rac{1}{2}$. $f'(x) = - rac{1}{x^2}$. Set $- rac{1}{c^2} = - rac{1}{2} \Rightarrow c^2 = 2 \Rightarrow c = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414 \in (1,2)$. **MVT working example 2: $f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2$ on $[0, 3]$.** Average slope: $ rac{(27-9+2)-2}{3} =  rac{20}{3}$. $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3$. Set $3x^2 - 3 =  rac{20}{3}$. Multiply by 3: $9x^2 - 9 = 20$, so $x^2 =  rac{29}{9}$, $x =  rac{\sqrt{29}}{3} \approx 1.795 \in (0,3)$ (positive root; negative discarded). **Root-counting application.** If $p(x)$ is a polynomial of degree $n$, then $p$ has at most $n$ real roots. Proof by contradiction: suppose $p$ has $n + 1$ distinct roots $r_1 < r_2 < \cdots < r_{n+1}$. Between consecutive roots $r_k$ and $r_{k+1}$, Rolle's Theorem gives a point $c_k$ with $p'(c_k) = 0$. This produces $n$ distinct roots of $p'(x)$. But $p'(x)$ has degree $n - 1$ and can have at most $n - 1$ roots — contradiction. **Key corollaries (what builds on Rolle's and MVT).** (1) Constant functions: if $f'(x) = 0$ for all $x \in (a,b)$, then $f$ is constant. (Apply MVT on any sub-interval; slope $= 0$ forces $f(x_2) = f(x_1)$.) (2) Functions with equal derivatives: if $f'(x) = g'(x)$ on an interval, then $f(x) = g(x) + C$. (3) Increasing/Decreasing Test: if $f'(x) > 0$ on $(a,b)$, then $f$ is strictly increasing there. These are the bridge to the First Derivative Test, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and Taylor's Theorem. **Proof of Rolle's Theorem (complete).** Assume $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and $f(a) = f(b)$. By the Extreme Value Theorem (which requires only continuity on a closed bounded interval), $f$ attains its absolute maximum $M$ at some $x_M \in [a, b]$ and its absolute minimum $m$ at some $x_m \in [a, b]$. If $M = m$, then $f$ is constant on $[a, b]$. Every point $c \in (a, b)$ satisfies $f'(c) = 0$, and the theorem holds trivially. If $M 
eq m$, then at least one of $M, m$ differs from $f(a) = f(b)$. Without loss of generality, suppose $M 
eq f(a)$. Then the maximum is not attained at $a$, and since $f(a) = f(b)$, it is not attained at $b$ either. So $x_M \in (a, b)$. Since $f$ is differentiable at $x_M$ and $x_M$ is an interior maximum, Fermat's Theorem gives $f'(x_M) = 0$. Set $c = x_M$. $\square$ **Fermat's Theorem (used above).** If $f$ has a local extremum at an interior point $c$ and $f'(c)$ exists, then $f'(c) = 0$. Proof: Suppose $c$ is a local maximum. For small $h > 0$, $f(c + h) \leq f(c)$, so $ rac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \leq 0$. Taking $h 	o 0^+$: $f'(c) \leq 0$. For small $h < 0$, $f(c + h) \leq f(c)$, but now the denominator $h$ is negative, so $ rac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \geq 0$. Taking $h 	o 0^-$: $f'(c) \geq 0$. Together: $f'(c) = 0$. (Symmetric argument for local minimum.) $\square$ **Why the hypotheses cannot be weakened.** (1) Continuity failure: define $f(x) = x$ for $x \in [0, 1)$ and $f(1) = 0$. Then $f(0) = f(1) = 0$ but $f'(x) = 1 
eq 0$ for all $x \in (0, 1)$. The jump at $x = 1$ breaks the Extreme Value Theorem. (2) Differentiability failure: $f(x) = 1 - |x|$ on $[-1, 1]$ has $f(-1) = f(1) = 0$, is continuous, but has a corner at $x = 0$ (the maximum) where $f'$ does not exist. The derivative is $-1$ for $x > 0$ and $+1$ for $x < 0$ — never zero. **Generalized Rolle's Theorem.** If $f$ vanishes at $n + 1$ distinct points, then $f'$ vanishes at $n$ distinct points (between consecutive roots of $f$), $f''$ vanishes at $n - 1$ points, and by induction $f^{(n)}$ vanishes at least once. This is used to prove error bounds in polynomial interpolation and Taylor's Theorem with remainder — topics we reach shortly. Fermat's Theorem (Interior Extrema) If $f$ has a local extremum at $c$ and $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then $f'(c) = 0$. WARNING: the converse is false. $f'(c) = 0$ does NOT imply $c$ is a local extremum — consider $f(x) = x^3$ at $c = 0$. Counterexamples When Hypotheses Fail Continuity dropped: $f(x) = x$ for $x \in [0,1)$ and $f(1) = 0$. Then $f(0) = f(1) = 0$ but $f'(x) = 1 
eq 0$. Differentiability dropped: $f(x) = 1 - |x|$ on $[-1,1]$ has $f(-1) = f(1) = 0$ but the maximum at $x = 0$ is a corner — no derivative exists there. Extreme Value Theorem + Fermat — The Proof Engine The proof of Rolle's Theorem relies on two earlier results working together. The EVT (continuity on a closed interval → max and min exist) hands you a candidate interior point. Fermat's Interior Extremum Theorem (differentiability at that interior extremum → derivative = 0) hands you the conclusion. Neither result alone is sufficient. All Three Hypotheses Are Necessary Rolle's Theorem requires: (1) $f$ continuous on $[a, b]$, (2) $f$ differentiable on $(a, b)$, (3) $f(a) = f(b)$. Drop any one and the conclusion can fail. A jump discontinuity, a corner, or unequal endpoint values can each prevent the existence of a horizontal tangent. The Mountain Pass Analogy Imagine hiking from a trailhead at elevation $h$ to another trailhead at the same elevation $h$, following a continuous smooth path. If you go uphill at any point, you must come back down — and at the highest point your trail is momentarily flat (horizontal tangent). If you go downhill first, the lowest point is flat. Either way, a flat point exists. Multiple Horizontal Tangents Are Fine Rolle's Theorem guarantees at least one $c$ with $f'(c) = 0$, but there may be many. $f(x) = \sin(x)$ on $[0, 2\pi]$ has $f(0) = f(2\pi) = 0$ and two such points: $c = \pi/2$ and $c = 3\pi/2$. The theorem guarantees a minimum of one — finding all of them requires solving $f'(x) = 0$. Michel Rolle (1652–1719) Ironically, Michel Rolle was a vocal critic of calculus who considered infinitesimals to be logically unsound. His theorem, published in 1691, was originally stated only for polynomials. The modern version for differentiable functions came later, after the foundations of calculus were made rigorous by Cauchy and Weierstrass. Rolle's Theorem If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and $f(a) = f(b)$, then there exists $c \in (a, b)$ with $f'(c) = 0$. Mean Value Theorem If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, then there exists $c \in (a, b)$ with $f'(c) =  rac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$. Rolle's Theorem is the special case $f(a) = f(b)$. The MVT Auxiliary Function Define $g(x) = f(x) - f(a) -  rac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}(x - a)$. Then $g(a) = g(b) = 0$. Rolle's Theorem gives $c$ with $g'(c) = 0$, and since $g'(x) = f'(x) -  rac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$, this yields $f'(c) =  rac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$. Rolle Does Not Find the Point Rolle's Theorem is purely existential. It guarantees $c$ exists but gives no formula. To locate $c$, solve $f'(x) = 0$ (Rolle's) or $f'(x) =  rac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ (MVT) explicitly. Key Corollaries to Memorize From MVT: (1) $f'=0$ everywhere $\Rightarrow$ $f$ constant. (2) $f'=g'$ everywhere $\Rightarrow$ $f - g$ is constant. (3) $f'>0$ on $(a,b)$ $\Rightarrow$ $f$ strictly increasing. These are used in every proof in the rest of this chapter. Enter any f(x) and interval, guess where the horizontal tangent is, then reveal the exact answer. Rolle's Theorem guarantee: equal endpoint heights plus smoothness force a horizontal tangent somewhere in the interior. The MVT auxiliary function construction: subtract the secant from f to get g with equal endpoints, then apply Rolle's to g. Rolle’s Theorem in action Rolle’s Theorem guarantees at least one horizontal tangent between equal endpoint values. Rolle walkthrough problems A guided Rolle walkthrough with multiple example functions and step-by-step visual reasoning. One complete Rolle problem A step-by-step Rolle's Theorem problem walkthrough with visual endpoint checks and derivative root confirmation. Verifying Rolle's Theorem for a Quadratic 	ext{Verify Rolle's Theorem for } f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 	ext{ on } [1, 3] 	ext{ and find the value of } c. Rolle's Theorem is verified: $c = 2$ is the point where $f'(c) = 0$. Geometrically, $f(x) = (x-1)(x-3)$ is a parabola opening upward with roots at 1 and 3, and its vertex (minimum) is at $x = 2$ — the horizontal tangent. f(1) = 1 - 4 + 3 = 0, \quad f(3) = 9 - 12 + 3 = 0 Check that $f(a) = f(b)$. Both endpoints give 0, so condition (iii) is satisfied. f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 	ext{ is a polynomial} Polynomials are continuous everywhere and differentiable everywhere. Conditions (i) and (ii) hold on any interval. f'(x) = 2x - 4 Differentiate $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3$. 2x - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2 Solve $f'(c) = 0$. The only solution is $c = 2$. c = 2 \in (1, 3) \; \checkmark Confirm that $c = 2$ lies in the open interval $(1, 3)$. Canonical Example: Rolle's on the Parabola 	ext{Verify Rolle's Theorem for the canonical case } f(x) = x^2 	ext{ on } [-1, 1] 	ext{ and find } c. The canonical Rolle's example. $c = 0$ is the vertex where the tangent is horizontal. Graphically: a symmetric bowl shape with equal endpoint heights, one flat point at the bottom. f(-1) = (-1)^2 = 1, \quad f(1) = 1^2 = 1 Check condition (iii): $f(-1) = f(1) = 1$. Equal. f(x) = x^2 	ext{ is a polynomial} \Rightarrow 	ext{continuous on } [-1,1], 	ext{ differentiable on } (-1,1) Conditions (i) and (ii) hold automatically. f'(x) = 2x Power rule. 2c = 0 \Rightarrow c = 0 Set $f'(c) = 0$. The only solution is $c = 0$. c = 0 \in (-1, 1) \; \checkmark Check: $0$ is strictly inside $(-1, 1)$. This is the vertex of the parabola — the horizontal tangent at the bottom. Rolle's Theorem with a Trigonometric Function 	ext{Show that } f(x) = \sin(x) 	ext{ on } [0, \pi] 	ext{ satisfies Rolle's Theorem and find all values of } c. The unique value is $c = \pi/2$. This is the peak of the sine arch — exactly where the sine function changes from increasing to decreasing, with a horizontal tangent at its crest. f(0) = \sin(0) = 0, \quad f(\pi) = \sin(\pi) = 0 Condition (iii): $f(0) = f(\pi) = 0$. \sin(x) 	ext{ is continuous on } [0, \pi] 	ext{ and differentiable on } (0, \pi) Sine is infinitely differentiable everywhere. Conditions (i) and (ii) hold. f'(x) = \cos(x) Differentiate. \cos(c) = 0 \Rightarrow c =  rac{\pi}{2} Solve $f'(c) = 0$ on $(0, \pi)$. The only solution is $c = \pi/2$. f(\pi/2) = \sin(\pi/2) = 1 	ext{ (the maximum)} At $c = \pi/2$, the function attains its maximum on $[0, \pi]$. The horizontal tangent occurs at the peak of the sine wave. Why Rolle Fails Without Differentiability 	ext{Show that } f(x) = |x| 	ext{ on } [-1, 1] 	ext{ does NOT satisfy the conclusion of Rolle's Theorem, and identify which hypothesis fails.} The absolute value function satisfies conditions (i) and (iii) but not (ii) — it is not differentiable at $x = 0$. This single point of non-differentiability is enough to break Rolle's Theorem. f(-1) = |-1| = 1, \quad f(1) = |1| = 1 Condition (iii): $f(-1) = f(1) = 1$. This condition holds. f(x) = |x| 	ext{ is continuous on } [-1, 1] \; \checkmark Condition (i): The absolute value function is continuous everywhere. This holds. f'(0) 	ext{ does not exist: } \lim_{h 	o 0^+}  rac{|h|}{h} = 1, \quad \lim_{h 	o 0^-}  rac{|h|}{h} = -1 At $x = 0$, the left and right derivatives differ. The function has a corner at the origin. f'(x) =  egin{cases} -1 & x < 0 \ +1 & x > 0 \end{cases} For $x 
eq 0$, $f'(x)$ is either $-1$ or $+1$. Neither value is zero. 	ext{No } c \in (-1, 1) 	ext{ with } f'(c) = 0 There is no point in $(-1, 1)$ where the derivative is zero. Rolle's conclusion fails because hypothesis (ii) fails at $x = 0$. Using Rolle to Prove a Polynomial Has Exactly One Real Root 	ext{Prove that } p(x) = x^3 + 3x + 1 	ext{ has exactly one real root.} The polynomial $p(x) = x^3 + 3x + 1$ has exactly one real root (in $(-1, 0)$). The IVT gives existence, and Rolle's Theorem (via the contrapositive) gives uniqueness. p(0) = 1 > 0, \quad p(-1) = -1 - 3 + 1 = -3 < 0 By the Intermediate Value Theorem, since $p$ is continuous and changes sign on $[-1, 0]$, there is at least one root in $(-1, 0)$. p'(x) = 3x^2 + 3 = 3(x^2 + 1) Differentiate $p(x)$. 3(x^2 + 1) > 0 	ext{ for all real } x Since $x^2 \geq 0$, we have $x^2 + 1 \geq 1 > 0$. So $p'(x) > 0$ everywhere — $p$ is strictly increasing. 	ext{Suppose } p 	ext{ had two roots } r_1 < r_2 Assume for contradiction that $p$ has two distinct roots. 	ext{Rolle's Theorem} \Rightarrow \exists\, c \in (r_1, r_2) 	ext{ with } p'(c) = 0 Rolle's Theorem would guarantee a point $c$ between the roots where $p'(c) = 0$. 	ext{But } p'(x) > 0 	ext{ for all } x. 	ext{ Contradiction.} We showed $p'(x) = 3(x^2 + 1) > 0$ everywhere, so no such $c$ can exist. The assumption of two roots is false. Rolle's Theorem with Multiple Interior Zeros 	ext{Find all values of } c 	ext{ satisfying Rolle's Theorem for } f(x) = \sin(2\pi x) 	ext{ on } [0, 1]. There are two values: $c = 1/4$ and $c = 3/4$. Rolle's Theorem guarantees at least one, but this function — a complete period of a sine wave — has two horizontal tangents: a maximum at $x = 1/4$ and a minimum at $x = 3/4$. f(0) = \sin(0) = 0, \quad f(1) = \sin(2\pi) = 0 Condition (iii): $f(0) = f(1) = 0$. f'(x) = 2\pi\cos(2\pi x) Differentiate using the chain rule. 2\pi\cos(2\pi c) = 0 \Rightarrow \cos(2\pi c) = 0 Set $f'(c) = 0$. Since $2\pi 
eq 0$, we need $\cos(2\pi c) = 0$. 2\pi c =  rac{\pi}{2} + n\pi \Rightarrow c =  rac{1}{4} +  rac{n}{2} Solve for $c$. c \in (0, 1): \quad c =  rac{1}{4} \;(n=0), \quad c =  rac{3}{4} \;(n=1) Keep only values in the open interval $(0, 1)$. Canonical MVT Example 	ext{Apply the Mean Value Theorem to } f(x) = x^2 	ext{ on } [0, 2] 	ext{ and find the guaranteed } c. The MVT guarantees $c = 1$. At this point the tangent line to $f(x) = x^2$ is parallel to the secant from $(0,0)$ to $(2,4)$. Both have slope 2. f(0) = 0, \quad f(2) = 4 Compute endpoint values. 	ext{Average slope} =  rac{f(2) - f(0)}{2 - 0} =  rac{4 - 0}{2} = 2 Compute the secant slope. f'(x) = 2x Differentiate. 2c = 2 \Rightarrow c = 1 Set $f'(c) = $ average slope. Solve for $c$. c = 1 \in (0, 2) \; \checkmark Check that $c$ is inside the interval. At $x=1$, the tangent slope equals 2 = the secant slope. MVT with a Rational Function 	ext{Apply the MVT to } f(x) =  rac{1}{x} 	ext{ on } [1, 2]. The MVT guarantees $c = \sqrt{2}$. At this point the tangent to $y = 1/x$ is parallel to the secant from $(1,1)$ to $(2,1/2)$. Both have slope $-1/2$. f(1) = 1, \quad f(2) = 	frac{1}{2} Evaluate endpoints. 	ext{Average slope} =  rac{1/2 - 1}{2 - 1} = - rac{1}{2} The secant slope is negative — $f$ is decreasing on $[1,2]$. f'(x) = - rac{1}{x^2} Differentiate using the power rule ($f(x) = x^{-1}$). - rac{1}{c^2} = - rac{1}{2} \Rightarrow c^2 = 2 \Rightarrow c = \sqrt{2} Set $f'(c) = $ secant slope. Take positive root since $c \in (1,2) > 0$. c = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414 \in (1, 2) \; \checkmark $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$ lies strictly between 1 and 2. MVT verified. Use Rolle's Theorem to prove that the equation $x^5 + 10x + 3 = 0$ has at most one real root. Compute $f'(x)$ and show it is always positive. Then use Rolle's Theorem by contradiction. 	ext{Since } f'(x) = 5x^4 + 10 > 0 	ext{ for all } x, 	ext{ Rolle's Theorem precludes two or more roots.} f(x) = x^5 + 10x + 3 \Rightarrow f'(x) = 5x^4 + 10 Differentiate the polynomial. 5x^4 + 10 \geq 10 > 0 	ext{ for all } x Since $x^4 \geq 0$, we have $f'(x) \geq 10 > 0$ everywhere. 	ext{If } f 	ext{ had two roots } r_1 < r_2, 	ext{ Rolle's gives } c \in (r_1, r_2) 	ext{ with } f'(c) = 0 Apply Rolle's Theorem to the interval $[r_1, r_2]$. f'(c) \geq 10 > 0 — contradiction No such $c$ exists since $f'$ is always positive. Verify Rolle's Theorem for $f(x) = x(x-2)e^x$ on $[0, 2]$ and find the value(s) of $c$. Check $f(0) = f(2) = 0$. Use the product rule to find $f'(x)$ and solve $f'(c) = 0$. c = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414 f(0) = 0 \cdot (-2) \cdot 1 = 0, \quad f(2) = 2 \cdot 0 \cdot e^2 = 0 Verify $f(0) = f(2) = 0$. f(x) = (x^2 - 2x)e^x \Rightarrow f'(x) = (2x - 2)e^x + (x^2 - 2x)e^x = (x^2 - 2)e^x Product rule: combine $(2x-2) + (x^2 - 2x) = x^2 - 2$. (c^2 - 2)e^c = 0 \Rightarrow c^2 = 2 \Rightarrow c = \pm\sqrt{2} Since $e^c > 0$ always, we need $c^2 - 2 = 0$. c = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414 \in (0, 2) \; \checkmark Only $c = \sqrt{2}$ lies in $(0, 2)$. If $f$ is a polynomial of degree 4 with 4 distinct real roots, how many real roots does $f'$ have at minimum? What about $f''$? Apply Rolle's Theorem between each consecutive pair of roots, then repeat for $f'$. f' 	ext{ has at least 3 real roots (exactly 3). } f'' 	ext{ has at least 2 real roots (exactly 2).} 	ext{Let } f 	ext{ have roots } r_1 < r_2 < r_3 < r_4 Label the four distinct real roots in order. 	ext{Rolle's: } f' 	ext{ has roots } c_1 \in (r_1,r_2),\; c_2 \in (r_2,r_3),\; c_3 \in (r_3,r_4) Between each consecutive pair of roots, Rolle gives at least one root of $f'$. At least 3 roots. f' 	ext{ has degree 3, so exactly 3 real roots} A cubic has at most 3 roots. Combined with at least 3, $f'$ has exactly 3 real roots. 	ext{Apply Rolle's again: } f'' 	ext{ has at least 2 real roots} Between consecutive roots of $f'$, Rolle gives roots of $f''$. Since $f''$ has degree 2, it has exactly 2 real roots. Mean Value Theorem The MVT generalizes Rolle's Theorem by dropping the requirement $f(a) = f(b)$. Rolle's Theorem is used to prove the MVT — the auxiliary function $g(x) = f(x) - L(x)$ trick reduces MVT directly to Rolle's. Curve Sketching Rolle's Theorem explains why between consecutive zeros of $f$, the derivative $f'$ must vanish — a fact used when analyzing the shape of graphs. Optimization Rolle's Theorem guarantees critical points exist under the right conditions, which is foundational for optimization problems. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step instantaneous rate of change slope dy/dx velocity marginal change real world engineering physics economics biology computer science
