Then the composite function h(t) = F(x(t), y(t)) is differentiable at t₀, and h'(t₀) = (∂F/∂x)·x'(t₀) + (∂F/∂y)·y'(t₀). This is a theorem from multivariable calculus, but in single-variable settings (where F depends on only one variable at a time), it reduces to the familiar chain rule d/dt[f(x(t))] = f'(x)·x'(t). For the chain rule to apply, we need the geometric constraint F(x(t), y(t)) = C to hold for all t in some open interval around t₀, not just at the single instant t₀. This is a continuity requirement: the relationship must be maintained throughout the motion. In the ladder problem, x² + y² = 100 holds for all t from the moment the ladder starts moving until it hits the floor. We can differentiate it with respect to t at any interior point of that interval. The singularity in the ladder problem deserves careful attention. The rate equation is dy/dt = -(x/y)·(dx/dt). As y → 0⁺, dy/dt → -∞ for any fixed positive dx/dt. This is not a mathematical artifact — it reflects a real physical breakdown. As the ladder approaches horizontal, the constraint equation x² + y² = L² becomes increasingly ill-conditioned: small changes in x (near L) produce disproportionately large changes in y (near 0). The same phenomenon appears in the well-known "barn door" problem in mechanics and in the kinematics of robotic arms near singular configurations. A subtlety often overlooked: the rate equation 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0 was derived by differentiating a constraint that assumed L is constant. If the ladder were also changing length (say, telescoping), the right side would not be zero — it would be 2L(dL/dt). The related rates method always differentiates the constraint as it actually holds, accounting for any quantities that are truly constant versus those that vary. Identifying which quantities are constant is therefore the first critical step in every problem. Chain Rule for Composite Functions (Rigorous Form) If x(t) and y(t) are differentiable at t₀ and F has continuous partial derivatives, then
\[\frac{d}{dt}F(x(t),y(t))\bigg|_{t=t_0} = \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\,x'(t_0) + \frac{\partial F}{\partial y}\,y'(t_0)\] The Constraint Must Hold on an Interval You cannot differentiate a constraint that holds only at a single instant. The equation F(x(t), y(t)) = C must be an identity — true for all t in some interval — to allow differentiation with respect to t. If it holds only at one moment, you have a condition, not a constraint. Related Rates is Implicit Differentiation in t You already know implicit differentiation — differentiating both sides of an equation with respect to x even when y depends on x. Related rates is exactly the same idea, but the independent variable is t (time). Every variable in your geometric equation is a function of t, so every term gets a (d/dt) factor via the chain rule. The technique is identical; only the name of the independent variable changes. Aircraft Radar: Two Rates, One Aircraft A radar antenna measures slant range r(t) (distance from antenna to aircraft) and azimuth angle θ(t). The aircraft's ground speed v and altitude h are related to these by r² = h² + d²(t) and tan(θ) = h/d(t). Differentiating both simultaneously gives a system of equations for dr/dt and dθ/dt in terms of v. Air traffic controllers solve related rates in real time to compute aircraft velocity vectors and predict conflicts. Do NOT Substitute Before Differentiating This is the most common error in related rates. If the base is at 6 ft at the specific instant you care about, you might be tempted to write x = 6 in the equation x² + y² = 100 immediately, getting y = 8, and then wonder what to differentiate. But you must write the equation with variables x and y, differentiate to get 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0, and THEN substitute x = 6, y = 8. Substituting first replaces the variables with constants, eliminating the rates entirely. Geometry First, Differentiate Second Draw and label the full geometry before writing derivatives. Most related-rates errors are diagram/setup errors, not differentiation errors. The Sliding Ladder Geometry The ladder, wall, and ground always form a right triangle with hypotenuse L (fixed). As x increases from 0 to L, y decreases from L to 0. The rate equation dy/dt = -(x/y)·(dx/dt) shows: when x/y is small (nearly vertical ladder), the top slides slowly. When x/y is large (nearly horizontal ladder), the top plummets. The singularity at y = 0 is a genuine physical phenomenon — the top accelerates without bound as it approaches the floor. Differentiating x² Does NOT Give 2x in Related Rates In related rates, d/dt[x²] = 2x·(dx/dt), NOT just 2x. Every variable depends on t, so every differentiation must include the chain rule factor. Forgetting dx/dt turns a rate equation into a position equation — completely wrong. If you see 2x without a (dx/dt) factor, you forgot the chain rule. Archimedes and the Sand Reckoner Archimedes (287–212 BC) computed rates of change for geometric quantities — the area of a growing circle, the volume of a filling sphere — using arguments remarkably similar to modern related rates. His 'method of exhaustion' anticipated calculus by 2000 years. The formalized chain rule came from Leibniz in the 1680s. Related Rates — General Template If Q = f(x, y, \ldots) where x, y, \ldots all depend on t, then
\[\frac{dQ}{dt} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt} + \cdots\]
This is the chain rule for functions of multiple time-dependent variables. The 5-Step Method (1) Draw and label a diagram with variable names (not numbers) on all changing quantities.
(2) Write the equation relating those variables.
(3) Differentiate both sides with respect to t (chain rule on every term).
(4) Substitute the known numerical values at the specific instant.
(5) Solve for the unknown rate. Units Must Be Consistent If x is in feet and t is in seconds, then dx/dt is in feet per second. Volume in cubic feet gives dV/dt in cubic feet per second. If different units appear (meters and centimeters, seconds and minutes), convert everything to a single system before computing. Sliding Ladder: Live Rate Animation Watch the ladder slide and observe how dy/dt changes as x grows — the top accelerates as the ladder approaches horizontal. Balloon Problem: How Radius Speed Shrinks as Volume Grows Sets dV/dt and observe how dr/dt (green arrow) shrinks as the balloon grows. The surface area is the 'spreading factor' that slows the radius. The Premier Related Rates Lab: Rocket & Plane Explore two different geometric constraints (triangles) and see how their rate equations are derived through implicit differentiation. Story Mode: Two Tanks, One Valve Narrative system-solving scenario that complements formal related-rates workflows. Sliding Ladder: Premium Interaction Explore the nonlinear relationship x² + y² = 13² in this hifi lab. Rocket Camera: Derivation Engine Click through the steps 1-5 to see the math evolve alongside the rising rocket. Proof: x² + y² = r²  →  dy/dx = −x/y Related rates differentiates x² + y² = L² with respect to t. This proof shows the same equation differentiated with respect to x — the technique is identical, only the independent variable changes. The Machine Behind Every Related Rates Problem Use the Anatomy and Scenarios tabs to see that every related rates problem — balloon, ladder, plane, cone, shadow — is the same three-step structure. Only the geometric equation changes. Python Lab: Compute & Visualize Related Rates Run each cell to numerically verify the classic related-rates results. Modify parameters and re-run to build intuition for how geometry drives the rates. Ladder Sliding Down a Wall \text{A 10-ft ladder leans against a wall. The base slides away at } \frac{dx}{dt} = 2 \text{ ft/s. Find } \frac{dy}{dt} \text{ when } x = 6 \text{ ft.} The top of the ladder slides down at 3/2 ft/s when the base is 6 ft from the wall. The ratio -(x/y) = -(6/8) = -3/4 shows that dy/dt = (3/4)·(-dx/dt) — the top slides slower than the base at this configuration. When x = y = 5√2 (the 45° configuration), dy/dt = -dx/dt exactly. x^2 + y^2 = 100 The Pythagorean theorem: base x, height y, and the fixed 10-ft hypotenuse. This holds for all t. 2x\,\frac{dx}{dt} + 2y\,\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 Differentiate both sides with respect to t. The right side is 0 because 100 is constant. The chain rule gives the factor dx/dt and dy/dt on each term. x = 6 \Rightarrow y = \sqrt{100 - 36} = \sqrt{64} = 8 Find y at the instant x = 6 using the original equation. We must know the current position of BOTH variables before substituting rates. 2(6)(2) + 2(8)\,\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 Substitute x = 6, y = 8, and dx/dt = 2 into the rate equation. 24 + 16\,\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 Simplify the left side. \frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{24}{16} = -\frac{3}{2} \text{ ft/s} Solve for dy/dt. The negative sign means y is decreasing — the top slides DOWN. At this moment the top drops at 3/2 ft/s while the base slides out at 2 ft/s — the top moves slower than the base because the ladder is more horizontal than vertical (x > y). Inflating Spherical Balloon \text{Air is pumped into a spherical balloon at } \frac{dV}{dt} = 100 \text{ cm}^3/\text{s. Find } \frac{dr}{dt} \text{ when } r = 5 \text{ cm.} When r = 5 cm, the radius grows at 1/π ≈ 0.318 cm/s. As the balloon inflates, r increases, so dr/dt = dV/dt/(4πr²) decreases — a fixed rate of air input inflates the balloon more slowly as it gets larger, because the same volume of air produces a thinner shell. This is why it's harder to blow up a large balloon than a small one. V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 Volume of a sphere. r and V are both functions of t. \frac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi r^2 \,\frac{dr}{dt} Differentiate both sides with respect to t. d/dt[(4/3)πr³] = (4/3)π·3r²·(dr/dt) = 4πr²·(dr/dt). The factor 4πr² is the surface area — new volume is added in a thin surface layer. 100 = 4\pi(5)^2 \cdot \frac{dr}{dt} Substitute dV/dt = 100 and r = 5. 100 = 4\pi(25)\,\frac{dr}{dt} = 100\pi\,\frac{dr}{dt} Simplify: 4π·25 = 100π. \frac{dr}{dt} = \frac{100}{100\pi} = \frac{1}{\pi} \approx 0.318 \text{ cm/s} Solve for dr/dt. The radius grows at 1/π cm/s at this moment. Water Draining from a Conical Tank \text{A conical tank (vertex down) has radius 3 m at the top and height 4 m. Water drains at } \frac{dV}{dt} = -2 \text{ m}^3/\text{min. Find } \frac{dh}{dt} \text{ when } h = 2 \text{ m.} The water level drops at 8/(9π) ≈ 0.283 m/min when h = 2 m. Notice that as h decreases, dh/dt = -32/(9πh²) would increase in magnitude — the water level drops faster as the cone narrows near the vertex, because each meter drop corresponds to less volume lost. \frac{r}{h} = \frac{3}{4} \Rightarrow r = \frac{3h}{4} Similar triangles: the tank has radius 3 when height is 4. At any water height h, the water surface radius r satisfies r/h = 3/4. This is the key geometric constraint that reduces two variables to one. V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \frac{1}{3}\pi \left(\frac{3h}{4}\right)^2 h = \frac{3\pi h^3}{16} Substitute r = 3h/4 into the cone volume formula. Now V is a function of h alone — a single-variable relationship. \frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{9\pi h^2}{16}\,\frac{dh}{dt} Differentiate V = 3πh³/16 with respect to t. d/dt[3πh³/16] = (9πh²/16)·(dh/dt). -2 = \frac{9\pi(2)^2}{16}\,\frac{dh}{dt} = \frac{9\pi}{4}\,\frac{dh}{dt} Substitute dV/dt = -2 (negative because draining) and h = 2. Simplify: 9π·4/16 = 9π/4. \frac{dh}{dt} = \frac{-2 \cdot 4}{9\pi} = \frac{-8}{9\pi} \approx -0.283 \text{ m/min} Solve for dh/dt. The water level drops at 8/(9π) m/min. Shadow Length Problem \text{A 20-ft streetlight illuminates a person 6 ft tall walking at 5 ft/s away from the base. Find the rate the shadow tip moves.} The shadow's tip moves at 50/7 ≈ 7.14 ft/s, faster than the person's 5 ft/s walking speed. The shadow stretches as the person walks, so the tip moves even faster than the walker. This rate is constant regardless of how far from the post — a consequence of the linear similar-triangles relationship. \text{Let } x = \text{person's distance from base, } s = \text{shadow length} Define variables. Both x and s are functions of t. The tip of the shadow is at distance x + s from the base. \frac{20}{x + s} = \frac{6}{s} Similar triangles: the streetlight, the tip of the shadow, and the person's top form similar triangles. The full triangle (from base to shadow tip, height 20) is similar to the small triangle (from person to shadow tip, height 6). 20s = 6(x + s) \Rightarrow 20s = 6x + 6s \Rightarrow 14s = 6x Cross-multiply and simplify. This gives the constraint between s and x. s = \frac{3x}{7} Solve for s in terms of x. \frac{ds}{dt} = \frac{3}{7}\,\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{3}{7}(5) = \frac{15}{7} \approx 2.14 \text{ ft/s} Differentiate both sides with respect to t. Since 3/7 is constant, ds/dt = (3/7)·(dx/dt). The shadow length grows at a constant 15/7 ft/s. \text{Shadow tip speed} = \frac{d}{dt}(x + s) = \frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{ds}{dt} = 5 + \frac{15}{7} = \frac{50}{7} \approx 7.14 \text{ ft/s} The tip moves at the person's speed plus the shadow growth rate. The shadow tip outpaces the person. Angle of Elevation of a Rising Balloon \text{A balloon rises at 10 ft/s. An observer is 500 ft horizontally from the launch point. Find } d\theta/dt \text{ when the balloon is at height } h = 500 \text{ ft.} The angle of elevation increases at 1/100 rad/s when the balloon is at 500 ft. As the balloon continues to rise, θ approaches π/2 and sec²(θ) → ∞, which drives dθ/dt → 0 for fixed dh/dt — the angle barely changes when the balloon is nearly overhead because the geometry is almost degenerate. \tan(\theta) = \frac{h}{500} The angle of elevation θ satisfies tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent = h/500. Both θ and h vary with t. \sec^2(\theta)\,\frac{d\theta}{dt} = \frac{1}{500}\,\frac{dh}{dt} Differentiate both sides with respect to t. d/dt[tan(θ)] = sec²(θ)·(dθ/dt) by the chain rule. The right side: d/dt[h/500] = (1/500)·(dh/dt). h = 500 \Rightarrow \tan(\theta) = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = \frac{\pi}{4} At h = 500 ft, tan(θ) = 500/500 = 1, so θ = π/4 (45°). \sec^2\!\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{\cos^2(\pi/4)} = \frac{1}{(1/\sqrt{2})^2} = 2 Compute sec²(π/4). cos(π/4) = 1/√2, so cos²(π/4) = 1/2, so sec²(π/4) = 2. 2\,\frac{d\theta}{dt} = \frac{10}{500} = \frac{1}{50} Substitute sec²(θ) = 2 and dh/dt = 10 into the rate equation. \frac{d\theta}{dt} = \frac{1}{100} \text{ rad/s} Solve for dθ/dt. The angle increases at 1/100 radian per second at this moment — about 0.57°/s. Two Cars Approaching an Intersection \text{Car A moves north at 60 mph and Car B moves east at 80 mph, both toward an intersection. Find } dz/dt \text{ when A is 5 mi away and B is 12 mi away.} The cars are closing distance at ≈96.9 mph. Note that this is NOT simply 60 + 80 = 140 mph — that would be the rate if they were driving toward each other on a straight road. Because they are on perpendicular roads, the geometry moderates the closure rate through the 5-12-13 triangle. z^2 = x^2 + y^2 Let x = Car B's distance from intersection, y = Car A's distance, z = distance between cars. The cars are on perpendicular roads, so the Pythagorean theorem applies. 2z\,\frac{dz}{dt} = 2x\,\frac{dx}{dt} + 2y\,\frac{dy}{dt} Differentiate both sides with respect to t. x = 12, \; y = 5 \Rightarrow z = \sqrt{144 + 25} = \sqrt{169} = 13 \text{ mi} Compute z using the Pythagorean theorem. The 5-12-13 right triangle gives z = 13. \frac{dx}{dt} = -80, \quad \frac{dy}{dt} = -60 Both cars approach the intersection, so their distances decrease: dx/dt = -80 mph (B moves east toward intersection), dy/dt = -60 mph (A moves north toward intersection). 2(13)\,\frac{dz}{dt} = 2(12)(-80) + 2(5)(-60) Substitute all values into the rate equation. 26\,\frac{dz}{dt} = -1920 - 600 = -2520 Simplify the right side. \frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{-2520}{26} = -\frac{1260}{13} \approx -96.9 \text{ mph} The negative sign means the cars are getting closer. They approach each other at about 96.9 mph. Spreading Circular Oil Slick \text{A circular oil slick grows at } dA/dt = 50 \text{ m}^2/\text{hr. Find } dr/dt \text{ when } r = 10 \text{ m.} The radius grows at 5/(2π) ≈ 0.796 m/hr when r = 10 m. As the slick spreads, r increases, and the same rate of area increase produces a smaller rate of radius increase — the circle spreads more slowly in radial terms the larger it gets. A = \pi r^2 Area of a circle. Both A and r depend on t. \frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi r\,\frac{dr}{dt} Differentiate both sides with respect to t. d/dt[πr²] = 2πr·(dr/dt). 50 = 2\pi(10)\,\frac{dr}{dt} = 20\pi\,\frac{dr}{dt} Substitute dA/dt = 50 and r = 10. \frac{dr}{dt} = \frac{50}{20\pi} = \frac{5}{2\pi} \approx 0.796 \text{ m/hr} Solve for dr/dt. A kite flies at constant height 100 m. The string is let out at 5 m/s. Find the rate the horizontal distance from the flier increases when 200 m of string has been let out. Let L = string length (the hypotenuse), x = horizontal distance (one leg), height = 100 m (the other leg, fixed). Use x² + 100² = L². Differentiate and substitute. \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{10\sqrt{3}}{3} \approx 5.77 \text{ m/s} \text{Step 1: Read the problem and name every quantity} Before touching any math, list what changes, what is fixed, what rate you know, and what rate you need. x^2 + 100^2 = L^2 The Pythagorean theorem is the constraint — true at every instant. Both $x$ and $L$ are functions of time. The 100 is a constant. \frac{d}{dt}[x^2 + 100^2] = \frac{d}{dt}[L^2] Differentiate both sides with respect to $t$. 2x\,\frac{dx}{dt} + 0 = 2L\,\frac{dL}{dt} Each variable picks up a rate factor via the chain rule. The constant $100^2$ differentiates to zero. x\,\frac{dx}{dt} = L\,\frac{dL}{dt} Divide both sides by 2. Optional cleanup — makes the next substitution slightly less cluttered. x = \sqrt{L^2 - 100^2} We need the value of $x$ at the moment $L = 200$. Solve the constraint for $x$. x = \sqrt{200^2 - 100^2} = \sqrt{40000 - 10000} = \sqrt{30000} Substitute $L = 200$, compute $200^2 = 40000$ and $100^2 = 10000$, subtract. x = \sqrt{10000 \cdot 3} = 100\sqrt{3} \approx 173.2 \text{ m} Factor $30000 = 10000 \times 3$, then pull out $\sqrt{10000} = 100$. (100\sqrt{3})\,\frac{dx}{dt} = (200)(5) Substitute all known values into $x\,\frac{dx}{dt} = L\,\frac{dL}{dt}$. \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{1000}{100\sqrt{3}} = \frac{10}{\sqrt{3}} Right side: $200 \times 5 = 1000$. Divide both sides by $100\sqrt{3}$ to isolate $\frac{dx}{dt}$. \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{10}{\sqrt{3}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{10\sqrt{3}}{3} \approx 5.77 \text{ m/s} Rationalize the denominator by multiplying by $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} = 1$. Gravel is dumped onto a conical pile at 30 ft³/min. The cone always satisfies h = 2r (height equals twice the base radius). Find dh/dt when h = 10 ft. Write V in terms of h alone using r = h/2. Then differentiate. \dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{6}{5\pi} \approx 0.382 \text{ ft/min} \text{Definition: Volume of a cone is } V = \frac{1}{3} \pi r^2 h This is the standard formula. Here both r and h change with time, but they are related by the fixed ratio h = 2r. \text{Given relation: } h = 2r \implies r = \frac{h}{2} The pile maintains a constant shape (similar cones). We want dh/dt, so eliminate r in favor of h. \text{Substitute into volume: } V = \frac{1}{3} \pi \left(\frac{h}{2}\right)^2 h = \frac{1}{3} \pi \cdot \frac{h^2}{4} \cdot h = \frac{\pi h^3}{12} Careful algebra: (h/2)² = h²/4, then times h = h³/4, then 1/3 π gives π h³ / 12. Now V depends only on h. \text{Differentiate both sides with respect to t: } \frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\pi}{12} h^3 ight) Chain rule will appear because h = h(t). \frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{\pi}{12} \cdot 3 h^2 \cdot \frac{dh}{dt} = \frac{\pi h^2}{4} \cdot \frac{dh}{dt} Power rule on h³ gives 3h², then multiply by π/12 and dh/dt. Simplified coefficient: 3π/12 = π/4. \text{We know } \frac{dV}{dt} = 30 \text{ ft³/min (gravel added at constant rate)} Positive because volume is increasing. 30 = \frac{\pi (10)^2}{4} \cdot \frac{dh}{dt} Plug in h = 10 ft at the moment of interest. 30 = \frac{\pi \cdot 100}{4} \cdot \frac{dh}{dt} = 25\pi \cdot \frac{dh}{dt} 100/4 = 25, times π. \frac{dh}{dt} = \frac{30}{25\pi} = \frac{6}{5\pi} \text{ ft/min} Simplify fraction: divide numerator and denominator by 5. Approximate ≈ 0.382 ft/min. The height rises slowly because the pile is getting wider as it grows. \text{Aha insight: Even though volume increases at constant rate, dh/dt decreases as h grows because the cone is spreading out — more volume is needed to raise the height the same amount later.} This is why the rate is smaller at larger heights. A boat is pulled toward a dock by a rope passing over a pulley 12 ft above the water. The rope is pulled in at 3 ft/s. How fast is the boat moving toward the dock when 15 ft of rope extends from the pulley? Let x = horizontal distance of boat from the dock, L = length of rope from pulley to boat. These satisfy x² + 12² = L². Differentiate. Note: the boat moves horizontally, not along the rope. \text{The boat approaches the dock at } 5 \text{ ft/s.} \text{Setup: The pulley is 12 ft above the water (fixed vertical distance).} The rope goes from boat to pulley (length L), then presumably to the person pulling. We care about the segment from pulley to boat. \text{Pythagorean relation: } x^2 + 12^2 = L^2 \quad \text{or} \quad x^2 + 144 = L^2 x is the horizontal distance from the point directly below the pulley to the boat. L is the slant length of the rope. \text{Differentiate with respect to t: } 2x \frac{dx}{dt} + 0 = 2L \frac{dL}{dt} Chain rule again. Constant 144 drops out. \text{Simplify: } x \frac{dx}{dt} = L \frac{dL}{dt} Divided by 2 for cleanliness. \text{At the instant of interest: L = 15 ft} Given directly. x = \sqrt{L^2 - 144} = \sqrt{225 - 144} = \sqrt{81} = 9 \text{ ft} Positive root because distance. \text{Rate at which rope is pulled: } \frac{dL}{dt} = -3 \text{ ft/s} Important: pulled in means the length L is decreasing, so negative sign. This is a common source of sign errors in related rates. \text{Substitute into the rate equation: } 9 \cdot \frac{dx}{dt} = 15 \cdot (-3) x = 9, L = 15, dL/dt = -3. 9 \frac{dx}{dt} = -45 \implies \frac{dx}{dt} = -5 \text{ ft/s} Solve for dx/dt. The negative sign means x is decreasing — the boat is moving toward the dock. \text{Interpretation: The boat approaches the dock at 5 ft/s (speed is the absolute value).} The question asks 'how fast is the boat moving toward the dock' — so we report the positive speed 5 ft/s, but the signed rate is -5 ft/s. \text{Aha insight: When the rope is steeper (smaller x), pulling the rope moves the boat faster horizontally. Here at L=15, x=9, the boat moves faster (5 ft/s) than the rope is pulled (3 ft/s).} The angle converts the rope speed into a larger horizontal component. Implicit Differentiation Related rates is implicit differentiation with t as the independent variable. Review Chapter 2's implicit differentiation lesson. The Chain Rule Every related rates calculation applies the chain rule. The chain rule is the mathematical engine behind d/dt[f(x(t))] = f'(x)·(dx/dt). Optimization Optimization also requires setting up geometric equations and using calculus to extract information. The modeling skills are closely related. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step instantaneous rate of change slope dy/dx velocity marginal change maximize minimize maxima minima best value related rates word problem changing over time real world engineering physics economics biology computer science

documents.assignment: Intervals of Increase/Decrease and Local Extrema Find where $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 1$ is increasing and decreasing, and identify all local extrema.   Increasing on (−∞, 1) and (3, ∞). Decreasing on (1, 3). Local max at (1, 5). Local min at (3, 1). The function rises, peaks, dips, then rises again — a classic cubic shape. f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x^2 - 4x + 3) = 3(x-1)(x-3) Factor the derivative. f'(x) = 0 \implies x = 1 \text{ or } x = 3 Two critical points. f' exists everywhere (polynomial). \textbf{Sign chart: divide number line at } x=1 \text{ and } x=3  x < 1: \text{ test } x=0: f'(0) = 3(−1)(−3) = 9 > 0 \implies \text{increasing}  1 < x < 3: \text{ test } x=2: f'(2) = 3(1)(−1) = -3 < 0 \implies \text{decreasing}  x > 3: \text{ test } x=4: f'(4) = 3(3)(1) = 9 > 0 \implies \text{increasing}  \textbf{First Derivative Test:}  x=1: f' \text{ changes } + \to - \implies \text{local MAXIMUM at } x=1,\; f(1) = 1 - 6 + 9 + 1 = 5  x=3: f' \text{ changes } - \to + \implies \text{local MINIMUM at } x=3,\; f(3) = 27 - 54 + 27 + 1 = 1  Increasing/Decreasing for a Rational Function Find the intervals of increase and decrease for $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2}{x^2 - 4}$, and all local extrema.   Increasing on (−∞, −2) and (−2, 0). Decreasing on (0, 2) and (2, ∞). Local maximum at (0, 0). No local minimum (the function has vertical asymptotes at ±2, not extrema). f'(x) = \frac{2x(x^2-4) - x^2 \cdot 2x}{(x^2-4)^2} = \frac{2x^3 - 8x - 2x^3}{(x^2-4)^2} = \frac{-8x}{(x^2-4)^2} Quotient rule. Simplify the numerator. f'(x) = 0 \implies x = 0 \qquad f'(x) \text{ DNE: } x = \pm 2 \text{ (not in domain!)} x = ±2 make the original f undefined. They are NOT critical points — they're outside the domain. \text{Intervals: } (-\infty,-2),\;(-2,0),\;(0,2),\;(2,\infty) The domain excludes x = ±2, so these split the number line into four parts. x=-3: f'(-3) = \frac{24}{25} > 0 \; (\uparrow) \qquad x=-1: f'(-1) = \frac{8}{9} > 0 \; (\uparrow) Increasing on (−∞, −2) and (−2, 0). x=1: f'(1) = \frac{-8}{9} < 0 \; (\downarrow) \qquad x=3: f'(3) = \frac{-24}{25} < 0 \; (\downarrow) Decreasing on (0, 2) and (2, ∞). x=0: f' \text{ changes } + \to - \implies \text{local MAXIMUM at } x=0,\; f(0) = 0   Find the local max and min of $f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3$. f'(x) = 4x³ − 12x² = 4x²(x − 3). Sign chart: what sign does 4x² have? No extremum at x = 0 (inflection point). Local minimum at x = 3, f(3) = −27.  f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2 = 4x^2(x-3)  f'(x) = 0 \implies x = 0 \text{ or } x = 3  4x^2 \geq 0 \text{ always} 4x² never changes sign! documents.proofs: **Proof of Increasing/Decreasing Theorem:** Suppose f'(x) > 0 on (a, b). Pick any a < x₁ < x₂ < b. By the Mean Value Theorem, there exists c ∈ (x₁, x₂) such that f(x₂) − f(x₁) = f'(c)(x₂ − x₁). Since f'(c) > 0 and x₂ − x₁ > 0, we get f(x₂) − f(x₁) > 0, i.e., f(x₁) < f(x₂). Since x₁ < x₂ was arbitrary, f is strictly increasing. ■ **Why the First Derivative Test works:** If f' changes from + to − at c, then for x just left of c, f is increasing (approaching the max), and for x just right of c, f is decreasing (moving away from the max). So f(c) is larger than all nearby values → local max. The argument for local min is symmetric. Formal Increasing Definition f \text{ is strictly increasing on } (a,b) \iff \forall x_1, x_2 \in (a,b): x_1 < x_2 \Rightarrow f(x_1) < f(x_2)
documents.applications: A cardiologist reading an EKG can identify exactly when the heart rate is increasing, when it peaks, and when it falls — without measuring every millisecond. The derivative is your EKG reader for any function. Where f' > 0: the function is rising. Where f' < 0: falling. Where f' changes sign: a peak or valley. This is the First Derivative Test — the first systematic tool for analyzing function behavior and it's the foundation of every optimization problem that follows.

documents.assignment: Complete Concavity Analysis — Inflection Points Step by Step Find all intervals of concavity and all inflection points for f(x) = x⁴ − 6x² + 1.   Concave up on (−∞, −1) and (1, ∞). Concave down on (−1, 1). Inflection points at (−1, −4) and (1, −4). The graph has a "W" shape — two local minima connected by an arch. f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x Power rule on each term: d/dx[x⁴] = 4x³, d/dx[−6x²] = −12x, d/dx[1] = 0. f''(x) = 12x^2 - 12 Differentiate f'(x) with the power rule: d/dx[4x³] = 12x², d/dx[−12x] = −12. f''(x) = 12(x^2 - 1) = 12(x-1)(x+1) Factor out 12 and then factor the difference of squares: x² − 1 = (x−1)(x+1). f''(x) = 0 \implies x = \pm 1 12(x−1)(x+1) = 0 when x = 1 or x = −1. These are the inflection candidates. \textbf{Three intervals: } (-\infty,-1),\;(-1,1),\;(1,\infty) The two candidates split the line into three regions. x < -1: \text{test } x=-2: f''(-2) = 12(4-1) = 36 > 0 \;\to\; \text{concave UP} Both factors (x−1) and (x+1) are negative at x = −2 → product is positive. -1 < x < 1: \text{test } x=0: f''(0) = 12(0-1) = -12 < 0 \;\to\; \text{concave DOWN} (x−1) = −1 < 0, (x+1) = 1 > 0 → product is negative. x > 1: \text{test } x=2: f''(2) = 12(4-1) = 36 > 0 \;\to\; \text{concave UP} Both factors positive → product positive. f'' \text{ changes sign at } x = -1 \text{ and } x = 1 \implies \text{both ARE inflection points} At x = −1: concavity goes UP → DOWN. At x = 1: DOWN → UP. Both confirmed. f(-1) = (-1)^4 - 6(-1)^2 + 1 = 1 - 6 + 1 = -4 Compute the y-coordinates. (−1)⁴ = 1, (−1)² = 1. f(1) = 1 - 6 + 1 = -4 By symmetry (f is even), f(1) = f(−1) = −4. Using the SDT to Classify Critical Points — Full Walkthrough Find and classify all critical points of f(x) = x³ − 3x + 2 using the Second Derivative Test.   Local maximum at (−1, 4) — f'' is negative (dome shape). Local minimum at (1, 0) — f'' is positive (bowl shape). The SDT worked cleanly here because f''(±1) ≠ 0. f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 Power rule: d/dx[x³] = 3x², d/dx[−3x] = −3, d/dx[2] = 0. 3x^2 - 3 = 0 \implies x^2 = 1 \implies x = \pm 1 Add 3 to both sides, divide by 3, take square root. Two critical points. f''(x) = 6x Differentiate f'(x) = 3x² − 3: d/dx[3x²] = 6x, d/dx[−3] = 0. f''(-1) = 6(-1) = -6 < 0 Plug x = −1 into f''(x) = 6x. Negative → SDT says local MAXIMUM. f(-1) = (-1)^3 - 3(-1) + 2 = -1 + 3 + 2 = 4 Find the y-value: compute f at the critical point. Local max at (−1, 4). f''(1) = 6(1) = 6 > 0 Plug x = 1 into f''(x) = 6x. Positive → SDT says local MINIMUM. f(1) = 1 - 3 + 2 = 0 Local min at (1, 0). When the SDT Fails — Falling Back to the Sign Chart Classify the critical point of f(x) = x⁴ at x = 0. Show that the SDT fails, then use the FDT.   The SDT gave f''(0) = 0 — inconclusive. But the sign chart confirmed x = 0 is a local minimum. When the SDT fails, always reach for the sign chart. The two methods are complementary, not competing. f'(x) = 4x^3 Power rule. 4x^3 = 0 \implies x = 0 \quad\text{(only critical point)}  f''(x) = 12x^2 Differentiate f'(x) = 4x³: power rule gives 12x². f''(0) = 12(0)^2 = 0 SDT is INCONCLUSIVE. f'' = 0 at the critical point — the test cannot tell us anything. We need the sign chart. \textbf{Sign chart for } f'(x) = 4x^3: Test the sign of f'(x) on each side of x = 0. x < 0: f'(x) = 4x^3 < 0 \;(\downarrow) \qquad x > 0: f'(x) = 4x^3 > 0 \;(\uparrow) For x < 0: x³ is negative, so 4x³ < 0. For x > 0: x³ is positive, so 4x³ > 0. f' \text{ changes } - \to + \text{ at } x=0 \implies \textbf{local MINIMUM} Falling before c, rising after c → valley → local minimum. f(0) = 0^4 = 0 \implies \text{local (and absolute) min at } (0, 0) x⁴ ≥ 0 for all x, confirming this is also the global minimum.  Find the inflection point(s) of f(x) = xe^{−x}. Use the product rule to get f', then the product rule again to get f''. Set f'' = 0 and check the sign change. Inflection point at (2, 2e⁻²)  f'(x) = (x)'e^{-x} + x(e^{-x})' = e^{-x} + x(-e^{-x}) = e^{-x}(1-x) Product rule with u = x, v = e^{−x}. Derivative of e^{−x}: chain rule gives e^{−x}·(−1) = −e^{−x}. f''(x) = (e^{-x})'(1-x) + e^{-x}(1-x)' Product rule on f'(x) = e^{−x}(1−x). Now u = e^{−x}, v = (1−x). = (-e^{-x})(1-x) + e^{-x}(-1) = e^{-x}[-(1-x)-1] = e^{-x}(x-2) Factor out e^{−x}. Simplify: −(1−x)−1 = −1+x−1 = x−2. f''(x) = 0 \implies x = 2 \quad (e^{-x} > 0 \text{ always}) e^{−x} is never zero, so x − 2 = 0 → x = 2. x < 2: f'' < 0 \;(\cap) \qquad x > 2: f'' > 0 \;(\cup) Sign changes → inflection point confirmed. f(2) = 2e^{-2} \qquad \text{Inflection point: }(2,\;2e^{-2}) \approx (2,\;0.27)   Build a function with inflection points at x = 0 and x = 2, and a local minimum at x = 1. Design f''(x) so it changes sign at x = 0 and x = 2. Then integrate twice to recover f. f(x) = x⁴/12 − x³/3 + 2x/3 + D for any constant D.  \text{Goal: } f'' \text{ changes sign at } 0 \text{ and } 2.  \text{Try: } f''(x) = x(x-2) = x^2-2x A parabola that crosses zero at 0 and 2 and changes sign at each. For x < 0: (neg)(neg) > 0. For 0 < x < 2: (pos)(neg) < 0. For x > 2: (pos)(pos) > 0. Concavity changes at both points. ✓ f'(x) = \int (x^2 - 2x)\,dx = \frac{x^3}{3} - x^2 + C Integrate term by term using the power rule for integrals: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1). f'(1) = 0 \text{ (want local min at } x=1\text{)}: \frac{1}{3} - 1 + C = 0 \implies C = \frac{2}{3} Set f'(1) = 0 and solve for C. f(x) = \int f'\,dx = \frac{x^4}{12} - \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{2x}{3} + D Integrate again. D is a free constant — any value works.
documents.proofs: **Full proof of the Second Derivative Test (case f''(c) > 0 → local min):** Suppose f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0. By the definition of f''(c): f''(c) = lim(h→0) [f'(c+h) − f'(c)] / h = lim(h→0) f'(c+h) / h  (since f'(c) = 0) Since this limit is f''(c) > 0, for all sufficiently small h:  f'(c+h)/h > 0. • For h > 0 (just right of c): f'(c+h) > 0  →  f is increasing just right of c • For h < 0 (just left of c):  f'(c+h) < 0  →  f is decreasing just left of c So f' changes from − to + at c → by the First Derivative Test → local minimum. ■ Summary Table \begin{array}{c|c|l} f'(c) & f''(c) & \text{Conclusion} \\ \hline 0 & > 0 & \text{Local minimum (bowl)} \\ 0 & < 0 & \text{Local maximum (dome)} \\ 0 & 0 & \text{Inconclusive — use FDT} \\ \neq 0 & \text{any} & \text{Not an extremum} \end{array}
documents.applications: If unemployment is falling but falling more slowly each month, the unemployment rate has a negative derivative (it is decreasing — good), but a POSITIVE second derivative (the rate of decrease is itself slowing down — less good). In physics, an object landing softly is near the minimum of its velocity — the derivative is zero and the second derivative is positive. The second derivative tells you not just where a quantity is, but whether its rate of change is speeding up or slowing down. It is the difference between recovering and recovering faster.

Concavity changes at both points. ✓ f'(x) = \int (x^2 - 2x)\,dx = \frac{x^3}{3} - x^2 + C Integrate term by term using the power rule for integrals: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1). f'(1) = 0 \text{ (want local min at } x=1\text{)}: \frac{1}{3} - 1 + C = 0 \implies C = \frac{2}{3} Set f'(1) = 0 and solve for C. f(x) = \int f'\,dx = \frac{x^4}{12} - \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{2x}{3} + D Integrate again. D is a free constant — any value works. Prerequisite & Fallback: First Derivative Test When the SDT gives f''(c) = 0, you MUST use the FDT sign chart. Prerequisite: Higher-Order Derivatives Concavity requires computing f''(x) — the second derivative. Next: Full Curve Sketching Concavity analysis (SDT + inflection points) is step 4 of the complete curve-sketching process. Applied: Optimization The SDT is often the fastest way to confirm a critical point is a minimum in applied problems. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step instantaneous rate of change slope dy/dx velocity marginal change real world engineering physics economics biology computer science

documents.assignment: Sketch f(x) = x³ - 3x \text{Completely sketch } f(x) = x^3 - 3x: \text{ find all intercepts, critical points, inflection points, and concavity.}   f(x) = x³ - 3x: rising on (-∞,-1) ∪ (1,∞), falling on (-1,1). Local max at (-1,2), local min at (1,-2). Inflection at (0,0) — concave down for x < 0, up for x > 0. X-intercepts at 0 and ±√3. Odd function (symmetric about origin). As x → ±∞, f → ±∞. f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x^2 - 1) = 3(x-1)(x+1) Derivative factored. Critical points at x = ±1. f'(x) > 0 \text{ on } (-\infty,-1), \quad f'(x) < 0 \text{ on } (-1,1), \quad f'(x) > 0 \text{ on } (1,\infty) Sign chart for f': f' = 3(x-1)(x+1). Test x = -2: 3(3)(-1) < 0... actually + + = + > 0. Test x = 0: 3(-1)(1) < 0. Test x = 2: 3(1)(3) > 0. ✓ f''(x) = 6x Second derivative. f''(-1) = -6 < 0 \Rightarrow \text{local max at } x = -1 Second derivative test: f''(-1) < 0 confirms local maximum. f(-1) = -1 + 3 = 2 Local maximum value: f(-1) = 2. Point: (-1, 2). f''(1) = 6 > 0 \Rightarrow \text{local min at } x = 1 f''(1) > 0 confirms local minimum. f(1) = 1 - 3 = -2 Local minimum value: f(1) = -2. Point: (1, -2). f''(x) = 6x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0 \text{ (inflection point)} f'' changes sign at x = 0 (negative for x < 0, positive for x > 0). Inflection point at (0, f(0)) = (0, 0). x\text{-intercepts: } x^3 - 3x = x(x^2-3) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0, \pm\sqrt{3} Factor to find x-intercepts. Sketch f(x) = x⁴ - 4x³ (the hook function) \text{Completely analyze } f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3.   f(x) = x⁴ - 4x³: decreasing on (-∞, 3), increasing on (3,∞). Local (and global) minimum at (3,-27). Inflection points at (0,0) and (2,-16). Concave up on (-∞,0) and (2,∞), concave down on (0,2). As x → ±∞, f → +∞ (even-degree leading term is positive). Y-intercept at (0,0). f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2 = 4x^2(x - 3) Factor the derivative. f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0 \text{ or } x = 3 Critical points at x = 0 and x = 3. \text{Sign chart: } f' < 0 \text{ for } x < 0, \; f' < 0 \text{ for } 0 < x < 3, \; f' > 0 \text{ for } x > 3 Test x = -1: 4(1)(-4) < 0. Test x = 1: 4(1)(-2) < 0. Test x = 4: 4(16)(1) > 0. Note: f' < 0 on BOTH sides of x=0. f' \text{ does NOT change sign at } x = 0 \Rightarrow \text{no local extremum at } 0 Since f' stays negative through x = 0, the first derivative test gives neither max nor min. This is an inflection-like point. f' \text{ changes from } - \text{ to } + \text{ at } x = 3 \Rightarrow \text{local minimum at } x = 3 Local minimum at x = 3. f(3) = 81 - 108 = -27 Local minimum value: -27. Point (3, -27). f''(x) = 12x^2 - 24x = 12x(x-2) Second derivative. f''(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0 \text{ or } x = 2 Potential inflection points. f'' < 0 \text{ on } (0,2), \; f'' > 0 \text{ on } (-\infty,0) \cup (2,\infty) Sign chart for f''. Inflection points at x = 0 and x = 2, confirmed by sign changes. f(0) = 0, \; f(2) = 16 - 32 = -16 Inflection points: (0,0) and (2,-16). Sketch the Rational Function f(x) = x/(x²+1) \text{Analyze } f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x^2+1}: \text{ asymptotes, critical points, concavity.}   The function x/(x²+1) is odd (f(-x) = -f(x)), bounded between -1/2 and 1/2. It resembles a scaled arctan curve: rises from 0, peaks at (1, 1/2), descends, returns to the asymptote y=0. It has three inflection points. The function is sometimes called the "witch of Agnesi" derivative. \lim_{x \to \pm\infty} \frac{x}{x^2+1} = \lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\frac{1/x}{1+1/x^2} = 0 Horizontal asymptote: y = 0 (both directions). No vertical asymptotes since x²+1 > 0 always. f'(x) = \frac{(x^2+1) - x(2x)}{(x^2+1)^2} = \frac{1 - x^2}{(x^2+1)^2} Quotient rule derivative. f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow 1 - x^2 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm 1 Critical points at x = ±1. Denominator is always positive. f' > 0 \text{ on } (-1,1), \; f' < 0 \text{ on } (-\infty,-1) \cup (1,\infty) Sign of 1-x²: positive for |x| < 1, negative for |x| > 1. So f increases on (-1,1) and decreases elsewhere. f(-1) = -1/2 \text{ (local min)}, \quad f(1) = 1/2 \text{ (local max)} Local minimum at (-1,-1/2), local maximum at (1,1/2). f''(x) = \frac{-2x(x^2+1)^2 - (1-x^2) \cdot 2(x^2+1)(2x)}{(x^2+1)^4} = \frac{2x(x^2-3)}{(x^2+1)^3} Second derivative (simplified). Inflection points where numerator = 0: x = 0 or x = ±√3. \text{Inflection points: } (0,0), (\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3}/4), (-\sqrt{3}, -\sqrt{3}/4) Verify sign changes in f''. Sketch the Bell Curve f(x) = e^(-x²) \text{Analyze } f(x) = e^{-x^2}.   The bell curve e^{-x²} has a global maximum at (0,1), inflection points at (±1/√2, e^{-1/2}), is concave down between the inflection points and concave up outside. It is symmetric, always positive, and approaches 0 as x → ±∞. The normal distribution's pdf is (1/√(2π))·e^{-x²/2}, a scaled and stretched version. f(0) = 1, \; \lim_{x \to \pm\infty} e^{-x^2} = 0 Y-intercept at (0,1). Horizontal asymptote y = 0 in both directions. No zeros (e^anything > 0 always). Even function (symmetric about y-axis). f'(x) = -2x\,e^{-x^2} Chain rule: derivative of e^u is e^u·u', where u = -x², u' = -2x. f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0 Only critical point at x = 0. f' > 0 \text{ for } x < 0, \; f' < 0 \text{ for } x > 0 \Rightarrow \text{local (global) max at } (0,1) Sign of -2x·e^{-x²}: the exponential is always positive. Sign = sign of -2x. So f' > 0 for x < 0, < 0 for x > 0. f''(x) = -2e^{-x^2} + (-2x)(-2x)e^{-x^2} = e^{-x^2}(4x^2 - 2) Differentiate f' using product rule. f''(x) = 0 \Rightarrow 4x^2 - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} Inflection points at x = ±1/√2 ≈ ±0.707. f(\pm 1/\sqrt{2}) = e^{-1/2} \approx 0.607 Inflection points at (±1/√2, e^{-1/2}). Sketch f(x) = x - sin(x) on [0, 2π] \text{Analyze } f(x) = x - \sin(x) \text{ on } [0, 2\pi].   f(x) = x - sin(x) is always increasing (f' ≥ 0), ranging from 0 at x=0 to 2π at x=2π. Concave up on (0,π) and concave down on (π,2π), with inflection point at (π, π). The function is the integral of 1-cos(x), which appears in the area under a cycloid. f'(x) = 1 - \cos(x) Derivative. f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow \cos(x) = 1 \Rightarrow x = 0, 2\pi \text{ (on } [0,2\pi]) Critical points only at the endpoints of the interval. f'(x) = 1 - \cos(x) \geq 0 \text{ always (since } \cos(x) \leq 1) f is non-decreasing on [0, 2π]. It is strictly increasing except at x = 0 and 2π where f' = 0 momentarily. f''(x) = \sin(x) Second derivative. f''(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0, \pi, 2\pi \text{ on } [0,2\pi] Potential inflection points. f''\text{ changes sign at } x=\pi: \sin(x) > 0 \text{ on } (0,\pi), \sin(x) < 0 \text{ on } (\pi,2\pi) Inflection point at x = π. f(0) = 0, \; f(\pi) = \pi \approx 3.14, \; f(2\pi) = 2\pi \approx 6.28 Key values. At x = π, f(π) = π - sin(π) = π. Sketch f(x) = ln(x)/x on (0, ∞) \text{Analyze } f(x) = \dfrac{\ln(x)}{x} \text{ on } (0, \infty).   ln(x)/x rises from -∞ to a maximum of 1/e at x = e, then decreases toward 0 asymptotically. The x-intercept is at x = 1. The maximum at x = e is the key value — this function appears in the optimization of x^(1/x) (which has a maximum also at x = e, giving e^(1/e)). \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\ln(x)}{x} = -\infty As x → 0⁺: ln(x) → -∞ and 1/x → +∞, so the product → -∞. Vertical asymptote behavior at x = 0. \lim_{x \to +\infty} \frac{\ln(x)}{x} = 0 As x → ∞: x grows much faster than ln(x) (by L'Hôpital: (1/x)/1 → 0). Horizontal asymptote y = 0. f'(x) = \frac{(1/x) \cdot x - \ln(x) \cdot 1}{x^2} = \frac{1 - \ln(x)}{x^2} Quotient rule. Numerator: (1/x)·x - ln(x)·1 = 1 - ln(x). f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow 1 - \ln(x) = 0 \Rightarrow \ln(x) = 1 \Rightarrow x = e Critical point at x = e. f' > 0 \text{ for } x \in (0, e), \; f' < 0 \text{ for } x > e \Rightarrow \text{local (global) max at } x = e Sign of 1 - ln(x): positive when ln(x) < 1 (x < e), negative when x > e. f(e) = \frac{\ln(e)}{e} = \frac{1}{e} Maximum value: 1/e at x = e. f(1) = 0 \text{ (x-intercept)} The function crosses zero at x = 1 (ln(1) = 0). All Local Extrema of a Cubic \text{Find all local extrema of } f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 4.   f(x) = 2x³ - 3x² - 12x + 4 has a local maximum at (-1, 11) and a local minimum at (2, -16). The function rises on (-∞,-1), falls on (-1,2), and rises on (2,∞). The inflection point is where f'' = 0: 12x - 6 = 0, x = 1/2, f(1/2) = 2(1/8) - 3(1/4) - 6 + 4 = 1/4 - 3/4 - 2 = -5/2. Inflection at (1/2, -5/2). f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6x - 12 = 6(x^2 - x - 2) = 6(x-2)(x+1) Factor the derivative. f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2 \text{ or } x = -1 Critical points. f''(x) = 12x - 6 Second derivative. f''(-1) = -12 - 6 = -18 < 0 \Rightarrow \text{local max at } x = -1 Second derivative test: f''(-1) < 0 → local max. f(-1) = -2 - 3 + 12 + 4 = 11 Local maximum value: 11. Point (-1, 11). f''(2) = 24 - 6 = 18 > 0 \Rightarrow \text{local min at } x = 2 Second derivative test: f''(2) > 0 → local min. f(2) = 16 - 12 - 24 + 4 = -16 Local minimum value: -16. Point (2, -16). Maximum Height of a Thrown Ball (Physics) A ball is thrown vertically upward from ground level with initial velocity $v_0 = 64$ ft/s. Its height is $h(t) = 64t - 16t^2$ feet. (a) Find the maximum height and when it occurs. (b) Interpret $h'(t)$ and $h''(t)$ physically. (c) Sketch $h(t)$, $h'(t)$, $h''(t)$ and identify all key features.   Maximum height of 64 ft at t=2 s, confirmed by three methods: (1) h'(2)=0 is a critical point, (2) h''=-32<0 confirms local max, (3) sign chart shows h' changes + to -. The constant h''=-32 means gravity pulls the ball down with constant acceleration throughout. The graph of h(t) is a downward parabola — symmetric about its peak. The graph of h'(t)=64-32t is a line crossing zero at t=2. The graph of h''(t)=-32 is a horizontal line below the axis. h'(t) = 64 - 32t Velocity: power rule gives d/dt[64t]=64 and d/dt[-16t²]=-32t. This is v(t) = 64 - 32t, which decreases linearly — the ball slows as it rises. h'(t) = 0 \Rightarrow 64 - 32t = 0 \Rightarrow t = 2 \text{ s} Maximum height when velocity = 0. The ball momentarily stops at t=2 s — this is the critical point. Set h'=0 and solve. h''(t) = -32 \text{ ft/s}^2 Acceleration is constant at -32 ft/s² — this is gravitational deceleration (g ≈ 32 ft/s² downward). h''< 0 everywhere confirms every critical point is a maximum. h(2) = 64(2) - 16(4) = 128 - 64 = 64 \text{ ft} Maximum height: substitute t=2 into h(t). The ball reaches 64 feet — same as the initial velocity numerically (not a coincidence: h_max = v₀²/64). h(t) = 0 \Rightarrow 16t(4 - t) = 0 \Rightarrow t = 0 \text{ and } t = 4 \text{ s} Ball returns to ground at t=4 s. Total airtime = 4 s = 2 × (time to peak), as expected by symmetry. \text{Sign chart: } h'(t) > 0 \text{ on } (0,2), \quad h'(t) < 0 \text{ on } (2,4) Ball rises for t∈(0,2) and falls for t∈(2,4). The maximum at t=2 is confirmed by the sign change + to -. h''(t) = -32 < 0 \text{ for all } t h''< 0 everywhere: h is concave down for its entire domain. This means h'(t) is always decreasing — the ball continuously decelerates under gravity.  Find constants a and b such that f(x) = ax³ + bx² has a local maximum at x = -1 with f(-1) = 4, and an inflection point at x = 1. Start with f'(-1) = 0 and f''(1) = 0 to relate a and b, then use f(-1) = 4 to pin down the scale. Afterward, check whether the resulting cubic really has an inflection at x = 1; if not, the conditions are inconsistent. a = 8, b = 12, giving f(x) = 8x³ + 12x². This satisfies f'(-1) = 0 and f(-1) = 4. The inflection point occurs at x = -b/(3a) = -12/24 = -1/2.  f'(x) = 3ax^2 + 2bx, \quad f''(x) = 6ax + 2b Compute derivatives. f'(-1) = 0: \quad 3a(-1)^2 + 2b(-1) = 3a - 2b = 0 Critical point condition at x = -1. f''(1) = 0: \quad 6a(1) + 2b = 6a + 2b = 0 Inflection condition at x = 1. \text{From } 6a + 2b = 0: b = -3a Solve for b in terms of a. \text{Substitute into } 3a - 2b = 0: 3a - 2(-3a) = 3a + 6a = 9a = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0? Hmm — a = 0 gives a degenerate solution. The conditions are inconsistent for a non-trivial cubic. Adjust: use f(-1) = 4 as the third equation. \text{From } 3a - 2b = 0 \Rightarrow b = 3a/2 Use this relation. f(-1) = a(-1)^3 + b(-1)^2 = -a + b = 4 Condition f(-1) = 4. -a + \frac{3a}{2} = \frac{a}{2} = 4 \Rightarrow a = 8, \; b = 12 Solve the system: a = 8, b = 12. f(x) = 8x^3 + 12x^2, \; f''(x) = 48x + 24 = 0 \Rightarrow x = -1/2 Inflection point is at x = -1/2, not x = 1. The original conditions (inflection at x=1) are incompatible with critical point at x=-1 for f = ax³+bx². Accept a = 8, b = 12 as the answer satisfying the available independent conditions.  Prove: if f'(c) = 0 and f changes from concave up to concave down at c, then c is a local maximum. If f'' changes from positive to negative at c, then f' is increasing then decreasing at c. Since f'(c) = 0, what can you conclude about the sign of f' on each side? The claim is actually false as stated for a "change of concavity" interpretation. A critical point where f'' changes sign is a horizontal inflection point (like f(x) = x³ at 0). The second derivative test for a local maximum requires f''(c) < 0 (strictly negative) at the critical point, not merely a sign change. This challenge illustrates why careful logical analysis of calculus conditions matters.  f'' > 0 \text{ on } (a,c) \text{ and } f'' < 0 \text{ on } (c,b) \text{ for some interval around } c Assumption: concavity changes from up (f''> 0) to down (f''< 0) at c. f'' > 0 \text{ on } (a,c) \Rightarrow f' \text{ is strictly increasing on } (a,c) Positive second derivative means f' is increasing (by the MVT corollary applied to f').  f'(c) = 0 \text{ and } f' \text{ increasing on } (a,c) \Rightarrow f'(x) < f'(c) = 0 \text{ for all } x \in (a,c) Since f' is increasing toward c, values before c are less than f'(c) = 0. So f'< 0 on (a,c)... but wait, if f' is increasing on (a,c) and equals 0 at c, then f' < 0 to the LEFT of c. f'' < 0 \text{ on } (c,b) \Rightarrow f' \text{ is strictly decreasing on } (c,b) Negative second derivative means f' is decreasing on (c,b). f'(c) = 0 \text{ and } f' \text{ decreasing on } (c,b) \Rightarrow f'(x) < 0 \text{ for all } x \in (c,b) Since f' decreases away from c, values after c are less than f'(c) = 0. So f'< 0 on (c,b) too? \text{Wait: } f' \text{ increasing on } (a,c) \Rightarrow f'(x) < f'(c)=0 \text{ for } x < c \checkmark Correct: f' increasing toward 0 means f' is negative to the left of c. f' \text{ decreasing from } 0 \text{ on } (c,b) \Rightarrow f'(x) < 0 \text{ for } x \in (c,b) \checkmark Decreasing from 0 means f' is negative to the right of c. \text{Both sides have } f' < 0 \Rightarrow \text{first derivative test? No sign change!} Actually if f'< 0 on both sides, the first derivative test says neither max nor min. Re-examine: f' increasing TO 0 means f' goes from negative to 0. f' decreasing FROM 0 means it goes from 0 to negative. So f'≤ 0 everywhere near c, but f'(c) = 0. The function is NON-increasing near c — not strictly decreasing. This is consistent with c being a local max if f is strictly above neighbors. \text{Use MVT: for } x < c, f(c) - f(x) = f'(s)(c-x) \text{ where } s \in (x,c) For x < c, apply MVT on [x,c]. Since s ∈ (a,c) and f' is increasing toward 0 with f'(s) ≤ f'(c) = 0 but s < c, actually f'(s) < 0. So f(c) - f(x) = f'(s)(c-x) where f'(s) < 0 and c-x > 0, giving f(c) - f(x) < 0. Hmm — that gives f(c) < f(x), a local minimum! \text{Correction: re-examine. } f' \text{ INCREASING on }(a,c) \text{ with } f'(c)=0 \Rightarrow f'(x) < 0 \text{ for } x < c. This means f is DECREASING on (a,c). Then f(c) < f(x) for x < c means f has smaller value at c — heading toward c, the function decreased. For x ∈ (c,b), f' also < 0, so f continues to decrease. There is no local extremum at c under these conditions — c is an inflection point! \text{Conclusion: the premise "f changes from concave up to concave down at c" with } f'(c)=0 \text{ means } c \text{ is an inflection point of f', not of f itself.} The statement as given is subtly incorrect. A critical point at a concavity change is an inflection point of f (where the tangent crosses the curve), not a local max. The second derivative test (f''(c) < 0 → local max) requires f''(c) < 0 STRICTLY, not just a sign change. The sign change at c with f'(c) = 0 produces a horizontal inflection point.  Sketch f(x) = x^{2/3}(x - 4). Note that f' is undefined at x = 0 — this creates a cusp. Write f as x^{5/3} - 4x^{2/3}. Differentiate term-by-term. Find where f'= 0 and where f' is undefined. The behavior at x = 0 is the key. f(x) = x^{2/3}(x-4) has a cusp (sharp peak) at x = 0 where f'is undefined, a local max value of 0 at the cusp, and a local minimum at x = 8/5. The cusp is not a smooth maximum — the tangent line is vertical on both sides, forming a sharp point.  f(x) = x^{5/3} - 4x^{2/3} Expand f to use the power rule. f'(x) = \frac{5}{3}x^{2/3} - \frac{8}{3}x^{-1/3} = \frac{x^{-1/3}}{3}(5x - 8) = \frac{5x - 8}{3x^{1/3}} Factor out x^{-1/3}/3. f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow 5x - 8 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \frac{8}{5} Critical point from numerator = 0. f'(x) \text{ undefined at } x = 0 \text{ (denominator } x^{1/3} = 0) Additional critical point where f' is undefined. At x = 0, the function has a cusp. \text{Sign chart: } f'(x) = \frac{5x-8}{3x^{1/3}} Test each region: x < 0: numerator < 0, denominator < 0, so f' > 0. x ∈ (0, 8/5): numerator < 0, denominator > 0, so f' < 0. x > 8/5: numerator > 0, denominator > 0, so f' > 0. \text{At } x=0: f' \text{ changes from } + \text{ to } - \Rightarrow \text{local max at } x=0 f' goes from + (for x < 0) to - (for x ∈ (0,8/5)), so local max at x = 0. f(0) = 0, \; f(8/5) = (8/5)^{2/3}(8/5 - 4) = (8/5)^{2/3}(-12/5) Local max at (0,0), local min at x = 8/5 ≈ 1.6. \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{5h - 8}{3h^{1/3}} = \lim_{h\to 0^+} \frac{-8}{3h^{1/3}} = -\infty The right derivative at 0 is -∞: the function plunges steeply to the right. Combined with the left derivative being +∞, this is a cusp — a sharp pointed maximum.
documents.proofs: Proof of the first derivative test from the MVT: Suppose f'(x) > 0 on (a,c) and f'(x) < 0 on (c,b). For any x ∈ (a,c), apply the MVT to f on [x,c]: f(c) - f(x) = f'(s)(c-x) for some s ∈ (x,c). Since s ∈ (a,c), f'(s) > 0 and c-x > 0, so f(c) - f(x) > 0, giving f(c) > f(x). For any x ∈ (c,b), apply MVT to f on [c,x]: f(x) - f(c) = f'(s)(x-c) for some s ∈ (c,x). Since s ∈ (c,b), f'(s) < 0 and x-c > 0, so f(x) - f(c) < 0, giving f(x) < f(c). Therefore f(c) ≥ f(x) for all x near c — this is a local maximum. The proof of the local minimum case is analogous. Why the second derivative test works — the Taylor expansion argument in full: Suppose f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0. We want to show f(c) is a local minimum. By continuity of f'', there exists δ > 0 such that f''(x) > 0 for all x ∈ (c-δ, c+δ). For any x ∈ (c-δ, c+δ) with x ≠ c, apply the MVT to f' on [c,x] (or [x,c]): f'(x) - f'(c) = f''(s)(x-c) for some s between c and x. Since s ∈ (c-δ, c+δ), f''(s) > 0. Also f'(c) = 0, so f'(x) = f''(s)(x-c). For x > c: x-c > 0 and f''(s) > 0, so f'(x) > 0. For x < c: x-c < 0 and f''(s) > 0, so f'(x) < 0. Therefore f' changes sign from - to + at c — by the first derivative test, c is a local minimum. ∎ This proof reveals the true logic: the second derivative test works because f''> 0 forces f' to be increasing, and f' going from - to + is exactly the first derivative test for a minimum. The second derivative test fails when f''(c) = 0 because f' might increase or decrease at c without f'' committing to a definite sign. The examples f(x) = x⁴ (local min at 0, f''(0) = 0), f(x) = -x⁴ (local max at 0, f''(0) = 0), and f(x) = x³ (inflection, f''(0) = 0) all have f'(0) = 0 and f''(0) = 0 but different behavior. The first derivative test always works in these cases and is the definitive test. Second Derivative Test = First Derivative Test + Continuity of f'' The second derivative test ultimately reduces to the first derivative test. If f''(c) > 0, then by continuity, f''> 0 near c, making f' increasing near c. Since f'(c) = 0, f' goes from negative (left of c) to positive (right of c) — exactly the first derivative test for a local minimum. The second derivative test is a shortcut that avoids computing the full sign chart.
