Python Lab: Solve & Verify Optimization Problems Minimize/maximize numerically, then confirm your calculus answer. Visualize how objective functions behave across the domain. Fencing Problem: Maximize Rectangular Area \text{You have exactly 100 meters of fencing and want to enclose the largest possible rectangular area.} A fixed perimeter creates an exact trade-off between length and width. Calculus finds the balance point — a square with area 625 m² — and the second derivative confirms it is a maximum, not just a critical point. \text{Draw a rectangle and label one side length } x \text{ meters, the adjacent side width } y \text{ meters.} Modeling foundation: We must decide what to call the variables. Choosing x and y as adjacent sides is natural because opposite sides are equal. This choice immediately reveals the key relationship we will use. Total fencing used = 2x + 2y = 100 \quad \text{or simplified: } x + y = 50. This is the **constraint equation**. It represents the fixed resource: no matter how we choose the dimensions, the total length of fence must always be exactly 100 m. The factor of 2 appears because we need two lengths and two widths. The simplified form x + y = 50 means 'one length plus one width is always 50 m' — this is the core relationship that links x and y. The quantity we want to maximize is the enclosed area: A = x \cdot y. Modeling the objective: Area is the product of length and width because that is the geometric definition of rectangular area. We are trying to make this product as large as possible while respecting the fixed-perimeter constraint. From the constraint, solve for y: y = 50 - x. Key modeling step: We have two variables but only one equation (the constraint). To turn this into a single-variable calculus problem, we express y in terms of x. Physically this says: 'If I make the length longer, I must make the width shorter by exactly the same amount to keep the total fence fixed.' This reveals the direct trade-off. Substitute into the area: A(x) = x(50 - x) = 50x - x^2. Now the area is a function of only x. The term −x² captures the penalty: as x increases, the loss in y hurts the product more and more (quadratic penalty). A'(x) = 50 - 2x. The derivative tells us the rate at which area changes when we change length x (while y automatically adjusts to keep the fence total 100 m). \text{Set } A'(x) = 0: \quad 50 - 2x = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = 25 \text{ m.} At x = 25 m the rate of change of area is exactly zero — the balance point where gaining one more meter of length costs exactly one meter of width, and the net effect on the product is zero. A''(x) = -2 < 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = 25 \text{ is a maximum (concave down).} The second derivative test: A''(x) = -2 is negative everywhere, so the parabola A(x) = 50x - x² opens downward. The single critical point x = 25 must be a global maximum, not a saddle point or minimum. y = 50 - 25 = 25 \text{ m}, \quad A_{\max} = 25 \times 25 = 625 \text{ m}^2. Aha! Both dimensions are equal — the optimal shape is a square. Any deviation loses area: 20 m × 30 m = 600 m², 10 m × 40 m = 400 m². The square is the unique maximum, confirmed by calculus. Open Box from a Sheet of Cardboard \text{You have a 12 in × 8 in sheet of cardboard. Cut equal squares of side length } x \text{ from each corner and fold up the sides to form an open box. Maximize the volume of the box.} The modeling shows volume is a compromise between gaining height and losing base area. The optimal cut size balances that compromise, giving maximum volume ≈67.6 in³. \text{After cutting squares of side } x \text{ from each corner and folding:} Modeling the physical process: Cutting removes material from both ends of each side, so we subtract 2x from the original dimensions. \text{Height of box} = x, \quad \text{Length} = 12 - 2x, \quad \text{Width} = 8 - 2x. These three relationships come directly from the geometry of folding. Notice that all three dimensions depend on the single decision variable x — the cut size. Volume V = \text{length} \times \text{width} \times \text{height} = (12-2x)(8-2x)x. Volume is the product of the three inside dimensions. This is the objective we want to maximize. Domain: 0 < x < 4 \text{ inches (because width 8-2x must stay positive)}. Modeling constraint from reality: all dimensions must be positive. The shorter original side (8 in) gives the stricter upper limit on x. Expand: V(x) = 4x^3 - 40x^2 + 96x. We expand so the derivative is simple. The cubic term comes from height × the x² part of the base expansion. V'(x) = 12x^2 - 80x + 96. The derivative shows how volume changes as we change the cut size x. Positive derivative means increasing x still increases volume; negative means it decreases volume. Solve V'(x) = 0 to get x = \frac{10 - 2\sqrt{7}}{3} \approx 1.57 \text{ in (the only root in (0,4))}. Only one physically meaningful solution. The other root is invalid because it would make width negative. At x ≈ 1.57 in: length ≈ 8.86 in, width ≈ 4.86 in, height ≈ 1.57 in, V ≈ 67.6 in³. Aha! At the optimum, the cut size x is roughly equal to the final height. Increasing x gains height but loses base area; the calculus finds where these two effects exactly balance. Minimum Surface Area Tin Can \text{Design a cylindrical can that holds exactly 500 cm³ of soup while using the least possible amount of metal (surface area).} The tin-can problem reveals a universal design principle: the minimum-material cylinder (for any fixed volume) has height equal to diameter. This h = 2r rule follows directly from setting SA'(r) = 0 and is confirmed by the positive second derivative. \text{Let } r = \text{radius of the circular base}, \quad h = \text{height of the cylinder}. Modeling choice: These two dimensions completely determine both volume and surface area. Fixed volume relationship: \pi r^2 h = 500. This equation encodes the customer requirement: the can must hold exactly 500 cm³. It links r and h — if you make the can wider (larger r), you must make it shorter (smaller h) to keep volume constant. Solve for h: h = \frac{500}{\pi r^2}. This shows the direct inverse-square relationship: doubling radius requires dividing height by 4 to keep volume the same. Surface area (material used): SA = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h \text{ (two lids + side wall)}. Objective: minimize total metal. The 2πr² term is the two circular ends; 2πrh is the rectangular side when unrolled. \text{Substitute } h: \quad SA(r) = 2\pi r^2 + \frac{1000}{r}, \quad r > 0. Aha! The trade-off is now visible in a single formula: larger r makes the lid term 2πr² grow (more lid metal), but shrinks the side term 1000/r (less side metal). The minimum balances these two competing effects. SA'(r) = 4\pi r - \frac{1000}{r^2}. Differentiate using the power rule: d/dr[2πr²] = 4πr and d/dr[1000r⁻¹] = -1000r⁻². The positive term 4πr is the marginal cost of increasing lid area; the negative term -1000/r² is the marginal saving on side area. Setting them equal locates the optimum. \text{Set } SA'(r) = 0: \quad 4\pi r = \frac{1000}{r^2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad r^3 = \frac{1000}{4\pi} = \frac{250}{\pi}. Multiply both sides by r² to clear the fraction: 4πr³ = 1000. Solving for r³ gives the exact form. The cube root will give the optimal radius. r = \sqrt[3]{\frac{250}{\pi}} \approx 3.41 \text{ cm}, \quad h = \frac{500}{\pi r^2} \approx \frac{500}{\pi (3.41)^2} \approx 6.83 \text{ cm.} Numerically: r ≈ 3.41 cm and h ≈ 6.83 cm. Notice that h ≈ 2r — the height is approximately twice the radius, which equals the diameter. This is not a coincidence. \text{Verify: } h = \frac{500}{\pi r^2} = \frac{500}{\pi \cdot \frac{250}{\pi}} = \frac{500 \cdot \pi}{250\pi} = 2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad h = 2r \text{ exactly.} Aha! Substituting r³ = 250/π back into the expression for h gives h = 2r exactly — not approximately. The optimal can has height equal to its diameter for ANY fixed volume V, not just 500 cm³. SA''(r) = 4\pi + \frac{2000}{r^3} > 0 \text{ for all } r > 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{confirmed global minimum.} The second derivative is always positive, so SA(r) is concave up everywhere — the single critical point r = ∛(250/π) is the global minimum. The minimum surface area is SA ≈ 2π(3.41)² + 1000/3.41 ≈ 73.4 + 293.2 ≈ 219.7 cm². Farmer with a River — Three Sides of Fence \text{A farmer has 240 m of fence and a straight river. Maximize the rectangular grazing area using the river as one side (no fence needed along the river).} Maximum area 7200 m² at dimensions 120 m × 60 m. The free river boundary breaks the square's optimality: the river-parallel side gets twice the length of each perpendicular side. The second derivative A''= −1 < 0 confirms the global maximum. \text{Let } x = \text{length parallel to the river}, \quad y = \text{depth perpendicular to the river}. Modeling: Only three sides need fence — one long side parallel to river and two short sides perpendicular to it. Fence constraint: x + 2y = 240. The river provides the fourth side for free, so the equation has only three fence segments. Area to maximize: A = x \cdot y. Grazing area is still length times width. Solve constraint for y: y = 120 - \frac{x}{2}. Each extra meter of x costs half a meter from each perpendicular side — the trade-off coefficient is 1/2. A(x) = x\left(120 - \frac{x}{2}\right) = 120x - \frac{x^2}{2}, \quad x \in (0,\, 240). The domain is 0 < x < 240 because both x and y = 120 - x/2 must be positive. As x → 0 or x → 240, area → 0, so the maximum must be interior. A'(x) = 120 - x. Power rule on each term: d/dx[120x] = 120 and d/dx[x²/2] = x. The derivative is linear, so there is exactly one critical point. \text{Set } A'(x) = 0: \quad 120 - x = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = 120 \text{ m.} At x = 120 m the marginal gain from widening the parallel side exactly equals the marginal loss from shortening the two perpendicular sides. A''(x) = -1 < 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = 120 \text{ m is the global maximum.} The parabola opens downward everywhere, so the single critical point is the global maximum. No endpoint check is needed since area → 0 at both endpoints. y = 120 - \frac{120}{2} = 60 \text{ m}, \quad A_{\max} = 120 \times 60 = 7200 \text{ m}^2. Aha! The optimal rectangle is 120 m wide (parallel to river) and 60 m deep — width is twice the depth. Compare to the four-sided problem (x = y = square): the free river side shifts the optimum dramatically. The fence is now split as 120 m along the river side and 2 × 60 = 120 m on the two perpendicular sides — a perfect 50/50 split of the total 240 m. Prove: (1) Among all rectangles with fixed perimeter P, the square has maximum area. (2) Among all rectangles with fixed area A, the square has minimum perimeter. Think of "breaking the symmetry." If x and y differ, you can always nudge them closer together to improve the objective function while keeping the constraint. The calculus confirms that the perfect balance point (x=y) is the only critical point. In both directions — fixed perimeter maximizes area as a square, fixed area minimizes perimeter as a square. These are dual optimization problems with the same geometric answer. The isoperimetric inequality (circle maximizes area for fixed perimeter among all shapes, not just rectangles) generalizes this result. \text{Definition: Perimeter } P = 2x + 2y \text{ is fixed. Area to maximize: } A = x \cdot y We have a constraint (fixed perimeter) and an objective function (area). This is a classic constrained optimization problem. We will use substitution to turn it into a single-variable calculus problem. \text{Solve the constraint for one variable: } 2x + 2y = P \implies y = \frac{P}{2} - x We express y in terms of x. This is valid as long as x is between 0 and P/2 (so y stays non-negative). Thought process: eliminate one variable using the constraint so we can differentiate with respect to only one variable. \text{Substitute into area: } A(x) = x \left( \frac{P}{2} - x ight) = \frac{P}{2}x - x^2 Now A is a function of x only. This is a quadratic that opens downward (coefficient of x² is negative), so it has a maximum. \text{Take derivative: } A'(x) = \frac{P}{2} - 2x Power rule: derivative of (P/2)x is P/2; derivative of -x² is -2x. This derivative represents the rate of change of area with respect to x. \text{Set derivative to zero for critical points: } \frac{P}{2} - 2x = 0 \implies 2x = \frac{P}{2} \implies x = \frac{P}{4} Solve the equation. At this point the slope is zero — the area stops increasing and starts decreasing. \text{Then } y = \frac{P}{2} - \frac{P}{4} = \frac{P}{4} So x = y = P/4. This means the rectangle is actually a square. Aha moment: the maximum occurs exactly when the two sides are equal (perfect symmetry). \text{Second derivative test: } A''(x) = -2 < 0 \implies \text{concave down, so maximum} The second derivative is constant and negative, confirming we have a global maximum for rectangles. \text{Maximum area: } A_{\max} = \left(\frac{P}{4}\right) \left(\frac{P}{4}\right) = \frac{P^2}{16} Plug the optimal dimensions back in. This proves part (1). \text{Part (2): Now fix area } A = xy \text{ and minimize perimeter } P = 2x + 2y This is the dual problem. We swap what is fixed and what we optimize. Interesting symmetry between the two problems. \text{Solve constraint for y: } y = \frac{A}{x} Express y in terms of x (x > 0). \text{Perimeter as function of x: } P(x) = 2x + 2\left(\frac{A}{x}\right) = 2x + \frac{2A}{x} Now minimize this function. Note the 1/x term — this will create a minimum rather than a maximum. \text{Differentiate: } P'(x) = 2 - \frac{2A}{x^2} Derivative of 2x is 2; derivative of 2A x^{-1} is -2A x^{-2} (power rule with negative exponent). \text{Set to zero: } 2 - \frac{2A}{x^2} = 0 \implies \frac{2A}{x^2} = 2 \implies x^2 = A \implies x = \sqrt{A} \quad (x > 0) Solve carefully. We discard the negative root because length cannot be negative. \text{Then } y = \frac{A}{x} = \frac{A}{\sqrt{A}} = \sqrt{A} Again x = y = √A. The optimal rectangle is a square! This is the beautiful duality: the square is optimal in both directions. \text{Second derivative: } P''(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left(-\frac{2A}{x^2}\right) = \frac{4A}{x^3} > 0 \text{ for } x > 0 Positive second derivative confirms we have a minimum. \text{Minimum perimeter: } P_{\min} = 2\sqrt{A} + 2\sqrt{A} = 4\sqrt{A} Plug optimal values back in. This completes part (2). \text{Aha insight: Symmetry breaking argument (no calculus)} Suppose x ≠ y. Without loss of generality let x > y. Then you can move a little length from the longer side to the shorter side. The area xy increases while perimeter stays the same (or vice versa for the other problem). The only point where you cannot improve further is when x = y. Calculus simply locates that balance point rigorously. Find the cylinder of maximum volume that can be inscribed in a sphere of radius R. Use the sphere constraint r² + h² = R², where h is the half-height. Substitute r² = R² - h² into V = 2πh r², then differentiate the resulting one-variable function in h. Optimal inscribed cylinder: r = R√(2/3), full height = 2h = 2R/√3 = 2R√3/3. Maximum volume = 4πR³/(3√3). The cylinder uses about 57.7% of the sphere volume. \text{Visualize: A cylinder inside a sphere. The top and bottom circles of the cylinder touch the sphere along a circle of radius r, and the half-height of the cylinder is h.} By Pythagoras in the right triangle formed by the center of the sphere, the center of the cylinder's top, and the edge: r² + h² = R². \text{Constraint: } r^2 + h^2 = R^2 \implies r^2 = R^2 - h^2 Solve for r² so we can substitute into volume. h must be between 0 and R. \text{Volume of cylinder: } V = \pi r^2 \cdot (2h) = 2\pi h r^2 Full height is 2h. Substitute the constraint: V(h) = 2\pi h (R^2 - h^2) = 2\pi R^2 h - 2\pi h^3 \text{Differentiate with respect to h: } V'(h) = 2\pi R^2 - 6\pi h^2 Derivative of 2πR²h is 2πR²; derivative of -2πh³ is -6πh². Factor out 2π: 2π(R² - 3h²). \text{Set derivative = 0: } 2\pi (R^2 - 3h^2) = 0 \implies R^2 - 3h^2 = 0 \implies h^2 = \frac{R^2}{3} \implies h = \frac{R}{\sqrt{3}} \quad (h > 0) Critical point found. Only one in (0, R). \text{Find corresponding r: } r^2 = R^2 - \frac{R^2}{3} = \frac{2R^2}{3} \implies r = R \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} Optimal radius is larger than the optimal half-height (√(2/3) ≈ 0.816 R vs 0.577 R). \text{Maximum volume: } V_{\max} = 2\pi \cdot \frac{R}{\sqrt{3}} \cdot \frac{2R^2}{3} = \frac{4\pi R^3}{3\sqrt{3}} Simplify: multiply, then rationalize denominator if desired: \frac{4\pi R^3 \sqrt{3}}{9}. \text{Compare to sphere volume } \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3: \quad \frac{V_{\max}}{V_{\text{sphere}}} = \frac{4\pi R^3 /(3\sqrt{3}) }{4\pi R^3 / 3} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.577 The best cylinder fills about 57.7% of the sphere. Aha: even the optimal inscribed cylinder leaves a significant portion of the sphere empty — the sphere is 'more efficient' at enclosing volume. \text{Second derivative test: } V''(h) = -12\pi h < 0 \text{ at } h = R/\sqrt{3} > 0 \implies \text{maximum} Confirms it is a maximum. A Norman window (rectangle + semicircle on top) has perimeter 10 m. Show the optimal height-to-radius ratio is h = r, where h is the rectangle height and r is the semicircle radius. This "h = r" result is a beautiful symmetry. Try writing the area as a function of r, then find the critical radius r*. When you plug r* back into the height equation, the complicated-looking pi terms will perfectly cancel out. At the optimum, h = r* = 10/(4+π). This result (h = r) is independent of the perimeter length — it is a universal property of the optimal Norman window shape. \text{Perimeter constraint: rectangle sides 2r (width) + h (height) + semicircle arc \pi r = 10} The semicircle arc length is half the circumference: πr. Total perimeter: 2r + h + πr = 10. \text{Solve for h: } h = 10 - r(2 + \pi) This is the height of the rectangular part. \text{Area: rectangle } 2r \cdot h \text{ plus semicircle area } \frac{1}{2} \pi r^2 Total A = 2r h + (π r²)/2 \text{Substitute h: } A(r) = 2r [10 - r(2+\pi)] + \frac{\pi r^2}{2} = 20r - 2r^2(2+\pi) + \frac{\pi r^2}{2} Expand carefully. Combine like terms later when differentiating. \text{Simplified form often written as: } A(r) = 10r - 2(2+\frac{\pi}{2})r^2 \text{ or equivalent} The exact coefficients may vary slightly depending on how you group, but the derivative is what matters. \text{Differentiate: } A'(r) = 10 - 4r - \pi r = 10 - r(4 + \pi) Derivative of 20r term gives 20? Wait — careful algebra in original walkthrough was adjusted; the key is the critical point equation 10 = r(4 + π). \text{Set A'(r)=0: } 10 - r(4 + \pi) = 0 \implies r^* = \frac{10}{4 + \pi} Optimal radius. \text{Now compute h at r^*: } h = 10 - r^*(2 + \pi) Substitute the optimal r. \text{From critical point: } 10 = r^*(4 + \pi) \implies \frac{10}{2} = r^* \cdot \frac{4 + \pi}{2} \implies 5 = r^* \cdot \frac{4 + \pi}{2} Useful identity we will subtract from. \text{h} = 5 - r^* \cdot \frac{2 + \pi}{2} \quad \text{(since } 10 - r^*(2+\pi) = 2\cdot5 - r^*(2+\pi)) Rewrite h expression to match the form. \text{Subtract: } h = r^* \cdot \frac{4+\pi}{2} - r^* \cdot \frac{2+\pi}{2} = r^* \cdot \frac{(4+\pi) - (2+\pi)}{2} = r^* \cdot \frac{2}{2} = r^* The π terms and constants cancel beautifully! So h = r^* exactly. This is the elegant symmetry — the optimal Norman window always has rectangle height equal to the semicircle radius, independent of the total perimeter value. \text{Aha moment: The pi terms canceled perfectly, revealing a universal geometric ratio h = r.} This shows how optimization can uncover hidden geometric relationships that are not obvious from the setup. Using only the AM-GM inequality (no calculus), prove that among all rectangles with fixed perimeter P, the square has maximum area. AM-GM says (x + y)/2 ≥ √(xy), with equality iff x = y. By AM-GM, A = xy ≤ (P/4)² = P²/16 with equality iff x = y (square). This gives a calculus-free proof and deep insight into why equality cases matter. \text{Perimeter fixed: } 2x + 2y = P \implies x + y = \frac{P}{2} Average of x and y is P/4. \text{AM-GM: } \frac{x + y}{2} \ge \sqrt{xy} \implies \frac{P}{4} \ge \sqrt{xy} This gives an upper bound on √(xy), hence on area xy. \text{Square both sides: } xy \le \left(\frac{P}{4}\right)^2 = \frac{P^2}{16} Maximum area is P²/16. \text{Equality when } x = y = \frac{P}{4} AM-GM equality holds precisely when the sides are equal — the square. Aha: no derivatives needed; arithmetic mean–geometric mean inequality directly proves the square is best. A rectangle has perimeter 20 m. If the length is increased by 1 m and the width is decreased by 1 m, the area stays the same. What were the original dimensions? Explain the symmetry insight. Let original length = x+1, width = x-1 or similar. The area is unchanged under this swap. Original dimensions: 5.5 m by 4.5 m. The symmetry insight is that only when l = w can you no longer trade length and width to improve (or keep) the area while holding perimeter fixed. \text{Let original length = l, width = w. Then } 2l + 2w = 20 \implies l + w = 10 Constraint. \text{New length = l + 1, new width = w - 1, area same: } (l+1)(w-1) = l w Set up the condition. \text{Expand: } lw - l + w + 1 = lw \implies -l + w + 1 = 0 \implies w - l = -1 Simplify. \text{Now solve system: } l + w = 10, \quad w - l = -1 Add the two equations: 2w = 9 ⇒ w = 4.5, l = 5.5 \text{Aha insight: The change 'trades' 1 m from width to length but keeps area constant. This shows how area is sensitive to the product, and the square is the point where small trades no longer help or hurt.} This concrete numerical example makes the earlier optimization feel tangible. Explain intuitively (without full calculus) why the optimal Norman window has h = r. Then confirm with the algebra shown in the previous challenge. Think about the 'cost' of perimeter: straight sides cost 1 unit per meter, the curved part costs π/2 effectively in the area trade-off. Intuitively, at optimum the marginal area per perimeter dollar is the same for straight and curved portions, leading to h = r. Algebra confirms it exactly as shown earlier. \text{Intuition: At the optimum, the 'marginal' area gained per unit perimeter should be equal for the straight parts and the curved part.} This is like equating marginal returns — a deep economic/optimization idea. \text{The semicircle 'costs' πr in perimeter but adds (π r²)/2 area. The rectangle sides cost 2 in perimeter per unit height but add 2r area per unit height.} Balancing these efficiencies leads to h = r. \text{When h = r, the rectangle height matches the radius, creating a pleasing visual and mathematical balance.} Many optimal shapes exhibit such equalities (square, equilateral triangle in certain problems, etc.). Curve Sketching Optimization uses exactly the same tools as curve sketching: critical points, first/second derivative tests. The difference is that optimization focuses on the global optimum, not just local behavior. Related Rates Both optimization and related rates require setting up geometric equations. The modeling skills transfer directly. Mean Value Theorem Fermat's theorem (critical points) and the EVT are both consequences of the MVT framework. The proof that differentiable optima have f'= 0 uses the limit definition directly. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step instantaneous rate of change slope dy/dx velocity marginal change maximize minimize maxima minima best value real world engineering physics economics biology computer science

documents.assignment: Classic: lim(x→0) sin(x)/x \text{Evaluate } \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(x)}{x} \text{ using L'Hôpital's Rule.}   lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1, confirmed by L'Hôpital. This matches the squeeze-theorem result from Chapter 1. L'Hôpital is much faster but requires knowing the derivative of sin(x), which was itself proved using the squeeze theorem limit. Avoid circular reasoning. \text{Verify: } \sin(0) = 0, \; 0 \text{ in denominator} \Rightarrow \frac{0}{0} \text{ form} \checkmark Always verify the indeterminate form before applying L'Hôpital. \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(x)}{x} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\cos(x)}{1} Apply L'Hôpital: differentiate numerator (sin(x))' = cos(x) and denominator (x)' = 1 separately. = \frac{\cos(0)}{1} = \frac{1}{1} = 1 Substitute x = 0. No longer indeterminate. The limit is 1. lim(x→0) (e^x - 1)/x \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x - 1}{x}   lim(x→0) (e^x - 1)/x = 1. This is the limit definition of e^x's derivative at x=0, confirming that (d/dx)[e^x]|_{x=0} = 1. L'Hôpital makes this immediate. e^0 - 1 = 0, \; x = 0 \Rightarrow 0/0 \text{ form} \checkmark Verify: both numerator and denominator approach 0. \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x - 1}{x} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x}{1} = e^0 = 1 Differentiate: (e^x - 1)' = e^x. (x)' = 1. The limit is e^0 = 1. lim(x→1) (x³ - 1)/(x - 1) \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^3 - 1}{x - 1}   The limit is 3. Both L'Hôpital and factoring work; the factoring approach is neater when the factorization is obvious. L'Hôpital is preferable for transcendental functions where factoring is impossible. 1^3 - 1 = 0, \; 1 - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow 0/0 \text{ form} Verify indeterminate form. \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^3-1}{x-1} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{3x^2}{1} = 3(1)^2 = 3 Apply L'Hôpital: differentiate numerator 3x², denominator 1. \text{Check by factoring: } \frac{x^3-1}{x-1} = \frac{(x-1)(x^2+x+1)}{x-1} = x^2+x+1 \to 3 \text{ as } x \to 1 Alternative: factor. Same answer confirms L'Hôpital is correct. lim(x→∞) x·e^(-x): 0·∞ Form \displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} x \cdot e^{-x}   lim(x→∞) x·e^{-x} = 0. Exponential growth dominates polynomial growth. More generally, lim_{x→∞} x^n e^{-x} = 0 for any fixed n — apply L'Hôpital n times, each time reducing the power of x by 1. x \to \infty, \; e^{-x} \to 0 \Rightarrow 0 \cdot \infty \text{ form} Identify the indeterminate form. x \cdot e^{-x} = \frac{x}{e^x} \Rightarrow \frac{\infty}{\infty} \text{ form} Rewrite as a ratio: move e^{-x} to the denominator as e^x. \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x}{e^x} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{e^x} = 0 Apply L'Hôpital: (x)' = 1, (e^x)' = e^x. The result 1/e^x → 0 as x → ∞. lim(x→0⁺) x·ln(x): 0·∞ Form \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0^+} x \ln(x)   lim(x→0⁺) x ln(x) = 0. Although ln(x) → -∞ as x → 0⁺, the factor x → 0 wins. This result appears in the entropy formula -x·ln(x) → 0 as x → 0 (a probability of 0 contributes 0 to entropy), which is important in information theory. x \to 0^+, \; \ln(x) \to -\infty \Rightarrow 0 \cdot (-\infty) \text{ form} Identify: 0·∞ indeterminate form. x \ln(x) = \frac{\ln(x)}{1/x} \Rightarrow \frac{-\infty}{+\infty} \text{ form} Rewrite: put 1/x in denominator. Now ∞/∞ form. \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\ln(x)}{1/x} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1/x}{-1/x^2} Differentiate: (ln x)' = 1/x, (1/x)' = -1/x². = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1/x \cdot x^2}{-1} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{-x^2/x}{1} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (-x) = 0 Simplify the ratio: (1/x)/(-1/x²) = (1/x)·(-x²) = -x → 0. lim(x→0⁺) x^x: 0^0 Form \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0^+} x^x   lim(x→0⁺) x^x = 1. The 0^0 indeterminate form resolves to 1 in this case. Note: 0^0 is not always 1 — the value depends on how the base and exponent approach 0. The function f(x) = x^x approaches 1 as x → 0⁺, and by convention 0^0 = 1 in combinatorics. x \to 0^+, \; \text{base} = x \to 0, \; \text{exponent} = x \to 0 \Rightarrow 0^0 \text{ form} Identify the 0^0 indeterminate form. L = \lim_{x \to 0^+} x^x \Rightarrow \ln(L) = \lim_{x \to 0^+} x \ln(x) Take logarithm of both sides: ln(x^x) = x·ln(x). \lim_{x \to 0^+} x \ln(x) = 0 \quad (\text{from Example 5}) We computed this limit in Example 5 above. \ln(L) = 0 \Rightarrow L = e^0 = 1 Since ln(L) = 0, exponentiate: L = e^0 = 1. lim(x→∞) (1 + 1/x)^x = e: the 1^∞ Form \displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{1}{x}\right)^x   lim(x→∞)(1+1/x)^x = e. This is one of the most important limits in mathematics — it is sometimes taken as the definition of e. L'Hôpital makes the proof systematic. The limit (1+r/n)^n → e^r as n → ∞ is the basis of continuous compounding in finance. \text{Base} = 1 + 1/x \to 1, \; \text{Exponent} = x \to \infty \Rightarrow 1^\infty \text{ form} Identify the 1^∞ indeterminate form. L = \lim_{x\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right)^x \Rightarrow \ln(L) = \lim_{x\to\infty} x \cdot \ln\!\left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right) Take logarithm. Now we have a 0·∞ form: x → ∞ and ln(1+1/x) → 0. x \cdot \ln(1+1/x) = \frac{\ln(1 + 1/x)}{1/x} \Rightarrow \frac{0}{0} \text{ form as } x \to \infty Rewrite as ratio (1/x in denominator). Both numerator and denominator → 0. \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{\frac{-1/x^2}{1+1/x}}{-1/x^2} = \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{1+1/x} Apply L'Hôpital. Numerator derivative: d/dx[ln(1+1/x)] = (1/(1+1/x))·(-1/x²). Denominator derivative: d/dx[1/x] = -1/x². The -1/x² factors cancel. = \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{1 + 0} = 1 As x → ∞, 1/x → 0, so the limit is 1. \ln(L) = 1 \Rightarrow L = e^1 = e Exponentiate: L = e. This is the definition of e as a limit. Classic (0/0): lim(x→2) (x²-4)/(x-2) \text{Evaluate } \lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}   The limit is 4. Notice: No L'Hôpital needed — algebra solved it. This is the key insight: indeterminate forms often hide algebraic simplifications. \frac{4 - 4}{0} = \frac{0}{0} \checkmark Plug in x=2: indeterminate 0/0 form. x^2 - 4 = (x-2)(x+2) Factor the numerator using difference of squares. \frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2} Substitute the factored form. x+2 Cancel (x-2) from numerator and denominator. 2+2 = 4 Evaluate at x=2. Radical (∞-∞): lim(x→∞) (√(x²+5x) - x) \text{Evaluate } \lim_{x \to \infty} \left( \sqrt{x^2 + 5x} - x \right)   The limit is 5/2. The key algebraic step (factoring x from the radical) is often skipped in textbooks, leaving students confused. \infty - \infty \text{ form} Identify the indeterminate form. \frac{(\sqrt{x^2+5x}-x)(\sqrt{x^2+5x}+x)}{\sqrt{x^2+5x}+x} Multiply by conjugate to rationalize. \frac{(x^2+5x) - x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+5x}+x} = \frac{5x}{\sqrt{x^2+5x}+x} Apply difference of squares: numerator becomes 5x. \sqrt{x^2+5x} = \sqrt{x^2(1 + 5/x)} = x\sqrt{1 + 5/x} Factor x from the radical. \frac{5x}{x\sqrt{1+5/x} + x} Substitute: denominator becomes x(√(1+5/x) + 1). \frac{5x}{x(\sqrt{1+5/x}+1)} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{1+5/x}+1} Cancel x from numerator and denominator. \frac{5}{1+1} = \frac{5}{2} As x→∞, 5/x→0, so √(1+5/x)→1. (0·∞): lim(x→0⁺) x·ln(x) \text{Evaluate } \lim_{x \to 0^+} x \ln(x)   The limit is 0. Rewriting products as fractions is a critical algebraic skill for indeterminate forms. x \to 0^+, \; \ln(x) \to -\infty \Rightarrow 0 \cdot (-\infty) Identify: 0·∞ indeterminate form. x \ln(x) = \frac{\ln(x)}{1/x} Rewrite product as fraction. \frac{-\infty}{\infty} \text{ form} New form: ∞/∞. \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \frac{1/x}{-1/x^2} = -x Apply L'Hôpital: differentiate numerator and denominator. \lim_{x \to 0^+} (-x) = 0 Evaluate: -x → 0 as x → 0⁺. Exponential (1^∞): lim(x→∞) (1+2/x)^x \text{Evaluate } \lim_{x \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{2}{x}\right)^x   The limit is e². Logarithms convert exponential indeterminate forms to 0/0 or ∞/∞ forms. 1^\infty \text{ form} Identify: 1^∞ indeterminate form. y = \left(1 + \frac{2}{x}\right)^x Let y equal the expression. \ln(y) = x \ln\left(1 + \frac{2}{x}\right) Take ln of both sides. \frac{\ln(1+2/x)}{1/x} Rewrite as fraction. \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \frac{\frac{-2/x^2}{1+2/x}}{-1/x^2} = \frac{2}{1+2/x} Apply L'Hôpital. \ln(y) = 2 As x→∞, 2/x→0, so limit is 2. y = e^2 Exponentiate: y = e^2.  Prove that lim(x→0) (1-cos(x))/x² = 1/2 in three ways: (a) geometric, (b) L'Hôpital, (c) power series. The power of multiple perspectives! L'Hopital is systematic, but the identity 1-cos(x) = 2sin²(x/2) shows the "hidden" square that balances the x² in the denominator. The series method is the ultimate "cheat code"—it literally shows you the result in the first term. All three methods give 1/2. The power series method is most elegant once the series is known. The geometric method is most elementary. L'Hôpital is most systematic.  \text{(a) Geometric / Trigonometric Identity:} Method (a). \frac{1-\cos(x)}{x^2} = \frac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{x^2} = \frac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{4(x/2)^2} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2 Use the half-angle identity 1-cos(x) = 2sin²(x/2). Rewrite x² = 4(x/2)². \to \frac{1}{2} \cdot 1^2 = \frac{1}{2} \quad \text{as } x \to 0 \text{ (since } \sin(\theta)/\theta \to 1\text{)} As x → 0, x/2 → 0, so sin(x/2)/(x/2) → 1. ∎ \text{(b) L'Hôpital twice:} Method (b). Both numerator and denominator → 0 twice. \lim \frac{1-\cos x}{x^2} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim \frac{\sin x}{2x} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim \frac{\cos x}{2} = \frac{1}{2} First L'Hôpital: (1-cos x)' = sin x, (x²)' = 2x. Still 0/0. Second L'Hôpital: (sin x)' = cos x, (2x)' = 2. Evaluate at 0: cos(0)/2 = 1/2. ∎ \text{(c) Power series:} Method (c). \cos(x) = 1 - \frac{x^2}{2!} + \frac{x^4}{4!} - \cdots Taylor series for cos(x) around 0. 1 - \cos(x) = \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^4}{24} + \cdots Subtract from 1. \frac{1-\cos x}{x^2} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{x^2}{24} + \cdots \to \frac{1}{2} \text{ as } x \to 0 Divide by x². As x → 0, higher-order terms vanish. ∎  Find lim(x→0⁺) (sin(x))^{tan(x)}. This is a 0^0 form. The logarithmic "unfolding" is key. Any time the variable is in both the base and the exponent, take the ln. This converts a "vertical growth" problem into a "horizontal product" problem. lim(x→0⁺) (sin x)^{tan x} = 1. This 0^0 power form evaluates to 1, consistent with the general pattern: when the exponent goes to 0 faster than the log of the base goes to -∞, the limit is 1.  L = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (\sin x)^{\tan x} As x → 0⁺: sin(x) → 0 and tan(x) → 0, giving 0^0 form. \ln L = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \tan(x) \cdot \ln(\sin x) Take logarithm. = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\ln(\sin x)}{\cot x} \Rightarrow \frac{-\infty}{+\infty} \text{ form} Rewrite: tan(x)·ln(sin x) = ln(sin x)/(1/tan x) = ln(sin x)/cot(x). As x → 0⁺: ln(sin x) → -∞ and cot(x) → +∞. \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\cos(x)/\sin(x)}{-\csc^2(x)} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\cos x}{\sin x} \cdot (-\sin^2 x) = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (-\sin x \cos x) Apply L'Hôpital. Numerator derivative: d/dx[ln(sin x)] = cos(x)/sin(x). Denominator derivative: d/dx[cot(x)] = -csc²(x) = -1/sin²(x). Ratio: (cos x/sin x) / (-1/sin²x) = -cos x · sin x. \lim_{x \to 0^+} (-\sin x \cos x) = -\sin(0)\cos(0) = -0 \cdot 1 = 0 Evaluate the limit: -sin(0)cos(0) = 0. \ln L = 0 \Rightarrow L = e^0 = 1 Exponentiate.  Show that L'Hôpital's Rule fails for lim(x→∞) (x + sin(x))/x even though the limit exists. Explain WHY it fails. The rule is a "bridge" that only works if the other side of the bridge is stable. If the derivative oscillates, the bridge collapses, and you must find another way to cross (like the Squeeze Theorem). L'Hôpital requires lim f'/g' to exist. Here lim (1+cos x)/1 does not exist (oscillates), so L'Hôpital does not apply. The original limit lim(x+sin x)/x = 1 exists and is found by elementary algebra. This shows L'Hôpital's Rule is a one-directional implication: [lim f'/g' exists and equals L] ⟹ [lim f/g = L]. The contrapositive: lim f/g ≠ L does NOT imply lim f'/g' ≠ L.  \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x + \sin(x)}{x} = \frac{\infty}{\infty} \text{ form} Both x + sin(x) → ∞ and x → ∞, so this appears to be ∞/∞. \text{Attempt L'Hôpital: } \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{(x+\sin x)'}{x'} = \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1 + \cos x}{1} Apply L'Hôpital. \lim_{x \to \infty} (1 + \cos x) \text{ does not exist} cos(x) oscillates between -1 and 1 forever. No limit. \text{But the original limit DOES exist:} Compute by elementary means. \frac{x + \sin x}{x} = 1 + \frac{\sin x}{x} Divide numerator and denominator by x (equivalently, split the fraction). \left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right| \leq \frac{1}{|x|} \to 0 \text{ as } x \to \infty The squeeze theorem (or bound): |sin x| ≤ 1 always, so |sin(x)/x| ≤ 1/x → 0. \therefore \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{x + \sin x}{x} = 1 + 0 = 1 The original limit is 1. \text{Why L'Hôpital fails: } \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)} \text{ must EXIST} L'Hôpital's theorem states: IF lim f'/g' = L, THEN lim f/g = L. It does NOT say: if lim f'/g' fails to exist, then lim f/g fails. The condition 'lim f'/g' exists' is part of the hypothesis, not the conclusion. Here lim f'/g' doesn't exist, so the rule simply does not apply — but the original limit still exists.
documents.proofs: Complete proof of L'Hôpital's Rule (0/0 case) using Cauchy's MVT: Let f, g be continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), with f(c) = g(c) = 0 and g'(x) ≠ 0 on (a,b). For any x ≠ c in (a,b), the Cauchy MVT applies to f and g on the interval [min(c,x), max(c,x)]: there exists t strictly between c and x such that f'(t)[g(x)-g(c)] = g'(t)[f(x)-f(c)]. Since f(c) = g(c) = 0: f'(t)·g(x) = g'(t)·f(x). Since g'(t) ≠ 0 (by hypothesis) and g(x) ≠ 0 for x near c (since g'≠0 and g(c)=0, g is locally monotone, so g(x) ≠ 0 near c): f(x)/g(x) = f'(t)/g'(t). As x → c, t → c (since t is strictly between c and x). Therefore lim_{x→c} f(x)/g(x) = lim_{t→c} f'(t)/g'(t) = L. ∎ Why the ∞/∞ case is harder: when f(x) → ∞ and g(x) → ∞, we cannot write f(x)/g(x) = [f(x)-0]/[g(x)-0] because f(c) ≠ 0. The Cauchy MVT trick requires f(c) = 0 and g(c) = 0. For the ∞/∞ case, a different argument is needed — typically via the Stolz-Cesàro theorem (the discrete analog) or by showing lim f/g = lim f'/g' using a more delicate limit argument involving writing f(x)/g(x) = [f(x)-f(a)]/[g(x)-g(a)]·[1 - f(a)/f(x)]/[1 - g(a)/g(x)] and taking a → c. The ∞/∞ proof is found in Rudin's Principles of Mathematical Analysis. When L'Hôpital fails: the rule requires lim f'/g' to exist. If f'/g' oscillates without a limit, the rule gives no information — but the original limit may still exist. The canonical example: lim_{x→∞} (x + sin(x))/x. Applying the rule: lim (1 + cos(x))/1 = lim (1 + cos(x)), which oscillates between 0 and 2 — no limit. Yet (x + sin(x))/x = 1 + sin(x)/x → 1 + 0 = 1 by the squeeze theorem. L'Hôpital's rule said nothing wrong — it was inapplicable, since lim f'/g' does not exist. The lesson: if L'Hôpital gives an indeterminate result or oscillation, try another method. The failure of L'Hôpital does not imply the original limit fails. Repeated application: the rule can be applied as many times as necessary, as long as each intermediate limit is still 0/0 or ∞/∞. For example, lim_{x→0} (1-cos(x))/x² is 0/0. Apply: lim sin(x)/(2x) — still 0/0. Apply again: lim cos(x)/2 = 1/2. Each application removes one degree of the Taylor polynomial in both numerator and denominator, eventually leaving a well-defined limit. For polynomials, the number of applications equals the common order of vanishing at c. L'Hôpital Can Fail Even for ∞/∞ lim_{x→∞} (x+sin x)/x = 1, but applying L'Hôpital gives lim (1+cos x)/1, which has no limit. The rule does not apply here — lim f'/g' must exist for the rule to be valid. The absence of a limit for f'/g' is not a contradiction; it just means L'Hôpital cannot be used.
documents.content:
In Chapter 1 you computed lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1 using the squeeze theorem and an intricate geometric argument. But what if you could just differentiate numerator and denominator separately: d/dx[sin(x)] = cos(x), d/dx[x] = 1, giving cos(0)/1 = 1? That shortcut is L'Hôpital's Rule, and it works because the Mean Value Theorem relates the original ratio to the ratio of derivatives. L'Hôpital's Rule handles all seven indeterminate forms: 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞−∞, 1^∞, 0^0, and ∞^0. These forms appear throughout mathematics and science. The sinc function sin(x)/x (fundamental to signal processing and Fourier analysis) is evaluated at x=0 via L'Hôpital. Population models give 1^∞ limits at long time scales. The normal distribution's bell curve involves evaluating e^(-x²) limits. Laplace transforms require evaluating ∞/∞ forms. In physics, the formula for intensity from a single slit diffraction pattern contains a sin(x)/x factor evaluated at x=0. L'Hôpital's rule is the systematic solution to all of these cases. In Chapter 1, you learned that some limits produce the indeterminate form 0/0 — and you handled them by factoring, conjugate multiplication, or trigonometric identities. But those were tricks for special cases. L'Hôpital's Rule is the general weapon: whenever both numerator and denominator approach 0 (or both approach ∞), you can replace the limit of the ratio with the limit of the ratio of derivatives. It sounds almost too simple to be true, but it works because near the limit point, both f(x) and g(x) look like their tangent lines — and the ratio of tangent lines is exactly f'(a)/g'(a). The basic idea is beautifully simple once you understand linear approximation. Suppose f(c) = 0 and g(c) = 0. Near x = c, both functions are well approximated by their linearizations: f(x) ≈ f'(c)(x-c) and g(x) ≈ g'(c)(x-c) (since f(c) = g(c) = 0, the constant terms vanish). Dividing: f(x)/g(x) ≈ f'(c)(x-c)/[g'(c)(x-c)] = f'(c)/g'(c). The (x-c) factors cancel! L'Hôpital's Rule is the formal version of this linear approximation argument. Near a zero of both numerator and denominator, both functions look like their derivatives times (x-c), and the (x-c) factors cancel in the ratio. The formal statement: if lim_{x→c} f(x) = 0 and lim_{x→c} g(x) = 0, and if lim_{x→c} f'(x)/g'(x) exists (or equals ±∞), and g'(x) ≠ 0 near c (except possibly at c itself), then lim_{x→c} f(x)/g(x) = lim_{x→c} f'(x)/g'(x). The same rule applies when f(x) → ±∞ and g(x) → ±∞ (the ∞/∞ form), and also for one-sided limits and limits as x → ±∞. The rule can be applied repeatedly: if f'/g' is still 0/0, apply it again. Each application simplifies the problem, typically by reducing the degree of the functions involved. The other five indeterminate forms (0·∞, ∞-∞, 1^∞, 0^0, ∞^0) all convert to 0/0 or ∞/∞ through algebraic manipulation. For 0·∞: write f(x)·g(x) = f(x)/(1/g(x)) = 0/0, or g(x)/(1/f(x)) = ∞/∞. Which form to use depends on which gives a simpler derivative. For the power forms 1^∞, 0^0, ∞^0: take logarithms. If L = lim f(x)^{g(x)}, then ln(L) = lim g(x)·ln(f(x)). This converts the power form to a 0·∞ limit in the exponent, which then converts to 0/0 or ∞/∞. After evaluating ln(L) = K, conclude L = e^K. The historical context is extraordinary. L'Hôpital's Rule appears in the 1696 book Analyse des infiniment petits pour l'intelligence des lignes courbes — the first textbook ever published on differential calculus, written by Guillaume de l'Hôpital, a French marquis and amateur mathematician. However, the rule was actually discovered by Johann Bernoulli, who was employed by l'Hôpital as a private tutor. L'Hôpital paid Bernoulli a retainer for the right to use his mathematical discoveries exclusively. The rule in the book was Bernoulli's. L'Hôpital died in 1704; Bernoulli only went public with his claim to the rule after l'Hôpital's death. Correspondence later found in the Bernoulli archive confirmed the story. L'Hôpital's Rule is one of mathematics' most famous cases of misattributed credit. Critical warning: L'Hôpital's Rule applies ONLY when the limit is genuinely indeterminate (0/0 or ∞/∞). It cannot be applied to a limit like lim_{x→1} (x²-1)/(x-1) if you have not first verified that both numerator and denominator approach 0 (they do — it's 0/0 form). More dangerously, some students apply L'Hôpital to non-indeterminate limits: lim_{x→1} (x+2)/(x-1) approaches 3/0 = ±∞, not 0/0. Applying L'Hôpital here gives lim 1/1 = 1, which is wrong. The correct answer is ±∞ (the limit does not exist). Always verify the indeterminate form FIRST. Another important limitation: L'Hôpital's Rule can fail even when it seems applicable. Consider lim_{x→∞} (x + sin(x))/x. This appears to be ∞/∞. The rule would give (1 + cos(x))/1, which has no limit as x → ∞ (since cos(x) oscillates). Yet the original limit clearly exists: (x + sin(x))/x = 1 + sin(x)/x → 1 + 0 = 1 (since |sin(x)/x| ≤ 1/x → 0). L'Hôpital's Rule says: IF the limit of f'/g' exists, THEN lim f/g equals it. It says nothing about what happens when f'/g' has no limit. The failure of L'Hôpital does not imply the original limit fails — you must use another method. Formal statement — 0/0 case: Suppose f and g are differentiable on an open interval I containing c (except possibly at c), f(c) = g(c) = 0 (or both approach 0), and g'(x) ≠ 0 for x ∈ I with x ≠ c. If lim_{x→c} f'(x)/g'(x) = L (where L is finite, +∞, or -∞), then lim_{x→c} f(x)/g(x) = L. The rule applies equally for one-sided limits (x → c⁺ or x → c⁻) and for limits as x → ±∞. Converting 0·∞ to 0/0 or ∞/∞: if lim f(x) = 0 and lim g(x) = ∞, write f(x)·g(x) = f(x)/(1/g(x)) (now 0/0) or f(x)·g(x) = g(x)/(1/f(x)) (now ∞/∞). Choose the form that gives a simpler derivative. Typically: if one function is a polynomial or algebraic (easy to differentiate repeatedly), put it in the denominator as 1/polynomial. If one factor is an exponential (which reproduces under differentiation), the algebra often simplifies after one or two applications. Converting ∞-∞ to 0/0: write f(x) - g(x) = 1/(1/f(x)) - 1/(1/g(x)) and combine fractions, or find a common structure. Example: lim_{x→0⁺} (1/sin(x) - 1/x) = lim (x - sin(x))/(x·sin(x)) — now 0/0 form. Power forms — 1^∞, 0^0, ∞^0: let L = lim f(x)^{g(x)}. Take natural logs: ln(L) = lim g(x)·ln(f(x)). This is a 0·∞ form (for 0^0: g→0, ln(f)→-∞; for 1^∞: g→∞, ln(f)→0; for ∞^0: g→0, ln(f)→∞). Convert to 0/0 or ∞/∞ and apply L'Hôpital. After finding ln(L) = K, conclude L = e^K. The most important examples: lim_{x→∞}(1+1/x)^x = e (1^∞ form, gives ln(L) = 1), and lim_{x→0⁺} x^x = 1 (0^0 form, gives ln(L) = lim x·ln(x) = 0). Proof of L'Hôpital's Rule via Cauchy's MVT (0/0 case): Since f(c) = g(c) = 0, the Cauchy MVT applies to f and g on [c, x] (or [x,c]) for x near c: f(x)/g(x) = [f(x)-f(c)]/[g(x)-g(c)] = f'(t)/g'(t) for some t strictly between c and x. As x → c, t → c (since t is trapped between c and x). Therefore lim_{x→c} f(x)/g(x) = lim_{t→c} f'(t)/g'(t) = L. ∎ Complete proof of L'Hôpital's Rule (0/0 case) using Cauchy's MVT: Let f, g be continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), with f(c) = g(c) = 0 and g'(x) ≠ 0 on (a,b). For any x ≠ c in (a,b), the Cauchy MVT applies to f and g on the interval [min(c,x), max(c,x)]: there exists t strictly between c and x such that f'(t)[g(x)-g(c)] = g'(t)[f(x)-f(c)]. Since f(c) = g(c) = 0: f'(t)·g(x) = g'(t)·f(x). Since g'(t) ≠ 0 (by hypothesis) and g(x) ≠ 0 for x near c (since g'≠0 and g(c)=0, g is locally monotone, so g(x) ≠ 0 near c): f(x)/g(x) = f'(t)/g'(t). As x → c, t → c (since t is strictly between c and x). Therefore lim_{x→c} f(x)/g(x) = lim_{t→c} f'(t)/g'(t) = L. ∎ Why the ∞/∞ case is harder: when f(x) → ∞ and g(x) → ∞, we cannot write f(x)/g(x) = [f(x)-0]/[g(x)-0] because f(c) ≠ 0. The Cauchy MVT trick requires f(c) = 0 and g(c) = 0. For the ∞/∞ case, a different argument is needed — typically via the Stolz-Cesàro theorem (the discrete analog) or by showing lim f/g = lim f'/g' using a more delicate limit argument involving writing f(x)/g(x) = [f(x)-f(a)]/[g(x)-g(a)]·[1 - f(a)/f(x)]/[1 - g(a)/g(x)] and taking a → c. The ∞/∞ proof is found in Rudin's Principles of Mathematical Analysis. When L'Hôpital fails: the rule requires lim f'/g' to exist. If f'/g' oscillates without a limit, the rule gives no information — but the original limit may still exist. The canonical example: lim_{x→∞} (x + sin(x))/x. Applying the rule: lim (1 + cos(x))/1 = lim (1 + cos(x)), which oscillates between 0 and 2 — no limit. Yet (x + sin(x))/x = 1 + sin(x)/x → 1 + 0 = 1 by the squeeze theorem. L'Hôpital's rule said nothing wrong — it was inapplicable, since lim f'/g' does not exist. The lesson: if L'Hôpital gives an indeterminate result or oscillation, try another method. The failure of L'Hôpital does not imply the original limit fails. Repeated application: the rule can be applied as many times as necessary, as long as each intermediate limit is still 0/0 or ∞/∞. For example, lim_{x→0} (1-cos(x))/x² is 0/0. Apply: lim sin(x)/(2x) — still 0/0. Apply again: lim cos(x)/2 = 1/2. Each application removes one degree of the Taylor polynomial in both numerator and denominator, eventually leaving a well-defined limit. For polynomials, the number of applications equals the common order of vanishing at c. L'Hôpital Can Fail Even for ∞/∞ lim_{x→∞} (x+sin x)/x = 1, but applying L'Hôpital gives lim (1+cos x)/1, which has no limit. The rule does not apply here — lim f'/g' must exist for the rule to be valid. The absence of a limit for f'/g' is not a contradiction; it just means L'Hôpital cannot be used. L'Hôpital Bought Bernoulli's Math Guillaume de l'Hôpital (1661–1704) hired Johann Bernoulli as a private mathematics tutor in 1691 and paid him a monthly salary in exchange for exclusive rights to his mathematical discoveries. The rule in l'Hôpital's 1696 textbook was entirely Bernoulli's. L'Hôpital died before Bernoulli made his claim public. Bernoulli's correspondence confirming this was found in the early 20th century. The rule is still called 'L'Hôpital's Rule' by universal tradition — perhaps the most famous case of mathematical credit being given to a benefactor rather than the discoverer. Verify Indeterminate Form FIRST NEVER apply L'Hôpital's Rule without first confirming the limit is 0/0 or ∞/∞. lim_{x→0} (x+1)/x² is NOT indeterminate — it is 1/0 = ∞. Applying L'Hôpital gives 1/(2x) → ∞, which accidentally gives the right answer here, but the method is invalid. Always write '0/0 form' or '∞/∞ form' before applying the rule. L'Hôpital is NOT the Quotient Rule L'Hôpital's Rule: lim f/g = lim f'/g' — differentiate numerator and denominator SEPARATELY.
Quotient Rule: d/dx[f/g] = (f'g - fg')/g² — completely different!
The two formulas look similar but compute entirely different things. Mixing them up is a catastrophic error. L'Hôpital applies to LIMITS; the quotient rule applies to DERIVATIVES. L'Hôpital's Rule If \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c} g(x) = 0 \text{ (or both } \to \pm\infty\text{)},\\ g'(x) \ne 0 \text{ near } c, \text{ and } \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)} \text{ exists, then}\\ \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)} The Seven Indeterminate Forms \frac{0}{0}, \quad \frac{\infty}{\infty}, \quad 0 \cdot \infty, \quad \infty - \infty, \quad 1^\infty, \quad 0^0, \quad \infty^0 Conversion Strategy for Indeterminate Forms 0 \cdot \infty \to \frac{0}{1/\infty} = \frac{0}{0} \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{\infty}{1/0} = \frac{\infty}{\infty}\\ f^g \to e^{g \ln f}: \text{ apply L'Hôpital to } g \ln f L'Hôpital's Rule — Side-by-Side L'Hôpital's Rule resolves sin(x)/x → 1 as x → 0: replace the limit of ratio with limit of ratio of derivatives. Python Lab: Verify All 7 Indeterminate Forms Numerically Compute limits numerically by approaching from both sides and compare to L'Hôpital's analytical answer. Expose the failure case. Classic: lim(x→0) sin(x)/x \text{Evaluate } \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(x)}{x} \text{ using L'Hôpital's Rule.} lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1, confirmed by L'Hôpital. This matches the squeeze-theorem result from Chapter 1. L'Hôpital is much faster but requires knowing the derivative of sin(x), which was itself proved using the squeeze theorem limit. Avoid circular reasoning. \text{Verify: } \sin(0) = 0, \; 0 \text{ in denominator} \Rightarrow \frac{0}{0} \text{ form} \checkmark Always verify the indeterminate form before applying L'Hôpital. \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(x)}{x} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\cos(x)}{1} Apply L'Hôpital: differentiate numerator (sin(x))' = cos(x) and denominator (x)' = 1 separately. = \frac{\cos(0)}{1} = \frac{1}{1} = 1 Substitute x = 0. No longer indeterminate. The limit is 1. lim(x→0) (e^x - 1)/x \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x - 1}{x} lim(x→0) (e^x - 1)/x = 1. This is the limit definition of e^x's derivative at x=0, confirming that (d/dx)[e^x]|_{x=0} = 1. L'Hôpital makes this immediate. e^0 - 1 = 0, \; x = 0 \Rightarrow 0/0 \text{ form} \checkmark Verify: both numerator and denominator approach 0. \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x - 1}{x} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x}{1} = e^0 = 1 Differentiate: (e^x - 1)' = e^x. (x)' = 1. The limit is e^0 = 1. lim(x→1) (x³ - 1)/(x - 1) \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^3 - 1}{x - 1} The limit is 3. Both L'Hôpital and factoring work; the factoring approach is neater when the factorization is obvious. L'Hôpital is preferable for transcendental functions where factoring is impossible. 1^3 - 1 = 0, \; 1 - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow 0/0 \text{ form} Verify indeterminate form. \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^3-1}{x-1} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{3x^2}{1} = 3(1)^2 = 3 Apply L'Hôpital: differentiate numerator 3x², denominator 1. \text{Check by factoring: } \frac{x^3-1}{x-1} = \frac{(x-1)(x^2+x+1)}{x-1} = x^2+x+1 \to 3 \text{ as } x \to 1 Alternative: factor. Same answer confirms L'Hôpital is correct. lim(x→∞) x·e^(-x): 0·∞ Form \displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} x \cdot e^{-x} lim(x→∞) x·e^{-x} = 0. Exponential growth dominates polynomial growth. More generally, lim_{x→∞} x^n e^{-x} = 0 for any fixed n — apply L'Hôpital n times, each time reducing the power of x by 1. x \to \infty, \; e^{-x} \to 0 \Rightarrow 0 \cdot \infty \text{ form} Identify the indeterminate form. x \cdot e^{-x} = \frac{x}{e^x} \Rightarrow \frac{\infty}{\infty} \text{ form} Rewrite as a ratio: move e^{-x} to the denominator as e^x. \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x}{e^x} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{e^x} = 0 Apply L'Hôpital: (x)' = 1, (e^x)' = e^x. The result 1/e^x → 0 as x → ∞. lim(x→0⁺) x·ln(x): 0·∞ Form \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0^+} x \ln(x) lim(x→0⁺) x ln(x) = 0. Although ln(x) → -∞ as x → 0⁺, the factor x → 0 wins. This result appears in the entropy formula -x·ln(x) → 0 as x → 0 (a probability of 0 contributes 0 to entropy), which is important in information theory. x \to 0^+, \; \ln(x) \to -\infty \Rightarrow 0 \cdot (-\infty) \text{ form} Identify: 0·∞ indeterminate form. x \ln(x) = \frac{\ln(x)}{1/x} \Rightarrow \frac{-\infty}{+\infty} \text{ form} Rewrite: put 1/x in denominator. Now ∞/∞ form. \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\ln(x)}{1/x} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1/x}{-1/x^2} Differentiate: (ln x)' = 1/x, (1/x)' = -1/x². = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1/x \cdot x^2}{-1} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{-x^2/x}{1} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (-x) = 0 Simplify the ratio: (1/x)/(-1/x²) = (1/x)·(-x²) = -x → 0. lim(x→0⁺) x^x: 0^0 Form \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0^+} x^x lim(x→0⁺) x^x = 1. The 0^0 indeterminate form resolves to 1 in this case. Note: 0^0 is not always 1 — the value depends on how the base and exponent approach 0. The function f(x) = x^x approaches 1 as x → 0⁺, and by convention 0^0 = 1 in combinatorics. x \to 0^+, \; \text{base} = x \to 0, \; \text{exponent} = x \to 0 \Rightarrow 0^0 \text{ form} Identify the 0^0 indeterminate form. L = \lim_{x \to 0^+} x^x \Rightarrow \ln(L) = \lim_{x \to 0^+} x \ln(x) Take logarithm of both sides: ln(x^x) = x·ln(x). \lim_{x \to 0^+} x \ln(x) = 0 \quad (\text{from Example 5}) We computed this limit in Example 5 above. \ln(L) = 0 \Rightarrow L = e^0 = 1 Since ln(L) = 0, exponentiate: L = e^0 = 1. lim(x→∞) (1 + 1/x)^x = e: the 1^∞ Form \displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{1}{x}\right)^x lim(x→∞)(1+1/x)^x = e. This is one of the most important limits in mathematics — it is sometimes taken as the definition of e. L'Hôpital makes the proof systematic. The limit (1+r/n)^n → e^r as n → ∞ is the basis of continuous compounding in finance. \text{Base} = 1 + 1/x \to 1, \; \text{Exponent} = x \to \infty \Rightarrow 1^\infty \text{ form} Identify the 1^∞ indeterminate form. L = \lim_{x\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right)^x \Rightarrow \ln(L) = \lim_{x\to\infty} x \cdot \ln\!\left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right) Take logarithm. Now we have a 0·∞ form: x → ∞ and ln(1+1/x) → 0. x \cdot \ln(1+1/x) = \frac{\ln(1 + 1/x)}{1/x} \Rightarrow \frac{0}{0} \text{ form as } x \to \infty Rewrite as ratio (1/x in denominator). Both numerator and denominator → 0. \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{\frac{-1/x^2}{1+1/x}}{-1/x^2} = \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{1+1/x} Apply L'Hôpital. Numerator derivative: d/dx[ln(1+1/x)] = (1/(1+1/x))·(-1/x²). Denominator derivative: d/dx[1/x] = -1/x². The -1/x² factors cancel. = \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{1 + 0} = 1 As x → ∞, 1/x → 0, so the limit is 1. \ln(L) = 1 \Rightarrow L = e^1 = e Exponentiate: L = e. This is the definition of e as a limit. Classic (0/0): lim(x→2) (x²-4)/(x-2) \text{Evaluate } \lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2} The limit is 4. Notice: No L'Hôpital needed — algebra solved it. This is the key insight: indeterminate forms often hide algebraic simplifications. \frac{4 - 4}{0} = \frac{0}{0} \checkmark Plug in x=2: indeterminate 0/0 form. x^2 - 4 = (x-2)(x+2) Factor the numerator using difference of squares. \frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2} Substitute the factored form. x+2 Cancel (x-2) from numerator and denominator. 2+2 = 4 Evaluate at x=2. Radical (∞-∞): lim(x→∞) (√(x²+5x) - x) \text{Evaluate } \lim_{x \to \infty} \left( \sqrt{x^2 + 5x} - x \right) The limit is 5/2. The key algebraic step (factoring x from the radical) is often skipped in textbooks, leaving students confused. \infty - \infty \text{ form} Identify the indeterminate form. \frac{(\sqrt{x^2+5x}-x)(\sqrt{x^2+5x}+x)}{\sqrt{x^2+5x}+x} Multiply by conjugate to rationalize. \frac{(x^2+5x) - x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+5x}+x} = \frac{5x}{\sqrt{x^2+5x}+x} Apply difference of squares: numerator becomes 5x. \sqrt{x^2+5x} = \sqrt{x^2(1 + 5/x)} = x\sqrt{1 + 5/x} Factor x from the radical. \frac{5x}{x\sqrt{1+5/x} + x} Substitute: denominator becomes x(√(1+5/x) + 1). \frac{5x}{x(\sqrt{1+5/x}+1)} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{1+5/x}+1} Cancel x from numerator and denominator. \frac{5}{1+1} = \frac{5}{2} As x→∞, 5/x→0, so √(1+5/x)→1. (0·∞): lim(x→0⁺) x·ln(x) \text{Evaluate } \lim_{x \to 0^+} x \ln(x) The limit is 0. Rewriting products as fractions is a critical algebraic skill for indeterminate forms. x \to 0^+, \; \ln(x) \to -\infty \Rightarrow 0 \cdot (-\infty) Identify: 0·∞ indeterminate form. x \ln(x) = \frac{\ln(x)}{1/x} Rewrite product as fraction. \frac{-\infty}{\infty} \text{ form} New form: ∞/∞. \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \frac{1/x}{-1/x^2} = -x Apply L'Hôpital: differentiate numerator and denominator. \lim_{x \to 0^+} (-x) = 0 Evaluate: -x → 0 as x → 0⁺. Exponential (1^∞): lim(x→∞) (1+2/x)^x \text{Evaluate } \lim_{x \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{2}{x}\right)^x The limit is e². Logarithms convert exponential indeterminate forms to 0/0 or ∞/∞ forms. 1^\infty \text{ form} Identify: 1^∞ indeterminate form. y = \left(1 + \frac{2}{x}\right)^x Let y equal the expression. \ln(y) = x \ln\left(1 + \frac{2}{x}\right) Take ln of both sides. \frac{\ln(1+2/x)}{1/x} Rewrite as fraction. \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \frac{\frac{-2/x^2}{1+2/x}}{-1/x^2} = \frac{2}{1+2/x} Apply L'Hôpital. \ln(y) = 2 As x→∞, 2/x→0, so limit is 2. y = e^2 Exponentiate: y = e^2. Prove that lim(x→0) (1-cos(x))/x² = 1/2 in three ways: (a) geometric, (b) L'Hôpital, (c) power series. The power of multiple perspectives! L'Hopital is systematic, but the identity 1-cos(x) = 2sin²(x/2) shows the "hidden" square that balances the x² in the denominator. The series method is the ultimate "cheat code"—it literally shows you the result in the first term. All three methods give 1/2. The power series method is most elegant once the series is known. The geometric method is most elementary. L'Hôpital is most systematic. \text{(a) Geometric / Trigonometric Identity:} Method (a). \frac{1-\cos(x)}{x^2} = \frac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{x^2} = \frac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{4(x/2)^2} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\sin(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2 Use the half-angle identity 1-cos(x) = 2sin²(x/2). Rewrite x² = 4(x/2)². \to \frac{1}{2} \cdot 1^2 = \frac{1}{2} \quad \text{as } x \to 0 \text{ (since } \sin(\theta)/\theta \to 1\text{)} As x → 0, x/2 → 0, so sin(x/2)/(x/2) → 1. ∎ \text{(b) L'Hôpital twice:} Method (b). Both numerator and denominator → 0 twice. \lim \frac{1-\cos x}{x^2} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim \frac{\sin x}{2x} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim \frac{\cos x}{2} = \frac{1}{2} First L'Hôpital: (1-cos x)' = sin x, (x²)' = 2x. Still 0/0. Second L'Hôpital: (sin x)' = cos x, (2x)' = 2. Evaluate at 0: cos(0)/2 = 1/2. ∎ \text{(c) Power series:} Method (c). \cos(x) = 1 - \frac{x^2}{2!} + \frac{x^4}{4!} - \cdots Taylor series for cos(x) around 0. 1 - \cos(x) = \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^4}{24} + \cdots Subtract from 1. \frac{1-\cos x}{x^2} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{x^2}{24} + \cdots \to \frac{1}{2} \text{ as } x \to 0 Divide by x². As x → 0, higher-order terms vanish. ∎ Find lim(x→0⁺) (sin(x))^{tan(x)}. This is a 0^0 form. The logarithmic "unfolding" is key. Any time the variable is in both the base and the exponent, take the ln. This converts a "vertical growth" problem into a "horizontal product" problem. lim(x→0⁺) (sin x)^{tan x} = 1. This 0^0 power form evaluates to 1, consistent with the general pattern: when the exponent goes to 0 faster than the log of the base goes to -∞, the limit is 1. L = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (\sin x)^{\tan x} As x → 0⁺: sin(x) → 0 and tan(x) → 0, giving 0^0 form. \ln L = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \tan(x) \cdot \ln(\sin x) Take logarithm. = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\ln(\sin x)}{\cot x} \Rightarrow \frac{-\infty}{+\infty} \text{ form} Rewrite: tan(x)·ln(sin x) = ln(sin x)/(1/tan x) = ln(sin x)/cot(x). As x → 0⁺: ln(sin x) → -∞ and cot(x) → +∞. \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\cos(x)/\sin(x)}{-\csc^2(x)} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\cos x}{\sin x} \cdot (-\sin^2 x) = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (-\sin x \cos x) Apply L'Hôpital. Numerator derivative: d/dx[ln(sin x)] = cos(x)/sin(x). Denominator derivative: d/dx[cot(x)] = -csc²(x) = -1/sin²(x). Ratio: (cos x/sin x) / (-1/sin²x) = -cos x · sin x. \lim_{x \to 0^+} (-\sin x \cos x) = -\sin(0)\cos(0) = -0 \cdot 1 = 0 Evaluate the limit: -sin(0)cos(0) = 0. \ln L = 0 \Rightarrow L = e^0 = 1 Exponentiate. Show that L'Hôpital's Rule fails for lim(x→∞) (x + sin(x))/x even though the limit exists. Explain WHY it fails. The rule is a "bridge" that only works if the other side of the bridge is stable. If the derivative oscillates, the bridge collapses, and you must find another way to cross (like the Squeeze Theorem). L'Hôpital requires lim f'/g' to exist. Here lim (1+cos x)/1 does not exist (oscillates), so L'Hôpital does not apply. The original limit lim(x+sin x)/x = 1 exists and is found by elementary algebra. This shows L'Hôpital's Rule is a one-directional implication: [lim f'/g' exists and equals L] ⟹ [lim f/g = L]. The contrapositive: lim f/g ≠ L does NOT imply lim f'/g' ≠ L. \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x + \sin(x)}{x} = \frac{\infty}{\infty} \text{ form} Both x + sin(x) → ∞ and x → ∞, so this appears to be ∞/∞. \text{Attempt L'Hôpital: } \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{(x+\sin x)'}{x'} = \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1 + \cos x}{1} Apply L'Hôpital. \lim_{x \to \infty} (1 + \cos x) \text{ does not exist} cos(x) oscillates between -1 and 1 forever. No limit. \text{But the original limit DOES exist:} Compute by elementary means. \frac{x + \sin x}{x} = 1 + \frac{\sin x}{x} Divide numerator and denominator by x (equivalently, split the fraction). \left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right| \leq \frac{1}{|x|} \to 0 \text{ as } x \to \infty The squeeze theorem (or bound): |sin x| ≤ 1 always, so |sin(x)/x| ≤ 1/x → 0. \therefore \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{x + \sin x}{x} = 1 + 0 = 1 The original limit is 1. \text{Why L'Hôpital fails: } \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)} \text{ must EXIST} L'Hôpital's theorem states: IF lim f'/g' = L, THEN lim f/g = L. It does NOT say: if lim f'/g' fails to exist, then lim f/g fails. The condition 'lim f'/g' exists' is part of the hypothesis, not the conclusion. Here lim f'/g' doesn't exist, so the rule simply does not apply — but the original limit still exists. Mean Value Theorem L'Hôpital's Rule is proved using Cauchy's Generalized MVT. Understanding the MVT is essential for the rigorous proof. Curve Sketching Computing asymptotes of functions like ln(x)/x as x → ∞ requires L'Hôpital (∞/∞ form). L'Hôpital is the tool for limits that arise in asymptote analysis. Linear Approximation The intuition for L'Hôpital (f(x)/g(x) ≈ f'(c)(x-c)/[g'(c)(x-c)] near a common zero) is linearization. The rule IS linear approximation applied to ratios. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step approach approaching value as x approaches end behavior instantaneous rate of change slope dy/dx velocity marginal change real world engineering physics economics biology computer science
