This converts (i-1) back to k so we can use the standard formula. \sum_{i=1}^n (i-1)^2 = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k^2 = 0^2 + \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} k^2 = \frac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{6} The k=0 term is 0 and drops out. Apply the sum formula with upper limit (n-1): replace n↦(n-1) in n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. L_n = \frac{1}{n^3}\cdot\frac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{6} = \frac{(n-1)(2n-1)}{6n^2} Cancel one factor of n: n/n³ = 1/n². = \frac{n(1-\tfrac{1}{n})\cdot n(2-\tfrac{1}{n})}{6n^2} = \frac{(1-\tfrac{1}{n})(2-\tfrac{1}{n})}{6} Rewrite (n-1)=n(1-1/n) and (2n-1)=n(2-1/n). The n² in numerator cancels the n² denominator. L_n = \frac{2-\tfrac{3}{n}+\tfrac{1}{n^2}}{6} = \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{2n} + \frac{1}{6n^2} FOIL: 1·2 + 1·(-1/n) + (-1/n)·2 + (-1/n)² = 2-3/n+1/n². Divide by 6. \lim_{n\to\infty} L_n = \frac{1}{3}\qquad(\text{same as }\lim R_n) The 1/n corrections vanish. Both left and right sums converge to 1/3. R_n - L_n = \frac{1}{n} = \Delta x\cdot(f(1)-f(0)) The gap between right and left sums equals Δx × (f(b)−f(a)) — one "sliver" at the right edge of Rₙ that Lₙ misses. This gap → 0 as n → ∞. Midpoint Sum Is Exact for f(x) = x on [0, 2] \text{Form the midpoint Riemann sum } M_n \text{ for } \int_0^2 x\,dx. \text{ Show that } M_n = 2 \text{ for every } n, \text{ and explain why.} For any linear f(x)=mx+b, the midpoint sum equals the exact integral for every n, because the overestimate on the right half of each subinterval and the underestimate on the left half cancel exactly. a=0,\quad b=2,\quad \Delta x = \frac{2}{n},\quad x_i = \frac{2i}{n} Uniform partition of [0,2]. Total length 2, so each of the n pieces has width 2/n. c_i = \frac{x_{i-1}+x_i}{2} = \frac{\tfrac{2(i-1)}{n}+\tfrac{2i}{n}}{2} = \frac{\tfrac{4i-2}{n}}{2} = \frac{2i-1}{n} Midpoint: average of the two endpoints. Combine over common denominator n, then divide by 2. f(c_i) = c_i = \frac{2i-1}{n} Since f(x)=x, evaluating at the midpoint just gives the midpoint itself. f(c_i)\,\Delta x = \frac{2i-1}{n}\cdot\frac{2}{n} = \frac{2(2i-1)}{n^2} One rectangle: height × width. M_n = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{2(2i-1)}{n^2} = \frac{2}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(2i-1) Factor the constant 2/n² out. Now evaluate the sum ∑(2i-1) by splitting it. \sum_{i=1}^n(2i-1) = 2\sum_{i=1}^n i - \sum_{i=1}^n 1 = 2\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2} - n = n(n+1)-n = n^2 Apply both formulas: ∑i = n(n+1)/2 and ∑1 = n. The result telescopes to n² exactly. M_n = \frac{2}{n^2}\cdot n^2 = 2\qquad\text{for every }n n²/n² = 1. No limit is needed — the sum already equals the exact integral for all n. \int_0^2 x\,dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^2 = 2\checkmark\qquad\text{(triangle: }\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot2\cdot2=2\text{)} Confirmed by antiderivative and by geometry (right triangle with base 2, height 2). \text{Why exact? }\quad f''(x) = 0 \text{ for } f(x)=x The midpoint rule's error is proportional to f'' (curvature). f(x)=x is perfectly straight so f''=0 everywhere — zero error for every n. This generalises: midpoint rule is exact for any linear or constant function. Right Sum for f(x) = 3x² − 2x + 1 on [1, 3] — Full Algebraic Expansion \text{Form } R_n \text{ for } \int_1^3(3x^2-2x+1)\,dx. \text{ Simplify } S_n \text{ completely and verify the limit equals } 20. The key skill: expand f(a+iΔx) step by step — square first, then distribute each polynomial coefficient, then collect by powers of i (constant / linear / quadratic). Every polynomial integrand on every interval follows this same pattern. a=1,\quad b=3,\quad \Delta x = \frac{2}{n} Step 2: interval length is b−a=2, so each rectangle has width 2/n. x_i = 1 + \frac{2i}{n},\qquad c_i = x_i = 1+\frac{2i}{n} Steps 3–4: right endpoints start at a=1 and add i·Δx = 2i/n each step. \left(1+\frac{2i}{n}\right)^2 = 1 + \frac{4i}{n} + \frac{4i^2}{n^2} Step 5 — expand the square FIRST before plugging into f. Use (A+B)²=A²+2AB+B²: A=1, B=2i/n. 3\left(1+\frac{4i}{n}+\frac{4i^2}{n^2}\right) = 3 + \frac{12i}{n} + \frac{12i^2}{n^2} Distribute the 3 across all three terms. -2\left(1+\frac{2i}{n}\right) = -2 - \frac{4i}{n} Distribute the -2. f(c_i) = \underbrace{3-2+1}_{=2} + \underbrace{\frac{12i-4i}{n}}_{=\frac{8i}{n}} + \frac{12i^2}{n^2} = 2 + \frac{8i}{n} + \frac{12i^2}{n^2} Collect: constants 3-2+1=2; linear-in-i terms 12i/n-4i/n=8i/n; quadratic 12i²/n². f(c_i)\,\Delta x = \left(2 + \frac{8i}{n} + \frac{12i^2}{n^2}\right)\cdot\frac{2}{n} = \frac{4}{n} + \frac{16i}{n^2} + \frac{24i^2}{n^3} Step 6: multiply every term by Δx=2/n. R_n = \frac{4}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n 1\ +\ \frac{16}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n i\ +\ \frac{24}{n^3}\sum_{i=1}^n i^2 Steps 7–8: split the sum into three separate sums, each with its constant factored out. = \frac{4}{n}\cdot n\ +\ \frac{16}{n^2}\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\ +\ \frac{24}{n^3}\cdot\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} Step 9: apply ∑1=n, ∑i=n(n+1)/2, ∑i²=n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. = 4\ +\ \frac{8(n+1)}{n}\ +\ \frac{4(n+1)(2n+1)}{n^2} Simplify: first term = 4; second = 16n(n+1)/(2n²) = 8(n+1)/n; third = 24n(n+1)(2n+1)/(6n³) = 4(n+1)(2n+1)/n². = 4 + 8\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right) + 4\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)\left(2+\frac{1}{n}\right) Rewrite (n+1)/n = 1+1/n and (2n+1)/n = 2+1/n. \lim_{n\to\infty} R_n = 4 + 8(1) + 4(1)(2) = 4 + 8 + 8 = 20 Step 10: every 1/n term vanishes. Limit = 20. \int_1^3(3x^2-2x+1)\,dx = \bigl[x^3-x^2+x\bigr]_1^3 = (27-9+3)-(1-1+1) = 21-1 = 20\checkmark Verified using antiderivative. The Riemann sum limit matches exactly. Compute L₄ and R₄ for ∫₀² (x² + 1) dx. Identify which sum overestimates and which underestimates, and why. f(x) = x²+1 is increasing on [0,2]. Δx = 0.5. Left endpoints: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5. Right endpoints: 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2. L_4 = 3.75 \text{ (underestimate)},\quad R_4 = 5.75 \text{ (overestimate)} \Delta x = 0.5, \quad f(x) = x^2 + 1 Uniform partition of [0,2] into 4 subintervals. L_4 = [f(0)+f(0.5)+f(1)+f(1.5)] \cdot 0.5 = [1+1.25+2+3.25] \cdot 0.5 = 7.5 \cdot 0.5 = 3.75 f(0)=1, f(0.5)=1.25, f(1)=2, f(1.5)=3.25. Sum=7.5. R_4 = [f(0.5)+f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2)] \cdot 0.5 = [1.25+2+3.25+5] \cdot 0.5 = 11.5 \cdot 0.5 = 5.75 f(2)=5. Sum=11.5. \text{True value: } \int_0^2(x^2+1)\,dx = \left[\tfrac{x^3}{3}+x\right]_0^2 = \tfrac{8}{3}+2 = \tfrac{14}{3} \approx 4.667 Exact value for comparison. L_4 = 3.75 < 14/3 \approx 4.667 < R_4 = 5.75 f is increasing, so L₄ underestimates and R₄ overestimates, as expected. Using sigma notation, derive a closed-form expression for Rₙ for ∫₀² x³ dx, and compute the exact limit to verify that ∫₀² x³ dx = 4. Use the sum formula Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ i³ = [n(n+1)/2]². With Δx = 2/n and xᵢ = 2i/n, Rₙ = Σ(2i/n)³·(2/n). Factor constants outside the sum. Apply the sum formula. Then take n → ∞. \displaystyle\int_0^2 x^3\,dx = 4 \Delta x = \frac{2}{n}, \quad x_i = \frac{2i}{n} Partition [0,2] uniformly. R_n = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{2i}{n}\right)^3 \cdot \frac{2}{n} = \frac{16}{n^4} \sum_{i=1}^n i^3 Factor: (2i/n)³·(2/n) = 8i³/n³·2/n = 16i³/n⁴. = \frac{16}{n^4} \cdot \left[\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2 = \frac{16}{n^4} \cdot \frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{4} = \frac{4(n+1)^2}{n^2} Apply the sum formula. \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{4(n+1)^2}{n^2} = \lim_{n\to\infty} 4\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^2 = 4 \cdot 1 = 4 As n→∞, (1+1/n)² → 1. Prove the following: for a function f that is increasing and continuous on [a, b], the error |Rₙ − ∫ₐᵇ f| satisfies |Rₙ − ∫ₐᵇ f| ≤ [f(b) − f(a)](b−a)/n. Interpret this formula: the error depends on the "total rise" of f and the interval width, but decreases like 1/n. On each subinterval [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ], the right rectangle overestimates by the area of a thin "sliver" at the top: the sliver has width Δx and height at most f(xᵢ)−f(xᵢ₋₁). Sum all slivers. |R_n - \int_a^b f| \leq \dfrac{(f(b)-f(a))(b-a)}{n}. \text{ Error } \to 0 \text{ as } n \to \infty. \text{On } [x_{i-1}, x_i]: \; \int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i} f\,dx \leq f(x_i)\,\Delta x \leq f(x_i)\,\Delta x Since f is increasing, f(x) ≤ f(xᵢ) for all x in [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ]. The right rectangle area is an overestimate. 0 \leq f(x_i)\,\Delta x - \int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i} f\,dx \leq (f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1}))\,\Delta x Upper bound on error per subinterval: max minus min of f times width. The "sliver" above the curve has area ≤ (f(xᵢ)−f(xᵢ₋₁))Δx. |R_n - \int_a^b f| \leq \sum_{i=1}^n (f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1}))\,\Delta x = \Delta x \cdot \sum_{i=1}^n (f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})) Sum all sub-errors. The total error is bounded by Δx times the telescoping sum. \sum_{i=1}^n (f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})) = f(x_n) - f(x_0) = f(b) - f(a) Telescoping sum: all intermediate terms cancel. Total rise = f(b)−f(a). |R_n - \int_a^b f| \leq (f(b)-f(a)) \cdot \Delta x = \frac{(f(b)-f(a))(b-a)}{n} Substitute Δx = (b−a)/n. This is the error bound. Area and Accumulation Lesson 0 introduced integrals informally as area. This lesson provides the precise definition as a limit of Riemann sums. The Definite Integral Lesson 2 develops the properties of the definite integral and computes it by geometry rather than Riemann sums. Fundamental Theorem of Calculus The FTC replaces Riemann sum limits with antiderivative evaluation — making exact computation of most integrals far more practical. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step antiderivative accumulation area under curve net area total change

documents.assignment: ∫₀³ (2x+1) dx by Geometry \text{Compute } \int_0^3 (2x+1)\,dx \text{ using the geometric interpretation (area of a trapezoid).}   ∫₀³ (2x+1) dx = 12. For any linear function, the integral equals the trapezoid area — no calculus machinery needed. This confirms our geometric intuition and sets up a check for Lesson 3 (FTC Part 2 will give the same answer: [x²+x]₀³ = 9+3−0 = 12). f(x) = 2x+1 \text{ is a straight line.} \quad f(0) = 1, \quad f(3) = 7 The integrand is linear. The region under the graph from x=0 to x=3 is a trapezoid. \text{Trapezoid: two parallel sides } f(0)=1 \text{ and } f(3)=7, \text{ width (height of trapezoid)} = 3. The "parallel sides" are the vertical heights at x=0 and x=3; the width is the length of the interval. \text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}(\text{side}_1 + \text{side}_2) \times \text{width} = \frac{1}{2}(1+7) \times 3 = \frac{1}{2}(8)(3) = 12 Trapezoid area formula: average of parallel sides times width. \int_0^3 (2x+1)\,dx = 12 Confirmed: the definite integral equals the geometric area of the trapezoid. ∫₀² √(4−x²) dx = π Using Geometry \text{Evaluate } \int_0^2 \sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx \text{ without computing an antiderivative.}   ∫₀²√(4−x²)dx = π. This elegant result requires no antiderivative (the antiderivative of √(4−x²) involves arcsin, which is not yet available). Geometric reasoning gives the exact answer immediately. This illustrates the power of the area interpretation. y = \sqrt{4-x^2} \Rightarrow y^2 = 4 - x^2 \Rightarrow x^2 + y^2 = 4 The equation y = √(4−x²) with y ≥ 0 describes the upper semicircle of radius 2 centered at the origin. \text{The region under } y = \sqrt{4-x^2} \text{ from } x=0 \text{ to } x=2 \text{ is a quarter-disk of radius } 2. On [0,2], the curve goes from (0,2) to (2,0), tracing a quarter-circle in the first quadrant. \text{Area of quarter-disk} = \frac{1}{4}\pi r^2 = \frac{1}{4}\pi(4) = \pi Area = πr²/4 = 4π/4 = π. \int_0^2 \sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx = \pi \approx 3.14159 The definite integral equals the area of the quarter-disk: exactly π. ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx = 0 by Symmetry \text{Evaluate } \int_{-1}^{1} x^3\,dx \text{ using symmetry, without computing.}   ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx = 0 by symmetry. No computation required — recognizing the odd function on a symmetric interval gives the answer instantly. This is one of the most powerful time-saving tricks in integral calculus. f(x) = x^3 \text{ is an odd function: } f(-x) = (-x)^3 = -x^3 = -f(x) Verify odd symmetry: f(−x) = −f(x) for all x. \text{Odd function on symmetric interval} \Rightarrow \int_{-1}^{1} x^3\,dx = 0 By the symmetry theorem: ∫₋ₐᵃ (odd function) dx = 0. The positive area on [0,1] is exactly canceled by the negative area on [−1,0]. \text{Verification: } \int_{-1}^{1} x^3\,dx = \left[\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_{-1}^{1} = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} = 0 The antiderivative of x³ is x⁴/4. Both endpoints give 1/4, so the difference is 0. Using Additivity: Finding ∫₃⁵ f from Partial Information \text{Given } \int_0^3 f(x)\,dx = 5 \text{ and } \int_0^5 f(x)\,dx = 12, \text{ find } \int_3^5 f(x)\,dx.   ∫₃⁵ f = 7. The additivity property lets us extract partial integrals from known combinations — like solving an equation. This technique is essential whenever you only have access to aggregate data. \int_0^5 f = \int_0^3 f + \int_3^5 f Interval additivity: the integral from 0 to 5 splits at x=3. 12 = 5 + \int_3^5 f Substitute the known values. \int_3^5 f(x)\,dx = 12 - 5 = 7 Solve for the unknown integral. Average Value and the MVT for Integrals \text{Find the average value of } f(x) = x^2 \text{ on } [0,3]. \text{ Then find } c \in (0,3) \text{ where } f(c) = f_{\text{avg}}.   The average value of x² on [0,3] is 3. The function achieves this average at c = √3 ≈ 1.73, which lies inside (0,3) as the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals guarantees. f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{3-0}\int_0^3 x^2\,dx Average value formula: (1/(b−a)) × integral. \int_0^3 x^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3 = \frac{27}{3} - 0 = 9 Antiderivative of x² is x³/3. Evaluate at 3 and 0. f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{3} \cdot 9 = 3 Average value of x² on [0,3] is 3. f(c) = f_{\text{avg}} \Rightarrow c^2 = 3 \Rightarrow c = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73 Solve f(c) = 3 for c. Since c must be in (0,3), we take the positive root c = √3. \sqrt{3} \in (0,3) \checkmark Confirmed: c = √3 ≈ 1.73 is in the open interval (0,3), as the MVT for integrals guarantees. ∫₋₂² |x| dx Using Geometry \text{Evaluate } \int_{-2}^{2} |x|\,dx \text{ using the geometric area interpretation.}   ∫₋₂² |x| dx = 4. The absolute value function is even, so we can double the integral over [0,2]. Geometrically, the "V" shape creates two triangles with total area 4. |x| = \begin{cases} -x & x < 0 \\ x & x \geq 0 \end{cases} The absolute value function forms a "V" shape with vertex at the origin. \int_{-2}^{2} |x|\,dx = \int_{-2}^{0} (-x)\,dx + \int_0^2 x\,dx Split at x=0 where the behavior changes. On [−2,0], |x| = −x; on [0,2], |x| = x. \text{Each piece is a right triangle with base 2 and height 2.} |x| on [−2,0] is a line from 2 to 0 (height at x=−2 is 2, at x=0 is 0). Same on [0,2]. \int_{-2}^{0} (-x)\,dx = \frac{1}{2}(2)(2) = 2 \quad \int_0^2 x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}(2)(2) = 2 Each triangle has area ½ × 2 × 2 = 2. \int_{-2}^{2} |x|\,dx = 2 + 2 = 4 Total area = 4. \text{Or by even symmetry: } \int_{-2}^{2} |x|\,dx = 2\int_0^2 x\,dx = 2 \cdot 2 = 4 Since |x| is even, we can use the symmetry shortcut: double the [0,2] piece. Displacement vs. Distance: Signed vs. Unsigned Integral \text{A particle moves with } v(t) = \sin(t). \text{ Find displacement and total distance over } [0, 2\pi].   Displacement = 0 (returns to start) but total distance = 4 (traveled 2 units forward and 2 units back). This distinction is fundamental in physics: displacement is a vector (signed); distance is a scalar (unsigned). \text{Displacement} = \int_0^{2\pi} \sin(t)\,dt Displacement is the signed integral of velocity. = [-\cos(t)]_0^{2\pi} = -\cos(2\pi) + \cos(0) = -1 + 1 = 0 Antiderivative of sin(t) is −cos(t). Evaluate from 0 to 2π. \text{The particle returns to its starting point after one full period.} Displacement = 0 means net change in position is zero — it started and ended at the same place. \text{Total distance} = \int_0^{2\pi} |\sin(t)|\,dt Distance ignores direction — integrate the absolute value. = \int_0^{\pi} \sin(t)\,dt + \int_{\pi}^{2\pi} (-\sin(t))\,dt sin(t) ≥ 0 on [0,π]; sin(t) ≤ 0 on [π,2π] so |sin| = −sin there. Split at the zero. = [-\cos(t)]_0^{\pi} + [\cos(t)]_{\pi}^{2\pi} = (1+1) + (-1-(-1)) = 2 + 2 = 4 First piece: −cos(π)+cos(0) = 1+1=2. Second piece: cos(2π)−cos(π) = 1−(−1)=2. \text{Displacement} = 0, \quad \text{Total distance} = 4. The particle traveled 4 units total but ended where it started.  Given ∫₋₃³ f(x) dx = 10 and ∫₋₃³ g(x) dx = 6, evaluate: (a) ∫₋₃³ [2f(x) − 3g(x)] dx. (b) If f is even and ∫₀³ f = 7, what is ∫₋₃⁰ f? Use linearity for part (a). For part (b), use the even-function symmetry: ∫₋₃³ f = 2∫₀³ f. Then use additivity to find ∫₋₃⁰ f. \text{(a) } 2 \qquad \text{(b) } \int_{-3}^0 f = 7  \text{(a) } \int_{-3}^3 [2f-3g]\,dx = 2\int_{-3}^3 f - 3\int_{-3}^3 g = 2(10) - 3(6) = 20 - 18 = 2 Linearity: pull out constants and split the integral. \text{(b) } f \text{ even} \Rightarrow \int_{-3}^3 f = 2\int_0^3 f For even f on symmetric interval: ∫₋ₐᵃ f = 2∫₀ᵃ f. \int_{-3}^3 f = 2(7) = 14 Since ∫₀³ f = 7, the full symmetric integral is 14. \int_{-3}^3 f = \int_{-3}^0 f + \int_0^3 f \Rightarrow 14 = \int_{-3}^0 f + 7 \Rightarrow \int_{-3}^0 f = 7 Split by additivity. Subtract ∫₀³ f = 7 from both sides. By symmetry, ∫₋₃⁰ f = ∫₀³ f = 7, as expected for an even function.  Find the average value of f(x) = sin(x) on [0, π]. Then find all c ∈ (0, π) where f(c) = f_avg. Compute ∫₀^π sin(x) dx using the antiderivative −cos(x). Divide by the interval length π. Then solve sin(c) = f_avg. f_{\text{avg}} = 2/\pi \approx 0.637. \text{ Achieved at } c \approx 0.690 \text{ and } c \approx 2.452.  \int_0^{\pi} \sin(x)\,dx = [-\cos(x)]_0^{\pi} = -\cos(\pi)+\cos(0) = -(-1)+1 = 2 Antiderivative of sin is −cos. f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{\pi - 0} \cdot 2 = \frac{2}{\pi} \approx 0.637 Average value = integral / interval length = 2/π. \sin(c) = \frac{2}{\pi} \Rightarrow c = \arcsin\!\left(\frac{2}{\pi}\right) \approx 0.690 \text{ or } c = \pi - \arcsin\!\left(\frac{2}{\pi}\right) \approx 2.452 On [0,π], sin(c) = 2/π has two solutions (sin is positive throughout). Both c ≈ 0.690 and c ≈ 2.452 are in (0,π).  Prove the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals from scratch using only the Extreme Value Theorem and Intermediate Value Theorem. Be explicit about where each theorem is used. Step 1: EVT gives min m and max M of f on [a,b]. Step 2: Comparison inequalities give m ≤ (1/(b−a))∫ₐᵇf ≤ M. Step 3: IVT gives a point where f equals this average value. \text{MVT for Integrals proved: } \exists c \in [a,b]: f(c) = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f\,dx.  \text{Since } f \text{ is continuous on } [a,b], \text{ the EVT guarantees } m = \min f \text{ and } M = \max f \text{ both exist.} EVT: continuous function on closed bounded interval attains its extrema. m \leq f(x) \leq M \text{ for all } x \in [a,b] Definition of min and max. m(b-a) \leq \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \leq M(b-a) Comparison property: integrating an inequality over [a,b] preserves it (and multiplies by width b−a). m \leq \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx \leq M Divide through by (b−a) > 0. \text{Let } \mu = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f\,dx. \text{ Then } m \leq \mu \leq M. The average value μ lies between the minimum and maximum of f. f \text{ is continuous and } m = f(d), M = f(e) \text{ for some } d, e \in [a,b]. \text{ By IVT, } \exists c \in [a,b]: f(c) = \mu. IVT: a continuous function takes all intermediate values between any two values it attains. Since f(d)=m ≤ μ ≤ M=f(e), there exists c between d and e (hence in [a,b]) with f(c)=μ. ∎
documents.proofs: The comparison property |∫ₐᵇ f| ≤ ∫ₐᵇ |f| deserves a careful proof, since it is used repeatedly in analysis. For any Riemann sum: |Σf(cᵢ)Δx| ≤ Σ|f(cᵢ)|Δx by the triangle inequality for finite sums. Taking the limit as n → ∞: the left side converges to |∫ₐᵇ f| and the right side to ∫ₐᵇ |f| (assuming both f and |f| are integrable, which follows from f being integrable — since |f| is integrable whenever f is). The inequality is preserved in the limit, giving the result. The MVT for integrals requires both the Extreme Value Theorem and the Intermediate Value Theorem. The EVT guarantees f attains m = min f and M = max f on [a, b] (requiring continuity + closed bounded interval). The bound m ≤ f_avg ≤ M follows from the comparison property. The IVT guarantees f takes every value between m and M on [a, b] (requiring continuity). Since m ≤ f_avg ≤ M, f must take the value f_avg somewhere — call it c. Thus f(c) = f_avg. The careful reader will note that the IVT gives c in [a, b], not necessarily the open interval (a, b). The strict interior can be guaranteed if f_avg is not equal to m or M (which holds when f is non-constant), by a sharper application of the IVT. documents.applications: The definite integral as a number appears constantly in physics and engineering. The average temperature in a room over 24 hours is an integral divided by time. The center of mass of an irregular solid is a ratio of two integrals. The probability that a random variable falls in an interval is an integral of the probability density function. In signal processing, the "DC component" of a periodic signal is its average value — an integral over one period. In structural engineering, the bending moment at a point in a beam is the integral of the distributed load. Understanding the definite integral as a number with specific algebraic properties allows these calculations to be systematized. Signed Area: Positive Above, Negative Below The integral ∫₀^(2π) sin(x) dx = 0, even though the graph of sin(x) is never zero except at 0, π, 2π. The positive area on [0, π] equals 2, and the negative area on [π, 2π] equals −2. They cancel exactly. This is not a coincidence — it reflects the perfect symmetry of sine. The displacement of a particle moving with v(t)=sin(t) over a full period is zero: it returns to its starting position. Average Value in Physics and Engineering The average value formula f_avg = (1/(b−a))∫ₐᵇ f has direct applications: average temperature over a day (used by HVAC systems), average power over a cycle (determines RMS voltage in AC circuits), average velocity over a time interval (used in GPS), average force over a displacement (gives work via W = F_avg × d). In every case, the continuous average replaces the discrete mean, and the definite integral plays the role of the sum. Symmetry: Odd and Even Functions You already know that polynomial terms xⁿ are odd when n is odd and even when n is even. More generally: sin(x), x³, x⁵ are odd; cos(x), x², x⁴ are even. Sums and products follow rules: (even)×(odd) = odd; (odd)×(odd) = even. Use these to instantly identify integrals that are zero over symmetric intervals without computing anything. Average Value ≠ Average of Endpoints The average value of f on [a,b] is (1/(b−a))∫ₐᵇ f dx — NOT (f(a)+f(b))/2. The endpoint average is a crude approximation (the trapezoidal rule with n=1). For f(x)=x² on [0,3]: endpoint average = (0+9)/2 = 4.5. True average = 3. The correct formula integrates the function, capturing its full behavior over the interval. ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx Is a Number, Not a Function The definite integral ∫₀³ x² dx = 9 is a NUMBER (9), not a function of x. The variable x is a 'dummy variable' — ∫₀³ t² dt = ∫₀³ u² du = 9. Do not confuse the definite integral (a number) with the indefinite integral ∫x² dx = x³/3 + C (a family of functions). The definite integral has limits; the indefinite integral does not. Cavalieri's Method of Indivisibles (1635) Bonaventura Cavalieri imagined a plane region as composed of infinitely many parallel lines — 'indivisibles.' By comparing the indivisibles of two regions line by line, he could prove they had equal areas without computing either area directly. His principle is the ancestor of ∫ₐᵇ [f(x)−g(x)] dx. It was logically incomplete (what IS an indivisible?) but profoundly influential, motivating both Newton and Leibniz.

This is the definite integral — not an approximation, but an exact real number. Now: what does the definite integral of ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx equal? Do you need to compute anything? Think about symmetry. It measures signed area: regions where f > 0 contribute positively, regions where f < 0 contribute negatively. The "signed" aspect is essential for physics — velocity can be negative (motion in the opposite direction), and the signed area gives displacement (net change in position), not total distance. Keeping track of signs is not a complication; it is the feature that makes the integral physically meaningful. Linearity is the most useful property in practice. ∫ₐᵇ [c·f(x) + g(x)] dx = c·∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx + ∫ₐᵇ g(x) dx. This means you can split a complicated integral into simpler pieces. To compute ∫₀² (3x² + 5√x) dx, you can compute ∫₀² 3x² dx and ∫₀² 5√x dx separately and add. Any polynomial, any sum of trigonometric functions, any linear combination of integrable functions can be integrated piece by piece. Linearity is the reason integration is "not that hard" for elementary functions. The interval additivity property ∫ₐᶜ f = ∫ₐᵇ f + ∫ᵦᶜ f allows you to break the domain of integration anywhere. To compute ∫₋₂⁵ f, split at x = 0: ∫₋₂⁰ f + ∫₀⁵ f. This is powerful when f behaves differently on different sub-intervals (for example, if f has a corner at 0, or changes sign at 0). For |f(x)| dx (total area), split at every zero of f and negate the negative pieces: ∫|f| = ∫₍positive regions₎ f − ∫₍negative regions₎ f. Symmetry is the most elegant shortcut for computing integrals. For an ODD function — one satisfying f(−x) = −f(x) — the graph is symmetric about the origin. The area above the x-axis on [0, b] is exactly canceled by the equal-and-opposite area below the x-axis on [−b, 0]. Therefore ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0 for any odd function integrated over a symmetric interval. For an EVEN function — f(−x) = f(x), symmetric about the y-axis — the areas on [−a, 0] and [0, a] are equal, so ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx. These shortcuts save enormous computational effort. The average value of f on [a, b] is defined as f_avg = (1/(b−a)) ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx. This is the continuous analog of the arithmetic mean (average) of a list of numbers: instead of summing n values and dividing by n, we integrate the function and divide by the interval length. Geometrically, f_avg is the height of the rectangle with base [a, b] that has exactly the same area as the region under f. The rectangle is the "flattened-out" version of f. The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals guarantees that f_avg is actually attained by f somewhere in (a, b), not just an abstract average. If f is continuous, then there exists at least one point c ∈ (a, b) where f(c) = f_avg. This is deeply intuitive: the continuous function must pass through its average. For f(x) = x² on [0, 3], f_avg = (1/3)∫₀³ x² dx = (1/3)(9) = 3. The equation f(c) = 3 gives c² = 3, so c = √3 ≈ 1.73. The function x² takes the value 3 at x = √3, which is inside (0, 3), exactly as the theorem predicts. The formal properties of the definite integral follow from the limit-of-Riemann-sums definition. Linearity: for constants c, d and integrable functions f, g on [a, b], ∫ₐᵇ [c·f(x) + d·g(x)] dx = c·∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx + d·∫ₐᵇ g(x) dx. Properties of the Definite Integral \[\int_a^b [c\,f(x)+d\,g(x)]\,dx = c\!\int_a^b\!f\,dx + d\!\int_a^b\!g\,dx \quad \text{(linearity)}\]
\[\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f \quad \text{(interval additivity)}\]
\[\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\right| \leq \int_a^b |f(x)|\,dx \quad \text{(triangle inequality)}\] Average Value of a Function The average value of \(f\) on \([a,b]\) is
\[f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.\]
Geometrically, \(f_{\text{avg}}\) is the height of the rectangle with base \(b-a\) that has the same area as the region under \(f\). Mean Value Theorem for Integrals If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), there exists \(c \in (a,b)\) such that
\[\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = f(c)(b-a).\]
Equivalently, \(f(c) = f_{\text{avg}}\) — a continuous function attains its average value. Symmetry Shortcuts If \(f\) is odd \((f(-x) = -f(x))\):
\[\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 0.\]
If \(f\) is even \((f(-x) = f(x))\):
\[\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 2\int_0^a f(x)\,dx.\] Signed Area: Positive and Negative Regions The shaded area above the x-axis is positive (green) and below is negative (red). The definite integral is the net signed area. Drag the endpoints to explore how the integral changes when more positive or negative region is included. ∫₀³ (2x+1) dx by Geometry \text{Compute } \int_0^3 (2x+1)\,dx \text{ using the geometric interpretation (area of a trapezoid).} ∫₀³ (2x+1) dx = 12. For any linear function, the integral equals the trapezoid area — no calculus machinery needed. This confirms our geometric intuition and sets up a check for Lesson 3 (FTC Part 2 will give the same answer: [x²+x]₀³ = 9+3−0 = 12). f(x) = 2x+1 \text{ is a straight line.} \quad f(0) = 1, \quad f(3) = 7 The integrand is linear. The region under the graph from x=0 to x=3 is a trapezoid. \text{Trapezoid: two parallel sides } f(0)=1 \text{ and } f(3)=7, \text{ width (height of trapezoid)} = 3. The "parallel sides" are the vertical heights at x=0 and x=3; the width is the length of the interval. \text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}(\text{side}_1 + \text{side}_2) \times \text{width} = \frac{1}{2}(1+7) \times 3 = \frac{1}{2}(8)(3) = 12 Trapezoid area formula: average of parallel sides times width. \int_0^3 (2x+1)\,dx = 12 Confirmed: the definite integral equals the geometric area of the trapezoid. ∫₀² √(4−x²) dx = π Using Geometry \text{Evaluate } \int_0^2 \sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx \text{ without computing an antiderivative.} ∫₀²√(4−x²)dx = π. This elegant result requires no antiderivative (the antiderivative of √(4−x²) involves arcsin, which is not yet available). Geometric reasoning gives the exact answer immediately. This illustrates the power of the area interpretation. y = \sqrt{4-x^2} \Rightarrow y^2 = 4 - x^2 \Rightarrow x^2 + y^2 = 4 The equation y = √(4−x²) with y ≥ 0 describes the upper semicircle of radius 2 centered at the origin. \text{The region under } y = \sqrt{4-x^2} \text{ from } x=0 \text{ to } x=2 \text{ is a quarter-disk of radius } 2. On [0,2], the curve goes from (0,2) to (2,0), tracing a quarter-circle in the first quadrant. \text{Area of quarter-disk} = \frac{1}{4}\pi r^2 = \frac{1}{4}\pi(4) = \pi Area = πr²/4 = 4π/4 = π. \int_0^2 \sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx = \pi \approx 3.14159 The definite integral equals the area of the quarter-disk: exactly π. ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx = 0 by Symmetry \text{Evaluate } \int_{-1}^{1} x^3\,dx \text{ using symmetry, without computing.} ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx = 0 by symmetry. No computation required — recognizing the odd function on a symmetric interval gives the answer instantly. This is one of the most powerful time-saving tricks in integral calculus. f(x) = x^3 \text{ is an odd function: } f(-x) = (-x)^3 = -x^3 = -f(x) Verify odd symmetry: f(−x) = −f(x) for all x. \text{Odd function on symmetric interval} \Rightarrow \int_{-1}^{1} x^3\,dx = 0 By the symmetry theorem: ∫₋ₐᵃ (odd function) dx = 0. The positive area on [0,1] is exactly canceled by the negative area on [−1,0]. \text{Verification: } \int_{-1}^{1} x^3\,dx = \left[\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_{-1}^{1} = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} = 0 The antiderivative of x³ is x⁴/4. Both endpoints give 1/4, so the difference is 0. Using Additivity: Finding ∫₃⁵ f from Partial Information \text{Given } \int_0^3 f(x)\,dx = 5 \text{ and } \int_0^5 f(x)\,dx = 12, \text{ find } \int_3^5 f(x)\,dx. ∫₃⁵ f = 7. The additivity property lets us extract partial integrals from known combinations — like solving an equation. This technique is essential whenever you only have access to aggregate data. \int_0^5 f = \int_0^3 f + \int_3^5 f Interval additivity: the integral from 0 to 5 splits at x=3. 12 = 5 + \int_3^5 f Substitute the known values. \int_3^5 f(x)\,dx = 12 - 5 = 7 Solve for the unknown integral. Average Value and the MVT for Integrals \text{Find the average value of } f(x) = x^2 \text{ on } [0,3]. \text{ Then find } c \in (0,3) \text{ where } f(c) = f_{\text{avg}}. The average value of x² on [0,3] is 3. The function achieves this average at c = √3 ≈ 1.73, which lies inside (0,3) as the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals guarantees. f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{3-0}\int_0^3 x^2\,dx Average value formula: (1/(b−a)) × integral. \int_0^3 x^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3 = \frac{27}{3} - 0 = 9 Antiderivative of x² is x³/3. Evaluate at 3 and 0. f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{3} \cdot 9 = 3 Average value of x² on [0,3] is 3. f(c) = f_{\text{avg}} \Rightarrow c^2 = 3 \Rightarrow c = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73 Solve f(c) = 3 for c. Since c must be in (0,3), we take the positive root c = √3. \sqrt{3} \in (0,3) \checkmark Confirmed: c = √3 ≈ 1.73 is in the open interval (0,3), as the MVT for integrals guarantees. ∫₋₂² |x| dx Using Geometry \text{Evaluate } \int_{-2}^{2} |x|\,dx \text{ using the geometric area interpretation.} ∫₋₂² |x| dx = 4. The absolute value function is even, so we can double the integral over [0,2]. Geometrically, the "V" shape creates two triangles with total area 4. |x| = \begin{cases} -x & x < 0 \\ x & x \geq 0 \end{cases} The absolute value function forms a "V" shape with vertex at the origin. \int_{-2}^{2} |x|\,dx = \int_{-2}^{0} (-x)\,dx + \int_0^2 x\,dx Split at x=0 where the behavior changes. On [−2,0], |x| = −x; on [0,2], |x| = x. \text{Each piece is a right triangle with base 2 and height 2.} |x| on [−2,0] is a line from 2 to 0 (height at x=−2 is 2, at x=0 is 0). Same on [0,2]. \int_{-2}^{0} (-x)\,dx = \frac{1}{2}(2)(2) = 2 \quad \int_0^2 x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}(2)(2) = 2 Each triangle has area ½ × 2 × 2 = 2. \int_{-2}^{2} |x|\,dx = 2 + 2 = 4 Total area = 4. \text{Or by even symmetry: } \int_{-2}^{2} |x|\,dx = 2\int_0^2 x\,dx = 2 \cdot 2 = 4 Since |x| is even, we can use the symmetry shortcut: double the [0,2] piece. Displacement vs. Distance: Signed vs. Unsigned Integral \text{A particle moves with } v(t) = \sin(t). \text{ Find displacement and total distance over } [0, 2\pi]. Displacement = 0 (returns to start) but total distance = 4 (traveled 2 units forward and 2 units back). This distinction is fundamental in physics: displacement is a vector (signed); distance is a scalar (unsigned). \text{Displacement} = \int_0^{2\pi} \sin(t)\,dt Displacement is the signed integral of velocity. = [-\cos(t)]_0^{2\pi} = -\cos(2\pi) + \cos(0) = -1 + 1 = 0 Antiderivative of sin(t) is −cos(t). Evaluate from 0 to 2π. \text{The particle returns to its starting point after one full period.} Displacement = 0 means net change in position is zero — it started and ended at the same place. \text{Total distance} = \int_0^{2\pi} |\sin(t)|\,dt Distance ignores direction — integrate the absolute value. = \int_0^{\pi} \sin(t)\,dt + \int_{\pi}^{2\pi} (-\sin(t))\,dt sin(t) ≥ 0 on [0,π]; sin(t) ≤ 0 on [π,2π] so |sin| = −sin there. Split at the zero. = [-\cos(t)]_0^{\pi} + [\cos(t)]_{\pi}^{2\pi} = (1+1) + (-1-(-1)) = 2 + 2 = 4 First piece: −cos(π)+cos(0) = 1+1=2. Second piece: cos(2π)−cos(π) = 1−(−1)=2. \text{Displacement} = 0, \quad \text{Total distance} = 4. The particle traveled 4 units total but ended where it started. Given ∫₋₃³ f(x) dx = 10 and ∫₋₃³ g(x) dx = 6, evaluate: (a) ∫₋₃³ [2f(x) − 3g(x)] dx. (b) If f is even and ∫₀³ f = 7, what is ∫₋₃⁰ f? Use linearity for part (a). For part (b), use the even-function symmetry: ∫₋₃³ f = 2∫₀³ f. Then use additivity to find ∫₋₃⁰ f. \text{(a) } 2 \qquad \text{(b) } \int_{-3}^0 f = 7 \text{(a) } \int_{-3}^3 [2f-3g]\,dx = 2\int_{-3}^3 f - 3\int_{-3}^3 g = 2(10) - 3(6) = 20 - 18 = 2 Linearity: pull out constants and split the integral. \text{(b) } f \text{ even} \Rightarrow \int_{-3}^3 f = 2\int_0^3 f For even f on symmetric interval: ∫₋ₐᵃ f = 2∫₀ᵃ f. \int_{-3}^3 f = 2(7) = 14 Since ∫₀³ f = 7, the full symmetric integral is 14. \int_{-3}^3 f = \int_{-3}^0 f + \int_0^3 f \Rightarrow 14 = \int_{-3}^0 f + 7 \Rightarrow \int_{-3}^0 f = 7 Split by additivity. Subtract ∫₀³ f = 7 from both sides. By symmetry, ∫₋₃⁰ f = ∫₀³ f = 7, as expected for an even function. Find the average value of f(x) = sin(x) on [0, π]. Then find all c ∈ (0, π) where f(c) = f_avg. Compute ∫₀^π sin(x) dx using the antiderivative −cos(x). Divide by the interval length π. Then solve sin(c) = f_avg. f_{\text{avg}} = 2/\pi \approx 0.637. \text{ Achieved at } c \approx 0.690 \text{ and } c \approx 2.452. \int_0^{\pi} \sin(x)\,dx = [-\cos(x)]_0^{\pi} = -\cos(\pi)+\cos(0) = -(-1)+1 = 2 Antiderivative of sin is −cos. f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{\pi - 0} \cdot 2 = \frac{2}{\pi} \approx 0.637 Average value = integral / interval length = 2/π. \sin(c) = \frac{2}{\pi} \Rightarrow c = \arcsin\!\left(\frac{2}{\pi}\right) \approx 0.690 \text{ or } c = \pi - \arcsin\!\left(\frac{2}{\pi}\right) \approx 2.452 On [0,π], sin(c) = 2/π has two solutions (sin is positive throughout). Both c ≈ 0.690 and c ≈ 2.452 are in (0,π). Prove the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals from scratch using only the Extreme Value Theorem and Intermediate Value Theorem. Be explicit about where each theorem is used. Step 1: EVT gives min m and max M of f on [a,b]. Step 2: Comparison inequalities give m ≤ (1/(b−a))∫ₐᵇf ≤ M. Step 3: IVT gives a point where f equals this average value. \text{MVT for Integrals proved: } \exists c \in [a,b]: f(c) = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f\,dx. \text{Since } f \text{ is continuous on } [a,b], \text{ the EVT guarantees } m = \min f \text{ and } M = \max f \text{ both exist.} EVT: continuous function on closed bounded interval attains its extrema. m \leq f(x) \leq M \text{ for all } x \in [a,b] Definition of min and max. m(b-a) \leq \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \leq M(b-a) Comparison property: integrating an inequality over [a,b] preserves it (and multiplies by width b−a). m \leq \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx \leq M Divide through by (b−a) > 0. \text{Let } \mu = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f\,dx. \text{ Then } m \leq \mu \leq M. The average value μ lies between the minimum and maximum of f. f \text{ is continuous and } m = f(d), M = f(e) \text{ for some } d, e \in [a,b]. \text{ By IVT, } \exists c \in [a,b]: f(c) = \mu. IVT: a continuous function takes all intermediate values between any two values it attains. Since f(d)=m ≤ μ ≤ M=f(e), there exists c between d and e (hence in [a,b]) with f(c)=μ. ∎ Riemann Sums The definite integral's properties (linearity, comparison) all follow from the limit-of-Riemann-sums definition established in Lesson 1. Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Lesson 3 shows how to COMPUTE definite integrals efficiently using antiderivatives. The properties in this lesson remain the foundation for understanding what we are computing. Applications of Integration Area between curves, net displacement, and average value — all developed in Lesson 5 — rely on the properties and signed-area interpretation built here. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step antiderivative accumulation area under curve net area total change

documents.assignment: FTC Part 1: Differentiating an Integral \text{Find } \frac{d}{dx}\int_0^x \sin(t^2)\,dt.   d/dx[∫₀ˣ sin(t²)dt] = sin(x²). FTC Part 1 applies even when the integrand has no elementary antiderivative. The theorem differentiates any continuous function — it does not require that an antiderivative be expressible in closed form. \text{Let } A(x) = \int_0^x \sin(t^2)\,dt Identify the accumulation function. The integrand is f(t) = sin(t²), which is continuous everywhere. \text{By FTC Part 1: } A'(x) = f(x) = \sin(x^2) Apply FTC Part 1 directly: the derivative of the accumulation function equals the integrand evaluated at the upper limit. \frac{d}{dx}\int_0^x \sin(t^2)\,dt = \sin(x^2) Final answer. Note: sin(t²) has no elementary antiderivative — without FTC Part 1, we could not differentiate this integral at all. Chain Rule + FTC Part 1 \text{Find } \frac{d}{dx}\int_3^{x^2} e^t\,dt.   d/dx[∫₃^(x²) eᵗ dt] = 2xe^(x²). The chain rule contribution 2x comes from the x² upper limit. Without the chain rule, you would incorrectly get just e^(x²). Always differentiate the upper limit and multiply. \text{Let } u = x^2. \text{ Define } A(u) = \int_3^u e^t\,dt. The upper limit is g(x) = x², not x itself. Use the chain rule: d/dx[A(g(x))] = A'(g(x))·g'(x). A'(u) = e^u \quad \text{(FTC Part 1)} The derivative of the accumulation function with respect to its upper limit is the integrand evaluated at the upper limit. \frac{d}{dx}\int_3^{x^2} e^t\,dt = A'(x^2) \cdot \frac{d}{dx}[x^2] = e^{x^2} \cdot 2x Chain rule: A'(g(x))·g'(x) = e^(x²)·2x. = 2x\,e^{x^2} Final answer. FTC Part 2: Evaluating ∫₀³ (2x+1) dx \text{Compute } \int_0^3 (2x+1)\,dx \text{ using FTC Part 2. Check against the geometric answer from Lesson 2.}   ∫₀³(2x+1)dx = 12. FTC Part 2 confirms the geometric calculation. This integral is simple enough to verify geometrically, which builds confidence in the algebraic method. \text{Find an antiderivative: } F(x) = x^2 + x F'(x) = 2x+1 ✓. We need any antiderivative — C=0 is the simplest choice. \int_0^3 (2x+1)\,dx = [x^2+x]_0^3 Apply FTC Part 2: ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a). = (3^2 + 3) - (0^2 + 0) = (9+3) - 0 = 12 Evaluate F at the upper limit (3) and subtract F at the lower limit (0). \text{Matches the geometric trapezoid calculation: } \frac{1}{2}(1+7)(3) = 12 \checkmark Confirmed: FTC Part 2 gives the same answer as the trapezoidal area computed geometrically in Lesson 2. ∫₀^π cos(x) dx = 0: Geometric and Algebraic \text{Compute } \int_0^{\pi} \cos(x)\,dx \text{ and interpret geometrically.}   ∫₀^π cos(x) dx = 0. The cosine function has equal positive and negative areas on [0, π], which cancel. This is a consequence of symmetry: cos(π−x) = −cos(x), so the second half mirrors the first half with opposite sign. \int_0^{\pi} \cos(x)\,dx = [\sin(x)]_0^{\pi} Antiderivative of cos(x) is sin(x). = \sin(\pi) - \sin(0) = 0 - 0 = 0 sin(π) = 0 and sin(0) = 0. \text{Geometric interpretation: cos is positive on } [0,\pi/2] \text{ and negative on } [\pi/2,\pi]. The positive area above the x-axis on [0,π/2] equals the negative area below on [π/2,π]. They cancel exactly. \int_0^{\pi/2}\cos(x)\,dx = [\sin x]_0^{\pi/2} = 1 \quad \int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\cos(x)\,dx = [\sin x]_{\pi/2}^{\pi} = -1 Each half contributes ±1. Total = 1+(−1) = 0. ∫₁ᵉ (1/x) dx and the Natural Logarithm \text{Compute } \int_1^e \frac{1}{x}\,dx.   ∫₁ᵉ(1/x)dx = 1. This is actually the most elegant way to define the natural logarithm: ln(x) = ∫₁ˣ (1/t) dt. The number e is then defined as the value where this integral equals 1. The logarithm defined by an integral has all the expected properties (ln(ab)=ln(a)+ln(b), etc.) which follow from properties of integrals. \int_1^e \frac{1}{x}\,dx = [\ln|x|]_1^e The antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|. On [1,e], x > 0 so |x| = x. = \ln(e) - \ln(1) = 1 - 0 = 1 ln(e) = 1 (by definition of e). ln(1) = 0 (since e⁰ = 1). \int_1^e \frac{1}{x}\,dx = 1 The area under y=1/x from x=1 to x=e is exactly 1. ∫₀¹ eˣ dx \text{Compute } \int_0^1 e^x\,dx.   ∫₀¹ eˣ dx = e − 1 ≈ 1.718. The area under y = eˣ from 0 to 1 is e − 1. This exact result from FTC contrasts dramatically with what would be required from Riemann sums. \int_0^1 e^x\,dx = [e^x]_0^1 The antiderivative of eˣ is eˣ itself — the exponential function is its own antiderivative. = e^1 - e^0 = e - 1 \approx 1.718 Evaluate: e¹ = e ≈ 2.718, e⁰ = 1. Displacement and Distance for a Velocity with Sign Change \text{A particle moves with } v(t) = 3t^2 - 6t \text{ m/s. Find displacement and total distance over } [0, 3].   Displacement = 0 m; total distance = 8 m. The particle travels 4 m in the negative direction (t∈[0,2]) then 4 m in the positive direction (t∈[2,3]), returning to its start. Always split the integral at velocity sign changes when computing distance. \text{Displacement} = \int_0^3 (3t^2-6t)\,dt = [t^3-3t^2]_0^3 Displacement = ∫v dt. Antiderivative of 3t²−6t is t³−3t². = (27-27) - (0-0) = 0 F(3) = 27−27 = 0. F(0) = 0. Displacement = 0 − 0 = 0. v(t) = 3t^2 - 6t = 3t(t-2) = 0 \Rightarrow t = 0 \text{ or } t = 2 Find when v changes sign. v < 0 on (0,2) (particle moves backward), v > 0 on (2,3) (moves forward). \text{Distance} = \int_0^2 |v|\,dt + \int_2^3 |v|\,dt = \int_0^2 (6t-3t^2)\,dt + \int_2^3 (3t^2-6t)\,dt On [0,2], v < 0 so |v| = −v = 6t−3t². On [2,3], v > 0 so |v| = v. \int_0^2(6t-3t^2)\,dt = [3t^2-t^3]_0^2 = (12-8)-0 = 4 First piece: antiderivative is 3t²−t³. Evaluate from 0 to 2. \int_2^3(3t^2-6t)\,dt = [t^3-3t^2]_2^3 = (27-27)-(8-12) = 0-(-4) = 4 Second piece. Evaluate from 2 to 3. \text{Total distance} = 4 + 4 = 8 \text{ m} The particle moved 4 m backward then 4 m forward, ending where it started (displacement = 0) but traveling 8 m total. Spotting the FTC Error: The Discontinuous Integrand \text{What is wrong with the calculation } \int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_{-1}^{1} = -1 - 1 = -2?   The calculation is invalid because 1/x² has a vertical asymptote at x=0 inside the interval [−1,1]. FTC Part 2 requires continuity on the entire closed interval. The true "integral" diverges to +∞ (not −2). This is one of the most important errors to avoid in calculus. f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2} > 0 \text{ everywhere it is defined.} 1/x² is positive wherever it exists. A positive function cannot have a negative integral. The answer −2 is immediately suspicious. f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2} \text{ is not defined at } x = 0 \in [-1,1]. The integrand has a vertical asymptote at x=0, which lies inside the integration interval [−1,1]. \text{FTC Part 2 requires } f \text{ to be continuous on } [a,b]. \text{ Here } f \text{ is discontinuous at } x=0 \in [-1,1]. The hypothesis of FTC Part 2 is violated. The theorem does not apply. \int_0^1 \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \lim_{t \to 0^+}\int_t^1 \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \lim_{t \to 0^+}\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_t^1 = \lim_{t \to 0^+}\left(-1+\frac{1}{t}\right) = +\infty The integral diverges as the lower limit approaches 0. The integral ∫₋₁¹ 1/x² dx does not exist.  Evaluate: (a) ∫₁⁴ (3√x − 2/x) dx. (b) ∫₀^(π/2) (sin x + cos x) dx. For (a): rewrite √x = x^(1/2), antiderivative is (2/3)x^(3/2) for x^(1/2) and ln|x| for 1/x. For (b): antiderivative of sin is −cos, of cos is sin. \text{(a) } 14 - 4\ln 2 \approx 11.23 \qquad \text{(b) } 2  \text{(a) } \int_1^4 \left(3x^{1/2} - \frac{2}{x}\right)dx = \left[3 \cdot \frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} - 2\ln|x|\right]_1^4 = \left[2x^{3/2} - 2\ln x\right]_1^4 Antiderivatives: ∫x^(1/2)dx = x^(3/2)/(3/2) = (2/3)x^(3/2); 3×(2/3)=2. ∫(1/x)dx = ln|x|; x > 0 on [1,4]. = (2(8) - 2\ln 4) - (2(1) - 2\ln 1) = (16 - 2\ln 4) - (2 - 0) = 14 - 2\ln 4 = 14 - 4\ln 2 4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 8. ln(1) = 0. Simplify 2ln(4) = 2ln(2²) = 4ln(2). \text{(b) } \int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin x + \cos x)\,dx = [-\cos x + \sin x]_0^{\pi/2} Antiderivative of sin is −cos; antiderivative of cos is sin. = (-\cos(\pi/2)+\sin(\pi/2)) - (-\cos(0)+\sin(0)) = (0+1) - (-1+0) = 1+1 = 2 cos(π/2)=0, sin(π/2)=1, cos(0)=1, sin(0)=0.  Find d/dx[∫_{x}^{x²} cos(t³) dt]. Use both the chain rule version of FTC Part 1 and the interval additivity property to handle both a variable lower and upper limit. Write ∫ₓ^(x²) cos(t³)dt = ∫ₐ^(x²) cos(t³)dt − ∫ₐˣ cos(t³)dt for any constant a. Differentiate each piece using FTC Part 1 with the chain rule. \dfrac{d}{dx}\int_x^{x^2}\cos(t^3)\,dt = 2x\cos(x^6) - \cos(x^3)  \int_x^{x^2} \cos(t^3)\,dt = \int_a^{x^2} \cos(t^3)\,dt - \int_a^x \cos(t^3)\,dt Split using additivity: ∫ₓ^(x²) = ∫ₐ^(x²) − ∫ₐˣ, for any constant a (e.g., a=0). \frac{d}{dx}\int_a^{x^2}\cos(t^3)\,dt = \cos((x^2)^3) \cdot 2x = \cos(x^6)\cdot 2x FTC Part 1 with chain rule: upper limit is g(x)=x², so derivative is cos(g(x)³)·g'(x) = cos(x⁶)·2x. \frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x \cos(t^3)\,dt = \cos(x^3) FTC Part 1 directly (upper limit is x). \frac{d}{dx}\int_x^{x^2}\cos(t^3)\,dt = 2x\cos(x^6) - \cos(x^3) Subtract the two derivatives.  Prove FTC Part 2 from Part 1, filling in every logical step. In particular: (a) show (A − F)' = 0 using the MVT, (b) conclude A − F = constant, (c) determine the constant, (d) derive ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a). A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f. Use Part 1: A' = f. Given F' = f. Define H = A − F. Show H' = 0. Apply the MVT corollary. Evaluate at x=a to find the constant. \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a). \text{ Proved from FTC Part 1 + the MVT corollary.}  A(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt. \text{ By FTC Part 1: } A'(x) = f(x). Hypothesis: f continuous. Part 1 guarantees A is differentiable and A' = f. H(x) = A(x) - F(x). \quad H'(x) = A'(x) - F'(x) = f(x) - f(x) = 0 Define H. Differentiate: H' = A' − F' = f − f = 0. \text{Since } H'(x) = 0 \text{ on } (a,b) \text{ and } H \text{ is continuous on } [a,b]: H \text{ is constant.} MVT corollary: if H' = 0 on an interval, H is constant. (Proof: for any x₁,x₂, MVT gives H(x₂)−H(x₁) = H'(c)(x₂−x₁) = 0, so H(x₁)=H(x₂).) H(a) = A(a) - F(a) = 0 - F(a) = -F(a) Evaluate at x=a: A(a) = ∫ₐᵃ f = 0. So the constant equals −F(a). A(x) - F(x) = -F(a) \Rightarrow A(x) = F(x) - F(a) Rearrange: A(x) = F(x) − F(a) for all x ∈ [a,b]. A(b) = F(b) - F(a) \Rightarrow \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a). \quad \square Set x = b. The definite integral equals the antiderivative evaluated at the endpoints. QED.  A particle has velocity v(t) = t² − 4t + 3 m/s for t ∈ [0, 4]. (a) Find all times when the particle changes direction. (b) Compute the total displacement over [0, 4]. (c) Compute the total distance traveled over [0, 4]. Factor v(t): v = (t−1)(t−3). Zeros at t=1 and t=3. v > 0 on [0,1] and [3,4]; v < 0 on [1,3]. Displacement = ∫₀⁴ v. Distance = ∫₀¹ v + |∫₁³ v| + ∫₃⁴ v. \text{Displacement} = \frac{4}{3} \text{ m}; \quad \text{Distance} = 4 \text{ m}.  v(t) = t^2-4t+3 = (t-1)(t-3). \text{ Zeros at } t=1,3. Factor. v > 0 on [0,1] and (3,4]; v < 0 on (1,3). \text{Displacement} = \int_0^4(t^2-4t+3)\,dt = \left[\frac{t^3}{3}-2t^2+3t\right]_0^4 Antiderivative: t³/3 − 2t² + 3t. = \left(\frac{64}{3}-32+12\right) - 0 = \frac{64}{3} - 20 = \frac{64-60}{3} = \frac{4}{3} \text{ m} 64/3 − 32 + 12 = 64/3 − 20 = 4/3. \int_0^1(t^2-4t+3)\,dt = \left[\frac{t^3}{3}-2t^2+3t\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3}-2+3 = \frac{4}{3} Piece on [0,1]: v ≥ 0. \int_1^3(t^2-4t+3)\,dt = \left[\frac{t^3}{3}-2t^2+3t\right]_1^3 = (9-18+9)-(\frac{1}{3}-2+3) = 0-\frac{4}{3} = -\frac{4}{3} Piece on [1,3]: v ≤ 0. The integral is negative. \int_3^4(t^2-4t+3)\,dt = \left[\frac{t^3}{3}-2t^2+3t\right]_3^4 = (\frac{64}{3}-32+12)-(9-18+9) = \frac{4}{3}-0 = \frac{4}{3} Piece on [3,4]: v ≥ 0. \text{Distance} = \frac{4}{3} + \frac{4}{3} + \frac{4}{3} = 4 \text{ m} Total distance = sum of |pieces| = 4/3 + 4/3 + 4/3 = 4 m.
documents.proofs: The proof of FTC Part 1 relies critically on two ingredients: the continuity of f (used in the MVT for integrals and in the passage to the limit f(c_h) → f(x)) and the fact that A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt is well-defined, which requires f to be integrable on [a, x] for each x ∈ [a, b]. Both conditions are guaranteed by f being continuous on [a, b]. If f is merely integrable but not continuous, A is still defined and still satisfies A(x₀)→A(x) as x₀→x (A is continuous), but A may fail to be differentiable at points where f is discontinuous. The derivative A'(x) = f(x) holds at every point of continuity of f. The key step in the proof — that (1/h)∫ₓˣ⁺ʰ f(t) dt → f(x) — deserves a fully explicit argument. For any ε > 0, by continuity of f at x, there exists δ > 0 such that |f(t) − f(x)| < ε whenever |t − x| < δ. For |h| < δ, every t ∈ [x, x+h] satisfies |t − x| ≤ |h| < δ, so |f(t) − f(x)| < ε. Therefore |(1/h)∫ₓˣ⁺ʰ f(t) dt − f(x)| = |(1/h)∫ₓˣ⁺ʰ [f(t)−f(x)] dt| ≤ (1/|h|)∫ₓˣ⁺ʰ ε|dt| = ε. Since ε was arbitrary, the limit equals f(x). This argument works for both positive and negative h. FTC Part 2 follows immediately from Part 1 and the Mean Value Theorem. Since A'(x) = f(x) and F'(x) = f(x), the function (A - F) has a zero derivative and must be a constant C. By checking the boundary at x=a, where A(a) = 0, we find C = -F(a). Thus A(b) = F(b) - F(a), which is the evaluation formula we use every day. A Function with Zero Derivative Is Constant (Connected Domain) If \(H'(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in (a,b)\), then \(H(x) = C\) (constant) on \((a,b)\). Proof: for any \(x_1, x_2 \in (a,b)\), the MVT gives \(H(x_2)-H(x_1) = H'(c)(x_2-x_1) = 0\). So \(H(x_1)=H(x_2)\) for all pairs — \(H\) is constant. FTC Requires Continuity on the Entire Interval The integral \(\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx\) appears to equal \([-1/x]_{-1}^{1} = -1-1=-2\). This is wrong. \(1/x^2\) is not defined at \(x=0\), which is inside \([-1,1]\). The function is not continuous on the interval, FTC Part 2 does not apply, and the integral does not exist (it diverges to \(+\infty\) as an improper integral). Always check for singularities before applying FTC Part 2.
documents.applications: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus is the reason calculus is computable. Without it, every integral would require evaluating a limit of Riemann sums — a process that, for most functions, cannot be completed in closed form. With it, any function whose antiderivative can be found algebraically can be integrated in seconds. The theorem was independently discovered by Isaac Newton (who called it the "method of fluxions") and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (who developed the ∫ and dx/dy notation still used today). Their parallel discovery in the 1660s–1680s, and the subsequent priority dispute, represent one of the most consequential — and contentious — episodes in the history of science. The theorem underlies every area, volume, center-of-mass, work, probability, and differential equation calculation in engineering and physics. Newton, Leibniz, and the Priority Dispute Isaac Newton developed the FTC around 1666 but did not publish it until 1687 (in Principia Mathematica). Gottfried Leibniz independently developed the same result around 1675–1676 and published it in 1684. Leibniz's notation — ∫ for integral, dx for differential — was adopted universally; Newton's "fluxion" notation (ẋ for derivative) is used only in mechanics today. The resulting dispute over who discovered calculus first split European mathematics into British and Continental camps for a century and retarded mathematical progress in England, which loyally used Newton's inferior notation long after the Continent had moved on with Leibniz's more flexible system. The historical lesson: good notation matters enormously. You Already Knew This Physically Position x(t) is the antiderivative of velocity v(t): v = dx/dt means x(t) = ∫v dt + x(0). You have used this in kinematics for years. The FTC is the formal theorem behind this: integrating the rate of change (v) gives back the quantity (x). The notation ∫₀ᵀ v(t) dt = x(T) − x(0) is precisely FTC Part 2 applied to the position-velocity relationship. Every kinematics calculation you have done was an application of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Discontinuity Invalidates the FTC FTC Part 2 requires that f be continuous on [a, b] — specifically, that f has no vertical asymptotes or jump discontinuities in the interval of integration. A famous "error" is ∫₋₁¹ (1/x) dx = [ln|x|]₋₁¹ = ln(1) − ln(1) = 0. This is WRONG. The function 1/x is not defined (let alone continuous) at x = 0, and the integral does not exist as an ordinary Riemann integral. The formula is not valid. Whenever a potential singularity exists inside [a, b], you must check continuity before applying FTC Part 2. d/dx[∫₀^(x²) f(t) dt] ≠ f(x²) — Don't Forget the Chain Rule! When differentiating ∫₀^(g(x)) f(t) dt, you MUST include the chain rule factor g'(x): the answer is f(g(x))·g'(x), not just f(g(x)). For d/dx[∫₀^(x²) sin(t) dt]: CORRECT = sin(x²)·2x. WRONG = sin(x²). The 2x factor from differentiating x² is essential. This is the #1 error students make with FTC Part 1.

Define A(x) = ∫₀ˣ t² dt — the area under the parabola from 0 to x. A(x) is a function of x. What is A'(x)? Without computing anything, make a guess. Then think: if A(x) is the "accumulated area so far," what happens to A when x increases by a tiny amount dx? How much new area is added? The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus is the reason calculus is computable. Without it, every integral would require evaluating a limit of Riemann sums — a process that, for most functions, cannot be completed in closed form. With it, any function whose antiderivative can be found algebraically can be integrated in seconds. The theorem was independently discovered by Isaac Newton (who called it the "method of fluxions") and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (who developed the ∫ and dx/dy notation still used today). Their parallel discovery in the 1660s–1680s, and the subsequent priority dispute, represent one of the most consequential — and contentious — episodes in the history of science. The theorem underlies every area, volume, center-of-mass, work, probability, and differential equation calculation in engineering and physics. The Fundamental Theorem has two parts, and both parts are surprising. Part 1 says: if you define A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt (the accumulated area from a to x), then A is differentiable and A'(x) = f(x). The derivative of the accumulated area is the original function. Differentiation undoes integration. Part 2 says: if F is any antiderivative of f (meaning F' = f), then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). To compute the area under f from a to b, find any antiderivative of f and subtract its values at the endpoints. Integration undoes differentiation (up to a constant). Part 1 can be understood physically. Imagine driving a car and tracking position A(x) at every moment. Your speedometer reads f(x) — the instantaneous rate of change of accumulated position. Part 1 says: if you know the accumulated position A(x), its derivative A'(x) is exactly your current speed f(x). The rate at which the "area counter" advances is equal to the height of the function at that exact moment. This is compelling: adding a thin strip of width dx and height f(x) to the accumulated area increases A by approximately f(x)·dx, so ΔA/Δx ≈ f(x), and in the limit A'(x) = f(x). Part 2 follows from Part 1 by a beautiful algebraic argument. Suppose F is any antiderivative of f, so F' = f. We also know A'= f where A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t)dt. So A' = F' on [a, b], which means A − F is a function with zero derivative — and by the Mean Value Theorem, A(x) − F(x) = constant. Call it C. Evaluate at x = a: A(a) − F(a) = C. But A(a) = ∫ₐᵃ f = 0. So C = −F(a), giving A(x) = F(x) − F(a) for all x. At x = b: ∫ₐᵇ f(t)dt = A(b) = F(b) − F(a). This derivation is the logical core of FTC Part 2. The notation F(b) − F(a) is so common it has its own shorthand: [F(x)]ₐᵇ, read "F of x evaluated from a to b." The calculation ∫₀³ x² dx = [x³/3]₀³ = 27/3 − 0/3 = 9 is a typical application: find the antiderivative (x³/3), evaluate at the upper limit (3³/3 = 9), subtract the value at the lower limit (0³/3 = 0). Result: 9. What would have taken a pages-long Riemann sum calculation is now three lines of algebra. Part 1 also has a chain rule version for when the upper limit of integration is a function of x rather than x itself. If g is differentiable, then d/dx[∫ₐ^(g(x)) f(t) dt] = f(g(x))·g'(x). This is FTC Part 1 composed with the chain rule: the outer derivative is f(g(x)) (the function evaluated at the upper limit), and g'(x) comes from the chain rule. For example, d/dx[∫₀^(x²) sin(t) dt] = sin(x²)·2x. This generalization appears constantly in differential equations and in the Leibniz integral rule. The historical importance of the FTC cannot be overstated. Before Newton and Leibniz, computing areas, volumes, and arc lengths required ad-hoc geometric arguments — brilliant but non-systematic. After the FTC, the problem of computing any definite integral was reduced to the problem of finding an antiderivative: a systematic algebraic task. The next century saw an explosion of mathematical physics, as Newton's laws of motion combined with the FTC to produce exact predictions for planetary orbits, projectile trajectories, wave propagation, and eventually Maxwell's equations of electromagnetism. Every model of physical reality that uses differential equations ultimately relies on the FTC. Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1: let f be continuous on [a, b], and define the accumulation function A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt for x ∈ [a, b]. Then A is differentiable on (a, b) and A'(x) = f(x). Proof: A'(x) = lim_{h→0} [A(x+h) − A(x)]/h = lim_{h→0} (1/h) ∫ₓˣ⁺ʰ f(t) dt. By the MVT for integrals, (1/h) ∫ₓˣ⁺ʰ f(t) dt = f(c_h) for some c_h between x and x+h. As h → 0, c_h → x, and by continuity of f, f(c_h) → f(x). Therefore A'(x) = f(x). ∎ Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2 (Evaluation Theorem): let f be continuous on [a, b] and let F be any antiderivative of f (F' = f). Then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). Proof: let A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt. By Part 1, A' = f. Also F' = f. So (A − F)' = 0 on (a, b). By Corollary to the MVT: A(x) − F(x) = C for some constant C. Evaluate at x = a: 0 − F(a) = C, so C = −F(a). Therefore A(x) = F(x) − F(a). At x = b: ∫ₐᵇ f = A(b) = F(b) − F(a). ∎ The Chain Rule version of FTC Part 1: if g is differentiable and f is continuous, then d/dx[∫ₐ^(g(x)) f(t) dt] = f(g(x))·g'(x). This follows from writing the integral as A(g(x)) where A(u) = ∫ₐᵘ f(t) dt, and applying the chain rule: d/dx[A(g(x))] = A'(g(x))·g'(x) = f(g(x))·g'(x). The lower limit can also depend on x: d/dx[∫_{h(x)}^{g(x)} f(t) dt] = f(g(x))·g'(x) − f(h(x))·h'(x). The notation [F(x)]ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a) is standard. An antiderivative F of f is sometimes called an "indefinite integral" and written ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C, where C is an arbitrary constant. The "+C" is essential: every antiderivative differs from every other by a constant, because if F' = f and G' = f, then (G − F)' = 0 so G − F = C. When applying FTC Part 2, any choice of C works because it cancels: (F(b)+C) − (F(a)+C) = F(b) − F(a). The proof of FTC Part 1 relies critically on two ingredients: the continuity of f (used in the MVT for integrals and in the passage to the limit f(c_h) → f(x)) and the fact that A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt is well-defined, which requires f to be integrable on [a, x] for each x ∈ [a, b]. Both conditions are guaranteed by f being continuous on [a, b]. If f is merely integrable but not continuous, A is still defined and still satisfies A(x₀)→A(x) as x₀→x (A is continuous), but A may fail to be differentiable at points where f is discontinuous. The derivative A'(x) = f(x) holds at every point of continuity of f. The key step in the proof — that (1/h)∫ₓˣ⁺ʰ f(t) dt → f(x) — deserves a fully explicit argument. For any ε > 0, by continuity of f at x, there exists δ > 0 such that |f(t) − f(x)| < ε whenever |t − x| < δ. For |h| < δ, every t ∈ [x, x+h] satisfies |t − x| ≤ |h| < δ, so |f(t) − f(x)| < ε. Therefore |(1/h)∫ₓˣ⁺ʰ f(t) dt − f(x)| = |(1/h)∫ₓˣ⁺ʰ [f(t)−f(x)] dt| ≤ (1/|h|)∫ₓˣ⁺ʰ ε|dt| = ε. Since ε was arbitrary, the limit equals f(x). This argument works for both positive and negative h. FTC Part 2 follows immediately from Part 1 and the Mean Value Theorem. Since A'(x) = f(x) and F'(x) = f(x), the function (A - F) has a zero derivative and must be a constant C. By checking the boundary at x=a, where A(a) = 0, we find C = -F(a). Thus A(b) = F(b) - F(a), which is the evaluation formula we use every day. A Function with Zero Derivative Is Constant (Connected Domain) If \(H'(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in (a,b)\), then \(H(x) = C\) (constant) on \((a,b)\). Proof: for any \(x_1, x_2 \in (a,b)\), the MVT gives \(H(x_2)-H(x_1) = H'(c)(x_2-x_1) = 0\). So \(H(x_1)=H(x_2)\) for all pairs — \(H\) is constant. FTC Requires Continuity on the Entire Interval The integral \(\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx\) appears to equal \([-1/x]_{-1}^{1} = -1-1=-2\). This is wrong. \(1/x^2\) is not defined at \(x=0\), which is inside \([-1,1]\). The function is not continuous on the interval, FTC Part 2 does not apply, and the integral does not exist (it diverges to \(+\infty\) as an improper integral). Always check for singularities before applying FTC Part 2. Newton, Leibniz, and the Priority Dispute Isaac Newton developed the FTC around 1666 but did not publish it until 1687 (in Principia Mathematica). Gottfried Leibniz independently developed the same result around 1675–1676 and published it in 1684. Leibniz's notation — ∫ for integral, dx for differential — was adopted universally; Newton's "fluxion" notation (ẋ for derivative) is used only in mechanics today. The resulting dispute over who discovered calculus first split European mathematics into British and Continental camps for a century and retarded mathematical progress in England, which loyally used Newton's inferior notation long after the Continent had moved on with Leibniz's more flexible system. The historical lesson: good notation matters enormously. You Already Knew This Physically Position x(t) is the antiderivative of velocity v(t): v = dx/dt means x(t) = ∫v dt + x(0). You have used this in kinematics for years. The FTC is the formal theorem behind this: integrating the rate of change (v) gives back the quantity (x). The notation ∫₀ᵀ v(t) dt = x(T) − x(0) is precisely FTC Part 2 applied to the position-velocity relationship. Every kinematics calculation you have done was an application of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Discontinuity Invalidates the FTC FTC Part 2 requires that f be continuous on [a, b] — specifically, that f has no vertical asymptotes or jump discontinuities in the interval of integration. A famous "error" is ∫₋₁¹ (1/x) dx = [ln|x|]₋₁¹ = ln(1) − ln(1) = 0. This is WRONG. The function 1/x is not defined (let alone continuous) at x = 0, and the integral does not exist as an ordinary Riemann integral. The formula is not valid. Whenever a potential singularity exists inside [a, b], you must check continuity before applying FTC Part 2. d/dx[∫₀^(x²) f(t) dt] ≠ f(x²) — Don't Forget the Chain Rule! When differentiating ∫₀^(g(x)) f(t) dt, you MUST include the chain rule factor g'(x): the answer is f(g(x))·g'(x), not just f(g(x)). For d/dx[∫₀^(x²) sin(t) dt]: CORRECT = sin(x²)·2x. WRONG = sin(x²). The 2x factor from differentiating x² is essential. This is the #1 error students make with FTC Part 1. Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1 If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(A(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt\), then \(A\) is differentiable and
\[A'(x) = f(x).\]
The accumulation function's derivative is the original integrand. Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2 If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(F' = f\), then
\[\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a) = \bigl[F(x)\bigr]_a^b.\]
To integrate \(f\), find any antiderivative \(F\) and subtract endpoint values. Chain Rule Form of FTC Part 1 If \(f\) is continuous and \(g\) is differentiable:
\[\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^{g(x)} f(t)\,dt = f(g(x))\cdot g'(x).\]
More generally:
\[\frac{d}{dx}\int_{h(x)}^{g(x)} f(t)\,dt = f(g(x))\,g'(x) - f(h(x))\,h'(x).\] The Accumulation Function A(x) and its Derivative The left panel shows f(t) with the accumulated area A(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt shaded. The right panel shows A(x) as a function of x. Drag the slider to change x and observe: A increases when f > 0, decreases when f < 0, and has a horizontal tangent when f = 0. The slope of A(x) at each x is exactly f(x) — FTC Part 1. Masterclass: The Mathematical Bridge A step-by-step masterclass peeling away the abstract math of the FTC Part 1 derivative proof. FTC Part 1: Differentiating an Integral \text{Find } \frac{d}{dx}\int_0^x \sin(t^2)\,dt. d/dx[∫₀ˣ sin(t²)dt] = sin(x²). FTC Part 1 applies even when the integrand has no elementary antiderivative. The theorem differentiates any continuous function — it does not require that an antiderivative be expressible in closed form. \text{Let } A(x) = \int_0^x \sin(t^2)\,dt Identify the accumulation function. The integrand is f(t) = sin(t²), which is continuous everywhere. \text{By FTC Part 1: } A'(x) = f(x) = \sin(x^2) Apply FTC Part 1 directly: the derivative of the accumulation function equals the integrand evaluated at the upper limit. \frac{d}{dx}\int_0^x \sin(t^2)\,dt = \sin(x^2) Final answer. Note: sin(t²) has no elementary antiderivative — without FTC Part 1, we could not differentiate this integral at all. Chain Rule + FTC Part 1 \text{Find } \frac{d}{dx}\int_3^{x^2} e^t\,dt. d/dx[∫₃^(x²) eᵗ dt] = 2xe^(x²). The chain rule contribution 2x comes from the x² upper limit. Without the chain rule, you would incorrectly get just e^(x²). Always differentiate the upper limit and multiply. \text{Let } u = x^2. \text{ Define } A(u) = \int_3^u e^t\,dt. The upper limit is g(x) = x², not x itself. Use the chain rule: d/dx[A(g(x))] = A'(g(x))·g'(x). A'(u) = e^u \quad \text{(FTC Part 1)} The derivative of the accumulation function with respect to its upper limit is the integrand evaluated at the upper limit. \frac{d}{dx}\int_3^{x^2} e^t\,dt = A'(x^2) \cdot \frac{d}{dx}[x^2] = e^{x^2} \cdot 2x Chain rule: A'(g(x))·g'(x) = e^(x²)·2x. = 2x\,e^{x^2} Final answer. FTC Part 2: Evaluating ∫₀³ (2x+1) dx \text{Compute } \int_0^3 (2x+1)\,dx \text{ using FTC Part 2. Check against the geometric answer from Lesson 2.} ∫₀³(2x+1)dx = 12. FTC Part 2 confirms the geometric calculation. This integral is simple enough to verify geometrically, which builds confidence in the algebraic method. \text{Find an antiderivative: } F(x) = x^2 + x F'(x) = 2x+1 ✓. We need any antiderivative — C=0 is the simplest choice. \int_0^3 (2x+1)\,dx = [x^2+x]_0^3 Apply FTC Part 2: ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a). = (3^2 + 3) - (0^2 + 0) = (9+3) - 0 = 12 Evaluate F at the upper limit (3) and subtract F at the lower limit (0). \text{Matches the geometric trapezoid calculation: } \frac{1}{2}(1+7)(3) = 12 \checkmark Confirmed: FTC Part 2 gives the same answer as the trapezoidal area computed geometrically in Lesson 2. ∫₀^π cos(x) dx = 0: Geometric and Algebraic \text{Compute } \int_0^{\pi} \cos(x)\,dx \text{ and interpret geometrically.} ∫₀^π cos(x) dx = 0. The cosine function has equal positive and negative areas on [0, π], which cancel. This is a consequence of symmetry: cos(π−x) = −cos(x), so the second half mirrors the first half with opposite sign. \int_0^{\pi} \cos(x)\,dx = [\sin(x)]_0^{\pi} Antiderivative of cos(x) is sin(x). = \sin(\pi) - \sin(0) = 0 - 0 = 0 sin(π) = 0 and sin(0) = 0. \text{Geometric interpretation: cos is positive on } [0,\pi/2] \text{ and negative on } [\pi/2,\pi]. The positive area above the x-axis on [0,π/2] equals the negative area below on [π/2,π]. They cancel exactly. \int_0^{\pi/2}\cos(x)\,dx = [\sin x]_0^{\pi/2} = 1 \quad \int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\cos(x)\,dx = [\sin x]_{\pi/2}^{\pi} = -1 Each half contributes ±1. Total = 1+(−1) = 0. ∫₁ᵉ (1/x) dx and the Natural Logarithm \text{Compute } \int_1^e \frac{1}{x}\,dx. ∫₁ᵉ(1/x)dx = 1. This is actually the most elegant way to define the natural logarithm: ln(x) = ∫₁ˣ (1/t) dt. The number e is then defined as the value where this integral equals 1. The logarithm defined by an integral has all the expected properties (ln(ab)=ln(a)+ln(b), etc.) which follow from properties of integrals. \int_1^e \frac{1}{x}\,dx = [\ln|x|]_1^e The antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|. On [1,e], x > 0 so |x| = x. = \ln(e) - \ln(1) = 1 - 0 = 1 ln(e) = 1 (by definition of e). ln(1) = 0 (since e⁰ = 1). \int_1^e \frac{1}{x}\,dx = 1 The area under y=1/x from x=1 to x=e is exactly 1. ∫₀¹ eˣ dx \text{Compute } \int_0^1 e^x\,dx. ∫₀¹ eˣ dx = e − 1 ≈ 1.718. The area under y = eˣ from 0 to 1 is e − 1. This exact result from FTC contrasts dramatically with what would be required from Riemann sums. \int_0^1 e^x\,dx = [e^x]_0^1 The antiderivative of eˣ is eˣ itself — the exponential function is its own antiderivative. = e^1 - e^0 = e - 1 \approx 1.718 Evaluate: e¹ = e ≈ 2.718, e⁰ = 1. Displacement and Distance for a Velocity with Sign Change \text{A particle moves with } v(t) = 3t^2 - 6t \text{ m/s. Find displacement and total distance over } [0, 3]. Displacement = 0 m; total distance = 8 m. The particle travels 4 m in the negative direction (t∈[0,2]) then 4 m in the positive direction (t∈[2,3]), returning to its start. Always split the integral at velocity sign changes when computing distance. \text{Displacement} = \int_0^3 (3t^2-6t)\,dt = [t^3-3t^2]_0^3 Displacement = ∫v dt. Antiderivative of 3t²−6t is t³−3t². = (27-27) - (0-0) = 0 F(3) = 27−27 = 0. F(0) = 0. Displacement = 0 − 0 = 0. v(t) = 3t^2 - 6t = 3t(t-2) = 0 \Rightarrow t = 0 \text{ or } t = 2 Find when v changes sign. v < 0 on (0,2) (particle moves backward), v > 0 on (2,3) (moves forward). \text{Distance} = \int_0^2 |v|\,dt + \int_2^3 |v|\,dt = \int_0^2 (6t-3t^2)\,dt + \int_2^3 (3t^2-6t)\,dt On [0,2], v < 0 so |v| = −v = 6t−3t². On [2,3], v > 0 so |v| = v. \int_0^2(6t-3t^2)\,dt = [3t^2-t^3]_0^2 = (12-8)-0 = 4 First piece: antiderivative is 3t²−t³. Evaluate from 0 to 2. \int_2^3(3t^2-6t)\,dt = [t^3-3t^2]_2^3 = (27-27)-(8-12) = 0-(-4) = 4 Second piece. Evaluate from 2 to 3. \text{Total distance} = 4 + 4 = 8 \text{ m} The particle moved 4 m backward then 4 m forward, ending where it started (displacement = 0) but traveling 8 m total. Spotting the FTC Error: The Discontinuous Integrand \text{What is wrong with the calculation } \int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_{-1}^{1} = -1 - 1 = -2? The calculation is invalid because 1/x² has a vertical asymptote at x=0 inside the interval [−1,1]. FTC Part 2 requires continuity on the entire closed interval. The true "integral" diverges to +∞ (not −2). This is one of the most important errors to avoid in calculus. f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2} > 0 \text{ everywhere it is defined.} 1/x² is positive wherever it exists. A positive function cannot have a negative integral. The answer −2 is immediately suspicious. f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2} \text{ is not defined at } x = 0 \in [-1,1]. The integrand has a vertical asymptote at x=0, which lies inside the integration interval [−1,1]. \text{FTC Part 2 requires } f \text{ to be continuous on } [a,b]. \text{ Here } f \text{ is discontinuous at } x=0 \in [-1,1]. The hypothesis of FTC Part 2 is violated. The theorem does not apply. \int_0^1 \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \lim_{t \to 0^+}\int_t^1 \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \lim_{t \to 0^+}\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_t^1 = \lim_{t \to 0^+}\left(-1+\frac{1}{t}\right) = +\infty The integral diverges as the lower limit approaches 0. The integral ∫₋₁¹ 1/x² dx does not exist. Evaluate: (a) ∫₁⁴ (3√x − 2/x) dx. (b) ∫₀^(π/2) (sin x + cos x) dx. For (a): rewrite √x = x^(1/2), antiderivative is (2/3)x^(3/2) for x^(1/2) and ln|x| for 1/x. For (b): antiderivative of sin is −cos, of cos is sin. \text{(a) } 14 - 4\ln 2 \approx 11.23 \qquad \text{(b) } 2 \text{(a) } \int_1^4 \left(3x^{1/2} - \frac{2}{x}\right)dx = \left[3 \cdot \frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} - 2\ln|x|\right]_1^4 = \left[2x^{3/2} - 2\ln x\right]_1^4 Antiderivatives: ∫x^(1/2)dx = x^(3/2)/(3/2) = (2/3)x^(3/2); 3×(2/3)=2. ∫(1/x)dx = ln|x|; x > 0 on [1,4]. = (2(8) - 2\ln 4) - (2(1) - 2\ln 1) = (16 - 2\ln 4) - (2 - 0) = 14 - 2\ln 4 = 14 - 4\ln 2 4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 8. ln(1) = 0. Simplify 2ln(4) = 2ln(2²) = 4ln(2). \text{(b) } \int_0^{\pi/2}(\sin x + \cos x)\,dx = [-\cos x + \sin x]_0^{\pi/2} Antiderivative of sin is −cos; antiderivative of cos is sin. = (-\cos(\pi/2)+\sin(\pi/2)) - (-\cos(0)+\sin(0)) = (0+1) - (-1+0) = 1+1 = 2 cos(π/2)=0, sin(π/2)=1, cos(0)=1, sin(0)=0. Find d/dx[∫_{x}^{x²} cos(t³) dt]. Use both the chain rule version of FTC Part 1 and the interval additivity property to handle both a variable lower and upper limit. Write ∫ₓ^(x²) cos(t³)dt = ∫ₐ^(x²) cos(t³)dt − ∫ₐˣ cos(t³)dt for any constant a. Differentiate each piece using FTC Part 1 with the chain rule. \dfrac{d}{dx}\int_x^{x^2}\cos(t^3)\,dt = 2x\cos(x^6) - \cos(x^3) \int_x^{x^2} \cos(t^3)\,dt = \int_a^{x^2} \cos(t^3)\,dt - \int_a^x \cos(t^3)\,dt Split using additivity: ∫ₓ^(x²) = ∫ₐ^(x²) − ∫ₐˣ, for any constant a (e.g., a=0). \frac{d}{dx}\int_a^{x^2}\cos(t^3)\,dt = \cos((x^2)^3) \cdot 2x = \cos(x^6)\cdot 2x FTC Part 1 with chain rule: upper limit is g(x)=x², so derivative is cos(g(x)³)·g'(x) = cos(x⁶)·2x. \frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x \cos(t^3)\,dt = \cos(x^3) FTC Part 1 directly (upper limit is x). \frac{d}{dx}\int_x^{x^2}\cos(t^3)\,dt = 2x\cos(x^6) - \cos(x^3) Subtract the two derivatives. Prove FTC Part 2 from Part 1, filling in every logical step. In particular: (a) show (A − F)' = 0 using the MVT, (b) conclude A − F = constant, (c) determine the constant, (d) derive ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a). A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f. Use Part 1: A' = f. Given F' = f. Define H = A − F. Show H' = 0. Apply the MVT corollary. Evaluate at x=a to find the constant. \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a). \text{ Proved from FTC Part 1 + the MVT corollary.} A(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt. \text{ By FTC Part 1: } A'(x) = f(x). Hypothesis: f continuous. Part 1 guarantees A is differentiable and A' = f. H(x) = A(x) - F(x). \quad H'(x) = A'(x) - F'(x) = f(x) - f(x) = 0 Define H. Differentiate: H' = A' − F' = f − f = 0. \text{Since } H'(x) = 0 \text{ on } (a,b) \text{ and } H \text{ is continuous on } [a,b]: H \text{ is constant.} MVT corollary: if H' = 0 on an interval, H is constant. (Proof: for any x₁,x₂, MVT gives H(x₂)−H(x₁) = H'(c)(x₂−x₁) = 0, so H(x₁)=H(x₂).) H(a) = A(a) - F(a) = 0 - F(a) = -F(a) Evaluate at x=a: A(a) = ∫ₐᵃ f = 0. So the constant equals −F(a). A(x) - F(x) = -F(a) \Rightarrow A(x) = F(x) - F(a) Rearrange: A(x) = F(x) − F(a) for all x ∈ [a,b]. A(b) = F(b) - F(a) \Rightarrow \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a). \quad \square Set x = b. The definite integral equals the antiderivative evaluated at the endpoints. QED. A particle has velocity v(t) = t² − 4t + 3 m/s for t ∈ [0, 4]. (a) Find all times when the particle changes direction. (b) Compute the total displacement over [0, 4]. (c) Compute the total distance traveled over [0, 4]. Factor v(t): v = (t−1)(t−3). Zeros at t=1 and t=3. v > 0 on [0,1] and [3,4]; v < 0 on [1,3]. Displacement = ∫₀⁴ v. Distance = ∫₀¹ v + |∫₁³ v| + ∫₃⁴ v. \text{Displacement} = \frac{4}{3} \text{ m}; \quad \text{Distance} = 4 \text{ m}. v(t) = t^2-4t+3 = (t-1)(t-3). \text{ Zeros at } t=1,3. Factor. v > 0 on [0,1] and (3,4]; v < 0 on (1,3). \text{Displacement} = \int_0^4(t^2-4t+3)\,dt = \left[\frac{t^3}{3}-2t^2+3t\right]_0^4 Antiderivative: t³/3 − 2t² + 3t. = \left(\frac{64}{3}-32+12\right) - 0 = \frac{64}{3} - 20 = \frac{64-60}{3} = \frac{4}{3} \text{ m} 64/3 − 32 + 12 = 64/3 − 20 = 4/3. \int_0^1(t^2-4t+3)\,dt = \left[\frac{t^3}{3}-2t^2+3t\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3}-2+3 = \frac{4}{3} Piece on [0,1]: v ≥ 0. \int_1^3(t^2-4t+3)\,dt = \left[\frac{t^3}{3}-2t^2+3t\right]_1^3 = (9-18+9)-(\frac{1}{3}-2+3) = 0-\frac{4}{3} = -\frac{4}{3} Piece on [1,3]: v ≤ 0. The integral is negative. \int_3^4(t^2-4t+3)\,dt = \left[\frac{t^3}{3}-2t^2+3t\right]_3^4 = (\frac{64}{3}-32+12)-(9-18+9) = \frac{4}{3}-0 = \frac{4}{3} Piece on [3,4]: v ≥ 0. \text{Distance} = \frac{4}{3} + \frac{4}{3} + \frac{4}{3} = 4 \text{ m} Total distance = sum of |pieces| = 4/3 + 4/3 + 4/3 = 4 m.
