Verify by differentiating: d/dx[(x²+1)⁶/6] = (x²+1)⁵ · 2x ✓ (chain rule). u = x^2 + 1 Choose u = the expression raised to the power 5. Its derivative 2x is already present in the integrand. du = 2x\,dx Differentiate u with respect to x. \int (x^2+1)^5 \cdot 2x\,dx = \int u^5\,du Substitute: (x²+1)⁵ = u⁵, and 2x dx = du. The entire integrand converts cleanly. = \frac{u^6}{6} + C Power rule in u: ∫uⁿ du = uⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C, with n=5. = \frac{(x^2+1)^6}{6} + C Back-substitute u = x²+1. Inserting a Missing Constant \text{Evaluate } \displaystyle\int x \cdot e^{x^2}\,dx. Answer: (1/2)e^(x²) + C. The "missing" factor of 2 in du = 2x dx is handled by dividing, which introduces the compensating factor 1/2. u = x^2 The exponent is the natural choice for u. du = 2x\,dx \implies x\,dx = \frac{du}{2} We have x dx in the integrand, but du = 2x dx. Solve for x dx. \int x \cdot e^{x^2}\,dx = \int e^u \cdot \frac{du}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\int e^u\,du Substitute: e^(x²) = eᵘ and x dx = du/2. Pull the constant 1/2 out front. = \frac{1}{2}e^u + C ∫eᵘ du = eᵘ + C. = \frac{1}{2}e^{x^2} + C Back-substitute u = x². Definite Integral — Changing Limits \text{Evaluate } \displaystyle\int_0^2 3x^2(x^3+1)^4\,dx. Answer: 59048/5 = 11809.6. Changing limits is the cleanest method for definite integrals — no back-substitution step at the end. u = x^3 + 1, \quad du = 3x^2\,dx u is the expression raised to the 4th power; 3x² dx = du is present exactly. \text{Change limits: } x=0 \Rightarrow u=0^3+1=1; \quad x=2 \Rightarrow u=2^3+1=9 Convert both limits using u = x³+1. \int_0^2 3x^2(x^3+1)^4\,dx = \int_1^9 u^4\,du Substitute. Notice the limits changed from [0,2] to [1,9]. = \left[\frac{u^5}{5}\right]_1^9 = \frac{9^5}{5} - \frac{1^5}{5} Evaluate the antiderivative at the new limits. = \frac{59049}{5} - \frac{1}{5} = \frac{59048}{5} = 11809.6 9⁵ = 59049. No back-substitution needed because we changed the limits. U-Sub with Trig — ∫sin(3x+2) dx \text{Evaluate } \displaystyle\int \sin(3x+2)\,dx. Answer: −(1/3)cos(3x+2) + C. General rule: ∫sin(ax+b) dx = −(1/a)cos(ax+b) + C. u = 3x+2, \quad du = 3\,dx \implies dx = \frac{du}{3} The argument of sine is the natural u. Its derivative is 3 (a constant). \int \sin(3x+2)\,dx = \int \sin(u) \cdot \frac{du}{3} = \frac{1}{3}\int \sin(u)\,du Substitute and pull the constant 1/3 out. = \frac{1}{3}(-\cos u) + C = -\frac{1}{3}\cos(3x+2) + C ∫sin(u)du = −cos(u). Back-substitute. Log Integral — ∫ f'/f dx \text{Evaluate } \displaystyle\int \frac{2x+3}{x^2+3x+7}\,dx. Answer: ln(x²+3x+7) + C. The pattern ∫ f'(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + C is one of the most important in integration — recognize the numerator as the derivative of the denominator. u = x^2 + 3x + 7 The denominator is u. Check: is the numerator a multiple of u'? du = (2x+3)\,dx The derivative of x²+3x+7 is 2x+3 — exactly the numerator! Perfect. \int \frac{2x+3}{x^2+3x+7}\,dx = \int \frac{du}{u} = \ln|u| + C The integrand is exactly du/u after substitution. = \ln|x^2+3x+7| + C Back-substitute. Since x²+3x+7 = (x+3/2)²+19/4 > 0 always, the absolute value is not needed here. Substitution with Algebra — ∫ x√(x+1) dx \text{Evaluate } \displaystyle\int x\sqrt{x+1}\,dx. Answer: (2/5)(x+1)^(5/2) − (2/3)(x+1)^(3/2) + C. When x appears separately from the composite, algebraically solve for x in terms of u to replace it. u = x+1 \implies x = u-1, \quad du = dx Let u = x+1 (the radicand). Crucially, solve for x: x = u−1. This lets us replace the remaining factor x. \int x\sqrt{x+1}\,dx = \int (u-1)\sqrt{u}\,du x = u−1, √(x+1) = √u, dx = du. All substituted. = \int (u-1)u^{1/2}\,du = \int (u^{3/2} - u^{1/2})\,du Distribute: (u−1)u^(1/2) = u^(3/2) − u^(1/2). = \frac{u^{5/2}}{5/2} - \frac{u^{3/2}}{3/2} + C = \frac{2}{5}u^{5/2} - \frac{2}{3}u^{3/2} + C Power rule: ∫uⁿ du = uⁿ⁺¹/(n+1). Here n=3/2 and n=1/2. = \frac{2}{5}(x+1)^{5/2} - \frac{2}{3}(x+1)^{3/2} + C Back-substitute u = x+1. Integral with Exponential — Area Under a Bell Curve Piece \text{Evaluate } \displaystyle\int_0^1 2x e^{-x^2}\,dx. \text{ (Part of the error function — core to probability and statistics.)} Answer: 1 − 1/e ≈ 0.6321. Note: the integrand 2xe^(−x²) is the Rayleigh distribution's PDF — it gives the probability that a Rayleigh-distributed distance (arising in 2D random walks and wireless signal strength) falls in [0,1]. The related error function erf(x) = (2/√π)∫₀ˣ e^(−t²) dt generalizes the idea to Gaussian integrals; both require substitution as their first step. u = -x^2, \quad du = -2x\,dx \implies 2x\,dx = -du Let u = −x². Its derivative −2x is almost the factor 2x present (off by a sign). \text{Limits: } x=0 \Rightarrow u=0; \quad x=1 \Rightarrow u=-1 Convert limits using u = −x². \int_0^1 2x e^{-x^2}\,dx = \int_0^{-1} e^u \cdot (-du) = \int_{-1}^0 e^u\,du Substitute: e^(−x²) = eᵘ, 2x dx = −du. Flip limits (negating the integral) to get ∫_{−1}^{0}. = [e^u]_{-1}^0 = e^0 - e^{-1} = 1 - \frac{1}{e} Evaluate. e⁰ = 1, e⁻¹ = 1/e. Evaluate ∫ cos(x)·sin²(x) dx. Let u = sin(x). What is du? \dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3} + C u = \sin x, \quad du = \cos x\,dx The derivative of sin is cos, which is already present. \int \cos x \cdot \sin^2 x\,dx = \int u^2\,du = \frac{u^3}{3} + C Substitute. cos(x) dx = du, sin²(x) = u². = \frac{\sin^3 x}{3} + C Back-substitute. Evaluate \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4} \tan x\,dx. (Recall \tan x = \sin x / \cos x.) Write tan x = sin(x)/cos(x). Let u = cos(x). \dfrac{\ln 2}{2} \approx 0.347 \int_0^{\pi/4} \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx Rewrite tan x. u = \cos x, \quad du = -\sin x\,dx \implies \sin x\,dx = -du The numerator sin x is (−1) times the derivative of cos x. \text{Limits: } x=0 \Rightarrow u=1; \quad x=\pi/4 \Rightarrow u=1/\sqrt{2} cos(0)=1, cos(π/4)=1/√2. \int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx = \int_1^{1/\sqrt{2}}\frac{-du}{u} = -[\ln|u|]_1^{1/\sqrt{2}} Substitute. = -(\ln(1/\sqrt{2}) - \ln 1) = -(-\tfrac{1}{2}\ln 2 - 0) = \frac{\ln 2}{2} ln(1/√2) = ln(2^(−1/2)) = −(1/2)ln 2. And ln(1) = 0. Evaluate \displaystyle\int \frac{e^x}{e^{2x}+1}\,dx. Let u = eˣ. What does the integrand become? You'll get ∫ 1/(u²+1) du. \arctan(e^x) + C u = e^x, \quad du = e^x\,dx Let u = eˣ. Then eˣ dx = du. \int \frac{e^x}{e^{2x}+1}\,dx = \int \frac{du}{u^2+1} Substitute: eˣ = u, e²ˣ = u², eˣ dx = du. = \arctan(u) + C = \arctan(e^x) + C Standard integral: ∫ 1/(u²+1) du = arctan(u) + C. Chain Rule (Prerequisite) U-substitution reverses the chain rule. If you can differentiate with the chain rule, you can integrate by substitution. Antiderivative Formulas The basic antiderivative table (∫xⁿ dx, ∫sin dx, etc.) provides f(u) once you make the substitution. Next: Integration by Parts When substitution fails (e.g., ∫x·sin(x) dx), integration by parts is the next technique to try. documents.assignment: Disk Method: Volume of a Cone \text{Find the volume of a cone of radius } R \text{ and height } h \text{ using the disk method. (Rotate } y = Rx/h \text{ around the x-axis on [0,h].)}   V = (1/3)πR²h — the classic cone volume formula, now derived rigorously from calculus. The 1/3 comes from the ∫x² factor. Compare with a cylinder (no 1/3): the cone has 1/3 the volume of the cylinder with same base and height. f(x) = \frac{R}{h}x \text{ (cross-sections are disks of radius } r = Rx/h\text{)} The slant side of the cone is a straight line from (0,0) to (h, R). V = \pi\int_0^h \left[\frac{R}{h}x\right]^2 dx = \pi\cdot\frac{R^2}{h^2}\int_0^h x^2\,dx Disk method: V = π∫r² dx. Factor out the constant. = \frac{\pi R^2}{h^2}\cdot\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^h = \frac{\pi R^2}{h^2}\cdot\frac{h^3}{3} = \frac{\pi R^2 h}{3} Antiderivative of x² is x³/3. Evaluate at limits. Washer Method: Volume Between Two Curves \text{Find the volume generated by rotating the region between } y = \sqrt{x} \text{ and } y = x \text{ on [0,1] around the x-axis.}   V = π/6. Interesting: this is the same as the AREA between y=x and y=x² (from earlier) times π — but that is a coincidence of the specific functions here, not a general rule. \text{On } [0,1]: \sqrt{x} \geq x \geq 0 \text{ (check at } x=1/4: 1/2 > 1/4\text{)} Outer radius R = √x, inner radius r = x. V = \pi\int_0^1 \left[(\sqrt{x})^2 - x^2\right]dx = \pi\int_0^1 (x - x^2)\,dx Washer formula: π∫(R² − r²) dx = π∫(x − x²) dx. = \pi\left[\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \pi\left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6} Evaluate: 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6. Shell Method: Rotation Around the y-Axis \text{Find the volume generated by rotating the region under } y = x^2 \text{ on [0,2] around the y-axis.}   V = 8π. The shell method was simpler here because expressing x as a function of y (inverting y = x² to get x = √y) would have required disk integration from y = 0 to y = 4 — still doable, but with a square root in the integrand. V = 2\pi\int_0^2 x \cdot f(x)\,dx = 2\pi\int_0^2 x \cdot x^2\,dx = 2\pi\int_0^2 x^3\,dx Shell method for y-axis rotation: V = 2π∫x·f(x)dx. Shell radius = x, height = f(x) = x². = 2\pi\left[\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^2 = 2\pi\cdot\frac{16}{4} = 2\pi\cdot 4 = 8\pi Antiderivative of x³ is x⁴/4. Evaluate at x=2: 16/4 = 4. Volume of a Sphere (Disk Method) \text{Derive the volume of a sphere of radius } R \text{ by rotating the semicircle } y = \sqrt{R^2 - x^2} \text{ around the x-axis.}   V = (4/3)πR³ — the sphere volume formula from calculus. Archimedes proved this without calculus using exhaustion, but note how naturally integration handles it: once you square the semicircle equation, the √ disappears and you integrate a simple polynomial! V = \pi\int_{-R}^R \left(\sqrt{R^2-x^2}\right)^2 dx = \pi\int_{-R}^R (R^2-x^2)\,dx Disk method. Squaring eliminates the square root! = \pi\left[R^2 x - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-R}^R Antiderivative: ∫(R²−x²)dx = R²x − x³/3. = \pi\left[\left(R^3 - \frac{R^3}{3}\right) - \left(-R^3 + \frac{R^3}{3}\right)\right] Evaluate at x = R and x = −R. = \pi\left[\frac{2R^3}{3} + \frac{2R^3}{3}\right] = \frac{4\pi R^3}{3} Combine: 2(2R³/3) = 4R³/3. Rotation Around a Non-Axis Line \text{Find the volume generated by rotating } y = x^2 \text{ from } x=0 \text{ to } x=2 \text{ around the line } y = 4.   V = 256π/15. When the axis of rotation is y = k, the disk radius is |f(x) − k|. Always draw the problem first — identify which side of the axis the curve lives on to get the correct sign. \text{Disk radius: } r(x) = 4 - x^2 We are rotating around y=4. At each x, the radius = distance from the axis y=4 down to the curve y=x². Since x²≤4 on [0,2], this is always positive: r = 4−x². \text{This is a disk (not washer) — the axis } y=4 \text{ is the outer boundary itself, so no hole.} The region sweeps solid disks of radius (4−x²) at each x. There is no inner hole because we are rotating the region between y=x² and the axis y=4. V = \pi\int_0^2 (4-x^2)^2\,dx = \pi\int_0^2(16-8x^2+x^4)\,dx Disk method with radius = 4−x². Expand the square. = \pi\left[16x - \frac{8x^3}{3} + \frac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^2 Integrate term by term. = \pi\left[32 - \frac{64}{3} + \frac{32}{5}\right] = \pi\cdot\frac{480 - 320 + 96}{15} = \frac{256\pi}{15} Common denominator 15: 32 = 480/15, 64/3 = 320/15, 32/5 = 96/15.  Use the disk method to find the volume generated by rotating y = 2x on [0, 3] around the x-axis. Verify using the cone formula V = (1/3)πR²h. Disk radius = 2x. R = f(3) = 6, h = 3. V = 36\pi  V = \pi\int_0^3(2x)^2\,dx = 4\pi\int_0^3 x^2\,dx Apply disk method. = 4\pi\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3 = 4\pi\cdot 9 = 36\pi Evaluate. \text{Verify: }\frac{1}{3}\pi(6)^2(3) = \frac{1}{3}\pi\cdot 36\cdot 3 = 36\pi\;\checkmark Cone formula with R=6, h=3.  Use BOTH the disk/washer method AND the shell method to find the volume of the solid generated by rotating the region bounded by y = x and y = x² around the y-axis. Show the two give the same answer. Disk (around y-axis): integrate in y, slicing perpendicular to y-axis. Shell (around y-axis): integrate in x. V = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ by both methods}  \text{Shell method: } V = 2\pi\int_0^1 x(x-x^2)\,dx = 2\pi\int_0^1(x^2-x^3)\,dx Shell radius = x, height = x − x² (top curve minus bottom). = 2\pi\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^1 = 2\pi\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}\right) = 2\pi\cdot\frac{1}{12} = \frac{\pi}{6} Evaluate. \text{Disk/Washer: rotate around y-axis. Slice at height } y: x_{\text{outer}}=\sqrt{y}, x_{\text{inner}}=y For y-axis disk, solve for x in terms of y. y=x² → x=√y; y=x → x=y. V = \pi\int_0^1(y - y^2)\,dy = \pi\left[\frac{y^2}{2}-\frac{y^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \pi\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6}\;\checkmark Outer radius √y, inner radius y. R²−r² = y−y². Same answer!  Use Pappus's centroid theorem to find the volume of the torus (donut) generated by rotating a disk of radius r with center at distance R from the rotation axis (R > r). Then verify with the washer method. The centroid of the disk is at distance R from the axis. Area of disk = πr². Pappus: V = 2π·R·(πr²). V = 2\pi^2 R r^2  V = 2\pi \bar{r} A = 2\pi R \cdot \pi r^2 = 2\pi^2 R r^2 Pappus's theorem directly. \text{Washer verify: disk has outer radius } R+r, \text{ inner radius } R-r, \text{ for each y-slice} More precisely, at height y above the disk center, the outer radius = R + √(r²−y²), inner = R − √(r²−y²). V = \pi\int_{-r}^{r}\left[(R+\sqrt{r^2-y^2})^2 - (R-\sqrt{r^2-y^2})^2\right]dy Washer method integrating in y. = \pi\int_{-r}^{r} 4R\sqrt{r^2-y^2}\,dy = 4\pi R \cdot \frac{\pi r^2}{2} = 2\pi^2 Rr^2\;\checkmark Since (A+B)²−(A−B)² = 4AB, and ∫₋ᵣʳ√(r²−y²)dy = πr²/2 (semicircle area).
documents.proofs:
The disk method formula V = π∫ₐᵇ [f(x)]² dx is rigorously justified by Cavalieri's principle and the definition of the definite integral. The volume of a solid with known cross-sectional area A(x) is V = ∫ₐᵇ A(x) dx (Cross-Section Formula). For a solid of revolution around the x-axis, the cross-section at x is a disk of radius f(x) and area A(x) = π[f(x)]². The disk method is therefore a special case of the cross-section formula. The shell method requires a different argument. Consider a thin cylindrical shell at radius x with height f(x) and thickness Δx. Its volume is (outer volume) − (inner volume) = π(x+Δx)²f(x) − πx²f(x) = π[(x+Δx)² − x²]f(x) = π[2xΔx + (Δx)²]f(x) ≈ 2πx·f(x)·Δx for small Δx. Summing: ΣᵢΔxᵢ 2πxᵢ·f(xᵢ) → ∫ 2πx·f(x) dx as Δx → 0. The equivalence of the disk and shell methods for the same solid follows from the fact that both compute the same volume — they are just different decompositions of the same 3D region. A rigorous proof uses Fubini's theorem (change of the order of integration in 2D), but the intuitive justification is sufficient for Calc 1. Cross-Section Formula (Cavalieri's Principle) If a solid has cross-sectional area $A(x)$ at position $x$, then its volume is
\[V = \int_a^b A(x)\,dx.\]
The disk method is the special case $A(x) = \pi[f(x)]^2$.
documents.applications:
Volumes of revolution are fundamental to manufacturing and engineering. Every lathe-turned object — wheels, axles, bolts, pistons, wine glasses, vases, turbine blades — is a solid of revolution. Pharmaceutical capsules are ellipsoids of revolution; their fill volumes require integration. The fuel tank on a rocket nose cone is a paraboloid (parabola rotated around its axis); its volume is π∫r²dx. In medicine, CT scans reconstruct 3D organ volumes by rotating 2D cross-sections — the mathematical structure is the disk method. Pappus's theorem (a 4th-century Greek result) computes the volume of any solid of revolution using the centroid of the generating region: V = 2πr̄A — no calculus, just clever geometry. Disk-Washer vs. Shell — Quick Decision Disk/Washer: slice ⊥ to rotation axis. Volume = π∫R² dx (or π∫(R²−r²) dx for washer).
Shell: slice ∥ to rotation axis. Volume = 2π∫r·h dr.
Choose whichever gives a simpler integral. Often: disk for x-axis rotation with y=f(x); shell for y-axis rotation with y=f(x) (avoids inverting). The Disk is Just a Very Thin Cylinder V = π r² h → for a thin slice of thickness dx, this becomes π[f(x)]² dx. Integrating sums up infinitely many disks. The same reasoning that gives ∫F(x)dx as work (summing tiny force × distance pieces) applies here: summing tiny volume pieces gives total volume. Pappus's Centroid Theorem The volume of a solid of revolution = 2π × (centroid distance to axis) × (area of the region). Classic application — the torus: rotate a disk of radius r whose center is at distance R from the axis (R > r). The centroid of the disk is at distance R, and the area is πr². So V = 2π·R·(πr²) = 2π²Rr². This gives the exact torus volume formula without setting up any integral — a stunning shortcut from 4th-century geometry! π is Outside the Integral V = π∫[f(x)]² dx, NOT ∫π[f(x)]² dx ... actually these are equal! Since π is a constant, it can move in and out of the integral. Both forms are correct. The first form (π outside) is traditional. Just don't forget π — it is the area of the circular cross-section and is always present in disk/washer methods.

How do you compute the volume of a vase, a bullet, or a donut? If the object has rotational symmetry — like virtually any machined part — you can generate it by rotating a 2D curve around an axis. Its volume is then a definite integral. Volumes of revolution are fundamental to manufacturing and engineering. Every lathe-turned object — wheels, axles, bolts, pistons, wine glasses, vases, turbine blades — is a solid of revolution. Pharmaceutical capsules are ellipsoids of revolution; their fill volumes require integration. The fuel tank on a rocket nose cone is a paraboloid (parabola rotated around its axis); its volume is π∫r²dx. In medicine, CT scans reconstruct 3D organ volumes by rotating 2D cross-sections — the mathematical structure is the disk method. Pappus's theorem (a 4th-century Greek result) computes the volume of any solid of revolution using the centroid of the generating region: V = 2πr̄A — no calculus, just clever geometry. Imagine spinning the region under y = f(x) on [a, b] around the x-axis. At each x-position, the spinning creates a circular cross-section (a disk) of radius r = f(x) and area πr² = π[f(x)]². The volume is the limit of the sum of thin disk volumes: ∑ π[f(x)]² Δx → ∫ₐᵇ π[f(x)]² dx. This is the **Disk Method**. When the region is between two curves f(x) ≥ g(x) ≥ 0 and you rotate around the x-axis, each cross-section is a **washer** with outer radius R = f(x) and inner radius r = g(x). Area of washer = π(R² − r²). Volume = ∫ₐᵇ π[f(x)² − g(x)²] dx. This is the **Washer Method** — disk method with a hole. The **Shell Method** takes a different slice. Instead of slicing perpendicular to the axis of rotation (giving disks), we slice parallel to the axis (giving cylindrical shells). The volume of a cylindrical shell of radius r, height h, and thickness dr is approximately 2πr·h·dr. When rotating around the y-axis: V = ∫ₐᵇ 2πx·f(x) dx. The shell method is often simpler when the natural integration variable is perpendicular to the rotation axis (e.g., rotating around the y-axis but expressing the curve as y = f(x)). Choosing disk vs. shell: if the axis of rotation is the x-axis, disk/washer slices in the x-direction and integrates in x (natural for y = f(x)). Shell slices in the x-direction and also integrates in x, but applies when rotating around the y-axis. A good rule: if you would need to invert the function x = f(y) to use disk method, try shells first. Rotation around other lines (y = k or x = h): shift the problem. If rotating y = f(x) around y = 2, the disk radius is |f(x) − 2| instead of f(x). If rotating around x = -1, the shell radius is (x + 1) instead of x. Always draw the problem to identify the correct radii. Disk Method (rotation around x-axis): if f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b], then V = π∫ₐᵇ [f(x)]² dx. Washer Method (rotation around x-axis, f ≥ g ≥ 0): V = π∫ₐᵇ {[f(x)]² − [g(x)]²} dx. Outer radius R = f(x), inner radius r = g(x). Shell Method (rotation around y-axis): V = 2π∫ₐᵇ x·f(x) dx, where [a,b] is on the x-axis and f(x) ≥ 0. Rotation around y = k: disk radius = |f(x) − k|, washer: outer and inner radii both adjusted by subtracting k. Rotation around x = h (shell method): shell radius = |x − h| instead of x. Converting between methods: any disk/washer integral can be converted to a shell integral and vice versa — they give the same answer. The choice is purely about which integral is easier to evaluate. The disk method formula V = π∫ₐᵇ [f(x)]² dx is rigorously justified by Cavalieri's principle and the definition of the definite integral. The volume of a solid with known cross-sectional area A(x) is V = ∫ₐᵇ A(x) dx (Cross-Section Formula). For a solid of revolution around the x-axis, the cross-section at x is a disk of radius f(x) and area A(x) = π[f(x)]². The disk method is therefore a special case of the cross-section formula. The shell method requires a different argument. Consider a thin cylindrical shell at radius x with height f(x) and thickness Δx. Its volume is (outer volume) − (inner volume) = π(x+Δx)²f(x) − πx²f(x) = π[(x+Δx)² − x²]f(x) = π[2xΔx + (Δx)²]f(x) ≈ 2πx·f(x)·Δx for small Δx. Summing: ΣᵢΔxᵢ 2πxᵢ·f(xᵢ) → ∫ 2πx·f(x) dx as Δx → 0. The equivalence of the disk and shell methods for the same solid follows from the fact that both compute the same volume — they are just different decompositions of the same 3D region. A rigorous proof uses Fubini's theorem (change of the order of integration in 2D), but the intuitive justification is sufficient for Calc 1. Cross-Section Formula (Cavalieri's Principle) If a solid has cross-sectional area $A(x)$ at position $x$, then its volume is
\[V = \int_a^b A(x)\,dx.\]
The disk method is the special case $A(x) = \pi[f(x)]^2$. Disk-Washer vs. Shell — Quick Decision Disk/Washer: slice ⊥ to rotation axis. Volume = π∫R² dx (or π∫(R²−r²) dx for washer).
Shell: slice ∥ to rotation axis. Volume = 2π∫r·h dr.
Choose whichever gives a simpler integral. Often: disk for x-axis rotation with y=f(x); shell for y-axis rotation with y=f(x) (avoids inverting). The Disk is Just a Very Thin Cylinder V = π r² h → for a thin slice of thickness dx, this becomes π[f(x)]² dx. Integrating sums up infinitely many disks. The same reasoning that gives ∫F(x)dx as work (summing tiny force × distance pieces) applies here: summing tiny volume pieces gives total volume. Pappus's Centroid Theorem The volume of a solid of revolution = 2π × (centroid distance to axis) × (area of the region). Classic application — the torus: rotate a disk of radius r whose center is at distance R from the axis (R > r). The centroid of the disk is at distance R, and the area is πr². So V = 2π·R·(πr²) = 2π²Rr². This gives the exact torus volume formula without setting up any integral — a stunning shortcut from 4th-century geometry! π is Outside the Integral V = π∫[f(x)]² dx, NOT ∫π[f(x)]² dx ... actually these are equal! Since π is a constant, it can move in and out of the integral. Both forms are correct. The first form (π outside) is traditional. Just don't forget π — it is the area of the circular cross-section and is always present in disk/washer methods. Volume Formulas Summary \text{Disk (x-axis): } V = \pi\int_a^b [f(x)]^2\,dx\\
\text{Washer (x-axis): } V = \pi\int_a^b \left([f(x)]^2-[g(x)]^2\right)dx\\
\text{Shell (y-axis): } V = 2\pi\int_a^b x\,f(x)\,dx Pappus's Centroid Theorem If a plane region $\mathcal{R}$ with area $A$ is revolved around an external axis, the volume of the solid of revolution is:
\[V = 2\pi \bar{r}\, A\]
where $\bar{r}$ is the distance from the centroid of $\mathcal{R}$ to the axis of revolution. 3D Solid of Revolution — Interactive Rotate the plane region around the axis and see the 3D solid form. Toggle between disk, washer, and shell representations. Drag n to see how more slices approximate the volume better. Biology: Integrating Laminar Blood Flow The Washer Method describes more than physical geometry—it describes total accumulation of concentric rings. In medicine, Poiseuilles Law integrates the velocity of blood layers across an artery to find total flow Q. Interactive Volume Calculator Choose disk or shell method and see exact volume calculations update in real time as you adjust the function and bounds. Disk Method: Volume of a Cone \text{Find the volume of a cone of radius } R \text{ and height } h \text{ using the disk method. (Rotate } y = Rx/h \text{ around the x-axis on [0,h].)} V = (1/3)πR²h — the classic cone volume formula, now derived rigorously from calculus. The 1/3 comes from the ∫x² factor. Compare with a cylinder (no 1/3): the cone has 1/3 the volume of the cylinder with same base and height. f(x) = \frac{R}{h}x \text{ (cross-sections are disks of radius } r = Rx/h\text{)} The slant side of the cone is a straight line from (0,0) to (h, R). V = \pi\int_0^h \left[\frac{R}{h}x\right]^2 dx = \pi\cdot\frac{R^2}{h^2}\int_0^h x^2\,dx Disk method: V = π∫r² dx. Factor out the constant. = \frac{\pi R^2}{h^2}\cdot\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^h = \frac{\pi R^2}{h^2}\cdot\frac{h^3}{3} = \frac{\pi R^2 h}{3} Antiderivative of x² is x³/3. Evaluate at limits. Washer Method: Volume Between Two Curves \text{Find the volume generated by rotating the region between } y = \sqrt{x} \text{ and } y = x \text{ on [0,1] around the x-axis.} V = π/6. Interesting: this is the same as the AREA between y=x and y=x² (from earlier) times π — but that is a coincidence of the specific functions here, not a general rule. \text{On } [0,1]: \sqrt{x} \geq x \geq 0 \text{ (check at } x=1/4: 1/2 > 1/4\text{)} Outer radius R = √x, inner radius r = x. V = \pi\int_0^1 \left[(\sqrt{x})^2 - x^2\right]dx = \pi\int_0^1 (x - x^2)\,dx Washer formula: π∫(R² − r²) dx = π∫(x − x²) dx. = \pi\left[\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \pi\left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6} Evaluate: 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6. Shell Method: Rotation Around the y-Axis \text{Find the volume generated by rotating the region under } y = x^2 \text{ on [0,2] around the y-axis.} V = 8π. The shell method was simpler here because expressing x as a function of y (inverting y = x² to get x = √y) would have required disk integration from y = 0 to y = 4 — still doable, but with a square root in the integrand. V = 2\pi\int_0^2 x \cdot f(x)\,dx = 2\pi\int_0^2 x \cdot x^2\,dx = 2\pi\int_0^2 x^3\,dx Shell method for y-axis rotation: V = 2π∫x·f(x)dx. Shell radius = x, height = f(x) = x². = 2\pi\left[\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^2 = 2\pi\cdot\frac{16}{4} = 2\pi\cdot 4 = 8\pi Antiderivative of x³ is x⁴/4. Evaluate at x=2: 16/4 = 4. Volume of a Sphere (Disk Method) \text{Derive the volume of a sphere of radius } R \text{ by rotating the semicircle } y = \sqrt{R^2 - x^2} \text{ around the x-axis.} V = (4/3)πR³ — the sphere volume formula from calculus. Archimedes proved this without calculus using exhaustion, but note how naturally integration handles it: once you square the semicircle equation, the √ disappears and you integrate a simple polynomial! V = \pi\int_{-R}^R \left(\sqrt{R^2-x^2}\right)^2 dx = \pi\int_{-R}^R (R^2-x^2)\,dx Disk method. Squaring eliminates the square root! = \pi\left[R^2 x - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-R}^R Antiderivative: ∫(R²−x²)dx = R²x − x³/3. = \pi\left[\left(R^3 - \frac{R^3}{3}\right) - \left(-R^3 + \frac{R^3}{3}\right)\right] Evaluate at x = R and x = −R. = \pi\left[\frac{2R^3}{3} + \frac{2R^3}{3}\right] = \frac{4\pi R^3}{3} Combine: 2(2R³/3) = 4R³/3. Rotation Around a Non-Axis Line \text{Find the volume generated by rotating } y = x^2 \text{ from } x=0 \text{ to } x=2 \text{ around the line } y = 4. V = 256π/15. When the axis of rotation is y = k, the disk radius is |f(x) − k|. Always draw the problem first — identify which side of the axis the curve lives on to get the correct sign. \text{Disk radius: } r(x) = 4 - x^2 We are rotating around y=4. At each x, the radius = distance from the axis y=4 down to the curve y=x². Since x²≤4 on [0,2], this is always positive: r = 4−x². \text{This is a disk (not washer) — the axis } y=4 \text{ is the outer boundary itself, so no hole.} The region sweeps solid disks of radius (4−x²) at each x. There is no inner hole because we are rotating the region between y=x² and the axis y=4. V = \pi\int_0^2 (4-x^2)^2\,dx = \pi\int_0^2(16-8x^2+x^4)\,dx Disk method with radius = 4−x². Expand the square. = \pi\left[16x - \frac{8x^3}{3} + \frac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^2 Integrate term by term. = \pi\left[32 - \frac{64}{3} + \frac{32}{5}\right] = \pi\cdot\frac{480 - 320 + 96}{15} = \frac{256\pi}{15} Common denominator 15: 32 = 480/15, 64/3 = 320/15, 32/5 = 96/15. Use the disk method to find the volume generated by rotating y = 2x on [0, 3] around the x-axis. Verify using the cone formula V = (1/3)πR²h. Disk radius = 2x. R = f(3) = 6, h = 3. V = 36\pi V = \pi\int_0^3(2x)^2\,dx = 4\pi\int_0^3 x^2\,dx Apply disk method. = 4\pi\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3 = 4\pi\cdot 9 = 36\pi Evaluate. \text{Verify: }\frac{1}{3}\pi(6)^2(3) = \frac{1}{3}\pi\cdot 36\cdot 3 = 36\pi\;\checkmark Cone formula with R=6, h=3. Use BOTH the disk/washer method AND the shell method to find the volume of the solid generated by rotating the region bounded by y = x and y = x² around the y-axis. Show the two give the same answer. Disk (around y-axis): integrate in y, slicing perpendicular to y-axis. Shell (around y-axis): integrate in x. V = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ by both methods} \text{Shell method: } V = 2\pi\int_0^1 x(x-x^2)\,dx = 2\pi\int_0^1(x^2-x^3)\,dx Shell radius = x, height = x − x² (top curve minus bottom). = 2\pi\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^1 = 2\pi\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}\right) = 2\pi\cdot\frac{1}{12} = \frac{\pi}{6} Evaluate. \text{Disk/Washer: rotate around y-axis. Slice at height } y: x_{\text{outer}}=\sqrt{y}, x_{\text{inner}}=y For y-axis disk, solve for x in terms of y. y=x² → x=√y; y=x → x=y. V = \pi\int_0^1(y - y^2)\,dy = \pi\left[\frac{y^2}{2}-\frac{y^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \pi\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6}\;\checkmark Outer radius √y, inner radius y. R²−r² = y−y². Same answer! Use Pappus's centroid theorem to find the volume of the torus (donut) generated by rotating a disk of radius r with center at distance R from the rotation axis (R > r). Then verify with the washer method. The centroid of the disk is at distance R from the axis. Area of disk = πr². Pappus: V = 2π·R·(πr²). V = 2\pi^2 R r^2 V = 2\pi \bar{r} A = 2\pi R \cdot \pi r^2 = 2\pi^2 R r^2 Pappus's theorem directly. \text{Washer verify: disk has outer radius } R+r, \text{ inner radius } R-r, \text{ for each y-slice} More precisely, at height y above the disk center, the outer radius = R + √(r²−y²), inner = R − √(r²−y²). V = \pi\int_{-r}^{r}\left[(R+\sqrt{r^2-y^2})^2 - (R-\sqrt{r^2-y^2})^2\right]dy Washer method integrating in y. = \pi\int_{-r}^{r} 4R\sqrt{r^2-y^2}\,dy = 4\pi R \cdot \frac{\pi r^2}{2} = 2\pi^2 Rr^2\;\checkmark Since (A+B)²−(A−B)² = 4AB, and ∫₋ᵣʳ√(r²−y²)dy = πr²/2 (semicircle area). Applications of Integration Area between curves, average value, and work — the foundational applications that lead into 3D volumes here. U-Substitution Some volume integrals require substitution to evaluate — trig sub for spheres and ellipsoids, power sub for compound forms. The Definite Integral All volume formulas are definite integrals. The cross-section formula V = ∫A(x)dx is the definite integral applied to 3D. Polar Coordinates Volumes of surfaces like spheres and cones often arise in polar/spherical coordinates in multivariable calculus. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step antiderivative accumulation area under curve net area total change

documents.assignment: Classic: ∫x·eˣ dx \text{Find } \int x e^x\,dx.   ∫xeˣ dx = eˣ(x−1) + C. One round of by-parts reduces the polynomial factor from degree 1 to degree 0. \text{Let } u = x, \quad dv = e^x\,dx LIATE: x is algebraic (A), eˣ is exponential (E). A has higher priority, so u = x. du = dx, \quad v = e^x Differentiate u, integrate dv. \int xe^x\,dx = xe^x - \int e^x\,dx Apply ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. = xe^x - e^x + C ∫eˣ dx = eˣ. = e^x(x-1) + C Factor out eˣ for a clean final form. \text{Verify: } \frac{d}{dx}[e^x(x-1)] = e^x(x-1) + e^x = e^x \cdot x \checkmark Product rule: eˣ(x−1) + eˣ·1 = xeˣ. ✓ Repeated Parts: ∫x²·sin(x) dx \text{Find } \int x^2\sin x\,dx.   ∫x²sin x dx = −x²cos x + 2x sin x + 2 cos x + C. Two rounds of by-parts reduce x² to a constant. \text{Let } u = x^2, \; dv = \sin x\,dx \Rightarrow du = 2x\,dx, \; v = -\cos x First round: u = x² (algebraic), dv = sin x dx. \int x^2\sin x\,dx = -x^2\cos x + \int 2x\cos x\,dx Apply by-parts. The new integral still has a polynomial × trig — apply again. \text{Second round: } u = 2x, \; dv = \cos x\,dx \Rightarrow du = 2\,dx, \; v = \sin x Reduce the polynomial degree by one more. \int 2x\cos x\,dx = 2x\sin x - \int 2\sin x\,dx = 2x\sin x + 2\cos x + C ∫2 sin x dx = −2 cos x. \int x^2\sin x\,dx = -x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x + C Combine all terms. \text{Verify: differentiate } -x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x Product rule on each term: 2x cos x + x² sin x + 2 sin x + 2x cos x − 2 sin x = x² sin x. ✓ Lone Function: ∫ln(x) dx \text{Find } \int \ln x\,dx.   ∫ln x dx = x ln x − x + C. The "trick" is writing ∫ln x dx as ∫1·ln x dx and choosing u = ln x. \text{Let } u = \ln x, \quad dv = dx Pair ln x with dv = dx. LIATE: logarithmic has highest priority. du = \frac{1}{x}\,dx, \quad v = x Differentiate u, integrate dv. \int \ln x\,dx = x\ln x - \int x \cdot \frac{1}{x}\,dx Apply the formula: uv − ∫v du. = x\ln x - \int 1\,dx = x\ln x - x + C The integral simplifies to ∫1 dx = x. \text{Verify: } \frac{d}{dx}[x\ln x - x] = \ln x + 1 - 1 = \ln x \checkmark Product rule on x ln x gives ln x + 1. Subtract 1. ✓ Cycling: ∫eˣ·sin(x) dx \text{Find } \int e^x\sin x\,dx.   ∫eˣ sin x dx = eˣ(sin x − cos x)/2 + C. The cycling trick: apply by-parts twice, then solve algebraically for the original integral. \text{Let } I = \int e^x\sin x\,dx. \text{ Round 1: } u = \sin x,\; dv = e^x\,dx Either choice of u works for cycling. We pick u = sin x. I = e^x\sin x - \int e^x\cos x\,dx du = cos x dx, v = eˣ. Apply formula. \text{Round 2: } u = \cos x,\; dv = e^x\,dx \Rightarrow du = -\sin x\,dx,\; v = e^x Apply by-parts to ∫eˣ cos x dx. \int e^x\cos x\,dx = e^x\cos x - \int e^x(-\sin x)\,dx = e^x\cos x + I The original integral I reappears! I = e^x\sin x - (e^x\cos x + I) = e^x\sin x - e^x\cos x - I Substitute back into the Round 1 result. 2I = e^x(\sin x - \cos x) \Rightarrow I = \frac{e^x(\sin x - \cos x)}{2} + C Add I to both sides and divide by 2. Inverse Trig: ∫arctan(x) dx \text{Find } \int \arctan x\,dx.   ∫arctan x dx = x arctan x − (1/2)ln(1+x²) + C. By-parts + u-sub working together — a common combination. \text{Let } u = \arctan x, \quad dv = dx LIATE: inverse trig (I) has high priority. Pair with dv = dx. du = \frac{1}{1+x^2}\,dx, \quad v = x Differentiate and integrate. \int \arctan x\,dx = x\arctan x - \int \frac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx Apply the formula. \text{For } \int \frac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx: \text{ let } w = 1+x^2,\; dw = 2x\,dx The remaining integral is a u-sub problem. \int \frac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\ln|1+x^2| + C = \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2) + C 1+x² > 0 always, so absolute value is unnecessary. \int \arctan x\,dx = x\arctan x - \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2) + C Combine the results.  Find ∫x·cos x dx and ∫x·e^(−x) dx. For both: u = x (algebraic), dv = the other factor. One round of by-parts each. \int x\cos x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x + C; \quad \int xe^{-x}dx = -e^{-x}(x+1)+C  \int x\cos x\,dx: u=x, dv=\cos x\,dx. \; = x\sin x - \int \sin x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x + C du = dx, v = sin x. ∫sin x dx = −cos x. \int xe^{-x}dx: u=x, dv=e^{-x}dx. \; = -xe^{-x} - \int -e^{-x}dx = -xe^{-x} - e^{-x} + C = -e^{-x}(x+1)+C du = dx, v = −e^(−x). ∫−e^(−x) dx = e^(−x)... wait: ∫e^(−x) dx = −e^(−x). So −∫−e^(−x) dx = −e^(−x).  Use the tabular method to find ∫x³·eˣ dx. Derivatives of x³: x³, 3x², 6x, 6, 0. Antiderivatives of eˣ: eˣ, eˣ, eˣ, eˣ, eˣ. Alternate signs +, −, +, −. e^x(x^3-3x^2+6x-6)+C  \text{Derivatives: } x^3,\; 3x^2,\; 6x,\; 6,\; 0 Differentiate x³ until you reach 0. \text{Antiderivatives: } e^x,\; e^x,\; e^x,\; e^x Integrate eˣ repeatedly (it stays eˣ). \text{Signs: } +,\; -,\; +,\; - Alternate starting with +. = (+)(x^3)(e^x) + (-)(3x^2)(e^x) + (+)(6x)(e^x) + (-)(6)(e^x) + C Multiply each derivative by the antiderivative one row below, with alternating sign. = e^x(x^3 - 3x^2 + 6x - 6) + C Factor out eˣ.  Derive the reduction formula: ∫sin^n(x) dx = −(1/n)sin^(n−1)(x)cos(x) + (n−1)/n · ∫sin^(n−2)(x) dx. Then use it to compute ∫sin⁴(x) dx. Write sin^n x = sin^(n−1) x · sin x. Let u = sin^(n−1) x, dv = sin x dx. Use cos²x = 1 − sin²x to handle the resulting integral. \int \sin^4 x\,dx = \frac{3x}{8} - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + \frac{\sin 4x}{32} + C  u = \sin^{n-1}x,\; dv = \sin x\,dx \Rightarrow du = (n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x\,dx,\; v = -\cos x Set up by-parts. \int \sin^n x\,dx = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\cos^2 x\,dx Apply formula. Note the cos²x factor. = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x(1-\sin^2 x)\,dx Replace cos²x = 1 − sin²x. = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\,dx - (n-1)\int \sin^n x\,dx Distribute. The last term contains the original integral! n\int \sin^n x\,dx = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\,dx Move the sin^n integral to the left: 1 + (n−1) = n. \int \sin^4 x\,dx = -\frac{1}{4}\sin^3 x\cos x + \frac{3}{4}\int \sin^2 x\,dx Apply with n=4. \int \sin^2 x\,dx = -\frac{1}{2}\sin x\cos x + \frac{1}{2}x + C = \frac{x}{2} - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + C Apply with n=2 (or use half-angle identity). \int \sin^4 x\,dx = -\frac{1}{4}\sin^3 x\cos x + \frac{3}{8}x - \frac{3}{16}\sin 2x + C Substitute back.
documents.proofs:
Derivation of integration by parts from the product rule. The product rule states: $d/dx[u(x)v(x)] = u'(x)v(x) + u(x)v'(x)$. Rearrange: $u(x)v'(x) = d/dx[u(x)v(x)] - u'(x)v(x)$. Integrate both sides over $[a,b]$: $\int_a^b u(x)v'(x)\,dx = [u(x)v(x)]_a^b - \int_a^b u'(x)v(x)\,dx$. This is exact — no approximation. The formula requires $u$ and $v$ to be differentiable, with $u'v$ and $uv'$ integrable. For continuously differentiable functions (the usual case), all conditions are satisfied. The indefinite version follows by omitting the evaluation limits: $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du + C$. The constant is conventionally absorbed into the final answer. Note: when computing $v = \int dv$, we do NOT include a $+C$ at this intermediate step — any choice of antiderivative for $v$ works, and the simplest (with $C = 0$) is preferred. Validity of the cycling method: when $\int u\,dv$ is computed by two rounds of by-parts and yields $I = A - I$ (where $A$ collects boundary terms), we solve algebraically: $2I = A$, so $I = A/2$. This is valid because $I$ is a NUMBER (for definite integrals) or a FUNCTION (for indefinite integrals, defined up to $+C$). The algebraic manipulation is justified by the linearity of integration. Reduction formulas and mathematical induction. The reduction $\int \sin^n x\,dx = -(1/n)\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)/n \int \sin^{n-2}x\,dx$ is proved by one round of by-parts with $u = \sin^{n-1}x$ and $dv = \sin x\,dx$. The identity $\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x$ is used to eliminate $\cos^2 x$ from the result. By induction, this gives the Wallis-type closed form for $\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^n x\,dx$. Derivation from the Product Rule \((uv)' = u'v + uv'\) implies \(uv' = (uv)' - u'v\). Integrating:
\[\int uv' = uv - \int u'v.\]
This is exact, not an approximation. It holds whenever \(u, v\) are \(C^1\) (continuously differentiable).
documents.applications: Integration by parts appears throughout engineering and physics. Fourier coefficients — the foundation of signal processing, audio compression (MP3), and image analysis (JPEG) — are computed by integrating products of functions with sines and cosines, requiring repeated by-parts. In quantum mechanics, expectation values involve integrals like ∫ψ*(x)·x·ψ(x)dx, solved by parts. Control engineers use Laplace transforms that rely on by-parts internally. Statisticians computing moments of probability distributions (mean, variance, skewness) integrate x^n times density functions — by parts is the standard method. When to Use Integration by Parts Use by-parts when the integrand is a product of two different "types" of functions (e.g., polynomial × exponential, polynomial × trig, logarithm × anything) and u-substitution does not apply (no inner derivative present). The LIATE rule tells you which factor to differentiate. Choosing u and dv Badly Bad choices make the integral harder. In ∫x·eˣ dx, if you choose u = eˣ and dv = x dx, then du = eˣ dx and v = x²/2, giving ∫x·eˣ dx = (x²/2)eˣ − ∫(x²/2)eˣ dx — the new integral is MORE complex (x² instead of x). LIATE prevents this: x (algebraic) has higher priority than eˣ (exponential), so u = x. By-Parts Is Not a Last Resort Students often try u-sub first and reach for by-parts only when stuck. But many integrals (∫x cos x dx, ∫ln x dx, ∫arctan x dx) are immediately recognizable as by-parts problems. Train yourself to spot products of different function types — that is the signal for by-parts. The Product Rule Is the Foundation By-parts IS the product rule, rearranged and integrated. If you remember (uv)' = u'v + uv', then ∫uv' = uv − ∫u'v follows immediately. Every by-parts problem is just the product rule run backwards, with a strategic choice of which factor to call u.
documents.content:
How do you integrate x·eˣ? There is no substitution that works — the x factor is not the derivative of the exponent, and the exponent is not the derivative of x. Yet d/dx[x·eˣ] = eˣ + x·eˣ by the product rule, so x·eˣ = d/dx[x·eˣ] − eˣ. Integrating both sides: ∫x·eˣ dx = x·eˣ − eˣ + C. Integration by parts formalizes this trick for any product. Integration by parts appears throughout engineering and physics. Fourier coefficients — the foundation of signal processing, audio compression (MP3), and image analysis (JPEG) — are computed by integrating products of functions with sines and cosines, requiring repeated by-parts. In quantum mechanics, expectation values involve integrals like ∫ψ*(x)·x·ψ(x)dx, solved by parts. Control engineers use Laplace transforms that rely on by-parts internally. Statisticians computing moments of probability distributions (mean, variance, skewness) integrate x^n times density functions — by parts is the standard method. The product rule says $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$. Rearranging: $uv' = (uv)' - u'v$. Integrate both sides: $\int u\,v'\,dx = uv - \int u'\,v\,dx$. That is the integration by parts formula. It trades the integral $\int u\,dv$ for a (hopefully simpler) integral $\int v\,du$. The art is choosing $u$ and $dv$ so that the new integral is easier than the original. Think of it as a strategic trade. You start with a product of two functions that you cannot integrate directly. You "differentiate one factor and integrate the other." If differentiating the first factor makes it simpler while integrating the second factor does not make it worse, you win: the new integral is easier. The classic example is $\int x \cdot e^x\,dx$: differentiating $x$ gives 1 (simpler!), and integrating $e^x$ gives $e^x$ (no worse). So the new integral $\int 1 \cdot e^x\,dx = e^x$ is trivial. The LIATE rule gives a priority order for choosing $u$: Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic (polynomials), Trigonometric, Exponential. Choose $u$ as the function highest on the list; the remaining factor becomes $dv$. Why? Functions higher on the list simplify when differentiated (ln x → 1/x, arctan x → 1/(1+x²), x² → 2x → 2 → 0), while functions lower on the list do not get worse when integrated (e^x → e^x, sin x → −cos x). Sometimes you need to apply by-parts more than once. For $\int x^2 \sin x\,dx$, one round reduces $x^2$ to $2x$; a second round reduces $2x$ to $2$; then the remaining integral is elementary. Each round peels off one power of $x$. The tabular method (also called the "tic-tac-toe" method) organizes repeated by-parts: list successive derivatives of $u$ in one column and successive antiderivatives of $dv$ in the other, alternating signs (+, −, +, −, …). Multiply diagonally and add. A beautiful special case is the "cycling" trick. For $\int e^x \sin x\,dx$, applying by-parts twice brings you back to an integral of the same form: $\int e^x \sin x\,dx = -e^x \cos x + e^x \sin x - \int e^x \sin x\,dx$. The original integral appears on both sides! Move it to the left: $2\int e^x \sin x\,dx = e^x(\sin x - \cos x)$. Divide by 2. This is algebra, not magic — it works whenever the same integral recurs after two rounds of by-parts. Integration by parts also handles functions that seem to have no partner to multiply. For $\int \ln x\,dx$, write it as $\int 1 \cdot \ln x\,dx$ with $u = \ln x$ and $dv = dx$. Then $du = dx/x$ and $v = x$, giving $x \ln x - \int x \cdot (1/x)\,dx = x \ln x - x + C$. The same trick works for $\int \arctan x\,dx$ and $\int \arcsin x\,dx$ — pair the inverse function with $dv = dx$. Reduction formulas use by-parts to express $\int f_n(x)\,dx$ in terms of $\int f_{n-2}(x)\,dx$ or $\int f_{n-1}(x)\,dx$. For example, $\int \sin^n x\,dx$ can be reduced by writing $\sin^n x = \sin^{n-1}x \cdot \sin x$, integrating by parts, and using $\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x$. The result is a formula linking the $n$-th integral to the $(n-2)$-th. Applied repeatedly, this reduces any $\int \sin^n x\,dx$ to either $\int \sin x\,dx$ or $\int dx$. The integration by parts formula: $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$. In function notation: if $u = u(x)$ and $v = v(x)$, then $\int u(x)v'(x)\,dx = u(x)v(x) - \int u'(x)v(x)\,dx$. For definite integrals: $\int_a^b u\,dv = [uv]_a^b - \int_a^b v\,du$. LIATE priority for choosing $u$: (L)ogarithmic: $\ln x$, $\log x$; (I)nverse trig: $\arctan x$, $\arcsin x$; (A)lgebraic: $x^n$, polynomials; (T)rigonometric: $\sin x$, $\cos x$; (E)xponential: $e^x$, $a^x$. Choose $u$ from the highest available category. The other factor (together with $dx$) is $dv$. Tabular method for repeated by-parts: when $u$ is a polynomial of degree $n$ and $dv$ involves $e^x$, $\sin x$, or $\cos x$, create two columns. Left column: successive derivatives of $u$ (each row differentiates once more, ending at 0). Right column: successive antiderivatives of $dv$. Alternate signs: $+, -, +, -, \ldots$ Multiply each left entry by the right entry one row below it, with the alternating sign. Sum all products. This gives the answer without writing intermediate integrals. Cycling integrals: for $\int e^{ax}\sin(bx)\,dx$ or $\int e^{ax}\cos(bx)\,dx$, two rounds of by-parts produce the original integral $I$ on the right side: $I = (\text{boundary terms}) - I$ or $I = (\text{terms}) + I$. Collect $I$: $2I = (\text{boundary terms})$, so $I = (\text{boundary terms})/2$. Results: $\int e^{ax}\sin(bx)\,dx = \frac{e^{ax}(a\sin bx - b\cos bx)}{a^2+b^2}+C$ and $\int e^{ax}\cos(bx)\,dx = \frac{e^{ax}(a\cos bx + b\sin bx)}{a^2+b^2}+C$. Reduction formula for $\int x^n e^x\,dx$: let $u = x^n$, $dv = e^x\,dx$. Then $\int x^n e^x\,dx = x^n e^x - n\int x^{n-1} e^x\,dx$. Applied $n$ times, this reduces to $\int e^x\,dx = e^x + C$. The general result is $\int x^n e^x\,dx = e^x \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k \frac{n!}{(n-k)!} x^{n-k} + C$. Derivation of integration by parts from the product rule. The product rule states: $d/dx[u(x)v(x)] = u'(x)v(x) + u(x)v'(x)$. Rearrange: $u(x)v'(x) = d/dx[u(x)v(x)] - u'(x)v(x)$. Integrate both sides over $[a,b]$: $\int_a^b u(x)v'(x)\,dx = [u(x)v(x)]_a^b - \int_a^b u'(x)v(x)\,dx$. This is exact — no approximation. The formula requires $u$ and $v$ to be differentiable, with $u'v$ and $uv'$ integrable. For continuously differentiable functions (the usual case), all conditions are satisfied. The indefinite version follows by omitting the evaluation limits: $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du + C$. The constant is conventionally absorbed into the final answer. Note: when computing $v = \int dv$, we do NOT include a $+C$ at this intermediate step — any choice of antiderivative for $v$ works, and the simplest (with $C = 0$) is preferred. Validity of the cycling method: when $\int u\,dv$ is computed by two rounds of by-parts and yields $I = A - I$ (where $A$ collects boundary terms), we solve algebraically: $2I = A$, so $I = A/2$. This is valid because $I$ is a NUMBER (for definite integrals) or a FUNCTION (for indefinite integrals, defined up to $+C$). The algebraic manipulation is justified by the linearity of integration. Reduction formulas and mathematical induction. The reduction $\int \sin^n x\,dx = -(1/n)\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)/n \int \sin^{n-2}x\,dx$ is proved by one round of by-parts with $u = \sin^{n-1}x$ and $dv = \sin x\,dx$. The identity $\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x$ is used to eliminate $\cos^2 x$ from the result. By induction, this gives the Wallis-type closed form for $\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^n x\,dx$. Derivation from the Product Rule \((uv)' = u'v + uv'\) implies \(uv' = (uv)' - u'v\). Integrating:
\[\int uv' = uv - \int u'v.\]
This is exact, not an approximation. It holds whenever \(u, v\) are \(C^1\) (continuously differentiable). When to Use Integration by Parts Use by-parts when the integrand is a product of two different "types" of functions (e.g., polynomial × exponential, polynomial × trig, logarithm × anything) and u-substitution does not apply (no inner derivative present). The LIATE rule tells you which factor to differentiate. Choosing u and dv Badly Bad choices make the integral harder. In ∫x·eˣ dx, if you choose u = eˣ and dv = x dx, then du = eˣ dx and v = x²/2, giving ∫x·eˣ dx = (x²/2)eˣ − ∫(x²/2)eˣ dx — the new integral is MORE complex (x² instead of x). LIATE prevents this: x (algebraic) has higher priority than eˣ (exponential), so u = x. By-Parts Is Not a Last Resort Students often try u-sub first and reach for by-parts only when stuck. But many integrals (∫x cos x dx, ∫ln x dx, ∫arctan x dx) are immediately recognizable as by-parts problems. Train yourself to spot products of different function types — that is the signal for by-parts. The Product Rule Is the Foundation By-parts IS the product rule, rearranged and integrated. If you remember (uv)' = u'v + uv', then ∫uv' = uv − ∫u'v follows immediately. Every by-parts problem is just the product rule run backwards, with a strategic choice of which factor to call u. Integration by Parts Formula \[\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du\]
Definite integral form:
\[\int_a^b u\,dv = [uv]_a^b - \int_a^b v\,du\] The Tabular Method For \(\int x^n f(x)\,dx\) where \(f\) has a pattern of antiderivatives (e.g., \(e^x, \sin x, \cos x\)):
1. Differentiate \(x^n\) repeatedly: \(x^n, nx^{n-1}, n(n-1)x^{n-2}, \ldots, n!, 0\)
2. Integrate \(f\) repeatedly: \(f, F_1, F_2, \ldots\)
3. Multiply diagonally with alternating signs and sum. Cycling Formula \[\int e^{ax}\sin(bx)\,dx = \frac{e^{ax}(a\sin bx - b\cos bx)}{a^2+b^2}+C\]
\[\int e^{ax}\cos(bx)\,dx = \frac{e^{ax}(a\cos bx + b\sin bx)}{a^2+b^2}+C\] Method Selection Trainer Try product-style integrands and see why by-parts ranks above substitution when no inner derivative is available. Integration by Parts: Trading Integrals The graph shows the original integrand u·v' (shaded) and the new integrand u'·v (lighter shade). By-parts trades the area under one curve for the area under a simpler curve, plus a boundary term uv. When the lighter region is easier to compute, the trade is profitable. Python Lab: Build & Verify Integration by Parts Implement the tabular method, verify antiderivatives by differentiation, and discover the cycling trick numerically before working it algebraically. Classic: ∫x·eˣ dx \text{Find } \int x e^x\,dx. ∫xeˣ dx = eˣ(x−1) + C. One round of by-parts reduces the polynomial factor from degree 1 to degree 0. \text{Let } u = x, \quad dv = e^x\,dx LIATE: x is algebraic (A), eˣ is exponential (E). A has higher priority, so u = x. du = dx, \quad v = e^x Differentiate u, integrate dv. \int xe^x\,dx = xe^x - \int e^x\,dx Apply ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. = xe^x - e^x + C ∫eˣ dx = eˣ. = e^x(x-1) + C Factor out eˣ for a clean final form. \text{Verify: } \frac{d}{dx}[e^x(x-1)] = e^x(x-1) + e^x = e^x \cdot x \checkmark Product rule: eˣ(x−1) + eˣ·1 = xeˣ. ✓ Repeated Parts: ∫x²·sin(x) dx \text{Find } \int x^2\sin x\,dx. ∫x²sin x dx = −x²cos x + 2x sin x + 2 cos x + C. Two rounds of by-parts reduce x² to a constant. \text{Let } u = x^2, \; dv = \sin x\,dx \Rightarrow du = 2x\,dx, \; v = -\cos x First round: u = x² (algebraic), dv = sin x dx. \int x^2\sin x\,dx = -x^2\cos x + \int 2x\cos x\,dx Apply by-parts. The new integral still has a polynomial × trig — apply again. \text{Second round: } u = 2x, \; dv = \cos x\,dx \Rightarrow du = 2\,dx, \; v = \sin x Reduce the polynomial degree by one more. \int 2x\cos x\,dx = 2x\sin x - \int 2\sin x\,dx = 2x\sin x + 2\cos x + C ∫2 sin x dx = −2 cos x. \int x^2\sin x\,dx = -x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x + C Combine all terms. \text{Verify: differentiate } -x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x Product rule on each term: 2x cos x + x² sin x + 2 sin x + 2x cos x − 2 sin x = x² sin x. ✓ Lone Function: ∫ln(x) dx \text{Find } \int \ln x\,dx. ∫ln x dx = x ln x − x + C. The "trick" is writing ∫ln x dx as ∫1·ln x dx and choosing u = ln x. \text{Let } u = \ln x, \quad dv = dx Pair ln x with dv = dx. LIATE: logarithmic has highest priority. du = \frac{1}{x}\,dx, \quad v = x Differentiate u, integrate dv. \int \ln x\,dx = x\ln x - \int x \cdot \frac{1}{x}\,dx Apply the formula: uv − ∫v du. = x\ln x - \int 1\,dx = x\ln x - x + C The integral simplifies to ∫1 dx = x. \text{Verify: } \frac{d}{dx}[x\ln x - x] = \ln x + 1 - 1 = \ln x \checkmark Product rule on x ln x gives ln x + 1. Subtract 1. ✓ Cycling: ∫eˣ·sin(x) dx \text{Find } \int e^x\sin x\,dx. ∫eˣ sin x dx = eˣ(sin x − cos x)/2 + C. The cycling trick: apply by-parts twice, then solve algebraically for the original integral. \text{Let } I = \int e^x\sin x\,dx. \text{ Round 1: } u = \sin x,\; dv = e^x\,dx Either choice of u works for cycling. We pick u = sin x. I = e^x\sin x - \int e^x\cos x\,dx du = cos x dx, v = eˣ. Apply formula. \text{Round 2: } u = \cos x,\; dv = e^x\,dx \Rightarrow du = -\sin x\,dx,\; v = e^x Apply by-parts to ∫eˣ cos x dx. \int e^x\cos x\,dx = e^x\cos x - \int e^x(-\sin x)\,dx = e^x\cos x + I The original integral I reappears! I = e^x\sin x - (e^x\cos x + I) = e^x\sin x - e^x\cos x - I Substitute back into the Round 1 result. 2I = e^x(\sin x - \cos x) \Rightarrow I = \frac{e^x(\sin x - \cos x)}{2} + C Add I to both sides and divide by 2. Inverse Trig: ∫arctan(x) dx \text{Find } \int \arctan x\,dx. ∫arctan x dx = x arctan x − (1/2)ln(1+x²) + C. By-parts + u-sub working together — a common combination. \text{Let } u = \arctan x, \quad dv = dx LIATE: inverse trig (I) has high priority. Pair with dv = dx. du = \frac{1}{1+x^2}\,dx, \quad v = x Differentiate and integrate. \int \arctan x\,dx = x\arctan x - \int \frac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx Apply the formula. \text{For } \int \frac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx: \text{ let } w = 1+x^2,\; dw = 2x\,dx The remaining integral is a u-sub problem. \int \frac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\ln|1+x^2| + C = \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2) + C 1+x² > 0 always, so absolute value is unnecessary. \int \arctan x\,dx = x\arctan x - \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2) + C Combine the results. Find ∫x·cos x dx and ∫x·e^(−x) dx. For both: u = x (algebraic), dv = the other factor. One round of by-parts each. \int x\cos x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x + C; \quad \int xe^{-x}dx = -e^{-x}(x+1)+C \int x\cos x\,dx: u=x, dv=\cos x\,dx. \; = x\sin x - \int \sin x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x + C du = dx, v = sin x. ∫sin x dx = −cos x. \int xe^{-x}dx: u=x, dv=e^{-x}dx. \; = -xe^{-x} - \int -e^{-x}dx = -xe^{-x} - e^{-x} + C = -e^{-x}(x+1)+C du = dx, v = −e^(−x). ∫−e^(−x) dx = e^(−x)... wait: ∫e^(−x) dx = −e^(−x). So −∫−e^(−x) dx = −e^(−x). Use the tabular method to find ∫x³·eˣ dx. Derivatives of x³: x³, 3x², 6x, 6, 0. Antiderivatives of eˣ: eˣ, eˣ, eˣ, eˣ, eˣ. Alternate signs +, −, +, −. e^x(x^3-3x^2+6x-6)+C \text{Derivatives: } x^3,\; 3x^2,\; 6x,\; 6,\; 0 Differentiate x³ until you reach 0. \text{Antiderivatives: } e^x,\; e^x,\; e^x,\; e^x Integrate eˣ repeatedly (it stays eˣ). \text{Signs: } +,\; -,\; +,\; - Alternate starting with +. = (+)(x^3)(e^x) + (-)(3x^2)(e^x) + (+)(6x)(e^x) + (-)(6)(e^x) + C Multiply each derivative by the antiderivative one row below, with alternating sign. = e^x(x^3 - 3x^2 + 6x - 6) + C Factor out eˣ. Derive the reduction formula: ∫sin^n(x) dx = −(1/n)sin^(n−1)(x)cos(x) + (n−1)/n · ∫sin^(n−2)(x) dx. Then use it to compute ∫sin⁴(x) dx. Write sin^n x = sin^(n−1) x · sin x. Let u = sin^(n−1) x, dv = sin x dx. Use cos²x = 1 − sin²x to handle the resulting integral. \int \sin^4 x\,dx = \frac{3x}{8} - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + \frac{\sin 4x}{32} + C u = \sin^{n-1}x,\; dv = \sin x\,dx \Rightarrow du = (n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x\,dx,\; v = -\cos x Set up by-parts. \int \sin^n x\,dx = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\cos^2 x\,dx Apply formula. Note the cos²x factor. = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x(1-\sin^2 x)\,dx Replace cos²x = 1 − sin²x. = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\,dx - (n-1)\int \sin^n x\,dx Distribute. The last term contains the original integral! n\int \sin^n x\,dx = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\,dx Move the sin^n integral to the left: 1 + (n−1) = n. \int \sin^4 x\,dx = -\frac{1}{4}\sin^3 x\cos x + \frac{3}{4}\int \sin^2 x\,dx Apply with n=4. \int \sin^2 x\,dx = -\frac{1}{2}\sin x\cos x + \frac{1}{2}x + C = \frac{x}{2} - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + C Apply with n=2 (or use half-angle identity). \int \sin^4 x\,dx = -\frac{1}{4}\sin^3 x\cos x + \frac{3}{8}x - \frac{3}{16}\sin 2x + C Substitute back. U-Substitution When u-sub fails (no inner derivative present), by-parts is the next technique. Many problems combine both methods. Trig Integrals Reduction formulas derived by parts are the foundation of trig integral techniques in Lesson 8. Indefinite Integrals By-parts extends the basic antiderivative table to products of functions. The Chain Rule The product rule gives by-parts; the chain rule gives u-sub. Together they handle most integrals. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step antiderivative accumulation area under curve net area total change

documents.assignment: Even Power: ∫sin²(x) dx \text{Find } \int \sin^2 x\,dx.   ∫sin²x dx = x/2 − sin(2x)/4 + C. This is the most important trig integral — memorize it or be able to derive it instantly. \sin^2 x = \frac{1-\cos 2x}{2} Both exponents are even (sin² = sin² · cos⁰). Use the half-angle identity. \int \sin^2 x\,dx = \int \frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\int(1-\cos 2x)\,dx Factor out 1/2. = \frac{1}{2}\left(x - \frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right) + C = \frac{x}{2} - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + C ∫cos 2x dx = sin(2x)/2 by linear substitution. \text{Verify: } \frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{x}{2}-\frac{\sin 2x}{4}\right] = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{2\cos 2x}{4} = \frac{1-\cos 2x}{2} = \sin^2 x \checkmark Differentiate and use the half-angle identity backwards. Odd Power: ∫sin³(x) dx \text{Find } \int \sin^3 x\,dx.   ∫sin³x dx = −cos x + cos³x/3 + C. The "save one, convert the rest" strategy makes odd powers straightforward. \int \sin^3 x\,dx = \int \sin^2 x \cdot \sin x\,dx Odd power of sin: save one sin x. = \int (1-\cos^2 x)\sin x\,dx Replace sin²x = 1 − cos²x. \text{Let } u = \cos x, \; du = -\sin x\,dx Now u-sub with u = cos x. = -\int (1-u^2)\,du = -u + \frac{u^3}{3} + C Integrate the polynomial in u. = -\cos x + \frac{\cos^3 x}{3} + C Substitute back u = cos x. Mixed: ∫sin²(x)cos³(x) dx \text{Find } \int \sin^2 x \cos^3 x\,dx.   ∫sin²x cos³x dx = sin³x/3 − sin⁵x/5 + C. When one exponent is odd, the integral reduces to a polynomial. \text{cos has odd power (3). Save one cos x:} Decision: n = 3 is odd → use Pythagorean identity strategy. \int \sin^2 x \cos^2 x \cdot \cos x\,dx = \int \sin^2 x(1-\sin^2 x)\cos x\,dx Replace cos²x = 1 − sin²x. \text{Let } u = \sin x,\; du = \cos x\,dx Substitute u = sin x. = \int u^2(1-u^2)\,du = \int (u^2-u^4)\,du Expand. = \frac{u^3}{3} - \frac{u^5}{5} + C = \frac{\sin^3 x}{3} - \frac{\sin^5 x}{5} + C Power rule, then substitute back. Both Even: ∫sin²(x)cos²(x) dx \text{Find } \int \sin^2 x \cos^2 x\,dx.   ∫sin²x cos²x dx = x/8 − sin(4x)/32 + C. Both even → half-angle, possibly twice. \sin^2 x\cos^2 x = \left(\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{\sin^2 2x}{4} Use sin x cos x = sin(2x)/2, then square. = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{1-\cos 4x}{2} = \frac{1-\cos 4x}{8} Apply half-angle to sin²(2x): sin²(2x) = (1 − cos 4x)/2. \int \sin^2 x\cos^2 x\,dx = \frac{1}{8}\int(1-\cos 4x)\,dx Now integrate a first-degree trig function. = \frac{1}{8}\left(x - \frac{\sin 4x}{4}\right) + C = \frac{x}{8} - \frac{\sin 4x}{32} + C ∫cos 4x dx = sin(4x)/4. Tangent Power: ∫tan⁴(x) dx \text{Find } \int \tan^4 x\,dx.   ∫tan⁴x dx = tan³x/3 − tan x + x + C. The reduction tan²x = sec²x − 1 is applied twice. \tan^4 x = \tan^2 x \cdot \tan^2 x = \tan^2 x(\sec^2 x - 1) Peel off tan²x and use tan²x = sec²x − 1. = \tan^2 x \sec^2 x - \tan^2 x Distribute. \int \tan^2 x\sec^2 x\,dx: u=\tan x,\; du=\sec^2 x\,dx \Rightarrow \int u^2\,du = \frac{\tan^3 x}{3} First integral: direct u-sub. \int \tan^2 x\,dx = \int(\sec^2 x-1)\,dx = \tan x - x + C Second integral: replace tan²x = sec²x − 1 again. \int \tan^4 x\,dx = \frac{\tan^3 x}{3} - \tan x + x + C Combine results. Secant Cubed: ∫sec³(x) dx \text{Find } \int \sec^3 x\,dx.   ∫sec³x dx = (1/2)[sec x tan x + ln|sec x + tan x|] + C. This is one of the most important results in trig integrals — it appears frequently in applications (arc length of parabolas, etc.). \text{Let } I = \int \sec^3 x\,dx. \text{ By parts: } u = \sec x,\; dv = \sec^2 x\,dx Odd power of sec → integration by parts. du = \sec x\tan x\,dx, \quad v = \tan x Differentiate and integrate. I = \sec x\tan x - \int \sec x\tan^2 x\,dx Apply the by-parts formula. = \sec x\tan x - \int \sec x(\sec^2 x - 1)\,dx Replace tan²x = sec²x − 1. = \sec x\tan x - I + \int \sec x\,dx Split: −∫sec³x dx = −I, and +∫sec x dx. 2I = \sec x\tan x + \ln|\sec x+\tan x| Collect I on the left. Recall ∫sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x|. I = \frac{1}{2}\left[\sec x\tan x + \ln|\sec x + \tan x|\right] + C Divide by 2.  Evaluate: (a) ∫cos²(x) dx, (b) ∫sin(x)cos³(x) dx. (a) Half-angle: cos²x = (1+cos 2x)/2. (b) Odd power of cos: save one cos x, let u = sin x. \text{(a) } \frac{x}{2}+\frac{\sin 2x}{4}+C \quad \text{(b) } -\frac{\cos^4 x}{4}+C  \text{(a) } \int \cos^2 x\,dx = \int\frac{1+\cos 2x}{2}dx = \frac{x}{2} + \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + C Half-angle identity, then integrate. \text{(b) } u = \sin x,\; du = \cos x\,dx.\; \int \sin x \cos^2 x \cdot \cos x\,dx = \int u(1-u^2)du Wait — cos has odd power 3. Save one cos x. sin x · cos²x · cos x dx. But more directly: just u = sin x... \text{Actually: } \int \sin x\cos^3 x\,dx,\; u=\cos x,\; du=-\sin x\,dx: -\int u^3\,du = -\frac{\cos^4 x}{4}+C Simpler: let u = cos x since sin x dx = −du. Then cos³x = u³.  Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin⁵(x) dx using the odd-power strategy, then verify using the Wallis formula. Save one sin x, convert sin⁴x = (1−cos²x)², substitute u = cos x. For Wallis: (4·2)/(5·3·1) · 1. \frac{8}{15}  \int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^5 x\,dx = \int_0^{\pi/2}(1-\cos^2 x)^2\sin x\,dx Save one sin x, write sin⁴x = (1−cos²x)². u=\cos x,\; x=0\Rightarrow u=1,\; x=\pi/2\Rightarrow u=0 Change limits. = -\int_1^0 (1-u^2)^2\,du = \int_0^1(1-2u^2+u^4)\,du Flip limits and expand. = \left[u-\frac{2u^3}{3}+\frac{u^5}{5}\right]_0^1 = 1-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{5} = \frac{15-10+3}{15} = \frac{8}{15} Evaluate. \text{Wallis: } \frac{4!!}{5!!} \cdot 1 = \frac{4\cdot2}{5\cdot3\cdot1} = \frac{8}{15} \checkmark n=5 is odd, so multiply by 1 (not π/2). Confirmed.  Find ∫tan³(x)sec³(x) dx. Save sec x tan x (so m is odd for tan). Write tan²x = sec²x − 1. documents.proofs:
The half-angle identities are derived from the double-angle formula $\cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x - 1$. Solving for $\sin^2 x$: $\sin^2 x = (1 - \cos 2x)/2$. Solving for $\cos^2 x$: $\cos^2 x = (1 + \cos 2x)/2$. These are exact algebraic identities, not approximations. The reduction formula for $\int \sin^n x\,dx$ is derived by integration by parts. Let $u = \sin^{n-1} x$, $dv = \sin x\,dx$. Then $du = (n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x\,dx$ and $v = -\cos x$. Applying by-parts: $\int \sin^n x\,dx = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\cos^2 x\,dx$. Replace $\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x$: $= -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\,dx - (n-1)\int \sin^n x\,dx$. Let $I_n = \int \sin^n x\,dx$. Then $I_n = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)I_{n-2} - (n-1)I_n$. Solving: $nI_n = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)I_{n-2}$, giving $I_n = -\frac{1}{n}\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + \frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}$. The Wallis formula for definite integrals over $[0, \pi/2]$ follows from the reduction formula evaluated at the endpoints. Since $\sin(0) = 0$ and $\sin(\pi/2) = 1$, the boundary term $[-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x]_0^{\pi/2}$ equals $-1^{n-1}\cdot 0 + 0 = 0$ for all $n \geq 1$. Thus $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^n x\,dx = \frac{n-1}{n}\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x\,dx$. Iterating: for even $n = 2k$, the chain terminates at $\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx = \pi/2$; for odd $n = 2k+1$, it terminates at $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\,dx = 1$. The Wallis product formula for $\pi$ follows from comparing $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2n}x\,dx$ and $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2n+1}x\,dx$. Since $0 \leq \sin x \leq 1$ on $[0, \pi/2]$, we have $\sin^{2n+1}x \leq \sin^{2n}x \leq \sin^{2n-1}x$. Integrating and dividing by $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2n+1}x\,dx$, then taking $n \to \infty$ (using the squeeze theorem), yields the Wallis product: $\pi/2 = \prod_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{4k^2}{4k^2-1}$. Reduction Formula for sin^n (Proof Sketch) By parts with \(u = \sin^{n-1}x\), \(dv = \sin x\,dx\):
\[I_n = -\frac{1}{n}\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + \frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}\]
The \(\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x\) substitution is the key algebraic step that makes the original integral reappear.

Structural engineers compute bending moments in beams under sinusoidal loads. In optics, interference patterns involve integrals of cos² and sin·cos products. Fourier analysis — the mathematical backbone of audio processing, telecommunications, and image compression — requires evaluating ∫sin^m(x)cos^n(x)dx for all combinations of m and n. How do you integrate sin²(x)? The power rule does not apply (sin²(x) is not x^n), and u-sub fails (the derivative of sin x is cos x, but there is no cos x factor). The key is a trig identity: sin²(x) = (1 − cos 2x)/2. This converts the integral to a basic form. Trig integrals are all about choosing the right identity to simplify the integrand — and this lesson gives you a complete decision flowchart. Trigonometric integrals arise naturally in any field involving periodic phenomena. Electrical engineers compute power dissipation in AC circuits by integrating sin²(ωt) over a period — giving the "RMS" (root mean square) values that appear on every voltmeter. Structural engineers compute bending moments in beams under sinusoidal loads. In optics, interference patterns involve integrals of cos² and sin·cos products. Fourier analysis — the mathematical backbone of audio processing, telecommunications, and image compression — requires evaluating ∫sin^m(x)cos^n(x)dx for all combinations of m and n. The fundamental challenge with trig integrals is that powers of trig functions are not in the basic antiderivative table. You know $\int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x$ and $\int \cos x\,dx = \sin x$, but $\int \sin^2 x\,dx$ is not directly available. The strategy is always the same: use trigonometric identities to convert the integrand into a form you CAN integrate. For products $\sin^m x \cos^n x$, the strategy depends on whether $m$ or $n$ is odd. If one exponent is odd, peel off one factor and use the Pythagorean identity to convert the rest. For example, $\int \sin^3 x \cos^2 x\,dx$: peel off one $\sin x$ to get $\sin^2 x \cos^2 x \cdot \sin x\,dx$, replace $\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x$, and substitute $u = \cos x$. The integral becomes a polynomial in $u$. If BOTH exponents are even, peeling off one factor does not help (it leaves an odd power that cannot be converted using $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$ cleanly). Instead, use the half-angle identities: $\sin^2 x = (1 - \cos 2x)/2$ and $\cos^2 x = (1 + \cos 2x)/2$. These reduce the powers by converting $\sin^2$ and $\cos^2$ into first-degree trig functions of $2x$. You may need to apply half-angle identities multiple times for higher even powers. For powers of tangent and secant, the strategies are different. The key identity is $\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1$. For $\int \tan^n x\,dx$, write $\tan^n x = \tan^{n-2} x \cdot \tan^2 x = \tan^{n-2} x(\sec^2 x - 1)$, which splits into $\int \tan^{n-2} x \sec^2 x\,dx$ (u-sub with $u = \tan x$) minus $\int \tan^{n-2} x\,dx$ (a lower power). This is a reduction formula. For $\int \sec^n x\,dx$ with even $n$, save a $\sec^2 x$ factor and convert the rest using $\sec^2 x = 1 + \tan^2 x$, then substitute $u = \tan x$. For odd powers of secant, integration by parts is needed — and $\int \sec^3 x\,dx$ is a famously tricky integral that combines by-parts with the identity $\sec^2 x = 1 + \tan^2 x$. Here is the complete decision flowchart for $\int \sin^m x \cos^n x\,dx$: (1) If $n$ is odd: save one $\cos x$, write the rest as $(1-\sin^2 x)^{(n-1)/2}$, substitute $u = \sin x$. (2) If $m$ is odd: save one $\sin x$, write the rest as $(1-\cos^2 x)^{(m-1)/2}$, substitute $u = \cos x$. (3) If both are even: use half-angle identities to reduce powers. For $\int \tan^m x \sec^n x\,dx$: (1) If $n$ is even: save $\sec^2 x$, convert remaining $\sec$ to $\tan$ via $\sec^2 = 1 + \tan^2$, substitute $u = \tan x$. (2) If $m$ is odd: save $\sec x \tan x$, convert remaining $\tan$ to $\sec$ via $\tan^2 = \sec^2 - 1$, substitute $u = \sec x$. The Wallis formulas give closed-form results for $\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^n x\,dx$ and $\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^n x\,dx$. By the reduction formula, $\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^n x\,dx = \frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\frac{n-3}{n-2}\cdots$ The product ends at $\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}$ if $n$ is even, or at $1$ if $n$ is odd. These formulas are used in physics (computing moments of inertia of spheres) and lead to the beautiful Wallis product for $\pi$: $\pi/2 = (2/1)(2/3)(4/3)(4/5)(6/5)(6/7)\cdots$ Case 1 — odd power of cosine: $\int \sin^m x \cos^{2k+1} x\,dx$. Save one $\cos x$: $= \int \sin^m x (\cos^2 x)^k \cos x\,dx = \int \sin^m x (1-\sin^2 x)^k \cos x\,dx$. Substitute $u = \sin x$, $du = \cos x\,dx$: $= \int u^m(1-u^2)^k\,du$. Expand $(1-u^2)^k$ and integrate each term by the power rule. Case 2 — odd power of sine: $\int \sin^{2k+1} x \cos^n x\,dx$. Save one $\sin x$: $= \int (\sin^2 x)^k \cos^n x \sin x\,dx = \int (1-\cos^2 x)^k \cos^n x \sin x\,dx$. Substitute $u = \cos x$, $du = -\sin x\,dx$: $= -\int (1-u^2)^k u^n\,du$. Case 3 — both even: use half-angle identities repeatedly. $\int \sin^{2m} x \cos^{2n} x\,dx$. Replace $\sin^2 x = (1-\cos 2x)/2$ and $\cos^2 x = (1+\cos 2x)/2$. Expand the product and integrate each term. For the resulting $\cos^2(2x)$ terms, apply the half-angle identity again with argument $4x$. Tangent powers: $\int \tan^n x\,dx = \int \tan^{n-2} x(\sec^2 x - 1)\,dx = \int \tan^{n-2} x \sec^2 x\,dx - \int \tan^{n-2} x\,dx$. The first integral is $\tan^{n-1} x/(n-1)$ by $u = \tan x$. This gives the reduction formula: $\int \tan^n x\,dx = \frac{\tan^{n-1} x}{n-1} - \int \tan^{n-2} x\,dx$. Secant powers (even): $\int \sec^{2k} x\,dx = \int (\sec^2 x)^{k-1} \sec^2 x\,dx = \int (1+\tan^2 x)^{k-1} \sec^2 x\,dx$. Substitute $u = \tan x$: $= \int (1+u^2)^{k-1}\,du$, a polynomial integral. Secant powers (odd, $\geq 3$): use integration by parts. The key result is $\int \sec^3 x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}[\sec x \tan x + \ln|\sec x + \tan x|] + C$. Wallis formulas: $\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^n x\,dx = \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^n x\,dx = \frac{(n-1)!!}{n!!} \cdot \begin{cases} \pi/2 & n \text{ even} \\ 1 & n \text{ odd} \end{cases}$, where $n!! = n(n-2)(n-4)\cdots$ (double factorial). For example, $\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^6 x\,dx = \frac{5\cdot3\cdot1}{6\cdot4\cdot2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{5\pi}{32}$. The half-angle identities are derived from the double-angle formula $\cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x - 1$. Solving for $\sin^2 x$: $\sin^2 x = (1 - \cos 2x)/2$. Solving for $\cos^2 x$: $\cos^2 x = (1 + \cos 2x)/2$. These are exact algebraic identities, not approximations. The reduction formula for $\int \sin^n x\,dx$ is derived by integration by parts. Let $u = \sin^{n-1} x$, $dv = \sin x\,dx$. Then $du = (n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x\,dx$ and $v = -\cos x$. Applying by-parts: $\int \sin^n x\,dx = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\cos^2 x\,dx$. Replace $\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x$: $= -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int \sin^{n-2}x\,dx - (n-1)\int \sin^n x\,dx$. Let $I_n = \int \sin^n x\,dx$. Then $I_n = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)I_{n-2} - (n-1)I_n$. Solving: $nI_n = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)I_{n-2}$, giving $I_n = -\frac{1}{n}\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + \frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}$. The Wallis formula for definite integrals over $[0, \pi/2]$ follows from the reduction formula evaluated at the endpoints. Since $\sin(0) = 0$ and $\sin(\pi/2) = 1$, the boundary term $[-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x]_0^{\pi/2}$ equals $-1^{n-1}\cdot 0 + 0 = 0$ for all $n \geq 1$. Thus $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^n x\,dx = \frac{n-1}{n}\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x\,dx$. Iterating: for even $n = 2k$, the chain terminates at $\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx = \pi/2$; for odd $n = 2k+1$, it terminates at $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\,dx = 1$. The Wallis product formula for $\pi$ follows from comparing $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2n}x\,dx$ and $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2n+1}x\,dx$. Since $0 \leq \sin x \leq 1$ on $[0, \pi/2]$, we have $\sin^{2n+1}x \leq \sin^{2n}x \leq \sin^{2n-1}x$. Integrating and dividing by $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2n+1}x\,dx$, then taking $n \to \infty$ (using the squeeze theorem), yields the Wallis product: $\pi/2 = \prod_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{4k^2}{4k^2-1}$. Reduction Formula for sin^n (Proof Sketch) By parts with \(u = \sin^{n-1}x\), \(dv = \sin x\,dx\):
\[I_n = -\frac{1}{n}\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + \frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}\]

documents.proofs:
The validity of trig substitution rests on the invertibility of the substitution on the relevant domain. For $x = a\sin\theta$ with $\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]$, the function $\sin$ is a bijection from $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ to $[-a, a]$ (after scaling by $a$). This ensures that $\theta = \arcsin(x/a)$ is well-defined, and the back-substitution is unambiguous. For $x = a\tan\theta$ with $\theta \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)$, $\tan$ is a bijection from $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$ to $(-\infty, \infty)$, so $\theta = \arctan(x/a)$ is always well-defined. For $x = a\sec\theta$, the situation is slightly more delicate: $\sec$ on $[0, \pi/2)$ maps to $[1, \infty)$, and on $(\pi/2, \pi]$ maps to $(-\infty, -1]$. We choose the branch matching the sign of $x$. The substitution theorem for definite integrals guarantees that $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} f(g(\theta))g'(\theta)\,d\theta$ when $x = g(\theta)$ is $C^1$ with $g(\alpha) = a$ and $g(\beta) = b$. The requirement that $g$ be $C^1$ is satisfied by $a\sin\theta$, $a\tan\theta$, and $a\sec\theta$ on their respective domains. The theorem does NOT require $g$ to be one-to-one for definite integrals (the formula holds regardless), but one-to-one ensures the back-substitution for indefinite integrals is well-defined. Geometric verification for the semicircle: $\int_{-a}^{a} \sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx$ should equal $\pi a^2/2$ (area of a semicircle). With $x = a\sin\theta$: the integral becomes $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} a\cos\theta \cdot a\cos\theta\,d\theta = a^2 \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos^2\theta\,d\theta = a^2 \cdot \pi/2 = \pi a^2/2$. The trig substitution method correctly reproduces the geometric result. Domain Restrictions Ensure Well-Defined Back-Substitution For \(x = a\sin\theta\): restrict \(\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]\) so \(\cos\theta \geq 0\) and \(\theta = \arcsin(x/a)\) is unique.
For \(x = a\tan\theta\): restrict \(\theta \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)\) so \(\sec\theta > 0\) and \(\theta = \arctan(x/a)\).
For \(x = a\sec\theta\): choose the branch matching \(\text{sgn}(x)\).
documents.applications:
Trig substitution appears whenever geometry meets calculus. Computing the area of an ellipse (∫√(a²−x²) dx) uses the sin substitution and yields πab. Gravitational and electric field calculations involve integrals with √(x²+a²) denominators. Orbital mechanics integrates √(r²−b²) terms for trajectory computations. The arc length of a parabola requires ∫√(1+4x²) dx — a tan substitution. In statistics, normalizing the t-distribution uses ∫(1+x²/n)^(−(n+1)/2) dx, simplified by trig substitution. Which Substitution to Use • √(a² − x²) → x = a sin θ (think: Pythagorean identity sin²+cos²=1)
• √(a² + x²) → x = a tan θ (think: 1+tan²=sec²)
• √(x² − a²) → x = a sec θ (think: sec²−1=tan²)
Mnemonic: the sign between a² and x² determines the identity. Always Draw the Reference Triangle After integrating in θ, you must convert back to x. Draw the right triangle: label the sides based on your substitution (e.g., for x = a sin θ: opp = x, hyp = a, adj = √(a²−x²)). Read off cos θ, tan θ, etc. from the triangle. This avoids algebraic errors in back-substitution. Trig Sub Is Not Just for Radicals Trig substitution also works for expressions like 1/(a²+x²)^n without a visible radical. For instance, ∫dx/(1+x²)² is solved by x = tan θ, giving ∫cos²θ dθ. Any expression involving a²±x² or x²−a² (even without a √) can potentially benefit from trig sub. Completing the Square If the expression under the radical is ax² + bx + c, complete the square first: a(x + b/2a)² + (c − b²/4a). Then let u = x + b/(2a) to put it in standard form (u² ± k²) before applying trig substitution.

How do you integrate √(4 − x²)? No algebraic trick or u-substitution removes the square root. But if you let x = 2 sin θ, then √(4 − x²) = √(4 − 4sin²θ) = 2cos θ — the radical vanishes! The integral becomes a trig integral, which you already know how to solve. Trigonometric substitution is a technique that uses the Pythagorean identity to eliminate radicals. On the unit circle, $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$, which means $\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta}$. The combination of eliminating the radical AND transforming $dx$ usually converts the integral into a standard trig integral from Lesson 8.
