All trig functions of θ can be read directly from the triangle, enabling back-substitution without memorization. Semicircle Area: ∫√(4−x²) dx \text{Find } \int \sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx. ∫√(4−x²) dx = 2 arcsin(x/2) + x√(4−x²)/2 + C. Evaluating from −2 to 2 gives 2π — the area of a semicircle of radius 2. \sqrt{a^2-x^2} \text{ form with } a=2. \text{ Let } x = 2\sin\theta, \; dx = 2\cos\theta\,d\theta Case 1 substitution. \sqrt{4-x^2} = \sqrt{4-4\sin^2\theta} = 2\cos\theta The radical becomes 2cosθ. \int \sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx = \int 2\cos\theta \cdot 2\cos\theta\,d\theta = 4\int \cos^2\theta\,d\theta Substitute everything. = 4\cdot\frac{1}{2}(\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta) + C = 2\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta + C ∫cos²θ dθ = θ/2 + sin(2θ)/4 = (θ + sinθ cosθ)/2. \text{Back-sub: } \theta = \arcsin(x/2),\; \sin\theta = x/2,\; \cos\theta = \sqrt{4-x^2}/2 Use the reference triangle: opp = x, hyp = 2, adj = √(4−x²). = 2\arcsin\frac{x}{2} + 2\cdot\frac{x}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{4-x^2}}{2} + C = 2\arcsin\frac{x}{2} + \frac{x\sqrt{4-x^2}}{2} + C Final answer in terms of x. ∫dx/(x²+1)^(3/2) \text{Find } \int \frac{dx}{(x^2+1)^{3/2}}. ∫dx/(x²+1)^(3/2) = x/√(x²+1) + C. The tan substitution turned a formidable-looking integral into ∫cosθ dθ. \sqrt{x^2+a^2} \text{ with } a=1. \text{ Let } x = \tan\theta, \; dx = \sec^2\theta\,d\theta Case 2 substitution. x^2+1 = \tan^2\theta+1 = \sec^2\theta, \; (x^2+1)^{3/2} = \sec^3\theta Simplify the denominator. \int \frac{\sec^2\theta}{\sec^3\theta}\,d\theta = \int \frac{d\theta}{\sec\theta} = \int \cos\theta\,d\theta Cancel sec²θ/sec³θ = 1/secθ = cosθ. = \sin\theta + C ∫cosθ dθ = sinθ + C. \text{Reference triangle: adj}=1, \text{ opp}=x, \text{ hyp}=\sqrt{x^2+1}. \; \sin\theta = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} Read sinθ from the triangle. = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} + C Final answer. ∫x²/√(9−x²) dx \text{Find } \int \frac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\,dx. ∫x²/√(9−x²) dx = (9/2)arcsin(x/3) − x√(9−x²)/2 + C. \text{Let } x = 3\sin\theta, \; dx = 3\cos\theta\,d\theta, \; \sqrt{9-x^2} = 3\cos\theta Case 1 with a = 3. \int \frac{9\sin^2\theta}{3\cos\theta}\cdot 3\cos\theta\,d\theta = 9\int \sin^2\theta\,d\theta The cosθ factors cancel. = 9\cdot\frac{1}{2}(\theta - \sin\theta\cos\theta) + C ∫sin²θ dθ = θ/2 − sin(2θ)/4 = (θ − sinθ cosθ)/2. = \frac{9}{2}\arcsin\frac{x}{3} - \frac{9}{2}\cdot\frac{x}{3}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{9-x^2}}{3} + C Back-sub: θ = arcsin(x/3), sinθ = x/3, cosθ = √(9−x²)/3. = \frac{9}{2}\arcsin\frac{x}{3} - \frac{x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{2} + C Simplify: 9/(2·9) = 1/2. ∫dx/√(x²−9) \text{Find } \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-9}} \text{ for } x > 3. ∫dx/√(x²−9) = ln|x + √(x²−9)| + C. This is equivalent to arccosh(x/3) + C. \text{Let } x = 3\sec\theta, \; dx = 3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta, \; \sqrt{x^2-9} = 3\tan\theta Case 3 with a = 3. \int \frac{3\sec\theta\tan\theta}{3\tan\theta}\,d\theta = \int \sec\theta\,d\theta The 3tanθ factors cancel. = \ln|\sec\theta + \tan\theta| + C Standard integral of secθ. \text{Reference triangle: hyp}=x,\text{ adj}=3,\text{ opp}=\sqrt{x^2-9} secθ = x/3, tanθ = √(x²−9)/3. = \ln\left|\frac{x}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}{3}\right| + C = \ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2-9}\right| - \ln 3 + C Simplify. The −ln 3 can be absorbed into C. = \ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2-9}\right| + C Final simplified form. Completing the Square: ∫dx/√(x²+4x+8) \text{Find } \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+4x+8}}. ∫dx/√(x²+4x+8) = ln|x+2+√(x²+4x+8)| + C. Completing the square is the essential first step when the quadratic has a linear term. x^2+4x+8 = (x+2)^2 + 4 Complete the square: x²+4x+4+4 = (x+2)²+4. \text{Let } u = x+2,\; du = dx. \text{ Then } \int\frac{du}{\sqrt{u^2+4}} Shift to standard form. \text{Let } u = 2\tan\theta,\; du = 2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta,\; \sqrt{u^2+4} = 2\sec\theta Case 2 with a = 2. \int\frac{2\sec^2\theta}{2\sec\theta}d\theta = \int \sec\theta\,d\theta = \ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|+C Simplify and integrate. \sec\theta = \frac{\sqrt{u^2+4}}{2},\; \tan\theta = \frac{u}{2} = \frac{x+2}{2} Back-substitute using the reference triangle. = \ln\left|\frac{\sqrt{(x+2)^2+4}}{2}+\frac{x+2}{2}\right|+C = \ln|x+2+\sqrt{x^2+4x+8}|+C Simplify, absorbing −ln 2 into C. Find ∫dx/√(1−x²). (You should recognize this from the antiderivative table — verify it using the sin substitution.) Let x = sinθ, dx = cosθ dθ. √(1−x²) = cosθ. \arcsin x + C x = \sin\theta,\; dx = \cos\theta\,d\theta,\; \sqrt{1-x^2}=\cos\theta Standard sin substitution with a = 1. \int \frac{\cos\theta}{\cos\theta}d\theta = \int d\theta = \theta + C = \arcsin x + C The integral is trivially θ, which equals arcsin(x). Evaluate ∫₀² √(4+x²) dx. Let x = 2tanθ. Change limits: x=0 → θ=0, x=2 → θ=π/4. You will need ∫sec³θ dθ from Lesson 8. 2\sqrt{2}+2\ln(1+\sqrt{2}) \approx 4.591 x = 2\tan\theta,\; dx = 2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta,\; \sqrt{4+x^2} = 2\sec\theta Case 2 with a = 2. \int_0^{\pi/4} 2\sec\theta\cdot 2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta = 4\int_0^{\pi/4}\sec^3\theta\,d\theta Limits: x=0→θ=0, x=2→θ=π/4. \int \sec^3\theta\,d\theta = \frac{1}{2}[\sec\theta\tan\theta + \ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|] From Lesson 8. = 4\cdot\frac{1}{2}[\sec\theta\tan\theta+\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|]_0^{\pi/4} Evaluate at limits. = 2[(\sqrt{2})(1)+\ln(\sqrt{2}+1) - (1)(0) - \ln(1+0)] At θ=π/4: secθ=√2, tanθ=1. At θ=0: secθ=1, tanθ=0. = 2[\sqrt{2}+\ln(1+\sqrt{2})] ln 1 = 0. Find ∫x³/√(x²+4) dx using trig substitution. Then verify by using the algebraic substitution u = x²+4 instead. Trig: x = 2tanθ. Algebraic: u = x²+4, then x² = u−4 and x dx = du/2. \frac{(x^2-8)\sqrt{x^2+4}}{3}+C \text{Trig sub: } x=2\tan\theta,\; x^3 = 8\tan^3\theta,\; \sqrt{x^2+4}=2\sec\theta,\; dx=2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta Set up. \int \frac{8\tan^3\theta}{2\sec\theta}\cdot 2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta = 8\int \tan^3\theta\sec\theta\,d\theta Simplify: 8·2/(2)·sec = 8 tanθ³ secθ. = 8\int \tan^2\theta\cdot\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta = 8\int(\sec^2\theta-1)\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta Write tan²θ = sec²θ−1, save secθ tanθ for du. u=\sec\theta: 8\int(u^2-1)du = 8(u^3/3-u)+C = \frac{8}{3}\sec^3\theta - 8\sec\theta + C Integrate. \sec\theta = \sqrt{x^2+4}/2: \; = \frac{8}{3}\cdot\frac{(x^2+4)^{3/2}}{8} - 8\cdot\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{2}+C Back-substitute. = \frac{(x^2+4)^{3/2}}{3} - 4\sqrt{x^2+4} + C = \frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{3}(x^2+4-12)+C = \frac{(x^2-8)\sqrt{x^2+4}}{3}+C Factor and simplify. Trig Integrals After trig substitution, you always face a trig integral. Master Lesson 8 first. U-Substitution Sometimes an algebraic u-sub is simpler than trig sub — always consider both approaches. Trig Review The three Pythagorean identities are the foundation of trig substitution. Improper Integrals Trig substitution often appears in improper integrals involving radicals. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step trig sine cosine tangent unit circle

documents.assignment: Distinct Linear: ∫(2x+1)/((x−1)(x+2)) dx \text{Find } \int \frac{2x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\,dx.   ∫(2x+1)/((x−1)(x+2)) dx = ln|(x−1)(x+2)| + C. Heaviside cover-up makes finding A and B almost instant. \frac{2x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{x+2} Set up the partial fraction form: distinct linear factors. \text{Heaviside: } A = \frac{2(1)+1}{1+2} = \frac{3}{3} = 1 Cover up (x−1), evaluate at x = 1. B = \frac{2(-2)+1}{-2-1} = \frac{-3}{-3} = 1 Cover up (x+2), evaluate at x = −2. \int \frac{2x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\,dx = \int\frac{1}{x-1}dx + \int\frac{1}{x+2}dx Both coefficients are 1. = \ln|x-1| + \ln|x+2| + C = \ln|(x-1)(x+2)| + C Each integrates to a logarithm. Combine using ln a + ln b = ln(ab). Repeated Factor: ∫x/((x−1)²(x+1)) dx \text{Find } \int \frac{x}{(x-1)^2(x+1)}\,dx.   ∫x/((x−1)²(x+1)) dx = (1/4)ln|(x−1)/(x+1)| − 1/(2(x−1)) + C. \frac{x}{(x-1)^2(x+1)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{(x-1)^2} + \frac{C}{x+1} Repeated factor (x−1)² requires TWO terms. \text{Heaviside for } B: \text{cover } (x-1)^2, \text{ eval at } x=1: \; B = \frac{1}{1+1} = \frac{1}{2} B is found directly. \text{Heaviside for } C: \text{cover } (x+1), \text{ eval at } x=-1: \; C = \frac{-1}{(-1-1)^2} = \frac{-1}{4} C is found directly. \text{For } A: \text{multiply out and compare. Set } x=0: \; \frac{0}{(−1)^2(1)} = A(−1)(1)+B(1)+C(−1)^2 Substitute a convenient value x = 0. 0 = -A + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{-1}{4} = -A + \frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow A = \frac{1}{4} Solve for A. \int \frac{x}{(x-1)^2(x+1)}dx = \frac{1}{4}\ln|x-1| - \frac{1}{2(x-1)} - \frac{1}{4}\ln|x+1| + C ∫A/(x−1) = A ln|x−1|; ∫B/(x−1)² = −B/(x−1); ∫C/(x+1) = C ln|x+1|. = \frac{1}{4}\ln\left|\frac{x-1}{x+1}\right| - \frac{1}{2(x-1)} + C Combine logarithms. Irreducible Quadratic: ∫(x²+1)/(x³+x) dx \text{Find } \int \frac{x^2+1}{x^3+x}\,dx.   ∫(x²+1)/(x³+x) dx = ln|x| + C. Lesson: always check for cancellation before setting up partial fractions. x^3+x = x(x^2+1) Factor the denominator. x²+1 is irreducible (discriminant = −4 < 0). \frac{x^2+1}{x(x^2+1)} = \frac{1}{x} Wait — x²+1 cancels! The fraction simplifies before decomposition. \int \frac{x^2+1}{x^3+x}\,dx = \int \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln|x| + C Always simplify first. True Quadratic: ∫(3x+5)/(x²+2x+5) dx \text{Find } \int \frac{3x+5}{x^2+2x+5}\,dx.   ∫(3x+5)/(x²+2x+5) dx = (3/2)ln(x²+2x+5) + arctan((x+1)/2) + C. The split into "derivative of denominator" and "constant over denominator" is the standard technique for irreducible quadratics. x^2+2x+5 = (x+1)^2+4 Complete the square. Discriminant = 4−20 < 0, so irreducible. 3x+5 = 3(x+1)+2 Rewrite numerator in terms of (x+1) to match the completed square. \int \frac{3(x+1)}{(x+1)^2+4}dx + \int \frac{2}{(x+1)^2+4}dx Split into two integrals. \text{First: } u=(x+1)^2+4,\; du=2(x+1)dx: \; \frac{3}{2}\ln[(x+1)^2+4] U-sub gives a logarithm. \text{Second: } \frac{2}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{1}\arctan\frac{x+1}{2} = \arctan\frac{x+1}{2} ∫du/(u²+a²) = (1/a)arctan(u/a). Here a = 2: 2·(1/2)arctan((x+1)/2). = \frac{3}{2}\ln(x^2+2x+5) + \arctan\frac{x+1}{2} + C Combine. Note: (x+1)²+4 = x²+2x+5 is always positive, no absolute value needed. Long Division First: ∫(x³−2x+3)/(x²−1) dx \text{Find } \int \frac{x^3-2x+3}{x^2-1}\,dx.   ∫(x³−2x+3)/(x²−1) dx = x²/2 + ln|x−1| − 2ln|x+1| + C. Always do long division when the numerator degree ≥ denominator degree. \frac{x^3-2x+3}{x^2-1} = x + \frac{-x+3}{x^2-1} Degree of numerator (3) ≥ degree of denominator (2). Long divide: x³ ÷ (x²−1) = x remainder −x+3. \frac{-x+3}{(x-1)(x+1)} = \frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+1} Factor x²−1 and decompose the proper fraction. A = \frac{-1+3}{1+1} = 1, \quad B = \frac{1+3}{-1-1} = -2 Heaviside cover-up. \int\left(x + \frac{1}{x-1} - \frac{2}{x+1}\right)dx Three simple integrals. = \frac{x^2}{2} + \ln|x-1| - 2\ln|x+1| + C Integrate each term.  Find ∫dx/((x+1)(x+3)) using the Heaviside cover-up method. A = 1/(1+3−1+1)... actually: cover (x+1), eval at x = −1: A = 1/(−1+3) = 1/2. Cover (x+3), eval at x = −3: B = 1/(−3+1) = −1/2. \frac{1}{2}\ln\left|\frac{x+1}{x+3}\right|+C  \frac{1}{(x+1)(x+3)} = \frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{B}{x+3} Standard form for distinct linear factors. A = \frac{1}{-1+3} = \frac{1}{2}, \quad B = \frac{1}{-3+1} = -\frac{1}{2} Cover-up method. \int \frac{dx}{(x+1)(x+3)} = \frac{1}{2}\ln|x+1|-\frac{1}{2}\ln|x+3|+C = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left|\frac{x+1}{x+3}\right|+C Integrate and combine logs.  Find ∫(2x²+3x+1)/(x³+x²) dx. Factor: x³+x² = x²(x+1). Repeated factor x² needs terms A/x + B/x² + C/(x+1). 2\ln|x|-\frac{1}{x}+C  \frac{2x^2+3x+1}{x^2(x+1)} = \frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x^2}+\frac{C}{x+1} Set up with repeated linear factor x². B:\text{ cover } x^2, x=0: B = \frac{1}{0+1} = 1. \quad C:\text{ cover } (x+1), x=-1: C = \frac{2-3+1}{(-1)^2} = 0 Heaviside for B and C. \text{For } A: \text{multiply by } x^2(x+1): 2x^2+3x+1 = Ax(x+1)+1\cdot(x+1)+0\cdot x^2 Substitute known B=1, C=0. \text{Compare } x^2: 2 = A. \text{ Check } x^1: 3 = A+1 = 3.\checkmark A = 2 confirmed. \int\left(\frac{2}{x}+\frac{1}{x^2}\right)dx = 2\ln|x|-\frac{1}{x}+C Integrate (C=0 term vanishes).  Find ∫(x²+2)/((x−1)(x²+x+1)) dx. Note that x³−1 = (x−1)(x²+x+1). Decompose into A/(x−1) + (Bx+C)/(x²+x+1). For the quadratic integral, complete the square: x²+x+1 = (x+1/2)² + 3/4. \ln|x-1|-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\arctan\frac{2x+1}{\sqrt{3}}+C  \frac{x^2+2}{(x-1)(x^2+x+1)} = \frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+x+1} x²+x+1 is irreducible (discriminant = 1−4 = −3 < 0). A = \frac{1+2}{1+1+1} = 1 Cover up (x−1), evaluate at x = 1. \text{Multiply out: } x^2+2 = 1\cdot(x^2+x+1)+(Bx+C)(x-1) Expand right side. x^2+2 = x^2+x+1+Bx^2-Bx+Cx-C = (1+B)x^2+(1-B+C)x+(1-C) Collect terms. x^2: 1=1+B \Rightarrow B=0. \quad x^0: 2=1-C \Rightarrow C=-1. \quad \text{Check } x^1: 0=1-0-1=0.\checkmark Compare coefficients. \int\frac{1}{x-1}dx + \int\frac{-1}{x^2+x+1}dx = \ln|x-1| - \int\frac{dx}{(x+1/2)^2+3/4} Complete the square: x²+x+1 = (x+1/2)² + 3/4. = \ln|x-1| - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}/2}\arctan\frac{x+1/2}{\sqrt{3}/2} + C = \ln|x-1|-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan\frac{2x+1}{\sqrt{3}}+C Apply ∫du/(u²+a²) = (1/a)arctan(u/a).
documents.proofs: The existence and uniqueness of partial fraction decomposition is guaranteed by algebra. Over a field $F$, the ring of polynomials $F[x]$ is a principal ideal domain, and partial fraction decomposition follows from the Chinese Remainder Theorem for $F[x]$-modules. In concrete terms: if $Q(x) = Q_1(x)Q_2(x)$ with $\gcd(Q_1, Q_2) = 1$, then for any $P$ with $\deg P < \deg Q$, there exist unique $P_1, P_2$ with $\deg P_i < \deg Q_i$ such that $P/Q = P_1/Q_1 + P_2/Q_2$. The proof of the Heaviside cover-up formula: $A_k = \lim_{x \to r_k}(x-r_k)\cdot P(x)/Q(x)$. Since $Q(x)$ has a simple root at $r_k$, write $Q(x) = (x-r_k)\tilde{Q}(x)$ where $\tilde{Q}(r_k) \neq 0$. Then $(x-r_k)P(x)/Q(x) = P(x)/\tilde{Q}(x) \to P(r_k)/\tilde{Q}(r_k)$ as $x \to r_k$. This equals the residue of $P/Q$ at $r_k$ — the same concept used in complex analysis for contour integrals. For repeated roots, the generalization uses derivatives: if $Q(x) = (x-r)^m \tilde{Q}(x)$, define $\phi(x) = (x-r)^m P(x)/Q(x) = P(x)/\tilde{Q}(x)$. Then $A_m = \phi(r)$, $A_{m-1} = \phi'(r)/1!$, $A_{m-2} = \phi''(r)/2!$, and in general $A_{m-j} = \phi^{(j)}(r)/j!$. This is the Taylor expansion of $\phi$ at $r$. The fact that every real polynomial factors into linear and irreducible quadratic factors follows from the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (every polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ complex roots, counted with multiplicity). Complex roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs $\alpha \pm \beta i$. Each pair gives a real quadratic factor $(x-\alpha)^2+\beta^2 = x^2-2\alpha x+\alpha^2+\beta^2$, which is irreducible over $\mathbb{R}$ (its discriminant $4\alpha^2-4(\alpha^2+\beta^2) = -4\beta^2 < 0$). Existence and Uniqueness For any proper rational function \(P(x)/Q(x)\), the partial fraction decomposition exists and is unique. This follows from the Chinese Remainder Theorem in the polynomial ring \(\mathbb{R}[x]\).
documents.applications: Partial fractions are essential in engineering. In control theory, the transfer function of a system H(s) = P(s)/Q(s) is decomposed into partial fractions to find the inverse Laplace transform — this is how engineers determine the time-domain response of circuits, mechanical systems, and feedback controllers. In signal processing, partial fractions decompose frequency-domain filters into first-order components. In pharmacokinetics, drug concentration models with multiple compartments produce rational functions of the Laplace variable, and partial fractions give the time-domain solution. The technique also appears in probability (generating functions) and number theory (formal power series). When to Use Partial Fractions Use partial fractions when the integrand is a rational function P(x)/Q(x) (polynomial over polynomial) and Q(x) can be factored. If the degree of P ≥ degree of Q, do long division first. This technique works for ALL rational functions — it is a complete method. Polynomial Long Division If deg(P) ≥ deg(Q), divide P by Q first. Example: (x³+2)/(x²−1) = x + remainder (x+2)/(x²−1). Only the proper fraction (x+2)/(x²−1) needs partial fraction decomposition. The polynomial part integrates directly. Factor Completely Before Decomposing Partial fractions require a fully factored denominator. x⁴−1 = (x²+1)(x−1)(x+1), not just (x²−1)(x²+1). If you miss a factorization, you will set up the wrong form and get stuck. Always check: can any quadratic factor be factored further? (Test discriminant: b²−4c < 0 means irreducible.) Laplace Transforms and Circuit Analysis In electrical engineering, the response of an RLC circuit to a step input is found by (1) writing the transfer function H(s) = 1/(s²+s+1), (2) decomposing into partial fractions (with complex or irreducible quadratic terms), and (3) inverse-transforming each piece. Partial fractions convert one hard transform into several easy ones. Repeated Factors Need Multiple Terms For (x−1)³ in the denominator, you need THREE terms: A/(x−1) + B/(x−1)² + C/(x−1)³. A common error is writing only A/(x−1)³. This gives too few unknowns and the decomposition fails.
documents.content:
How do you integrate 1/((x−1)(x+2))? Neither u-sub nor by-parts helps. But if you write 1/((x−1)(x+2)) = A/(x−1) + B/(x+2) for suitable constants A and B, each piece integrates to a logarithm. Partial fraction decomposition breaks any rational function into a sum of simple fractions, each of which has a known antiderivative. It is the algebraic key to integrating all rational functions. Partial fractions are essential in engineering. In control theory, the transfer function of a system H(s) = P(s)/Q(s) is decomposed into partial fractions to find the inverse Laplace transform — this is how engineers determine the time-domain response of circuits, mechanical systems, and feedback controllers. In signal processing, partial fractions decompose frequency-domain filters into first-order components. In pharmacokinetics, drug concentration models with multiple compartments produce rational functions of the Laplace variable, and partial fractions give the time-domain solution. The technique also appears in probability (generating functions) and number theory (formal power series). You already know how to add fractions: $1/(x-1) + 1/(x+2) = ((x+2)+(x-1))/((x-1)(x+2)) = (2x+1)/((x-1)(x+2))$. Partial fraction decomposition is this process in REVERSE. Given a complicated fraction like $(2x+1)/((x-1)(x+2))$, we break it back into $A/(x-1) + B/(x+2)$. Each simple fraction is easy to integrate: $\int A/(x-1)\,dx = A\ln|x-1| + C$. The method works because rational functions (polynomial over polynomial) can always be decomposed into a polynomial part (if the degree of the numerator is $\geq$ the degree of the denominator) plus a sum of "partial fractions" — terms of the form $A/(x-a)^k$ for real roots and $(Bx+C)/(x^2+bx+c)^k$ for irreducible quadratic factors. Each type has a known antiderivative. The first step is always: check degrees. If the numerator degree $\geq$ denominator degree, perform polynomial long division first to get a polynomial plus a proper fraction (numerator degree $<$ denominator degree). Only proper fractions get decomposed. For example, $\int (x^3+2)/(x^2-1)\,dx$: divide to get $x + (x+2)/(x^2-1)$, then decompose the proper fraction. For distinct linear factors, the decomposition is straightforward. Factor the denominator completely: $Q(x) = (x-r_1)(x-r_2)\cdots(x-r_n)$. Write $P(x)/Q(x) = A_1/(x-r_1) + A_2/(x-r_2) + \cdots + A_n/(x-r_n)$. Find $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ by multiplying both sides by $Q(x)$ and substituting the roots, or by comparing coefficients. The Heaviside cover-up method is a fast shortcut for distinct linear factors. To find the coefficient $A_k$ of $1/(x-r_k)$: "cover up" the factor $(x-r_k)$ in the denominator and evaluate the rest at $x = r_k$. Formally, $A_k = P(r_k)/\prod_{j \neq k}(r_k - r_j)$. This avoids setting up a system of equations and is extremely efficient for denominators with 3 or more distinct factors. For repeated linear factors like $(x-r)^m$, you need $m$ terms: $A_1/(x-r) + A_2/(x-r)^2 + \cdots + A_m/(x-r)^m$. The Heaviside method gives $A_m$ directly (plug in $x = r$), but the other coefficients require either comparing coefficients or differentiating the cover-up equation. Each term $A_k/(x-r)^k$ integrates as $A_k(x-r)^{1-k}/(1-k)$ for $k \geq 2$, or $A_1 \ln|x-r|$ for $k = 1$. For irreducible quadratic factors $(x^2+bx+c)$ (where $b^2-4c < 0$), the partial fraction has the form $(Bx+C)/(x^2+bx+c)$. To integrate: complete the square in the denominator, then split into two integrals — one giving a logarithm (via u-sub) and one giving an arctangent. For repeated quadratics $(x^2+bx+c)^k$, you need terms $(B_j x + C_j)/(x^2+bx+c)^j$ for $j = 1, 2, \ldots, k$. Setup for partial fractions. Let $P(x)/Q(x)$ be a proper rational function (deg $P$ < deg $Q$). Factor $Q(x)$ into linear and irreducible quadratic factors over $\mathbb{R}$: $Q(x) = (x-r_1)^{m_1}\cdots(x-r_p)^{m_p}(x^2+b_1x+c_1)^{n_1}\cdots(x^2+b_qx+c_q)^{n_q}$. The partial fraction decomposition is: $\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = \sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}\frac{A_{ij}}{(x-r_i)^j} + \sum_{i=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}\frac{B_{ij}x+C_{ij}}{(x^2+b_ix+c_i)^j}$. The constants $A_{ij}$, $B_{ij}$, $C_{ij}$ are uniquely determined. Finding coefficients — three methods: (1) Multiply both sides by $Q(x)$ and substitute the roots $x = r_i$ to find some constants (Heaviside). (2) Compare coefficients of like powers of $x$ on both sides. (3) Substitute convenient non-root values of $x$ (e.g., $x = 0$) to generate additional equations. In practice, a mix of all three is fastest. Integration of each type: $\int A/(x-r)\,dx = A\ln|x-r|+C$. $\int A/(x-r)^k\,dx = A(x-r)^{1-k}/(1-k)+C$ for $k \geq 2$. $\int (Bx+C)/(x^2+bx+c)\,dx$: complete the square, split into $\int (\text{du/u}) + \int (\text{d}\theta/(1+\theta^2))$, giving a $\ln$ and an $\arctan$. Integration of the quadratic type in detail: let $x^2+bx+c = (x+b/2)^2 + (c-b^2/4) = (x+b/2)^2+d^2$ where $d = \sqrt{c-b^2/4}$. Split $Bx+C = B(x+b/2) + (C-Bb/2)$. Then: $\int \frac{B(x+b/2)}{(x+b/2)^2+d^2}dx = \frac{B}{2}\ln[(x+b/2)^2+d^2]+C_1$ (u-sub with $u = (x+b/2)^2+d^2$). And: $\int \frac{C-Bb/2}{(x+b/2)^2+d^2}dx = \frac{C-Bb/2}{d}\arctan\frac{x+b/2}{d}+C_2$. The existence and uniqueness of partial fraction decomposition is guaranteed by algebra. Over a field $F$, the ring of polynomials $F[x]$ is a principal ideal domain, and partial fraction decomposition follows from the Chinese Remainder Theorem for $F[x]$-modules. In concrete terms: if $Q(x) = Q_1(x)Q_2(x)$ with $\gcd(Q_1, Q_2) = 1$, then for any $P$ with $\deg P < \deg Q$, there exist unique $P_1, P_2$ with $\deg P_i < \deg Q_i$ such that $P/Q = P_1/Q_1 + P_2/Q_2$. The proof of the Heaviside cover-up formula: $A_k = \lim_{x \to r_k}(x-r_k)\cdot P(x)/Q(x)$. Since $Q(x)$ has a simple root at $r_k$, write $Q(x) = (x-r_k)\tilde{Q}(x)$ where $\tilde{Q}(r_k) \neq 0$. Then $(x-r_k)P(x)/Q(x) = P(x)/\tilde{Q}(x) \to P(r_k)/\tilde{Q}(r_k)$ as $x \to r_k$. This equals the residue of $P/Q$ at $r_k$ — the same concept used in complex analysis for contour integrals. For repeated roots, the generalization uses derivatives: if $Q(x) = (x-r)^m \tilde{Q}(x)$, define $\phi(x) = (x-r)^m P(x)/Q(x) = P(x)/\tilde{Q}(x)$. Then $A_m = \phi(r)$, $A_{m-1} = \phi'(r)/1!$, $A_{m-2} = \phi''(r)/2!$, and in general $A_{m-j} = \phi^{(j)}(r)/j!$. This is the Taylor expansion of $\phi$ at $r$. The fact that every real polynomial factors into linear and irreducible quadratic factors follows from the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (every polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ complex roots, counted with multiplicity). Complex roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs $\alpha \pm \beta i$. Each pair gives a real quadratic factor $(x-\alpha)^2+\beta^2 = x^2-2\alpha x+\alpha^2+\beta^2$, which is irreducible over $\mathbb{R}$ (its discriminant $4\alpha^2-4(\alpha^2+\beta^2) = -4\beta^2 < 0$). Existence and Uniqueness For any proper rational function \(P(x)/Q(x)\), the partial fraction decomposition exists and is unique. This follows from the Chinese Remainder Theorem in the polynomial ring \(\mathbb{R}[x]\). When to Use Partial Fractions Use partial fractions when the integrand is a rational function P(x)/Q(x) (polynomial over polynomial) and Q(x) can be factored. If the degree of P ≥ degree of Q, do long division first. This technique works for ALL rational functions — it is a complete method. Polynomial Long Division If deg(P) ≥ deg(Q), divide P by Q first. Example: (x³+2)/(x²−1) = x + remainder (x+2)/(x²−1). Only the proper fraction (x+2)/(x²−1) needs partial fraction decomposition. The polynomial part integrates directly. Factor Completely Before Decomposing Partial fractions require a fully factored denominator. x⁴−1 = (x²+1)(x−1)(x+1), not just (x²−1)(x²+1). If you miss a factorization, you will set up the wrong form and get stuck. Always check: can any quadratic factor be factored further? (Test discriminant: b²−4c < 0 means irreducible.) Laplace Transforms and Circuit Analysis In electrical engineering, the response of an RLC circuit to a step input is found by (1) writing the transfer function H(s) = 1/(s²+s+1), (2) decomposing into partial fractions (with complex or irreducible quadratic terms), and (3) inverse-transforming each piece. Partial fractions convert one hard transform into several easy ones. Repeated Factors Need Multiple Terms For (x−1)³ in the denominator, you need THREE terms: A/(x−1) + B/(x−1)² + C/(x−1)³. A common error is writing only A/(x−1)³. This gives too few unknowns and the decomposition fails. Partial Fraction Forms Distinct linear \((x-r)\): \(\frac{A}{x-r}\)
Repeated linear \((x-r)^m\): \(\frac{A_1}{x-r}+\frac{A_2}{(x-r)^2}+\cdots+\frac{A_m}{(x-r)^m}\)
Irreducible quadratic \((x^2+bx+c)\): \(\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+bx+c}\)
Repeated quadratic: similar pattern with increasing powers. Heaviside Cover-Up Method For distinct linear factors: to find the coefficient of \(1/(x-r_k)\), cover up \((x-r_k)\) in the original fraction and evaluate at \(x = r_k\).
Example: \(\frac{5}{(x-1)(x+3)}\): coefficient of \(1/(x-1)\) is \(5/(1+3) = 5/4\). Coefficient of \(1/(x+3)\) is \(5/(-3-1) = -5/4\). Every Rational Function Is Integrable Since every polynomial factors over \(\mathbb{R}\) into linear and irreducible quadratic factors, and each partial fraction type has a known antiderivative (ln, power, arctan), every rational function has an elementary antiderivative. This is one of the great computational triumphs of calculus. Method Selection Trainer Switch on the rational/factorable trait and verify when partial fractions should be your first move. Decomposing a Rational Function The original rational function (dark curve) equals the sum of its partial fractions (lighter curves). Each simple fraction has a vertical asymptote at a root of the denominator. The decomposition separates the behavior near each asymptote into independent, integrable pieces. Distinct Linear: ∫(2x+1)/((x−1)(x+2)) dx \text{Find } \int \frac{2x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\,dx. ∫(2x+1)/((x−1)(x+2)) dx = ln|(x−1)(x+2)| + C. Heaviside cover-up makes finding A and B almost instant. \frac{2x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{x+2} Set up the partial fraction form: distinct linear factors. \text{Heaviside: } A = \frac{2(1)+1}{1+2} = \frac{3}{3} = 1 Cover up (x−1), evaluate at x = 1. B = \frac{2(-2)+1}{-2-1} = \frac{-3}{-3} = 1 Cover up (x+2), evaluate at x = −2. \int \frac{2x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\,dx = \int\frac{1}{x-1}dx + \int\frac{1}{x+2}dx Both coefficients are 1. = \ln|x-1| + \ln|x+2| + C = \ln|(x-1)(x+2)| + C Each integrates to a logarithm. Combine using ln a + ln b = ln(ab). Repeated Factor: ∫x/((x−1)²(x+1)) dx \text{Find } \int \frac{x}{(x-1)^2(x+1)}\,dx. ∫x/((x−1)²(x+1)) dx = (1/4)ln|(x−1)/(x+1)| − 1/(2(x−1)) + C. \frac{x}{(x-1)^2(x+1)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{(x-1)^2} + \frac{C}{x+1} Repeated factor (x−1)² requires TWO terms. \text{Heaviside for } B: \text{cover } (x-1)^2, \text{ eval at } x=1: \; B = \frac{1}{1+1} = \frac{1}{2} B is found directly. \text{Heaviside for } C: \text{cover } (x+1), \text{ eval at } x=-1: \; C = \frac{-1}{(-1-1)^2} = \frac{-1}{4} C is found directly. \text{For } A: \text{multiply out and compare. Set } x=0: \; \frac{0}{(−1)^2(1)} = A(−1)(1)+B(1)+C(−1)^2 Substitute a convenient value x = 0. 0 = -A + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{-1}{4} = -A + \frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow A = \frac{1}{4} Solve for A. \int \frac{x}{(x-1)^2(x+1)}dx = \frac{1}{4}\ln|x-1| - \frac{1}{2(x-1)} - \frac{1}{4}\ln|x+1| + C ∫A/(x−1) = A ln|x−1|; ∫B/(x−1)² = −B/(x−1); ∫C/(x+1) = C ln|x+1|. = \frac{1}{4}\ln\left|\frac{x-1}{x+1}\right| - \frac{1}{2(x-1)} + C Combine logarithms. Irreducible Quadratic: ∫(x²+1)/(x³+x) dx \text{Find } \int \frac{x^2+1}{x^3+x}\,dx. ∫(x²+1)/(x³+x) dx = ln|x| + C. Lesson: always check for cancellation before setting up partial fractions. x^3+x = x(x^2+1) Factor the denominator. x²+1 is irreducible (discriminant = −4 < 0). \frac{x^2+1}{x(x^2+1)} = \frac{1}{x} Wait — x²+1 cancels! The fraction simplifies before decomposition. \int \frac{x^2+1}{x^3+x}\,dx = \int \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln|x| + C Always simplify first. True Quadratic: ∫(3x+5)/(x²+2x+5) dx \text{Find } \int \frac{3x+5}{x^2+2x+5}\,dx. ∫(3x+5)/(x²+2x+5) dx = (3/2)ln(x²+2x+5) + arctan((x+1)/2) + C. The split into "derivative of denominator" and "constant over denominator" is the standard technique for irreducible quadratics. x^2+2x+5 = (x+1)^2+4 Complete the square. Discriminant = 4−20 < 0, so irreducible. 3x+5 = 3(x+1)+2 Rewrite numerator in terms of (x+1) to match the completed square. \int \frac{3(x+1)}{(x+1)^2+4}dx + \int \frac{2}{(x+1)^2+4}dx Split into two integrals. \text{First: } u=(x+1)^2+4,\; du=2(x+1)dx: \; \frac{3}{2}\ln[(x+1)^2+4] U-sub gives a logarithm. \text{Second: } \frac{2}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{1}\arctan\frac{x+1}{2} = \arctan\frac{x+1}{2} ∫du/(u²+a²) = (1/a)arctan(u/a). Here a = 2: 2·(1/2)arctan((x+1)/2). = \frac{3}{2}\ln(x^2+2x+5) + \arctan\frac{x+1}{2} + C Combine. Note: (x+1)²+4 = x²+2x+5 is always positive, no absolute value needed. Long Division First: ∫(x³−2x+3)/(x²−1) dx \text{Find } \int \frac{x^3-2x+3}{x^2-1}\,dx. ∫(x³−2x+3)/(x²−1) dx = x²/2 + ln|x−1| − 2ln|x+1| + C. Always do long division when the numerator degree ≥ denominator degree. \frac{x^3-2x+3}{x^2-1} = x + \frac{-x+3}{x^2-1} Degree of numerator (3) ≥ degree of denominator (2). Long divide: x³ ÷ (x²−1) = x remainder −x+3. \frac{-x+3}{(x-1)(x+1)} = \frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+1} Factor x²−1 and decompose the proper fraction. A = \frac{-1+3}{1+1} = 1, \quad B = \frac{1+3}{-1-1} = -2 Heaviside cover-up. \int\left(x + \frac{1}{x-1} - \frac{2}{x+1}\right)dx Three simple integrals. = \frac{x^2}{2} + \ln|x-1| - 2\ln|x+1| + C Integrate each term. Find ∫dx/((x+1)(x+3)) using the Heaviside cover-up method. A = 1/(1+3−1+1)... actually: cover (x+1), eval at x = −1: A = 1/(−1+3) = 1/2. Cover (x+3), eval at x = −3: B = 1/(−3+1) = −1/2. \frac{1}{2}\ln\left|\frac{x+1}{x+3}\right|+C \frac{1}{(x+1)(x+3)} = \frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{B}{x+3} Standard form for distinct linear factors. A = \frac{1}{-1+3} = \frac{1}{2}, \quad B = \frac{1}{-3+1} = -\frac{1}{2} Cover-up method. \int \frac{dx}{(x+1)(x+3)} = \frac{1}{2}\ln|x+1|-\frac{1}{2}\ln|x+3|+C = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left|\frac{x+1}{x+3}\right|+C Integrate and combine logs. Find ∫(2x²+3x+1)/(x³+x²) dx. Factor: x³+x² = x²(x+1). Repeated factor x² needs terms A/x + B/x² + C/(x+1). 2\ln|x|-\frac{1}{x}+C \frac{2x^2+3x+1}{x^2(x+1)} = \frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x^2}+\frac{C}{x+1} Set up with repeated linear factor x². B:\text{ cover } x^2, x=0: B = \frac{1}{0+1} = 1. \quad C:\text{ cover } (x+1), x=-1: C = \frac{2-3+1}{(-1)^2} = 0 Heaviside for B and C. \text{For } A: \text{multiply by } x^2(x+1): 2x^2+3x+1 = Ax(x+1)+1\cdot(x+1)+0\cdot x^2 Substitute known B=1, C=0. \text{Compare } x^2: 2 = A. \text{ Check } x^1: 3 = A+1 = 3.\checkmark A = 2 confirmed. \int\left(\frac{2}{x}+\frac{1}{x^2}\right)dx = 2\ln|x|-\frac{1}{x}+C Integrate (C=0 term vanishes). Find ∫(x²+2)/((x−1)(x²+x+1)) dx. Note that x³−1 = (x−1)(x²+x+1). Decompose into A/(x−1) + (Bx+C)/(x²+x+1). For the quadratic integral, complete the square: x²+x+1 = (x+1/2)² + 3/4. \ln|x-1|-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\arctan\frac{2x+1}{\sqrt{3}}+C \frac{x^2+2}{(x-1)(x^2+x+1)} = \frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+x+1} x²+x+1 is irreducible (discriminant = 1−4 = −3 < 0). A = \frac{1+2}{1+1+1} = 1 Cover up (x−1), evaluate at x = 1. \text{Multiply out: } x^2+2 = 1\cdot(x^2+x+1)+(Bx+C)(x-1) Expand right side. x^2+2 = x^2+x+1+Bx^2-Bx+Cx-C = (1+B)x^2+(1-B+C)x+(1-C) Collect terms. x^2: 1=1+B \Rightarrow B=0. \quad x^0: 2=1-C \Rightarrow C=-1. \quad \text{Check } x^1: 0=1-0-1=0.\checkmark Compare coefficients. \int\frac{1}{x-1}dx + \int\frac{-1}{x^2+x+1}dx = \ln|x-1| - \int\frac{dx}{(x+1/2)^2+3/4} Complete the square: x²+x+1 = (x+1/2)² + 3/4. = \ln|x-1| - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}/2}\arctan\frac{x+1/2}{\sqrt{3}/2} + C = \ln|x-1|-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan\frac{2x+1}{\sqrt{3}}+C Apply ∫du/(u²+a²) = (1/a)arctan(u/a). U-Substitution Partial fractions reduce rational integrals to simple forms, some of which need u-sub (e.g., ∫x/(x²+1) dx). Indefinite Integrals The antiderivative table entries ln|x|, arctan x, and power rules are the building blocks for partial fraction integration. Improper Integrals Partial fractions help evaluate improper integrals of rational functions by splitting them into convergent pieces. Integration by Parts Irreducible quadratic terms with higher powers may require by-parts in addition to partial fractions. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step

documents.assignment: Type 1: ∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx \text{Evaluate } \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx.   ∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx = 1. The infinite tail has finite area. This is the p-test with p = 2 > 1. \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty}\int_1^b x^{-2}\,dx Replace ∞ with a finite limit b. = \lim_{b \to \infty}\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_1^b = \lim_{b \to \infty}\left(-\frac{1}{b}+1\right) Antiderivative of x⁻² is −x⁻¹. Evaluate at limits. = 0 + 1 = 1 As b → ∞, 1/b → 0. Type 1 (Divergent): ∫₁^∞ 1/x dx \text{Show that } \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x}\,dx \text{ diverges.}   ∫₁^∞ 1/x dx diverges. Despite 1/x → 0, it approaches zero too slowly for the tail area to be finite. This is the borderline case p = 1. \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty}\int_1^b \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty}[\ln x]_1^b Set up the limit. = \lim_{b \to \infty}(\ln b - \ln 1) = \lim_{b \to \infty}\ln b = \infty ln b grows without bound. Type 1: ∫₀^∞ e^(−x) dx \text{Evaluate } \int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx.   ∫₀^∞ e^(−x) dx = 1. Exponentials decay fast enough for convergence. This integral is the total area of the exponential distribution with λ = 1. \int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty}\int_0^b e^{-x}\,dx Replace ∞ with b. = \lim_{b \to \infty}[-e^{-x}]_0^b = \lim_{b \to \infty}(-e^{-b}+e^0) Antiderivative of e^(−x) is −e^(−x). = 0 + 1 = 1 e^(−b) → 0 as b → ∞ (exponential decay). Type 2: ∫₀¹ 1/√x dx \text{Evaluate } \int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx.   ∫₀¹ 1/√x dx = 2. This is the p-test at 0 with p = 1/2 < 1 — convergent. \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \to \infty \text{ as } x \to 0^+ The integrand has a vertical asymptote at x = 0. This is Type 2. \int_0^1 x^{-1/2}dx = \lim_{\epsilon \to 0^+}\int_\epsilon^1 x^{-1/2}dx Replace 0 with ε and take the limit. = \lim_{\epsilon \to 0^+}[2x^{1/2}]_\epsilon^1 = \lim_{\epsilon \to 0^+}(2-2\sqrt{\epsilon}) Power rule: ∫x^(−1/2) dx = 2x^(1/2). = 2 - 0 = 2 √ε → 0 as ε → 0. Comparison Test: ∫₁^∞ 1/(x²+x) dx \text{Determine whether } \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2+x}\,dx \text{ converges and find its value.}   ∫₁^∞ 1/(x²+x) dx = ln 2. We confirmed convergence by comparison and computed the exact value by partial fractions. \frac{1}{x^2+x} \leq \frac{1}{x^2} \text{ for } x \geq 1 Comparison: x²+x > x², so 1/(x²+x) < 1/x². Since ∫1/x² converges, so does ∫1/(x²+x). \frac{1}{x^2+x} = \frac{1}{x(x+1)} = \frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{x+1} But we can also compute exactly using partial fractions! \int_1^b \left(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\right)dx = [\ln x - \ln(x+1)]_1^b = \ln\frac{b}{b+1}-\ln\frac{1}{2} Telescoping with logs. = \ln\frac{b}{b+1}+\ln 2 \to \ln 1 + \ln 2 = \ln 2 As b → ∞, b/(b+1) → 1, so ln(b/(b+1)) → 0. Gabriel's Horn: Finite Volume, Infinite Surface Area \text{Show that rotating } y = 1/x \text{ for } x \geq 1 \text{ around the x-axis gives volume } \pi \text{ but infinite surface area.}   Volume = π (finite), surface area = ∞. The horn can be filled with a finite amount of paint, but its surface cannot be painted. The paradox hinges on the difference between p = 2 (converges) and p = 1 (diverges). V = \pi\int_1^\infty \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)^2 dx = \pi\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \pi\cdot 1 = \pi Disk method. ∫1/x² from 1 to ∞ = 1 (Example 1). S = 2\pi\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{x^4}}\,dx Surface area formula for revolution. S \geq 2\pi\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x}\cdot 1\,dx = 2\pi\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \infty √(1+1/x⁴) ≥ 1, so S ≥ 2π∫1/x dx = ∞.  Evaluate ∫₂^∞ 1/x³ dx and ∫₀¹ 1/x^(2/3) dx. Both are p-integrals. First: p = 3 > 1, converges. Second: p = 2/3 < 1 at x = 0, converges. \frac{1}{8} \text{ and } 3  \int_2^\infty x^{-3}dx = \lim_{b\to\infty}\left[-\frac{1}{2x^2}\right]_2^b = 0+\frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{8} p = 3 > 1. Antiderivative: x^(−2)/(−2). \int_0^1 x^{-2/3}dx = \lim_{\epsilon\to 0^+}\left[3x^{1/3}\right]_\epsilon^1 = 3-0 = 3 p = 2/3 < 1. Antiderivative: x^(1/3)/(1/3) = 3x^(1/3).  Use the limit comparison test to determine whether ∫₁^∞ (x+3)/(x³−x+1) dx converges. For large x, (x+3)/(x³−x+1) behaves like x/x³ = 1/x². Compare with ∫1/x² dx. \text{Converges (by limit comparison with } 1/x^2\text{)}  \text{Let } f(x) = \frac{x+3}{x^3-x+1},\; g(x) = \frac{1}{x^2} Choose g based on dominant terms for large x. \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{(x+3)x^2}{x^3-x+1} = \frac{x^3+3x^2}{x^3-x+1} Compute the ratio. \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x^3+3x^2}{x^3-x+1} = \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1+3/x}{1-1/x^2+1/x^3} = 1 Divide numerator and denominator by x³. L = 1 \in (0,\infty), \text{ and } \int_1^\infty 1/x^2\,dx \text{ converges, so } \int_1^\infty f \text{ converges.} Limit comparison test applies.  Evaluate ∫₀^∞ x·e^(−x) dx. This integral gives the mean of the exponential distribution with λ = 1. Integration by parts with u = x, dv = e^(−x) dx, then take the limit. documents.proofs: The improper integral $\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx$ is defined as $\lim_{b \to \infty}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, provided this limit exists in $\mathbb{R}$. The ordinary Riemann integral $\int_a^b f$ is well-defined for each finite $b$ (assuming $f$ is integrable on every $[a,b]$). The improper integral extends this to an infinite interval by taking the limit of the finitely-defined object. For Type 2, the integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ where $f$ has a singularity at $a$ is defined as $\lim_{\epsilon \to 0^+}\int_{a+\epsilon}^b f(x)\,dx$. If $f$ is unbounded near $a$ but integrable on every $[a+\epsilon, b]$, this limit may or may not exist. The $p$-test provides the criterion: $f(x) \sim C/(x-a)^p$ near $a$ implies convergence iff $p < 1$. Proof of the $p$-test ($\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$). For $p \neq 1$: $\int_1^b x^{-p}\,dx = [x^{1-p}/(1-p)]_1^b = b^{1-p}/(1-p) - 1/(1-p)$. As $b \to \infty$: if $1-p < 0$ (i.e., $p > 1$), then $b^{1-p} \to 0$, giving limit $-1/(1-p) = 1/(p-1)$. If $1-p > 0$ (i.e., $p < 1$), then $b^{1-p} \to \infty$, giving divergence. If $1-p = 0$ (i.e., $p = 1$): $\int_1^b 1/x\,dx = \ln b \to \infty$. Gabriel's Horn — formal verification. Volume: $V = \pi\int_1^\infty (1/x)^2\,dx = \pi\int_1^\infty x^{-2}\,dx = \pi[−1/x]_1^\infty = \pi(0-(-1)) = \pi$. Surface area: $S = 2\pi\int_1^\infty (1/x)\sqrt{1+1/x^4}\,dx \geq 2\pi\int_1^\infty 1/x\,dx = \infty$ (since $\sqrt{1+1/x^4} \geq 1$). The volume integral converges ($p = 2 > 1$) while the surface area integral diverges (bounded below by a $p = 1$ integral). p-Test Proof \(\int_1^\infty x^{-p}dx = \frac{b^{1-p}-1}{1-p}\). As \(b \to \infty\): \(b^{1-p} \to 0\) iff \(1-p < 0\) iff \(p > 1\). The borderline case \(p = 1\) gives \(\ln b \to \infty\). This sharp cutoff explains why \(1/x^2\) is integrable but \(1/x\) is not.

Improper integrals are fundamental to probability theory: every continuous probability distribution satisfies ∫₋∞^∞ f(x) dx = 1 — an improper integral. The normal distribution integral ∫₋∞^∞ e^(−x²/2) dx = √(2π) is one of the most important results in statistics. Can you find the area under y = 1/x² from x = 1 to infinity? The region extends infinitely to the right, so the area must be infinite... right? Wrong. ∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx = [−1/x]₁^∞ = 0−(−1) = 1. An infinitely long region with FINITE area. How is this possible? And how do we know when an infinite integral gives a finite answer versus when it diverges to infinity? Improper integrals are fundamental to probability theory: every continuous probability distribution satisfies ∫₋∞^∞ f(x) dx = 1 — an improper integral. The normal distribution integral ∫₋∞^∞ e^(−x²/2) dx = √(2π) is one of the most important results in statistics. In physics, the total energy radiated by a black body is ∫₀^∞ ν³/(e^(hν/kT)−1) dν — an improper integral that Planck evaluated to derive quantum theory. In economics, the present value of a perpetual income stream is ∫₀^∞ R·e^(−rt) dt = R/r — the foundation of bond pricing and asset valuation. An improper integral arises when the "standard" Riemann integral definition breaks down — either because the interval is infinite or because the integrand blows up somewhere on the interval. There are two types: Type 1 has an infinite limit of integration (like $\int_1^\infty 1/x^2\,dx$), and Type 2 has a discontinuous integrand (like $\int_0^1 1/\sqrt{x}\,dx$, where $1/\sqrt{x} \to \infty$ as $x \to 0^+$). The idea for handling both types is the same: replace the problematic part with a finite limit, compute the ordinary integral, and then take the limit. For Type 1: $\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty} \int_1^b f(x)\,dx$. For Type 2 (discontinuity at $a$): $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{\epsilon \to 0^+} \int_{a+\epsilon}^b f(x)\,dx$. If the limit exists and is finite, the integral converges. If the limit is $\pm\infty$ or does not exist, the integral diverges. The $p$-integral test is the most important convergence test: $\int_1^\infty 1/x^p\,dx$ converges if and only if $p > 1$. At the boundary $p = 1$, we get $\int_1^\infty 1/x\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty} \ln b = \infty$ — divergent. For $p > 1$: $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx = [x^{1-p}/(1-p)]_1^\infty = 0 - 1/(1-p) = 1/(p-1)$ — convergent. The cutoff is sharp: $1/x^{1.001}$ has finite total area, but $1/x^{0.999}$ does not. There is also a $p$-test near zero: $\int_0^1 1/x^p\,dx$ converges if and only if $p < 1$. This is the mirror image: near zero, $1/x^p$ blows up, but for $p < 1$ it does not blow up fast enough to make the area infinite. At $p = 1$, $\int_0^1 1/x\,dx = \lim_{\epsilon \to 0^+}(-\ln \epsilon) = \infty$. So $1/x$ is the "boundary function" for both types. The comparison test lets you determine convergence without computing the integral. If $0 \leq f(x) \leq g(x)$ for all $x$ large enough, then: if $\int g$ converges, so does $\int f$ (smaller function, smaller area). If $\int f$ diverges, so does $\int g$ (larger function, larger area). Typically you compare against a known $p$-integral. For example, $\int_1^\infty e^{-x}\,dx$ converges because $e^{-x} \leq 1/x^2$ for large $x$ (exponentials decay faster than any power). The limit comparison test is often easier: if $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x)/g(x) = L$ with $0 < L < \infty$, then $\int f$ and $\int g$ either both converge or both diverge. This avoids proving an inequality; you just need the ratio to approach a positive constant. Compare $\int_1^\infty (3x+1)/(x^3+x^2)\,dx$ with $\int_1^\infty 3/x^2\,dx$: the ratio approaches 1, so both converge. Gabriel's Horn (Torricelli's trumpet) is a stunning paradox. Rotate $y = 1/x$ for $x \geq 1$ around the $x$-axis. The volume is $\pi\int_1^\infty 1/x^2\,dx = \pi$ — finite! But the surface area is $2\pi\int_1^\infty (1/x)\sqrt{1+1/x^4}\,dx \geq 2\pi\int_1^\infty 1/x\,dx = \infty$. You can fill the horn with paint (finite volume), but you cannot paint its surface (infinite area). This is not a contradiction — it reflects the difference between $\int 1/x^2$ (converges) and $\int 1/x$ (diverges). Type 1 (infinite limits): $\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$. Similarly, $\int_{-\infty}^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{a \to -\infty}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$. For $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx$: split at any point $c$: $\int_{-\infty}^c f + \int_c^\infty f$. Both must converge independently. Type 2 (discontinuous integrand): if $f$ has a vertical asymptote at $x = c \in [a,b]$, split at $c$: $\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$, where $\int_a^c f = \lim_{\epsilon \to 0^+}\int_a^{c-\epsilon}f$ and $\int_c^b f = \lim_{\epsilon \to 0^+}\int_{c+\epsilon}^b f$. If $1-p > 0$ (i.e., $p < 1$), then $b^{1-p} \to \infty$, giving divergence. If $1-p = 0$ (i.e., $p = 1$): $\int_1^b 1/x\,dx = \ln b \to \infty$. Gabriel's Horn — formal verification. The volume integral converges ($p = 2 > 1$) while the surface area integral diverges (bounded below by a $p = 1$ integral). p-Test Proof \(\int_1^\infty x^{-p}dx = \frac{b^{1-p}-1}{1-p}\). Convergence and Divergence An improper integral converges if the defining limit exists and is finite. Otherwise it diverges. A divergent integral may tend to \(+\infty\), \(-\infty\), or oscillate without approaching any limit. Comparison Tests Direct: if \(0 \leq f \leq g\) and \(\int g\) converges, then \(\int f\) converges.
Limit: if \(f/g \to L \in (0,\infty)\), then \(\int f\) and \(\int g\) share convergence behavior.
Usual comparison targets: \(1/x^p\) and \(e^{-x}\). Gaussian Integral \[\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\]
This integral has no elementary antiderivative but has a finite value, computed by a polar-coordinates trick (squaring and converting to 2D). It is the foundation of the normal distribution in statistics. Convergent vs. Divergent Improper Integrals Compare 1/x² (convergent, total area = 1) with 1/x (divergent, area grows without bound). Both approach the x-axis, but 1/x² approaches fast enough for the tail area to be finite. Python Lab: Watch Improper Integrals Converge (or Diverge) Compute ∫₁^b f(x)dx as b grows, see partial areas accumulate, and watch the p-test cutoff at p=1 in real time. Type 1: ∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx \text{Evaluate } \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx. ∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx = 1. The infinite tail has finite area. This is the p-test with p = 2 > 1. \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty}\int_1^b x^{-2}\,dx Replace ∞ with a finite limit b. = \lim_{b \to \infty}\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_1^b = \lim_{b \to \infty}\left(-\frac{1}{b}+1\right) Antiderivative of x⁻² is −x⁻¹. Evaluate at limits. = 0 + 1 = 1 As b → ∞, 1/b → 0. Type 1 (Divergent): ∫₁^∞ 1/x dx \text{Show that } \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x}\,dx \text{ diverges.} ∫₁^∞ 1/x dx diverges. documents.proofs: The trapezoidal rule error bound is derived from Taylor expansion. On each subinterval $[x_i, x_{i+1}]$, expand $f(x)$ around the midpoint $\bar{x}_i = (x_i+x_{i+1})/2$: $f(x) = f(\bar{x}_i) + f'(\bar{x}_i)(x-\bar{x}_i) + \frac{1}{2}f''(c_x)(x-\bar{x}_i)^2$. The trapezoid approximation on this interval is $h[f(x_i)+f(x_{i+1})]/2$. The error on this interval is $\int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}}f(x)\,dx - h[f(x_i)+f(x_{i+1})]/2 = -h^3 f''(c_i)/12$ for some $c_i \in [x_i, x_{i+1}]$. Summing over all $n$ subintervals: $E_T = -\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} h^3 f''(c_i)/12 = -nh^3 f''(\bar{c})/12 = -(b-a)h^2 f''(\bar{c})/12$, using the intermediate value theorem to replace the sum of $f''(c_i)$ by $nf''(\bar{c})$. The midpoint rule error is derived similarly. The local error on $[x_i, x_{i+1}]$ is $h^3 f''(c_i)/24$, giving $E_M = (b-a)h^2 f''(\bar{c})/24$. Note the OPPOSITE sign compared to the trapezoidal error — the midpoint rule overshoots where the trapezoidal undershoots (for concave-up functions), and vice versa. This is why their weighted average $(2M+T)/3$ achieves cancellation. Simpson's rule error requires the fourth derivative. The local error of Simpson's rule on $[x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}]$ (a double interval of width $2h$) is $-(2h)^5 f^{(4)}(c_i)/(2880)$. Summing over $n/2$ double intervals gives $E_S = -(b-a)h^4 f^{(4)}(\bar{c})/180$. The key fact is that Simpson's rule is exact not just for quadratics but for cubics — the $f'''$ error term vanishes by symmetry of the parabolic fit. This extra order of exactness is "free" and gives Simpson's its remarkable efficiency. Exactness for cubics (proof sketch): on a symmetric interval $[-h, h]$, the Simpson approximation for $f(x) = x^3$ gives $(h/3)[(-h)^3 + 4(0)^3 + h^3] = (h/3)(-h^3+h^3) = 0$. The exact integral $\int_{-h}^{h} x^3\,dx = 0$ by symmetry. So the error is zero. Since Simpson's rule is exact for polynomials of degree $\leq 2$ (by construction) and exact for degree 3 (by this symmetry argument), its leading error term involves $f^{(4)}$ rather than $f^{(3)}$. Simpson's Rule Is Exact for Cubics Even though Simpson's rule fits parabolas (degree 2), it integrates cubics (degree 3) exactly. This is because the cubic error term vanishes by symmetry of the fitting interval. The leading error is therefore proportional to \(f^{(4)}\) and \(h^4\), not \(f^{(3)}\) and \(h^3\).
documents.applications:
Numerical integration is one of the most widely used computational techniques in science and engineering. Weather prediction models integrate atmospheric equations at millions of grid points. Finite element analysis (used in bridge design, aircraft engineering, and crash simulations) is fundamentally numerical integration over complex domains. Monte Carlo integration computes high-dimensional integrals in finance (option pricing), physics (particle scattering), and machine learning (Bayesian inference). Modern graphics/path tracing evaluates the rendering equation by sampling and averaging illumination integrals over light directions. GPS satellites compute orbital integrals numerically. Every spreadsheet "SUM" over a column of measured data is a crude numerical integral. Which Method to Use For quick hand calculations: Trapezoidal rule (simple formula, easy to remember).
For high accuracy with few points: Simpson's rule (error ∝ 1/n⁴).
For data from experiments: Trapezoidal rule (only needs function values at endpoints).
For computer implementations: Adaptive Simpson's (automatically chooses n to meet a target accuracy). Simpson's Rule Requires Even n Simpson's rule fits parabolas through groups of THREE points, spanning TWO subintervals. This requires n (the number of subintervals) to be EVEN. If you use odd n, the formula does not apply. Always check: is n even? Riemann Sums Are the Foundation All numerical integration methods are refinements of Riemann sums. Left Riemann sums use the left endpoint; right sums use the right; midpoint sums use the center. The trapezoidal rule averages left and right. Simpson's rule goes further by fitting curves. Each refinement reduces the error for smooth functions. Numerical Integration in Engineering Software MATLAB's "integral" function, Python's scipy.integrate.quad, and Wolfram Alpha all use adaptive numerical integration internally. They start with a coarse grid, estimate the error, and refine only where needed. The underlying method is usually Gauss-Kronrod quadrature — a sophisticated descendant of Simpson's rule that achieves machine precision (15-16 digits) in milliseconds. Path Tracing = Monte Carlo Integration Photorealistic rendering evaluates integrals of incoming light over a hemisphere. More samples reduce variance like 1/sqrt(N), so numerical integration quality directly controls image noise and render time. More Points Is Not Always Better In theory, increasing n always reduces the error. In practice (on a computer), round-off errors from floating-point arithmetic eventually dominate. For n beyond a few thousand, the accumulated round-off can exceed the approximation error. The optimal n balances approximation error (decreasing) against round-off error (increasing).

How do you compute ∫₀¹ e^(−x²) dx? This function has no elementary antiderivative — no combination of polynomials, trig functions, exponentials, and logarithms will give you an answer. Yet the integral exists (it is about 0.7468). Numerical integration provides systematic methods to approximate any definite integral to arbitrary precision, complete with guaranteed error bounds. Numerical integration is one of the most widely used computational techniques in science and engineering. Weather prediction models integrate atmospheric equations at millions of grid points. Finite element analysis (used in bridge design, aircraft engineering, and crash simulations) is fundamentally numerical integration over complex domains. Monte Carlo integration computes high-dimensional integrals in finance (option pricing), physics (particle scattering), and machine learning (Bayesian inference). Modern graphics/path tracing evaluates the rendering equation by sampling and averaging illumination integrals over light directions. GPS satellites compute orbital integrals numerically. Every spreadsheet "SUM" over a column of measured data is a crude numerical integral. Numerical integration goes back to the original idea of Riemann sums: approximate the area under a curve by summing the areas of simple shapes. The question is not WHETHER we can approximate (we always can), but HOW ACCURATELY and HOW EFFICIENTLY. Different methods use different shapes — rectangles, trapezoids, parabolic arcs — and achieve different levels of accuracy for the same number of function evaluations. The midpoint rule uses rectangles whose height is the function value at the midpoint of each subinterval. If you divide $[a,b]$ into $n$ equal subintervals of width $h = (b-a)/n$, the midpoint rule gives $M_n = h\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(\bar{x}_i)$, where $\bar{x}_i = a + (i-1/2)h$ is the midpoint of the $i$-th subinterval. Geometrically, each rectangle touches the curve at the center, which tends to balance overestimates and underestimates. The trapezoidal rule replaces each rectangle with a trapezoid: connect the function values at the left and right endpoints with a straight line. The area of each trapezoid is $h \cdot [f(x_i) + f(x_{i+1})]/2$. Summing: $T_n = h[f(x_0)/2 + f(x_1) + f(x_2) + \cdots + f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)/2]$. The first and last function values get half weight; all interior points get full weight. The trapezoidal rule is exact for linear functions. Simpson's rule is the star of numerical integration. Instead of fitting a straight line through two points, it fits a parabola through three consecutive points. Over two subintervals $[x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}]$, the area under the parabola is $(h/3)[f(x_{i-1}) + 4f(x_i) + f(x_{i+1})]$. Summing over all pairs (requiring $n$ to be even): $S_n = (h/3)[f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) + 4f(x_3) + \cdots + 4f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)]$. The coefficients alternate: 1, 4, 2, 4, 2, ..., 4, 1. The error bounds reveal why Simpson's rule is so powerful. Midpoint rule: $|E_M| \leq (b-a)^3/(24n^2) \cdot \max|f''|$. Trapezoidal rule: $|E_T| \leq (b-a)^3/(12n^2) \cdot \max|f''|$. Both have errors that shrink like $1/n^2$ — doubling $n$ cuts the error by a factor of 4. Simpson's rule: $|E_S| \leq (b-a)^5/(180n^4) \cdot \max|f^{(4)}|$. The error shrinks like $1/n^4$ — doubling $n$ cuts the error by a factor of 16! Simpson's rule with just $n = 10$ often gives 8+ digits of accuracy. An important relationship: Simpson's rule is a weighted average of the midpoint and trapezoidal rules: $S_{2n} = (2M_n + T_n)/3$. This means you can compute $M_n$ and $T_n$ and combine them to get $S_{2n}$ for free, effectively tripling your accuracy without additional function evaluations. When do you NEED numerical methods? (1) The integrand has no elementary antiderivative: $e^{-x^2}$, $\sin(x)/x$, $\sqrt{1+x^4}$. (2) The function is given by data (measured temperatures, experimental readings) rather than a formula — you cannot find an antiderivative of a table. (3) The antiderivative exists but is too complicated to evaluate reliably (some partial fraction or trig sub results). In all these cases, numerical integration gives the answer directly. Error bound: $|E_M| \leq \frac{(b-a)^3}{24n^2}\max_{[a,b]}|f''(x)|$. The midpoint rule is exact for polynomials of degree $\leq 1$ (and, due to cancellation, also exact for degree 2 over symmetric intervals). Trapezoidal rule: $T_n = \frac{h}{2}[f(x_0) + 2f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) + \cdots + 2f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)]$. Error bound: $|E_T| \leq \frac{(b-a)^3}{12n^2}\max_{[a,b]}|f''(x)|$. Note that $|E_T| \leq 2|E_M|$ — the midpoint rule is typically twice as accurate as the trapezoidal rule for the same $n$. Simpson's rule ($n$ even): $S_n = \frac{h}{3}[f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) + 4f(x_3) + 2f(x_4) + \cdots + 4f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)]$. Not bad for just 5 function evaluations! h = (1-0)/4 = 0.25, \quad x_i = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 Set up the partition. f(x_i): f(0)=1, \; f(0.25)=e^{-0.0625}\approx 0.9394, \; f(0.5)=e^{-0.25}\approx 0.7788 Evaluate f at grid points. f(0.75) = e^{-0.5625} \approx 0.5698, \quad f(1) = e^{-1} \approx 0.3679 Remaining function values. T_4 = \frac{0.25}{2}[f(0)+2f(0.25)+2f(0.5)+2f(0.75)+f(1)] Trapezoidal formula: endpoints get weight 1, interior points get weight 2. = 0.125[1+2(0.9394)+2(0.7788)+2(0.5698)+0.3679] Substitute values. = 0.125[1+1.8788+1.5576+1.1396+0.3679] = 0.125 \times 5.9439 \approx 0.7430 Sum and multiply. Simpson's Rule: ∫₀¹ e^(−x²) dx with n = 4 \text{Approximate } \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx \text{ using Simpson's rule with } n = 4. S₄ ≈ 0.7469. The true value is 0.7468..., so the error is about 0.0001 — roughly 40 times more accurate than T₄ with the same data points! h = 0.25, \text{ same grid as Example 1} Same partition, same function values. S_4 = \frac{h}{3}[f(x_0)+4f(x_1)+2f(x_2)+4f(x_3)+f(x_4)] Simpson's coefficients: 1, 4, 2, 4, 1. = \frac{0.25}{3}[1+4(0.9394)+2(0.7788)+4(0.5698)+0.3679] Substitute. = \frac{0.25}{3}[1+3.7576+1.5576+2.2792+0.3679] Multiply coefficients. = \frac{0.25}{3}\times 8.9623 = \frac{2.2406}{3} \approx 0.7469 Sum and compute. From Experimental Data \text{A vehicle's speed (m/s) is measured every 2 seconds: } v(0)=0, v(2)=5, v(4)=9, v(6)=11, v(8)=10, v(10)=8. \text{ Estimate distance traveled.} Distance ≈ 78 m using the trapezoidal rule. With data (not a formula), the trapezoidal rule is the standard method. n = 5 \text{ subintervals}, \; h = 2 \text{ s} Five intervals of width 2. T_5 = \frac{2}{2}[0+2(5)+2(9)+2(11)+2(10)+8] Trapezoidal rule (works with odd n, unlike Simpson's). = 1[0+10+18+22+20+8] = 78 \text{ m} Sum up. \text{Note: } n=5 \text{ is odd, so Simpson's rule is not directly applicable.} We cannot use Simpson's with 5 subintervals. We could use it on the first 4 intervals (n=4) and the trapezoidal rule on the last. Error Bound: How Many Points for 6-Digit Accuracy? \text{How large must } n \text{ be for Simpson's rule to approximate } \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}dx \text{ with error} \leq 10^{-6}? n = 18 subintervals (19 function evaluations) give 6-digit accuracy with Simpson's rule. The trapezoidal rule would need n ≈ 816 for the same accuracy. f(x) = e^{-x^2}. \text{ Need } \max_{[0,1]}|f^{(4)}(x)|. Simpson's error uses the 4th derivative. f'(x) = -2xe^{-x^2},\; f''(x) = (4x^2-2)e^{-x^2} Compute derivatives. f^{(4)}(x) = (16x^4-48x^2+12)e^{-x^2} Fourth derivative (tedious but doable). \max_{[0,1]}|f^{(4)}(x)| \leq 12 \quad (\text{occurs at } x=0: f^{(4)}(0) = 12) Check: |f⁴(0)| = 12, and the function decreases as x increases. Use M₄ = 12. \frac{(1-0)^5 \cdot 12}{180 n^4} \leq 10^{-6} \Rightarrow n^4 \geq \frac{12}{180 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{12}{1.8\times 10^{-4}} \approx 66667 Set error bound ≤ 10⁻⁶ and solve for n. n \geq 66667^{1/4} \approx 16.1 \Rightarrow n = 18 \text{ (next even integer)} Round up to next even n. Midpoint Rule: ∫₁³ 1/x dx with n = 4 \text{Approximate } \int_1^3 \frac{1}{x}\,dx \text{ using the midpoint rule with } n = 4. \text{ Compare with the exact value } \ln 3 \approx 1.0986. M₄ ≈ 1.0897 with error 0.0089. The midpoint rule is slightly more accurate than the trapezoidal rule for the same n (T₄ ≈ 1.1167, error 0.0181). h = (3-1)/4 = 0.5, \quad \bar{x}_i = 1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 2.75 Midpoints of each subinterval. M_4 = 0.5[f(1.25)+f(1.75)+f(2.25)+f(2.75)] Midpoint rule formula. = 0.5[0.8000+0.5714+0.4444+0.3636] f(x) = 1/x. = 0.5 \times 2.1794 = 1.0897 Sum and multiply. |E_M| = |1.0986-1.0897| = 0.0089 Error compared to ln 3. Use the trapezoidal rule with n = 4 to approximate ∫₀² x² dx. Compare with the exact value 8/3. h = 0.5. Grid points: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2. Function values: 0, 0.25, 1, 2.25, 4. T_4 = 2.75, \text{ exact} = 8/3 \approx 2.6667, \text{ error} \approx 0.083 T_4 = \frac{0.5}{2}[0+2(0.25)+2(1)+2(2.25)+4] = 0.25[0+0.5+2+4.5+4] Apply trapezoidal formula. = 0.25 \times 11 = 2.75 Sum. \text{Exact: } \int_0^2 x^2\,dx = [x^3/3]_0^2 = 8/3 \approx 2.6667 Compare. \text{Error: } |2.75-2.6667| = 0.0833 About 3% error. Use Simpson's rule with n = 2 to approximate ∫₀^π sin(x) dx. Show that the result is exact for this function. Explain why. n = 2 means 3 points: 0, π/2, π. Simpson's: (h/3)[f(0)+4f(π/2)+f(π)]. The exact value is 2. S_2 = 2\pi/3 \approx 2.094. \text{ Not exact (sin x is not a cubic polynomial). Error} \approx 0.094. h = \pi/2. \; S_2 = \frac{\pi/2}{3}[\sin 0+4\sin(\pi/2)+\sin \pi] Three points: 0, π/2, π. = \frac{\pi}{6}[0+4(1)+0] = \frac{4\pi}{6} = \frac{2\pi}{3} \approx 2.094 Compute. \text{Exact: } \int_0^\pi \sin x\,dx = [-\cos x]_0^\pi = 1+1 = 2 The exact value. \text{Error: } |2.094-2| = 0.094. \text{ NOT exact — sin is not a polynomial of degree} \leq 3! Simpson's is exact for cubics, but sin(x) is not a polynomial. Close but not exact. Prove that the trapezoidal rule is exact for linear functions f(x) = mx + b, and that Simpson's rule is exact for cubic polynomials f(x) = ax³ + bx² + cx + d. (For the Simpson's case, it suffices to show exactness for f(x) = x³ on [−h, h].) For the trapezoidal rule: compute both the exact integral and the trapezoidal approximation of mx+b over [x_i, x_{i+1}] and show they agree. For Simpson's on x³: compute (h/3)[f(−h)+4f(0)+f(h)] and ∫_{−h}^{h} x³ dx separately. \text{Trapezoidal: exact for degree } \leq 1. \text{ Simpson: exact for degree } \leq 3. \text{Trap for } f(x)=mx+b \text{ on } [x_i, x_{i+1}]: Single subinterval. \text{Exact: } \int_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}}(mx+b)dx = [mx^2/2+bx]_{x_i}^{x_{i+1}} = m(x_{i+1}^2-x_i^2)/2+b\cdot h Direct integration. \text{Trap: } \frac{h}{2}[f(x_i)+f(x_{i+1})] = \frac{h}{2}[(mx_i+b)+(mx_{i+1}+b)] = \frac{h}{2}[m(x_i+x_{i+1})+2b] Trapezoidal approximation. m(x_{i+1}^2-x_i^2)/2 = m(x_{i+1}+x_i)(x_{i+1}-x_i)/2 = mh(x_i+x_{i+1})/2 Factor the difference of squares. Both expressions equal mh(x_i+x_{i+1})/2 + bh. ✓ \text{Simpson for } f(x)=x^3 \text{ on } [-h,h]: Three points: −h, 0, h. \frac{h}{3}[(-h)^3+4(0)^3+h^3] = \frac{h}{3}(-h^3+h^3) = 0 Simpson's approximation. \int_{-h}^{h}x^3\,dx = 0 \text{ (odd function on symmetric interval).} Exact integral. Both are zero. ✓ Exact for cubics. Area and Accumulation Riemann sums from Lesson 0 are the conceptual foundation of all numerical integration methods. Indefinite Integrals Numerical methods are used when the antiderivative table from Lesson 4 does not cover the integrand. Improper Integrals Numerical methods can approximate improper integrals by truncating the infinite domain and estimating the tail. Applications of Integration Many real-world applications require numerical integration because the integrands come from measured data, not formulas. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step instantaneous rate of change slope dy/dx velocity marginal change antiderivative accumulation area under curve net area total change

documents.title: Volumes: Disk and Washer Methods
documents.subtitle: Rotate a curve around an axis and integrate circular cross-sections to find solid volume
