documents.proofs: Formally, piecewise constant-acceleration motion is defined by a partition of the time axis $[0, T]$ into $n$ subintervals $[T_{k-1}, T_k]$ with $T_0 = 0$. On each subinterval, the acceleration $a_k$ is constant. The position and velocity functions are then $C^1$ on $(0, T)$ — continuously differentiable — even though the acceleration is only piecewise constant (i.e., it has jump discontinuities at the boundaries). The invariant that makes the connection well-posed is the requirement that $x$ and $v$ are determined uniquely at each boundary by a single value, not a left-hand and right-hand limit. If both sides agree — which they must, because the ODE $\ddot x = a$ has unique solutions given initial conditions — then the global trajectory is uniquely determined by specifying $(x_0, v_0)$ once at $t = 0$. Geometrically, the x–t curve is a piecewise parabola (or line, when $a = 0$). At each phase boundary, the parabolic arcs share a common point (position continuity) and a common tangent slope (velocity continuity). The curvature, however, jumps — which is why the x–t graph develops a visible kink in its second-derivative character even though the first derivative (slope) is smooth. In more advanced mechanics, this piecewise structure is replaced by integrating the equation of motion when $a(t)$ is a given continuous function. The result is the same handoff logic, but expressed as a single integral: $v(t) = v_0 + \int_0^t a(\tau)\,d\tau$. Two-phase motion is the special case where $a(\tau)$ is a step function — making the integral piecewise linear and the position piecewise quadratic. Piecewise SUVAT — state evolution v_k(t) = v_{0,k} + a_k t,\quad x_k(t) = x_{0,k} + v_{0,k}t + \tfrac{1}{2}a_k t^2,\quad t \in [0, T_k]

Vehicles have acceleration, cruise, and braking phases. Each phase obeys its own SUVAT equations, but the final speed and position of one phase must feed seamlessly into the next. Five-step phase handoff procedure 1. Identify all phases — wherever acceleration changes, draw a phase boundary.
2. Solve phase 1 completely: find its final velocity $v_{1,f}$ and displacement $\Delta x_1$.
3. Hand off: set $v_{0,2} = v_{1,f}$ and (if needed) $x_{0,2} = x_{0,1} + \Delta x_1$.
4. Restart the local clock ($t = 0$ at the phase boundary) and solve phase 2.
5. Add displacements (or track absolute positions) to answer the question. What is continuous vs. what can jump Position $x$ and velocity $v$ are always continuous at a phase boundary — they cannot teleport or spike. Acceleration $a$ can (and usually does) change abruptly at the boundary. That discontinuity in $a$ is what defines the boundary in the first place. Restart the clock for each phase Each phase has its own local time variable starting at $t = 0$. Do not use the global elapsed time in phase-2 equations — it will give wrong answers. The handoff gives you $v_{0,2}$ and $x_{0,2}$; treat everything else as a fresh problem.

documents.assignment: Dropped from rest — full walkthrough An object is dropped from rest at height $y_0 = 44.1$ m above the ground (up-positive, $g = 9.8$ m/s²). Find (a) the time to reach the ground and (b) the impact velocity.   Time to ground is 3 s; impact velocity is $-29.4$ m/s (downward). The object accelerates from rest to nearly 30 m/s — about 106 km/h — in just three seconds. v_0 = 0,\quad a = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2,\quad y_0 = 44.1\text{ m},\quad y_f = 0 List knowns with signs. Dropped from rest means $v_0 = 0$; released from 44.1 m means $y_f = 0$ is the ground. y_f = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}g t^2 \implies 0 = 44.1 - \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 Choose SUVAT equation 2. $v_0 = 0$ kills the linear term, leaving a simple quadratic. t = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 44.1}{9.8}} = \sqrt{9} = 3\text{ s} Solve for $t$. The answer is exactly 3 s because 44.1 was chosen as $\tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(9)$. v_f = v_0 - g t = 0 - 9.8(3) = -29.4\text{ m/s} Impact velocity. Negative sign confirms downward direction (up-positive convention). Object dropped from a known height — use energy-like equation A rock is dropped from a cliff of height $h = 80$ m (up-positive). Find its speed just before impact without computing the fall time.   Impact speed is approximately 39.6 m/s. Using the no-time equation is faster when the problem doesn't ask for $t$. v_0 = 0,\quad \Delta y = -80\text{ m},\quad a = -g = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2 $\Delta y$ is negative because the rock moves downward. We want $v_f$ and do not need $t$, so use the no-time equation. v_f^2 = v_0^2 - 2g\Delta y = 0 - 2(9.8)(-80) = 1568\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2 Substituting $\Delta y = -80$ m and $v_0 = 0$. Two negatives multiply to a positive — the speed squared is positive, as required. |v_f| = \sqrt{1568} \approx 39.6\text{ m/s} Take the positive root for speed. The sign of $v_f$ is negative (downward); the speed (magnitude) is 39.6 m/s ≈ 142 km/h. Object thrown downward from a window A ball is thrown downward at $v_0 = -8$ m/s from a window 30 m above the ground (up-positive). Find (a) the time to reach the ground and (b) the impact velocity.   Flight time ≈ 1.79 s, impact velocity ≈ −25.5 m/s. Compare to dropping from rest from 30 m: $t = \sqrt{60/9.8} \approx 2.47$ s and $v_f \approx -24.3$ m/s. The initial downward throw shortens fall time by 0.68 s. v_0 = -8\text{ m/s},\quad y_0 = 30\text{ m},\quad y_f = 0,\quad a = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2 Thrown downward: $v_0$ is negative in the up-positive convention. Ground is $y_f = 0$. 0 = 30 + (-8)t - \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 \implies 4.9t^2 + 8t - 30 = 0 Substitute into $y_f = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ and rearrange to standard quadratic form. t = \frac{-8 + \sqrt{64 + 4(4.9)(30)}}{2(4.9)} = \frac{-8 + \sqrt{652}}{9.8} \approx \frac{-8 + 25.53}{9.8} \approx 1.79\text{ s} Quadratic formula; take the positive root because $t > 0$. The ball reaches the ground in about 1.79 s. v_f = -8 - 9.8(1.79) \approx -8 - 17.5 = -25.5\text{ m/s} Impact velocity is about $-25.5$ m/s (downward). Throwing it down gives a faster impact than dropping from rest.  A ball is thrown upward at $v_0 = 19.6$ m/s from ground level (up-positive). Find (a) maximum height, (b) time to reach the peak, and (c) total airtime. At maximum height, $v = 0$. Total airtime is twice the rise time by symmetry.   v_f = 0\text{ at peak} \implies 0 = v_0^2 - 2g\Delta y_{\text{max}} Use the no-time equation with the apex condition $v_f = 0$. \Delta y_{\text{max}} = \frac{v_0^2}{2g} = \frac{(19.6)^2}{2(9.8)} = \frac{384.16}{19.6} = 19.6\text{ m} Maximum height is 19.6 m. Notice $v_0^2 / (2g)$ with $v_0 = 19.6$ m/s and $g = 9.8$ m/s² gives exactly $19.6$ m. t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g} = \frac{19.6}{9.8} = 2\text{ s} Time to peak from $v_f = v_0 - g t$ with $v_f = 0$. T_{\text{total}} = 2 t_{\text{peak}} = 4\text{ s} By symmetry (no air resistance), the fall time from peak back to launch height equals the rise time. Total airtime is 4 s.  An object dropped from rest hits the ground after exactly 4 s. Find (a) the height it was dropped from and (b) its impact speed. Use $\Delta y = -\tfrac{1}{2}g t^2$ for part (a). The negative sign means downward displacement.   \Delta y = v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}g t^2 = 0 - \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(16) = -78.4\text{ m} Displacement is $-78.4$ m, meaning the ground is 78.4 m below the drop point. The drop height is $h = 78.4$ m. v_f = v_0 - g t = 0 - 9.8(4) = -39.2\text{ m/s} Impact velocity is $-39.2$ m/s. Speed (magnitude) is 39.2 m/s ≈ 141 km/h. \text{Cross-check: }v_f^2 = -2g\Delta y = 2(9.8)(78.4) = 1536.6 \implies |v_f| = 39.2\text{ m/s}\checkmark Verify using the no-time equation. Both methods agree, confirming the answer.  A stone is thrown upward from the edge of a 45-m cliff at $v_0 = 14.7$ m/s (up-positive, $g = 9.8$ m/s²). The stone eventually lands at the base of the cliff. Find (a) the time of flight and (b) the impact velocity. The stone starts at $y_0 = 45$ m and lands at $y_f = 0$. Set up $y_f = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}g t^2 = 0$ and solve the quadratic.   0 = 45 + 14.7 t - \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 \implies 4.9 t^2 - 14.7 t - 45 = 0 Rearrange to standard form $4.9t^2 - 14.7t - 45 = 0$. t = \frac{14.7 + \sqrt{(14.7)^2 + 4(4.9)(45)}}{2(4.9)} = \frac{14.7 + \sqrt{216.09 + 882}}{9.8} = \frac{14.7 + \sqrt{1098.09}}{9.8} Quadratic formula; take the positive root. $\sqrt{1098.09} \approx 33.1$. t \approx \frac{14.7 + 33.1}{9.8} = \frac{47.8}{9.8} \approx 4.88\text{ s} The stone is in the air for about 4.88 s — including the upward phase, descent to launch height, and the extra 45 m of fall. v_f = 14.7 - 9.8(4.88) \approx 14.7 - 47.8 = -33.1\text{ m/s} Impact velocity is $\approx -33.1$ m/s (downward). Note $|v_f| \approx \sqrt{1098} \approx 33.1$ m/s matches, confirming the quadratic root.
documents.proofs: Near Earth's surface, the gravitational force on an object of (gravitational) mass $m_g$ is $F = m_g g$. By Newton's second law, $F = m_i a$, where $m_i$ is the inertial mass. The empirical equivalence $m_g = m_i$ (which holds to at least one part in $10^{12}$ in precision experiments) gives $a = g$ independent of mass. Free-fall kinematics is therefore a corollary of Newton's laws plus the equivalence principle. The constant-acceleration assumption holds as long as height changes are small compared to Earth's radius ($\approx 6400$ km). For a fall of 100 m, the fractional change in $g$ is roughly $2(100)/6{,}400{,}000 \approx 3 \times 10^{-5}$ — negligible for all introductory-physics purposes. Over kilometer-scale heights, $g$ begins to vary and the constant-$a$ model must be replaced by integrating $F = -GMm/r^2$. Geometrically, free-fall trajectories in one dimension are parabolas in the $y$–$t$ plane (since $y = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}g t^2$ is a quadratic in $t$) and straight lines in the $v$–$t$ plane ($v = v_0 - gt$ is linear). The slope of the $v$–$t$ line is $-g$ everywhere — a constant — which is the defining feature of constant acceleration. Curvature of $y(t)$ is $\ddot y = -g < 0$, meaning the parabola always opens downward regardless of the direction of $v_0$. Free fall is the special case $a = -g$ of the general constant-acceleration model. In chapter 3, when Newton's second law introduces $a = F_{\text{net}}/m$, free fall becomes the example where $F_{\text{net}} = -mg$ and $m$ cancels. In chapter 4 (projectile motion), free fall governs the vertical component while horizontal motion is inertial ($a_x = 0$). Every projectile problem decomposes into two simultaneous free-fall sub-problems along perpendicular axes. Free-fall position and velocity (up-positive) y(t) = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}g t^2,\qquad v(t) = v_0 - g t

Free fall is the purest application of constant-acceleration kinematics. Galileo established that (without air resistance) all objects fall equally. This underpins every projectile calculation. Four-step free-fall setup checklist 1. Choose your axis direction (up-positive is standard) and write it at the top of your work.
2. Assign signs to all known quantities: velocities, positions, and accelerations must all use the same convention.
3. Write $a = -g = -9.8$ m/s² (up-positive) or $a = +g = +9.8$ m/s² (down-positive).
4. Select the SUVAT equation that contains your unknown and not the quantity you don't care about. Solve and check the sign of the answer for physical sense. Free-fall acceleration a = -g \approx -9.8\,\text{m/s}^2 \quad (\text{up-positive convention}) Convention first — commit and never switch If you choose down-positive, then $a = +g$, a thrown-upward initial velocity is negative, and heights above the launch point are negative. Both conventions give the same physical answer, but mixing them mid-problem gives garbage. Pick one and annotate it at the top of every free-fall problem.

Free fall means only gravity acts on the object — air resistance is neglected. Near Earth's surface, that gravitational pull gives every object the same downward acceleration, roughly 9.8 m/s², regardless of mass. This surprising result — that a feather and a cannonball fall together with no air — was demonstrated by Galileo and confirmed spectacularly on the Moon by Apollo 15 in 1971. The reason mass cancels is that the same property of matter (inertial mass) that resists acceleration is what couples the object to gravity (gravitational mass). Newton's law $F = ma$ with $F = mg$ gives $a = g$ — the mass divides out completely. This equivalence is so fundamental that it became one of Einstein's starting points for general relativity. In practice, free-fall kinematics means substituting $a = \pm g$ into the four SUVAT equations, where the sign depends on your axis convention. Choosing up as positive (the most common convention) gives $a = -9.8$ m/s² because gravity points in the negative direction. Choosing down as positive gives $a = +9.8$ m/s². Either works — you just have to be consistent throughout the problem. The most critical bookkeeping step is deciding the convention before writing a single equation. A stone thrown upward with $v_0 = +15$ m/s in the up-positive system has the same motion as one thrown with $v_0 = -15$ m/s in the down-positive system. The physics is identical; only the sign labels differ. Free fall is constant-acceleration kinematics with one substitution: replace $a$ with $-g$ (up-positive) or $+g$ (down-positive). All four SUVAT equations apply directly. A reliable workflow: list the five kinematic quantities $(v_0, v_f, a, t, \Delta y)$. Mark the ones you know (and their signs), identify the unknown, and note the quantity not mentioned in the problem. Choose the SUVAT equation that omits the unneeded quantity. Always assign $a = \mp g$ first, before touching the other quantities. documents.title: Free Fall Symmetry
documents.subtitle: In ideal free fall, ascent and descent mirror each other about the apex.
documents.tags: free fall symmetry projectile
documents.assignment: Apex time and total flight time A ball is thrown upward at $v_0 = 19.6$ m/s from ground level (up-positive, $g = 9.8$ m/s²). Find (a) time to the apex and (b) total flight time back to the ground.   Apex at $t = 2$ s, lands at $t = 4$ s with speed 19.6 m/s — same as the launch speed. The v–t graph is a straight line from $+19.6$ to $-19.6$ m/s over 4 s. t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g} = \frac{19.6}{9.8} = 2\text{ s} At the apex, $v = 0$. Set $v = v_0 - gt = 0$ and solve for $t$. T_{\text{total}} = 2 t_{\text{peak}} = 2 \times 2 = 4\text{ s} By time symmetry: descent time equals ascent time. Alternatively, set $y = v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = 0$ and factor out $t$ to get $t = 2v_0/g = 4$ s. v_{\text{land}} = v_0 - g T = 19.6 - 9.8(4) = -19.6\text{ m/s} Landing velocity is $-19.6$ m/s (downward). Magnitude equals launch speed — confirming speed symmetry. Speed at equal heights on ascent and descent A ball is thrown upward at $v_0 = 24.5$ m/s. A ledge is located 15 m above the launch point. Find the ball's speed when it passes the ledge height (a) on the way up and (b) on the way down.   The speed is 17.5 m/s at 15 m on both the ascent and descent. This is the speed symmetry: $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2gh$ gives the same value on both passes because height $h$ is the only position-dependent term. v_{\text{up}}^2 = v_0^2 - 2g h = (24.5)^2 - 2(9.8)(15) = 600.25 - 294 = 306.25 On the way up: substitute $h = +15$ m into the no-time equation. |v_{\text{up}}| = \sqrt{306.25} \approx 17.5\text{ m/s} Speed on the way up at 15 m. The ball is still moving upward ($v > 0$). v_{\text{down}}^2 = v_0^2 - 2g h = 306.25\text{ (identical)} On the way down at the same height: the right-hand side is identical because $h$ is the same. So $v^2$ is the same. |v_{\text{down}}| = \sqrt{306.25} \approx 17.5\text{ m/s} Speed on the way down at 15 m — exactly the same as on the way up. Only the direction differs: upward (+17.5) vs downward (−17.5). Finding launch speed from total flight time A ball is thrown upward from the ground and returns to the ground after exactly 6 s. Find the launch speed and the maximum height.   Launch speed is 29.4 m/s and maximum height is 44.1 m. When total flight time is given, the symmetry formula $T = 2v_0/g$ is the fastest path to the launch speed. T_{\text{total}} = \frac{2v_0}{g} \implies v_0 = \frac{g T}{2} = \frac{9.8 \times 6}{2} = 29.4\text{ m/s} Invert the total flight time formula. The flight time determines the launch speed directly — no quadratic needed. y_{\text{max}} = \frac{v_0^2}{2g} = \frac{(29.4)^2}{2(9.8)} = \frac{864.36}{19.6} = 44.1\text{ m} Maximum height from the apex formula. t_{\text{peak}} = T/2 = 3\text{ s},\quad v_{\text{land}} = -v_0 = -29.4\text{ m/s} Apex at 3 s, landing speed 29.4 m/s downward — confirming symmetry.  Prove algebraically that when a ball is thrown upward with speed $v_0$ and lands back at the same height, the landing speed equals the launch speed. Use only the SUVAT equations. The direction is negative (downward), but the magnitude equals the launch speed. The midpoint between the two passes is the apex. The half-time from one pass to the apex is 1.2 s. documents.proofs: Formally, the time symmetry is a consequence of the time-reversal symmetry of Newton's second law when only conservative forces act. With $\ddot y = -g$ (constant), if $y(t)$ is a solution, then $y(T - t)$ (time-reversed trajectory) satisfies the same differential equation with reversed initial conditions. The midpoint $t = T/2 = t_{\text{peak}}$ is fixed under this reversal. The speed symmetry is equivalent to conservation of mechanical energy. With only gravity (a conservative force), total mechanical energy $E = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgy$ is conserved. At any height $y = h$ on either pass, $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2 + mg(0)$, giving $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2gh$ on both the ascent and descent. Free-fall symmetry and energy conservation are two sides of the same coin. In the y–t plane, the trajectory $y(t) = v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ is a parabola with vertex at $(t_{\text{peak}}, y_{\text{max}}) = (v_0/g,\, v_0^2/(2g))$ and roots at $t = 0$ and $t = 2v_0/g$. The axis of symmetry is the vertical line $t = v_0/g$. The parabola's shape confirms that the two halves are mirror images — the left half (ascent) and right half (descent) are reflections across this axis. When air resistance is present, the equation of motion becomes $m\ddot y = -mg - bv$ (linear drag) or $-mg - b v|v|$ (quadratic drag). Neither is time-reversible in the same way, breaking both symmetries. The ball reaches a lower peak (more work done against drag on the way up) and has a lower impact speed (less potential energy converted to kinetic on the way down). The symmetry of free fall is an idealization valid when drag forces are negligible compared to gravity. Symmetry from the quadratic roots y = v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = 0 \implies t = 0 \text{ or } t = \frac{2v_0}{g} = 2t_{\text{peak}}

Why does an object thrown straight up return with the same speed it had at launch? Ballistics and sports physics rely on this symmetry as a first-order model before adding drag. Understanding which symmetry properties hold (and why they break with air resistance) is essential for any realistic projectile analysis. Before reading on, predict: a ball is thrown upward at 20 m/s. After it rises, reaches the apex, and falls back down to the exact height from which it was thrown, what is its speed? More than 20 m/s, exactly 20 m/s, or less than 20 m/s? Write your prediction and the reason for it before continuing. Free-fall symmetry has two parts. First, the time to rise from any height to the apex equals the time to fall from the apex back to that same height. Second, the speed at any height on the way up equals the speed at that same height on the way down. Both symmetries follow from a single fact: acceleration is constant throughout the flight. The clearest way to see the time symmetry is to look at the v–t graph. With $a = -g$, velocity is $v(t) = v_0 - gt$ — a straight line that crosses zero at $t_{\text{peak}} = v_0/g$. The line is perfectly symmetric about $t_{\text{peak}}$: whatever the velocity was at time $t_{\text{peak}} - \tau$, the velocity at time $t_{\text{peak}} + \tau$ is its exact negative. Same magnitude, opposite direction. The speed symmetry follows algebraically from the no-time equation $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2g\Delta y$. At any specific height $\Delta y$, the right-hand side is the same regardless of whether the object is on the way up or the way down. So $v^2$ is the same at that height on both passes — which means speed is the same. The direction differs (positive on the way up, negative on the way down), but the magnitude is identical. Both symmetries break as soon as you add air resistance. Drag opposes velocity, so on the way up it acts downward (adding to gravity) and on the way down it acts upward (opposing gravity). The upward phase is shortened, the downward phase is slowed, and the ball returns with less speed than it left with. Real balls, shuttlecocks, and artillery shells all land slower than they launched — symmetry is an idealization. The symmetry claims can be proven directly from the SUVAT equations. The midpoint is $v_0/g = t_{\text{peak}}$, confirming equal rise and fall times. For speed symmetry: at any height $h$ on the way up, $v_{\text{up}}^2 = v_0^2 - 2gh$. On the way down at the same height, the same equation gives $v_{\text{down}}^2 = v_0^2 - 2gh$. So $|v_{\text{up}}| = |v_{\text{down}}|$ at every common height. At $h = 0$ (launch/landing height), this gives $|v_{\text{land}}| = |v_0|$ — the quantitative statement that impact speed equals launch speed. These two symmetry results together mean that the v–t graph for a full up-and-down flight is a straight line that passes through zero at $t_{\text{peak}}$ and has equal positive and negative regions. The y–t parabola is symmetric about the vertical line $t = t_{\text{peak}}$. Formally, the time symmetry is a consequence of the time-reversal symmetry of Newton's second law when only conservative forces act. With $\ddot y = -g$ (constant), if $y(t)$ is a solution, then $y(T - t)$ (time-reversed trajectory) satisfies the same differential equation with reversed initial conditions. The midpoint $t = T/2 = t_{\text{peak}}$ is fixed under this reversal. The speed symmetry is equivalent to conservation of mechanical energy. With only gravity (a conservative force), total mechanical energy $E = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgy$ is conserved. At any height $y = h$ on either pass, $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2 + mg(0)$, giving $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2gh$ on both the ascent and descent. Free-fall symmetry and energy conservation are two sides of the same coin. In the y–t plane, the trajectory $y(t) = v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ is a parabola with vertex at $(t_{\text{peak}}, y_{\text{max}}) = (v_0/g,\, v_0^2/(2g))$ and roots at $t = 0$ and $t = 2v_0/g$. The axis of symmetry is the vertical line $t = v_0/g$. The parabola's shape confirms that the two halves are mirror images — the left half (ascent) and right half (descent) are reflections across this axis. When air resistance is present, the equation of motion becomes $m\ddot y = -mg - bv$ (linear drag) or $-mg - b v|v|$ (quadratic drag). Neither is time-reversible in the same way, breaking both symmetries. The ball reaches a lower peak (more work done against drag on the way up) and has a lower impact speed (less potential energy converted to kinetic on the way down). The symmetry of free fall is an idealization valid when drag forces are negligible compared to gravity. Symmetry from the quadratic roots y = v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = 0 \implies t = 0 \text{ or } t = \frac{2v_0}{g} = 2t_{\text{peak}} Using symmetry to solve quickly 1. Identify if the problem involves return to the same height — if so, return speed equals launch speed instantly.
2. Identify if you need total flight time — if landing at launch height, $T = 2v_0/g$ without solving a quadratic.
3. Identify if you need speed at a specific height — use $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2g\Delta y$; speed is the same on ascent and descent at that height.
4. Only when the landing height differs from the launch height do you need the full quadratic $y = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. The v–t line is the engine of symmetry $v(t) = v_0 - gt$ is a straight line. The apex occurs at the midpoint $t_{\text{peak}} = v_0/g$. For any time offset $\tau$ from the apex, $v(t_{\text{peak}} - \tau) = g\tau = -v(t_{\text{peak}} + \tau)$. Same magnitude, opposite sign — this is exactly what "symmetric about the apex" means. Symmetry only holds when landing at launch height If the ball lands at a different height (e.g., thrown from a cliff), the return speed no longer equals the launch speed — though the no-time equation $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2g\Delta y$ still tells you the exact impact speed. The time symmetry also breaks: more (or less) time is spent on one side of the apex. Free-fall symmetry (land at launch height) t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g},\quad T_{\text{total}} = \frac{2v_0}{g},\quad |v_{\text{land}}| = v_0 Speed at height $h$ on both passes v^2 = v_0^2 - 2gh \implies |v_{\text{up}}(h)| = |v_{\text{down}}(h)| Symmetric trajectory about the apex The trajectory y(t) = v₀t − ½gt² is a downward-opening parabola. The apex is the axis of symmetry — equal horizontal distances on the t-axis correspond to equal heights on both sides. Apex time and total flight time A ball is thrown upward at $v_0 = 19.6$ m/s from ground level (up-positive, $g = 9.8$ m/s²). Find (a) time to the apex and (b) total flight time back to the ground. Apex at $t = 2$ s, lands at $t = 4$ s with speed 19.6 m/s — same as the launch speed. The v–t graph is a straight line from $+19.6$ to $-19.6$ m/s over 4 s. t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g} = \frac{19.6}{9.8} = 2\text{ s} At the apex, $v = 0$. Set $v = v_0 - gt = 0$ and solve for $t$. T_{\text{total}} = 2 t_{\text{peak}} = 2 \times 2 = 4\text{ s} By time symmetry: descent time equals ascent time. Alternatively, set $y = v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = 0$ and factor out $t$ to get $t = 2v_0/g = 4$ s. v_{\text{land}} = v_0 - g T = 19.6 - 9.8(4) = -19.6\text{ m/s} Landing velocity is $-19.6$ m/s (downward). Magnitude equals launch speed — confirming speed symmetry. Speed at equal heights on ascent and descent A ball is thrown upward at $v_0 = 24.5$ m/s. A ledge is located 15 m above the launch point. Find the ball's speed when it passes the ledge height (a) on the way up and (b) on the way down. The speed is 17.5 m/s at 15 m on both the ascent and descent. This is the speed symmetry: $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2gh$ gives the same value on both passes because height $h$ is the only position-dependent term. v_{\text{up}}^2 = v_0^2 - 2g h = (24.5)^2 - 2(9.8)(15) = 600.25 - 294 = 306.25 On the way up: substitute $h = +15$ m into the no-time equation. |v_{\text{up}}| = \sqrt{306.25} \approx 17.5\text{ m/s} Speed on the way up at 15 m. The ball is still moving upward ($v > 0$). v_{\text{down}}^2 = v_0^2 - 2g h = 306.25\text{ (identical)} On the way down at the same height: the right-hand side is identical because $h$ is the same. So $v^2$ is the same. |v_{\text{down}}| = \sqrt{306.25} \approx 17.5\text{ m/s} Speed on the way down at 15 m — exactly the same as on the way up. Only the direction differs: upward (+17.5) vs downward (−17.5). Finding launch speed from total flight time A ball is thrown upward from the ground and returns to the ground after exactly 6 s. Find the launch speed and the maximum height. Launch speed is 29.4 m/s and maximum height is 44.1 m. When total flight time is given, the symmetry formula $T = 2v_0/g$ is the fastest path to the launch speed. T_{\text{total}} = \frac{2v_0}{g} \implies v_0 = \frac{g T}{2} = \frac{9.8 \times 6}{2} = 29.4\text{ m/s} Invert the total flight time formula. The flight time determines the launch speed directly — no quadratic needed. y_{\text{max}} = \frac{v_0^2}{2g} = \frac{(29.4)^2}{2(9.8)} = \frac{864.36}{19.6} = 44.1\text{ m} Maximum height from the apex formula. t_{\text{peak}} = T/2 = 3\text{ s},\quad v_{\text{land}} = -v_0 = -29.4\text{ m/s} Apex at 3 s, landing speed 29.4 m/s downward — confirming symmetry. Prove algebraically that when a ball is thrown upward with speed $v_0$ and lands back at the same height, the landing speed equals the launch speed. Use only the SUVAT equations. Use $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2g\Delta y$ with $\Delta y = 0$ at the landing height. \Delta y = y_{\text{land}} - y_0 = 0\text{ (same height)} The ball returns to the same height, so the net displacement is zero. v_{\text{land}}^2 = v_0^2 - 2g(\Delta y) = v_0^2 - 2g(0) = v_0^2 Substitute $\Delta y = 0$ into the no-time equation. The $g$ term vanishes. |v_{\text{land}}| = \sqrt{v_0^2} = v_0\quad (v_0 > 0) Taking the positive square root gives $|v_{\text{land}}| = v_0$. The direction is negative (downward), but the magnitude equals the launch speed. A ball is thrown upward and is observed to pass a window ledge at 12 m above launch on both the way up and the way down. The time between the two passes is 2.4 s. Find the launch speed $v_0$. The midpoint between the two passes is the apex. The half-time from one pass to the apex is 1.2 s. Find the velocity at the window height first. \Delta t_{\text{half}} = 1.2\text{ s (from window to apex)} By symmetry, the time from the window (12 m) to the apex, and from the apex back to the window, are both 1.2 s. So the ball is at the apex at time $t_{\text{pass1}} + 1.2$ s. v_{\text{window}} + g \cdot 1.2 = 0 \implies v_{\text{window}} = 9.8 \times 1.2 = 11.76\text{ m/s} At the window on the way up, the ball decelerates to zero over 1.2 s. So $v_{\text{window}} = g \cdot 1.2 = 11.76$ m/s. v_0^2 = v_{\text{window}}^2 + 2g h = (11.76)^2 + 2(9.8)(12) = 138.3 + 235.2 = 373.5 Use $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2gh$ to relate launch speed to window speed. v_0 = \sqrt{373.5} \approx 19.3\text{ m/s} Launch speed is about 19.3 m/s. documents.title: Free Fall Sign Convention
documents.subtitle: Pick one positive direction and keep all quantities consistent.
documents.tags: sign convention free fall kinematics
documents.assignment: Same drop, two conventions — full comparison An object is dropped from rest and falls for 2 s. Compute displacement and final velocity under both up-positive and down-positive conventions.   Displacement magnitude: 19.6 m. Impact speed: 19.6 m/s. Both conventions give the same physics; only the sign of the result differs. \text{Up-positive: }v_0 = 0,\;a = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2 Gravity acts downward, which is negative in up-positive. \Delta y_{\text{up}+} = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(-9.8)(4) = -19.6\text{ m},\quad v_{\text{up}+} = -9.8(2) = -19.6\text{ m/s} Negative results: the object moved downward and is moving downward. Physically: fell 19.6 m at 19.6 m/s downward. \text{Down-positive: }v_0 = 0,\;a = +9.8\text{ m/s}^2 Gravity acts downward, which is positive in down-positive. \Delta y_{\text{dn}+} = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(+9.8)(4) = +19.6\text{ m},\quad v_{\text{dn}+} = +9.8(2) = +19.6\text{ m/s} Positive results: the object moved in the positive (downward) direction and is moving in the positive (downward) direction. |\Delta y_{\text{up}+}| = |\Delta y_{\text{dn}+}| = 19.6\text{ m},\quad |v_{\text{up}+}| = |v_{\text{dn}+}| = 19.6\text{ m/s} Same physical fall, same physical speed — only the sign differs. Convention changes labels, not physics. Downward throw — sign of v₀ differs by convention A ball is thrown downward at 5 m/s from a height of 20 m above the ground. Find the time to land using (a) up-positive and (b) down-positive.   Flight time is ≈ 1.57 s under both conventions. The quadratic equation is identical — the sign convention affects how you write the equation, not what the equation is. \text{Up+: }v_0 = -5\text{ m/s},\;a = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2,\;y_0 = 20\text{ m},\;y_f = 0 Thrown downward means $v_0$ is negative. Initial height is +20 m (above ground reference). 0 = 20 + (-5)t + \tfrac{1}{2}(-9.8)t^2 \implies 4.9t^2 + 5t - 20 = 0 Standard form. Take the positive root. t = \frac{-5 + \sqrt{25 + 4(4.9)(20)}}{9.8} = \frac{-5 + \sqrt{417}}{9.8} \approx \frac{-5 + 20.42}{9.8} \approx 1.57\text{ s} Up-positive gives $t \approx 1.57$ s. \text{Down+: }v_0 = +5\text{ m/s},\;a = +9.8\text{ m/s}^2,\;\Delta y = +20\text{ m} Thrown downward is positive. Fall distance is +20 m (in the positive/downward direction). 20 = 5t + \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 \implies 4.9t^2 + 5t - 20 = 0 Same quadratic equation! Only the interpretation of signs differed. t \approx 1.57\text{ s (identical)} Same answer. The two conventions are algebraically equivalent when applied consistently. Upward throw under down-positive convention A ball is thrown upward at 14.7 m/s. Using the down-positive convention, find the time to the apex and the maximum height.   Apex at 1.5 s, height 11.025 m — identical to the up-positive result. The negative $\Delta y$ in down-positive is expected: it means the ball moved in the upward (negative) direction. v_0 = -14.7\text{ m/s (upward = negative in down+)},\quad a = +9.8\text{ m/s}^2 In down-positive, upward motion is in the negative direction, so $v_0 = -14.7$ m/s. Gravity still acts in the positive (downward) direction: $a = +9.8$. v = 0\text{ at apex}: 0 = -14.7 + 9.8 t \implies t = \frac{14.7}{9.8} = 1.5\text{ s} Solve $v = 0$. The negative divided by positive gives a positive time — physically sensible. \Delta y = -14.7(1.5) + \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(2.25) = -22.05 + 11.025 = -11.025\text{ m} Displacement is $-11.025$ m. In down-positive, negative means upward — so the apex is 11.025 m above the launch point.  h = |\Delta y| = 11.025\text{ m}\quad (\text{same as up-positive: }v_0^2/(2g) = (14.7)^2/19.6 = 11.025\text{ m}) Maximum height is 11.025 m regardless of convention. The negative sign in down-positive just means the apex is above the reference point.  A ball is thrown upward at 9.8 m/s from ground level. Solve for the total flight time (a) using up-positive and (b) using down-positive. Confirm the answers match. In down-positive, the ball starts at $\Delta y = 0$, moves to a negative maximum, then returns to $\Delta y = 0$. Set $\Delta y = 0$ in each convention and factor the quadratic.   \text{Up+: }v_0 = +9.8,\;a = -9.8\;\Rightarrow\; 0 = 9.8t - \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 = t(9.8 - 4.9t) Factor out $t$: the non-zero solution is $t = 9.8/4.9 = 2$ s. T_{\text{up+}} = 2\text{ s} Total flight time under up-positive convention. \text{Down+: }v_0 = -9.8,\;a = +9.8\;\Rightarrow\; 0 = -9.8t + \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 = t(-9.8 + 4.9t) Same structure. Factor out $t$: non-zero solution is $t = 9.8/4.9 = 2$ s. T_{\text{dn+}} = 2\text{ s}\quad (\text{identical}) Both conventions give 2 s. The flight time is a physical quantity — it cannot depend on the sign convention.  A rock is dropped into a well. Using down-positive (which is natural here), the rock lands at $\Delta y = +78.4$ m. Find the time of fall and impact speed. Then restate the problem in up-positive and verify the same answers. In down-positive, $v_0 = 0$ (dropped from rest) and $a = +g = +9.8$ m/s². In up-positive, $\Delta y = -78.4$ m.   \text{Down+: }v_0 = 0,\;a = +9.8,\;\Delta y = +78.4\text{ m} All positive — down-positive is natural for a downward-only problem. 78.4 = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 \implies t = \sqrt{78.4/4.9} = \sqrt{16} = 4\text{ s} Clean algebra: $t = 4$ s. v_f = 0 + 9.8(4) = 39.2\text{ m/s (downward, positive)} Impact speed 39.2 m/s in the positive (downward) direction. \text{Up+: }v_0 = 0,\;a = -9.8,\;\Delta y = -78.4\text{ m}\;\Rightarrow\; -78.4 = -\tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 \implies t = 4\text{ s}\checkmark Same answer, but with negative signs throughout. Down-positive was simpler here. v_f = -9.8(4) = -39.2\text{ m/s}\quad |v_f| = 39.2\text{ m/s}\checkmark Same speed magnitude. Negative sign means downward in up-positive — correct. documents.proofs: Formally, switching from up-positive to down-positive is a coordinate transformation $y' = -y$ (flip the axis). Under this transformation, velocity transforms as $v' = dy'/dt = -dy/dt = -v$, and acceleration transforms as $a' = -a$. Starting from $\ddot y = -g$ (up-positive), the transformed equation is $\ddot y' = -\ddot y = -(-g) = +g$. So the equation of motion under down-positive is $\ddot y' = +g$ — exactly as expected. The invariant is the physical trajectory: the path through space that the object actually follows. Two equations $(y(t), \text{up+})$ and $(y'(t), \text{down+})$ with $y'(t) = -y(t)$ describe the same worldline — just labeled with opposite signs. Any physical question (time of flight, speed, where it lands) has the same numerical answer regardless of which labeling you use. This is a special case of Galilean covariance: the Newtonian equation of motion $F = ma$ is form-invariant under spatial reflections (flipping an axis). Physical laws do not depend on which direction you call positive. Only computational conventions — sign bookkeeping — change. In more advanced treatments, this extends to choosing arbitrary positive directions in 3D and to choosing rotating reference frames. The principle is the same: pick a consistent set of basis vectors, assign signs accordingly, and the physics is unchanged. Sign conventions are a human bookkeeping device, not a physical constraint. Axis-flip invariance y' = -y \implies \ddot{y}' = -g \cdot (-1) = +g \quad \text{(down-positive equation of motion)}

Most free-fall mistakes are sign mistakes, not algebra mistakes. Building a disciplined sign-assignment habit eliminates an entire class of errors across kinematics, dynamics, and projectile motion. Sign-assignment checklist 1. Write your convention at the top: "up = positive" or "down = positive."
2. Assign $a$: $-g$ (up+) or $+g$ (down+). This is always the first number you assign.
3. Assign $v_0$: positive if the initial velocity points in your positive direction, negative if opposite.
4. Assign positions and displacements consistently: positive = in your chosen direction.
5. Solve and check: if displacement is negative in up-positive, the object moved downward — that makes sense. Mixing conventions is the #1 free-fall error If you choose down-positive, do NOT write $a = -g$. If you choose up-positive, do NOT write an upward-thrown ball as $v_0 = -v$ (negative). Flip only if you also flip the convention for every other quantity in the problem. When to choose each convention Up-positive is the standard in most textbooks and gives negative velocities for falling objects (which feels natural: downward = bad sign). Down-positive is sometimes easier when everything in the problem moves downward (e.g., a rock falling into a well), because you avoid a page full of minus signs. Either works — choose the one that minimizes minus signs in your specific problem.

Why do students get different answers from the same equation set? Most free-fall mistakes are sign mistakes, not algebra mistakes. Building a disciplined sign-assignment habit eliminates an entire class of errors across kinematics, dynamics, and projectile motion. Before reading on, predict: a ball is thrown downward at 8 m/s from a window. You choose up as positive. What values do you write for $v_0$ and $a$? Now switch to down as positive. Write the values again. Do you get the same final answers for time and impact speed? Think through it before reading on. A sign convention is a choice: which direction gets the positive label. In free-fall problems, the two standard choices are up-positive and down-positive. The physics — how fast the object falls, where it lands, how long it takes — is the same regardless. What changes is only the sign of each number in your equations. With up-positive: velocities that point upward are positive, velocities pointing downward are negative, and $a = -9.8$ m/s² (gravity pulls in the negative direction). With down-positive: downward velocities are positive, upward velocities are negative, and $a = +9.8$ m/s² (gravity pulls in the positive direction). The equations look different, but they model the same physics. The golden rule: all quantities in a given problem must use the same convention. The moment you write $a = +9.8$ m/s² (down-positive) but then treat a downward throw as $v_0 = -8$ m/s (as if up-positive), the equation becomes a contradiction. Both the numerical values and the signs must be chosen from one consistent framework. The best practice is to write your convention explicitly at the top of every free-fall problem — even a single line like "up = positive" — before assigning any numbers. This forced declaration is cheap insurance against the most common category of kinematics error. The two conventions produce equations that look different but are algebraically equivalent. Under up-positive: $v = v_0 - gt$, $y = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, and $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2g\Delta y$. Under down-positive with $v_0' = -v_0$ (upward throw becomes negative), $a' = +g$, $\Delta y' = -\Delta y$: the same equations hold with all signs flipped. The cleanest way to verify this is to compute a physical quantity — say, the time for a drop from height $h$ — in both conventions. Up-positive: $0 = h - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 \Rightarrow t = \sqrt{2h/g}$. Down-positive: $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 \Rightarrow t = \sqrt{2h/g}$. Same formula, same result. When the initial velocity has components in both the positive and negative directions (e.g., a throw at an angle), the sign convention must be extended consistently to all components. This is the foundation for 2D projectile motion in chapter 4. Formally, switching from up-positive to down-positive is a coordinate transformation $y' = -y$ (flip the axis). Under this transformation, velocity transforms as $v' = dy'/dt = -dy/dt = -v$, and acceleration transforms as $a' = -a$. Starting from $\ddot y = -g$ (up-positive), the transformed equation is $\ddot y' = -\ddot y = -(-g) = +g$. So the equation of motion under down-positive is $\ddot y' = +g$ — exactly as expected. The invariant is the physical trajectory: the path through space that the object actually follows. Two equations $(y(t), \text{up+})$ and $(y'(t), \text{down+})$ with $y'(t) = -y(t)$ describe the same worldline — just labeled with opposite signs. Any physical question (time of flight, speed, where it lands) has the same numerical answer regardless of which labeling you use. This is a special case of Galilean covariance: the Newtonian equation of motion $F = ma$ is form-invariant under spatial reflections (flipping an axis). Physical laws do not depend on which direction you call positive. Only computational conventions — sign bookkeeping — change. In more advanced treatments, this extends to choosing arbitrary positive directions in 3D and to choosing rotating reference frames. The principle is the same: pick a consistent set of basis vectors, assign signs accordingly, and the physics is unchanged. Sign conventions are a human bookkeeping device, not a physical constraint. Axis-flip invariance y' = -y \implies \ddot{y}' = -g \cdot (-1) = +g \quad \text{(down-positive equation of motion)} Sign-assignment checklist 1. Write your convention at the top: "up = positive" or "down = positive."
2. Assign $a$: $-g$ (up+) or $+g$ (down+). This is always the first number you assign.
3. Assign $v_0$: positive if the initial velocity points in your positive direction, negative if opposite.
4. Assign positions and displacements consistently: positive = in your chosen direction.
5. Solve and check: if displacement is negative in up-positive, the object moved downward — that makes sense. Mixing conventions is the #1 free-fall error If you choose down-positive, do NOT write $a = -g$. If you choose up-positive, do NOT write an upward-thrown ball as $v_0 = -v$ (negative). Flip only if you also flip the convention for every other quantity in the problem. When to choose each convention Up-positive is the standard in most textbooks and gives negative velocities for falling objects (which feels natural: downward = bad sign). Down-positive is sometimes easier when everything in the problem moves downward (e.g., a rock falling into a well), because you avoid a page full of minus signs. Either works — choose the one that minimizes minus signs in your specific problem. SUVAT under two conventions (same height problem) \underbrace{v = v_0 - gt,\; \Delta y = v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2}_{\text{up-positive}} \equiv \underbrace{v' = v_0' + gt,\; \Delta y' = v_0' t + \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2}_{\text{down-positive, primed}} Common pitfall Mixing up-positive formula $v = v_0 - gt$ with a down-positive number $a = +9.8$ in the same line. This gives $v = v_0 - (+9.8)t$, which looks like up-positive but the sign of $a$ is wrong. Axis orientation and sign of g The physics is axis-independent. Choosing +y upward makes a = −g (negative). Choosing +y downward makes a = +g (positive). Both give the same trajectory — only the sign labels differ. Same drop, two conventions — full comparison An object is dropped from rest and falls for 2 s. Compute displacement and final velocity under both up-positive and down-positive conventions. Displacement magnitude: 19.6 m. Impact speed: 19.6 m/s. Both conventions give the same physics; only the sign of the result differs. \text{Up-positive: }v_0 = 0,\;a = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2 Gravity acts downward, which is negative in up-positive. \Delta y_{\text{up}+} = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(-9.8)(4) = -19.6\text{ m},\quad v_{\text{up}+} = -9.8(2) = -19.6\text{ m/s} Negative results: the object moved downward and is moving downward. Physically: fell 19.6 m at 19.6 m/s downward. \text{Down-positive: }v_0 = 0,\;a = +9.8\text{ m/s}^2 Gravity acts downward, which is positive in down-positive. \Delta y_{\text{dn}+} = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(+9.8)(4) = +19.6\text{ m},\quad v_{\text{dn}+} = +9.8(2) = +19.6\text{ m/s} Positive results: the object moved in the positive (downward) direction and is moving in the positive (downward) direction. |\Delta y_{\text{up}+}| = |\Delta y_{\text{dn}+}| = 19.6\text{ m},\quad |v_{\text{up}+}| = |v_{\text{dn}+}| = 19.6\text{ m/s} Same physical fall, same physical speed — only the sign differs. Convention changes labels, not physics. Downward throw — sign of v₀ differs by convention A ball is thrown downward at 5 m/s from a height of 20 m above the ground. Find the time to land using (a) up-positive and (b) down-positive. Flight time is ≈ 1.57 s under both conventions. The quadratic equation is identical — the sign convention affects how you write the equation, not what the equation is. \text{Up+: }v_0 = -5\text{ m/s},\;a = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2,\;y_0 = 20\text{ m},\;y_f = 0 Thrown downward means $v_0$ is negative. Initial height is +20 m (above ground reference). 0 = 20 + (-5)t + \tfrac{1}{2}(-9.8)t^2 \implies 4.9t^2 + 5t - 20 = 0 Standard form. Take the positive root. t = \frac{-5 + \sqrt{25 + 4(4.9)(20)}}{9.8} = \frac{-5 + \sqrt{417}}{9.8} \approx \frac{-5 + 20.42}{9.8} \approx 1.57\text{ s} Up-positive gives $t \approx 1.57$ s. \text{Down+: }v_0 = +5\text{ m/s},\;a = +9.8\text{ m/s}^2,\;\Delta y = +20\text{ m} Thrown downward is positive. Fall distance is +20 m (in the positive/downward direction). 20 = 5t + \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 \implies 4.9t^2 + 5t - 20 = 0 Same quadratic equation! Only the interpretation of signs differed. t \approx 1.57\text{ s (identical)} Same answer. The two conventions are algebraically equivalent when applied consistently. Upward throw under down-positive convention A ball is thrown upward at 14.7 m/s. Using the down-positive convention, find the time to the apex and the maximum height. Apex at 1.5 s, height 11.025 m — identical to the up-positive result. The negative $\Delta y$ in down-positive is expected: it means the ball moved in the upward (negative) direction. v_0 = -14.7\text{ m/s (upward = negative in down+)},\quad a = +9.8\text{ m/s}^2 In down-positive, upward motion is in the negative direction, so $v_0 = -14.7$ m/s. Gravity still acts in the positive (downward) direction: $a = +9.8$. v = 0\text{ at apex}: 0 = -14.7 + 9.8 t \implies t = \frac{14.7}{9.8} = 1.5\text{ s} Solve $v = 0$. The negative divided by positive gives a positive time — physically sensible. \Delta y = -14.7(1.5) + \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(2.25) = -22.05 + 11.025 = -11.025\text{ m} Displacement is $-11.025$ m. In down-positive, negative means upward — so the apex is 11.025 m above the launch point.  h = |\Delta y| = 11.025\text{ m}\quad (\text{same as up-positive: }v_0^2/(2g) = (14.7)^2/19.6 = 11.025\text{ m}) Maximum height is 11.025 m regardless of convention. The negative sign in down-positive just means the apex is above the reference point. A ball is thrown upward at 9.8 m/s from ground level. Solve for the total flight time (a) using up-positive and (b) using down-positive. Confirm the answers match. In down-positive, the ball starts at $\Delta y = 0$, moves to a negative maximum, then returns to $\Delta y = 0$. Set $\Delta y = 0$ in each convention and factor the quadratic. \text{Up+: }v_0 = +9.8,\;a = -9.8\;\Rightarrow\; 0 = 9.8t - \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 = t(9.8 - 4.9t) Factor out $t$: the non-zero solution is $t = 9.8/4.9 = 2$ s. T_{\text{up+}} = 2\text{ s} Total flight time under up-positive convention. \text{Down+: }v_0 = -9.8,\;a = +9.8\;\Rightarrow\; 0 = -9.8t + \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 = t(-9.8 + 4.9t) Same structure. Factor out $t$: non-zero solution is $t = 9.8/4.9 = 2$ s. T_{\text{dn+}} = 2\text{ s}\quad (\text{identical}) Both conventions give 2 s. The flight time is a physical quantity — it cannot depend on the sign convention. A rock is dropped into a well. Using down-positive (which is natural here), the rock lands at $\Delta y = +78.4$ m. documents.assignment: Max height and full trajectory summary A ball is launched upward at $v_0 = 14$ m/s from ground level (up-positive, $g = 9.8$ m/s²). Find (a) maximum height, (b) time to apex, (c) total airtime, and (d) velocity at $t = 2$ s.   Max height 10 m, apex at 1.43 s, lands at 2.86 s with speed 14 m/s. At $t = 2$ s the ball is falling at 5.6 m/s. h_{\text{max}} = \frac{v_0^2}{2g} = \frac{196}{19.6} = 10\text{ m} Apply the apex height formula. Since $v_0 = 14$ m/s, $v_0^2 = 196$ m²/s². t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g} = \frac{14}{9.8} \approx 1.43\text{ s} Time to the apex from $v = 0$ in $v = v_0 - gt$. T_{\text{total}} = 2 t_{\text{peak}} \approx 2.86\text{ s} By symmetry (landing at same height as launch), total flight time is double the apex time. v(2) = 14 - 9.8(2) = 14 - 19.6 = -5.6\text{ m/s} At $t = 2$ s (which is after the apex at 1.43 s), the ball is moving downward — consistent with the negative sign. Ball thrown from an elevated platform A ball is thrown upward at $v_0 = 10$ m/s from a platform 15 m above the ground. Find when it hits the ground and its impact speed.   Flight time ≈ 3.05 s; impact speed ≈ 19.9 m/s. The extra height above the ground means the ball falls farther than it rose, gaining more than the launch speed on impact. y_0 = 15\text{ m},\quad v_0 = +10\text{ m/s},\quad a = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2,\quad y_f = 0 Set up with up-positive: platform is 15 m above ground ($y_f = 0$). 0 = 15 + 10t - \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 \implies 4.9t^2 - 10t - 15 = 0 Rearrange to standard quadratic form. t = \frac{10 + \sqrt{100 + 4(4.9)(15)}}{9.8} = \frac{10 + \sqrt{394}}{9.8} \approx \frac{10 + 19.85}{9.8} \approx 3.05\text{ s} Quadratic formula; take positive root. The ball is in the air for about 3.05 s. v_f = 10 - 9.8(3.05) \approx -19.9\text{ m/s} Impact velocity is about $-19.9$ m/s (downward). Speed ≈ 19.9 m/s — much larger than the 10 m/s launch speed because the ball gained extra speed falling from 15 m above the ground. Find launch speed given maximum height A safety engineer needs a component to reach exactly 12.5 m above its launch point. What launch speed is required?   Required launch speed is $\sqrt{2g \cdot h} = \sqrt{245} \approx 15.65$ m/s. This is the inverse of the apex formula — solving for $v_0$ given $h_{\text{max}}$. h_{\text{max}} = \frac{v_0^2}{2g} = 12.5\text{ m} Set the apex height formula equal to the required height. v_0^2 = 2g \cdot h_{\text{max}} = 2(9.8)(12.5) = 245\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2 Solve for $v_0^2$. v_0 = \sqrt{245} \approx 15.65\text{ m/s} Take the positive square root. A launch speed of about 15.65 m/s will deliver exactly 12.5 m apex height. \text{Check: }h = \frac{(15.65)^2}{2(9.8)} = \frac{244.9}{19.6} \approx 12.5\text{ m}\checkmark Verify by substituting back.  A ball is thrown upward from a rooftop 20 m above the ground. The ball reaches a maximum height of 5 m above the rooftop. Find (a) the launch speed, (b) the time to the apex, and (c) the impact speed when it hits the ground. The apex height is measured from the launch point (rooftop), not the ground. For part (c), use the no-time equation with $\Delta y = -(20 + 5) = -25$ m from apex to ground, or track absolute positions.   h_{\text{max}} = 5\text{ m (above rooftop)} \implies v_0 = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2(9.8)(5)} = \sqrt{98} \approx 9.9\text{ m/s} Invert the apex formula: $v_0 = \sqrt{2g h_{\text{max}}}$. t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g} = \frac{9.9}{9.8} \approx 1.01\text{ s} Time from rooftop to apex. y_{\text{apex}} = 20 + 5 = 25\text{ m (absolute, above ground)} The apex is 25 m above the ground (20 m of building + 5 m of rise). v_f^2 = 0 - 2g(-25) = 2(9.8)(25) = 490 \implies |v_f| = \sqrt{490} \approx 22.1\text{ m/s} From apex (speed = 0) to ground ($\Delta y = -25$ m from apex), use the no-time equation.  A ball thrown upward passes a window 6 m above the launch point on the way up. Two seconds later, it passes the same window on the way down. Find the launch speed. Set up $y = v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = 6$ m. The two solutions differ by 2 s: $t_2 - t_1 = 2$ s. Use Vieta's formulas on the quadratic roots.   v_0 t - 4.9 t^2 = 6 \implies 4.9t^2 - v_0 t + 6 = 0 Rearrange to standard form. The two roots $t_1$ and $t_2$ are the times the ball is at 6 m. t_1 + t_2 = \frac{v_0}{4.9},\quad t_1 \cdot t_2 = \frac{6}{4.9} Vieta's formulas: sum of roots = $b/a$ (with sign change), product = $c/a$. Sum gives $t_1 + t_2 = v_0/4.9$. t_2 - t_1 = 2\text{ s (given)} \implies (t_2 - t_1)^2 = (t_2 + t_1)^2 - 4t_1 t_2 Use the algebraic identity to relate sum/difference/product of roots. 4 = \left(\frac{v_0}{4.9}\right)^2 - 4\cdot\frac{6}{4.9} \implies \frac{v_0^2}{24.01} = 4 + \frac{24}{4.9} \approx 4 + 4.898 = 8.898 Substitute and solve for $v_0^2$. v_0^2 = 8.898 \times 24.01 \approx 213.6 \implies v_0 \approx 14.6\text{ m/s} Launch speed is approximately 14.6 m/s. This is a clever application of Vieta's formulas to avoid solving the full quadratic.  A ball is thrown upward at $v_0 = 20$ m/s. A second ball is dropped from rest at height $H$ at the same instant. The two balls collide at the apex of the first ball's trajectory. Find $H$. The first ball's apex is at $h = v_0^2/(2g)$ and occurs at $t_{\text{peak}} = v_0/g$. At that same time, the second ball has fallen from $H$ to the same height.   t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g} = \frac{20}{9.8} \approx 2.04\text{ s},\quad h_{\text{apex}} = \frac{v_0^2}{2g} = \frac{400}{19.6} \approx 20.4\text{ m} Compute the apex time and height for the first ball. \text{Ball 2: }y_2(t) = H - \tfrac{1}{2}g t^2 Dropped from rest at height $H$. At $t = t_{\text{peak}}$, ball 2 must be at height $h_{\text{apex}}$. h_{\text{apex}} = H - \tfrac{1}{2}g t_{\text{peak}}^2 \implies H = h_{\text{apex}} + \tfrac{1}{2}g t_{\text{peak}}^2 Solve for $H$. H = 20.4 + \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(2.04)^2 \approx 20.4 + 20.4 = 40.8\text{ m} The second ball must be dropped from 40.8 m — exactly twice the apex height. The second ball falls $h_{\text{apex}}$ meters while the first rises $h_{\text{apex}}$ meters, so $H = 2h_{\text{apex}}$.
documents.proofs: The upward-launch equations are the same constant-acceleration SUVAT family with $a = -g$. The apex results follow by substitution, not by separate derivation: from $v = v_0 - gt$ with $v = 0$, $t_{\text{peak}} = v_0/g$. Substituting into $y = v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ gives $y_{\text{max}} = v_0(v_0/g) - \tfrac{1}{2}g(v_0/g)^2 = v_0^2/g - v_0^2/(2g) = v_0^2/(2g)$. The scaling $h_{\text{max}} \propto v_0^2$ is fundamental: it reflects that kinetic energy $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2$ is completely converted to potential energy $mgh_{\text{max}}$ at the apex. This energy-based derivation gives the same result and connects kinematics to the energy chapter: $h_{\text{max}} = v_0^2/(2g)$ is just the work-energy theorem with $mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. The symmetry property from ch2-013 applies fully here: for a ball that returns to its launch height, total flight time is $T = 2v_0/g$ and the return speed equals $v_0$. These are direct consequences of the constant-acceleration, time-symmetric trajectory, not separate facts. In a full two-dimensional projectile (chapter 4), the vertical component of motion is exactly this upward-launch analysis: $v_y = v_0 \sin\theta - gt$, $y = v_0 \sin\theta \cdot t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, with $v_0 \sin\theta$ replacing $v_0$ throughout. Mastering the 1D case now means the 2D case is just a notation change. Apex height derivation v = 0 \text{ at apex} \implies t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g},\quad h_{\text{max}} = v_0 \cdot \frac{v_0}{g} - \frac{1}{2}g\left(\frac{v_0}{g}\right)^2 = \frac{v_0^2}{2g}

How high does it go, and how long until it returns? Projectile prediction in sports and safety engineering starts with this idealized vertical model. A basketball free throw, a fireworks shell, and a safety drop-test all use the same equations. Before reading on, predict: a ball is thrown straight up at 20 m/s. At the highest point, what are the velocity and acceleration? Many students say both are zero at the top. Think carefully about whether that makes sense physically — if the acceleration were zero at the apex, what would happen next? An upward launch is not two separate problems (going up, then coming down) — it is one continuous trajectory governed by a single, unchanging acceleration $a = -g$ throughout. The object decelerates on the way up, momentarily stops at the apex, then accelerates downward. At no point does acceleration pause or reverse. The apex is a velocity event, not an acceleration event. At the top, $v = 0$ (instantaneously at rest) but $a = -9.8$ m/s² (still pulling downward). This non-zero acceleration is precisely what causes the ball to start falling immediately after reaching the top. If $a$ were zero at the apex, the ball would hover indefinitely. The two most useful apex results follow directly from substituting $v = 0$ into the standard equations: $t_{\text{peak}} = v_0/g$ (from $v = v_0 - gt$) and $h_{\text{max}} = v_0^2/(2g)$ (from $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2g\Delta y$). Notice that $h_{\text{max}}$ scales as the square of $v_0$ — doubling the launch speed quadruples the maximum height. After the apex, the object is in standard free fall: starts from rest at the peak height and accelerates downward at $g$. The descent phase of the upward-launch problem is exactly the dropped-from-rest problem from ch2-012, just with a different starting height. For an upward launch from position $y_0$ with initial speed $v_0$ (up-positive), the three most-used relations are: $v = v_0 - gt$ (velocity at time $t$), $y = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ (position at time $t$), and $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2g(y - y_0)$ (velocity at position $y$, no $t$ needed). The apex condition $v = 0$ applied to each equation yields the two key results: $t_{\text{peak}} = v_0/g$ and $h_{\text{max}} = v_0^2/(2g)$. These are not separate formulas to memorize — they are what you get when you substitute $v = 0$ into the standard equations. This derivation should be automatic. When the ball must land at a height different from $y_0$ (e.g., on a cliff, through a window, or at ground level from an elevated platform), use the quadratic $y_f = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. Rearrange to $\tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 - v_0 t + (y_f - y_0) = 0$ and apply the quadratic formula; take the positive root. The upward-launch equations are the same constant-acceleration SUVAT family with $a = -g$. The apex results follow by substitution, not by separate derivation: from $v = v_0 - gt$ with $v = 0$, $t_{\text{peak}} = v_0/g$. Substituting into $y = v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ gives $y_{\text{max}} = v_0(v_0/g) - \tfrac{1}{2}g(v_0/g)^2 = v_0^2/g - v_0^2/(2g) = v_0^2/(2g)$. The scaling $h_{\text{max}} \propto v_0^2$ is fundamental: it reflects that kinetic energy $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2$ is completely converted to potential energy $mgh_{\text{max}}$ at the apex. This energy-based derivation gives the same result and connects kinematics to the energy chapter: $h_{\text{max}} = v_0^2/(2g)$ is just the work-energy theorem with $mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. The symmetry property from ch2-013 applies fully here: for a ball that returns to its launch height, total flight time is $T = 2v_0/g$ and the return speed equals $v_0$. These are direct consequences of the constant-acceleration, time-symmetric trajectory, not separate facts. In a full two-dimensional projectile (chapter 4), the vertical component of motion is exactly this upward-launch analysis: $v_y = v_0 \sin\theta - gt$, $y = v_0 \sin\theta \cdot t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, with $v_0 \sin\theta$ replacing $v_0$ throughout. Mastering the 1D case now means the 2D case is just a notation change. Apex height derivation v = 0 \text{ at apex} \implies t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g},\quad h_{\text{max}} = v_0 \cdot \frac{v_0}{g} - \frac{1}{2}g\left(\frac{v_0}{g}\right)^2 = \frac{v_0^2}{2g} Upward-launch problem template 1. Assign: $v_0 > 0$ (upward), $a = -g = -9.8$ m/s² (up-positive).
2. Apex: set $v = 0$ to find $t_{\text{peak}} = v_0/g$ and $h_{\text{max}} = v_0^2/(2g)$.
3. Return to launch height: $T_{\text{total}} = 2v_0/g$ by symmetry; return speed = $v_0$.
4. If the ball lands below or above launch height: use the full quadratic $y = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = y_f$ and solve for $t$. Apex ≠ equilibrium At the apex, $v = 0$ but $a = -g \neq 0$. Zero velocity is not the same as equilibrium. Equilibrium requires zero net force, which would mean no gravity — physically impossible near Earth. The apex is a momentary stop, not a rest state. Height quadruples when launch speed doubles $h_{\text{max}} = v_0^2/(2g)$ is quadratic in $v_0$. To reach 4× the height, you need only 2× the launch speed. To reach 9× the height, you need 3× the speed. This non-linear scaling is why slight variations in launch speed have large effects on range in athletics. Apex results (up-positive, launched from $y_0$) t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g},\qquad h_{\text{max}} = y_0 + \frac{v_0^2}{2g} When to use each equation If a problem does NOT mention time, use $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2g\Delta y$ — it skips $t$ entirely. If it mentions time, use $v = v_0 - gt$ and/or $y = y_0 + v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. Upward launch: v₀ > 0, a = −g v₀ is positive (upward). a = −9.8 m/s² (downward, always). The object decelerates, reaches apex where v = 0, then accelerates downward. The sign of v changes at the apex; the sign of a never does. Max height and full trajectory summary A ball is launched upward at $v_0 = 14$ m/s from ground level (up-positive, $g = 9.8$ m/s²). Find (a) maximum height, (b) time to apex, (c) total airtime, and (d) velocity at $t = 2$ s. Max height 10 m, apex at 1.43 s, lands at 2.86 s with speed 14 m/s. At $t = 2$ s the ball is falling at 5.6 m/s. h_{\text{max}} = \frac{v_0^2}{2g} = \frac{196}{19.6} = 10\text{ m} Apply the apex height formula. Since $v_0 = 14$ m/s, $v_0^2 = 196$ m²/s². t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g} = \frac{14}{9.8} \approx 1.43\text{ s} Time to the apex from $v = 0$ in $v = v_0 - gt$. T_{\text{total}} = 2 t_{\text{peak}} \approx 2.86\text{ s} By symmetry (landing at same height as launch), total flight time is double the apex time. v(2) = 14 - 9.8(2) = 14 - 19.6 = -5.6\text{ m/s} At $t = 2$ s (which is after the apex at 1.43 s), the ball is moving downward — consistent with the negative sign. Ball thrown from an elevated platform A ball is thrown upward at $v_0 = 10$ m/s from a platform 15 m above the ground. Find when it hits the ground and its impact speed. Flight time ≈ 3.05 s; impact speed ≈ 19.9 m/s. The extra height above the ground means the ball falls farther than it rose, gaining more than the launch speed on impact. y_0 = 15\text{ m},\quad v_0 = +10\text{ m/s},\quad a = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2,\quad y_f = 0 Set up with up-positive: platform is 15 m above ground ($y_f = 0$). 0 = 15 + 10t - \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 \implies 4.9t^2 - 10t - 15 = 0 Rearrange to standard quadratic form. t = \frac{10 + \sqrt{100 + 4(4.9)(15)}}{9.8} = \frac{10 + \sqrt{394}}{9.8} \approx \frac{10 + 19.85}{9.8} \approx 3.05\text{ s} Quadratic formula; take positive root. The ball is in the air for about 3.05 s. v_f = 10 - 9.8(3.05) \approx -19.9\text{ m/s} Impact velocity is about $-19.9$ m/s (downward). Speed ≈ 19.9 m/s — much larger than the 10 m/s launch speed because the ball gained extra speed falling from 15 m above the ground. Find launch speed given maximum height A safety engineer needs a component to reach exactly 12.5 m above its launch point. What launch speed is required? Required launch speed is $\sqrt{2g \cdot h} = \sqrt{245} \approx 15.65$ m/s. This is the inverse of the apex formula — solving for $v_0$ given $h_{\text{max}}$. h_{\text{max}} = \frac{v_0^2}{2g} = 12.5\text{ m} Set the apex height formula equal to the required height. v_0^2 = 2g \cdot h_{\text{max}} = 2(9.8)(12.5) = 245\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2 Solve for $v_0^2$. v_0 = \sqrt{245} \approx 15.65\text{ m/s} Take the positive square root. A launch speed of about 15.65 m/s will deliver exactly 12.5 m apex height. \text{Check: }h = \frac{(15.65)^2}{2(9.8)} = \frac{244.9}{19.6} \approx 12.5\text{ m}\checkmark Verify by substituting back. A ball is thrown upward from a rooftop 20 m above the ground. The ball reaches a maximum height of 5 m above the rooftop. Find (a) the launch speed, (b) the time to the apex, and (c) the impact speed when it hits the ground. The apex height is measured from the launch point (rooftop), not the ground. For part (c), use the no-time equation with $\Delta y = -(20 + 5) = -25$ m from apex to ground, or track absolute positions. h_{\text{max}} = 5\text{ m (above rooftop)} \implies v_0 = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2(9.8)(5)} = \sqrt{98} \approx 9.9\text{ m/s} Invert the apex formula: $v_0 = \sqrt{2g h_{\text{max}}}$. t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g} = \frac{9.9}{9.8} \approx 1.01\text{ s} Time from rooftop to apex. y_{\text{apex}} = 20 + 5 = 25\text{ m (absolute, above ground)} The apex is 25 m above the ground (20 m of building + 5 m of rise). v_f^2 = 0 - 2g(-25) = 2(9.8)(25) = 490 \implies |v_f| = \sqrt{490} \approx 22.1\text{ m/s} From apex (speed = 0) to ground ($\Delta y = -25$ m from apex), use the no-time equation. A ball thrown upward passes a window 6 m above the launch point on the way up. Two seconds later, it passes the same window on the way down. Find the launch speed. Set up $y = v_0 t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = 6$ m. The two solutions differ by 2 s: $t_2 - t_1 = 2$ s. Use Vieta's formulas on the quadratic roots. v_0 t - 4.9 t^2 = 6 \implies 4.9t^2 - v_0 t + 6 = 0 Rearrange to standard form. The two roots $t_1$ and $t_2$ are the times the ball is at 6 m. t_1 + t_2 = \frac{v_0}{4.9},\quad t_1 \cdot t_2 = \frac{6}{4.9} Vieta's formulas: sum of roots = $b/a$ (with sign change), product = $c/a$. Sum gives $t_1 + t_2 = v_0/4.9$. t_2 - t_1 = 2\text{ s (given)} \implies (t_2 - t_1)^2 = (t_2 + t_1)^2 - 4t_1 t_2 Use the algebraic identity to relate sum/difference/product of roots. 4 = \left(\frac{v_0}{4.9}\right)^2 - 4\cdot\frac{6}{4.9} \implies \frac{v_0^2}{24.01} = 4 + \frac{24}{4.9} \approx 4 + 4.898 = 8.898 Substitute and solve for $v_0^2$. v_0^2 = 8.898 \times 24.01 \approx 213.6 \implies v_0 \approx 14.6\text{ m/s} Launch speed is approximately 14.6 m/s. This is a clever application of Vieta's formulas to avoid solving the full quadratic. A ball is thrown upward at $v_0 = 20$ m/s. A second ball is dropped from rest at height $H$ at the same instant. The two balls collide at the apex of the first ball's trajectory. Find $H$. The first ball's apex is at $h = v_0^2/(2g)$ and occurs at $t_{\text{peak}} = v_0/g$. At that same time, the second ball has fallen from $H$ to the same height. t_{\text{peak}} = \frac{v_0}{g} = \frac{20}{9.8} \approx 2.04\text{ s},\quad h_{\text{apex}} = \frac{v_0^2}{2g} = \frac{400}{19.6} \approx 20.4\text{ m} Compute the apex time and height for the first ball. \text{Ball 2: }y_2(t) = H - \tfrac{1}{2}g t^2 Dropped from rest at height $H$. At $t = t_{\text{peak}}$, ball 2 must be at height $h_{\text{apex}}$. h_{\text{apex}} = H - \tfrac{1}{2}g t_{\text{peak}}^2 \implies H = h_{\text{apex}} + \tfrac{1}{2}g t_{\text{peak}}^2 Solve for $H$. H = 20.4 + \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(2.04)^2 \approx 20.4 + 20.4 = 40.8\text{ m} The second ball must be dropped from 40.8 m — exactly twice the apex height. The second ball falls $h_{\text{apex}}$ meters while the first rises $h_{\text{apex}}$ meters, so $H = 2h_{\text{apex}}$. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step

documents.title: Free Fall: Downward Throw
documents.subtitle: When initial velocity is downward, gravity compounds the speed increase from the very start.
documents.tags: downward throw free fall kinematics
documents.assignment: Throw from balcony — impact speed and time From a 20-m balcony, an object is thrown downward at 5 m/s (down-positive, $g = 9.8$ m/s²). Find (a) the impact speed and (b) the time of impact.   Impact speed ≈ 20.4 m/s, time ≈ 1.57 s. Dropping from rest gives ≈ 19.8 m/s in 2.02 s — the 5 m/s initial throw provides a 22% time reduction but only a 3% speed increase. v_0 = +5\text{ m/s (down+)},\quad a = +9.8\text{ m/s}^2,\quad h = 20\text{ m} All positive in down-positive convention: initial speed, acceleration, and fall distance. v_{\text{impact}}^2 = v_0^2 + 2gh = 25 + 2(9.8)(20) = 25 + 392 = 417\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2 No-time SUVAT equation. Both terms are positive and add together. v_{\text{impact}} = \sqrt{417} \approx 20.4\text{ m/s (downward)} Impact speed. Compare to dropping from rest: $v_{\text{drop}} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 20} = \sqrt{392} \approx 19.8$ m/s. The initial 5 m/s adds only 0.6 m/s to the impact speed. \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 + 5t - 20 = 0 \implies 4.9t^2 + 5t - 20 = 0 Rearrange $h = v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}g t^2$ to quadratic form. t = \frac{-5 + \sqrt{25 + 4(4.9)(20)}}{2(4.9)} = \frac{-5 + \sqrt{417}}{9.8} \approx \frac{-5 + 20.4}{9.8} \approx 1.57\text{ s} Positive root gives impact time ≈ 1.57 s. Cross-check: $v_0 + gt = 5 + 9.8(1.57) \approx 20.4$ m/s ✓ Comparison table — drop vs downward throw From 45 m height, compare: (a) drop from rest, (b) throw downward at 10 m/s, (c) throw downward at 20 m/s. Find impact speed and time for each.   As initial downward speed increases, impact time decreases substantially (linearly dominated), while impact speed increases modestly (sublinearly, because of the square root). Initial speed is more effective at reducing time than boosting impact speed. \text{(a) Drop: }v_{\text{impact}} = \sqrt{2(9.8)(45)} = \sqrt{882} \approx 29.7\text{ m/s},\quad t = \sqrt{2h/g} = \sqrt{9.18} \approx 3.03\text{ s} Reference case: $v_0 = 0$. \text{(b) }v_0 = 10\text{ m/s: }v_{\text{impact}} = \sqrt{100 + 882} = \sqrt{982} \approx 31.3\text{ m/s} Extra 10 m/s initial speed adds only 1.6 m/s to impact speed (5% increase). \text{(b) time: }4.9t^2 + 10t - 45 = 0 \implies t = \frac{-10 + \sqrt{982}}{9.8} \approx \frac{21.3}{9.8} \approx 2.17\text{ s} Impact time reduced from 3.03 s to 2.17 s (28% reduction). \text{(c) }v_0 = 20\text{ m/s: }v_{\text{impact}} = \sqrt{400 + 882} = \sqrt{1282} \approx 35.8\text{ m/s} Extra 20 m/s initial speed adds 6.1 m/s to impact speed. Still subadditive. \text{(c) time: }4.9t^2 + 20t - 45 = 0 \implies t \approx 1.57\text{ s} Impact time further reduced to 1.57 s (48% shorter than drop from rest). Find height from impact data An object is thrown downward at 4 m/s and hits the ground at 22 m/s. Find the drop height.   The drop height is approximately 23.9 m. This inverse problem — finding height from impact data — uses the no-time equation rearranged for $h$. v_{\text{impact}}^2 = v_0^2 + 2gh \implies h = \frac{v_{\text{impact}}^2 - v_0^2}{2g} Rearrange the no-time equation to solve for $h$. h = \frac{(22)^2 - (4)^2}{2(9.8)} = \frac{484 - 16}{19.6} = \frac{468}{19.6} \approx 23.9\text{ m} The drop height is approximately 23.9 m. \text{Verify with time: }t = \frac{v_{\text{impact}} - v_0}{g} = \frac{22 - 4}{9.8} \approx 1.84\text{ s} Using $v = v_0 + at$: the impact takes 1.84 s. h_{\text{check}} = v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = 4(1.84) + \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(3.38) \approx 7.36 + 16.56 = 23.9\text{ m}\checkmark Cross-check confirms $h \approx 23.9$ m.  An object is dropped from rest from height $h$ and hits the ground at time $t_1$. An identical object is thrown downward at speed $v_0$ from the same height and hits at time $t_2 < t_1$. Derive an expression for $t_2$ in terms of $v_0$, $g$, and $t_1$. Use $h = \tfrac{1}{2}g t_1^2$ (drop from rest) to eliminate $h$, then solve the quadratic for $t_2$.   h = \tfrac{1}{2}g t_1^2 From the drop-from-rest case: $h$ expressed in terms of $t_1$. h = v_0 t_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}g t_2^2 \implies \tfrac{1}{2}g t_1^2 = v_0 t_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}g t_2^2 Substitute the thrown-object equation and replace $h$. \tfrac{1}{2}g t_2^2 + v_0 t_2 - \tfrac{1}{2}g t_1^2 = 0 Quadratic in $t_2$. t_2 = \frac{-v_0 + \sqrt{v_0^2 + g^2 t_1^2}}{g} Positive root of the quadratic. As $v_0 \to 0$, this gives $t_2 \to t_1$, confirming the drop-from-rest limit.  An object is thrown downward at 8 m/s from a building and hits the ground at 30 m/s. (a) Find the building height. (b) How much faster did it hit compared to dropping from rest? Use $h = (v_f^2 - v_0^2)/(2g)$ for part (a). For part (b), compute drop-from-rest impact speed from the same height.   h = \frac{(30)^2 - (8)^2}{2(9.8)} = \frac{900 - 64}{19.6} = \frac{836}{19.6} \approx 42.7\text{ m} Height from the inverse no-time equation. v_{\text{drop}} = \sqrt{2(9.8)(42.7)} = \sqrt{836.9} \approx 28.9\text{ m/s} Drop-from-rest impact speed from the same height. \Delta v = 30 - 28.9 = 1.1\text{ m/s (about 3.8\%)} Throwing downward at 8 m/s only adds 1.1 m/s to the 28.9 m/s drop speed. The subadditive effect is clear: a large initial downward speed gives a tiny impact speed boost.  Two objects are thrown downward simultaneously from heights $h_1 = 30$ m and $h_2 = 50$ m with the same initial speed $v_0 = 6$ m/s. How much sooner does the first object hit the ground than the second? Find $t_1$ and $t_2$ separately from $\tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 + v_0 t - h = 0$, then compute $t_2 - t_1$.   4.9t_1^2 + 6t_1 - 30 = 0 \implies t_1 = \frac{-6 + \sqrt{36 + 588}}{9.8} = \frac{-6 + \sqrt{624}}{9.8} \approx \frac{-6 + 24.98}{9.8} \approx 1.94\text{ s} Impact time for the 30-m throw. 4.9t_2^2 + 6t_2 - 50 = 0 \implies t_2 = \frac{-6 + \sqrt{36 + 980}}{9.8} = \frac{-6 + \sqrt{1016}}{9.8} \approx \frac{-6 + 31.87}{9.8} \approx 2.64\text{ s} Impact time for the 50-m throw. \Delta t = t_2 - t_1 \approx 2.64 - 1.94 = 0.70\text{ s} The first object hits the ground about 0.70 s before the second.
documents.proofs: A downward throw is the constant-acceleration model with the initial condition $v_0 < 0$ (up-positive) instead of $v_0 > 0$ (upward throw) or $v_0 = 0$ (drop from rest). The differential equation $\ddot y = -g$ (up-positive) is unchanged; only the boundary condition at $t = 0$ differs. All SUVAT equations hold without modification. The energy interpretation clarifies why impact speed is $\sqrt{v_0^2 + 2gh}$: at launch, the kinetic energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2$ and the potential energy (relative to the ground) is $mgh$. At impact, all energy converts to kinetic energy $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\text{impact}}^2$. Energy conservation gives $v_{\text{impact}}^2 = v_0^2 + 2gh$ — identical to the SUVAT result, confirming that both approaches are equivalent for conservative forces. The subadditive behavior $v_{\text{impact}} < v_0 + \sqrt{2gh}$ follows from the inequality $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} < a + b$ for $a, b > 0$. More precisely, $\sqrt{v_0^2 + 2gh} = \sqrt{(v_0 + \sqrt{2gh})^2 - 2v_0\sqrt{2gh}} < v_0 + \sqrt{2gh}$. The "shortfall" $2v_0\sqrt{2gh}/(v_0 + \sqrt{2gh})$ increases with $v_0$, so higher initial speeds are increasingly less effective at boosting the impact speed. For very large $v_0$ (initial speed much greater than the free-fall contribution), $v_{\text{impact}} \approx v_0 + gh/v_0$ — the gravitational boost becomes a small additive correction. Conversely, for small $v_0$, $v_{\text{impact}} \approx \sqrt{2gh} + v_0/\sqrt{2gh} \cdot v_0/2$. These asymptotic behaviors are useful for building physical intuition about when initial speed dominates vs. when gravity dominates. Impact speed from energy conservation \tfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2 + mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\text{impact}}^2 \implies v_{\text{impact}} = \sqrt{v_0^2 + 2gh}
