The book does not accelerate vertically. Many students incorrectly identify the weight (Earth pulling book down) and the normal force (table pushing book up) as a Third Law pair. They are NOT. They act on the SAME object (the book), they are different types of forces (gravitational vs contact), and they cancel only because the book is in equilibrium — not because of the Third Law. The actual Third Law pairs are: Earth pulls book down ↔ book pulls Earth up (gravitational pair between Earth and book); table pushes book up ↔ book pushes table down (contact pair between table and book). Learning to identify true Third Law pairs is a skill that takes practice. **Walking, swimming, and propulsion — all Third Law.** You walk by pushing your foot backward on the ground. The ground pushes your foot forward (Third Law). You swim by pushing water backward with your hands. The water pushes you forward (Third Law). A propeller pushes air backward; the air pushes the plane forward (Third Law). A fan pushes air; the air pushes the fan and its housing backward (this is why you should anchor a fan). Every propulsion system in history works by pushing something backward and using the Third Law reaction to move forward. Understanding this makes the mechanics of every vehicle, animal, and machine immediately clear. **Momentum and the Third Law: why the universe conserves momentum.** The Third Law has a profound mathematical consequence. In a system of two interacting objects, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite: F₁₂ = −F₂₁. By Newton's Second Law, F₁₂ = dp₁/dt and F₂₁ = dp₂/dt. Adding: dp₁/dt + dp₂/dt = 0, which means d(p₁ + p₂)/dt = 0 — the total momentum is constant. Conservation of momentum is not a separate law; it is a direct consequence of Newton's Third Law. Every collision, every explosion, every rocket burn conserves the total momentum of the system for the same reason: internal forces always come in equal-and-opposite pairs. The Third Law pair has a simple algebraic statement: F_{A on B} = −F_{B on A}. The magnitudes are equal; the signs are opposite. When analyzing systems with multiple objects, you apply Newton's Second Law to each object separately. The Third Law tells you the forces that connect them are equal and opposite. For two objects m₁ and m₂ in contact, the contact force that m₁ exerts on m₂ is equal and opposite to the contact force m₂ exerts on m₁. This is how you 'chain' the equations of motion for connected objects. Newton's Third Law is deeply connected to conservation of momentum. Consider an isolated system of two particles. documents.assignment: Block on horizontal surface with applied force and friction A 10 kg block on a horizontal surface is pushed to the right by F = 50 N. Kinetic friction is f_k = 20 N. Find the acceleration and the normal force. Use g = 10 m/s².   Acceleration = 3 m/s² to the right; Normal force = 100 N. \text{FBD forces: } F_{\text{app}} = 50\,\text{N (right)}, f_k = 20\,\text{N (left)}, W = 100\,\text{N (down)}, N = ?\,(\text{up}) List all four forces before writing equations. \sum F_y = N - W = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad N = W = mg = 100\,\text{N} No vertical acceleration; normal force balances weight. \sum F_x = 50 - 20 = 30\,\text{N} \quad\Rightarrow\quad a = \frac{30}{10} = 3\,\text{m/s}^2 Net horizontal force = 30 N; divide by mass for acceleration. Hanging mass on two ropes at angles A 6 kg traffic light hangs from two ropes: rope 1 makes 53° with the horizontal, rope 2 makes 37° with the horizontal. Find tensions T₁ and T₂. (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8, sin 53° = 0.8, cos 53° = 0.6.) Use g = 10 m/s².   T₁ = 48 N (steeper rope carries more force), T₂ = 36 N. Verify: 0.8(48) + 0.6(36) = 38.4 + 21.6 = 60 N ✓ W = mg = 6 \times 10 = 60\,\text{N (down)} Weight of the traffic light. \sum F_x = T_2 \cos 37° - T_1 \cos 53° = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 0.8 T_2 - 0.6 T_1 = 0 Horizontal equilibrium: x-components of both tensions must cancel. \sum F_y = T_1 \sin 53° + T_2 \sin 37° - 60 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 0.8 T_1 + 0.6 T_2 = 60 Vertical equilibrium: upward tension components support the weight. \text{From x-equation: } T_1 = \frac{0.8}{0.6} T_2 = \frac{4}{3} T_2 Express T₁ in terms of T₂. 0.8 \cdot \frac{4}{3} T_2 + 0.6 T_2 = 60 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{3.2 + 1.8}{3} T_2 = \frac{5}{3} T_2 = 60 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_2 = 36\,\text{N} Substitute and solve for T₂. T_1 = \frac{4}{3}(36) = 48\,\text{N} Back-substitute for T₁.  Draw the FBD for a 5 kg block sliding down a frictionless ramp. Identify the TWO forces acting. Write their names, directions, and the axis equations. Use g = 10 m/s². On a ramp, only weight and normal force act (frictionless). Normal is perpendicular to the ramp surface, not vertical. Two forces: W (down) and N (perpendicular to slope). N = mg cosθ; a = g sinθ along slope.  \text{Forces: Weight } W = 50\,\text{N (vertically down)}, \quad N \perp \text{ramp surface} Two forces only on a frictionless ramp: gravity and normal. \sum F_{\perp} = N - mg\cos\theta = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad N = mg\cos\theta Perpendicular to ramp: no acceleration in this direction. \sum F_{\parallel} = mg\sin\theta = ma \quad\Rightarrow\quad a = g\sin\theta Along ramp: weight component drives acceleration down the slope.  A 4 kg block is pushed against a vertical wall by a horizontal force of 80 N. The coefficient of static friction between block and wall is μ_s = 0.4. Does the block slide? Find the friction force and normal force. Use g = 10 m/s². The normal force here comes from the horizontal push, not from gravity. Draw the FBD carefully. N = 80 N (horizontal), maximum friction = 32 N. Since weight (40 N) exceeds maximum friction (32 N), the block slides down.  N = F_{\text{push}} = 80\,\text{N} \qquad (\text{normal to the vertical wall}) The wall's normal force balances the horizontal push. N ≠ mg here! W = mg = 4 \times 10 = 40\,\text{N (down)} Weight pulls the block downward. f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N = 0.4 \times 80 = 32\,\text{N} Maximum static friction the wall can provide. W = 40\,\text{N} > f_{s,\max} = 32\,\text{N} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{block slides down} Gravity exceeds maximum friction — the block cannot be held.  A 3 kg block is suspended by two vertical ropes. Then a horizontal rope pulls it to the right so it hangs at 30° from vertical. The left-upper rope is now at angle 30° from vertical. Find: (a) the tension in the diagonal rope, (b) the tension in the horizontal rope. Use g = 10 m/s². (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.866.) Draw the FBD with three forces: T₁ (diagonal, upper-left), T₂ (horizontal, right), W (down). Use equilibrium equations. Diagonal rope tension T₁ ≈ 34.6 N; horizontal rope tension T₂ ≈ 17.3 N.  W = 3 \times 10 = 30\,\text{N} Weight is 30 N downward. \sum F_y = T_1 \cos 30° - W = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_1 = \frac{30}{\cos 30°} = \frac{30}{0.866} \approx 34.6\,\text{N} Vertical component of T₁ supports the entire weight. \sum F_x = T_1 \sin 30° - T_2 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_2 = 34.6 \times 0.5 = 17.3\,\text{N} Horizontal component of T₁ is balanced by the horizontal tension.
documents.proofs: The FBD method is a systematic application of particle mechanics. The key assumption is that the object can be treated as a point mass — all forces effectively act at one point, and we ignore rotation (torque). Every force in an FBD is a vector F⃗ with components (Fₓ, Fᵧ). The vector sum ΣF⃗ = Σ(Fₓ, Fᵧ) = (ΣFₓ, ΣFᵧ). By the Second Law, (ΣFₓ, ΣFᵧ) = m(aₓ, aᵧ). This gives two independent scalar equations. The choice of coordinate axes does not change the physics — only the algebra. Aligning one axis with the acceleration direction zeros out one component equation and simplifies the other. For inclined planes, tilting the axes with the slope is standard and reduces computation. The FBD is the interface between the physical world and the mathematical model. A correct FBD guarantees a solvable system; an incorrect FBD (wrong forces, wrong directions) gives nonsensical results every time. FBD → equations systematically \sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \begin{cases} \sum F_x = m a_x \\ \sum F_y = m a_y \end{cases}
documents.applications: Free body diagrams (FBDs) are the universal language of mechanics. Every structural engineer, roboticist, and physicist draws them before writing a single equation. An FBD isolates one object and shows every force acting on it as a labeled vector. Without an FBD, even simple problems become confusing. With one, even complex problems become systematic. Free Body Diagram (FBD) A diagram showing a single isolated object with all external forces drawn as vector arrows, each labeled with its magnitude and direction. Internal forces are omitted. Normal Force (N) The contact force exerted by a surface on an object, always perpendicular (normal) to the surface. N is NOT always equal to mg — that is only true on a horizontal surface with no vertical applied forces. Tension (T) The pulling force exerted by a rope, cable, or string along its length, directed away from the object (ropes pull, never push). For a massless rope, tension is the same throughout. 5-step FBD procedure (1) Isolate the object. (2) Identify all contact and field forces. (3) Draw each as a vector with label. (4) Choose coordinate axes (align with acceleration if possible). (5) Write ΣF = ma for each axis.
documents.content: How do engineers design a bridge without knowing in advance which direction each internal force points? Free body diagrams (FBDs) are the universal language of mechanics. Every structural engineer, roboticist, and physicist draws them before writing a single equation. An FBD isolates one object and shows every force acting on it as a labeled vector. Without an FBD, even simple problems become confusing. With one, even complex problems become systematic. A free body diagram is a picture of ONE object in isolation, with every external force drawn as an arrow at the point of application (or at the center for simplicity). Internal forces — interactions between parts of the object — are NOT drawn. The five common forces you will draw in every introductory problem: (1) Weight W = mg, always straight down from the center of mass. (2) Normal force N, perpendicular to any surface the object touches. (3) Tension T, along a rope or cable, always pulling away from the object. (4) Friction f, parallel to the surface, opposing motion (or tendency of motion). (5) Applied force F_app, in whatever direction stated. After drawing the FBD, choose a coordinate system (usually x right, y up — or tilted to align with the acceleration direction). Project every force onto your axes. Then write ΣFₓ = maₓ and ΣFᵧ = maᵧ. You now have algebra equations that you can solve. The FBD is not decoration — it IS the physics. Skipping it leads to sign errors, missing forces, and wrong answers. Professional engineers draw FBDs even for problems they've solved hundreds of times. Once you have an FBD, the mathematical work is mechanical: resolve each force into x and y components, then sum each component and set equal to maₓ or maᵧ. For an object on a horizontal surface with a horizontal push F, kinetic friction f_k, mass m, and acceleration a: ΣFₓ = F − f_k = ma (horizontal); ΣFᵧ = N − mg = 0 (vertical, no vertical acceleration). Two equations, solve for a and N. For a hanging mass in equilibrium on two ropes at angles θ₁ and θ₂: ΣFₓ = T₂cosθ₂ − T₁cosθ₁ = 0; ΣFᵧ = T₁sinθ₁ + T₂sinθ₂ − mg = 0. Two equations, two unknowns T₁ and T₂. The FBD method is a systematic application of particle mechanics. The key assumption is that the object can be treated as a point mass — all forces effectively act at one point, and we ignore rotation (torque). Every force in an FBD is a vector F⃗ with components (Fₓ, Fᵧ). The vector sum ΣF⃗ = Σ(Fₓ, Fᵧ) = (ΣFₓ, ΣFᵧ). By the Second Law, (ΣFₓ, ΣFᵧ) = m(aₓ, aᵧ). This gives two independent scalar equations. The choice of coordinate axes does not change the physics — only the algebra. Aligning one axis with the acceleration direction zeros out one component equation and simplifies the other. For inclined planes, tilting the axes with the slope is standard and reduces computation. The FBD is the interface between the physical world and the mathematical model. A correct FBD guarantees a solvable system; an incorrect FBD (wrong forces, wrong directions) gives nonsensical results every time. FBD → equations systematically \sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \begin{cases} \sum F_x = m a_x \\ \sum F_y = m a_y \end{cases} Free Body Diagram (FBD) A diagram showing a single isolated object with all external forces drawn as vector arrows, each labeled with its magnitude and direction. Internal forces are omitted. Normal Force (N) The contact force exerted by a surface on an object, always perpendicular (normal) to the surface. N is NOT always equal to mg — that is only true on a horizontal surface with no vertical applied forces. Tension (T) The pulling force exerted by a rope, cable, or string along its length, directed away from the object (ropes pull, never push). For a massless rope, tension is the same throughout. 5-step FBD procedure (1) Isolate the object. (2) Identify all contact and field forces. (3) Draw each as a vector with label. (4) Choose coordinate axes (align with acceleration if possible). (5) Write ΣF = ma for each axis. Standard FBD equations for block on horizontal surface \sum F_x = F_{\text{app}} - f = ma_x \qquad \sum F_y = N - mg = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad N = mg When N ≠ mg Normal force equals mg only for an object on a horizontal surface with no vertical applied forces. If the surface is tilted, if a force pushes vertically, or if the object is accelerating vertically, then N ≠ mg. Always derive N from ΣFᵧ = maᵧ. FBD of a block on a horizontal surface being pushed Applied force F_app (right), friction f (left), weight W (down), normal N (up). All four forces are drawn as arrows from the center. The FBD makes it clear that only the horizontal forces affect horizontal acceleration. Hanging mass: two tension forces in balance FBD converts a 2D geometry problem into a system of algebra equations. Step-by-step FBD construction Physics thinking (FBD) converts directly to mathematical equations. Block on horizontal surface with applied force and friction A 10 kg block on a horizontal surface is pushed to the right by F = 50 N. Kinetic friction is f_k = 20 N. Find the acceleration and the normal force. Use g = 10 m/s². Acceleration = 3 m/s² to the right; Normal force = 100 N. \text{FBD forces: } F_{\text{app}} = 50\,\text{N (right)}, f_k = 20\,\text{N (left)}, W = 100\,\text{N (down)}, N = ?\,(\text{up}) List all four forces before writing equations. \sum F_y = N - W = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad N = W = mg = 100\,\text{N} No vertical acceleration; normal force balances weight. \sum F_x = 50 - 20 = 30\,\text{N} \quad\Rightarrow\quad a = \frac{30}{10} = 3\,\text{m/s}^2 Net horizontal force = 30 N; divide by mass for acceleration. Hanging mass on two ropes at angles A 6 kg traffic light hangs from two ropes: rope 1 makes 53° with the horizontal, rope 2 makes 37° with the horizontal. Find tensions T₁ and T₂. (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8, sin 53° = 0.8, cos 53° = 0.6.) Use g = 10 m/s². T₁ = 48 N (steeper rope carries more force), T₂ = 36 N. Verify: 0.8(48) + 0.6(36) = 38.4 + 21.6 = 60 N ✓ W = mg = 6 \times 10 = 60\,\text{N (down)} Weight of the traffic light. \sum F_x = T_2 \cos 37° - T_1 \cos 53° = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 0.8 T_2 - 0.6 T_1 = 0 Horizontal equilibrium: x-components of both tensions must cancel. \sum F_y = T_1 \sin 53° + T_2 \sin 37° - 60 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 0.8 T_1 + 0.6 T_2 = 60 Vertical equilibrium: upward tension components support the weight. \text{From x-equation: } T_1 = \frac{0.8}{0.6} T_2 = \frac{4}{3} T_2 Express T₁ in terms of T₂. 0.8 \cdot \frac{4}{3} T_2 + 0.6 T_2 = 60 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{3.2 + 1.8}{3} T_2 = \frac{5}{3} T_2 = 60 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_2 = 36\,\text{N} Substitute and solve for T₂. T_1 = \frac{4}{3}(36) = 48\,\text{N} Back-substitute for T₁. Draw the FBD for a 5 kg block sliding down a frictionless ramp. Identify the TWO forces acting. Write their names, directions, and the axis equations. Use g = 10 m/s². On a ramp, only weight and normal force act (frictionless). Normal is perpendicular to the ramp surface, not vertical. Two forces: W (down) and N (perpendicular to slope). N = mg cosθ; a = g sinθ along slope. \text{Forces: Weight } W = 50\,\text{N (vertically down)}, \quad N \perp \text{ramp surface} Two forces only on a frictionless ramp: gravity and normal. \sum F_{\perp} = N - mg\cos\theta = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad N = mg\cos\theta Perpendicular to ramp: no acceleration in this direction. \sum F_{\parallel} = mg\sin\theta = ma \quad\Rightarrow\quad a = g\sin\theta Along ramp: weight component drives acceleration down the slope. A 4 kg block is pushed against a vertical wall by a horizontal force of 80 N. The coefficient of static friction between block and wall is μ_s = 0.4. Does the block slide? Find the friction force and normal force. Use g = 10 m/s². The normal force here comes from the horizontal push, not from gravity. Draw the FBD carefully. N = 80 N (horizontal), maximum friction = 32 N. Since weight (40 N) exceeds maximum friction (32 N), the block slides down. N = F_{\text{push}} = 80\,\text{N} \qquad (\text{normal to the vertical wall}) The wall's normal force balances the horizontal push. N ≠ mg here! W = mg = 4 \times 10 = 40\,\text{N (down)} Weight pulls the block downward. f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N = 0.4 \times 80 = 32\,\text{N} Maximum static friction the wall can provide. W = 40\,\text{N} > f_{s,\max} = 32\,\text{N} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{block slides down} Gravity exceeds maximum friction — the block cannot be held. A 3 kg block is suspended by two vertical ropes. Then a horizontal rope pulls it to the right so it hangs at 30° from vertical. The left-upper rope is now at angle 30° from vertical. Find: (a) the tension in the diagonal rope, (b) the tension in the horizontal rope. Use g = 10 m/s². (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.866.) Draw the FBD with three forces: T₁ (diagonal, upper-left), T₂ (horizontal, right), W (down). Use equilibrium equations. Diagonal rope tension T₁ ≈ 34.6 N; horizontal rope tension T₂ ≈ 17.3 N. W = 3 \times 10 = 30\,\text{N} Weight is 30 N downward. \sum F_y = T_1 \cos 30° - W = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_1 = \frac{30}{\cos 30°} = \frac{30}{0.866} \approx 34.6\,\text{N} Vertical component of T₁ supports the entire weight. \sum F_x = T_1 \sin 30° - T_2 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_2 = 34.6 \times 0.5 = 17.3\,\text{N} Horizontal component of T₁ is balanced by the horizontal tension. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step

documents.title: Friction: Static and Kinetic
documents.subtitle: Static friction prevents motion; kinetic friction opposes it. Both depend on the normal force and surface properties.
documents.tags: friction static-friction kinetic-friction normal-force coefficient-of-friction dynamics
documents.assignment: Minimum force to start sliding a crate A 30 kg crate sits on a floor with μ_s = 0.45 and μ_k = 0.30. (a) What minimum force starts it sliding? (b) Once sliding, what force keeps it moving at constant velocity? Use g = 10 m/s².   Need 135 N to start sliding; only 90 N to maintain constant sliding speed. The 45 N difference is why it "feels easier" once the crate is moving. N = mg = 30 \times 10 = 300\,\text{N} Normal force on horizontal surface. (a)\; F_{\min} = \mu_s N = 0.45 \times 300 = 135\,\text{N} Must exceed maximum static friction to initiate sliding. (b)\; f_k = \mu_k N = 0.30 \times 300 = 90\,\text{N} Once sliding, kinetic friction requires 90 N to maintain constant velocity (zero acceleration). Block pushed with downward-angled force A 10 kg block is pushed along the floor by a 50 N force directed 30° below horizontal. μ_k = 0.25. Find the normal force and the acceleration. (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.866.) Use g = 10 m/s².   N = 125 N (not mg = 100 N!); a ≈ 1.2 m/s². The angled push increases N, which increases friction — the block accelerates less than if the push were horizontal. F_x = 50\cos 30° = 43.3\,\text{N (forward)}, \quad F_y = -50\sin 30° = -25\,\text{N (downward)} The push is angled downward, so it adds to the downward forces. \sum F_y = 0: N - mg - 25 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad N = 100 + 25 = 125\,\text{N} Normal force increases because the downward push component presses the block into the floor. f_k = \mu_k N = 0.25 \times 125 = 31.25\,\text{N} Kinetic friction is larger because N is larger — notice the coupling. a = \frac{F_x - f_k}{m} = \frac{43.3 - 31.25}{10} = \frac{12.05}{10} \approx 1.2\,\text{m/s}^2 Net horizontal force divided by mass.  A 20 kg box on a horizontal floor has μ_s = 0.5 and μ_k = 0.35. A horizontal force of 80 N is applied. Does the box move? If so, find its acceleration. Use g = 10 m/s². First compute maximum static friction. Compare to applied force. If it moves, use kinetic friction. The box does not move. Static friction = 80 N (matching the push). Acceleration = 0.  N = mg = 200\,\text{N}, \quad f_{s,\max} = 0.5 \times 200 = 100\,\text{N} Maximum static friction is 100 N. F_{\text{app}} = 80\,\text{N} < 100\,\text{N} = f_{s,\max} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{Box does NOT move} Applied force is less than maximum static friction. f_s = 80\,\text{N (exactly matches applied force)}, \quad a = 0 Static friction equals the applied force to maintain equilibrium.  A 15 kg sled is pulled across snow by a rope at 20° above horizontal with tension T = 60 N. μ_k = 0.10. Find N, f_k, and the acceleration. Use g = 10 m/s². (sin 20° ≈ 0.34, cos 20° ≈ 0.94.) The upward component of T reduces N — which reduces friction. Find N from ΣFᵧ = 0 first. N = 129.6 N, f_k = 13.0 N, a ≈ 2.9 m/s².  T_x = 60\cos 20° = 56.4\,\text{N}, \quad T_y = 60\sin 20° = 20.4\,\text{N (up)} Decompose tension into horizontal and vertical components. N = mg - T_y = 150 - 20.4 = 129.6\,\text{N} The upward pull reduces normal force. f_k = 0.10 \times 129.6 = 13.0\,\text{N} Reduced N means reduced kinetic friction. a = \frac{T_x - f_k}{m} = \frac{56.4 - 13.0}{15} = \frac{43.4}{15} \approx 2.9\,\text{m/s}^2 Net force divided by mass.  A 5 kg block is on a 40° ramp. μ_s = 0.6. Will the block slide? If not, what is the friction force? If it does slide and μ_k = 0.4, find the acceleration. (sin 40° ≈ 0.643, cos 40° ≈ 0.766.) Use g = 10 m/s². Find N, then maximum static friction, and compare to the component of gravity along the ramp. Block slides (W_∥ = 32.15 N > f_{s,max} = 23.0 N). Kinetic friction = 15.32 N. Acceleration ≈ 3.4 m/s² down the slope.  N = mg\cos 40° = 5 \times 10 \times 0.766 = 38.3\,\text{N} Normal force perpendicular to ramp. W_{\parallel} = mg\sin 40° = 5 \times 10 \times 0.643 = 32.15\,\text{N (down slope)} Gravity component along the slope — this tends to cause sliding. f_{s,\max} = 0.6 \times 38.3 = 23.0\,\text{N} Maximum static friction available. W_{\parallel} = 32.15 > f_{s,\max} = 23.0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{Block slides!} Gravity exceeds maximum static friction — sliding occurs. f_k = 0.4 \times 38.3 = 15.32\,\text{N (up slope)} Kinetic friction opposes the sliding direction (acts up the slope). a = \frac{W_{\parallel} - f_k}{m} = \frac{32.15 - 15.32}{5} = \frac{16.83}{5} \approx 3.4\,\text{m/s}^2 \text{ (down slope)} Net force along slope divided by mass.
documents.proofs: Friction is an emergent macroscopic effect of microscopic contact interactions. At the atomic level, surfaces have asperities (tiny bumps) that interlock; the friction force is the net horizontal component of all those microscopic normal forces. The empirical Coulomb friction model (f ≤ μN for static, f = μN for kinetic) is not derived from first principles — it is a mathematical model that fits experimental data extremely well over a wide range of conditions. It breaks down at very high speeds, very high pressures, or for lubricated surfaces. Mathematically, the piecewise nature of friction makes it a non-smooth function. The equation of motion for a block with friction has different forms before and during motion: m(d²x/dt²) = F_app − μ_s N (if |F_app| ≤ μ_s N, then actually d²x/dt² = 0) and m(d²x/dt²) = F_app − μ_k N (when sliding). This piecewise ODE requires careful handling. The transition between static and kinetic: f_s,max = μ_s N is the threshold. For F_applied < f_s,max: static, a = 0. For F_applied = f_s,max: on the verge of sliding. For F_applied > f_s,max: kinetic friction takes over at f_k = μ_k N < f_s,max. Piecewise equation of motion with friction m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |F_{\text{app}}| \leq \mu_s N \text{ (static)} \\ F_{\text{app}} - \mu_k N \cdot \text{sgn}(v) & \text{if sliding} \end{cases}
documents.applications: Friction is everywhere: tires gripping roads, brakes stopping cars, bolts staying tight, shoes walking without slipping. Understanding friction allows engineers to design brake systems, prevent structural failures, and analyze machine efficiency. The distinction between static and kinetic friction — and the insight that normal force drives both — unlocks every friction problem in physics. Static friction f_s \leq \mu_s N \qquad \text{(prevents motion; automatically adjusts up to maximum \(\mu_s N\))} Kinetic friction f_k = \mu_k N \qquad \text{(opposes motion in progress; constant value)} Coefficient of friction \mu = \text{dimensionless number characterizing surface pair}; \quad \mu_k < \mu_s \text{ always} Normal force is NOT always mg On a horizontal surface with no vertical applied forces: N = mg. But on a ramp, N = mg cosθ. If a force pushes the object into the surface or lifts it, N changes. Always derive N from ΣFᵧ = maᵧ.
documents.content: Why is it harder to START sliding a heavy box than to KEEP it sliding once it's already moving? Friction is everywhere: tires gripping roads, brakes stopping cars, bolts staying tight, shoes walking without slipping. Understanding friction allows engineers to design brake systems, prevent structural failures, and analyze machine efficiency. The distinction between static and kinetic friction — and the insight that normal force drives both — unlocks every friction problem in physics. Static friction is the friction force that prevents an object from moving. It adjusts to whatever value is needed to maintain equilibrium, up to a maximum. When you push lightly on a box, static friction matches your push exactly. Push harder, and it matches you harder — until you exceed its maximum. Kinetic friction acts when the object IS moving. It has a fixed value (not adjustable) equal to μ_k × N. It always opposes the direction of motion. Always: μ_k < μ_s. It takes more force to START sliding something than to KEEP it sliding. This is why pushing a heavy box over a threshold feels like the resistance suddenly drops — once kinetic friction replaces static, the resisting force decreases. Both friction forces depend on N (the normal force) through the coefficient of friction μ — a dimensionless number that characterizes the roughness of the surface pair. μ does NOT depend on contact area — a wide flat box and a narrow tall box with the same mass and surface type have the same friction force. For a block on a horizontal surface: N = mg, so f_k = μ_k·mg and f_{s,max} = μ_s·mg. For a block on a ramp at angle θ: N = mg cosθ, so f_k = μ_k·mg cosθ. To find the minimum force to start sliding: F_min = f_{s,max} = μ_s·N. For horizontal surface: F_min = μ_s·mg. To find the acceleration of a sliding block: ΣF = F_applied − f_k = F_applied − μ_k·N = ma → a = (F_applied − μ_k·N)/m. Friction is an emergent macroscopic effect of microscopic contact interactions. At the atomic level, surfaces have asperities (tiny bumps) that interlock; the friction force is the net horizontal component of all those microscopic normal forces. The empirical Coulomb friction model (f ≤ μN for static, f = μN for kinetic) is not derived from first principles — it is a mathematical model that fits experimental data extremely well over a wide range of conditions. It breaks down at very high speeds, very high pressures, or for lubricated surfaces. Mathematically, the piecewise nature of friction makes it a non-smooth function. The equation of motion for a block with friction has different forms before and during motion: m(d²x/dt²) = F_app − μ_s N (if |F_app| ≤ μ_s N, then actually d²x/dt² = 0) and m(d²x/dt²) = F_app − μ_k N (when sliding). This piecewise ODE requires careful handling. The transition between static and kinetic: f_s,max = μ_s N is the threshold. For F_applied < f_s,max: static, a = 0. For F_applied = f_s,max: on the verge of sliding. For F_applied > f_s,max: kinetic friction takes over at f_k = μ_k N < f_s,max. Piecewise equation of motion with friction m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |F_{\text{app}}| \leq \mu_s N \text{ (static)} \\ F_{\text{app}} - \mu_k N \cdot \text{sgn}(v) & \text{if sliding} \end{cases} Static friction f_s \leq \mu_s N \qquad \text{(prevents motion; automatically adjusts up to maximum \(\mu_s N\))} Kinetic friction f_k = \mu_k N \qquad \text{(opposes motion in progress; constant value)} Coefficient of friction \mu = \text{dimensionless number characterizing surface pair}; \quad \mu_k < \mu_s \text{ always} Normal force is NOT always mg On a horizontal surface with no vertical applied forces: N = mg. But on a ramp, N = mg cosθ. If a force pushes the object into the surface or lifts it, N changes. Always derive N from ΣFᵧ = maᵧ. Friction equations on a horizontal surface N = mg, \quad f_k = \mu_k m g, \quad f_{s,\max} = \mu_s m g Minimum force to start sliding (horizontal) F_{\min} = \mu_s N = \mu_s m g Friction is piecewise The friction force as a function of applied force is NOT smooth — it has a kink at the onset of motion. Mathematically, friction is a piecewise-defined function: f = F_applied (static regime) or f = μ_k N (kinetic regime). This is important in calculus: friction is not differentiable at the transition point. FBD: block on surface with friction Applied force F_app (right), kinetic friction f_k (left, opposing motion), weight W (down), normal N (up). The friction force is f_k = μ_k N, not μ_k mg unless N = mg. Static vs kinetic friction: force-vs-applied-force graph Friction is not constant — static is variable (up to a maximum); kinetic is fixed. Interactive: apply force to block with friction The threshold between static and kinetic friction is the maximum static friction force. Static-to-kinetic transition and piecewise dynamics Real friction requires knowing the motion state before writing the equation of motion. Minimum force to start sliding a crate A 30 kg crate sits on a floor with μ_s = 0.45 and μ_k = 0.30. (a) What minimum force starts it sliding? (b) Once sliding, what force keeps it moving at constant velocity? Use g = 10 m/s². Need 135 N to start sliding; only 90 N to maintain constant sliding speed. The 45 N difference is why it "feels easier" once the crate is moving. N = mg = 30 \times 10 = 300\,\text{N} Normal force on horizontal surface. (a)\; F_{\min} = \mu_s N = 0.45 \times 300 = 135\,\text{N} Must exceed maximum static friction to initiate sliding. (b)\; f_k = \mu_k N = 0.30 \times 300 = 90\,\text{N} Once sliding, kinetic friction requires 90 N to maintain constant velocity (zero acceleration). Block pushed with downward-angled force A 10 kg block is pushed along the floor by a 50 N force directed 30° below horizontal. μ_k = 0.25. Find the normal force and the acceleration. (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.866.) Use g = 10 m/s². N = 125 N (not mg = 100 N!); a ≈ 1.2 m/s². The angled push increases N, which increases friction — the block accelerates less than if the push were horizontal. F_x = 50\cos 30° = 43.3\,\text{N (forward)}, \quad F_y = -50\sin 30° = -25\,\text{N (downward)} The push is angled downward, so it adds to the downward forces. \sum F_y = 0: N - mg - 25 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad N = 100 + 25 = 125\,\text{N} Normal force increases because the downward push component presses the block into the floor. f_k = \mu_k N = 0.25 \times 125 = 31.25\,\text{N} Kinetic friction is larger because N is larger — notice the coupling. a = \frac{F_x - f_k}{m} = \frac{43.3 - 31.25}{10} = \frac{12.05}{10} \approx 1.2\,\text{m/s}^2 Net horizontal force divided by mass. The upward component of T reduces N — which reduces friction. Find N from ΣFᵧ = 0 first. N = 129.6 N, f_k = 13.0 N, a ≈ 2.9 m/s². T_x = 60\cos 20° = 56.4\,\text{N}, \quad T_y = 60\sin 20° = 20.4\,\text{N (up)} Decompose tension into horizontal and vertical components. N = mg - T_y = 150 - 20.4 = 129.6\,\text{N} The upward pull reduces normal force. f_k = 0.10 \times 129.6 = 13.0\,\text{N} Reduced N means reduced kinetic friction. a = \frac{T_x - f_k}{m} = \frac{56.4 - 13.0}{15} = \frac{43.4}{15} \approx 2.9\,\text{m/s}^2 Net force divided by mass. Use g = 10 m/s². Find N, then maximum static friction, and compare to the component of gravity along the ramp. Block slides (W_∥ = 32.15 N > f_{s,max} = 23.0 N). Kinetic friction = 15.32 N. Acceleration ≈ 3.4 m/s² down the slope. N = mg\cos 40° = 5 \times 10 \times 0.766 = 38.3\,\text{N} Normal force perpendicular to ramp. W_{\parallel} = mg\sin 40° = 5 \times 10 \times 0.643 = 32.15\,\text{N (down slope)} Gravity component along the slope — this tends to cause sliding. f_{s,\max} = 0.6 \times 38.3 = 23.0\,\text{N} Maximum static friction available. W_{\parallel} = 32.15 > f_{s,\max} = 23.0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{Block slides!} Gravity exceeds maximum static friction — sliding occurs. f_k = 0.4 \times 38.3 = 15.32\,\text{N (up slope)} Kinetic friction opposes the sliding direction (acts up the slope). a = \frac{W_{\parallel} - f_k}{m} = \frac{32.15 - 15.32}{5} = \frac{16.83}{5} \approx 3.4\,\text{m/s}^2 \text{ (down slope)} Net force along slope divided by mass. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step

documents.assignment: Sign hanging from two cables at equal angles A 40 N sign hangs from two cables, each making 50° with the horizontal. Find the tension in each cable. (sin 50° ≈ 0.766, cos 50° ≈ 0.643.)   Each cable carries 26.1 N — more than half the weight (20 N) because the cables are not vertical. \text{By symmetry: } T_1 = T_2 = T Equal angles → equal tensions. Symmetry simplifies the problem. \sum F_x = T\cos 50° - T\cos 50° = 0 \quad\checkmark Horizontal: the two x-components cancel automatically by symmetry. \sum F_y = 2T\sin 50° - 40 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T = \frac{40}{2 \times 0.766} = \frac{40}{1.532} \approx 26.1\,\text{N} Two upward components support the weight. Ladder against a frictionless wall A 5 m, 20 kg ladder leans against a frictionless vertical wall, making 60° with the floor. The floor has friction. Find the normal force from the wall (N_w) and the normal force from the floor (N_f). (Treat as translational equilibrium only; treat the ladder weight as acting at its midpoint.) Use g = 10 m/s². (sin 60° ≈ 0.866, cos 60° = 0.5.)   N_f = 200 N (floor supports all weight vertically); N_w = f_floor ≈ 57.7 N (wall pushes horizontally, balanced by floor friction). Note: torque balance is needed for the full solution. W = 20 \times 10 = 200\,\text{N (down at midpoint)} Weight acts at the center of mass (midpoint of ladder). \sum F_y = 0: N_f - W = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad N_f = 200\,\text{N} Vertical: only the floor normal force and weight are vertical. (Wall is frictionless, so no vertical wall force.) \sum F_x = 0: N_w - f_{\text{floor}} = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad N_w = f_{\text{floor}} Horizontal: wall normal force is balanced by floor friction. \text{Full solution requires torque balance: } N_w = \frac{W \cdot \frac{L}{2}\cos 60°}{L \sin 60°} = \frac{200 \times 0.5}{2 \times 0.866} \approx 57.7\,\text{N} Torque equation (preview): moment arm geometry gives N_w. Full derivation in rotational statics chapter.  A 60 N picture frame hangs from a single vertical wire attached at two equal points. The wire makes a V-shape; each side makes 70° with the horizontal. Find the tension in each segment of wire. (sin 70° ≈ 0.940.) Two symmetric tension forces, both angled upward. ΣFᵧ = 0. T ≈ 31.9 N in each wire segment.  2T\sin 70° = 60 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T = \frac{60}{2 \times 0.940} = \frac{60}{1.88} \approx 31.9\,\text{N} Each wire segment carries equal tension by symmetry.  A 50 N weight hangs from two unequal cables: cable A makes 45° with the horizontal, cable B is horizontal. Find T_A and T_B. (sin 45° = cos 45° ≈ 0.707.) A horizontal cable (B) provides only a horizontal force. Cable A provides both horizontal and vertical components. Use ΣFᵧ = 0 to find T_A first. T_A ≈ 70.7 N; T_B ≈ 50 N. The horizontal cable carries as much tension as the weight itself.  \sum F_y = T_A \sin 45° - 50 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_A = \frac{50}{0.707} \approx 70.7\,\text{N} Only cable A has a vertical component to support the weight. \sum F_x = T_A \cos 45° - T_B = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_B = 70.7 \times 0.707 \approx 50\,\text{N} Horizontal cable B cancels the horizontal component of T_A.  Three cables support a 120 N chandelier: cable 1 (T₁) makes 30° with horizontal on the left, cable 2 (T₂) makes 60° with horizontal on the right, cable 3 (T₃) hangs vertically downward from the junction to the chandelier. Write the full system of equilibrium equations at the junction and solve for T₁, T₂, and T₃. (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.866, sin 60° = 0.866, cos 60° = 0.5.) T₃ = W = 120 N directly from ΣFᵧ on the chandelier alone. Then analyze the junction with T₁, T₂, T₃ as forces. T₁ = 60 N, T₂ ≈ 103.9 N, T₃ = 120 N. The steeper cable (T₂ at 60°) carries more tension.  T_3 = W = 120\,\text{N} \quad\text{(vertical cable supports chandelier weight)} Apply equilibrium to the chandelier alone: only T₃ (up) and W (down). \text{At junction: } \sum F_y = T_1 \sin 30° + T_2 \sin 60° - T_3 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 0.5 T_1 + 0.866 T_2 = 120 Upward components of T₁ and T₂ must support T₃. \sum F_x = T_2 \cos 60° - T_1 \cos 30° = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 0.5 T_2 = 0.866 T_1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_2 = 1.732 T_1 Horizontal components of T₁ (left) and T₂ (right) must cancel. 0.5 T_1 + 0.866(1.732 T_1) = 120 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 0.5 T_1 + 1.5 T_1 = 120 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_1 = 60\,\text{N} Substitute and solve. T_2 = 1.732 \times 60 \approx 103.9\,\text{N}, \quad T_3 = 120\,\text{N} Back-substitute for T₂.
documents.proofs: Static equilibrium is a special case of Newton's Second Law: ΣF = ma = 0 because a = 0. The two component equations ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣFᵧ = 0 together constitute the full translational equilibrium condition. Mathematically, the equilibrium equations form a linear system Ax = b where x is the vector of unknown force magnitudes, A is the matrix of direction cosines (from the geometry), and b is the vector of known forces (usually weight components). If A is invertible, there is a unique equilibrium solution. When the system is underdetermined (more unknowns than equations), the structure is statically indeterminate — cannot be solved from statics alone. When overdetermined, there is generally no solution (the structure fails). Well-designed structures are statically determinate: exactly as many unknowns as equilibrium equations. Calculus perspective: equilibrium means the position function x(t) is constant. Its derivative dx/dt = v = 0 and its second derivative d²x/dt² = a = 0. Both kinematic quantities are zero. The calculus of statics is trivial — the richness is entirely in the geometry and algebra of force decomposition. Linear system form of static equilibrium A \vec{T} = \vec{W} \quad \text{where} \quad A = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta_1 & -\cos\theta_2 \\ \sin\theta_1 & \sin\theta_2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \vec{T} = \begin{pmatrix} T_1 \\ T_2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \vec{W} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ W \end{pmatrix}

documents.content: How does a bridge cable know exactly how much tension to carry — and why does the tension change depending on the cable angle? Static equilibrium is the physics of things that are NOT moving: buildings, bridges, cranes, hanging signs, ladders against walls. Engineers design structures to be in static equilibrium under all expected loads. Every structural analysis starts with ΣF = 0. Mastering statics means mastering the algebra of force balance — a skill used constantly in mechanical and civil engineering. An object in static equilibrium has zero acceleration (a = 0) and zero velocity (at rest). From Newton's Second Law: ΣF = ma = m(0) = 0. So ΣF = 0 — every force is balanced by other forces. In 2D, this means TWO conditions: ΣFₓ = 0 (horizontal forces balance) AND ΣFᵧ = 0 (vertical forces balance). Each condition gives one equation. Two unknowns (like two tension magnitudes) → two equations → solvable. The key skill: decompose every angled force into x and y components, then apply the two balance equations. The geometry of the angles determines the component values. Note: Complete statics also requires Στ = 0 (torques balance). We will only address translational equilibrium (force balance) here. Rotational equilibrium (torque balance) comes in a later chapter. For any statics problem, the result is a system of linear equations. In 2D with two unknown forces, you get exactly two equations (ΣFₓ = 0, ΣFᵧ = 0) and two unknowns — a well-determined system. If a force F acts at angle θ above the positive x-axis: Fₓ = F cosθ (positive = rightward), Fᵧ = F sinθ (positive = upward). Careful with signs — forces pointing left or down contribute negative components. The system of equations is a 2×2 linear system: aT₁ + bT₂ = c and dT₁ + eT₂ = f (where a,b,c,d,e,f come from the geometry). Solve by substitution or elimination. Force balance as a 2×2 linear system Statics is geometry + Newton's Law → linear algebra. Sign hanging from two cables at equal angles A 40 N sign hangs from two cables, each making 50° with the horizontal. Find the tension in each cable. (sin 50° ≈ 0.766, cos 50° ≈ 0.643.) Each cable carries 26.1 N — more than half the weight (20 N) because the cables are not vertical. \text{By symmetry: } T_1 = T_2 = T Equal angles → equal tensions. Symmetry simplifies the problem. \sum F_x = T\cos 50° - T\cos 50° = 0 \quad\checkmark Horizontal: the two x-components cancel automatically by symmetry. \sum F_y = 2T\sin 50° - 40 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T = \frac{40}{2 \times 0.766} = \frac{40}{1.532} \approx 26.1\,\text{N} Two upward components support the weight. Find the normal force from the wall (N_w) and the normal force from the floor (N_f). (Treat as translational equilibrium only; treat the ladder weight as acting at its midpoint.) Use g = 10 m/s². documents.assignment: Block sliding down a ramp with friction A 8 kg block slides down a 30° ramp with μ_k = 0.20. Find: (a) the normal force, (b) the friction force, (c) the acceleration, (d) the speed after sliding 5 m from rest. Use g = 10 m/s². (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.866.)   N = 69.3 N, f_k = 13.9 N, a = 3.27 m/s² down the slope, speed after 5 m = 5.72 m/s. N = mg\cos 30° = 8 \times 10 \times 0.866 = 69.3\,\text{N} Normal force is perpendicular to slope — not equal to mg. f_k = \mu_k N = 0.20 \times 69.3 = 13.9\,\text{N} Kinetic friction opposes sliding (acts up the slope). a = g(\sin 30° - \mu_k \cos 30°) = 10(0.5 - 0.20 \times 0.866) = 10(0.5 - 0.173) = 3.27\,\text{m/s}^2 Acceleration along the slope (downward). v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x = 0 + 2(3.27)(5) = 32.7 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = \sqrt{32.7} \approx 5.72\,\text{m/s} Kinematic equation for constant acceleration over displacement 5 m. Finding the critical angle A rubber block is placed on a wooden ramp. μ_s = 0.70. At what angle will the block begin to slide? What is the acceleration just after it begins sliding if μ_k = 0.50? Use g = 10 m/s².   The block starts sliding at θ_c ≈ 35°. Just after sliding, it accelerates at 1.64 m/s² down the slope. \theta_c = \arctan(\mu_s) = \arctan(0.70) \approx 35° Critical angle: tan θ_c = μ_s. Rubber on wood is quite rough — steeper threshold. a = g(\sin 35° - \mu_k \cos 35°) = 10(0.574 - 0.50 \times 0.819) = 10(0.574 - 0.410) = 1.64\,\text{m/s}^2 At θ = 35°, using kinetic friction after sliding begins.  A frictionless ramp makes 25° with the horizontal. A 4 kg block starts from rest at the top. Find: (a) the normal force, (b) the acceleration, (c) speed after traveling 3 m. Use g = 10 m/s². (sin 25° ≈ 0.423, cos 25° ≈ 0.906.) No friction → friction force = 0. Use a = g sinθ. N = 36.2 N, a = 4.23 m/s², v ≈ 5.04 m/s after 3 m.  N = mg\cos 25° = 4 \times 10 \times 0.906 = 36.2\,\text{N} Normal force on frictionless ramp. a = g\sin 25° = 10 \times 0.423 = 4.23\,\text{m/s}^2 No friction term — full weight component along slope drives acceleration. v^2 = 2a\Delta x = 2(4.23)(3) = 25.4 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v \approx 5.04\,\text{m/s} v² = v₀² + 2aΔx with v₀ = 0.  A block on a 40° ramp with μ_s = 0.55 and μ_k = 0.40 is given an initial push up the ramp at 6 m/s. (a) Does the block slide down on its own after stopping? (b) Find the acceleration while moving up and the deceleration distance. Use g = 10 m/s². (sin 40° ≈ 0.643, cos 40° ≈ 0.766.) While moving UP, friction acts DOWN the slope (opposing upward motion). Check if θ > arctan(μ_s) to determine if it slides back. Yes, it slides back (θ = 40° > θ_c ≈ 28.8°). Deceleration while going up = 9.49 m/s². Stops after 1.90 m.  \theta_c = \arctan(0.55) \approx 28.8° < 40° \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{Block slides back after stopping} The ramp is steeper than the critical angle, so gravity overcomes static friction. a_{\text{up}} = -(g\sin 40° + \mu_k g\cos 40°) = -10(0.643 + 0.40 \times 0.766) = -10(0.643 + 0.306) = -9.49\,\text{m/s}^2 Going up: both gravity component and friction act DOWN (deceleration). v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x \Rightarrow 0 = 36 + 2(-9.49)d \Rightarrow d = \frac{36}{18.98} \approx 1.90\,\text{m} Distance traveled up the ramp before stopping.  A 6 kg block on a 35° ramp is connected by a rope over a frictionless pulley at the top to a hanging 4 kg mass. μ_k = 0.20 for the ramp. Does the ramp block slide up or down? Find its acceleration and the rope tension. Use g = 10 m/s². (sin 35° ≈ 0.574, cos 35° ≈ 0.819.) First determine which direction the system moves (compare driving forces). Then write F=ma for each mass separately and solve simultaneously. The system is in static equilibrium — a = 0. The net tendency (5.6 N) is less than maximum static friction. Tension T = m₂g = 40 N (hanging mass in equilibrium). This illustrates why checking static equilibrium FIRST is essential.  N = m_1 g\cos 35° = 6 \times 10 \times 0.819 = 49.1\,\text{N}; \quad f_k = 0.20 \times 49.1 = 9.82\,\text{N} Normal force and kinetic friction for the block on the ramp. W_1^{\parallel} = m_1 g\sin 35° = 6 \times 10 \times 0.574 = 34.4\,\text{N (down slope)} Gravity component of ramp block along slope. W_2 = m_2 g = 4 \times 10 = 40\,\text{N (down)} Weight of hanging mass. 40 > 34.4 + 9.82 = 44.2? \;\text{No: } 40 < 44.2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{Try: hanging mass goes DOWN} Hanging mass pulls the ramp block UP. Check if W₂ > W₁_parallel + friction. 40 N vs 34.4 + 9.82 = 44.2 N — hanging mass can't lift the block. Try the other direction. \text{Check: block slides DOWN, hanging mass goes UP.}\; W_1^{\parallel} = 34.4 > W_2 - f_k = 40 - 9.82? \;34.4 > 30.2\;\checkmark The ramp block slides down, pulling the hanging mass up. (m_1 + m_2)a = m_1 g\sin 35° - f_k - m_2 g = 34.4 - 9.82 - 40 = -15.4\,\text{N} Wait — this is negative, meaning block actually does NOT slide down. System is in static equilibrium! \text{Static check: } |W_1^{\parallel} - W_2| = |34.4 - 40| = 5.6\,\text{N} < f_{s,\max} \approx \mu_s N \approx 0.25 \times 49.1 = 12.3\,\text{N} The net driving force (5.6 N) is less than maximum static friction — the system is in static equilibrium, a = 0.
documents.proofs: The inclined plane is a perfect demonstration that the choice of coordinate system is a mathematical tool, not a physical law. Physics doesn't care which axes you choose — Newton's Second Law holds in any inertial frame and any orientation. In standard axes (x horizontal, y vertical): weight = (0, −mg), Normal = (N sinθ, N cosθ), friction = (−f cosθ, f sinθ) for a block sliding down. Setting ΣF = ma gives two coupled equations. Solving them is more work but gives the same answer. In tilted axes (x along slope, y perpendicular): weight = (−mg sinθ, −mg cosθ), Normal = (0, N), friction = (f, 0). The two equations decouple completely: N = mg cosθ from the y-equation, and ma = mg sinθ − f from the x-equation. This is why tilted axes are preferred. Calculus connection: the equation a = g(sinθ − μcosθ) is a constant (for given θ and μ). This means d²x/dt² = a = constant, giving the standard kinematic equations: v(t) = v₀ + at and x(t) = x₀ + v₀t + ½at². Ramp problems with constant slope are constant-acceleration problems. Tilted axis decoupling \text{y-axis (⊥ slope): } N - mg\cos\theta = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad N = mg\cos\theta \\ \text{x-axis (∥ slope): } mg\sin\theta - \mu_k N = ma \quad\Rightarrow\quad a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)

The key technique — tilting your coordinate axes to align with the acceleration — reduces a 2D problem to two independent 1D problems. Master this and you can solve any ramp problem in three steps. Weight components in tilted coordinates W_{\parallel} = mg\sin\theta \;(\text{down slope}), \qquad W_{\perp} = mg\cos\theta \;(\text{into surface}) Normal force on ramp N = mg\cos\theta \qquad (\text{perpendicular to slope; less than mg for any } \theta > 0) Acceleration on ramp with friction a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k \cos\theta) \qquad (\text{if } \sin\theta > \mu_s\cos\theta) Critical angle for sliding \theta_c = \arctan(\mu_s) \qquad \text{(block slides if } \theta > \theta_c\text{)}
documents.content: Why does a steeper ramp accelerate a sliding box more — and at exactly what angle does the box start sliding on its own? Inclined planes are the master example of force decomposition in physics. Every ramp, ski slope, conveyor belt, and hillside road is an inclined plane problem. The key technique — tilting your coordinate axes to align with the acceleration — reduces a 2D problem to two independent 1D problems. Master this and you can solve any ramp problem in three steps. The standard (horizontal/vertical) coordinate system is not the most efficient for ramp problems. Instead, tilt your axes so that x points along the slope (in the direction of motion) and y points perpendicular to the slope. Now the normal force is purely in the y-direction and the acceleration is purely in the x-direction. In the tilted system, the weight W = mg (straight down) has two components: W_∥ = mg sinθ (along the slope, pointing down the ramp — the component that causes sliding) and W_⊥ = mg cosθ (perpendicular to slope, into the surface — the component that determines normal force). The normal force N balances W_⊥: N = mg cosθ. Note this is LESS than mg on a ramp — the normal force decreases as the angle increases. At θ = 90° (vertical wall), N = 0 (no contact force). Friction on the ramp: f = μN = μmg cosθ (if the object slides). Net force along the slope: F_net = mg sinθ − μmg cosθ = mg(sinθ − μcosθ). Divide by m: a = g(sinθ − μcosθ). This elegant formula contains all the physics. Setup for any inclined plane problem: (1) Define x-axis along the slope (positive = up the slope or down, choose consistently), y-axis perpendicular to slope. (2) Decompose weight: W_x = −mg sinθ (down slope), W_y = −mg cosθ (into slope). (3) Normal: N_y = +mg cosθ. (4) Friction: ±μN along slope (opposes motion). (5) Write ΣFₓ = ma and ΣFᵧ = 0. The perpendicular equation ΣFᵧ = 0 always gives N = mg cosθ immediately. Substitute into the parallel equation ΣFₓ = ma to find a. For a block sliding DOWN: a = g sinθ − μ_k g cosθ = g(sinθ − μ_k cosθ). For a block pushed UP the ramp, friction now acts downward along the slope: a = −g sinθ − μ_k g cosθ (decelerating). Physics doesn't care which axes you choose — Newton's Second Law holds in any inertial frame and any orientation. Find: (a) the normal force, (b) the friction force, (c) the acceleration, (d) the speed after sliding 5 m from rest. Use g = 10 m/s². (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.866.) N = 69.3 N, f_k = 13.9 N, a = 3.27 m/s² down the slope, speed after 5 m = 5.72 m/s. N = mg\cos 30° = 8 \times 10 \times 0.866 = 69.3\,\text{N} Normal force is perpendicular to slope — not equal to mg. f_k = \mu_k N = 0.20 \times 69.3 = 13.9\,\text{N} Kinetic friction opposes sliding (acts up the slope). a = g(\sin 30° - \mu_k \cos 30°) = 10(0.5 - 0.20 \times 0.866) = 10(0.5 - 0.173) = 3.27\,\text{m/s}^2 Acceleration along the slope (downward). v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x = 0 + 2(3.27)(5) = 32.7 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = \sqrt{32.7} \approx 5.72\,\text{m/s} Kinematic equation for constant acceleration over displacement 5 m. Finding the critical angle A rubber block is placed on a wooden ramp. μ_s = 0.70. At what angle will the block begin to slide? What is the acceleration just after it begins sliding if μ_k = 0.50? Use g = 10 m/s². The block starts sliding at θ_c ≈ 35°. Just after sliding, it accelerates at 1.64 m/s² down the slope. \theta_c = \arctan(\mu_s) = \arctan(0.70) \approx 35° Critical angle: tan θ_c = μ_s. Rubber on wood is quite rough — steeper threshold. a = g(\sin 35° - \mu_k \cos 35°) = 10(0.574 - 0.50 \times 0.819) = 10(0.574 - 0.410) = 1.64\,\text{m/s}^2 At θ = 35°, using kinetic friction after sliding begins. A frictionless ramp makes 25° with the horizontal. A 4 kg block starts from rest at the top. Find: (a) the normal force, (b) the acceleration, (c) speed after traveling 3 m. Use g = 10 m/s². (sin 25° ≈ 0.423, cos 25° ≈ 0.906.) No friction → friction force = 0. Use a = g sinθ. N = 36.2 N, a = 4.23 m/s², v ≈ 5.04 m/s after 3 m. N = mg\cos 25° = 4 \times 10 \times 0.906 = 36.2\,\text{N} Normal force on frictionless ramp. a = g\sin 25° = 10 \times 0.423 = 4.23\,\text{m/s}^2 No friction term — full weight component along slope drives acceleration. v^2 = 2a\Delta x = 2(4.23)(3) = 25.4 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v \approx 5.04\,\text{m/s} v² = v₀² + 2aΔx with v₀ = 0. A block on a 40° ramp with μ_s = 0.55 and μ_k = 0.40 is given an initial push up the ramp at 6 m/s. (a) Does the block slide down on its own after stopping? (b) Find the acceleration while moving up and the deceleration distance. Use g = 10 m/s². (sin 40° ≈ 0.643, cos 40° ≈ 0.766.) While moving UP, friction acts DOWN the slope (opposing upward motion). Check if θ > arctan(μ_s) to determine if it slides back. Yes, it slides back (θ = 40° > θ_c ≈ 28.8°). Deceleration while going up = 9.49 m/s². Stops after 1.90 m. \theta_c = \arctan(0.55) \approx 28.8° < 40° \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{Block slides back after stopping} The ramp is steeper than the critical angle, so gravity overcomes static friction. a_{\text{up}} = -(g\sin 40° + \mu_k g\cos 40°) = -10(0.643 + 0.40 \times 0.766) = -10(0.643 + 0.306) = -9.49\,\text{m/s}^2 Going up: both gravity component and friction act DOWN (deceleration). v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x \Rightarrow 0 = 36 + 2(-9.49)d \Rightarrow d = \frac{36}{18.98} \approx 1.90\,\text{m} Distance traveled up the ramp before stopping. A 6 kg block on a 35° ramp is connected by a rope over a frictionless pulley at the top to a hanging 4 kg mass. μ_k = 0.20 for the ramp. Does the ramp block slide up or down? Find its acceleration and the rope tension. Use g = 10 m/s². (sin 35° ≈ 0.574, cos 35° ≈ 0.819.) First determine which direction the system moves (compare driving forces). Then write F=ma for each mass separately and solve simultaneously. The system is in static equilibrium — a = 0. The net tendency (5.6 N) is less than maximum static friction. Tension T = m₂g = 40 N (hanging mass in equilibrium). This illustrates why checking static equilibrium FIRST is essential. N = m_1 g\cos 35° = 6 \times 10 \times 0.819 = 49.1\,\text{N}; \quad f_k = 0.20 \times 49.1 = 9.82\,\text{N} Normal force and kinetic friction for the block on the ramp. W_1^{\parallel} = m_1 g\sin 35° = 6 \times 10 \times 0.574 = 34.4\,\text{N (down slope)} Gravity component of ramp block along slope. W_2 = m_2 g = 4 \times 10 = 40\,\text{N (down)} Weight of hanging mass. 40 > 34.4 + 9.82 = 44.2? \;\text{No: } 40 < 44.2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{Try: hanging mass goes DOWN} Hanging mass pulls the ramp block UP. documents.assignment: Classic Atwood machine m₁ = 5 kg, m₂ = 3 kg, g = 10 m/s². Find: (a) the acceleration, (b) the tension, (c) the speed of m₁ after it falls 0.8 m from rest.   a = 2.5 m/s², T = 37.5 N, speed after 0.8 m = 2 m/s. a = \frac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{(5-3) \times 10}{5+3} = \frac{20}{8} = 2.5\,\text{m/s}^2 Heavier mass m₁ descends; acceleration is positive. T = \frac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{2 \times 5 \times 3 \times 10}{8} = \frac{300}{8} = 37.5\,\text{N} Tension lies between m₂g = 30 N and m₁g = 50 N — sanity check passed. v^2 = 2a\Delta x = 2 \times 2.5 \times 0.8 = 4 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = 2\,\text{m/s} Constant acceleration kinematic equation from rest. Near-balanced Atwood machine m₁ = 4.1 kg, m₂ = 3.9 kg, g = 10 m/s². Find the acceleration and tension. Why is T nearly equal to both weights?   a = 0.25 m/s² (barely moving), T ≈ 40 N. This is how the Atwood machine was historically used to measure g — tiny a magnifies small measurement errors into measurable time intervals. a = \frac{(4.1-3.9) \times 10}{4.1+3.9} = \frac{0.2 \times 10}{8} = \frac{2}{8} = 0.25\,\text{m/s}^2 Small mass difference → small acceleration. T = \frac{2 \times 4.1 \times 3.9 \times 10}{8} = \frac{319.8}{8} \approx 40\,\text{N} T ≈ mg = 4 kg × 10 = 40 N. Nearly balanced → tension is nearly the weight of either mass.  An Atwood machine has m₁ = 6 kg and m₂ = 2 kg. g = 10 m/s². Find a and T. How far does m₁ fall in 2 s from rest? Use a = (m₁−m₂)g/(m₁+m₂), then x = ½at². a = 5 m/s², T = 30 N, m₁ falls 10 m in 2 s.  a = \frac{(6-2) \times 10}{6+2} = \frac{40}{8} = 5\,\text{m/s}^2 Large mass difference gives large acceleration. T = \frac{2 \times 6 \times 2 \times 10}{8} = \frac{240}{8} = 30\,\text{N} Check: m₂g = 20 N < T = 30 N < m₁g = 60 N. ✓ x = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 4 = 10\,\text{m} m₁ falls 10 m in 2 seconds. Rearrange a = (m₁−m₂)g/(m₁+m₂) to solve for m₁. m₁ = 6 kg, T = 48 N.  a(m_1+m_2) = (m_1-m_2)g \;\Rightarrow\; am_1 + am_2 = m_1 g - m_2 g Cross-multiply and expand. m_1(g-a) = m_2(g+a) \;\Rightarrow\; m_1 = m_2\frac{g+a}{g-a} = 4 \times \frac{12}{8} = 6\,\text{kg} Isolate m₁: collect terms. T = \frac{2 \times 6 \times 4 \times 10}{10} = \frac{480}{10} = 48\,\text{N} Tension with m₁ = 6, m₂ = 4.  A modified Atwood machine: m₁ = 5 kg sits on a frictionless horizontal table. documents.proofs: Define positive directions carefully: let positive be the direction of expected motion — downward for m₁ and upward for m₂. With this convention, both masses have the same positive acceleration scalar a > 0. The rope constraint enforces that if m₁ moves down by dx, m₂ moves up by exactly dx. Differentiating twice: a₁ = a₂ = a. This is the geometric foundation — from it, we can write one acceleration for the whole system. Notice that T cancels when the two equations are added. This is not a coincidence — it reflects the fact that tension is an internal force of the system. The system as a whole accelerates under the net external force (m₁ − m₂)g acting on the total mass (m₁ + m₂). The Atwood machine is a perfect illustration of treating a connected system as a single object with an effective mass. System perspective F_{\text{net,ext}} = (m_1 - m_2)g, \quad m_{\text{total}} = m_1 + m_2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad a = \frac{(m_1-m_2)g}{m_1+m_2}
documents.applications: Pulleys redirect force. Cranes, elevators, and window-washing rigs all use pulley systems. The Atwood machine — two masses over a single pulley — is the textbook model because it isolates one subtle idea: when two objects are connected, their accelerations are equal in magnitude. You can't solve the system by looking at just one mass. You must write Newton's second law for each mass separately, then solve together. How to solve any Atwood machine Step 1: Draw a free-body diagram for EACH mass separately. Step 2: Choose consistent sign conventions (e.g., down positive for m₁, up positive for m₂). Step 3: Write F = ma for each mass. Step 4: Note that both equations share the same a and the same T. Step 5: Add the equations to eliminate T and solve for a. Step 6: Substitute a back to find T. The constraint Because the rope is inextensible, both masses have the same acceleration magnitude: |a₁| = |a₂| = a. This "constraint equation" is what connects the two Newton's-law equations into a solvable system. The tension is NOT equal to either weight Students often set T = m₁g or T = m₂g. This is wrong — it would only be true if the system were in static equilibrium (a = 0). In a moving Atwood machine, T lies strictly between m₂g and m₁g (when m₁ > m₂). Calculus connection The acceleration a = (m₁−m₂)g/(m₁+m₂) is a constant (for fixed masses). This means d²x/dt² = a = constant, so v(t) = at and x(t) = ½at². Atwood machines are constant-acceleration problems — all the kinematic equations apply directly.
documents.content: If you hang a 3 kg mass and a 1 kg mass over a frictionless pulley, what is the tension in the rope? Pulleys redirect force. Cranes, elevators, and window-washing rigs all use pulley systems. The Atwood machine — two masses over a single pulley — is the textbook model because it isolates one subtle idea: when two objects are connected, their accelerations are equal in magnitude. You can't solve the system by looking at just one mass. You must write Newton's second law for each mass separately, then solve together. Imagine two tug-of-war teams, one on each end of a rope draped over a pulley. If both teams are equally matched, nobody moves — the rope is taut and still. If one team is stronger, the heavier side wins. But here is the beautiful constraint: both sides move at exactly the same speed. The rope doesn't stretch or compress. The pulley just changes the direction of force, not its magnitude. A pulley has one powerful property: the tension T in an ideal (massless, frictionless) rope is the same everywhere along the rope. The rope pulls m₁ upward with force T and pulls m₂ upward with force T — the exact same T. This single number is what links the two masses into a coupled system. Change one mass and you change the tension felt by both. The key constraint: m₁ and m₂ have the same magnitude of acceleration. If m₁ descends by 1 m, m₂ rises by exactly 1 m. The rope length is fixed, so one side can only go down by the same amount the other side goes up. This geometric fact — the constraint equation — is the bridge between the two Newton's law equations. So the Atwood machine has exactly two unknowns: the shared acceleration a and the rope tension T. You get exactly two equations by applying F = ma to each mass separately with consistent sign conventions. Two equations, two unknowns — the system is fully determined. The algebra is simple; the conceptual setup is everything. There's a beautiful limit: if m₁ = m₂, then a = 0 and T = mg. The masses balance like a scale — the system is in equilibrium, rope taut but motionless. As the mass difference grows, a increases toward g (free fall). At the extreme, one mass is so much larger the other that it's effectively in free fall pulling a negligible mass. Every Atwood machine lives on this spectrum between perfect balance and free fall. Step 1 — Free body diagram for each mass separately. For m₁ (the heavier mass, taking down as positive): net downward force = m₁g − T. Newton's 2nd law: m₁g − T = m₁a. Step 2 — Free body diagram for m₂ (taking upward as positive, since it rises): net upward force = T − m₂g. Newton's 2nd law: T − m₂g = m₂a. Step 3 — Notice both equations share the same a and the same T. Add the two equations to eliminate T: m₁g − T + T − m₂g = m₁a + m₂a → (m₁ − m₂)g = (m₁ + m₂)a. Solving for acceleration: a = (m₁ − m₂)g / (m₁ + m₂). Substituting back into T − m₂g = m₂a gives T = m₂(g + a). Simplifying: T = 2m₁m₂g / (m₁ + m₂). Sanity checks: (1) If m₁ = m₂ = m: a = 0 and T = mg — balanced system, nothing moves. (2) If m₂ → 0: a → g and T → 0 — m₁ is in free fall, rope goes slack. (3) T is always less than m₁g and greater than m₂g when the system moves. Define positive directions carefully: let positive be the direction of expected motion — downward for m₁ and upward for m₂. With this convention, both masses have the same positive acceleration scalar a > 0. The rope constraint enforces that if m₁ moves down by dx, m₂ moves up by exactly dx. Differentiating twice: a₁ = a₂ = a. This is the geometric foundation — from it, we can write one acceleration for the whole system. Notice that T cancels when the two equations are added. This is not a coincidence — it reflects the fact that tension is an internal force of the system. The system as a whole accelerates under the net external force (m₁ − m₂)g acting on the total mass (m₁ + m₂). The Atwood machine is a perfect illustration of treating a connected system as a single object with an effective mass. System perspective F_{\text{net,ext}} = (m_1 - m_2)g, \quad m_{\text{total}} = m_1 + m_2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad a = \frac{(m_1-m_2)g}{m_1+m_2} How to solve any Atwood machine Step 1: Draw a free-body diagram for EACH mass separately. Step 2: Choose consistent sign conventions (e.g., down positive for m₁, up positive for m₂). Step 3: Write F = ma for each mass. Step 4: Note that both equations share the same a and the same T. Step 5: Add the equations to eliminate T and solve for a. Step 6: Substitute a back to find T. The constraint Because the rope is inextensible, both masses have the same acceleration magnitude: |a₁| = |a₂| = a. This "constraint equation" is what connects the two Newton's-law equations into a solvable system. The tension is NOT equal to either weight Students often set T = m₁g or T = m₂g. This is wrong — it would only be true if the system were in static equilibrium (a = 0). In a moving Atwood machine, T lies strictly between m₂g and m₁g (when m₁ > m₂). Atwood machines are constant-acceleration problems — all the kinematic equations apply directly. documents.title: Circular Motion Dynamics
documents.subtitle: Centripetal force is not a new force — it is whatever real force points toward the center.
documents.tags: circular-motion centripetal-force centripetal-acceleration orbital-mechanics banking
documents.assignment: Car on a flat curve A 1200 kg car rounds a flat curve of radius 60 m. μ_s = 0.70, g = 10 m/s². (a) What maximum speed can the car maintain without skidding? (b) At 20 m/s, what friction force is required?   Max speed ≈ 20.5 m/s (73.7 km/h). At 20 m/s, friction must supply 8000 N inward — within the 8400 N max (0.70 × 1200 × 10). v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g} = \sqrt{0.70 \times 60 \times 10} = \sqrt{420} \approx 20.5\,\text{m/s} \approx 73.7\,\text{km/h} Friction provides centripetal force; mass cancels. v_max depends only on μ, r, and g. F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{1200 \times 400}{60} = 8000\,\text{N} At 20 m/s: required centripetal force. This must be supplied by friction. Ball on a string in a vertical circle A 0.4 kg ball on a 0.8 m string moves in a vertical circle. (a) What is the minimum speed at the top to keep the string taut? (b) At the bottom, moving at 6 m/s, what is the tension? g = 10 m/s².   v_min at top = 2.83 m/s. Tension at bottom at 6 m/s = 22 N (5.5× the ball's weight — the bottom of a loop is the most stressful point for the string). \text{Top: } mg + N = \frac{mv^2}{r} \;\Rightarrow\; N = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; v_{\min} = \sqrt{rg} = \sqrt{0.8 \times 10} = 2.83\,\text{m/s} Minimum speed: gravity alone provides centripetal force; string just barely taut (N=0). \text{Bottom: } T - mg = \frac{mv^2}{r} \;\Rightarrow\; T = mg + \frac{mv^2}{r} = 0.4 \times 10 + \frac{0.4 \times 36}{0.8} = 4 + 18 = 22\,\text{N} At the bottom: centripetal direction is upward. Net upward force = T − mg = mv²/r. Tension is largest at the bottom.  A satellite orbits at altitude 400 km above Earth's surface. Earth's radius = 6.4×10⁶ m, g at that altitude ≈ 8.7 m/s². Find the orbital speed and period. (Use v = √(gr).) r = R_Earth + altitude. Period T = 2πr/v. v ≈ 7692 m/s (7.7 km/s), T ≈ 92.5 min.  r = 6.4 \times 10^6 + 4 \times 10^5 = 6.8 \times 10^6\,\text{m} Orbital radius = Earth's radius + altitude. v = \sqrt{g r} = \sqrt{8.7 \times 6.8 \times 10^6} = \sqrt{5.916 \times 10^7} \approx 7692\,\text{m/s} \approx 7.7\,\text{km/s} Gravity provides centripetal force: mg = mv²/r → v = √(gr). T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi \times 6.8 \times 10^6}{7692} \approx 5552\,\text{s} \approx 92.5\,\text{min} The ISS orbits at ~400 km and has a period of ~92 minutes — this matches!  A highway curve has radius 150 m. Design it to be safe at 30 m/s without relying on friction (ideal banking angle). Also find the maximum speed with μ_s = 0.55 on the banked curve at this angle. g = 10 m/s². Ideal angle: tanθ = v²/(rg). With banking and friction: v_max = √(rg(tanθ + μ_s)/(1 − μ_s tanθ)). Ideal banking angle θ ≈ 31°. The word "centripetal" means "center-seeking," and the remarkable insight is that it's never a new mysterious force: it's always an existing force (gravity, normal, tension, friction) doing double duty as the redirector. Tie a ball to a string and swing it in a circle over your head. Your hand pulls the string inward. That inward pull is the centripetal force — and if you let go, the ball flies off in a straight line tangent to the circle (Newton's 1st law at work). The string was constantly changing the ball's direction without changing its speed. This is the defining feature of centripetal force: it acts perpendicular to velocity, so it changes direction but does no work. Changing direction means changing the velocity vector, even if the speed (magnitude) is constant. Changing velocity means acceleration. So circular motion at constant speed still involves acceleration — directed toward the center at every instant. This is centripetal acceleration: a_c = v²/r. The faster you go or the tighter the curve, the larger the centripetal acceleration needed. The required centripetal force is just F_c = ma_c = mv²/r. The question in every circular dynamics problem is the same: which physical force provides mv²/r? For a satellite: gravity. For a car on a flat curve: static friction. For a ball on a string: tension. For a roller coaster at the top of a loop: gravity plus normal force. The "centripetal force" is not a new entry on your free body diagram — it's the label for the net inward force supplied by existing forces. Here is the most persistent misconception in circular dynamics: "centrifugal force." In the inertial (ground) reference frame, there is no outward force on the object. What feels like an outward push to a passenger in a turning car is really just inertia — the car pushes the passenger inward (centripetally), and the passenger's inertia makes it feel like they're being pushed outward. If friction disappears on an icy road, the car doesn't fly outward — it goes straight, tangent to the curve. Outward is the direction of missing centripetal force. Four canonical examples build all the intuition you need: (1) Ball on a string — tension is purely centripetal. (2) Car on a flat curve — friction provides the centripetal force; max speed = √(μ_s rg). (3) Satellite orbit — gravity is the centripetal force; orbital speed v = √(GM/r). This is not an approximation — it is exact for uniform circular motion. Required centripetal force: F_c = ma_c = mv²/r = mω²r. This must be supplied by a real force or the net inward component of multiple forces. The algebra is simple; the physics is identifying which force does the supplying. Flat curve (friction as centripetal force): f_s = mv²/r. Maximum friction = μ_s N = μ_s mg. So max speed: μ_s mg = mv²_max/r → v_max = √(μ_s rg). Mass cancels — a heavier car and a lighter car have the same maximum safe speed on the same road. Vertical circle (at the top of a loop): weight + normal force both point toward center. mg + N = mv²/r. At minimum speed, N = 0: mg = mv²_min/r → v_min = √(rg). Below this speed, the string goes slack or the car leaves the track. Banked curve (no friction, ideal angle): Normal force N has horizontal component N sinθ (centripetal) and vertical component N cosθ (balancing weight). N sinθ = mv²/r and N cosθ = mg. A weightlifter holds a 100 kg barbell perfectly still above their head for 3 minutes — arms shaking, muscles burning. According to physics, exactly how much work have they done on the barbell? Make a genuine guess before reading on. Your intuitive sense of "effort" and physics "work" are deliberately different things. Physics work measures one specific thing: energy transferred into an object's motion or position change. When that transfer is zero, the work is zero — regardless of how hard you tried. This is not pedantic. It is the key to understanding where energy goes in every engine, every machine, and every biological system. **The answer that surprises everyone:** The weightlifter has done exactly zero joules of work on the barbell. The barbell didn't move — displacement is zero — so no energy was transferred to its motion or position. The muscles burned ATP (biological energy), but that energy became heat and muscle tension, not mechanical work on the barbell. Biology and physics measure "work" differently on purpose. **Push a concrete wall.** You push with maximum force. The wall doesn't move. Displacement: zero. Work done on the wall: zero. Exhausting yourself without moving something is not work in physics. This forces the question: what exactly *is* work? **The contradiction that builds the model:** If a horse pulls a cart along a flat road, work is done. If the same horse stands motionless in harness, no work is done. If a roller coaster car rolls along a horizontal track, gravity (pointing down) does no work — because gravity is perpendicular to the motion. The pattern emerging: work requires both force AND displacement, and only the force component *in the direction of motion* counts. **Building the rule:** We need a formula capturing: (1) more force → more work, (2) more displacement → more work, (3) force aligned with motion → maximum work, (4) force perpendicular → zero work. There is exactly one product of two vectors that behaves this way: the **dot product**. Math doesn't impose this — physics demands it, and the dot product is the compression that satisfies all four conditions at once. For a **constant force** \(\vec{F}\) acting through displacement \(\vec{d}\): \(W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = Fd\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between force and displacement. For a **variable force** \(F(x)\) that changes as position changes, we sum infinitesimal work contributions: \(W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x)\,dx\) — this is the area under the force-vs-position graph. documents.assignment: Ball thrown upward — energy analysis \text{A 0.5 kg ball is thrown upward at 14 m/s. Using energy methods, find the maximum height.}   Maximum height = 10 m. No kinematics equations needed — energy gives the answer directly. KE_i = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.5)(14)^2 = 49\,\text{J} Initial kinetic energy at launch. PE_{\text{top}} = mgh_{\text{max}} At maximum height, all KE has converted to PE (speed = 0 at peak). 49 = (0.5)(9.8)h_{\text{max}} \Rightarrow h_{\text{max}} = \frac{49}{4.9} = 10\,\text{m} Set KE = PE at maximum height and solve. Spring launcher — finding launch speed \text{A spring (k = 800 N/m) is compressed 0.15 m and launches a 0.2 kg ball horizontally. Find the ball's speed after leaving the spring.}   Launch speed ≈ 9.5 m/s. The spring's stored energy completely transfers to kinetic energy. PE_s = \tfrac{1}{2}(800)(0.15)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(800)(0.0225) = 9\,\text{J} Elastic PE stored in the compressed spring. 9 = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.2)v^2 \Rightarrow v^2 = 90 All spring PE converts to ball's KE (ignoring friction and vertical motion). v = \sqrt{90} \approx 9.49\,\text{m/s} Launch speed.  \text{Find the gravitational PE of a 3 kg book on a shelf 1.2 m above the floor. Take g = 9.8 m/s².} PE = mgh. PE = 35.3 J.  PE = (3)(9.8)(1.2) = 35.3\,\text{J} Relative to floor level.  \text{A 0.3 kg object slides down a frictionless ramp from height 2 m, then compresses a spring (k = 600 N/m) at the bottom. Find maximum compression.} All gravitational PE converts to elastic PE at maximum compression. Maximum compression x = 0.14 m.  mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 Set gravitational PE equal to elastic PE at maximum compression. (0.3)(9.8)(2) = \tfrac{1}{2}(600)x^2 \Rightarrow x^2 = \frac{5.88}{300} = 0.0196 Solve for compression x. x = 0.14\,\text{m} Maximum compression = 14 cm.  \text{Verify that } F = -kx \text{ is recoverable from } PE_s = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 \text{ using } F = -dPE/dx. \text{Then show that gravity } F = -mg \text{ is recoverable from } PE_g = mgy \text{ where y is height.} Differentiate each PE function with respect to the displacement variable, then negate. F = −dPE/dx recovers both Hooke's Law and gravity exactly. Force is the negative gradient of potential energy.  F_s = -\frac{d}{dx}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2\right) = -kx Hooke's Law recovered from elastic PE. The negative sign means the force restores toward zero. documents.applications:
Potential energy is the physics of stored capability. A stretched bowstring, a raised counterweight, a compressed spring, a charged battery — all store energy that was once work done against a force, waiting to be released. Hydroelectric dams convert gravitational PE of water into electrical energy. Springs in watches convert elastic PE into kinetic energy of gears. The concept of potential energy is what allows us to predict motion without tracking every instant of force application. Lesson 3 of 6 — Where does work go when motion stops? **Lesson 2 established:** Net work = ΔKE. When net work is positive, the object speeds up.
**The gap:** What about work done against gravity while rising? The object slows — so ΔKE is negative. But the energy must go *somewhere*.
**This lesson:** That energy goes into potential energy — the stored capacity to do work later.
**Next lesson:** Conservation of Energy — KE + PE = constant for systems with only conservative forces. Conservative force A force is conservative if the work it does between two points is path-independent. Equivalently: the work done by the force around any closed loop is zero. Examples: gravity, spring force, electrostatic force. Counter-examples: friction, air resistance. Gravitational PE (near Earth's surface) PE_g = mgh \qquad \text{where } h = \text{height above reference level} Elastic PE (spring) PE_s = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 \qquad \text{where } x = \text{displacement from natural length} PE is relative to a chosen reference level Only changes in PE have physical meaning. You can set h = 0 anywhere convenient. A ball on a table has different PE depending on whether you measure from the table surface or the floor — but the change in PE between any two points is always the same. Calculus connection: W = −ΔPE For a conservative force \(F(x)\), potential energy is defined as: \(PE(x) = -\int_{x_0}^x F(x')\,dx'\), so \(F = -\dfrac{dPE}{dx}\). Force is the negative gradient of potential energy. This is why PE curves "slope toward" equilibrium.
