documents.assignment: Parametric and Symmetric Equations of a Line Find the parametric and symmetric equations of the line through $P_0 = (1, 2, -1)$ with direction $\mathbf{d} = [3, -1, 2]$.   Parametric: $(1+3t,\ 2-t,\ -1+2t)$. Symmetric: $\frac{x-1}{3} = \frac{y-2}{-1} = \frac{z+1}{2}$. Both describe the same infinite line. \mathbf{r}(t) = (1, 2, -1) + t[3, -1, 2] Plug the base point $P_0 = (1,2,-1)$ and direction $\mathbf{d} = [3,-1,2]$ into the parametric form $\mathbf{r}(t) = P_0 + t\mathbf{d}$. The parameter $t$ ranges over all reals, tracing the full infinite line. x = 1 + 3t, \quad y = 2 - t, \quad z = -1 + 2t Write the three component equations. Each is linear in $t$ — a line in each of the coordinate directions. t = \frac{x-1}{3}, \quad t = \frac{y-2}{-1}, \quad t = \frac{z+1}{2} Solve each component equation for $t$. Since all three expressions equal the same $t$, they must all be equal to each other. \frac{x-1}{3} = \frac{y-2}{-1} = \frac{z+1}{2} Set all three expressions equal — this is the symmetric (or Cartesian) form of the line. Each denominator is a component of $\mathbf{d}$; each numerator is the distance from $P_0$ in that coordinate. Equation of a Plane from Three Points Find the equation of the plane through $A = (1,0,0)$, $B = (0,1,0)$, $C = (0,0,2)$.   The plane through $A$, $B$, $C$ has equation $2x + 2y + z = 2$. Normal vector $[2,2,1]$ is perpendicular to every vector lying in the plane. \mathbf{u} = B - A = [-1, 1, 0], \quad \mathbf{v} = C - A = [-1, 0, 2] Form two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ lying IN the plane by subtracting the base point $A$ from the other two points. Any vector from one point on the plane to another is a displacement within the plane. \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\-1&1&0\\-1&0&2\end{vmatrix} Compute the cross product $\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}$. The cross product is perpendicular to both $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, so it is perpendicular to the plane — it IS the normal vector. \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{i}(1\cdot2 - 0\cdot0) - \mathbf{j}((-1)\cdot2 - 0\cdot(-1)) + \mathbf{k}((-1)\cdot0 - 1\cdot(-1)) = [2, 2, 1] Expand the $3 \times 3$ determinant cofactor by cofactor. Result: $\mathbf{n} = [2, 2, 1]$. \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - A) = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad 2(x-1) + 2(y-0) + 1(z-0) = 0 Use point $A = (1,0,0)$ in the point-normal form $\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - P_0) = 0$. Every point $\mathbf{x}$ on the plane satisfies this — the vector from $A$ to $\mathbf{x}$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}$. 2x + 2y + z = 2 Expand and simplify: $2x - 2 + 2y + z = 0$ → $2x + 2y + z = 2$. The scalar equation $ax + by + cz = d$ has the normal vector $[a,b,c] = [2,2,1]$ as its coefficients. Line-Plane Intersection Find where the line $\mathbf{r}(t) = (2, 0, 1) + t[1, -1, 3]$ intersects the plane $x + 2y - z = 4$.   The line hits the plane at $\left(\frac{5}{4}, \frac{3}{4}, -\frac{5}{4}\right)$. \mathbf{n} = [1, 2, -1], \quad d = 4, \quad P_0 = (2,0,1), \quad \mathbf{d}_{\text{line}} = [1,-1,3] Identify the ingredients: $\mathbf{n} = [1,2,-1]$ is the normal to the plane (read from the coefficients), $d = 4$ is the plane offset, $P_0$ is the line base point, and $\mathbf{d}_{\text{line}}$ is the line direction. \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}_{\text{line}} = (1)(1) + (2)(-1) + (-1)(3) = 1 - 2 - 3 = -4 Compute the denominator first. Since $-4 \neq 0$, the line is NOT parallel to the plane — intersection exists. t = \frac{d - \mathbf{n} \cdot P_0}{\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}_{\text{line}}} = \frac{4 - (1\cdot2 + 2\cdot0 + (-1)\cdot1)}{-4} = \frac{4 - 1}{-4} = -\frac{3}{4} Apply the intersection formula. Numerator: $\mathbf{n} \cdot P_0 = 2 + 0 - 1 = 1$, so $4 - 1 = 3$. Denominator: $-4$. Result: $t = -3/4$. \mathbf{r}\!\left(-\tfrac{3}{4}\right) = \left(2 - \tfrac{3}{4},\ 0 + \tfrac{3}{4},\ 1 - \tfrac{9}{4}\right) = \left(\tfrac{5}{4},\ \tfrac{3}{4},\ -\tfrac{5}{4}\right) Substitute $t = -3/4$ into $\mathbf{r}(t) = P_0 + t\mathbf{d}_{\text{line}}$: $x = 2 + (-3/4)(1) = 5/4$, $y = 0 + (-3/4)(-1) = 3/4$, $z = 1 + (-3/4)(3) = -5/4$. Distance from a Point to a Plane Find the distance from $Q = (1, 2, 3)$ to the plane $2x - y + 2z = 6$.   Distance = 0, meaning $Q = (1, 2, 3)$ lies on the plane $2x - y + 2z = 6$. The distance formula gives 0 whenever the query point satisfies the plane equation. \mathbf{n} = [2, -1, 2], \quad d = 6, \quad \|\mathbf{n}\| = \sqrt{4+1+4} = \sqrt{9} = 3 Extract the normal vector $\mathbf{n} = [2,-1,2]$ from the plane coefficients. Compute $\|\mathbf{n}\| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2} = 3$. This normalizer is crucial — without dividing by $\|\mathbf{n}\|$, you get the unnormalized projection, not the actual distance. \mathbf{n} \cdot Q = 2(1) + (-1)(2) + 2(3) = 2 - 2 + 6 = 6 Compute the dot product $\mathbf{n} \cdot Q$. We get 6, which equals $d = 6$, so the numerator $|\mathbf{n} \cdot Q - d| = |6 - 6| = 0$. \text{dist} = \frac{|\mathbf{n} \cdot Q - d|}{\|\mathbf{n}\|} = \frac{|0|}{3} = 0 Distance is 0 — meaning $Q$ is ON the plane. This makes sense: $Q$ satisfies $2(1) - (2) + 2(3) = 6$, which is exactly the plane equation.  Write parametric equations for the line through $P = (0, 1, -2)$ and $Q = (3, -1, 4)$.  $\mathbf{r}(t) = (3t,\ 1-2t,\ -2+6t)$ for $t \in \mathbb{R}$.  \mathbf{d} = Q - P = [3, -2, 6] The direction vector points from P toward Q. Any nonzero scalar multiple of d gives the same line — both P→Q and Q→P describe the same infinite line. \mathbf{r}(t) = (0,1,-2) + t[3,-2,6] = (3t,\ 1-2t,\ -2+6t) Use P as the base point in the formula r(t) = P₀ + t·d. At t=0 you get P; at t=1 you get Q. t=0:\ (0,1,-2)=P\ ✓;\quad t=1:\ (3,-1,4)=Q\ ✓ Verify both endpoints. t=0 returns P, t=1 returns Q. The line passes through both.  Find the plane containing the three points $P=(2,1,0)$, $Q=(1,3,-1)$, $R=(0,0,4)$. Give the equation in the form $ax+by+cz=d$.  $7x + 6y + 5z = 20$  \mathbf{u}=Q-P=[-1,2,-1],\quad\mathbf{v}=R-P=[-2,-1,4] Two vectors lying in the plane: subtract the base point P from each of the other two points. \mathbf{n}=\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\-1&2&-1\\-2&-1&4\end{vmatrix}=[7,6,5] Cross product gives the normal. Verify: n·u = -7+12-5=0 ✓ and n·v = -14-6+20=0 ✓. 7(x-2)+6(y-1)+5(z-0)=0 Point-normal form using P=(2,1,0). Expand: 7x-14+6y-6+5z=0. 7x+6y+5z=20 Scalar form. Verify: P: 14+6+0=20 ✓; Q: 7+18-5=20 ✓; R: 0+0+20=20 ✓.  Find the distance between the two parallel planes $x + 2y - 2z = 4$ and $x + 2y - 2z = 13$.  Distance = 3 units.  \|\mathbf{n}\|=\sqrt{1^2+2^2+(-2)^2}=\sqrt{9}=3 Extract the normal n=[1,2,-2] from both planes (same coefficients since the planes are parallel). Compute its magnitude once — you will use it for the distance formula. Q=(4,0,0)\ \in\ P_1:\quad 1(4)+2(0)-2(0)=4\ ✓ Pick any point on plane P₁ by setting y=z=0, giving x=4. \text{dist}=\dfrac{|1(4)+2(0)-2(0)-13|}{3}=\dfrac{|4-13|}{3}=\dfrac{9}{3}=3 Apply the distance formula from Q to plane P₂. Shortcut: for parallel planes ax+by+cz=d₁ and d₂, the distance is |d₂-d₁|/‖n‖ = |13-4|/3 = 3.
documents.proofs:
**Affine subspaces.** A **line** in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the set $\{P_0 + t\mathbf{d} : t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ — a 1-dimensional affine subspace. A **plane** is $\{P_0 + s\mathbf{u} + t\mathbf{v} : s, t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ — a 2-dimensional affine subspace. "Affine" means a linear subspace shifted away from the origin. A subspace must contain the origin; an affine subspace need not. If $P_0 = \mathbf{0}$, the affine subspace is a genuine linear subspace. **Hyperplanes.** The equation $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = d$ defines a **hyperplane** — a subspace of codimension 1 in $\mathbb{R}^n$. In $\mathbb{R}^3$: a plane (dimension 2). In $\mathbb{R}^2$: a line (dimension 1). In $\mathbb{R}^n$: an $(n-1)$-dimensional flat. The kernel of the linear map $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x}$ is a linear subspace; the level set $f(\mathbf{x}) = d$ is the affine hyperplane. The normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ spans the orthogonal complement of the hyperplane. **Intersection of planes is a system.** Two planes $\mathbf{n}_1 \cdot \mathbf{x} = d_1$ and $\mathbf{n}_2 \cdot \mathbf{x} = d_2$ with linearly independent normals intersect in a line (codimension 2 in $\mathbb{R}^3$). Three planes with linearly independent normals intersect in a point — which is exactly a $3 \times 3$ linear system. This is the bridge between geometry (intersecting planes) and algebra (Gaussian elimination). Every intersection question in 3D is secretly a linear system. **General position.** In $\mathbb{R}^n$, a line is a 1-flat (parametric = one free parameter). A plane is a 2-flat. In general, a $k$-flat has $k$ free parameters and is defined by $n - k$ independent linear equations. The "dimension" of an intersection of two flats of dimensions $p$ and $q$ is at least $p + q - n$ (when they are not parallel). This is the dimension formula for affine subspaces, and it connects back to the rank-nullity theorem from the next chapter. Affine Subspace (Formal) An **affine subspace** of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a set of the form $P_0 + W$ where $W$ is a linear subspace.

**Line** = $P_0 + \text{span}\{\mathbf{d}\}$ (1-dimensional)
**Plane** = $P_0 + \text{span}\{\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}\}$ (2-dimensional)

Difference from a subspace: affine subspaces need not pass through the origin. Codimension and Equations Every hyperplane in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is defined by exactly ONE linear equation. A line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ needs TWO equations (intersection of two planes). Generally: a $k$-dimensional affine subspace is the solution set of $n - k$ independent linear equations. The Normal Vector Is the "Perpendicular Coordinate" The normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ is to a plane what the $z$-axis is to the $xy$-plane. It points in the one direction that has ZERO component within the plane. The distance from any point $Q$ to the plane is the magnitude of $Q$'s component in the $\mathbf{n}$ direction — literally a projection of $(Q - P_0)$ onto $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$.
documents.applications:
Every 3D graphics engine, robotics planner, and physics simulator must answer questions about lines and planes thousands of times per second. Collision detection is a line-plane intersection test. Flight simulators check whether a wing intersects the ground plane. Ray tracing (the rendering algorithm inside Pixar films) fires rays — lines — and finds intersections with planes to determine what a camera sees. The math is all here. Lesson 5 of 6 — Vectors & Spaces **Previous:** Systems of Linear Equations — Gaussian elimination and pivot structure.
**This lesson:** Lines and Planes — the geometric picture of linear constraints and intersections in 3D.
**Next:** Gauss-Jordan RREF — the complete algorithm for solving any linear system. Two Ways to Describe a Line **Parametric:** $\mathbf{r}(t) = P_0 + t\mathbf{d}$
Travel from $P_0$ in direction $\mathbf{d}$.

**Symmetric (when $d_i \neq 0$):** $\dfrac{x-x_0}{d_x} = \dfrac{y-y_0}{d_y} = \dfrac{z-z_0}{d_z}$
Eliminate $t$ to get the ratio form. If one component of $\mathbf{d}$ is zero (say $d_z = 0$), write $z = z_0$ separately and use the symmetric form for the other two. Two Ways to Describe a Plane **Normal form:** $\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - P_0) = 0$
Every point $\mathbf{x}$ on the plane satisfies this.

**Scalar form:** $ax + by + cz = d$
where $\mathbf{n} = [a, b, c]$ and $d = \mathbf{n} \cdot P_0$. Procedure: Line-Plane Intersection Step 1. From the plane $ax+by+cz=d$, read off $\mathbf{n}=[a,b,c]$ and $d$.
Step 2. From the parametric line, read off base point $P_0$ and direction $\mathbf{d}_{\text{line}}$.
Step 3. Compute the denominator: $\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}_{\text{line}}$. If zero — line is parallel to the plane (stop).
Step 4. Compute $t = (d - \mathbf{n}\cdot P_0)\;/\;(\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}_{\text{line}})$.
Step 5. Compute the intersection point: $\mathbf{r}(t) = P_0 + t\,\mathbf{d}_{\text{line}}$.
Step 6. Verify: substitute the intersection point into $ax+by+cz$ and confirm it equals $d$. Common Mistake: Confusing the Normal Vector with a Direction Vector For a **line**, you need a direction vector $\mathbf{d}$ that points ALONG the line. For a **plane**, you need a normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ that points PERPENDICULAR to the plane.

**Wrong:** Using the normal vector $\mathbf{n} = [1, 2, -1]$ as the line direction when the plane equation is $x + 2y - z = 4$.

**What you actually get:** A line through $P_0$ in direction $[1, 2, -1]$ is PERPENDICULAR to the plane, not lying in it.

**Right rule:** For the plane $ax + by + cz = d$, the normal is $\mathbf{n} = [a,b,c]$. A direction vector for a line IN the plane must satisfy $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} = 0$. A Line in 3D ≠ A Single Equation In 2D, a line = one equation ($ax + by = c$). In 3D, a line = the INTERSECTION of two planes = TWO equations. One equation in 3D defines a **plane**, not a line. This trips up many students. When to Use This Use **parametric line form** when you need to:
- Trace a path through space (robotics, animation, physics)
- Test if a point lies on a line (check whether all components give the same $t$)
- Find where a ray hits a surface (ray tracing, collision detection)

Use **plane normal form** when you need to:
- Test if a point is on a plane: evaluate $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} - d$; zero means on the plane, sign tells which side
- Measure distance from a point to a plane: $\frac{|\mathbf{n} \cdot Q - d|}{\|\mathbf{n}\|}$
- Find the normal to a surface given two edges: take the cross product
documents.content:
You're designing a robot arm. The end-effector must travel in a straight line in 3D space. How do you describe that line mathematically — and how do you tell if two robot paths will collide? Every 3D graphics engine, robotics planner, and physics simulator must answer questions about lines and planes thousands of times per second. Collision detection is a line-plane intersection test. Flight simulators check whether a wing intersects the ground plane. Ray tracing (the rendering algorithm inside Pixar films) fires rays — lines — and finds intersections with planes to determine what a camera sees. The math is all here. Start at the point $(1, 2, -1)$ and walk in direction $[3, -1, 2]$. After $t = 0$: you are at $(1, 2, -1)$. After $t = 1$: $(4, 1, 1)$. After $t = -1$: $(-2, 3, -3)$. The formula $(1+3t,\ 2-t,\ -1+2t)$ visits every point on an infinite straight line — one free parameter $t$ traces the whole thing. This is the **parametric form** of a line. Now, to describe a flat surface (a plane) in 3D, a direction to walk *along* the surface is not enough — you need the one direction that is perpendicular to the entire surface: the **normal vector**. Think of a line in 3D. You need two pieces of information: a **point** you start from, and a **direction** to travel. If you start at point $P_0$ and walk in direction $\mathbf{d}$, after time $t$ you are at $P_0 + t\mathbf{d}$. That simple idea is the parametric equation of a line. A plane needs a different description. Instead of a direction to travel ALONG the plane, it is easier to give a direction PERPENDICULAR to the plane — the **normal vector** $\mathbf{n}$. Every point $\mathbf{x}$ on the plane satisfies $\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - P_0) = 0$: the vector from $P_0$ to $\mathbf{x}$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}$. **Why does the cross product appear here?** If you know two vectors lying IN a plane (say the edges of a triangle), their cross product is perpendicular to both — it IS the normal vector. So the cross product is the machine for finding plane equations from geometric data. **Predict before reading the intersection formula:** the line $\mathbf{r}(t) = (2,0,1) + t[1,-1,3]$ and the plane $x + 2y - z = 4$. Compute $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}_{\text{line}} = [1,2,-1]\cdot[1,-1,3]$ mentally: $1 - 2 - 3 = -4 \neq 0$. The denominator is nonzero, so the line will intersect the plane at exactly one point. Verify this in Example 3. Lines and planes are the 1D and 2D linear subspaces (shifted by a point) of 3D space. Every linear algebra concept — span, basis, orthogonality — has a concrete geometric home in lines and planes. **CNC and robotics applications.** Every CNC toolpath segment is a line in 3D space — parametrically $\mathbf{r}(t) = P_0 + t\mathbf{d}$ where $\mathbf{d}$ is the feed direction and $t$ is proportional to time. The machined surface is (locally) a plane with a specific normal. The controller must constantly check: is the tool axis aligned with the surface normal? Is the feedrate vector tangent to the surface (dot product with normal = 0)? In 5-axis machining, the tool orientation is defined by two vectors — the tool axis and the surface normal — and keeping these properly aligned is a geometric problem entirely expressed through lines, planes, and their intersections. **Where this is heading.** When you have multiple plane equations (a system of linear equations), finding where the planes all intersect simultaneously is a system of equations problem — which is exactly what Gauss-Jordan RREF (the next lesson) solves. Every row of an $m \times n$ linear system is one plane in $n$-dimensional space, and the solution is the set of points where all those hyperplanes meet. **Parametric equation of a line.** Given a point $P_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0)$ and a nonzero direction vector $\mathbf{d} = [d_x, d_y, d_z]$, the line through $P_0$ in direction $\mathbf{d}$ is:
$$\mathbf{r}(t) = P_0 + t\mathbf{d} = (x_0 + td_x,\ y_0 + td_y,\ z_0 + td_z), \quad t \in \mathbb{R}$$
The scalar $t$ is the parameter — it tells you how far along the line you are. **Symmetric equations.** If none of $d_x, d_y, d_z$ is zero, solve each parametric equation for $t$ and set them equal:
$$\frac{x - x_0}{d_x} = \frac{y - y_0}{d_y} = \frac{z - z_0}{d_z}$$
If one component is zero (say $d_z = 0$), then $z = z_0$ is one of the equations and the symmetric form uses just the other two ratios. **Equation of a plane.** A plane is determined by a point $P_0$ and a normal vector $\mathbf{n} = [a, b, c]$ perpendicular to every vector in the plane. The condition for a point $\mathbf{x} = (x, y, z)$ to lie on the plane is:
$$\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - P_0) = 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad a(x - x_0) + b(y - y_0) + c(z - z_0) = 0$$
Expanding and collecting: $ax + by + cz = d$ where $d = ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0$. **Distance from a point to a plane.** The distance from point $Q$ to the plane $ax + by + cz = d$ is:
$$\text{dist} = \frac{|a q_x + b q_y + c q_z - d|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}} = \frac{|\mathbf{n} \cdot Q - d|}{\|\mathbf{n}\|}$$
This is projection: you project $Q - P_0$ onto the unit normal. If $Q$ is on the plane, $\mathbf{n} \cdot Q = d$ and the distance is 0. **Line-plane intersection.** To find where a line $P_0 + t\mathbf{d}$ meets a plane $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = d$, substitute:
$$\mathbf{n} \cdot (P_0 + t\mathbf{d}) = d \quad \Rightarrow \quad t = \frac{d - \mathbf{n} \cdot P_0}{\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}}$$
If $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} = 0$, the line is parallel to the plane (no intersection, or the line lies in the plane if also $\mathbf{n} \cdot P_0 = d$). **Parallel planes.** Two planes $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = d_1$ and $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = d_2$ with the SAME normal vector are parallel. If $d_1 \neq d_2$, they never intersect; the distance between them is $|d_2 - d_1| / \|\mathbf{n}\|$. If $d_1 = d_2$, they are the same plane. **Affine subspaces.** A **line** in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the set $\{P_0 + t\mathbf{d} : t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ — a 1-dimensional affine subspace. A **plane** is $\{P_0 + s\mathbf{u} + t\mathbf{v} : s, t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ — a 2-dimensional affine subspace. "Affine" means a linear subspace shifted away from the origin. A subspace must contain the origin; an affine subspace need not. If $P_0 = \mathbf{0}$, the affine subspace is a genuine linear subspace. **Hyperplanes.** The equation $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = d$ defines a **hyperplane** — a subspace of codimension 1 in $\mathbb{R}^n$. In $\mathbb{R}^3$: a plane (dimension 2). In $\mathbb{R}^2$: a line (dimension 1). In $\mathbb{R}^n$: an $(n-1)$-dimensional flat. The kernel of the linear map $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x}$ is a linear subspace; the level set $f(\mathbf{x}) = d$ is the affine hyperplane. The normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ spans the orthogonal complement of the hyperplane. **Intersection of planes is a system.** Two planes $\mathbf{n}_1 \cdot \mathbf{x} = d_1$ and $\mathbf{n}_2 \cdot \mathbf{x} = d_2$ with linearly independent normals intersect in a line (codimension 2 in $\mathbb{R}^3$). Three planes with linearly independent normals intersect in a point — which is exactly a $3 \times 3$ linear system. This is the bridge between geometry (intersecting planes) and algebra (Gaussian elimination). Every intersection question in 3D is secretly a linear system. **General position.** In $\mathbb{R}^n$, a line is a 1-flat (parametric = one free parameter). A plane is a 2-flat. In general, a $k$-flat has $k$ free parameters and is defined by $n - k$ independent linear equations. The "dimension" of an intersection of two flats of dimensions $p$ and $q$ is at least $p + q - n$ (when they are not parallel). This is the dimension formula for affine subspaces, and it connects back to the rank-nullity theorem from the next chapter. Affine Subspace (Formal) An **affine subspace** of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a set of the form $P_0 + W$ where $W$ is a linear subspace.

**Line** = $P_0 + \text{span}\{\mathbf{d}\}$ (1-dimensional)
**Plane** = $P_0 + \text{span}\{\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}\}$ (2-dimensional)

Difference from a subspace: affine subspaces need not pass through the origin. Codimension and Equations Every hyperplane in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is defined by exactly ONE linear equation. A line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ needs TWO equations (intersection of two planes). Generally: a $k$-dimensional affine subspace is the solution set of $n - k$ independent linear equations. The Normal Vector Is the "Perpendicular Coordinate" The normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ is to a plane what the $z$-axis is to the $xy$-plane. It points in the one direction that has ZERO component within the plane. The distance from any point $Q$ to the plane is the magnitude of $Q$'s component in the $\mathbf{n}$ direction — literally a projection of $(Q - P_0)$ onto $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$. Lesson 5 of 6 — Vectors & Spaces **Previous:** Systems of Linear Equations — Gaussian elimination and pivot structure.
**This lesson:** Lines and Planes — the geometric picture of linear constraints and intersections in 3D.
**Next:** Gauss-Jordan RREF — the complete algorithm for solving any linear system. Two Ways to Describe a Line **Parametric:** $\mathbf{r}(t) = P_0 + t\mathbf{d}$
Travel from $P_0$ in direction $\mathbf{d}$.

**Symmetric (when $d_i \neq 0$):** $\dfrac{x-x_0}{d_x} = \dfrac{y-y_0}{d_y} = \dfrac{z-z_0}{d_z}$
Eliminate $t$ to get the ratio form. If one component of $\mathbf{d}$ is zero (say $d_z = 0$), write $z = z_0$ separately and use the symmetric form for the other two. Two Ways to Describe a Plane **Normal form:** $\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - P_0) = 0$
Every point $\mathbf{x}$ on the plane satisfies this.

**Scalar form:** $ax + by + cz = d$
where $\mathbf{n} = [a, b, c]$ and $d = \mathbf{n} \cdot P_0$. Procedure: Line-Plane Intersection Step 1. From the plane $ax+by+cz=d$, read off $\mathbf{n}=[a,b,c]$ and $d$.
Step 2. From the parametric line, read off base point $P_0$ and direction $\mathbf{d}_{\text{line}}$.
Step 3. Compute the denominator: $\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}_{\text{line}}$. If zero — line is parallel to the plane (stop).
Step 4. Compute $t = (d - \mathbf{n}\cdot P_0)\;/\;(\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}_{\text{line}})$.
Step 5. Compute the intersection point: $\mathbf{r}(t) = P_0 + t\,\mathbf{d}_{\text{line}}$.
Step 6. Verify: substitute the intersection point into $ax+by+cz$ and confirm it equals $d$. Common Mistake: Confusing the Normal Vector with a Direction Vector For a **line**, you need a direction vector $\mathbf{d}$ that points ALONG the line. For a **plane**, you need a normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ that points PERPENDICULAR to the plane.

**Wrong:** Using the normal vector $\mathbf{n} = [1, 2, -1]$ as the line direction when the plane equation is $x + 2y - z = 4$.

**What you actually get:** A line through $P_0$ in direction $[1, 2, -1]$ is PERPENDICULAR to the plane, not lying in it.

**Right rule:** For the plane $ax + by + cz = d$, the normal is $\mathbf{n} = [a,b,c]$. A direction vector for a line IN the plane must satisfy $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} = 0$. A Line in 3D ≠ A Single Equation In 2D, a line = one equation ($ax + by = c$). In 3D, a line = the INTERSECTION of two planes = TWO equations. One equation in 3D defines a **plane**, not a line. This trips up many students. When to Use This Use **parametric line form** when you need to:
- Trace a path through space (robotics, animation, physics)
- Test if a point lies on a line (check whether all components give the same $t$)
- Find where a ray hits a surface (ray tracing, collision detection)

Use **plane normal form** when you need to:
- Test if a point is on a plane: evaluate $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} - d$; zero means on the plane, sign tells which side
- Measure distance from a point to a plane: $\frac{|\mathbf{n} \cdot Q - d|}{\|\mathbf{n}\|}$
- Find the normal to a surface given two edges: take the cross product Point-Normal Form of a Plane \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - P_0) = 0

or equivalently: $ax + by + cz = d$

$\mathbf{n} = [a,b,c]$ is perpendicular to every vector lying in the plane. Normal Vector A vector $\mathbf{n}$ is **normal** to a plane if it is perpendicular to every vector that lies in the plane.

Given two non-parallel vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$ in the plane, $\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}$. Cross Product Gives the Normal Immediately If you know two edges of a triangle (vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$), then $\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}$ is immediately perpendicular to both — it IS the normal to the plane containing the triangle. No algebra required. Lines and Planes: Geometric Intuition Direction vectors drive lines; normal vectors define planes. Lines and Planes in OpenMAT / MATLAB Lines and planes in MATLAB — also exactly how CNC and robotics check for workspace violations. Code: Lines, Planes, and 3D Geometry Use Python to build geometric intuition with 2D projection visualizations. Projection and Perpendicularity Distance = projection onto the unit normal. Parametric and Symmetric Equations of a Line Find the parametric and symmetric equations of the line through $P_0 = (1, 2, -1)$ with direction $\mathbf{d} = [3, -1, 2]$. Parametric: $(1+3t,\ 2-t,\ -1+2t)$. Symmetric: $\frac{x-1}{3} = \frac{y-2}{-1} = \frac{z+1}{2}$. Both describe the same infinite line. \mathbf{r}(t) = (1, 2, -1) + t[3, -1, 2] Plug the base point $P_0 = (1,2,-1)$ and direction $\mathbf{d} = [3,-1,2]$ into the parametric form $\mathbf{r}(t) = P_0 + t\mathbf{d}$. The parameter $t$ ranges over all reals, tracing the full infinite line. x = 1 + 3t, \quad y = 2 - t, \quad z = -1 + 2t Write the three component equations. Each is linear in $t$ — a line in each of the coordinate directions. t = \frac{x-1}{3}, \quad t = \frac{y-2}{-1}, \quad t = \frac{z+1}{2} Solve each component equation for $t$. Since all three expressions equal the same $t$, they must all be equal to each other. \frac{x-1}{3} = \frac{y-2}{-1} = \frac{z+1}{2} Set all three expressions equal — this is the symmetric (or Cartesian) form of the line. Each denominator is a component of $\mathbf{d}$; each numerator is the distance from $P_0$ in that coordinate. Equation of a Plane from Three Points Find the equation of the plane through $A = (1,0,0)$, $B = (0,1,0)$, $C = (0,0,2)$. The plane through $A$, $B$, $C$ has equation $2x + 2y + z = 2$. Normal vector $[2,2,1]$ is perpendicular to every vector lying in the plane. \mathbf{u} = B - A = [-1, 1, 0], \quad \mathbf{v} = C - A = [-1, 0, 2] Form two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ lying IN the plane by subtracting the base point $A$ from the other two points. Any vector from one point on the plane to another is a displacement within the plane. \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\-1&1&0\\-1&0&2\end{vmatrix} Compute the cross product $\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}$. The cross product is perpendicular to both $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, so it is perpendicular to the plane — it IS the normal vector. \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{i}(1\cdot2 - 0\cdot0) - \mathbf{j}((-1)\cdot2 - 0\cdot(-1)) + \mathbf{k}((-1)\cdot0 - 1\cdot(-1)) = [2, 2, 1] Expand the $3 \times 3$ determinant cofactor by cofactor. Result: $\mathbf{n} = [2, 2, 1]$. \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - A) = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad 2(x-1) + 2(y-0) + 1(z-0) = 0 Use point $A = (1,0,0)$ in the point-normal form $\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - P_0) = 0$. Every point $\mathbf{x}$ on the plane satisfies this — the vector from $A$ to $\mathbf{x}$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}$. 2x + 2y + z = 2 Expand and simplify: $2x - 2 + 2y + z = 0$ → $2x + 2y + z = 2$. The scalar equation $ax + by + cz = d$ has the normal vector $[a,b,c] = [2,2,1]$ as its coefficients. Line-Plane Intersection Find where the line $\mathbf{r}(t) = (2, 0, 1) + t[1, -1, 3]$ intersects the plane $x + 2y - z = 4$. The line hits the plane at $\left(\frac{5}{4}, \frac{3}{4}, -\frac{5}{4}\right)$. \mathbf{n} = [1, 2, -1], \quad d = 4, \quad P_0 = (2,0,1), \quad \mathbf{d}_{\text{line}} = [1,-1,3] Identify the ingredients: $\mathbf{n} = [1,2,-1]$ is the normal to the plane (read from the coefficients), $d = 4$ is the plane offset, $P_0$ is the line base point, and $\mathbf{d}_{\text{line}}$ is the line direction. \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}_{\text{line}} = (1)(1) + (2)(-1) + (-1)(3) = 1 - 2 - 3 = -4 Compute the denominator first. Since $-4 \neq 0$, the line is NOT parallel to the plane — intersection exists. t = \frac{d - \mathbf{n} \cdot P_0}{\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}_{\text{line}}} = \frac{4 - (1\cdot2 + 2\cdot0 + (-1)\cdot1)}{-4} = \frac{4 - 1}{-4} = -\frac{3}{4} Apply the intersection formula. Numerator: $\mathbf{n} \cdot P_0 = 2 + 0 - 1 = 1$, so $4 - 1 = 3$. Denominator: $-4$. Result: $t = -3/4$. \mathbf{r}\!\left(-\tfrac{3}{4}\right) = \left(2 - \tfrac{3}{4},\ 0 + \tfrac{3}{4},\ 1 - \tfrac{9}{4}\right) = \left(\tfrac{5}{4},\ \tfrac{3}{4},\ -\tfrac{5}{4}\right) Substitute $t = -3/4$ into $\mathbf{r}(t) = P_0 + t\mathbf{d}_{\text{line}}$: $x = 2 + (-3/4)(1) = 5/4$, $y = 0 + (-3/4)(-1) = 3/4$, $z = 1 + (-3/4)(3) = -5/4$. Distance from a Point to a Plane Find the distance from $Q = (1, 2, 3)$ to the plane $2x - y + 2z = 6$. Distance = 0, meaning $Q = (1, 2, 3)$ lies on the plane $2x - y + 2z = 6$. The distance formula gives 0 whenever the query point satisfies the plane equation. \mathbf{n} = [2, -1, 2], \quad d = 6, \quad \|\mathbf{n}\| = \sqrt{4+1+4} = \sqrt{9} = 3 Extract the normal vector $\mathbf{n} = [2,-1,2]$ from the plane coefficients. Compute $\|\mathbf{n}\| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2} = 3$. This normalizer is crucial — without dividing by $\|\mathbf{n}\|$, you get the unnormalized projection, not the actual distance. \mathbf{n} \cdot Q = 2(1) + (-1)(2) + 2(3) = 2 - 2 + 6 = 6 Compute the dot product $\mathbf{n} \cdot Q$. We get 6, which equals $d = 6$, so the numerator $|\mathbf{n} \cdot Q - d| = |6 - 6| = 0$. \text{dist} = \frac{|\mathbf{n} \cdot Q - d|}{\|\mathbf{n}\|} = \frac{|0|}{3} = 0 Distance is 0 — meaning $Q$ is ON the plane. This makes sense: $Q$ satisfies $2(1) - (2) + 2(3) = 6$, which is exactly the plane equation. Write parametric equations for the line through $P = (0, 1, -2)$ and $Q = (3, -1, 4)$. $\mathbf{r}(t) = (3t,\ 1-2t,\ -2+6t)$ for $t \in \mathbb{R}$. \mathbf{d} = Q - P = [3, -2, 6] The direction vector points from P toward Q. Any nonzero scalar multiple of d gives the same line — both P→Q and Q→P describe the same infinite line. \mathbf{r}(t) = (0,1,-2) + t[3,-2,6] = (3t,\ 1-2t,\ -2+6t) Use P as the base point in the formula r(t) = P₀ + t·d. At t=0 you get P; at t=1 you get Q. t=0:\ (0,1,-2)=P\ ✓;\quad t=1:\ (3,-1,4)=Q\ ✓ Verify both endpoints. t=0 returns P, t=1 returns Q. The line passes through both. Find the plane containing the three points $P=(2,1,0)$, $Q=(1,3,-1)$, $R=(0,0,4)$. Give the equation in the form $ax+by+cz=d$. $7x + 6y + 5z = 20$ \mathbf{u}=Q-P=[-1,2,-1],\quad\mathbf{v}=R-P=[-2,-1,4] Two vectors lying in the plane: subtract the base point P from each of the other two points. \mathbf{n}=\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\-1&2&-1\\-2&-1&4\end{vmatrix}=[7,6,5] Cross product gives the normal. Verify: n·u = -7+12-5=0 ✓ and n·v = -14-6+20=0 ✓. 7(x-2)+6(y-1)+5(z-0)=0 Point-normal form using P=(2,1,0). Expand: 7x-14+6y-6+5z=0. 7x+6y+5z=20 Scalar form. Verify: P: 14+6+0=20 ✓; Q: 7+18-5=20 ✓; R: 0+0+20=20 ✓. Find the distance between the two parallel planes $x + 2y - 2z = 4$ and $x + 2y - 2z = 13$. Distance = 3 units. \|\mathbf{n}\|=\sqrt{1^2+2^2+(-2)^2}=\sqrt{9}=3 Extract the normal n=[1,2,-2] from both planes (same coefficients since the planes are parallel). Compute its magnitude once — you will use it for the distance formula. Q=(4,0,0)\ \in\ P_1:\quad 1(4)+2(0)-2(0)=4\ ✓ Pick any point on plane P₁ by setting y=z=0, giving x=4. \text{dist}=\dfrac{|1(4)+2(0)-2(0)-13|}{3}=\dfrac{|4-13|}{3}=\dfrac{9}{3}=3 Apply the distance formula from Q to plane P₂. Shortcut: for parallel planes ax+by+cz=d₁ and d₂, the distance is |d₂-d₁|/‖n‖ = |13-4|/3 = 3. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step parametric equations x(t) y(t) parameterized curve vector-valued velocity acceleration trajectory

documents.assignment: 3×3 System — Full Gauss-Jordan to RREF Solve via RREF: $2x_1 + x_2 - x_3 = 8$, $-3x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 = -11$, $-2x_1 + x_2 + 2x_3 = -3$.   Unique solution: $x_1 = 2$, $x_2 = 3$, $x_3 = -1$. The RREF is the identity matrix on the left — all three variables are pivot variables, confirming no free variables and exactly one solution. \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2&1&-1&8\\-3&-1&2&-11\\-2&1&2&-3\end{array}\right] Write as augmented matrix $[A|\mathbf{b}]$. The three coefficient columns correspond to $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$; the last column is the right-hand side $\mathbf{b} = [8, -11, -3]^\top$. \xrightarrow{\frac{1}{2}R_1} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&\frac{1}{2}&-\frac{1}{2}&4\\-3&-1&2&-11\\-2&1&2&-3\end{array}\right] Scale row 1 by $\frac{1}{2}$ so the first pivot (top-left entry) equals 1. Now the pivot variable $x_1$ has coefficient 1 in row 1, which makes the elimination multipliers below it exact integers. \xrightarrow{R_2+3R_1,\;R_3+2R_1} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&\frac{1}{2}&-\frac{1}{2}&4\\0&\frac{1}{2}&\frac{1}{2}&1\\0&2&1&5\end{array}\right] Forward elimination on column 1: add 3 times row 1 to row 2 (the multiplier is $-(-3) = 3$), and 2 times row 1 to row 3 (the multiplier is $-(-2) = 2$). All entries below the first pivot are now zero. \xrightarrow{2R_2} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&\frac{1}{2}&-\frac{1}{2}&4\\0&1&1&2\\0&2&1&5\end{array}\right] \xrightarrow{R_3-2R_2} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&\frac{1}{2}&-\frac{1}{2}&4\\0&1&1&2\\0&0&-1&1\end{array}\right] Scale row 2 by 2 so the second pivot = 1, giving $x_2$ coefficient 1. Then subtract $2 \times$ (scaled) row 2 from row 3 to zero out the column-2 entry in row 3. Row 3 becomes $[0,0,-1,1]$. \xrightarrow{-R_3} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&\frac{1}{2}&-\frac{1}{2}&4\\0&1&1&2\\0&0&1&-1\end{array}\right] Scale row 3 by $-1$ to get the third pivot = 1. The matrix is now in Row Echelon Form (REF) — all pivots are 1 and zeros below each. The next step (back-elimination) is what makes it RREF. \xrightarrow{R_2-R_3,\;R_1+\frac{1}{2}R_3} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&\frac{1}{2}&0&\frac{7}{2}\\0&1&0&3\\0&0&1&-1\end{array}\right] \xrightarrow{R_1-\frac{1}{2}R_2} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&0&0&2\\0&1&0&3\\0&0&1&-1\end{array}\right] Back-eliminate: subtract row 3 from row 2 to zero out the $x_3$ entry above pivot 3. Add $\frac{1}{2}$ row 3 to row 1. Then subtract $\frac{1}{2}$ row 2 from row 1. RREF is $[I | \mathbf{c}]$ — solution reads from the last column: $x_1 = 2$, $x_2 = 3$, $x_3 = -1$. Detecting Inconsistency — the Contradiction Row Determine whether the system is consistent: $x + 2y = 3$, $2x + 4y = 7$, $3x + 6y = 9$.   The system is inconsistent — no solution exists. Geometrically, all three equations describe lines with the same slope, but equations 1 and 2 have different intercepts ($x+2y=3$ and $x+2y=7/2$). Parallel lines never intersect. \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&2&3\\2&4&7\\3&6&9\end{array}\right] Form the $3 \times 3$ augmented matrix. Notice: the coefficient column vectors are $[1,2,3]^\top$ and $[2,4,6]^\top = 2[1,2,3]^\top$ — they are proportional. All three coefficient rows are multiples of $[1,2]$, meaning every equation describes the same family of lines $x + 2y = k$. \xrightarrow{R_2-2R_1,\;R_3-3R_1} \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&2&3\\0&0&1\\0&0&0\end{array}\right] Forward elimination: subtract $2 \times$ row 1 from row 2, and $3 \times$ row 1 from row 3. The left sides go to zero (as expected from proportional rows), but the right sides give $7 - 2(3) = 1$ and $9 - 3(3) = 0$. Row 2 becomes the contradiction row $[0\ 0\ |\ 1]$. [0\ 0\ |\ 1] \quad \text{reads as} \quad 0x + 0y = 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad 0 = 1 The row translates to $0 = 1$ — false for any $(x,y)$. This is the definitive inconsistency test: a **pivot in the augmented column** (last column). Compare with row 3: $[0\ 0\ |\ 0]$ reads $0 = 0$ — that row is harmless (redundant). The single contradiction row in row 2 kills the entire system. Free Variables — Writing the General Solution Find all solutions to: $x_1 + 2x_2 - x_3 = 4$ and $x_3 = 2$.   Infinitely many solutions. General solution: $(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (6-2t,\ t,\ 2)$ for $t \in \mathbb{R}$. The solution set is a line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ — one degree of freedom (one free variable). \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&2&-1&4\\0&0&1&2\end{array}\right] Write the $2 \times 4$ augmented matrix. Column 1 has a pivot (the 1 in row 1). Column 2 has NO pivot entry — no row has a leading 1 in column 2. Column 3 has a pivot (the 1 in row 2). So: pivot variables are $x_1$ and $x_3$; free variable is $x_2$. \xrightarrow{R_1+R_2} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&2&0&6\\0&0&1&2\end{array}\right] Back-eliminate: add row 2 to row 1 to zero out the $-1$ entry above the second pivot in column 3. Now both pivot columns (1 and 3) have a leading 1 and zeros everywhere else — this is RREF. x_2 = t \in \mathbb{R} \quad \text{(free — assign parameter } t \text{)} Assign the free variable $x_2$ a parameter $t$. The parameter $t$ can be ANY real number. Every distinct value of $t$ gives a different solution — this is why the system has infinitely many. x_3 = 2, \quad x_1 = 6 - 2x_2 = 6 - 2t Read the pivot variables from RREF: row 2 gives $x_3 = 2$ directly. Row 1 gives $x_1 + 2t = 6$, so $x_1 = 6 - 2t$. REF vs RREF — Why the Extra Step Matters Given the augmented matrix $\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2&4&10\\1&3&8\end{array}\right]$, first reach REF, then go all the way to RREF. documents.proofs: **Uniqueness of RREF.** Every matrix $A$ has a unique RREF, regardless of the sequence of row operations used to reach it. This is a non-trivial theorem proved by induction on the number of rows. The proof shows that if $R$ and $S$ are both in RREF and row-equivalent to $A$, then $R = S$. This uniqueness makes RREF a canonical form for the row equivalence class of $A$. **Row operations as matrix multiplication.** Each elementary row operation corresponds to multiplying on the left by an elementary matrix $E$. The RREF process computes $E_k \cdots E_2 E_1 A = R$. This means $R = MA$ where $M = E_k \cdots E_1$ is invertible. Therefore $A$ and $R$ are row-equivalent, and $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is equivalent to $R\mathbf{x} = M\mathbf{b}$. **Geometric picture of the solution set.** The solution set of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is either empty, a single point, or an affine subspace. If $\mathbf{x}_p$ is any particular solution and $N(A)$ is the null space (all $\mathbf{x}$ with $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$), the full solution set is $\mathbf{x}_p + N(A)$. The RREF free variable columns give the null space basis directly: for each free variable $x_j$, set $x_j = 1$ and all other free variables to $0$, then read the pivot variables from RREF — that gives one null space basis vector. A unique solution means $N(A) = \{\mathbf{0}\}$ (a single point); infinitely many means $N(A)$ is a positive-dimensional subspace (a line, plane, or higher). **Connection to LU decomposition and future methods.** RREF is conceptually central but rarely used in large-scale numerical computation. For numerical work, Gaussian elimination reaching only REF is used to compute the $LU$ decomposition $PA = LU$, where $P$ is a permutation, $L$ is lower triangular, and $U$ is upper triangular (REF). Two triangular solves then give $\mathbf{x}$ in $O(n^2)$ additional operations, after the $O(n^3)$ factorization is stored and reused for multiple right-hand sides. RREF's power is conceptual: it reveals rank, null space, column dependencies, and solution structure in a canonical form. The Rank-Nullity Theorem (la6-004) formalizes the observation that (number of pivot columns) + (number of free columns) = $n$ — a counting identity that runs through all of linear algebra. Why RREF is Unique Suppose $R$ and $S$ are both RREF matrices row-equivalent to $A$. Then $S = M R$ for some invertible $M$. Consider the pivot columns of $R$: they are the standard basis vectors $\mathbf{e}_{i_1}, \ldots, \mathbf{e}_{i_r}$. The corresponding columns of $S = MR$ would be $M\mathbf{e}_{i_1}, \ldots, M\mathbf{e}_{i_r}$. For $S$ to also be in RREF, these must be standard basis vectors. Proceeding column by column (left to right), one shows by induction that every leading 1 in $R$ corresponds to the same column position in $S$, and that all entries of $R$ and $S$ agree.

RREF is the universal algorithm for solving any linear system, finding the rank of any matrix, testing linear independence, and computing null spaces. Every major linear algebra software package (NumPy, MATLAB, Mathematica) uses a variant of this algorithm internally. A data scientist uses it when fitting models with too few observations. A robotics engineer uses it to find the joint angles that achieve a given end-effector position. The algorithm's three outputs — unique solution, no solution, infinite solutions — correspond directly to three geometric configurations you will encounter throughout your career. Procedure: Gauss-Jordan Elimination (Full RREF) Step 1. Form the augmented matrix $[A \mid \mathbf{b}]$.
Step 2. Forward pass — for each column left to right:
  a. If no nonzero entry in that column at or below current row: skip (free variable column).
  b. Swap to bring the best nonzero entry to the current pivot row.
  c. Scale: divide the pivot row by the pivot entry so pivot = 1.
  d. Eliminate BELOW: subtract multiples of the pivot row from all rows BELOW.
Step 3. Back pass — for each pivot row (bottom to top): eliminate ABOVE by subtracting multiples of the pivot row from all rows ABOVE.
Step 4. Check the augmented column: any row $[0\cdots 0 \mid k \ne 0]$ → INCONSISTENT.
Step 5. Assign parameter $t$ to each free variable. Express pivot variables in terms of parameters. Lesson 6 of 6 — Vectors & Spaces **Previous:** Lines and Planes — geometric picture of linear constraints.

**Next (Chapter 2):** Matrices as Linear Transformations — the matrix not as a spreadsheet but as a function that warps space. Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF) A matrix is in RREF if:
1. The first nonzero entry in each row is 1 (called a **leading 1** or **pivot**).
2. All other entries in each pivot column are 0.
3. The pivot in row $i+1$ is to the right of the pivot in row $i$.
4. Zero rows (all zeros) are at the bottom.

Every matrix has a unique RREF. Rank-Nullity Preview For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$:
$$\text{rank}(A) + \text{nullity}(A) = n$$

**rank** = number of pivot columns = number of nonzero rows in RREF.
**nullity** = number of free variable columns.

This identity (proven in Chapter 6) is one of the deepest theorems in linear algebra. Common Mistake: Skipping Back-Elimination Gaussian elimination creates zeros only **below** each pivot — stopping at Row Echelon Form (REF). Gauss-Jordan elimination creates zeros **above AND below** each pivot — reaching RREF.

**Wrong (stops at REF):**
$\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&2&5\\0&1&3\end{array}\right]$ — this is REF, NOT RREF (the $2$ above the second pivot is still there).

**Correct (RREF):** Apply $R_1 \to R_1 - 2R_2$ to get $\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&0&-1\\0&1&3\end{array}\right]$.

REF requires back-substitution to read the solution; RREF lets you read it directly. Free Variables Need a Parameter Name When a variable $x_3$ is free, assign it a parameter: $x_3 = t \in \mathbb{R}$. Then express all pivot variables in terms of $t$. If there are two free variables, use $s$ and $t$. The solution set is $\{\mathbf{x}_p + s\,\mathbf{v}_1 + t\,\mathbf{v}_2 : s, t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ — a translate of the null space. When to Use This Use RREF (Gauss-Jordan) when you need to:

- **Read the solution directly** with no back-substitution — ideal for paper-and-pencil work
- **Find all free variables** in a system — each non-pivot column is one
- **Determine the rank** of a matrix — count the nonzero rows in RREF
- **Test linear independence** of vectors — form a matrix with them as rows and check if RREF has all nonzero rows

Solution Existence and Uniqueness A system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$:

**Consistent** iff $\text{rank}(A) = \text{rank}([A|\mathbf{b}])$

**Unique solution** iff consistent AND $\text{rank}(A) = n$

**Infinitely many** iff consistent AND $\text{rank}(A) < n$ Elementary Row Operations **E1 (Swap):** Interchange rows $i$ and $j$: $R_i \leftrightarrow R_j$

**E2 (Scale):** Multiply row $i$ by nonzero scalar $c$: $R_i \leftarrow c R_i$

**E3 (Replace):** Add $c$ times row $j$ to row $i$: $R_i \leftarrow R_i + c R_j$

Each operation is **reversible** and preserves the solution set of the system. RREF Step-by-Step Visualizer Interactive Gauss-Jordan elimination showing all three solution types. RREF in OpenMAT Interactive OpenMAT cells for RREF practice. Code: RREF Three Ways — NumPy, SymPy, and Manual Use SymPy when you need to see the math; use NumPy when you need to solve numerically. Linear Systems & Row Reduction — Interactive Module Step through every elementary row operation to reach RREF — see exactly which rows are active at each stage. 3×3 System — Full Gauss-Jordan to RREF Solve via RREF: $2x_1 + x_2 - x_3 = 8$, $-3x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 = -11$, $-2x_1 + x_2 + 2x_3 = -3$. Unique solution: $x_1 = 2$, $x_2 = 3$, $x_3 = -1$. The RREF is the identity matrix on the left — all three variables are pivot variables, confirming no free variables and exactly one solution. \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2&1&-1&8\\-3&-1&2&-11\\-2&1&2&-3\end{array}\right] Write as augmented matrix $[A|\mathbf{b}]$. The three coefficient columns correspond to $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$; the last column is the right-hand side $\mathbf{b} = [8, -11, -3]^\top$. \xrightarrow{\frac{1}{2}R_1} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&\frac{1}{2}&-\frac{1}{2}&4\\-3&-1&2&-11\\-2&1&2&-3\end{array}\right] Scale row 1 by $\frac{1}{2}$ so the first pivot (top-left entry) equals 1. Now the pivot variable $x_1$ has coefficient 1 in row 1, which makes the elimination multipliers below it exact integers. \xrightarrow{R_2+3R_1,\;R_3+2R_1} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&\frac{1}{2}&-\frac{1}{2}&4\\0&\frac{1}{2}&\frac{1}{2}&1\\0&2&1&5\end{array}\right] Forward elimination on column 1: add 3 times row 1 to row 2 (the multiplier is $-(-3) = 3$), and 2 times row 1 to row 3 (the multiplier is $-(-2) = 2$). All entries below the first pivot are now zero. \xrightarrow{2R_2} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&\frac{1}{2}&-\frac{1}{2}&4\\0&1&1&2\\0&2&1&5\end{array}\right] \xrightarrow{R_3-2R_2} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&\frac{1}{2}&-\frac{1}{2}&4\\0&1&1&2\\0&0&-1&1\end{array}\right] Scale row 2 by 2 so the second pivot = 1, giving $x_2$ coefficient 1. Then subtract $2 \times$ (scaled) row 2 from row 3 to zero out the column-2 entry in row 3. Row 3 becomes $[0,0,-1,1]$. \xrightarrow{-R_3} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&\frac{1}{2}&-\frac{1}{2}&4\\0&1&1&2\\0&0&1&-1\end{array}\right] Scale row 3 by $-1$ to get the third pivot = 1. The matrix is now in Row Echelon Form (REF) — all pivots are 1 and zeros below each. The next step (back-elimination) is what makes it RREF. \xrightarrow{R_2-R_3,\;R_1+\frac{1}{2}R_3} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&\frac{1}{2}&0&\frac{7}{2}\\0&1&0&3\\0&0&1&-1\end{array}\right] \xrightarrow{R_1-\frac{1}{2}R_2} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&0&0&2\\0&1&0&3\\0&0&1&-1\end{array}\right] Back-eliminate: subtract row 3 from row 2 to zero out the $x_3$ entry above pivot 3. Add $\frac{1}{2}$ row 3 to row 1. Then subtract $\frac{1}{2}$ row 2 from row 1. RREF is $[I | \mathbf{c}]$ — solution reads from the last column: $x_1 = 2$, $x_2 = 3$, $x_3 = -1$. Detecting Inconsistency — the Contradiction Row Determine whether the system is consistent: $x + 2y = 3$, $2x + 4y = 7$, $3x + 6y = 9$. The system is inconsistent — no solution exists. Geometrically, all three equations describe lines with the same slope, but equations 1 and 2 have different intercepts ($x+2y=3$ and $x+2y=7/2$). Parallel lines never intersect. \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&2&3\\2&4&7\\3&6&9\end{array}\right] Form the $3 \times 3$ augmented matrix. Notice: the coefficient column vectors are $[1,2,3]^\top$ and $[2,4,6]^\top = 2[1,2,3]^\top$ — they are proportional. All three coefficient rows are multiples of $[1,2]$, meaning every equation describes the same family of lines $x + 2y = k$. \xrightarrow{R_2-2R_1,\;R_3-3R_1} \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&2&3\\0&0&1\\0&0&0\end{array}\right] Forward elimination: subtract $2 \times$ row 1 from row 2, and $3 \times$ row 1 from row 3. The left sides go to zero (as expected from proportional rows), but the right sides give $7 - 2(3) = 1$ and $9 - 3(3) = 0$. Row 2 becomes the contradiction row $[0\ 0\ |\ 1]$. [0\ 0\ |\ 1] \quad \text{reads as} \quad 0x + 0y = 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad 0 = 1 The row translates to $0 = 1$ — false for any $(x,y)$. This is the definitive inconsistency test: a **pivot in the augmented column** (last column). Compare with row 3: $[0\ 0\ |\ 0]$ reads $0 = 0$ — that row is harmless (redundant). The single contradiction row in row 2 kills the entire system. Free Variables — Writing the General Solution Find all solutions to: $x_1 + 2x_2 - x_3 = 4$ and $x_3 = 2$. Infinitely many solutions. General solution: $(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (6-2t,\ t,\ 2)$ for $t \in \mathbb{R}$. The solution set is a line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ — one degree of freedom (one free variable). \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&2&-1&4\\0&0&1&2\end{array}\right] Write the $2 \times 4$ augmented matrix. Column 1 has a pivot (the 1 in row 1). Column 2 has NO pivot entry — no row has a leading 1 in column 2. Column 3 has a pivot (the 1 in row 2). So: pivot variables are $x_1$ and $x_3$; free variable is $x_2$. \xrightarrow{R_1+R_2} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&2&0&6\\0&0&1&2\end{array}\right] Back-eliminate: add row 2 to row 1 to zero out the $-1$ entry above the second pivot in column 3. Now both pivot columns (1 and 3) have a leading 1 and zeros everywhere else — this is RREF. x_2 = t \in \mathbb{R} \quad \text{(free — assign parameter } t \text{)} Assign the free variable $x_2$ a parameter $t$. The parameter $t$ can be ANY real number. Every distinct value of $t$ gives a different solution — this is why the system has infinitely many. x_3 = 2, \quad x_1 = 6 - 2x_2 = 6 - 2t Read the pivot variables from RREF: row 2 gives $x_3 = 2$ directly. Row 1 gives $x_1 + 2t = 6$, so $x_1 = 6 - 2t$. Compare the reading effort. Solution: $x = -1$, $y = 3$. From RREF, the solution is immediate. From REF, you need back-substitution. Both give the same answer — RREF just removes the extra work. \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2&4&10\\1&3&8\end{array}\right] \xrightarrow{R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2} \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&3&8\\2&4&10\end{array}\right] Swap rows to get a leading 1 in position $(1,1)$ without fractions. Then scale row 2 by $-\frac{1}{2}$ so the second pivot = 1. **This is Row Echelon Form (REF)** — note the $3$ still above the second pivot. \xrightarrow{R_1 - 3R_2} \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&0&-1\\0&1&3\end{array}\right] Back-eliminate: subtract $3 \times$ row 2 from row 1 to zero out the $3$ above the second pivot. **This is RREF** — both pivot columns are identity columns $[1,0]^\top$ and $[0,1]^\top$. After the forward pass (zeros below pivots) you have REF — continue with back-elimination to zero out entries ABOVE the second pivot. Unique solution: $x = -1$, $y = 3$. Both columns 1 and 2 are pivot columns — no free variables. R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2:\;\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&3&8\\2&4&10\end{array}\right] Swap to bring a leading 1 to position (1,1). This avoids fractions from scaling row 1 by 1/2. R_2-2R_1:\;\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&3&8\\0&-2&-6\end{array}\right] Forward elimination: subtract 2 × row 1 from row 2. The entry below pivot 1 is now zero. -\tfrac{1}{2}R_2:\;\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&3&8\\0&1&3\end{array}\right] Scale row 2 so second pivot = 1. This is REF — note the 3 above the second pivot is still nonzero. R_1-3R_2:\;\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&0&-1\\0&1&3\end{array}\right] Back-eliminate: subtract 3 × row 2 from row 1. Both pivot columns are now identity columns — this is RREF. Read: x = −1, y = 3. Classify without solving Without fully reducing, determine whether the system with augmented matrix $\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&2&3&4\\ 2&4&6&9\\ 3&6&9&12\end{array}\right]$ has 0, 1, or infinitely many solutions. Justify using rank arguments. Build a rank-2 system with two outcomes Construct a $3 \times 3$ coefficient matrix $A$ with rank 2. Then find two different right-hand sides $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ such that: (a) $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}_1$ is consistent with infinitely many solutions, and (b) $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}_2$ is inconsistent. documents.proofs:
**Formal definition of a linear map.** A function $T: V \to W$ between vector spaces is called a **linear transformation** (or linear map) if and only if for all $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V$ and all scalars $c$:

1. **Additivity:** $T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v})$
2. **Homogeneity:** $T(c\mathbf{v}) = cT(\mathbf{v})$

Combining these: $T(c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{v}) = cT(\mathbf{u}) + dT(\mathbf{v})$ for all scalars $c, d$. By induction, $T$ preserves arbitrary linear combinations: $T\bigl(\sum_i c_i \mathbf{v}_i\bigr) = \sum_i c_i T(\mathbf{v}_i)$. **Matrix representation theorem.** The critical fact: every linear transformation $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is uniquely represented by an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ such that $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ for all $\mathbf{x}$. How do we find $A$? Apply $T$ to each standard basis vector $\mathbf{e}_j$ and make the results the columns of $A$:

$$A = \begin{bmatrix} T(\mathbf{e}_1) & T(\mathbf{e}_2) & \cdots & T(\mathbf{e}_n) \end{bmatrix}$$

This is the deepest reason the columns of a matrix are the destinations of the basis vectors. **Proof sketch.** For any $\mathbf{x} = x_1 \mathbf{e}_1 + \cdots + x_n \mathbf{e}_n$:

$$T(\mathbf{x}) = T(x_1 \mathbf{e}_1 + \cdots + x_n \mathbf{e}_n) = x_1 T(\mathbf{e}_1) + \cdots + x_n T(\mathbf{e}_n) = A\mathbf{x}$$

The first equality uses the representation in the standard basis. The second uses linearity. The third uses the definition $A = [T(\mathbf{e}_1) \cdots T(\mathbf{e}_n)]$. **The space of linear maps.** The set of all linear maps $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ forms a vector space (called $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{R}^m)$ or $\text{Hom}(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{R}^m)$), isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$. The identification $T \leftrightarrow A$ is a linear isomorphism. This is the formal statement that matrices and linear maps are the same thing. **Kernel and image.** For $T: V \to W$, the **kernel** (null space) is $\ker(T) = \{\mathbf{v} \in V : T(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}\}$. The **image** (column space) is $\text{im}(T) = \{T(\mathbf{v}) : \mathbf{v} \in V\}$. Both are subspaces. The Rank-Nullity theorem (LA1-006 preview) states $\dim(\ker T) + \dim(\text{im}\, T) = \dim(V) = n$. The image of $A$ is exactly the span of $A$'s columns — this is why column space matters. Matrix Representation of Linear Maps **Theorem:** Every linear map $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ has a unique matrix representation $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with $A_{ij} = [T(\mathbf{e}_j)]_i$ (the $i$-th component of where the $j$-th basis vector goes).

**Corollary:** The set of $m \times n$ matrices is in bijection with the set of linear maps $\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$. Matrix multiplication corresponds to function composition. The Origin Must Be Fixed For any linear map $T$, $T(\mathbf{0}) = T(0 \cdot \mathbf{0}) = 0 \cdot T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$ by homogeneity. So $T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$ — the origin is always a fixed point of any linear transformation. A transformation that moves the origin (e.g., $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} \neq \mathbf{0}$) is called affine, not linear. Image = Column Space The image of $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ is the set of all possible outputs: $\{A\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\}$. Expanding: $A\mathbf{x} = x_1\mathbf{a}_1 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{a}_n$ where $\mathbf{a}_j$ are the columns of $A$. So the image is exactly $\text{span}(\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n)$ — the **column space** of $A$.

In other words: the columns of the matrix span the entire set of possible outputs. Composition Order Matters — Matrices Do Not Commute Composing two linear maps corresponds to multiplying their matrices. But $AB \neq BA$ in general — matrix multiplication is **not** commutative.

Geometrically: "first rotate, then shear" gives a different result than "first shear, then rotate." Order matters because you are applying transformations to an already-warped space.
documents.applications:
When an engineer designs a video game or an iPhone app, they don't write a loop that calculates the new position of every single pixel one by one. That would be far too slow. Instead, they define a 'Linear Transformation'—a single rule that universally twists and stretches the entire fabric of space. Because space is locked to a grid, the computer only needs to calculate where the two fundamental basis vectors move. Everything else just gets dragged along for the ride. The mathematical 'recipe' that holds the instructions for where those two basis vectors go is called a Matrix. Procedure: Apply a Matrix to a Vector (Column Method) Step 1. Write the input vector $\mathbf{v} = [x, y]^T$ and identify its two components $x$ and $y$.
Step 2. Read column 1 of $A$ — this is where $\hat{i} = [1,0]^T$ lands after the transformation.
Step 3. Read column 2 of $A$ — this is where $\hat{j} = [0,1]^T$ lands.
Step 4. Scale and add: $A\mathbf{v} = x \cdot (\text{column 1}) + y \cdot (\text{column 2})$.
Step 5. Verify with the row formula: row 1 of $A$ dotted with $\mathbf{v}$ gives the first output component; row 2 dotted with $\mathbf{v}$ gives the second. Lesson 1 of 12 — Matrices & Transformations **Previous (Chapter 1):** Static vectors, dot products, systems of equations, RREF.
**This lesson:** Matrices as active functions that warp space — the “verb” to LA1's “nouns.”
**Next (Lesson 2):** Matrix Multiplication — chaining two transformations into one. The Secret of the Columns The columns of a matrix tell you **exactly** where the basis vectors $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ land:

$$A = \begin{bmatrix} | & | \\ \hat{i}_{new} & \hat{j}_{new} \\ | & | \end{bmatrix}$$

This is the most crucial insight in all of linear algebra. Read every matrix you encounter this way from now on. What Makes a Transformation "Linear"? Exactly two rules must hold for all vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$ and scalars $c$:

1. **Additivity:** $T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v})$
2. **Homogeneity:** $T(c\mathbf{v}) = cT(\mathbf{v})$

Together these imply $T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$ — the origin stays fixed. Any transformation that moves the origin (like "add 2 to every x-coordinate") is **not** linear (it is called affine). Affine vs. Linear — A Critical Distinction CNC work offsets (G54, G55) **translate** the origin — they shift every coordinate by a constant amount. That is an **affine** transformation, not a linear one. G68 coordinate rotation **is** linear — it preserves the origin. In robotics and computer graphics, the standard workaround is homogeneous coordinates: embed the 2D plane in 3D and represent translations as matrix multiplications. When to Read a Matrix Geometrically **Use the column-reading method when you want to understand WHAT a matrix does:** Is it a rotation? A stretch? A shear? Does it collapse the plane onto a line?

**Use the row-dot-column formula when you just need the number:** computing $A\mathbf{v}$ for a specific $\mathbf{v}$, or running machine computations.

**The test for linearity:** if a transformation preserves the origin AND satisfies $T(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})=T(\mathbf{u})+T(\mathbf{v})$, it can be represented as a matrix. If it moves the origin or bends grid lines, it cannot.

If you take a photo on your phone and want to skew it horizontally, how does the computer know where to move every single one of the 12 million pixels? When an engineer designs a video game or an iPhone app, they don't write a loop that calculates the new position of every single pixel one by one. That would be far too slow. Instead, they define a 'Linear Transformation'—a single rule that universally twists and stretches the entire fabric of space. Because space is locked to a grid, the computer only needs to calculate where the two fundamental basis vectors move. Everything else just gets dragged along for the ride. The mathematical 'recipe' that holds the instructions for where those two basis vectors go is called a Matrix. Take $[3, 1]^T$ and apply $A = \begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$. Output: $[-1, 3]^T$. Apply $A$ to $[5, 2]^T$: output is $[-2, 5]^T$. Apply $A$ to $[0, -4]^T$: output is $[4, 0]^T$. Every vector rotates 90° counter-clockwise. The matrix $A$ is not storing data — it is a **function** that warps the entire plane simultaneously. This lesson is about that shift: from matrix as spreadsheet to matrix as **verb** that transforms space. You may have seen matrices before as grids of data — like a spreadsheet. That is the database view. The **geometric view** is far more powerful: a matrix is a *function* that transforms every point in space simultaneously. Picture a rubber sheet covered in a grid. A matrix transformation grabs that sheet and stretches it, rotates it, or shears it into a new shape. Every point on the sheet moves with it. The key constraint of a **linear** transformation: the rubber sheet cannot crinkle, tear, or move the origin. Grid lines stay parallel and evenly spaced — just scaled, rotated, or skewed. **The basis vector shortcut.** Because the grid stays uniform, you do not need to track where every point goes. Track only two points: where $\hat{i} = [1,0]$ and $\hat{j} = [0,1]$ land. Once you know those, every other point is forced — because every vector is a linear combination of $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$, and the combination rules do not change under a linear transformation. **The matrix is the cheat sheet.** A $2 \times 2$ matrix stores exactly two pieces of information: the new coordinates of $\hat{i}$ (first column) and the new coordinates of $\hat{j}$ (second column). That is the whole secret. **Predict before reading on.** You have the shear matrix $S = \begin{bmatrix}1&3\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$. Without computing: what does $S$ send $\hat{i} = [1,0]^T$ to? What does it send $\hat{j} = [0,1]^T$ to? Where does the corner $(0,1)$ of the unit square end up? Write your prediction, then check it against Example 3. **CNC machine connection — G68 coordinate rotation.** On a CNC milling machine, parts are sometimes clamped at an angle. Rather than rewriting every coordinate in the G-code program, the operator uses `G68` (Coordinate Rotation). The CNC controller secretly multiplies every tool position by a rotation matrix:

$$\begin{bmatrix}X' \\ Y'\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}X \\ Y\end{bmatrix}$$

If the part is clamped 5° off — the controller applies this matrix to every single move, invisibly rotating the entire work coordinate system. You write the G-code as if the part were perfectly aligned; the transformation matrix handles the rest. **Where this is heading:** Once we understand what ONE matrix does to space, we chain matrices together (Matrix Multiplication) and ask whether transformations can be undone (Matrix Inverses). A 2D linear transformation relies on $2 \times 2$ matrices. When applying a matrix $A$ to an input vector $\vec{v}$, the output vector is written as $A\vec{v}$. Let's build a matrix $A$. Suppose we want to transform space such that $\hat{i}$ lands at $[a, c]$ and $\hat{j}$ lands at $[b, d]$. Remember that $\vec{v}$ is just a set of instructions: "Take $x$ steps along $\hat{i}$ and $y$ steps along $\hat{j}$". Because the grid lines remain straight and evenly spaced, the new vector will just take $x$ steps along the *new* $\hat{i}$ and $y$ steps along the *new* $\hat{j}$. Algebraically, we are just taking a linear combination of the columns of the matrix: $ \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = x\begin{bmatrix} a \\ c \end{bmatrix} + y\begin{bmatrix} b \\ d \end{bmatrix} $ This equation is the definition of Matrix-Vector multiplication. $$T(\mathbf{x}) = T(x_1 \mathbf{e}_1 + \cdots + x_n \mathbf{e}_n) = x_1 T(\mathbf{e}_1) + \cdots + x_n T(\mathbf{e}_n) = A\mathbf{x}$$

The first equality uses the representation in the standard basis. The second uses linearity. The third uses the definition $A = [T(\mathbf{e}_1) \cdots T(\mathbf{e}_n)]$. **The space of linear maps.** The set of all linear maps $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ forms a vector space (called $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{R}^m)$ or $\text{Hom}(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{R}^m)$), isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$. The identification $T \leftrightarrow A$ is a linear isomorphism. This is the formal statement that matrices and linear maps are the same thing. **Kernel and image.** For $T: V \to W$, the **kernel** (null space) is $\ker(T) = \{\mathbf{v} \in V : T(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}\}$. The **image** (column space) is $\text{im}(T) = \{T(\mathbf{v}) : \mathbf{v} \in V\}$. Both are subspaces. Matrix Representation of Linear Maps **Theorem:** Every linear map $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ has a unique matrix representation $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with $A_{ij} = [T(\mathbf{e}_j)]_i$ (the $i$-th component of where the $j$-th basis vector goes).

**Corollary:** The set of $m \times n$ matrices is in bijection with the set of linear maps $\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$. Matrix multiplication corresponds to function composition. The Origin Must Be Fixed For any linear map $T$, $T(\mathbf{0}) = T(0 \cdot \mathbf{0}) = 0 \cdot T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$ by homogeneity. So $T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$ — the origin is always a fixed point of any linear transformation. A transformation that moves the origin (e.g., $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} \neq \mathbf{0}$) is called affine, not linear. Image = Column Space The image of $T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ is the set of all possible outputs: $\{A\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\}$. Expanding: $A\mathbf{x} = x_1\mathbf{a}_1 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{a}_n$ where $\mathbf{a}_j$ are the columns of $A$. So the image is exactly $\text{span}(\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n)$ — the **column space** of $A$.

In other words: the columns of the matrix span the entire set of possible outputs. Composition Order Matters — Matrices Do Not Commute Composing two linear maps corresponds to multiplying their matrices. But $AB \neq BA$ in general — matrix multiplication is **not** commutative.

Geometrically: "first rotate, then shear" gives a different result than "first shear, then rotate." Order matters because you are applying transformations to an already-warped space. Procedure: Apply a Matrix to a Vector (Column Method) Step 1. Write the input vector $\mathbf{v} = [x, y]^T$ and identify its two components $x$ and $y$.
Step 2. Read column 1 of $A$ — this is where $\hat{i} = [1,0]^T$ lands after the transformation.
Step 3. Read column 2 of $A$ — this is where $\hat{j} = [0,1]^T$ lands.
Step 4. Scale and add: $A\mathbf{v} = x \cdot (\text{column 1}) + y \cdot (\text{column 2})$.
Step 5. Verify with the row formula: row 1 of $A$ dotted with $\mathbf{v}$ gives the first output component; row 2 dotted with $\mathbf{v}$ gives the second. Lesson 1 of 12 — Matrices & Transformations **Previous (Chapter 1):** Static vectors, dot products, systems of equations, RREF.
**This lesson:** Matrices as active functions that warp space — the “verb” to LA1's “nouns.”
**Next (Lesson 2):** Matrix Multiplication — chaining two transformations into one. The Secret of the Columns The columns of a matrix tell you **exactly** where the basis vectors $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ land:

$$A = \begin{bmatrix} | & | \\ \hat{i}_{new} & \hat{j}_{new} \\ | & | \end{bmatrix}$$

This is the most crucial insight in all of linear algebra. Read every matrix you encounter this way from now on. What Makes a Transformation "Linear"? Exactly two rules must hold for all vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$ and scalars $c$:

1. **Additivity:** $T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v})$
2. **Homogeneity:** $T(c\mathbf{v}) = cT(\mathbf{v})$

Together these imply $T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$ — the origin stays fixed. Any transformation that moves the origin (like "add 2 to every x-coordinate") is **not** linear (it is called affine). Affine vs. Linear — A Critical Distinction CNC work offsets (G54, G55) **translate** the origin — they shift every coordinate by a constant amount. That is an **affine** transformation, not a linear one. G68 coordinate rotation **is** linear — it preserves the origin. In robotics and computer graphics, the standard workaround is homogeneous coordinates: embed the 2D plane in 3D and represent translations as matrix multiplications. When to Read a Matrix Geometrically **Use the column-reading method when you want to understand WHAT a matrix does:** Is it a rotation? A stretch? A shear? Does it collapse the plane onto a line?

**Use the row-dot-column formula when you just need the number:** computing $A\mathbf{v}$ for a specific $\mathbf{v}$, or running machine computations.

**The test for linearity:** if a transformation preserves the origin AND satisfies $T(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})=T(\mathbf{u})+T(\mathbf{v})$, it can be represented as a matrix. If it moves the origin or bends grid lines, it cannot. Matrix-Vector Product Formula $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} ax + by \\ cx + dy \end{bmatrix}$ Rows vs Columns Many textbooks teach matrix multiplication as "multiply the rows by the columns" and taking a dot product. While true for computing, the "Linear Combination of Columns" perspective shown above is far better for geometric intuition. Warping the Grid — Interactive A linear transformation is completely determined by where it sends the two basis vectors. Why Columns Equal Basis Vector Destinations The linear combination law forces column 1 = destination of î, column 2 = destination of ĵ. Transform Lab — Place, Rotate, Mirror, Chain Build hands-on intuition by constructing rotation, reflection, and composition matrices yourself. OpenMAT: Matrices as Transformations Four cells: matrix-vector multiply, common transforms, rotation derivation, and CNC G68. Code: Matrices as Transformations Apply transformations to vectors and visualize how the grid warps. Projection — A Linear Map That Loses Information A rank-1 matrix collapses the plane onto a line. Many inputs share the same output — the kernel is all vectors perpendicular to the projection axis. Linear Transformations — Step-by-Step T(x) = Ax Every linear transformation is multiplication by its standard matrix — the columns are where the basis vectors land. Apply a Matrix — Read the Output as a Linear Combination Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$. Where does the vector $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ land after the transformation? A\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Set up the matrix-vector product $A\mathbf{v}$. The matrix $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ transformation; $\mathbf{v}$ is a $2 \times 1$ column vector. The result will also be $2 \times 1$. = 4 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + 1 \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} Rewrite as a **linear combination of the columns** of $A$: the first component of $\mathbf{v}$ (which is 4) scales column 1 $= [2,0]^T$, and the second component (which is 1) scales column 2 $= [-1,3]^T$. This is the geometric interpretation — $\mathbf{v}$ says "go 4 steps along new $\hat{i}$ and 1 step along new $\hat{j}$." = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} Scale: $4 \cdot [2,0]^T = [8,0]^T$ and $1 \cdot [-1,3]^T = [-1,3]^T$. = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} Add the scaled columns: $[8,0]^T + [-1,3]^T = [7,3]^T$. The vector $\mathbf{v} = [4,1]^T$ lands at $[7,3]^T$ after transformation $A$. Build a Matrix from Geometry — 90° Rotation Construct the $2 \times 2$ matrix that rotates every vector in the 2D plane $90^\circ$ counter-clockwise. \hat{i} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \xrightarrow{\text{90° CCW}} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Strategy: track only the two basis vectors. $\hat{i} = [1,0]^T$ points right. After rotating 90° counter-clockwise it points straight up: $[0,1]^T$. This will become column 1 of the matrix. \hat{j} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \xrightarrow{\text{90° CCW}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} $\hat{j} = [0,1]^T$ points up. After 90° CCW it points left: $[-1,0]^T$. This becomes column 2 of the matrix. R_{90} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} Paste the two landing vectors in as columns: column 1 = destination of $\hat{i}$ = $[0,1]^T$, column 2 = destination of $\hat{j}$ = $[-1,0]^T$. Every vector in the plane is rotated 90° CCW by this matrix. R_{90} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = 3\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + 1\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} Verify: apply $R_{90}$ to a test vector $[3,1]^T$. The result $[-1,3]^T$ should be $[3,1]^T$ rotated 90° CCW. Length preserved: $\sqrt{9+1} = \sqrt{1+9}$ ✓. Direction rotated 90° ✓. Read a Matrix — Identify the Transformation Geometrically Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, describe geometrically what this transformation does to the plane. Then apply it to the square with corners at $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(1,1)$, $(0,1)$. \text{Column 1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \text{Column 2} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Read the columns: $\hat{i} = [1,0]^T$ stays at $[1,0]^T$ (unchanged). $\hat{j} = [0,1]^T$ moves to $[3,1]^T$ — it slides 3 units to the right while staying at height 1. This is a **horizontal shear**. A\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}, \quad A\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\1\end{bmatrix}, \quad A\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix} Apply $A$ to three corners of the unit square. The corner $(0,0)$ stays at $(0,0)$ (origin fixed). $(1,0) \to (1,0)$ (on x-axis, unaffected). $(0,1) \to (3,1)$. $(1,1) \to (4,1)$. \text{Square} \to \text{Parallelogram with corners } (0,0),(1,0),(4,1),(3,1) The unit square shears into a parallelogram. The bottom edge stays on the x-axis (unaffected). The top edge slides 3 units right. **Key insight:** area is preserved in this shear — the parallelogram has the same area as the original square ($= |\det(A)| = |1\cdot1 - 3\cdot0| = 1$). Calculate the output of $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}$. Take 5 times the first column [1, 3], and add it to -2 times the second column [2, 4]. \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} + (-2) \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} Write as a linear combination of the columns. \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 15 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ -8 \end{bmatrix} Scale the columns. \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} Add them together. Construct a matrix that shrinks space by half horizontally, but leaves everything unchanged vertically. Where does [1,0] go? Where does [0,1] go? Make those your columns. $\begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ \hat{i} \to \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} Since horizontal scale is halved, i-hat shrinks to 0.5. \hat{j} \to \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Vertical scale is unchanged, so j-hat stays where it is. \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} Paste into columns. A $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ maps $[1,0]^T \to [2,3]^T$ and $[0,1]^T \to [-1,4]^T$. (a) Write $A$. (b) Where does $A$ send the vector $[5, -2]^T$? (c) Is the transformation area-preserving? (Hint: compute $|\det(A)|$.) Columns of $A$ are the destinations of the basis vectors. For (c): $\det(A) = ad - bc$; $|\det| = 1$ means area-preserving. $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$, $A[5,-2]^T = [12,7]^T$, and $|\det(A)| = 11$ — the transformation scales area by 11. A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} Paste destinations as columns: column 1 = $[2,3]^T$ (where $\hat{i}$ lands), column 2 = $[-1,4]^T$ (where $\hat{j}$ lands). A\begin{bmatrix}5\\-2\end{bmatrix} = 5\begin{bmatrix}2\\3\end{bmatrix} + (-2)\begin{bmatrix}-1\\4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}10\\15\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2\\-8\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}12\\7\end{bmatrix} Linear combination of columns: $5 \times$ col 1 plus $-2 \times$ col 2. \det(A) = (2)(4) - (-1)(3) = 8 + 3 = 11 The determinant equals 11, so $|\det| = 11 \neq 1$. The transformation scales area by a factor of 11 — it is NOT area-preserving. Regions expand to 11 times their original area. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step vector-valued velocity acceleration trajectory

The product $AB$ means $B$ acts on a vector first, then $A$ acts on the result. Dimension check: $A$ is $2 	imes 2$, $B$ is $2 	imes 2$ — inner dimensions match (2 = 2), so the product is defined and $2 	imes 2$.
