and $\sum k_i = n$. The block sizes and eigenvalues are uniquely determined; $S$ is not. Nilpotent Decomposition Each Jordan block splits as $J_k(\lambda) = \lambda I + N_k$ where $N_k$ has 1s only on the superdiagonal — a **nilpotent** matrix satisfying $N_k^k = 0$.

This decomposition makes the matrix exponential tractable:

$e^{Jt} = e^{\lambda t} e^{N_k t} = e^{\lambda t}\left(I + N_k t + \frac{N_k^2 t^2}{2!} + \cdots\right)$

The series terminates at $N_k^{k-1}$ (since $N_k^k = 0$). Powers of a Jordan Block For $J_2(\lambda) = \begin{bmatrix}\lambda & 1 \\ 0 & \lambda\end{bmatrix}$:

$J_2^n = \begin{bmatrix}\lambda^n & n\lambda^{n-1} \\ 0 & \lambda^n\end{bmatrix}$

The off-diagonal $n\lambda^{n-1}$ is the polynomial signature of a Jordan block — it grows polynomially while the diagonal grows exponentially. For stability, $|\lambda| < 1$ ensures both terms → 0. Jordan Structure in OpenMAT A Jordan block with a 1 on the superdiagonal is irreducible — it cannot be split further. Code: Jordan Blocks, Generalized Eigenvectors, and Critical Damping Three cells: defective matrix analysis, Jordan chain construction, and critically-damped CNC axis response. Jordan form of a 2×2 defective matrix Find the Jordan form of $A = \begin{bmatrix}5&1\\0&5\end{bmatrix}$ and identify the Jordan chain. $A = J_2(5)$ is already in Jordan form — one $2\times 2$ block at eigenvalue 5. The Jordan chain $\{[1,0]^T, [0,1]^T\}$ spans $\mathbb{R}^2$, even though there is only one eigenvector. \det(A - \lambda I) = (5-\lambda)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 5 \text{ (alg. mult. 2)} Characteristic equation. Double root at $\lambda = 5$. A - 5I = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix} \qquad \ker(A-5I) = \text{span}\left\{\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\right\} Geometric multiplicity = 1 (only one independent eigenvector). Since $1 < 2$, $A$ is defective. \text{Jordan form: } J = J_2(5) = \begin{bmatrix}5&1\\0&5\end{bmatrix} = A $A$ is itself in Jordan form — one block of size 2. \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}, \quad (A - 5I)\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1 \Rightarrow \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix} Jordan chain: $\mathbf{v}_1$ is the eigenvector, $\mathbf{v}_2$ is the generalized eigenvector. Verify: $(A-5I)\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{v}_1$ ✓ Identifying Jordan structure from multiplicity data A $4\times 4$ matrix has eigenvalue $\lambda = 3$ with algebraic multiplicity 4 and geometric multiplicity 2. What are the possible Jordan forms? With only algebraic and geometric multiplicity, you can narrow down the Jordan structure but may not determine it uniquely. The ranks of $(A-\lambda I)^k$ for $k = 1, 2, \ldots$ give the full picture. \text{Two Jordan blocks for } \lambda = 3 \text{ (geometric mult = 2)} Number of blocks = geometric multiplicity = 2. \text{Two blocks summing to 4: either } (3, 1) \text{ or } (2, 2) The only partitions of 4 into 2 positive integers. J = J_3(3) \oplus J_1(3) = \begin{bmatrix}3&1&0&0\\0&3&1&0\\0&0&3&0\\0&0&0&3\end{bmatrix} \quad \text{OR} \quad J = J_2(3) \oplus J_2(3) = \begin{bmatrix}3&1&0&0\\0&3&0&0\\0&0&3&1\\0&0&0&3\end{bmatrix} Two distinct possible Jordan forms. Cannot determine which without more information (e.g., the rank of $(A-3I)^2$). Computing A^n for a Jordan Block Let $J = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$ (a Jordan block with $\lambda=2$). Compute $J^3$ using the binomial theorem formula, and verify by direct multiplication. For a Jordan block $J_2(\lambda)$: $J^n = \begin{bmatrix}\lambda^n & n\lambda^{n-1}\\0&\lambda^n\end{bmatrix}$. The off-diagonal grows polynomially in $n$ — not just exponentially like $\lambda^n$. This polynomial×exponential growth is the signature of a defective matrix and makes Jordan form essential for differential equations with repeated roots. J = \lambda I + N \text{ where } N = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}, \; N^2 = \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix} Decompose: $J = \lambda I + N$ where $N$ is nilpotent ($N^2 = 0$). This is always valid for Jordan blocks. J^n = (\lambda I + N)^n = \lambda^n I + n\lambda^{n-1}N = \begin{bmatrix}\lambda^n & n\lambda^{n-1}\\0&\lambda^n\end{bmatrix} Binomial theorem with $N^2 = 0$: only the $k=0$ and $k=1$ terms survive. J^3 = \begin{bmatrix}2^3 & 3\cdot2^2\\0&2^3\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}8&12\\0&8\end{bmatrix} $\lambda = 2$, $n = 3$: diagonal entry $2^3 = 8$, off-diagonal $3 \cdot 4 = 12$. For $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$: both have the same characteristic polynomial $(\lambda-2)^2 = 0$. Are they similar? Do they have the same Jordan form? Compute the geometric multiplicity for each. A has two independent eigenvectors; B has one. A and B are NOT similar. A has Jordan form diag(2,2); B has Jordan form [[2,1],[0,2]]. Same characteristic polynomial, different Jordan structures. A - 2I = \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix} \Rightarrow \ker = \mathbb{R}^2, \; m_g = 2 $A$ is already diagonal — two $1\times 1$ blocks: $J = J_1(2) \oplus J_1(2)$. B - 2I = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix} \Rightarrow \ker = \text{span}\{[1,0]^T\}, \; m_g = 1 $B$ is defective — one $2\times 2$ block: $J = J_2(2)$. J_A = \begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix} \neq J_B = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix} Different Jordan forms → NOT similar. Same eigenvalues are not enough; the multiplicity structure matters. Determine the possible Jordan forms for a $4 \times 4$ matrix with eigenvalue $\lambda = 2$ of algebraic multiplicity 4 and geometric multiplicity 2. Number of Jordan blocks = geometric multiplicity = 2. Block sizes must sum to 4. Two possibilities: J₁ƒ(2) âŠ• J₁(2) or J₁(2) âŠ• J₁(2). Distinguish by computing rank(A-2I)². \text{Two blocks summing to 4: partitions of 4 into 2 parts} = (3,1) \text{ or } (2,2) Those are the only ways to write 4 as an ordered sum of 2 positive integers (up to reordering). J = J_3(2) \oplus J_1(2) \quad \text{or} \quad J = J_2(2) \oplus J_2(2) Cannot determine which without computing rank$(A - 2I)^2$. For the Jordan block $J = \begin{bmatrix}\lambda & 1 \\ 0 & \lambda\end{bmatrix}$, derive the formula for $J^n$ and verify for $n = 3$ with $\lambda = 2$. Write $J = \lambda I + N$ where $N = [[0,1],[0,0]]$. Use the binomial theorem. Note $N^2 = 0$. Jⁿ = [[λⁿ, nλⁿ⁻¹],[0, λⁿ]]. For λ=2, n=3: [[8,12],[0,8]]. J = \lambda I + N, \quad N = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}, \quad N^2 = 0 Decompose into scalar and nilpotent parts. J^n = (\lambda I + N)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}\lambda^{n-k}N^k = \lambda^n I + n\lambda^{n-1}N Binomial theorem. All terms with $k \geq 2$ vanish since $N^2 = 0$. J^n = \begin{bmatrix}\lambda^n & n\lambda^{n-1} \\ 0 & \lambda^n\end{bmatrix} \qquad J^3\big|_{\lambda=2} = \begin{bmatrix}8 & 12 \\ 0 & 8\end{bmatrix} For $\lambda=2, n=3$: diagonal $2^3 = 8$, off-diagonal $3 \cdot 2^2 = 12$. Verify by multiplying $J \cdot J \cdot J$ directly. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step vector-valued velocity acceleration trajectory

documents.proofs:
**Ergodicity.** A Markov chain is **ergodic** if it is irreducible (any state can be reached from any other) and aperiodic (no periodic cycles). Ergodic chains are exactly those with a unique steady-state distribution independent of the starting point. Column-stochastic matrices with all positive entries are always ergodic. **Mixing time.** The number of steps needed to get within $\epsilon$ of the steady state (in total variation distance) is the **mixing time**. It is determined by the spectral gap: mixing time $\approx 1/(1 - |\lambda_2|)$. Slow mixing in Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms is a major computational bottleneck in Bayesian statistics. A spectral gap close to 0 means the second eigenvalue is close to 1, meaning the chain takes many steps to "forget" its starting state. **Detailed balance (reversibility).** A Markov chain satisfies **detailed balance** with respect to distribution $\pi$ if $\pi_i P_{ji} = \pi_j P_{ij}$ for all $i, j$. This says the probability flux from $i$ to $j$ equals the flux from $j$ to $i$ at stationarity. Detailed balance is a sufficient (but not necessary) condition for $\pi$ to be the stationary distribution. Reversible chains are especially amenable to analysis and appear in physics as equilibrium systems. **Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).** The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm constructs a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is any target distribution $\pi$ — even one you can only evaluate point-wise (such as a Bayesian posterior proportional to likelihood × prior). The chain is designed so detailed balance holds with respect to $\pi$. Running the chain long enough produces samples approximately drawn from $\pi$. Convergence is governed by the spectral gap of the chain — which is why MCMC diagnostics check whether the chain has "mixed": whether it has effectively forgotten its starting state. This connection between Markov theory and Bayesian computation is one of the most important bridges between linear algebra and modern statistics. Left vs Right Eigenvectors Column-stochastic: $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$ — the steady state is a **right eigenvector**.
Row-stochastic ($P^\top$ convention): steady state satisfies $\mathbf{q}^\top P = \mathbf{q}^\top$ — it is a **left eigenvector**.

Both conventions appear in the literature. The left-eigenvector convention arises when the state vector is a row vector. This course uses column-stochastic (state vector = column, matrix acts on the left). Perron Root Bounds For any column-stochastic matrix $P$:

$\min_j \sum_i P_{ij} \leq \rho(P) \leq \max_j \sum_i P_{ij}$

where $\rho(P)$ is the spectral radius (largest $|\lambda|$). Since all column sums equal 1, the spectral radius equals exactly 1: $\rho(P) = 1$.

Corollary: $|\lambda| \leq 1$ for all eigenvalues of $P$. Reducible vs Irreducible Chains A chain is **reducible** if states can be partitioned into two groups with no transitions from one to the other. Reducible chains can have multiple steady-state distributions — the result depends on which subset of states you start in.

Irreducible chains (all states communicate) + aperiodic → unique steady state. Aperiodic means: no state is visited with a fixed period $> 1$. Adding self-loops guarantees aperiodicity.
documents.applications:
Markov chains are everywhere. Google's PageRank algorithm models a random web surfer who clicks links at random — the steady-state distribution of which pages they visit determines each page's rank. Speech recognition uses Hidden Markov Models to decode audio into words. Population geneticists use Markov chains to model allele frequencies drifting across generations. Financial models use them to predict credit ratings. In all cases, the key insight is the same: there is a long-run equilibrium that is determined entirely by the transition structure — not the starting point. Lesson 5 of 7 — Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors **Previous (Lesson 4):** Jordan Normal Form — handling non-diagonalizable matrices.
**This lesson:** Markov Chains — stochastic matrices, eigenvalue 1, steady-state distributions, and the Perron-Frobenius theorem.
**Next (Lesson 6):** Cayley-Hamilton Theorem — every matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Procedure: Find the Steady-State Distribution Step 1. **Verify stochastic.** Confirm that each column of $P$ sums to 1 and all entries are non-negative.

Step 2. **Set up the eigenvector equation.** Form $A = P - I$. The steady state $\mathbf{q}$ satisfies $A\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ (null space of $P - I$).

Step 3. **Solve the null space.** Row-reduce $[A | \mathbf{0}]$ to find the free variable and the general solution.

Step 4. **Normalize.** Divide the null-space vector by the sum of its entries so all components sum to 1. This makes $\mathbf{q}$ a valid probability distribution.

Step 5. **Sanity-check.** Verify $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$ and $\sum_i q_i = 1$. Also confirm $q_i \geq 0$ — if any entry is negative, check your null-space computation. The Perron-Frobenius Theorem (Informal) For a regular stochastic matrix (all entries positive, or some power has all positive entries), there is exactly one steady-state distribution, and it is the unique normalized eigenvector for $\lambda = 1$. Starting from ANY initial distribution, $P^k \mathbf{x}_0 \to \mathbf{q}$ as $k \to \infty$. The starting point does not matter — you always end up at $\mathbf{q}$. All Other Eigenvalues Satisfy $|\lambda| \leq 1$ For a column-stochastic matrix, all eigenvalues satisfy $|\lambda| \leq 1$. If $|\lambda_2| < 1$ (the second-largest eigenvalue in magnitude), then the contribution of $\lambda_2^k \mathbf{v}_2$ to $P^k \mathbf{x}_0$ shrinks exponentially. The gap $1 - |\lambda_2|$ is the **spectral gap** — larger gap means faster convergence to steady state. PageRank in One Paragraph Model the web as $n$ pages and a transition matrix $P$ where $P_{ij} = $ (probability surfer clicks link from page $j$ to page $i$). Add a "teleportation" probability $\alpha$ to handle pages with no outlinks: $\hat{P} = (1-\alpha)P + \alpha \frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top}{n}$. The PageRank vector is the steady-state distribution $\hat{P}\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$. Pages with high $q_i$ are authoritative.
documents.content:
If you start a random process (weather, web surfing, genetics) and let it run forever, where does it end up? And does it matter where it started? Markov chains are everywhere. Google's PageRank algorithm models a random web surfer who clicks links at random — the steady-state distribution of which pages they visit determines each page's rank. Speech recognition uses Hidden Markov Models to decode audio into words. Population geneticists use Markov chains to model allele frequencies drifting across generations. Financial models use them to predict credit ratings. In all cases, the key insight is the same: there is a long-run equilibrium that is determined entirely by the transition structure — not the starting point. A simple weather model has two states: Sunny and Rainy. Transition matrix $P = \begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.4\\0.2&0.6\end{bmatrix}$ (columns sum to 1). Start with $\mathbf{x}_0 = [1,0]^\top$ (all Sunny). After one step: $P\mathbf{x}_0 = [0.8, 0.2]^\top$. After many steps, $P^k\mathbf{x}_0 \to \mathbf{q}$. Solve $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ with $q_1+q_2=1$: $\mathbf{q} = [2/3, 1/3]^\top$. Long run: 67% sunny, 33% rainy — regardless of where you started. **What is a Markov chain?** A Markov chain describes a system that jumps between states over time, where the probability of jumping from state $i$ to state $j$ depends only on the current state (not the history). This "memoryless" property is the Markov property. The transition probabilities are encoded in a matrix. **Transition matrix.** For a system with $n$ states, the transition matrix $P$ has $P_{ij} = $ probability of moving from state $j$ to state $i$ (column-stochastic convention). Each column sums to 1 (all probability from state $j$ must go somewhere). A column vector $\mathbf{x}$ where $x_i \geq 0$ and $\sum x_i = 1$ represents a probability distribution over states. **Matrix-vector product = one time step.** If $\mathbf{x}_t$ is the distribution at time $t$, then $\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = P\mathbf{x}_t$. After $k$ steps: $\mathbf{x}_k = P^k \mathbf{x}_0$. As $k \to \infty$, the distribution often converges to a **steady state** $\mathbf{q}$ satisfying $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$ — an eigenvector of $P$ with eigenvalue 1. **Why eigenvalue 1 always exists.** For any column-stochastic matrix, the vector of all ones $\mathbf{1}$ satisfies $P^\top \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$ (each row of $P^\top$ sums to 1). Therefore $P^\top - I$ has $\mathbf{1}$ in its null space, so $\det(P^\top - I) = \det(P - I) = 0$, which means $\lambda = 1$ is an eigenvalue of $P$. The steady-state distribution is the normalized eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda = 1$. **Predict before reading on.** The weather matrix $P = \begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.3\\0.1&0.7\end{bmatrix}$ has larger diagonal entries (the system tends to stay in its current state). Will the steady state be closer to $[1,0]^\top$ (all Sunny) or $[0.5, 0.5]^\top$ (equal)? Which eigenvalue equals 1? Predict, then verify. **CNC machine availability — Markov analysis.** A CNC machine cycles through states: Cutting, Setup/Tool-change, Idle (waiting for parts), and Fault. From shift data, you can estimate transition probabilities between these states. The steady-state distribution tells you the long-run fraction of time in each state — and therefore machine **availability** (fraction of time Cutting). Availability = $q_{\text{Cutting}}$ where $\mathbf{q}$ is the steady-state distribution. If the fault-recovery probability is low, availability can be optimized by improving it — eigenvalue analysis shows exactly how much the steady state shifts per unit improvement. **Formal definition.** A matrix $P$ is **column-stochastic** if all entries are non-negative and each column sums to 1: $P_{ij} \geq 0$ for all $i,j$, and $\mathbf{1}^\top P = \mathbf{1}^\top$. A probability vector $\mathbf{x}$ satisfies $x_i \geq 0$ and $\sum x_i = 1$. Stochastic matrices preserve probability vectors: if $\mathbf{x}$ is a probability vector, so is $P\mathbf{x}$. **Existence of eigenvalue 1.** Since $P^\top \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$ (row sums of $P^\top$ = column sums of $P = 1$), $\mathbf{1}$ is an eigenvector of $P^\top$ for $\lambda = 1$. Since $P$ and $P^\top$ have the same characteristic polynomial, $\lambda = 1$ is also an eigenvalue of $P$. The corresponding left eigenvector is $\mathbf{1}^\top$. **Convergence.** Expand $\mathbf{x}_0$ in the eigenbasis of $P$: $\mathbf{x}_0 = c_1 \mathbf{q} + \sum_{k \geq 2} c_k \mathbf{v}_k$. Then $P^n \mathbf{x}_0 = c_1 \mathbf{q} + \sum_{k \geq 2} c_k \lambda_k^n \mathbf{v}_k$. If $|\lambda_k| < 1$ for all $k \geq 2$, the sum vanishes and $P^n \mathbf{x}_0 \to c_1 \mathbf{q}$. Since both $\mathbf{x}_0$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are probability vectors, $c_1 = 1$ and $P^n \mathbf{x}_0 \to \mathbf{q}$. **Ergodicity.** A Markov chain is **ergodic** if it is irreducible (any state can be reached from any other) and aperiodic (no periodic cycles). Ergodic chains are exactly those with a unique steady-state distribution independent of the starting point. Column-stochastic matrices with all positive entries are always ergodic. **Mixing time.** The number of steps needed to get within $\epsilon$ of the steady state (in total variation distance) is the **mixing time**. It is determined by the spectral gap: mixing time $\approx 1/(1 - |\lambda_2|)$. Slow mixing in Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms is a major computational bottleneck in Bayesian statistics. A spectral gap close to 0 means the second eigenvalue is close to 1, meaning the chain takes many steps to "forget" its starting state. **Detailed balance (reversibility).** A Markov chain satisfies **detailed balance** with respect to distribution $\pi$ if $\pi_i P_{ji} = \pi_j P_{ij}$ for all $i, j$. This says the probability flux from $i$ to $j$ equals the flux from $j$ to $i$ at stationarity. Detailed balance is a sufficient (but not necessary) condition for $\pi$ to be the stationary distribution. Reversible chains are especially amenable to analysis and appear in physics as equilibrium systems. **Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).** The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm constructs a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is any target distribution $\pi$ — even one you can only evaluate point-wise (such as a Bayesian posterior proportional to likelihood × prior). The chain is designed so detailed balance holds with respect to $\pi$. Running the chain long enough produces samples approximately drawn from $\pi$. Convergence is governed by the spectral gap of the chain — which is why MCMC diagnostics check whether the chain has "mixed": whether it has effectively forgotten its starting state. This connection between Markov theory and Bayesian computation is one of the most important bridges between linear algebra and modern statistics. Left vs Right Eigenvectors Column-stochastic: $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$ — the steady state is a **right eigenvector**.
Row-stochastic ($P^\top$ convention): steady state satisfies $\mathbf{q}^\top P = \mathbf{q}^\top$ — it is a **left eigenvector**.

Both conventions appear in the literature. The left-eigenvector convention arises when the state vector is a row vector. This course uses column-stochastic (state vector = column, matrix acts on the left). Perron Root Bounds For any column-stochastic matrix $P$:

$\min_j \sum_i P_{ij} \leq \rho(P) \leq \max_j \sum_i P_{ij}$

where $\rho(P)$ is the spectral radius (largest $|\lambda|$). Since all column sums equal 1, the spectral radius equals exactly 1: $\rho(P) = 1$.

Corollary: $|\lambda| \leq 1$ for all eigenvalues of $P$. Reducible vs Irreducible Chains A chain is **reducible** if states can be partitioned into two groups with no transitions from one to the other. Reducible chains can have multiple steady-state distributions — the result depends on which subset of states you start in.

Irreducible chains (all states communicate) + aperiodic → unique steady state. Aperiodic means: no state is visited with a fixed period $> 1$. Adding self-loops guarantees aperiodicity. Lesson 5 of 7 — Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors **Previous (Lesson 4):** Jordan Normal Form — handling non-diagonalizable matrices.
**This lesson:** Markov Chains — stochastic matrices, eigenvalue 1, steady-state distributions, and the Perron-Frobenius theorem.
**Next (Lesson 6):** Cayley-Hamilton Theorem — every matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Procedure: Find the Steady-State Distribution Step 1. **Verify stochastic.** Confirm that each column of $P$ sums to 1 and all entries are non-negative.

Step 2. **Set up the eigenvector equation.** Form $A = P - I$. The steady state $\mathbf{q}$ satisfies $A\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ (null space of $P - I$).

Step 3. **Solve the null space.** Row-reduce $[A | \mathbf{0}]$ to find the free variable and the general solution.

Step 4. **Normalize.** Divide the null-space vector by the sum of its entries so all components sum to 1. This makes $\mathbf{q}$ a valid probability distribution.

Step 5. **Sanity-check.** Verify $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$ and $\sum_i q_i = 1$. Also confirm $q_i \geq 0$ — if any entry is negative, check your null-space computation. The Perron-Frobenius Theorem (Informal) For a regular stochastic matrix (all entries positive, or some power has all positive entries), there is exactly one steady-state distribution, and it is the unique normalized eigenvector for $\lambda = 1$. Starting from ANY initial distribution, $P^k \mathbf{x}_0 \to \mathbf{q}$ as $k \to \infty$. The starting point does not matter — you always end up at $\mathbf{q}$. All Other Eigenvalues Satisfy $|\lambda| \leq 1$ For a column-stochastic matrix, all eigenvalues satisfy $|\lambda| \leq 1$. If $|\lambda_2| < 1$ (the second-largest eigenvalue in magnitude), then the contribution of $\lambda_2^k \mathbf{v}_2$ to $P^k \mathbf{x}_0$ shrinks exponentially. The gap $1 - |\lambda_2|$ is the **spectral gap** — larger gap means faster convergence to steady state. PageRank in One Paragraph Model the web as $n$ pages and a transition matrix $P$ where $P_{ij} = $ (probability surfer clicks link from page $j$ to page $i$). Add a "teleportation" probability $\alpha$ to handle pages with no outlinks: $\hat{P} = (1-\alpha)P + \alpha \frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top}{n}$. The PageRank vector is the steady-state distribution $\hat{P}\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$. Pages with high $q_i$ are authoritative. Perron-Frobenius (Matrix Form) If $P$ is a column-stochastic matrix with all positive entries, then:
1. $\lambda = 1$ is a simple eigenvalue (multiplicity 1)
2. All other eigenvalues satisfy $|\lambda| < 1$
3. There is a unique steady-state distribution $\mathbf{q} > 0$
4. For any probability vector $\mathbf{x}_0$: $P^n \mathbf{x}_0 \to \mathbf{q}$ Convergence Proof Sketch Expand $\mathbf{x}_0$ in the eigenbasis of $P$: $\mathbf{x}_0 = c_1 \mathbf{q} + \sum_{k\geq 2} c_k \mathbf{v}_k$

Then: $P^n \mathbf{x}_0 = c_1 \mathbf{q} + \sum_{k \geq 2} c_k \lambda_k^n \mathbf{v}_k$

Since $|\lambda_k| < 1$ for $k \geq 2$, the sum $\to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. Since $\mathbf{x}_0$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are both probability vectors, $c_1 = 1$ and $P^n \mathbf{x}_0 \to \mathbf{q}$. Finding the Steady State The steady state $\mathbf{q}$ satisfies $P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}$, i.e., $(P - I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ with $\sum_i q_i = 1$.

**Algorithm:**
1. Form $A = P - I$
2. Solve $A\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ (find null space)
3. Normalize: divide by $\sum_i q_i$

In MATLAB: `[V,D] = eig(P)` → column of $V$ corresponding to eigenvalue 1. Markov Chain Simulation Any starting distribution converges to the same steady-state eigenvector. Code: Markov Chains, Steady State, and CNC Machine Availability Three cells: finding steady state, simulating convergence, and CNC machine availability analysis. Two-state weather chain — finding the steady state The transition matrix $P = \begin{bmatrix}0.9 & 0.4\\ 0.1 & 0.6\end{bmatrix}$ models Sunny (col/row 1) and Rainy (col/row 2). Column convention: column $j$ = probabilities of leaving state $j$. Find the long-run fraction of sunny days. Steady state: 80% sunny, 20% rainy. This is the long-run distribution regardless of whether today is sunny or rainy. P - I = \begin{bmatrix}0.9-1 & 0.4\\0.1 & 0.6-1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-0.1 & 0.4\\0.1 & -0.4\end{bmatrix} Form $P - I$. Since $\lambda = 1$ is an eigenvalue, this matrix is singular (both rows are multiples of each other — check: row 2 = $-$row 1). \text{Row 1: } -0.1 q_1 + 0.4 q_2 = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad q_1 = 4 q_2 Solve the null space equation. q_1 + q_2 = 1, \quad q_1 = 4q_2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad 4q_2 + q_2 = 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad q_2 = 0.2, \; q_1 = 0.8 Apply the normalization constraint. PageRank on a 3-page web Three web pages: A links to B and C; B links to C only; C links to A only. Build the column-stochastic transition matrix and find the PageRank. PageRank: A = 40%, B = 20%, C = 40%. Despite B only linking to C, A and C share equal rank because of the cycle. B is lowest because it has only one inlink (from A with weight 1/2). P = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1/2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1/2 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} Column $j$ = outlink distribution from page $j$. Page A has 2 outlinks so $P_{BA} = P_{CA} = 1/2$. Page B has 1 outlink so $P_{CB} = 1$. Page C has 1 outlink so $P_{AC} = 1$. (P - I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}: \quad -q_A + q_C = 0, \quad \frac{1}{2}q_A - q_B = 0, \quad \frac{1}{2}q_A + q_B - q_C = 0 Three equations from $(P - I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$. q_A = q_C \quad (\text{from eq 1}), \quad q_B = \frac{1}{2}q_A \quad (\text{from eq 2}) Solve in terms of $q_A$. q_A + \frac{1}{2}q_A + q_A = 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad q_A = \frac{2}{5}, \quad q_B = \frac{1}{5}, \quad q_C = \frac{2}{5} Normalize. Pages A and C are equally ranked; B has half their rank. Convergence Rate via the Second Eigenvalue For $P = \begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.4\\0.2&0.6\end{bmatrix}$, find both eigenvalues and determine how many steps are needed to be within 1% of the steady state starting from $\mathbf{x}_0 = [1,0]^\top$. With $\lambda_2 = 0.4$ (spectral gap $= 0.6$), this chain converges quickly: within 6 steps. The spectral gap $1 - |\lambda_2|$ directly controls convergence rate. Large gap → fast convergence to steady state. \det(P - \lambda I) = (0.8-\lambda)(0.6-\lambda) - 0.08 = \lambda^2 - 1.4\lambda + 0.4 = 0 Characteristic equation. Products: $(0.8)(0.6) = 0.48$ and $(0.4)(0.2) = 0.08$, so constant term = $0.48 - 0.08 = 0.40$. \lambda = \frac{1.4 \pm \sqrt{1.96 - 1.6}}{2} = \frac{1.4 \pm 0.6}{2} \implies \lambda_1 = 1, \; \lambda_2 = 0.4 Two eigenvalues: 1 (steady state) and 0.4 (convergence rate). |\lambda_2^k| < 0.01 \implies |0.4|^k < 0.01 \implies k > \ln(0.01)/\ln(0.4) \approx 4.6/0.916 \approx 5.0 After $k$ steps, the error is proportional to $|\lambda_2|^k = 0.4^k$. For error $< 1\%$: $k > 5$. A two-state machine is either Working (W) or Broken (B). Each hour, a working machine breaks with probability 0.05. A broken machine is fixed with probability 0.3. Write the $2\times 2$ column-stochastic transition matrix and find the steady-state availability. Column W: prob(stay W) = 0.95, prob(go to B) = 0.05. Column B: prob(get fixed) = 0.3, prob(stay B) = 0.7. P = [[0.95, 0.3],[0.05, 0.7]]. Steady state: W = 6/7 â‰ˆ 85.7%, B = 1/7 â‰ˆ 14.3%. P = \begin{bmatrix}0.95 & 0.3 \\ 0.05 & 0.7\end{bmatrix} Column W: [0.95, 0.05] (95% stay working, 5% break). Column B: [0.3, 0.7] (30% fixed, 70% stay broken). (P - I)\mathbf{q} = 0: \quad -0.05 q_W + 0.3 q_B = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad q_W = 6 q_B Solve the null-space equation. q_W + q_B = 1, \quad q_W = 6q_B \quad \Rightarrow \quad q_B = 1/7 \approx 0.143, \; q_W = 6/7 \approx 0.857 Machine is working 85.7% of the time in the long run. Design a $2 \times 2$ column-stochastic matrix $P$ with steady-state distribution $\mathbf{q} = [0.6, 0.4]^\top$ and second eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = 0.3$. Use the fact that eigenvalues of a 2×2 stochastic matrix are $\lambda_1 = 1$ and $\lambda_2 = \text{tr}(P) - 1$. So $\text{tr}(P) = 1.3$. Also use the steady-state equation to relate the off-diagonal entries. With $\mathbf{q}=[0.6,0.4]^T$ and $\lambda_2=0.3$: steady-state equation gives $p_{12}=0.4 p_{21}/0.6$ and trace constraint $p_{11}+p_{22}=1.3$. One valid solution: $P=\begin{bmatrix}0.7+0.3t & 0.4(1-t)/0.6 \\ \cdots\end{bmatrix}$ for appropriate $t$. The constraints are consistent and the problem has a 1-parameter family of solutions. \text{tr}(P) = 1 + \lambda_2 = 1 + 0.3 = 1.3 \quad \Rightarrow \quad p_{11} + p_{22} = 1.3 For a $2\times 2$ stochastic matrix with eigenvalues 1 and $\lambda_2$, trace = sum of eigenvalues = $1 + \lambda_2$. P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}: \quad p_{11}(0.6) + p_{12}(0.4) = 0.6 \quad \text{and} \quad p_{22} = 1 - p_{12} Stochastic: $p_{21} = 1 - p_{11}$ and $p_{12} = 1 - p_{22}$. The steady-state equation for row 1 gives a relationship between $p_{11}$ and $p_{12}$. p_{11} = 0.6 + 0.3 = 0.9, \quad p_{22} = 0.4 \quad \Rightarrow \quad P = \begin{bmatrix}0.9 & 0.15 \\ 0.1 & 0.85\end{bmatrix} Wait — check: $p_{11} + p_{22} = 0.9 + 0.85 = 1.75 \neq 1.3$. Correct approach: $p_{22} = 1.3 - p_{11}$; use steady-state equation to pin $p_{11}$. $p_{11}(0.6) + (1-p_{22})(0.4) = 0.6$ → $p_{11}(0.6) + (1 - (1.3-p_{11}))(0.4) = 0.6$ → $p_{11}(0.6) + (p_{11} - 0.3)(0.4) = 0.6$ → $p_{11} = 0.6/0.8 \cdot$ ... solve to get $p_{11} = 0.7, p_{22} = 0.6$. Then $P = \begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.2\\0.3&0.8\end{bmatrix}$. Verify: $0.7(0.6)+0.2(0.4) = 0.42+0.08 = 0.5 \neq 0.6$. P = \begin{bmatrix}1 - p_{12} & p_{12} \\ p_{12} & 1-p_{12}\end{bmatrix}\text{ fails} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{Use }P = \begin{bmatrix}0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7\end{bmatrix} Verify: steady state of this $P$? $(P-I)\mathbf{q}=0$: $-0.2q_1+0.3q_2=0 \Rightarrow q_1=1.5q_2$. Normalize: $q_1=0.6, q_2=0.4$ ✓. Eigenvalues: trace$=1.5$, det$=0.56-0.06=0.50$. Char poly: $\lambda^2-1.5\lambda+0.5=0 \Rightarrow (\lambda-1)(\lambda-0.5)=0$. $\lambda_2=0.5 \neq 0.3$. Targeting $\lambda_2=0.3$ requires trace = 1.3: $P=\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.5\\0.3&0.6\end{bmatrix}$ gives steady state check $-0.3q_1+0.5q_2=0 \Rightarrow q_1=(5/3)q_2$. Normalize: $q_1=5/8, q_2=3/8 \neq [0.6,0.4]$. The two constraints (steady state and spectral gap) together pin both off-diagonal entries. For the weather chain $P = \begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.4\\0.1&0.6\end{bmatrix}$, find both eigenvalues. The second eigenvalue $|\lambda_2|$ determines the convergence rate. Estimate how many steps it takes for any initial distribution to be within 0.01 of the steady state. Find eigenvalues from trace = 1.5, det = 0.54. Then convergence: $|\lambda_2|^k < 0.01$. λ₁ = 0.5. About 7 steps to reach within 0.01 of steady state. Spectral gap = 0.5. \text{tr}(P) = 1.5, \; \det(P) = 0.9(0.6)-0.4(0.1) = 0.54 - 0.04 = 0.5 Characteristic polynomial: $\lambda^2 - 1.5\lambda + 0.5 = 0$. \lambda = \frac{1.5 \pm \sqrt{2.25 - 2}}{2} = \frac{1.5 \pm 0.5}{2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \lambda_1 = 1, \; \lambda_2 = 0.5 Two eigenvalues: 1 (steady state) and 0.5 (convergence rate). 0.5^k < 0.01 \quad \Rightarrow \quad k > \frac{\ln 0.01}{\ln 0.5} = \frac{-4.605}{-0.693} \approx 6.64 \quad \Rightarrow \quad k \geq 7 After 7 steps, the error is below 0.01. Spectral gap = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5 (relatively fast mixing). assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step vector-valued velocity acceleration trajectory

documents.assignment: Verify Cayley-Hamilton for a 2×2 matrix For $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{bmatrix}$, verify that $p(A) = 0$ where $p$ is the characteristic polynomial.   $p(A) = A^2 - 5A + I = 0$ ✓. Rearranging: $A^2 = 5A - I$. This means any higher power of $A$ can be written in terms of $\{I, A\}$ alone. p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - \text{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A) = \lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 1 Characteristic polynomial. trace $= 2+3 = 5$. det $= 2\cdot 3 - 1\cdot 5 = 1$. A^2 = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{bmatrix}^2 = \begin{bmatrix}9&5\\25&14\end{bmatrix} Compute $A^2$ by matrix multiplication. p(A) = A^2 - 5A + I = \begin{bmatrix}9&5\\25&14\end{bmatrix} - 5\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}9-10+1 & 5-5+0 \\ 25-25+0 & 14-15+1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix} Substitute. Every entry is exactly 0. ✓ Finding A⁻¹ via Cayley-Hamilton Use Cayley-Hamilton to find $A^{-1}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix}3&1\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$ without row reduction.   Cayley-Hamilton gives a one-formula shortcut for the inverse: $A^{-1} = (\text{tr}(A)I - A)/\det(A)$ for any invertible $2\times 2$ matrix. p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 trace $= 7$, det $= 12 - 2 = 10$. p(A) = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad A^2 - 7A + 10I = 0 Apply Cayley-Hamilton. A^2 - 7A + 10I = 0 \quad \xrightarrow{\times A^{-1}} \quad A - 7I + 10A^{-1} = 0 Multiply both sides by $A^{-1}$ (valid since det $\neq 0$). A^{-1} = \frac{7I - A}{10} = \frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix} Solve for $A^{-1}$. This matches the standard formula $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det(A)}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}$. Minimal polynomial strictly less than characteristic polynomial For $A = \begin{bmatrix}3&0&0\\0&3&0\\0&0&2\end{bmatrix}$, find the characteristic polynomial, then find the minimal polynomial and verify $m(A) = 0$.   The minimal polynomial $(\lambda-3)(\lambda-2)$ has degree 2, while the characteristic polynomial has degree 3. Cayley-Hamilton still holds (both annihilate $A$), but the minimal polynomial is the smallest one that does. Rule: for diagonal matrices, each distinct eigenvalue appears exactly once in $m(\lambda)$. p(\lambda) = (\lambda-3)^2(\lambda-2) = \lambda^3 - 8\lambda^2 + 21\lambda - 18 $A$ is diagonal, so eigenvalues are 3 (multiplicity 2) and 2 (multiplicity 1). m(\lambda) = (\lambda-3)(\lambda-2) = \lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 6 Since $A$ is diagonal (diagonalizable), the minimal polynomial has each distinct eigenvalue appearing exactly once — no repeated roots needed. m(A) = A^2 - 5A + 6I = \begin{bmatrix}9&0&0\\0&9&0\\0&0&4\end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix}15&0&0\\0&15&0\\0&0&10\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}6&0&0\\0&6&0\\0&0&6\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix} Diagonal: $9-15+6=0$ ✓, $9-15+6=0$ ✓, $4-10+6=0$ ✓.  For $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$, find the characteristic polynomial and verify $p(A) = 0$ directly. trace = 3, det = 2. So p(λ) = λ² - 3λ + 2. Compute A² - 3A + 2I. p(λ) = λ² - 3λ + 2. A² - 3A + 2I = [[0,0],[0,0]] ✓  p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 3\lambda + 2 trace = 3, det = 2. A^2 = \begin{bmatrix}1&3\\0&4\end{bmatrix} \qquad A^2 - 3A + 2I = \begin{bmatrix}1-3+2 & 3-3+0 \\ 0-0+0 & 4-6+2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix} Verified. ✓  For $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&4\end{bmatrix}$, use Cayley-Hamilton to express $A^3$ as a linear combination of $I$ and $A$. Find p(λ), use C-H to get A² = 6A - 5I. Then compute A³ = A·A² = A(6A-5I) = 6A² - 5A. A³ = 31A - 30I. Verify: A³ = [[8+3, 6+12],[2+4, 3+16]] = [[11,18],[6,19]] and 31[[2,3],[1,4]] - 30I = [[62-30,93],[31,124-30]] = [[32,93],[31,94]]... compute numerically to confirm.  p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 5 = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad A^2 = 6A - 5I trace = 6, det = 5. A^3 = A \cdot A^2 = A(6A - 5I) = 6A^2 - 5A = 6(6A-5I) - 5A = 36A - 30I - 5A = 31A - 30I Substitute $A^2 = 6A-5I$ again.  For $A = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}$ (90° rotation matrix), find the minimal polynomial. Then verify that $A^4 = I$ using only the Cayley-Hamilton identity, without computing $A^4$ directly by multiplication. Char poly: trace = 0, det = 1, so $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 + 1$. Therefore $A^2 = -I$. Use this to find $A^4$. Minimal polynomial: $\lambda^2 + 1$. $A^4 = I$ follows from $A^2 = -I$ via $(A^2)^2 = (-I)^2 = I$.  p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - \text{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A) = \lambda^2 + 1 trace = 0, det = 0·0 - 1·(-1) = 1. p(A) = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad A^2 + I = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad A^2 = -I Cayley-Hamilton. Note: $A^2 = -I$ means two 90° rotations = 180° rotation = negation. ✓ A^4 = (A^2)^2 = (-I)^2 = I Four 90° rotations = 360° = identity. ✓ No matrix multiplication required — only scalar reasoning about $A^2 = -I$. m(\lambda) = p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 + 1 Minimal polynomial equals the characteristic polynomial here. Check: is there a degree-1 annihilator? That would require $A = cI$ for some scalar $c$, but $A = [[0,1],[-1,0]] \neq cI$. So $m = p$.

**Proof via the adjugate.** The rigorous proof uses the **adjugate matrix** (matrix of cofactors). Since $(A - \lambda I)\text{adj}(A - \lambda I) = \det(A - \lambda I) I = p(\lambda) I$, write $\text{adj}(A - \lambda I) = B_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1} + \cdots + B_0$ (each $B_k$ is an $n\times n$ matrix with polynomial entries). Collect powers of $\lambda$ from both sides of $(A - \lambda I)(B_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1} + \cdots + B_0) = (c_n \lambda^n + \cdots + c_0) I$ and identify the matrix coefficient of each power. This gives $n+1$ matrix equations; summing them correctly (each multiplied by the appropriate power of $A$) yields $p(A) = 0$. **Over commutative rings.** The Cayley-Hamilton theorem holds for any $n \times n$ matrix over a commutative ring $R$ (not just fields). The adjugate proof carries through unchanged since it only uses the commutativity of $R$. This makes the theorem valid over $\mathbb{Z}$, polynomial rings $\mathbb{Z}[x]$, and more, which is important in algebraic K-theory and number theory. **Relationship between minimal and characteristic polynomials.** The minimal polynomial $m(\lambda)$ divides the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$, and they have the same set of distinct roots. The exact divisibility structure encodes the Jordan block sizes: if $\lambda_0$ has largest Jordan block of size $k$, then $(\lambda - \lambda_0)^k | m(\lambda)$ but $(\lambda - \lambda_0)^{k+1} \nmid m(\lambda)$. The characteristic polynomial has $(\lambda - \lambda_0)^{m_a(\lambda_0)}$ (the full algebraic multiplicity). **Hamiltonian systems and symplectic matrices.** In classical mechanics, the time-evolution of a Hamiltonian system is described by a symplectic matrix $M$ satisfying $M^\top J M = J$ where $J = \begin{bmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{bmatrix}$ is the standard symplectic form. Cayley-Hamilton applied to symplectic matrices reveals that their characteristic polynomial is palindromic: if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue, so is $1/\lambda$. This symmetry has deep consequences — it forces all eigenvalues to come in reciprocal pairs, constraining the long-term stability of Hamiltonian dynamics. In control theory, the analogous result for Riccati equations guarantees that optimal control gains can be found from the stable half of the spectrum of the Hamiltonian matrix. Outline: Adjugate Proof 1. Write $\text{adj}(A-\lambda I) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} B_k \lambda^k$ (matrix coefficients $B_k$)

The characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I)$ is a polynomial in the scalar $\lambda$. What happens if you replace $\lambda$ with the matrix $A$ itself? You get the zero matrix — every single time. The Cayley-Hamilton theorem has a surprisingly practical consequence: it gives you an efficient way to compute high powers of matrices and to find matrix inverses without computing determinants. In control theory, it is used to prove that any polynomial in a matrix can be reduced to degree $\leq n-1$. In signal processing, it bounds the order of recurrence relations. In robotics, it simplifies the computation of matrix exponentials used in joint kinematics. Wherever you need to evaluate a function of a matrix, Cayley-Hamilton is in the background. **A strange idea: plug a matrix into a polynomial.** The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is $p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I)$ — a polynomial in a scalar variable $\lambda$. Normally you evaluate $p$ at a number to find eigenvalues. But what happens if you replace $\lambda$ with the matrix $A$ itself? This sounds absurd — the polynomial was built from $A$ in the first place. Yet every time you do it, you get the zero matrix. That is the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, and it is far from obvious. **Verify the claim on a $2 \times 2$.** Let $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{bmatrix}$. Trace $= 5$, det $= 1$, so $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 1$. Now compute $p(A) = A^2 - 5A + I$. First, $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix}9&5\\25&14\end{bmatrix}$. Then $5A = \begin{bmatrix}10&5\\25&15\end{bmatrix}$. Subtract: $A^2 - 5A = \begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix} = -I$. Add $I$: result is $\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$. The matrix zeroes out its own characteristic polynomial. **Application 1: computing the inverse symbolically.** From $A^2 - 5A + I = 0$, multiply both sides by $A^{-1}$: $A - 5I + A^{-1} = 0$, so $A^{-1} = 5I - A = \begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\-5&2\end{bmatrix}$. No row reduction, no formula lookup — Cayley-Hamilton gives the inverse directly from the characteristic polynomial. This works whenever det$(A) \neq 0$ (so that $c_0 = \det(A)$ in the characteristic polynomial is nonzero). **Application 2: reducing high powers.** From $A^2 = 5A - I$, compute $A^3 = A \cdot A^2 = A(5A - I) = 5A^2 - A = 5(5A - I) - A = 24A - 5I$. Every higher power follows the same pattern: $A^k$ is always a linear combination $\alpha_k A + \beta_k I$ for some scalars $\alpha_k, \beta_k$. The characteristic polynomial acts as a recurrence relation for the coefficients. For an $n \times n$ matrix, any $A^k$ reduces to a linear combination of $I, A, A^2, \ldots, A^{n-1}$. **Minimal polynomial.** The minimal polynomial $m(\lambda)$ is the monic polynomial of smallest degree that annihilates $A$: $m(A) = 0$. The characteristic polynomial is always an annihilating polynomial, but it may not be the smallest. For a diagonalizable matrix with distinct eigenvalues, $m = p$. For the identity matrix $I_n$, $p(\lambda) = (\lambda - 1)^n$ but $m(\lambda) = \lambda - 1$ (since $I - I = 0$). The minimal polynomial divides the characteristic polynomial. **Predict before reading on.** For $B = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$, trace $= 4$, det $= 3$, so $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3$. Before computing: what is $B^2 - 4B + 3I$? And what is $B^{-1}$ using Cayley-Hamilton? Write your predictions, then verify by computing $B^2 = \begin{bmatrix}1&8\\0&9\end{bmatrix}$ and checking. **CNC robot kinematics — Rodrigues' formula.** In 5-axis CNC and robotic arms, every joint rotation is a $3 \times 3$ rotation matrix $R$. To compute the path of the tool, you need $e^{\hat{\omega}t}$ where $\hat{\omega}$ is the skew-symmetric angular velocity matrix. Cayley-Hamilton says $\hat{\omega}^3 = -\|\omega\|^2 \hat{\omega}$ for any skew-symmetric matrix, so $e^{\hat{\omega}t} = I + \sin(t)\hat{\omega} + (1 - \cos t)\hat{\omega}^2$. This is Rodrigues' rotation formula — and it comes directly from Cayley-Hamilton. CNC controllers compute this 50—200 times per second for every joint. **Where this is heading.** Cayley-Hamilton is the bridge from eigenvalues to functions of matrices. If you know $p(A) = 0$ and $p$ factors as $(\lambda - \lambda_1)\cdots(\lambda - \lambda_n)$, then the matrix exponential $e^{At}$ reduces to a sum involving $e^{\lambda_i t}$ times low-degree matrix polynomials — that is the next lesson, Matrix Exponential. Understanding Cayley-Hamilton also unlocks the theory of linear recurrences: any sequence satisfying a linear recurrence is secretly computing powers of a companion matrix. **Proof sketch (via Jordan form).** Over $\mathbb{C}$, every $A$ is similar to its Jordan form $J$: $A = SJS^{-1}$. Then $p(A) = Sp(J)S^{-1}$. The characteristic polynomial factors as $p(\lambda) = \prod_i (\lambda - \lambda_i)^{m_i}$. For a Jordan block $J_k(\lambda_0)$, we have $(J_k(\lambda_0) - \lambda_0 I)^k = 0$ (the nilpotent part raised to its degree). Since $p(\lambda) = (\lambda - \lambda_0)^{m_0} \cdot q(\lambda)$ where $m_0 \geq k$, $p(J_k(\lambda_0)) = 0$. Block-diagonal application completes the proof. **Minimal polynomial.** Define $m(\lambda)$ as the monic polynomial of least degree with $m(A) = 0$. It divides the characteristic polynomial: $p(\lambda) = m(\lambda) \cdot q(\lambda)$ for some polynomial $q$. The minimal polynomial has the same roots as the characteristic polynomial (just possibly smaller multiplicities). For a diagonalizable matrix, $m(\lambda) = \prod_i (\lambda - \lambda_i)$ (all roots simple). For $J_k(\lambda_0)$ (a single Jordan block), $m(\lambda) = (\lambda - \lambda_0)^k$. **Proof via the adjugate.** The rigorous proof uses the **adjugate matrix** (matrix of cofactors). Since $(A - \lambda I)\text{adj}(A - \lambda I) = \det(A - \lambda I) I = p(\lambda) I$, write $\text{adj}(A - \lambda I) = B_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1} + \cdots + B_0$ (each $B_k$ is an $n\times n$ matrix with polynomial entries). Collect powers of $\lambda$ from both sides of $(A - \lambda I)(B_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1} + \cdots + B_0) = (c_n \lambda^n + \cdots + c_0) I$ and identify the matrix coefficient of each power. This gives $n+1$ matrix equations; summing them correctly (each multiplied by the appropriate power of $A$) yields $p(A) = 0$. **Over commutative rings.** The Cayley-Hamilton theorem holds for any $n \times n$ matrix over a commutative ring $R$ (not just fields). The adjugate proof carries through unchanged since it only uses the commutativity of $R$. This makes the theorem valid over $\mathbb{Z}$, polynomial rings $\mathbb{Z}[x]$, and more, which is important in algebraic K-theory and number theory. **Relationship between minimal and characteristic polynomials.** The minimal polynomial $m(\lambda)$ divides the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$, and they have the same set of distinct roots. The exact divisibility structure encodes the Jordan block sizes: if $\lambda_0$ has largest Jordan block of size $k$, then $(\lambda - \lambda_0)^k | m(\lambda)$ but $(\lambda - \lambda_0)^{k+1} \nmid m(\lambda)$. The characteristic polynomial has $(\lambda - \lambda_0)^{m_a(\lambda_0)}$ (the full algebraic multiplicity). **Hamiltonian systems and symplectic matrices.** In classical mechanics, the time-evolution of a Hamiltonian system is described by a symplectic matrix $M$ satisfying $M^\top J M = J$ where $J = \begin{bmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{bmatrix}$ is the standard symplectic form. Cayley-Hamilton applied to symplectic matrices reveals that their characteristic polynomial is palindromic: if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue, so is $1/\lambda$. This symmetry has deep consequences — it forces all eigenvalues to come in reciprocal pairs, constraining the long-term stability of Hamiltonian dynamics. In control theory, the analogous result for Riccati equations guarantees that optimal control gains can be found from the stable half of the spectrum of the Hamiltonian matrix. Outline: Adjugate Proof 1. Write $\text{adj}(A-\lambda I) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} B_k \lambda^k$ (matrix coefficients $B_k$)

2. Use $(A-\lambda I)\text{adj}(A-\lambda I) = p(\lambda)I$ and expand both sides

3. Match coefficients of $\lambda^k$ for $k = 0, 1, \ldots, n$: get $n+1$ matrix equations

4. Left-multiply equation $k$ by $A^k$, sum all $n+1$ equations — a telescoping collapse gives $p(A) = 0$ $\blacksquare$ Span of Matrix Powers By Cayley-Hamilton, $A^n = -c_{n-1}A^{n-1} - \cdots - c_0 I$. So every $A^k$ for $k \geq n$ is a linear combination of $\{I, A, \ldots, A^{n-1}\}$.

Consequence: the subalgebra generated by $A$ has dimension $\leq n$. The exact dimension equals the degree of the **minimal polynomial** of $A$. Cayley-Hamilton in Control Theory A discrete-time system $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A\mathbf{x}_k$ is **completely reachable** (can reach any state from any other) if and only if the controllability matrix $\mathcal{C} = [B, AB, A^2B, \ldots, A^{n-1}B]$ has full rank.

By Cayley-Hamilton, $A^n B$ is already a combination of the columns in $\mathcal{C}$, so there is no point looking at higher powers. This is why the controllability matrix only needs $n$ columns. Cayley-Hamilton Theorem Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix and $p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I)$ its characteristic polynomial. Then $p(A) = 0$ (the zero matrix). Computing the Inverse via Cayley-Hamilton If $p(\lambda) = \lambda^n + c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1} + \cdots + c_1 \lambda + c_0$ and $c_0 = (-1)^n \det(A) \neq 0$, then:
$A^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1} + \cdots + c_1 A + c_0 I = 0$
Multiply by $A^{-1}$:
$A^{-1} = -c_0^{-1}(A^{n-1} + c_{n-1}A^{n-2} + \cdots + c_1 I)$ Lesson 6 of 7 — Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors **Previous (Lesson 5):** Markov Chains — eigenvalue 1, steady-state distributions.
**This lesson:** Cayley-Hamilton Theorem — every matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation; using it to compute powers and inverses symbolically.
**Next (Lesson 7):** Matrix Exponential — solving differential equations $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x}$ via $e^{At}$. Procedure: Apply Cayley-Hamilton Step 1. **Find the characteristic polynomial.** For a $2\times 2$ matrix: $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - \text{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A)$. For larger matrices, expand $\det(A - \lambda I)$.

Step 2. **Interpret $p(A)$.** Replace every $\lambda^k$ with $A^k$, and replace every scalar constant $c$ with $cI$. For example, $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 1$ becomes $p(A) = A^2 - 5A + I$.

Step 3. **Verify $p(A) = 0$.** Compute each term and sum — you should get the zero matrix.

Step 4. **Derive consequences.** From $p(A) = 0$:
- Multiply by $A^{-1}$ to get the **inverse**: $A^{-1} = (\text{tr}(A)I - A)/\det(A)$.
- Rearrange to express $A^n$ as a lower-degree combination: e.g., $A^2 = \text{tr}(A)A - \det(A)I$, then use this recurrence for $A^3, A^4, \ldots$ Do Not Prove It by Substitution A common mistake: writing $p(A) = \det(A - A \cdot I) = \det(0) = 0$ and thinking the theorem is obvious. This is wrong — $\det(A - \lambda I)$ is a scalar polynomial, and you cannot just substitute a matrix for the scalar and call it done. The actual proof requires care with polynomial rings and matrix algebra. Cayley-Hamilton via Minimal Polynomial The minimal polynomial $m(\lambda)$ divides the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$. Since $m(A) = 0$, and $p(\lambda) = m(\lambda) q(\lambda)$, we get $p(A) = m(A) q(A) = 0 \cdot q(A) = 0$. The Minimal Polynomial Determines the Jordan Structure The degree of the largest Jordan block for eigenvalue $\lambda_0$ equals the multiplicity of $\lambda_0$ as a root of the minimal polynomial. So the minimal polynomial encodes the Jordan structure more precisely than the characteristic polynomial. Cayley-Hamilton and the Power Basis Any polynomial $f(A)$ in a matrix can be reduced modulo the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$:

$f(A) = r(A)$ where $r$ is the remainder of $f$ divided by $p$ (degree $< n$)

This means $\{I, A, A^2, \ldots, A^{n-1}\}$ spans the entire space of polynomials in $A$. You never need $A^n$ or higher — it is always a linear combination of lower powers. Cayley-Hamilton Verification The matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Code: Cayley-Hamilton Verification, Inverse, and Rodrigues Formula Three cells: verify C-H, compute inverse via polynomial algebra, and apply to 3D rotation via Rodrigues formula. Verify Cayley-Hamilton for a 2×2 matrix For $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{bmatrix}$, verify that $p(A) = 0$ where $p$ is the characteristic polynomial. $p(A) = A^2 - 5A + I = 0$ ✓. Rearranging: $A^2 = 5A - I$. This means any higher power of $A$ can be written in terms of $\{I, A\}$ alone. p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - \text{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A) = \lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 1 Characteristic polynomial. trace $= 2+3 = 5$. det $= 2\cdot 3 - 1\cdot 5 = 1$. A^2 = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{bmatrix}^2 = \begin{bmatrix}9&5\\25&14\end{bmatrix} Compute $A^2$ by matrix multiplication. p(A) = A^2 - 5A + I = \begin{bmatrix}9&5\\25&14\end{bmatrix} - 5\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}9-10+1 & 5-5+0 \\ 25-25+0 & 14-15+1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix} Substitute. Every entry is exactly 0. ✓ Finding A⁻¹ via Cayley-Hamilton Use Cayley-Hamilton to find $A^{-1}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix}3&1\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$ without row reduction. Cayley-Hamilton gives a one-formula shortcut for the inverse: $A^{-1} = (\text{tr}(A)I - A)/\det(A)$ for any invertible $2\times 2$ matrix. p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 trace $= 7$, det $= 12 - 2 = 10$. p(A) = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad A^2 - 7A + 10I = 0 Apply Cayley-Hamilton. A^2 - 7A + 10I = 0 \quad \xrightarrow{\times A^{-1}} \quad A - 7I + 10A^{-1} = 0 Multiply both sides by $A^{-1}$ (valid since det $\neq 0$). A^{-1} = \frac{7I - A}{10} = \frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix} Solve for $A^{-1}$. This matches the standard formula $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det(A)}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}$. Minimal polynomial strictly less than characteristic polynomial For $A = \begin{bmatrix}3&0&0\\0&3&0\\0&0&2\end{bmatrix}$, find the characteristic polynomial, then find the minimal polynomial and verify $m(A) = 0$. The minimal polynomial $(\lambda-3)(\lambda-2)$ has degree 2, while the characteristic polynomial has degree 3. Cayley-Hamilton still holds (both annihilate $A$), but the minimal polynomial is the smallest one that does. Rule: for diagonal matrices, each distinct eigenvalue appears exactly once in $m(\lambda)$. p(\lambda) = (\lambda-3)^2(\lambda-2) = \lambda^3 - 8\lambda^2 + 21\lambda - 18 $A$ is diagonal, so eigenvalues are 3 (multiplicity 2) and 2 (multiplicity 1). m(\lambda) = (\lambda-3)(\lambda-2) = \lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 6 Since $A$ is diagonal (diagonalizable), the minimal polynomial has each distinct eigenvalue appearing exactly once — no repeated roots needed. m(A) = A^2 - 5A + 6I = \begin{bmatrix}9&0&0\\0&9&0\\0&0&4\end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix}15&0&0\\0&15&0\\0&0&10\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}6&0&0\\0&6&0\\0&0&6\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix} Diagonal: $9-15+6=0$ ✓, $9-15+6=0$ ✓, $4-10+6=0$ ✓. For $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$, find the characteristic polynomial and verify $p(A) = 0$ directly. trace = 3, det = 2. So p(λ) = λ² - 3λ + 2. Compute A² - 3A + 2I. p(λ) = λ² - 3λ + 2. A² - 3A + 2I = [[0,0],[0,0]] ✓ p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 3\lambda + 2 trace = 3, det = 2. A^2 = \begin{bmatrix}1&3\\0&4\end{bmatrix} \qquad A^2 - 3A + 2I = \begin{bmatrix}1-3+2 & 3-3+0 \\ 0-0+0 & 4-6+2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix} Verified. ✓ For $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&4\end{bmatrix}$, use Cayley-Hamilton to express $A^3$ as a linear combination of $I$ and $A$. Find p(λ), use C-H to get A² = 6A - 5I. Then compute A³ = A·A² = A(6A-5I) = 6A² - 5A. A³ = 31A - 30I. Then verify that $A^4 = I$ using only the Cayley-Hamilton identity, without computing $A^4$ directly by multiplication. Char poly: trace = 0, det = 1, so $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 + 1$. Therefore $A^2 = -I$. Use this to find $A^4$. documents.assignment: Matrix exponential of a diagonal matrix Compute $e^{At}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix}-2&0\\0&-3\end{bmatrix}$ and classify the stability.   $e^{At} = \text{diag}(e^{-2t}, e^{-3t})$. The system is asymptotically stable — every initial condition decays to zero exponentially. e^{Dt} = \begin{bmatrix}e^{-2t} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} For a diagonal matrix, exponentiate each entry independently: $(e^{Dt})_{ii} = e^{d_{ii} t}$. \text{Eigenvalues: } \lambda_1 = -2, \lambda_2 = -3 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{Re}(\lambda_i) < 0 Both eigenvalues are real and negative. e^{At}\mathbf{x}_0 = \begin{bmatrix}e^{-2t} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_1(0) \\ x_2(0)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}x_1(0)e^{-2t} \\ x_2(0)e^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix} \text{ as } t\to\infty Both components decay exponentially. The second decays faster ($e^{-3t}$ vs $e^{-2t}$). ODE system solution via eigendecomposition Solve $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x}$ with $A = \begin{bmatrix}-1&2\\0&-3\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{x}(0) = [1,\,1]^\top$.   $\mathbf{x}(t) = [2e^{-t} - e^{-3t},\, e^{-3t}]^\top$. The system is stable (both eigenvalues $< 0$). The $e^{-t}$ mode dominates at large $t$ since it decays more slowly. \lambda_1 = -1 \text{ (eigenvec: } \mathbf{v}_1 = [1,0]^\top), \quad \lambda_2 = -3 \text{ (eigenvec: } \mathbf{v}_2 = [1,-1]^\top) Eigenvalues of upper-triangular = diagonal entries. Eigenvectors from $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=0$. \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1 e^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} + c_2 e^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix} General solution: linear combination of modes. \mathbf{x}(0) = c_1\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} + c_2\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix} \quad \Rightarrow \quad c_1 + c_2 = 1, \; -c_2 = 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad c_2 = -1, \; c_1 = 2 Match initial condition to find constants. \mathbf{x}(t) = 2e^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} - e^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2e^{-t} - e^{-3t}\\e^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} Explicit solution. Both components decay. As $t\to\infty$: $x_1 \to 0$, $x_2 \to 0$. Matrix exponential of a Jordan block Compute $e^{At}$ for the Jordan block $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$ and write the ODE solution from $\mathbf{x}_0 = [1,0]^\top$.   $e^{At} = e^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$. **Spectral mapping theorem.** If $A = PDP^{-1}$ (diagonalizable), then $e^A = Pe^D P^{-1}$, and the eigenvalues of $e^A$ are exactly $\{e^\lambda : \lambda \in \text{spec}(A)\}$. More generally, for any analytic function $f$, $f(A)$ has eigenvalues $\{f(\lambda) : \lambda \in \text{spec}(A)\}$. This is the spectral mapping theorem. **Matrix logarithm.** The inverse of the matrix exponential (when it exists) is the matrix logarithm. $\log(e^A) = A$ for matrices near 0. The logarithm exists for all invertible matrices near $I$, but may not be unique (the complex logarithm is multi-valued). Applications: computing rotations in robotics (Lie algebras), interpolating between rotations in animation and computer vision. **Fundamental matrix solutions.** For a system $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x}$, the **fundamental matrix** $\Phi(t) = e^{At}$ satisfies $\dot{\Phi} = A\Phi$ and $\Phi(0) = I$. The general solution is $\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t)\mathbf{x}_0$. For non-autonomous systems $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A(t)\mathbf{x}$, a fundamental matrix still exists but is not simply $e^{\int A\,dt}$ unless $A(t)$ commutes with itself at different times. **Sylvester's formula and functions of matrices.** For a diagonalizable matrix $A$ with distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n$, any analytic function $f(A)$ can be written as $f(A) = \sum_{i=1}^n f(\lambda_i) Z_i$ where $Z_i = \prod_{j \neq i} \frac{A - \lambda_j I}{\lambda_i - \lambda_j}$ are the **spectral projectors** satisfying $Z_i Z_j = 0$ for $i \neq j$ and $\sum Z_i = I$. For the matrix exponential: $e^{At} = \sum_i e^{\lambda_i t} Z_i$. This is Sylvester's formula — it makes the dependence of $e^{At}$ on both the eigenvalues and the initial condition completely explicit, and generalizes to any analytic function: $\sin(A)$, $\log(A)$, $A^{1/2}$, etc. Spectral Mapping Theorem For any analytic function $f$ and matrix $A$:
- If $A = PDP^{-1}$ (diagonalizable), then $f(A) = Pf(D)P^{-1}$
- The eigenvalues of $f(A)$ are $\{f(\lambda) : \lambda \in \sigma(A)\}$

Special cases:
- Eigenvalues of $e^A$: $\{e^\lambda\}$
- Eigenvalues of $A^{-1}$: $\{1/\lambda\}$ (for invertible $A$)
- Eigenvalues of $e^{At}$: $\{e^{\lambda t}\}$ Lie Groups and Lie Algebras The matrix exponential maps the **Lie algebra** (a vector space of matrices, closed under commutator $[A,B] = AB-BA$) to the **Lie group** (a manifold of invertible matrices):

$\mathfrak{so}(3) \xrightarrow{\exp} SO(3)$ (skew-symmetric → rotation matrices)

$\mathfrak{se}(3) \xrightarrow{\exp} SE(3)$ (rigid body motions → transformation matrices)

This is the mathematical foundation of modern robotics and computer graphics. Numerical Computation of e^A The power series $\sum A^k/k!$ is accurate only for small $\|A\|$. MATLAB's `expm` and SciPy's `scipy.linalg.expm` use the **Padé approximant** + **scaling and squaring**:

1. Scale: compute $B = A/2^s$ so $\|B\| \approx 1$
2. Compute $e^B \approx$ Padé approximant (rational function approximation)
3. Square: $e^A = (e^B)^{2^s}$

This is $O(n^3)$ and numerically stable. Never use the raw power series.

In robotics, matrix exponentials compute the position of a robot arm as it sweeps through a rotation. In control theory, $e^{At}$ is the state transition matrix. Understanding this formula unifies ODEs and linear algebra into a single framework. **You already know the scalar case.** If $\dot{x} = ax$, the unique solution satisfying $x(0) = x_0$ is $x(t) = e^{at}x_0$. When $a < 0$ the solution decays; when $a > 0$ it blows up. Now suppose you have a system: $\dot{x}_1 = -2x_1$, $\dot{x}_2 = -3x_2$. In matrix form, $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x}$ with $A = \begin{bmatrix}-2&0\\0&-3\end{bmatrix}$. By analogy, the solution should be $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}_0$ — and it is. The object $e^{At}$ is the **matrix exponential**, defined by the same power series as its scalar cousin: $e^{At} = I + At + \frac{(At)^2}{2!} + \frac{(At)^3}{3!} + \cdots$ **Verify it works on the diagonal case.** For $A = \begin{bmatrix}-2&0\\0&-3\end{bmatrix}$, each power $A^k = \begin{bmatrix}(-2)^k&0\\0&(-3)^k\end{bmatrix}$, so the power series sums to $e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix}e^{-2t}&0\\0&e^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}$. With $\mathbf{x}_0 = [1,1]^\top$, the solution at $t=1$ is $\mathbf{x}(1) = [e^{-2}, e^{-3}]^\top \approx [0.135, 0.050]^\top$. Both components decay because both eigenvalues are negative. Eigenvectors from $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=0$. \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1 e^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} + c_2 e^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix} General solution: linear combination of modes. \mathbf{x}(0) = c_1\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} + c_2\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix} \quad \Rightarrow \quad c_1 + c_2 = 1, \; -c_2 = 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad c_2 = -1, \; c_1 = 2 Match initial condition to find constants. \mathbf{x}(t) = 2e^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} - e^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2e^{-t} - e^{-3t}\\e^{-3t}\end{bmatrix} Explicit solution. Both components decay. As $t\to\infty$: $x_1 \to 0$, $x_2 \to 0$. Matrix exponential of a Jordan block Compute $e^{At}$ for the Jordan block $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$ and write the ODE solution from $\mathbf{x}_0 = [1,0]^\top$. $e^{At} = e^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$. Jordan blocks produce $t^k e^{\lambda t}$ terms in solutions — the off-diagonal $t$ factor is the hallmark of defective (non-diagonalizable) matrices. The system is unstable since $\lambda = 2 > 0$. A = 2I + N, \quad N = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}, \quad N^2 = 0 Decompose: scalar part $\lambda I = 2I$ plus nilpotent $N$. Since $N^2 = 0$, the exponential series for $N$ truncates. e^{At} = e^{(2I+N)t} = e^{2It} \cdot e^{Nt} = e^{2t}I \cdot (I + Nt) = e^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{bmatrix} Since $2I$ and $N$ commute ($2I$ commutes with everything), $e^{(2I+N)t} = e^{2It}e^{Nt}$. Then $e^{Nt} = I + Nt + N^2t^2/2 + \cdots = I + Nt$. \mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}_0 = e^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} = e^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix} For $\mathbf{x}_0 = [1,0]^\top$, the solution is $e^{2t}[1,0]^\top$. The $t \cdot e^{2t}$ term does not appear for this initial condition. For $A = \begin{bmatrix}0&-\omega\\\omega&0\end{bmatrix}$ (pure rotation at rate $\omega$), compute $e^{At}$ and describe the motion. Eigenvalues are $\pm i\omega$. The system neither grows nor decays. Look for sine/cosine in $e^{At}$. e^(At) = rotation matrix by angle ωt. All solutions are circles in phase space — neutrally stable (oscillates forever). \det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 + \omega^2 = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \lambda = \pm i\omega Pure imaginary eigenvalues — neutral stability. e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix}\cos(\omega t) & -\sin(\omega t)\\ \sin(\omega t) & \cos(\omega t)\end{bmatrix} The matrix exponential of a skew-symmetric rotation matrix is a rotation matrix! Euler's formula: $e^{\pm i\omega t} = \cos(\omega t) \pm i\sin(\omega t)$. \mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix}\cos(\omega t) & -\sin(\omega t)\\ \sin(\omega t) & \cos(\omega t)\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}_0 Every solution traces a circle at angular speed $\omega$. The system is neutrally stable: trajectories never decay. Classify stability of the damped harmonic oscillator: $A = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-\omega^2&-2\zeta\omega\end{bmatrix}$ for $\zeta > 0, \omega > 0$. Compute the characteristic polynomial. Use the quadratic formula. What is the real part of the eigenvalues? Asymptotically stable for all ζ > 0, ω > 0. Underdamped (ζ < 1): decaying oscillation. Critically/overdamped (ζ ≥ 1): pure decay without oscillation. p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 + 2\zeta\omega\lambda + \omega^2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \lambda = -\zeta\omega \pm \omega\sqrt{\zeta^2 - 1} Quadratic formula with trace $= -2\zeta\omega$, det $= \omega^2$. \text{Re}(\lambda) = -\zeta\omega < 0 \text{ for all } \zeta > 0 If $\zeta < 1$ (underdamped): complex eigenvalues $-\zeta\omega \pm i\omega\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$ — decaying oscillation. If $\zeta \geq 1$: real negative eigenvalues — pure exponential decay. For the Jordan block $A = \begin{bmatrix}-1&1\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}$, compute $e^{At}$ using the decomposition $A = -I + N$ where $N = [[0,1],[0,0]]$. Then write the ODE solution from $\mathbf{x}_0 = [0,1]^\top$ and identify the $t e^{\lambda t}$ term. Decompose A into scalar and nilpotent parts. Since $-I$ and $N$ commute, $e^{At} = e^{-It} e^{Nt}$. Use $N^2 = 0$ to truncate the series. $e^{At} = e^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$. From $\mathbf{x}_0 = [0,1]^T$: $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{-t}[t, 1]^T$. The $te^{-t}$ term peaks at $t=1$ then decays — stable Jordan mode. A = -I + N, \quad N = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}, \quad N^2 = 0 Decompose: the scalar part $-I$ commutes with everything, enabling $e^{At} = e^{-It} e^{Nt}$. e^{Nt} = I + Nt = \begin{bmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{bmatrix} Since $N^2 = 0$, the series terminates: $e^{Nt} = I + Nt + N^2t^2/2! + \cdots = I + Nt$. e^{At} = e^{-t} \begin{bmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{bmatrix} $e^{-It} = e^{-t}I$ (scalar). Combined: $e^{At} = e^{-t}(I + Nt)$. \mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}_0 = e^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix} = e^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}t\\1\end{bmatrix} $x_1(t) = te^{-t}$ — the classical $te^{\lambda t}$ Jordan term. The system is stable ($\lambda = -1 < 0$) so this decays to 0 despite the polynomial factor. assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step growth decay e^x logarithm ln sequence convergence power series taylor maclaurin vector-valued velocity acceleration trajectory
