A 480V, 60Hz single-phase motor has winding resistance R = 5Ω and winding inductance L = 20mH. What current does it draw? What is the power factor? What is the reactive power demand? How does this change if you add a 200μF power factor correction capacitor in series? Real motor windings are RL circuits. At 60Hz: XL = 2π×60×0.02 = 7.54Ω. Z = √(5² + 7.54²) = 9.05Ω. I = 480/9.05 = 53A. PF = cos(arctan(7.54/5)) = cos(56.5°) = 0.55 lagging. Real power P = 480×53×0.55 = 14kW. Reactive power Q = 480×53×0.835 = 21.2kVAr. Adding 200μF: XC = 13.3Ω. Net X = XL − XC = 7.54 − 13.3 = −5.76Ω (now capacitive — overcorrected). A smaller capacitor (say 100μF, XC = 26.5Ω) brings X = 7.54−26.5 = −19Ω... still overcorrected. For exact unity PF: XC = XL = 7.54Ω → C = 1/(2π×60×7.54) = 352μF. With C=352μF: Z = R = 5Ω. I = 96A. But P = 96²×5 = 46kW — the motor is not drawing 46kW; this analysis is wrong because the motor speed and back-EMF changed. Series PF correction on motors is non-trivial — parallel is standard. **Series voltage divider with phasors.** In a series RLC, each element's voltage is I × Z_element. For R: V_R = I × R (in phase with I). For L: V_L = I × jXL (leads I by 90°). For C: V_C = I × (−jXC) (lags I by 90°). The component voltages are 90° apart from each other and sum by vector addition to give V_s. This is exactly the impedance triangle scaled by I. **Practical measurement: series circuit with motor.** A technician measures V = 480V at the supply and V_R = 266V across a sense resistor (measuring current). V_L = 400V across the motor winding. Phasor KVL: V_source² = V_R² + V_L² only if perfectly inductive. More precisely: V_s = V_R + j×V_L, |V_s| = √(266² + 400²) = 480V ✓. Current = 266/R. This confirms the measurement is consistent — a quick sanity check using phasor math. **Filter design with series RLC.** A series RLC bandpass filter has its output across R. The voltage across R peaks at resonance (Z is minimum, current is maximum, V_R = I × R = (Vs/R) × R = Vs). At frequencies far from resonance, Z increases, current decreases, V_R drops. The bandwidth is determined by Q = XL₀/R = f₀/BW — high Q gives narrow bandwidth. This is how radio tuners select a single station from the entire frequency spectrum. **Voltage phasor diagram in series RLC.** With I = I∠0° as reference phasor:

$$V_R = IR\angle 0° \quad V_L = IX_L\angle +90° \quad V_C = IX_C\angle -90°$$

$$V_s = V_R + j(V_L - V_C) = I(R + jX)$$

$$|V_s| = I\sqrt{R^2 + X^2} = I|Z| \checkmark$$

The angle between V_s and I is φ = arctan(X/R). When X>0 (inductive): V_s leads I. When X<0 (capacitive): V_s lags I (i.e., I leads V_s). Series RLC Impedance $$Z = R + jX = R + j(X_L - X_C)$$

$$|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$$

$$\phi = \arctan\!\left(\frac{X_L - X_C}{R}\right)$$

**AC Ohm's Law:**
$$I = \frac{V_s}{|Z|} \qquad I_{phasor} = \frac{V_s}{Z}$$

**Component voltages:**
$$V_R = IR \quad V_L = IX_L \quad V_C = IX_C$$

**Phasor KVL:** $V_s^2 = V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2$ Series RLC Circuit Analysis 1. Find XL = 2πfL and XC = 1/(2πfC)
2. Calculate net reactance X = XL − XC
3. Calculate |Z| = √(R² + X²)
4. Calculate phase angle φ = arctan(X/R)
5. Current magnitude I = Vs/|Z|
6. Component voltages: VR = IR, VL = IXL, VC = IXC
7. Real power P = I²R = Vs × I × cos(φ)
8. Reactive power Q = I²X = Vs × I × sin(φ)
9. Apparent power S = Vs × I = √(P² + Q²)

Verify: VR² + (VL−VC)² = Vs² ✓ The Voltmeter Paradox In a series RLC circuit, it is possible for individual component voltages to exceed the source voltage. At resonance, V_L = V_C = I × XL₀. If Q = XL₀/R = 10, then V_L = V_C = 10 × Vs. A 120V source can produce 1200V across L and C!

This voltage magnification is used in: RF filters (high Q for selectivity), induction heating (resonant tank voltage), Tesla coils. In industrial power systems, unintended resonance between cable capacitance and transformer inductance can create dangerous overvoltages — this is called ferroresonance. Series vs. Parallel Resonance in Real Circuits Industrial power systems are never purely series or purely parallel — they contain both. Resonance can occur unintentionally when:
- Capacitor banks (for PF correction) resonate with transformer leakage inductance
- Cable capacitance resonates with motor winding inductance
- Harmonic currents from VFDs excite resonant frequencies

Resonant frequencies f_r = 1/(2π√LC). If a 5th harmonic (300Hz) coincides with a capacitor-transformer resonance, harmonic voltages can amplify 10–100×. This is why harmonic analysis is required before installing large capacitor banks in industrial plants. Power Analysis of Series RLC Given: Vs=120V, R=100Ω, XL=150Ω, XC=80Ω (at 60Hz)

|Z| = √(100² + (150−80)²) = √(10000 + 4900) = 122.1Ω
φ = arctan(70/100) = +34.99° ≈ 35° (inductive)
I = 120/122.1 = 0.983A

Real power:    P = I²R = 0.966 × 100 = 96.6W
Reactive power: Q = I²X = 0.966 × 70 = 67.6VAr (inductive)
Apparent power: S = √(P²+Q²) = √(9331+4570) = 117.9VA
PF = P/S = 96.6/117.9 = 0.819 lagging Series RLC Impedance Triangle assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step sequence convergence power series taylor maclaurin

documents.title: Parallel RLC Circuits — Admittance, Susceptance, and Current Division
documents.subtitle: How to analyze AC parallel circuits using admittance — the reciprocal of impedance.
documents.tags: parallel RLC admittance susceptance conductance current divider AC parallel
documents.applications:
Industrial distribution panels have multiple parallel loads. To find total current, work in phasors: Heater: P=10kW, PF=1, I_R = 10000/480 = 20.83A ∠0°. Motor: P=15kW, PF=0.8, S=18.75kVA, I_M = 18750/480 = 39.1A ∠-36.9°. Capacitor bank: Q=50kVAr, I_C = 50000/480 = 104.2A ∠+90°. Total current = phasor sum of these three — you must add real and imaginary parts separately, not the magnitudes. This is why parallel AC analysis requires admittance (or phasor addition): naive scalar addition is completely wrong. Admittance, Conductance, Susceptance $$Y = \frac{1}{Z} = G + jB$$

where:
- G = conductance = 1/R (siemens, S)
- B = susceptance (siemens, S)
  - Inductive: $B_L = -\dfrac{1}{X_L}$ (negative)
  - Capacitive: $B_C = +\dfrac{1}{X_C}$ (positive)

**Parallel combination:**
$$Y_{total} = Y_1 + Y_2 + Y_3 = \sum G_i + j\sum B_i$$

**Total impedance:** $Z_{total} = 1/Y_{total}$
**Total current:** $I_{total} = V \cdot Y_{total}$ Parallel RLC Analysis Steps 1. Identify the common voltage V across all branches
2. Calculate each branch impedance: Z_R = R, Z_L = jXL, Z_C = −jXC
3. Calculate admittances: Y_R = 1/R, Y_L = −j/XL, Y_C = +j/XC
4. Sum admittances: Y_total = (1/R) + j(1/XC − 1/XL)
5. Total current: I_total = V × |Y_total|
6. Phase angle: φ = arctan(B_total/G) = arctan((1/XC − 1/XL)/(1/R))
7. Branch currents: IR = V/R, IL = V/XL, IC = V/XC
8. Verify: phasor sum of IR, IL, IC = I_total Parallel Resonance — Maximum Impedance In a parallel LC (or RLC) circuit, at resonance B_L = B_C:
$$\frac{1}{X_L} = \frac{1}{X_C} \Rightarrow X_L = X_C \Rightarrow f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$$

At resonance, B_L and B_C cancel. Y_total = G (purely conductive). Impedance Z_total = 1/G = R — maximum impedance. Circulating current in the LC tank can be Q times the source current. This is called a 'tank circuit' — energy circulates between L and C without the source needing to supply it (except resistive losses). Used in radio transmitters, oscillators, and notch filters. Current Division in AC Parallel Circuits **Scalar rule fails for AC.** In DC: I_branch = I_total × R_other/(R1+R2). In AC, you cannot apply this rule without using phasors.

**Correct AC current divider:**
$$I_1 = I_{total} \times \frac{Z_2}{Z_1 + Z_2}$$

Note Z_2 in numerator (opposite branch impedance, as in DC). For complex Z, this involves complex multiplication — magnitude of I1 ≠ |I_total| × |Z2|/|Z1+Z2| in general.

A common mistake: measuring I1=5A and I2=5A and concluding I_total=10A. If they're 90° apart, I_total=7.07A.
documents.content:
A 480V, 60Hz bus supplies three parallel loads: a 10kW heater (purely resistive), a 15kW motor (0.8 PF lagging), and a 50kVAr capacitor bank. What is the total current from the bus? What is the combined power factor? Industrial distribution panels have multiple parallel loads. To find total current, work in phasors: Heater: P=10kW, PF=1, I_R = 10000/480 = 20.83A ∠0°. Motor: P=15kW, PF=0.8, S=18.75kVA, I_M = 18750/480 = 39.1A ∠-36.9°. Capacitor bank: Q=50kVAr, I_C = 50000/480 = 104.2A ∠+90°. Total current = phasor sum of these three — you must add real and imaginary parts separately, not the magnitudes. This is why parallel AC analysis requires admittance (or phasor addition): naive scalar addition is completely wrong. **Why parallel currents don't just add.** Suppose branch 1 draws 10A at 0° and branch 2 draws 10A at 90°. Total = √(10² + 10²) = 14.14A, not 20A. The 90° phase difference means they peak at different times — they partially 'cancel' in the total current. This is the power of phasor analysis: it correctly accounts for time relationships, not just magnitudes. **Industrial plant power analysis.** When auditing plant power consumption: Resistive loads (heaters, incandescent lights): current in phase with voltage, PF=1. Inductive loads (motors, transformers): current lags voltage, PF<1 (lagging). Capacitive loads (capacitor banks, long cable runs with light load): current leads voltage, PF<1 (leading). The utility sees the phasor sum of all load currents. A combination of inductive and capacitive loads at the same site can self-correct PF — capacitor banks are installed precisely for this purpose. **Three-phase balanced parallel loads.** For balanced three-phase: each phase sees the same impedance. Calculate one phase (line-to-neutral voltage, single-phase current), multiply by √3 for three-phase total kVA. Line current = phase current for wye-connected loads. Line current = √3 × phase current for delta-connected loads (different because each delta element sees line-to-line voltage). This is why delta/wye transformer connections must be understood before calculating currents. **Admittance diagrams.** Just like the impedance triangle (R horizontal, X vertical, Z hypotenuse), admittance has the same structure: G horizontal, B vertical, Y hypotenuse. G = 1/R, B_C = 1/XC (upward, capacitive), B_L = −1/XL (downward, inductive). The total admittance magnitude |Y| = √(G² + B²). Total current I = V × |Y|. Phase angle of current relative to voltage: φ = arctan(B/G). **Converting between parallel and series equivalents.** A parallel RL (R_p ∥ jXL_p) can be converted to its series equivalent (R_s + jXL_s). From the admittance:

$$Y_p = \frac{1}{R_p} - \frac{j}{X_{L_p}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad Z_p = \frac{1}{Y_p} = \frac{R_p(jX_{L_p})}{R_p + jX_{L_p}}$$

Multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate gives R_s and X_s expressions. This conversion matters for filter design and transformer modeling where you need to switch between equivalent circuit forms. Admittance, Conductance, Susceptance $$Y = \frac{1}{Z} = G + jB$$

where:
- G = conductance = 1/R (siemens, S)
- B = susceptance (siemens, S)
  - Inductive: $B_L = -\dfrac{1}{X_L}$ (negative)
  - Capacitive: $B_C = +\dfrac{1}{X_C}$ (positive)

**Parallel combination:**
$$Y_{total} = Y_1 + Y_2 + Y_3 = \sum G_i + j\sum B_i$$

**Total impedance:** $Z_{total} = 1/Y_{total}$
**Total current:** $I_{total} = V \cdot Y_{total}$ Parallel RLC Analysis Steps 1. Identify the common voltage V across all branches
2. Calculate each branch impedance: Z_R = R, Z_L = jXL, Z_C = −jXC
3. Calculate admittances: Y_R = 1/R, Y_L = −j/XL, Y_C = +j/XC
4. Sum admittances: Y_total = (1/R) + j(1/XC − 1/XL)
5. Total current: I_total = V × |Y_total|
6. Phase angle: φ = arctan(B_total/G) = arctan((1/XC − 1/XL)/(1/R))
7. Branch currents: IR = V/R, IL = V/XL, IC = V/XC
8. Verify: phasor sum of IR, IL, IC = I_total Parallel Resonance — Maximum Impedance In a parallel LC (or RLC) circuit, at resonance B_L = B_C:
$$\frac{1}{X_L} = \frac{1}{X_C} \Rightarrow X_L = X_C \Rightarrow f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$$

At resonance, B_L and B_C cancel. Y_total = G (purely conductive). Impedance Z_total = 1/G = R — maximum impedance. Circulating current in the LC tank can be Q times the source current. This is called a 'tank circuit' — energy circulates between L and C without the source needing to supply it (except resistive losses). Used in radio transmitters, oscillators, and notch filters. Current Division in AC Parallel Circuits **Scalar rule fails for AC.** In DC: I_branch = I_total × R_other/(R1+R2). In AC, you cannot apply this rule without using phasors.

**Correct AC current divider:**
$$I_1 = I_{total} \times \frac{Z_2}{Z_1 + Z_2}$$

Note Z_2 in numerator (opposite branch impedance, as in DC). For complex Z, this involves complex multiplication — magnitude of I1 ≠ |I_total| × |Z2|/|Z1+Z2| in general.

A common mistake: measuring I1=5A and I2=5A and concluding I_total=10A. If they're 90° apart, I_total=7.07A. Industrial Plant Power Factor Calculation Loads on a 480V 3-phase bus:
- Load A: 100kW, PF=1.0 → P_A=100kW, Q_A=0
- Load B: 200kW, PF=0.8 lag → Q_B=200×tan(36.9°)=150kVAr
- Load C: 50kVAr capacitor bank → Q_C=−50kVAr

Total P = 100+200+0 = 300kW
Total Q = 0+150−50 = 100kVAr (lagging)
Total S = √(300²+100²) = 316kVA
PF = 300/316 = 0.949 lagging
Line current = 316000/(√3×480) = 380A Parallel RLC — Admittance and Impedance assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step

documents.title: Resonance — Q Factor, Bandwidth, and Frequency Selection
documents.subtitle: How resonant circuits select frequencies, amplify voltages, and form the core of every tuned electronic system.
documents.tags: resonance Q factor bandwidth tank circuit series resonance parallel resonance filter
documents.aliases: sequence convergence power series taylor maclaurin
documents.applications:
Bandwidth required: 200kHz (±100kHz either side). Q = f₀/BW = 101.1MHz/0.2MHz = 505. For C=10pF: L = 1/(4π²f₀²C) = 1/(4π² × (101.1×10⁶)² × 10×10⁻¹²) = 24.8nH. The LC tank achieves the needed selectivity. At 100.9MHz (Δf = 200kHz = BW): the signal is down −3dB (70.7%). At 200kHz off (2×BW): −6dB. For professional receivers, Q must be 500–2000 to prevent adjacent-channel interference. Industrial applications use resonance for induction heating, RF sensors, and wireless power transfer. Resonance Equations **Resonant frequency:**
$$f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$$

**Q factor — series:**
$$Q = \frac{X_{L_0}}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{f_0}{BW}$$

**Q factor — parallel:**
$$Q = \frac{R}{X_{L_0}} = R\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}$$

**Bandwidth:**
$$BW = f_{high} - f_{low} = \frac{f_0}{Q} = \frac{R}{2\pi L}$$

**Voltage magnification (series):** $V_L = V_C = Q \times V_s$ at resonance Resonant Circuit Design **Given:** f₀, Q, impedance level Z₀ (= √(L/C))

1. Choose Z₀ based on source/load impedance (match for max power transfer)
2. L = Z₀/(2πf₀) = Q × R / (2πf₀)
3. C = 1/(Z₀ × 2πf₀) = 1/(Q × R × 2πf₀)
4. R is the total series resistance (inductor DCR + source resistance + load resistance)
5. Q = Z₀/R — verify Q meets selectivity requirement

**Example:** f₀=1MHz, Q=50, Z₀=1kΩ:
L = 1000/(2π×10⁶) = 159μH
C = 1/(1000×2π×10⁶) = 159pF
Required R = Z₀/Q = 1000/50 = 20Ω Ferroresonance — The Dangerous Resonance Ferroresonance occurs when a transformer (nonlinear inductor) resonates with circuit capacitance. Unlike linear resonance, ferroresonance can:
- Jump between multiple stable operating points
- Produce sustained overvoltages (2–5× normal)
- Generate high-amplitude harmonics
- Damage equipment and cause fires

Triggers: switching a transformer with light load, long unloaded cable on a transformer, single-phase switching on a three-phase system.

Prevention: never leave transformer secondary unloaded with long cable runs; use damping resistors on vulnerable systems; analyze capacitance before installing VFDs or cable runs near transformers.
documents.content:
A radio receiver needs to select 101.1 MHz FM from a crowded band with stations at 100.9, 101.1, and 101.3 MHz — only 200kHz apart. What Q factor does the tuned circuit need? If C = 10pF, what is L? What happens to the signal at 100.9 MHz? Bandwidth required: 200kHz (±100kHz either side). Q = f₀/BW = 101.1MHz/0.2MHz = 505. For C=10pF: L = 1/(4π²f₀²C) = 1/(4π² × (101.1×10⁶)² × 10×10⁻¹²) = 24.8nH. The LC tank achieves the needed selectivity. At 100.9MHz (Δf = 200kHz = BW): the signal is down −3dB (70.7%). At 200kHz off (2×BW): −6dB. For professional receivers, Q must be 500–2000 to prevent adjacent-channel interference. Industrial applications use resonance for induction heating, RF sensors, and wireless power transfer. **Series resonance: maximum current, maximum component voltages.** At f₀: Z = R (minimum). I = Vs/R (maximum). V_L = I × XL₀ = Vs × Q. V_C = I × XC₀ = Vs × Q. Both V_L and V_C are Q times the source voltage — equal in magnitude but 180° apart. They cancel each other, leaving V_source = V_R only. Series resonance is used in: bandpass filters (output across R), induction heaters (high-Q tank drives current through workpiece), Tesla coils (Q=50–200, produces spectacular voltage amplification). **Parallel resonance: minimum source current, energy circulation.** At f₀: admittance Y = G = 1/R (minimum). Source current I_source = V/R (minimum — the load looks like a pure resistance R). But internal to the tank: I_tank = I_source × Q. All the energy is circulating between L and C, re-supplied only for resistive losses. A parallel tank with Q=100 draws 1A from the source while 100A circulates internally. Used in: RF power amplifier loads (high-impedance load matches transistor output), oscillator frequency-setting, notch filters (high impedance at one frequency blocks that frequency). **Bandwidth and Q in filter design.** For a bandpass filter centered at f₀ = 1kHz with BW = 100Hz: Q = 1000/100 = 10. For a narrower filter (BW = 10Hz): Q = 100. Achieving high Q requires low resistance — low-loss components (high-Q inductors, low-ESR capacitors). At RF frequencies, air-core inductors and NPO/C0G ceramic capacitors achieve Q = 200–500. At power frequencies, losses from core materials and wire resistance limit Q to 10–50. **Stagger tuning and flatness.** Multiple resonant circuits can be cascaded with slightly different f₀ values ('stagger-tuned') to create a flat-topped, steep-sided bandpass response. A single tuned circuit gives a rounded peak (Butterworth response). Two stagger-tuned circuits give a flatter top. This is how intermediate frequency (IF) strips in AM/FM radios are designed for consistent audio bandwidth across the IF band. **Frequency response near resonance.** For series RLC, normalized response H(f) = I(f)/I_max:

$$|H(f)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + Q^2\left(\dfrac{f}{f_0} - \dfrac{f_0}{f}\right)^2}}$$

At f = f₀: H = 1 (maximum). At f = f₀ ± BW/2: H = 1/√2 (−3dB). Far from resonance (f >> f₀ or f << f₀): H → 0. This is the universal resonance curve — the same shape whether the resonance is mechanical, acoustic, optical, or electrical. Resonance Equations **Resonant frequency:**
$$f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$$

**Q factor — series:**
$$Q = \frac{X_{L_0}}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{f_0}{BW}$$

**Q factor — parallel:**
$$Q = \frac{R}{X_{L_0}} = R\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}$$

**Bandwidth:**
$$BW = f_{high} - f_{low} = \frac{f_0}{Q} = \frac{R}{2\pi L}$$

**Voltage magnification (series):** $V_L = V_C = Q \times V_s$ at resonance Resonant Circuit Design **Given:** f₀, Q, impedance level Z₀ (= √(L/C))

1. Choose Z₀ based on source/load impedance (match for max power transfer)
2. L = Z₀/(2πf₀) = Q × R / (2πf₀)
3. C = 1/(Z₀ × 2πf₀) = 1/(Q × R × 2πf₀)
4. R is the total series resistance (inductor DCR + source resistance + load resistance)
5. Q = Z₀/R — verify Q meets selectivity requirement

**Example:** f₀=1MHz, Q=50, Z₀=1kΩ:
L = 1000/(2π×10⁶) = 159μH
C = 1/(1000×2π×10⁶) = 159pF
Required R = Z₀/Q = 1000/50 = 20Ω Ferroresonance — The Dangerous Resonance Ferroresonance occurs when a transformer (nonlinear inductor) resonates with circuit capacitance. Unlike linear resonance, ferroresonance can:
- Jump between multiple stable operating points
- Produce sustained overvoltages (2–5× normal)
- Generate high-amplitude harmonics
- Damage equipment and cause fires

Triggers: switching a transformer with light load, long unloaded cable on a transformer, single-phase switching on a three-phase system.

Prevention: never leave transformer secondary unloaded with long cable runs; use damping resistors on vulnerable systems; analyze capacitance before installing VFDs or cable runs near transformers. Measuring Q Factor Experimentally **Method 1: Bandwidth measurement**
1. Sweep frequency through resonance, measure output amplitude
2. Find f₀ (peak), f_low, f_high (−3dB points)
3. Q = f₀/(f_high − f_low)

**Method 2: Voltage magnification (series)**
1. Apply V_s at resonance
2. Measure V_C or V_L
3. Q = V_C/V_s = V_L/V_s

**Method 3: Phase shift**
1. At f₀, phase between V and I = 0° (series) or max (parallel)
2. Find frequencies where phase = ±45° → these are f_low, f_high
3. Q = f₀/(f_high − f_low) Resonance Explorer — Frequency Response assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step sequence convergence power series taylor maclaurin

documents.title: AC Power — Real, Reactive, Apparent, and Power Factor
documents.subtitle: Why the utility bills you for apparent power (VA) but your load only does real work (watts) — and how power factor correction saves money.
documents.tags: AC power real power reactive power apparent power power factor PF correction power triangle kVAr
documents.applications:
At 0.75 PF: S = P/PF = 500/0.75 = 667kVA. Q_initial = √(667²−500²) = 441kVAr inductive. Target Q at 0.92 PF: Q_target = 500 × tan(arccos(0.92)) = 500 × 0.426 = 213kVAr. Q_C needed = 441 − 213 = 228kVAr. For 480V 3-phase: C per phase = Q_C/(3 × ω × V²_LN) = 228000/(3 × 377 × 277²) = 2.63mF per phase. Original line current: 667kVA/(√3 × 480) = 802A. Corrected current: √(500²+213²)kVA/(√3×480) = 539kVA/831 = 648A. Annual savings from 154A reduction in 100m of 3-phase cable (100mΩ/phase): ΔP = 3 × I² × R loss reduction ≈ 3 × (802²−648²) × 0.1 = 66kW × 8760h = 578MWh/year. This is why PF correction pays back in 1–3 years in industrial plants. Power Triangle $$P = VI\cos\phi \text{ (watts, W or kW)}$$
$$Q = VI\sin\phi \text{ (volt-amperes reactive, VAr or kVAr)}$$
$$S = VI = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2} \text{ (volt-amperes, VA or kVA)}$$
$$PF = \cos\phi = \frac{P}{S}$$

Sign of Q: positive (lagging, inductive), negative (leading, capacitive).

**Alternative forms:**
$$P = I^2R \qquad Q = I^2X \qquad S = I^2|Z|$$
$$P = \frac{V_R^2}{R} \qquad Q = \frac{V_X^2}{X} \qquad S = \frac{V^2}{|Z|}$$ PF Correction Capacitor Sizing Given: P (kW), PF_initial, target PF_final (typically 0.90–0.95)

1. Q_initial = P × tan(arccos(PF_initial))
2. Q_target  = P × tan(arccos(PF_final))
3. Q_C = Q_initial − Q_target (kVAr to install)
4. For single-phase: C = Q_C/(ω × V²_rms)
5. For 3-phase wye: C per phase = Q_C/(3 × ω × V²_LN)
6. Capacitor voltage rating ≥ 1.1 × V_nominal (allow 10% harmonic overvoltage)
7. Verify no resonance between capacitor bank and transformer leakage inductance Three-Phase Power Formulas **Balanced 3-phase:**
$$P_{3\phi} = \sqrt{3}\,V_{LL}\,I_L\cos\phi = 3\,V_{LN}\,I_L\cos\phi$$
$$Q_{3\phi} = \sqrt{3}\,V_{LL}\,I_L\sin\phi$$
$$S_{3\phi} = \sqrt{3}\,V_{LL}\,I_L$$

**Single-phase equivalent:** analyze per phase (V_LN, single-phase current), then multiply by 3.

**Motor nameplate:** 480V, 3-phase, 30HP, 0.85 PF, 34A → S = √3×480×34 = 28.3kVA, P = 28.3×0.85 = 24kW ≈ 32HP (motor efficiency ≈ 95% → shaft power = 22.8kW = 30.5HP ✓) Harmonic Resonance with PF Capacitors Adding capacitor banks to a plant with VFDs or other harmonic-generating loads can cause harmonic resonance. The capacitors resonate with transformer leakage inductance at: f_r = f₁ × √(S_sc/Q_C) where f₁=60Hz, S_sc=short-circuit kVA, Q_C=capacitor kVAr.

If f_r coincides with the 5th (300Hz) or 7th (420Hz) harmonic from VFDs, those harmonics amplify dramatically — potentially 10–40×. Symptoms: capacitor fuses blowing, overheating, harmonic voltage distortion.

Solution: use detuned capacitor banks (series reactor raises f_r above the dominant harmonic) or active harmonic filters (inject equal and opposite harmonics).
documents.content:
A factory has 500kW of motor load at 0.75 PF lagging. The utility charges a PF penalty below 0.9. How much reactive power must a capacitor bank supply to correct PF to 0.92? At 480V 3-phase, what kVAr rating and capacitance per phase is needed? What is the annual current reduction on the supply cables? At 0.75 PF: S = P/PF = 500/0.75 = 667kVA. Q_initial = √(667²−500²) = 441kVAr inductive. Target Q at 0.92 PF: Q_target = 500 × tan(arccos(0.92)) = 500 × 0.426 = 213kVAr. Q_C needed = 441 − 213 = 228kVAr. For 480V 3-phase: C per phase = Q_C/(3 × ω × V²_LN) = 228000/(3 × 377 × 277²) = 2.63mF per phase. Original line current: 667kVA/(√3 × 480) = 802A. Corrected current: √(500²+213²)kVA/(√3×480) = 539kVA/831 = 648A. Annual savings from 154A reduction in 100m of 3-phase cable (100mΩ/phase): ΔP = 3 × I² × R loss reduction ≈ 3 × (802²−648²) × 0.1 = 66kW × 8760h = 578MWh/year. This is why PF correction pays back in 1–3 years in industrial plants. **Why the utility cares about reactive power.** The utility's generators, transformers, and cables must carry S (apparent) amps to deliver P (real) watts. A motor drawing 100A at 0.8 PF needs the same generator capacity as a resistive heater drawing 100A — but only delivers 80kW of real work vs 100kW. The generator is 'wasting' 20% capacity on reactive current. This is why utilities penalize industrial customers for low PF: they occupy grid capacity without being billed for it. **Displacement PF vs. true PF.** Classic PF = cos(φ) is displacement power factor — it accounts for phase displacement only. True PF also includes harmonic distortion: PF_true = P/(V_rms × I_rms). VFDs and switching power supplies draw non-sinusoidal currents — harmonic currents increase I_rms without increasing real power, reducing true PF. A VFD with displacement PF = 0.95 may have true PF = 0.75 due to harmonics. This requires active harmonic filters or multi-pulse rectifiers, not just capacitor banks. **Metering and billing.** Industrial utility meters measure: kWh (real energy), kVAh (apparent energy), or kVArh (reactive energy). PF penalty: if demand kVAr > kW × tan(arccos(PF_threshold)), a penalty charge applies. A $0.20/kVArh charge on 441kVAr for 720 hours/month = $63,504/month in avoidable charges. PF correction capacitor banks (say $50,000 installed) pay back in under a year. **Power factor correction placement.** Global correction: capacitor bank at the utility entry point, reduces billing charges. Local correction: capacitors at each motor terminal, reduces current in all distribution wiring upstream. Local correction also reduces transformer kVA loading. Standard practice: 75–100% local correction at each large motor (kVAr rating = 30–40% of motor kVA). Remaining imbalance corrected at switchboard level. **Complex power — the complete picture.** Define complex power S = V × I* (V times the conjugate of I). For V = V∠0° and I = I∠−φ (lagging current), I* = I∠+φ:

$$\mathbf{S} = |V||I|\angle\phi = P + jQ$$

Real part: P = |V||I|cos(φ) — real power. Imaginary part: Q = |V||I|sin(φ) — reactive power. Magnitude: |S| = |V||I| — apparent power. This compact notation handles all power components simultaneously and extends directly to three-phase systems. Power Triangle $$P = VI\cos\phi \text{ (watts, W or kW)}$$
$$Q = VI\sin\phi \text{ (volt-amperes reactive, VAr or kVAr)}$$
$$S = VI = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2} \text{ (volt-amperes, VA or kVA)}$$
$$PF = \cos\phi = \frac{P}{S}$$

Sign of Q: positive (lagging, inductive), negative (leading, capacitive).

**Alternative forms:**
$$P = I^2R \qquad Q = I^2X \qquad S = I^2|Z|$$
$$P = \frac{V_R^2}{R} \qquad Q = \frac{V_X^2}{X} \qquad S = \frac{V^2}{|Z|}$$ PF Correction Capacitor Sizing Given: P (kW), PF_initial, target PF_final (typically 0.90–0.95)

1. Q_initial = P × tan(arccos(PF_initial))
2. Q_target  = P × tan(arccos(PF_final))
3. Q_C = Q_initial − Q_target (kVAr to install)
4. For single-phase: C = Q_C/(ω × V²_rms)
5. For 3-phase wye: C per phase = Q_C/(3 × ω × V²_LN)
6. Capacitor voltage rating ≥ 1.1 × V_nominal (allow 10% harmonic overvoltage)
7. Verify no resonance between capacitor bank and transformer leakage inductance Three-Phase Power Formulas **Balanced 3-phase:**
$$P_{3\phi} = \sqrt{3}\,V_{LL}\,I_L\cos\phi = 3\,V_{LN}\,I_L\cos\phi$$
$$Q_{3\phi} = \sqrt{3}\,V_{LL}\,I_L\sin\phi$$
$$S_{3\phi} = \sqrt{3}\,V_{LL}\,I_L$$

**Single-phase equivalent:** analyze per phase (V_LN, single-phase current), then multiply by 3.

**Motor nameplate:** 480V, 3-phase, 30HP, 0.85 PF, 34A → S = √3×480×34 = 28.3kVA, P = 28.3×0.85 = 24kW ≈ 32HP (motor efficiency ≈ 95% → shaft power = 22.8kW = 30.5HP ✓) Harmonic Resonance with PF Capacitors Adding capacitor banks to a plant with VFDs or other harmonic-generating loads can cause harmonic resonance. The capacitors resonate with transformer leakage inductance at: f_r = f₁ × √(S_sc/Q_C) where f₁=60Hz, S_sc=short-circuit kVA, Q_C=capacitor kVAr.

If f_r coincides with the 5th (300Hz) or 7th (420Hz) harmonic from VFDs, those harmonics amplify dramatically — potentially 10–40×. Symptoms: capacitor fuses blowing, overheating, harmonic voltage distortion.

Solution: use detuned capacitor banks (series reactor raises f_r above the dominant harmonic) or active harmonic filters (inject equal and opposite harmonics). PF Penalty Calculation Utility rate: $8.00/kW demand + $0.15/kVAr demand above kW × 0.330 (= PF > 0.95)

Load: P = 800kW, Q = 600kVAr, S = 1000kVA, PF = 0.80

Allowable Q = 800 × 0.330 = 264kVAr (at PF 0.95)
Excess Q = 600 − 264 = 336kVAr (penalized)
Monthly Q penalty = 336 × $0.15 = $50.40/month
Annual penalty = $604.80

Capacitor bank to correct to 0.95: Q_C = 600 − 264 = 336kVAr
Capacitor bank cost (installed, 480V): ≈ $336 × $50/kVAr = $16,800
Simple payback = $16,800/$604.80 = 27.8 months AC Power Triangle and Waveforms assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step

documents.title: Transformers — Turns Ratio, Impedance Matching, and Practical Design
documents.subtitle: How transformers step voltage up and down, match impedances, and provide isolation — and why they only work with AC.
documents.tags: transformer turns ratio step-up step-down isolation impedance matching core loss leakage inductance
documents.applications:
Control transformers are in every industrial control panel. Primary current: Ip = Is/n = 3.5/(480/120) = 3.5/4 = 0.875A. Secondary load: 3.5A × 120V = 420VA. Adding 200W heater: S_total = √((420W + 200W)² + Q²) ≈ 620VA — exceeds 500VA rating. Result: transformer overheats, insulation degrades, shortened lifespan. Short circuit: transformer must supply short-circuit current limited only by its leakage inductance and winding resistance. Transformers are not self-protecting — fusing on both sides is required. Primary fuse: 500VA/480V = 1.04A → use 2A fuse. Secondary fuse: 500VA/120V = 4.17A → use 5A fuse. Ideal Transformer Equations **Turns ratio:** $n = N_s/N_p$

$$\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p} = n$$

$$\frac{I_s}{I_p} = \frac{N_p}{N_s} = \frac{1}{n}$$

**Power conservation:** $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$ (ideal)

**Impedance reflection:**
$$Z_{primary} = n^2 \times Z_{secondary}$$

**Three-winding/autotransformer:** additional secondary windings, all linked by common flux. Voltage ratios = turns ratios. Control Transformer Sizing 1. List all 120VAC loads: VA for each (relays: 10–50VA, PLC cards: 25–150VA, indicators: 5VA, solenoids: 30–200VA)
2. Sum continuous loads: S_continuous = Σ VA
3. Account for inrush: relays/solenoids have 3–10× inrush on pickup. Use inrush factor for sizing if many are simultaneously energized
4. Add 25% design margin: S_transformer = 1.25 × S_continuous
5. Round up to nearest standard size (50, 100, 150, 250, 500, 750, 1000VA)
6. Verify primary fuse: I_primary = S_transformer/V_primary; fuse = 125–175% of rated primary current
7. Secondary fuse: 125% of rated secondary current Transformer Nameplate Ratings | Nameplate item | Meaning |
|---|---|
| kVA | Apparent power capacity — depends on temperature rise, not real power type |
| Voltage (primary/secondary) | Nominal voltages — assume rated V at no load |
| % Impedance | Percentage of V_rated that causes full rated current in short-circuit test |
| Class H, F, B | Insulation temperature class (180°C, 155°C, 130°C max winding temp) |
| Frequency | 50 or 60Hz — running 60Hz transformer at 50Hz increases core losses and reduces kVA rating |
| Regulation % | Voltage drop from no-load to full-load, expressed as % of full-load voltage | Never Open-Circuit a CT Secondary A current transformer (CT) normally has a very low-impedance secondary (5Ω meter or relay). When current flows in the primary (line), the secondary current is forced by the primary ampere-turns. If the secondary is open-circuited while primary current flows:

1. No secondary current → no opposing MMF
2. Core flux rises until saturation
3. Very high dΦ/dt at saturation corners → kilovolt EMF spikes
4. Insulation failure, equipment damage, potentially fatal electric shock

Always: short the CT secondary before disconnecting meter/relay. Use CT shorting terminals. Label all CTs clearly. This is a Code requirement and a safety-critical procedure.
documents.content:
A control panel uses a 480V:120V control transformer to power 120V relays and PLC cards. The transformer is rated 500VA. The control loads draw 3.5A at 120V. What primary current is drawn? If you add a 200W heater to the 120V circuit, does the 500VA rating limit you? What happens if the secondary short-circuits? Control transformers are in every industrial control panel. Primary current: Ip = Is/n = 3.5/(480/120) = 3.5/4 = 0.875A. Secondary load: 3.5A × 120V = 420VA. Adding 200W heater: S_total = √((420W + 200W)² + Q²) ≈ 620VA — exceeds 500VA rating. Result: transformer overheats, insulation degrades, shortened lifespan. Short circuit: transformer must supply short-circuit current limited only by its leakage inductance and winding resistance. Transformers are not self-protecting — fusing on both sides is required. Primary fuse: 500VA/480V = 1.04A → use 2A fuse. Secondary fuse: 500VA/120V = 4.17A → use 5A fuse. **Real transformer model.** An ideal transformer is a good first approximation. A real transformer adds: magnetizing inductance (keeps core flux even at no load), core resistance (represents hysteresis and eddy current losses), primary and secondary leakage inductances (flux that doesn't link both coils), and winding resistances (copper losses I²R). The leakage inductance causes voltage to droop under load — important for fault current calculation and voltage regulation. **Voltage regulation.** A transformer's voltage regulation is how much secondary voltage drops from no-load to full-load: VR% = (V_NL − V_FL)/V_FL × 100%. A good power transformer: VR < 5%. A control transformer: 5–10%. High-leakage transformers (for current limiting): 20–50% (used as current-limited transformers for safe welding and charging circuits). Low VR is essential for voltage-sensitive loads (PLCs, VFDs); high VR is desired for inherently current-limited loads. **Core losses and efficiency.** Transformer losses: Copper losses P_Cu = I² × R_winding (load-dependent, proportional to I²). Core losses P_Fe = hysteresis + eddy current losses (load-independent, proportional to V² and f). Maximum efficiency occurs when P_Cu = P_Fe, typically at 50–80% of full load. A transformer idling at no load still draws full core losses (magnetizing current at no-load). Large plant transformers left energized 24/7 should be selected for low core losses (amorphous core or premium efficiency units). **Instrument transformers: CTs and PTs.** Current transformers (CTs) step down line current to 5A or 1A for meter/relay input. A 200:5 CT turns 200A line current into 5A for an ammeter. The CT secondary must never be open-circuited while current flows — all EMF drives into a very high impedance, producing dangerous kilovolt spikes that can destroy insulation and injure personnel. Potential transformers (PTs) step down line voltage (480V → 120V) for voltage measurement. PTs can be open on secondary safely — no current flows at no load. **Referred equivalent circuit.** To analyze a real transformer, 'refer' all secondary quantities to the primary side using n = Ns/Np:

$$V'_s = V_s/n \quad I'_s = n I_s \quad Z'_{load} = n^2 Z_{load}$$

The equivalent circuit becomes a single loop: V_p − I_p(R1 + jX1) − I_m(Rc ∥ jXm) − I'_s(R'2 + jX'2) − V'_s = 0

For most calculations, the shunt branch (Rc ∥ jXm) is ignored (no-load current is small). This leaves a simple series circuit: Z_total = (R1 + R'2) + j(X1 + X'2) plus the load. This is how transformer voltage regulation and short-circuit current are calculated. Ideal Transformer Equations **Turns ratio:** $n = N_s/N_p$

$$\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p} = n$$

$$\frac{I_s}{I_p} = \frac{N_p}{N_s} = \frac{1}{n}$$

**Power conservation:** $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$ (ideal)

**Impedance reflection:**
$$Z_{primary} = n^2 \times Z_{secondary}$$

**Three-winding/autotransformer:** additional secondary windings, all linked by common flux. Voltage ratios = turns ratios. Control Transformer Sizing 1. List all 120VAC loads: VA for each (relays: 10–50VA, PLC cards: 25–150VA, indicators: 5VA, solenoids: 30–200VA)
2. Sum continuous loads: S_continuous = Σ VA
3. Account for inrush: relays/solenoids have 3–10× inrush on pickup. Use inrush factor for sizing if many are simultaneously energized
4. Add 25% design margin: S_transformer = 1.25 × S_continuous
5. Round up to nearest standard size (50, 100, 150, 250, 500, 750, 1000VA)
6. Verify primary fuse: I_primary = S_transformer/V_primary; fuse = 125–175% of rated primary current
7. Secondary fuse: 125% of rated secondary current Transformer Nameplate Ratings | Nameplate item | Meaning |
|---|---|
| kVA | Apparent power capacity — depends on temperature rise, not real power type |
| Voltage (primary/secondary) | Nominal voltages — assume rated V at no load |
| % Impedance | Percentage of V_rated that causes full rated current in short-circuit test |
| Class H, F, B | Insulation temperature class (180°C, 155°C, 130°C max winding temp) |
| Frequency | 50 or 60Hz — running 60Hz transformer at 50Hz increases core losses and reduces kVA rating |
| Regulation % | Voltage drop from no-load to full-load, expressed as % of full-load voltage | Never Open-Circuit a CT Secondary A current transformer (CT) normally has a very low-impedance secondary (5Ω meter or relay). When current flows in the primary (line), the secondary current is forced by the primary ampere-turns. If the secondary is open-circuited while primary current flows:

1. No secondary current → no opposing MMF
2. Core flux rises until saturation
3. Very high dΦ/dt at saturation corners → kilovolt EMF spikes
4. Insulation failure, equipment damage, potentially fatal electric shock

Always: short the CT secondary before disconnecting meter/relay. Use CT shorting terminals. Label all CTs clearly. This is a Code requirement and a safety-critical procedure. Autotransformer vs. Isolation Transformer **Isolation transformer:** primary and secondary are electrically isolated — no shared conductors. Provides galvanic isolation. Required for medical equipment, GFCI protection, and grounding reference changes.

**Autotransformer:** uses a single winding with a tap. Primary and secondary share conductors. No isolation — ground faults propagate. More efficient (smaller core, less copper) for small step ratios.

Example: 480V → 208V as autotransformer uses 272V winding (the difference) as the 'transformer' part, while 208V is common. Saves ~43% copper vs. isolation transformer for the same kVA. Not permitted in some NEC applications requiring isolation (hazardous locations, certain medical). documents.title: Three-Phase Power — Delta, Wye, and Industrial Distribution
documents.subtitle: How three-phase systems deliver more power with less conductor, and why delta and wye connections produce different voltages and currents.

documents.applications:
150HP motors × 746W/HP ÷ 0.9 efficiency ÷ 0.85 PF ≈ 147kVA motor load. Plus 20kVA single-phase = 167kVA total. Specify a 200kVA transformer (25% margin). For 480V 3-phase with 120/208V single-phase: use a 480V delta primary, 120Y/208V wye secondary. The secondary wye provides: 208V line-to-line (3-phase for possible future use), 120V line-to-neutral (single-phase lighting and controls from any phase-to-neutral), true neutral for grounding. Primary current: 200kVA / (√3 × 480V) = 240A. Secondary current at 208V: 200kVA / (√3 × 208V) = 555A. This is standard for industrial facilities throughout North America. Wye and Delta Voltage/Current Relationships **Wye (Y) connection:**
$$V_{LL} = \sqrt{3}\,V_{LN} \approx 1.732\,V_{LN}$$
$$I_L = I_{phase}$$

**Delta (Δ) connection:**
$$V_{LL} = V_{phase}$$
$$I_L = \sqrt{3}\,I_{phase}$$

**Common voltages:**
| V_LL | V_LN | Connection |
|---|---|---|
| 480V | 277V | 480Y/277V |
| 208V | 120V | 208Y/120V |
| 4160V | 2400V | 4160Y/2400V |

1. Electrical input power: P_elec = P_shaft/η = 75/0.94 = 79.8kW
2. Apparent power: S = P/PF = 79.8/0.88 = 90.6kVA
3. Line current: I_L = S/(√3 × V_LL) = 90600/(1.732 × 480) = 108.9A
4. Verify: I_L at unity PF = 79800/(1.732×480) = 95.8A (less current at PF=1)

**For balanced load analysis:** work per phase:
- V_LN = 480/√3 = 277V
- Per-phase Z = V_LN/I_phase = 277/108.9 = 2.54Ω
- Per-phase P = I²×R = 108.9² × 2.54×0.88 = 26.6kW × 3 phases = 79.8kW ✓ Open-Delta (V-V) Transformer Connection If one transformer in a delta-delta bank fails, the remaining two can supply three-phase power in an 'open delta' or 'V' connection — at 57.7% of original capacity.

This allows temporary operation while the failed transformer is replaced. Critical industrial facilities sometimes intentionally design open-delta banks for cheaper transformer cost and quick recovery from single transformer failure, accepting the 42.3% capacity reduction.

$$\% \text{unbalance} = \frac{\text{max deviation from average}}{\text{average V}_{LL}} \times 100$$

- 1% unbalance: 3% derating
- 2% unbalance: 8% derating  
- 3% unbalance: 20% derating
- 5% unbalance: motor should not be operated

Causes: single-phase loads unevenly distributed, blown fuse in three-phase bank, failing transformer, unequal cable lengths to three-phase load.

Measure: take V_LL between all three pairs (AB, BC, CA). The differences should be <1% at the motor terminals.

4. Verify: I_L at unity PF = 79800/(1.732×480) = 95.8A (less current at PF=1)

- 1% unbalance: 3% derating
- 2% unbalance: 8% derating  
- 3% unbalance: 20% derating
- 5% unbalance: motor should not be operated

1. Sum all 3-phase motor loads: kVA = kW/(η × PF)
2. Sum all single-phase loads: kVA
3. Total kVA (with 25% margin): T_kVA = 1.25 × (3-phase kVA + single-phase kVA)
4. Primary voltage: utility supply (typically 4160V, 13.8kV, or 34.5kV)
5. Secondary: 480Y/277V for motor/VFD loads OR 208Y/120V for small facility
6. Specify: kVA rating, primary voltage, secondary voltage, % impedance (5–6% typical), insulation class
7. Include: transformer protection (fuses or breaker on primary), secondary main breaker or fuse disconnect Three-Phase Waveforms assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step

documents.title: Semiconductor Fundamentals — Doping, Band Gaps, and Carrier Types
documents.subtitle: Why silicon conducts sometimes, how adding impurities creates N-type and P-type material, and what band theory actually tells a working engineer.
documents.tags: semiconductor silicon doping N-type P-type band gap intrinsic extrinsic covalent bond hole electron carrier
documents.applications:
A MOSFET or IGBT will read open collector-to-emitter with the gate floating — this is correct operation. The device is a voltage-controlled switch: with no gate signal, the channel doesn't exist. A failed short would read near zero ohms both ways; a failed open in a bipolar transistor would read open in the reverse-biased direction. Understanding semiconductor fundamentals means you can interpret multimeter readings on solid-state devices without guessing. The same physics — controlled carrier injection — governs every transistor, thyristor, and diode in that drive cabinet. Intrinsic Carrier Concentration $$n_i = \sqrt{N_c N_v}\, \exp\!\left(\frac{-E_g}{2kT}\right)$$

where:
- Nc, Nv = effective density of states in conduction/valence bands
- Eg = band gap (1.12 eV for Si, 0.67 eV for Ge)
- k = Boltzmann constant (8.617 × 10⁻⁵ eV/K)
- T = temperature in Kelvin

At 300 K: ni(Si) ≈ 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³. Doubles roughly every 11°C. Mass Action Law In any semiconductor at thermal equilibrium:
$$n \cdot p = n_i^2$$

For N-type silicon with ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³:
- n ≈ ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ (majority carriers)
- p = ni² / n = (1.5×10¹⁰)² / 10¹⁶ = **2.25 × 10⁴ cm⁻³** (minority)

Minority carriers are 12 orders of magnitude less dense — yet they control diode and transistor behavior at the junction. Why Silicon Replaced Germanium Germanium was first (transistors, 1947) but silicon won commercially by the 1960s. Silicon's larger band gap (1.12 vs 0.67 eV) means lower leakage at room temperature, higher maximum junction temperature (~150°C vs ~75°C for Ge), and better high-voltage capability. Silicon also forms SiO₂ natively — a high-quality insulator enabling MOSFETs. Silicon is also the second most abundant element on Earth. Modern power electronics favors SiC and GaN for even wider band gaps, but these cost 10–20× more per wafer. Conductivity of Doped Silicon $$\sigma = q(n\mu_n + p\mu_p)$$

where:
- q = electron charge (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
- n = electron density (cm⁻³), μn = electron mobility ≈ 1350 cm²/V·s
- p = hole density (cm⁻³), μp = hole mobility ≈ 450 cm²/V·s

For N-type with ND = 10¹⁶: σ ≈ q × 10¹⁶ × 1350 ≈ 2.16 (Ω·cm)⁻¹, ρ ≈ 0.46 Ω·cm ESD Damage and Semiconductor Handling A static discharge of 200–500V can permanently destroy a MOS gate oxide (only ~10 nm thick). Human body can generate 2000–35000V of static. Always handle ICs and bare transistors with ESD wrist strap and mat. Store in anti-static bags. On an industrial job site, ESD damage often looks like random bit errors or logic failure at startup — not catastrophic device failure. Replacing boards without ESD precautions on a carpeted floor will damage the replacement too. Identifying N-Type vs P-Type with a Multimeter A quick field test with an analog meter (internal battery):
1. Set to low-resistance range (×1 or ×10).
2. Touch probes to a piece of semiconductor bar (e.g., a transistor junction with the case cracked open — rarely needed).
3. In practice: identify type from the device datasheet or markings. For discrete transistors, the middle letter in NPN/PNP tells you the base type.

For IC process: N-type substrates have phosphorus or arsenic (donor) doping; P-type substrates have boron (acceptor) doping. Datasheet always specifies.

A 480V industrial drive board has failed. The technician tests a power transistor with a multimeter and finds it reads open in both directions between collector and emitter — with the gate disconnected. The transistor is brand new. Why might a brand-new transistor read open, and is this a sign of failure or normal behavior? A MOSFET or IGBT will read open collector-to-emitter with the gate floating — this is correct operation. The device is a voltage-controlled switch: with no gate signal, the channel doesn't exist. A failed short would read near zero ohms both ways; a failed open in a bipolar transistor would read open in the reverse-biased direction. Understanding semiconductor fundamentals means you can interpret multimeter readings on solid-state devices without guessing. The same physics — controlled carrier injection — governs every transistor, thyristor, and diode in that drive cabinet. **Intrinsic vs extrinsic semiconductors.** Intrinsic (pure) silicon has equal numbers of electrons and holes generated by thermal excitation: n = p = ni ≈ 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ at 300 K. Extrinsic silicon has intentionally added impurities. N-type adds donor atoms (group V: P, As, Sb) — the extra electron is weakly bound and easily ionized at room temperature, so donor concentration ND ≈ n (free electrons). P-type adds acceptor atoms (group III: B, Al, In) — each creates a hole, so NA ≈ p. In both cases, the majority carrier is the one provided by doping; the minority carrier comes from thermal generation. **Holes: the engineering fiction that is physically real.** A hole is not just an absence of an electron — it behaves as a positive charge carrier with its own effective mass and mobility. When an electron moves left through the lattice to fill a hole, the hole effectively moves right. Hole mobility in silicon (450 cm²/V·s) is about half electron mobility (1350 cm²/V·s). This asymmetry matters: P-type devices are slower than N-type, which is why engineers prefer NMOS transistors for speed-critical paths and NPN BJTs over PNP in most amplifier designs. **Temperature effects on semiconductors.** Carrier density increases exponentially with temperature: ni ∝ exp(−Eg/2kT). At 150°C, intrinsic carrier density rises ~1000× vs. room temperature. For heavily doped silicon, this eventually swamps the intentional doping — the semiconductor becomes intrinsic, PN junctions fail to block, and device leakage skyrockets. This is why silicon devices are rated to 150–175°C junction temperature. SiC (band gap 3.26 eV) stays controllable to 200°C+ — critical for EV inverters and aircraft power electronics. **Resistivity and conductivity of doped silicon.** Intrinsic silicon resistivity ≈ 2300 Ω·cm. Heavily doped (10²⁰ cm⁻³) silicon resistivity ≈ 0.001 Ω·cm. Metal copper: ~1.7 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·cm. Semiconductor conductivity sits between metal and insulator — but critically, it is tuneable over six orders of magnitude by doping. This controlled conductivity is the basis of all solid-state devices. In a MOSFET, the applied gate voltage modulates channel conductivity continuously from near-insulating to near-conducting. **Drift current and mobility.** When an electric field E (V/cm) is applied, electrons drift at velocity vd = μn × E. Current density J = q × n × vd = q × n × μn × E = σ × E (Ohm's law in material form). For silicon with ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ in a field of 100 V/cm: vd = 1350 × 100 = 1.35 × 10⁵ cm/s. Current density J = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 10¹⁶ × 1.35×10⁵ = 216 A/cm². This is why small silicon devices can carry enormous current densities — but thermal management becomes critical immediately. **Diffusion current.** Carriers also move from high to low concentration (diffusion). Diffusion current density: Jn = q × Dn × (dn/dx), where Dn = μn × kT/q ≈ 1350 × 0.026 = 35 cm²/s is the diffusion coefficient. The thermal voltage kT/q = 0.026V at 300 K (often written VT = 26 mV) appears throughout semiconductor device equations. Diffusion is the dominant transport mechanism inside PN junctions and transistor base regions. Intrinsic Carrier Concentration $$n_i = \sqrt{N_c N_v}\, \exp\!\left(\frac{-E_g}{2kT}\right)$$

documents.title: The P-N Junction Diode — Depletion Region, Bias, and the Shockley Equation
documents.subtitle: How joining P-type and N-type silicon creates a one-way valve for current, and the exponential math that governs every diode in industry.
documents.tags: PN junction depletion region forward bias reverse bias Shockley equation diode built-in voltage breakdown diffusion drift
documents.aliases: growth decay e^x logarithm ln
documents.applications:
Two silicon diodes in the rectifier bridge each drop ~0.6–0.7V in the forward direction. Full-wave bridge rectification passes current through two diodes in series, dropping 1.2–1.4V total from the peak DC voltage. The transformer is usually wound to compensate, but at heavy load or high temperature (where Vf drops ~2mV/°C), you can see 22–23V. PLC digital inputs typically accept 18–30V DC — so 22.8V is acceptable. But if you swapped standard silicon diodes for Schottky diodes (Vf ≈ 0.3V), the output rises to ~23.4V, and efficiency improves. Understanding junction physics lets you choose the right diode for the application. Shockley Diode Equation $$I_D = I_S \left( e^{\frac{V_D}{nV_T}} - 1 \right)$$

where:
- IS = reverse saturation current (~10⁻¹² A for small-signal Si, ~10⁻⁶ A for power Si)
- VD = diode forward voltage (V)
- n = ideality factor (1.0–2.0; n=1 ideal, n=2 recombination dominant)
- VT = kT/q = 26 mV at 300 K (thermal voltage)

**Approximation for VD >> VT:** ID ≈ IS × e^(VD/nVT) Built-In Junction Potential $$V_0 = \frac{kT}{q} \ln\!\left(\frac{N_A N_D}{n_i^2}\right)$$

For silicon at 300 K with NA = ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³:
$$V_0 = 0.026 \ln\!\left(\frac{10^{32}}{(1.5\times10^{10})^2}\right) \approx 0.026 \times 27 \approx 0.70\text{ V}$$

Higher doping → higher V₀. This is not externally measurable but sets the knee of the I-V curve. Testing a Diode with a Multimeter **Diode test mode (most digital meters):**
1. Red probe → anode (P-side), Black → cathode (N-side): should read 0.50–0.75V (silicon), 0.25–0.45V (Schottky), 1.5–2.2V (LED)
2. Reverse probes: should read OL (open) for a good diode
3. Both directions read near 0V: shorted junction (failed)
4. Both directions read OL: open junction (failed) or MOSFET body diode with gate floating (normal)

**Resistance mode:** Not recommended for diodes — meter current is too small to fully forward-bias silicon. Use diode test mode. Why 0.7V? (And When It Isn't) The '0.7V diode drop' is a room-temperature approximation for a silicon junction at moderate current. It varies:
- Small-signal Si at 1 mA: ~0.6V
- Power diode at 10A: 0.8–1.1V (bulk resistance adds to junction voltage)
- At 125°C junction: subtract ~0.2V → 0.5V typical
- Schottky diode: 0.2–0.4V (metal-semiconductor junction, no minority storage)
- GaN Schottky: 0.5–0.7V (but fast recovery)

In a 5V logic circuit, 0.7V is 14% of supply — significant. In a 480V rectifier, 0.7V is 0.15% — negligible for most calculations. Peak Inverse Voltage — Selecting Rectifier Diodes The PIV (Peak Inverse Voltage) rating must exceed the peak reverse voltage the diode sees in circuit, with derating. For a full-wave bridge on 240VAC: peak voltage = 240 × √2 = 340V. Add transient margin: use 600V or 800V diodes. Never operate at rated PIV continuously — use 50% derating for industrial reliability. On inductive loads (transformers, motors), voltage spikes can reach 2–3× line voltage. Install MOV or RC snubbers, and select diodes with 2× margin over calculated peak. Small-Signal Diode Resistance At a DC operating point ID, the incremental (small-signal) resistance of a diode is:
$$r_d = \frac{nV_T}{I_D} = \frac{n \times 26\,\text{mV}}{I_D}$$

At ID = 1 mA, n=1: rd = 26 Ω
At ID = 10 mA: rd = 2.6 Ω
At ID = 100 mA: rd = 0.26 Ω

This small-signal resistance governs AC ripple voltage across a diode biased at DC — important for peak detector and precision rectifier design.

You're commissioning a 480VAC 3-phase to 24VDC power supply for a control panel. The output voltage is 22.8V at full load instead of the specified 24V. The transformer secondary is correct. Where is the 1.2V going, and does it matter for PLC 24V I/O reliability? Two silicon diodes in the rectifier bridge each drop ~0.6–0.7V in the forward direction. Full-wave bridge rectification passes current through two diodes in series, dropping 1.2–1.4V total from the peak DC voltage. The transformer is usually wound to compensate, but at heavy load or high temperature (where Vf drops ~2mV/°C), you can see 22–23V. PLC digital inputs typically accept 18–30V DC — so 22.8V is acceptable. But if you swapped standard silicon diodes for Schottky diodes (Vf ≈ 0.3V), the output rises to ~23.4V, and efficiency improves. Understanding junction physics lets you choose the right diode for the application. **Forward bias operation.** Applying positive voltage to P-side reduces the depletion width and lowers the energy barrier. Majority carriers (electrons from N, holes from P) are injected across the junction. Once across, they become minority carriers and recombine — this recombination current is the forward current. For silicon at room temperature: threshold ~0.6–0.7V. The forward current rises exponentially — at 0.7V a small-signal silicon diode might carry 10 mA; at 0.75V it carries 50 mA; at 0.8V it could carry 200 mA. The diode's bulk resistance eventually limits current at high currents (series resistance effect). **Reverse bias operation.** Applying negative voltage to P-side widens the depletion region — the barrier grows, and majority carrier injection stops. Only thermally generated minority carriers (a tiny population) can cross. This gives the reverse saturation current IS — extremely small (picoamperes for small-signal diodes, microamperes for power diodes). Reverse current is nearly independent of voltage until breakdown. Practically, a silicon diode blocks current until its peak inverse voltage (PIV) rating is exceeded. **Breakdown: avalanche and Zener.** At high reverse voltage, the electric field in the depletion region accelerates carriers enough that they ionize silicon atoms on collision — each ionization creates a new electron-hole pair, which accelerates and ionizes more atoms. This avalanche breakdown is the mechanism in most power rectifiers and most diodes marked 'reverse voltage Vr.' It is destructive if not current-limited. Zener breakdown (tunneling, occurs at lower voltages, <5V) is exploited for voltage regulation — see lesson elec3-004. **Temperature effects on forward voltage.** Forward voltage Vf decreases approximately 2 mV/°C for silicon. A diode conducting 1A at 25°C with Vf = 0.7V will have Vf ≈ 0.5V at 125°C junction temperature. This thermal coefficient is why power diode datasheets show Vf vs. temperature curves, and why you cannot assume 0.7V drop in a hot power supply. For paralleled diodes in a rectifier, Vf mismatch causes unequal current sharing — another thermal runaway risk requiring current-balancing resistors. **Depletion width and capacitance.** The depletion width W grows with reverse voltage VR: W = √(2ε(V₀ + VR)/q × (NA + ND)/(NA×ND)). For a one-sided abrupt junction (NA >> ND): W ≈ √(2ε(V₀ + VR)/(q×ND)). The depletion region acts as a capacitor with plates separated by W: Cj = ε×A/W ∝ (V₀ + VR)^(-1/2). This voltage-variable capacitance is exploited in varactor diodes for RF tuning. It also limits the switching speed of rectifier diodes — the capacitance must charge/discharge at each half-cycle. **Diffusion capacitance in forward bias.** In forward bias, minority carrier charge is stored in the neutral regions adjacent to the junction. This diffusion capacitance Cd = ID × τ/(nVT) is proportional to current, where τ is minority carrier lifetime. At high currents, Cd >> Cj and dominates switching time. Fast-recovery diodes are engineered with short τ (gold or platinum doping introduces recombination centers) to minimize stored charge and enable fast turn-off. Standard 60Hz rectifier diodes have τ on the order of microseconds — they cannot switch at 100 kHz. Shockley Diode Equation $$I_D = I_S \left( e^{\frac{V_D}{nV_T}} - 1 \right)$$

where:
- IS = reverse saturation current (~10⁻¹² A for small-signal Si, ~10⁻⁶ A for power Si)
- VD = diode forward voltage (V)
- n = ideality factor (1.0–2.0; n=1 ideal, n=2 recombination dominant)
- VT = kT/q = 26 mV at 300 K (thermal voltage)

**Approximation for VD >> VT:** ID ≈ IS × e^(VD/nVT) Built-In Junction Potential $$V_0 = \frac{kT}{q} \ln\!\left(\frac{N_A N_D}{n_i^2}\right)$$

For silicon at 300 K with NA = ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³:
$$V_0 = 0.026 \ln\!\left(\frac{10^{32}}{(1.5\times10^{10})^2}\right) \approx 0.026 \times 27 \approx 0.70\text{ V}$$

Higher doping → higher V₀. This is not externally measurable but sets the knee of the I-V curve. Testing a Diode with a Multimeter **Diode test mode (most digital meters):**
1. Red probe → anode (P-side), Black → cathode (N-side): should read 0.50–0.75V (silicon), 0.25–0.45V (Schottky), 1.5–2.2V (LED)
2. Reverse probes: should read OL (open) for a good diode
3. Both directions read near 0V: shorted junction (failed)
4. Both directions read OL: open junction (failed) or MOSFET body diode with gate floating (normal)

**Resistance mode:** Not recommended for diodes — meter current is too small to fully forward-bias silicon. Use diode test mode. Why 0.7V? (And When It Isn't) The '0.7V diode drop' is a room-temperature approximation for a silicon junction at moderate current. It varies:
- Small-signal Si at 1 mA: ~0.6V
- Power diode at 10A: 0.8–1.1V (bulk resistance adds to junction voltage)
- At 125°C junction: subtract ~0.2V → 0.5V typical
- Schottky diode: 0.2–0.4V (metal-semiconductor junction, no minority storage)
- GaN Schottky: 0.5–0.7V (but fast recovery)

In a 5V logic circuit, 0.7V is 14% of supply — significant. In a 480V rectifier, 0.7V is 0.15% — negligible for most calculations. Peak Inverse Voltage — Selecting Rectifier Diodes The PIV (Peak Inverse Voltage) rating must exceed the peak reverse voltage the diode sees in circuit, with derating. For a full-wave bridge on 240VAC: peak voltage = 240 × √2 = 340V. Add transient margin: use 600V or 800V diodes. Never operate at rated PIV continuously — use 50% derating for industrial reliability. On inductive loads (transformers, motors), voltage spikes can reach 2–3× line voltage. Install MOV or RC snubbers, and select diodes with 2× margin over calculated peak. Small-Signal Diode Resistance At a DC operating point ID, the incremental (small-signal) resistance of a diode is:
$$r_d = \frac{nV_T}{I_D} = \frac{n \times 26\,\text{mV}}{I_D}$$

At ID = 1 mA, n=1: rd = 26 Ω
At ID = 10 mA: rd = 2.6 Ω
At ID = 100 mA: rd = 0.26 Ω

This small-signal resistance governs AC ripple voltage across a diode biased at DC — important for peak detector and precision rectifier design. Rectifier Diode Selection — Step by Step 1. **Average current** IF(avg): for a bridge rectifier, IF(avg) per diode = 0.5 × Iload
2. **Peak current** IFSM: inrush current at startup (capacitor filter); select IFSM >> Icap_inrush
3. **PIV**: for bridge on Vrms: PIV = √2 × Vrms. Derate to 50%: Vrated ≥ 2 × PIV
4. **Switching speed**: for line frequency (50/60 Hz), standard rectifier grade OK. For SMPS > 10 kHz, use fast/ultrafast recovery (trr < 50–200 ns) or Schottky.
5. **Thermal**: Pdiode = IF(avg) × Vf. Check junction temp: Tj = Tambient + Pdiode × (Rθja or Rθjc + heatsink). Silicon Diode I-V Characteristic assignment homework quiz exam practice problems worked example step by step growth decay e^x logarithm ln

documents.title: Diode Circuits — Rectifiers, Clippers, Clampers, and Current Limiting
documents.subtitle: The practical circuits every power electronics technician builds from diodes: converting AC to DC, protecting circuits from voltage spikes, and limiting current to LEDs and sensors.

Electrolytic filter capacitors are the single most common cause of low-output-voltage failure in DC power supplies. The capacitor bank after a bridge rectifier smooths the pulsating DC — when capacitance drops due to age or temperature stress, ripple voltage increases and average output drops. Swollen tops on electrolytics are a visual giveaway of venting due to internal pressure from failed electrolyte. You can confirm with an in-circuit ESR meter (high ESR = failing cap) or by measuring ripple on the DC rail with a scope. Understanding the full-wave bridge circuit — why ripple depends on capacitance, load current, and frequency — lets you specify the correct replacement capacitor. Full-Wave Bridge Rectifier Output **DC output voltage (with capacitor filter, light load):**
$$V_{dc} \approx V_{peak} - 2V_f = \sqrt{2}\,V_{rms} - 1.4\text{ V}$$

**Ripple voltage (peak-to-peak):**
$$V_{ripple} \approx \frac{I_L}{2f\,C}$$

where: IL = DC load current (A), f = line frequency (Hz), C = filter capacitance (F)

**Example:** IL = 2A, f = 60 Hz, C = 2200 μF:
$$V_{ripple} = \frac{2}{2 \times 60 \times 0.0022} = \frac{2}{0.264} \approx 7.6\text{ V pp}$$ Measuring Ripple on a DC Power Supply 1. Set oscilloscope to AC coupling (removes DC component, shows only ripple)
2. Set time/div to capture 2–3 cycles of ripple (at 60 Hz, ripple is 120 Hz → period 8.3 ms; set 5 ms/div)
3. Measure peak-to-peak ripple amplitude
4. For a 24V supply: acceptable ripple < 2V pp (< 8%). Above 5V pp → investigate capacitors
5. Check ripple frequency: should be 2 × line frequency for full-wave (120 Hz on 60 Hz mains). If ripple is at line frequency (60 Hz) → one diode in bridge has failed (half-wave mode)
6. ESR check: good filter cap ESR < 0.1–0.5Ω at 100 kHz. Measure with LCR meter or ESR meter. Why Electrolytic Capacitors Fail in Power Supplies Industrial electrolytic capacitors have a rated life of 2000–5000 hours at rated temperature (usually 85°C or 105°C). Every 10°C above rated reduces life by half (Arrhenius law). A capacitor in a 55°C cabinet at 105°C rating runs at 50°C below max — fine. But if the supply runs hotter due to poor ventilation, or if ripple current exceeds the capacitor's rated ripple current (causing internal heating), life drops rapidly. Signs of failure: swollen or cracked vents, elevated ESR, reduced capacitance. Replace electrolytics in industrial equipment every 10 years as preventive maintenance, regardless of visible condition. LED Current-Limiting Resistor $$R = \frac{V_{supply} - V_f}{I_{LED}}$$

Typical LED values: Vf = 2.0V (red), 2.2V (green), 3.2V (blue/white), ILED = 10–20 mA

**Example:** 24V supply, red LED (Vf = 2V), ILED = 10 mA:
$$R = \frac{24 - 2}{0.010} = \frac{22}{0.010} = 2200\,\Omega \text{ (2.2 kΩ)}$$

Power dissipated in resistor: P = (Vsupply − Vf) × ILED = 22 × 0.01 = 0.22 W → use ¼W resistor minimum. Inrush Current Stress on Rectifier Diodes At power-up, the filter capacitor is fully discharged and looks like a short circuit. Inrush current can be 50–200× the steady-state load current for tens of milliseconds. This is why:
- Bridge diodes must be rated for repetitive surge current (IFSM), not just average current
- Slow-blow fuses are used on AC inputs to power supplies
- NTC thermistors or inrush limiters are often added in series with the AC line
- Large power supplies use soft-start circuits (timed relay bypassing a resistor)

A diode rated 3A average current may need to handle 100A inrush — check the IFSM spec and the I²t rating. Cockroft-Walton Voltage Multiplier Cascaded clamper/rectifier stages can multiply AC voltage without a transformer:
$$V_{out} \approx 2n \times V_{peak}$$
where n = number of stages (diode-capacitor pairs per rail)

A 2-stage doubler on 120VAC (Vpeak = 170V) gives ~340V DC. Used in CRT monitors (historically), microwave oven magnetrons, ion pumps, and particle accelerators. Each capacitor must be rated for the full output voltage. Output impedance rises with n — not suitable for high current. In industrial control: voltage multipliers appear in ESD test equipment (generating kV pulses) and in RF bias circuits.

A 24VDC PLC power supply shows 19V at its output terminals under full load. The incoming 120VAC is confirmed at 118V. The fuse and transformer secondary (measured) are both fine. Capacitors look swollen. What is failing, how would you confirm it, and what is the underlying circuit principle that explains the symptom? The capacitor bank after a bridge rectifier smooths the pulsating DC — when capacitance drops due to age or temperature stress, ripple voltage increases and average output drops. You can confirm with an in-circuit ESR meter (high ESR = failing cap) or by measuring ripple on the DC rail with a scope. Understanding the full-wave bridge circuit — why ripple depends on capacitance, load current, and frequency — lets you specify the correct replacement capacitor. **Half-wave rectifier waveforms.** Input: Vm sin(ωt). Output: Vm sin(ωt) for 0 < ωt < π (diode conducts), 0 for π < ωt < 2π (diode blocks). Average (no capacitor): Vavg = Vm/π ≈ 0.318 Vm. With capacitor at light load: Vout ≈ Vm − Vf. The capacitor must hold charge for a full half-period (8.3 ms at 60 Hz), so ripple is larger than full-wave for the same capacitance. PIV = Vm + Vc ≈ 2Vm (the capacitor voltage adds to the reverse-biased diode in the negative half-cycle). Always specify half-wave rectifier diodes with PIV ≥ 2 × Vpeak. **Bridge rectifier current paths.** Positive half-cycle: current flows through D1 (anode to load positive), through load, through D4 (cathode to transformer). D2 and D3 are reverse-biased. Negative half-cycle: current flows through D3, load, D2. D1 and D4 block. At all times, current through the load flows in one direction (top rail positive). Two diodes are always in series with the load — hence two diode voltage drops (1.2–1.4V total). On a 5V supply, this is significant; on 240V, negligible. **Clipper circuits: voltage limiting.** A series diode and reference voltage clips (limits) the signal at a set level. Shunt clippers use a diode to ground (or reference) — when input exceeds threshold, the diode conducts and clamps the output. Used to protect analog inputs, limit signal swings in comm circuits, and protect CMOS logic inputs from overvoltage. In industrial practice: transient voltage suppressors (TVS diodes) are the high-energy version — they clamp at a rated voltage and absorb energy in joules. Every motor terminal block in a control cabinet should have TVS or MOV protection. **Clamper circuits: DC level shifting.** A series capacitor + shunt diode shifts the DC level of a waveform without changing its shape. Positive clamper: diode in shunt to ground, capacitor in series — the output waveform is shifted so its negative peaks sit at 0V (or a reference). Output DC component = Vpeak. Used in CRT flyback circuits (historically), voltage multiplier ladders (Cockroft-Walton), and signal conditioning to establish a known DC baseline. The capacitor stores the DC offset — if the load draws too much current, the clamping effect degrades. **Transformer sizing for a bridge rectifier.** The transformer secondary must supply: (1) the DC output voltage Vdc = Vrms×√2 − 2Vf, so Vrms(secondary) = (Vdc + 2Vf)/√2; (2) the RMS current including ripple and conduction angle effects. For a capacitor-filtered bridge, transformer secondary RMS current = Idc × π/2 × (1/η) where η accounts for transformer efficiency (~0.85 typical). The transformer kVA rating must include both average and reactive (capacitor charging) current. Rule of thumb: transformer VA = 1.75 × Pdc for a capacitor-input filter at full load. **Voltage doubler for 120V/240V switching.** Many universal power supplies (switch-mode) use a bridge rectifier in voltage-doubler mode for 120VAC input or normal bridge for 240VAC input, configured with a voltage selector switch. At 120VAC: two capacitors in series charge to ~Vpeak each, yielding ~2×170 = 340V DC bus. At 240VAC: single bridge rectifier gives ~320V DC bus. Both configurations produce ~320–340V for the SMPS input stage, allowing one design to serve both markets. The switch disconnects one capacitor from the doubler circuit. $$V_{dc} \approx V_{peak} - 2V_f = \sqrt{2}\,V_{rms} - 1.4\text{ V}$$

**Ripple voltage (peak-to-peak):**
$$V_{ripple} \approx \frac{I_L}{2f\,C}$$

where: IL = DC load current (A), f = line frequency (Hz), C = filter capacitance (F)

**Example:** IL = 2A, f = 60 Hz, C = 2200 μF:
$$V_{ripple} = \frac{2}{2 \times 60 \times 0.0022} = \frac{2}{0.264} \approx 7.6\text{ V pp}$$ Measuring Ripple on a DC Power Supply 1. Set oscilloscope to AC coupling (removes DC component, shows only ripple)
2. Set time/div to capture 2–3 cycles of ripple (at 60 Hz, ripple is 120 Hz → period 8.3 ms; set 5 ms/div)
3. Measure peak-to-peak ripple amplitude
4. For a 24V supply: acceptable ripple < 2V pp (< 8%). Above 5V pp → investigate capacitors
5. Check ripple frequency: should be 2 × line frequency for full-wave (120 Hz on 60 Hz mains). If ripple is at line frequency (60 Hz) → one diode in bridge has failed (half-wave mode)
6. ESR check: good filter cap ESR < 0.1–0.5Ω at 100 kHz. Measure with LCR meter or ESR meter. Why Electrolytic Capacitors Fail in Power Supplies Industrial electrolytic capacitors have a rated life of 2000–5000 hours at rated temperature (usually 85°C or 105°C). Every 10°C above rated reduces life by half (Arrhenius law). A capacitor in a 55°C cabinet at 105°C rating runs at 50°C below max — fine. But if the supply runs hotter due to poor ventilation, or if ripple current exceeds the capacitor's rated ripple current (causing internal heating), life drops rapidly. Signs of failure: swollen or cracked vents, elevated ESR, reduced capacitance. Replace electrolytics in industrial equipment every 10 years as preventive maintenance, regardless of visible condition. LED Current-Limiting Resistor $$R = \frac{V_{supply} - V_f}{I_{LED}}$$

Typical LED values: Vf = 2.0V (red), 2.2V (green), 3.2V (blue/white), ILED = 10–20 mA

**Example:** 24V supply, red LED (Vf = 2V), ILED = 10 mA:
$$R = \frac{24 - 2}{0.010} = \frac{22}{0.010} = 2200\,\Omega \text{ (2.2 kΩ)}$$

Power dissipated in resistor: P = (Vsupply − Vf) × ILED = 22 × 0.01 = 0.22 W → use ¼W resistor minimum. Inrush current can be 50–200× the steady-state load current for tens of milliseconds. This is why:
- Bridge diodes must be rated for repetitive surge current (IFSM), not just average current
- Slow-blow fuses are used on AC inputs to power supplies
- NTC thermistors or inrush limiters are often added in series with the AC line
- Large power supplies use soft-start circuits (timed relay bypassing a resistor)
